data.query: How do NRC regulatory requirements for protection against natural phenomena hazards define the geographic scope that must be considered when establishing site parameters for nuclear power plant design?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory requirements for protection against natural phenomena hazards define the geographic scope for establishing site parameters by mandating consideration of both the site and its surrounding area. Specifically, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2 in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of the most severe natural phenomena—such as earthquakes, tornadoes, hurricanes, floods, tsunami, and seiches—that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area. The design bases must include sufficient margin to account for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time over which historical data have been accumulated (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; SRP 2.3.1, II. Acceptance Criteria).

Additionally, 10 CFR 52.79(a)(iii) and 10 CFR Part 100 (§100.10(c)(2), §100.20(c)(2), and §100.21(d)) reinforce the requirement to identify and characterize the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, and to evaluate regional meteorological characteristics and other physical site characteristics that may impact plant design and safety. These regulations ensure that the geographic scope for data collection and analysis encompasses not only the immediate site but also the broader surrounding area and relevant regional characteristics, as necessary for a comprehensive safety analysis and establishment of site parameters.

In summary, NRC regulations require that the geographic scope for natural phenomena hazard assessment includes the site, its surrounding area, and, where relevant, regional characteristics, to ensure that the most severe historically reported hazards are considered in nuclear power plant design.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
Requirements
Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations:
1. 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, “Design Bases for Protection Against Natural Phenomena,” as it relates to consideration of the most severe of the natural phenomena that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated.
...
4. 10 CFR 52.79(a)(iii) requires a COL applicant to identify the most severe of the natural phenomena that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area and with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and time in which the historical data have been accumulated.
5. 10 CFR Part 100, §100.10(c)(2), §100.20(c)(2), and §100.21(d) with respect to the consideration given to the regional meteorological characteristics of the site.
...
The technical rationale for application of these acceptance criteria to the areas of review addressed by this SRP section is discussed in the following paragraph:
GDC 4 requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety be appropriately protected against dynamic effects that may result from events and conditions outside the nuclear power unit.  GDC 2 (or 10 CFR 52.17(a)(1)(vi) for ESP applications) requires consideration of the most severe of the natural phenomena. 10 CFR 100.10(c)(2) and 10 CFR 100.20(c)(2) require meteorological characteristics of the site that are necessary for safety analysis or that may have an impact upon plant design (such as maximum probable wind speed and precipitation) to be identified and characterized, so that they may be taken into consideration in determining the acceptability of the site.  10 CFR 100.21(d) requires physical characteristics of the site, including meteorology, to be evaluated and site parameters established such that potential threats from such physical characteristics will pose no undue risk to the type of facility proposed to be located at the site.  Application of GDC 2 (or 10 CFR 52.17(a)(1)(vi) for ESP applications), GDC 4, 10 CFR 100.10(c)(2), 10 CFR 100.20(c)(2), and 10 CFR 100.21(d) provides assurance that the most severe meteorological conditions at the chosen plant site have been identified.

evidence_chain.evidence_text: General Design Criterion 2—Design bases for protection against natural phenomena. Structures, systems, and components important to safety shall be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena such as earthquakes, tornadoes, hurricanes, floods, tsunami, and seiches without loss of capability to perform their safety functions. The design bases for these structures, systems, and components shall reflect: (1) Appropriate consideration of the most severe of the natural phenomena that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated, (2) appropriate combinations of the effects of normal and accident conditions with the effects of the natural phenomena, and (3) the importance of the safety functions to be performed.

data.query: In the context of nuclear power plant design, how do general design criteria for environmental protection relate to the selection of climatological and meteorological parameters for site-independent designs?
data.answer:
The general design criteria for environmental protection, specifically General Design Criterion (GDC) 2 from 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, establish that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety at nuclear power plants must be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including climatological and meteorological events, without loss of safety function. According to SRP 2.3.1, Section II, and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2, the design bases for these SSCs must consider the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin to account for uncertainties in historical data. This means that when selecting climatological and meteorological parameters for site-independent designs, the criteria require identification and characterization of the most severe conditions (such as maximum probable wind speed and precipitation) that could impact plant safety.

Furthermore, 10 CFR 100.10(c)(2), 100.20(c)(2), and 100.21(d), as referenced in SRP 2.3.1, require that regional meteorological characteristics necessary for safety analysis or that may impact plant design be identified and evaluated. For site-independent designs, this ensures that the selected parameters are sufficiently conservative to account for the range of possible site conditions, thereby providing assurance that the plant design will be robust against the most severe credible environmental challenges. In summary, the general design criteria for environmental protection directly inform the selection of climatological and meteorological parameters by requiring that the most severe, historically reported natural phenomena be considered, with appropriate margins, in the design of nuclear power plants, regardless of site specificity.

data.query: What are the NRC requirements for identifying meteorological site parameters used in the safety analysis of nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC requirements for identifying meteorological site parameters used in the safety analysis of nuclear power plants are grounded in several regulatory documents and criteria. According to SRP 2.3.1 Section II, applicants must meet the requirements of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, which mandates that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated. This is further detailed in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2, which specifies that the design bases must reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe natural phenomena, combinations of normal and accident conditions with natural phenomena, and the importance of the safety functions to be performed.

Additionally, 10 CFR 52.47(a)(1) and 10 CFR 52.79(a)(iii) require design certification and combined license applicants, respectively, to identify and justify the site parameters and the most severe natural phenomena for the site. For early site permit applications, 10 CFR 52.17(a)(1)(vi) specifically requires identification of climatic site characteristics considering the most severe historical phenomena with sufficient margin.

Regarding specific meteorological parameters, Regulatory Guide 1.76 Section C provides accepted methods for defining the design-basis tornado, including parameter values such as maximum wind speed, translational speed, maximum rotational speed, radius of maximum rotational speed, pressure drop, and rate of pressure drop, which are region-specific. If less-conservative values are proposed, a comprehensive analysis must justify their use.

In summary, NRC requirements mandate the identification and justification of meteorological site parameters based on the most severe historical data, with sufficient margin for uncertainties, and the use of accepted parameter values or justified alternatives for phenomena such as tornadoes.

evidence_chain.section: C. REGULATORY POSITION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
The NRC staff has established the following regulatory positions for licensees and applicants to use in selecting the design-basis tornado and design-basis tornado-generated missiles that a nuclear power plant should be designed to withstand to prevent undue risk to the health and safety of the public.

1. Design-Basis Tornado Parameters
Nuclear power plants should be designed to withstand the design-basis tornado. The parameter values specified in Table 1 for the appropriate regions identified in Figure 1 are generally acceptable to the NRC staff for defining the design-basis tornado for a nuclear power plant. If a design-basis tornado proposed for a given site is characterized by less-conservative parameter values than the regional values in Table 1, a comprehensive analysis should be provided to justify the selection of the less-conservative design-basis tornado. Sites located near the general boundaries of adjoining regions may involve additional considerations. The radius of maximum rotational speed of 45.7 meters (150 feet) is used for all three tornado intensity regions.

data.query: How are meteorological site parameters expected to be linked to the design and operation of safety-related structures, systems, and components according to NRC regulatory guidance?
data.answer:
According to NRC regulatory guidance, meteorological site parameters are integrally linked to the design and operation of safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) to ensure plant safety under both normal and extreme weather conditions. As outlined in SRP 2.3.1, the NRC reviews site-specific meteorological data—including averages and extremes of climatic conditions and regional meteorological phenomena—to establish design and operating bases for SSCs. These parameters include, but are not limited to, snowpack and precipitation loads for structural design, ultimate heat sink meteorological conditions for cooling system performance, tornado and wind parameters for structural and missile loadings, and ambient temperature and humidity for heat removal and HVAC system design. The findings from these reviews are communicated to ensure SSCs are adequately designed to withstand these conditions (SRP 2.3.1, Section I).

This approach is grounded in regulatory requirements such as 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, which mandates that SSCs important to safety must be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena—including meteorological events—without loss of safety function. The design bases must reflect the most severe historically reported phenomena for the site, account for uncertainties in historical data, and consider the importance of the safety functions performed (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; RG 1.76, Section A). Furthermore, 10 CFR Part 100.20(c)(2) and 100.21(d) require that meteorological characteristics necessary for safety analysis or impacting plant design be evaluated and that site parameters be established to ensure no undue risk from such characteristics (RG 1.76, Section A).

In summary, NRC guidance requires that meteorological site parameters be systematically evaluated and incorporated into the design and operational bases of safety-related SSCs to ensure their capability to perform safety functions under the most severe credible meteorological conditions.

evidence_chain.section: A. INTRODUCTION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, “Design Bases for Protection Against Natural Phenomena,” of Appendix A, “General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants,” to Title 10, Part 50, of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR Part 50), “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities” (Ref. 1), requires that structures, systems, and components that are important to safety shall be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, such as tornadoes, without loss of capability to perform their safety functions.  GDC 2 also requires that the design bases for these structures, systems, and components shall reflect (1) appropriate consideration of the most severe of the natural phenomena that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated, (2) appropriate combinations of the effects of normal and accident conditions with the effects of the natural phenomena, and (3) the importance of the safety functions to be performed.
GDC 4, “Environmental and Dynamic Effects Design Bases,” of Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50 requires, in part, that structures, systems, and components that are important to safety shall be adequately protected against the effects of missiles resulting from events and conditions outside the plant.
For stationary power reactor site applications submitted on or after January 10, 1997, paragraph 100.20(c)(2) of 10 CFR Part 100 requires that meteorological characteristics of the site that are necessary for safety analysis or may have an impact upon plant design (such as maximum probable wind speed) must be considered in determining the acceptability of a site for a nuclear power plant.  In addition, paragraph 100.21(d) of 10 CFR Part 100 requires that the physical characteristics of the site, including meteorology, must be evaluated and site parameters established such that potential threats from such physical characteristics will pose no undue risk to the type of facility proposed to be located at the site.

data.query: For a new nuclear power plant design, what is the NRC-recommended process for ensuring that all meteorological site parameters are properly cross-referenced to the sections of the safety analysis where they are used, and how should this process support future combined license applicants in demonstrating compliance with site-specific requirements?
data.answer:
The NRC-recommended process for ensuring that all meteorological site parameters are properly cross-referenced to the sections of the safety analysis where they are used is detailed in SRP 2.3.1. Applicants are required to identify all references to FSAR (Final Safety Analysis Report) sections in which meteorological conditions are used (SRP 2.3.1, Section I.6). This includes site characteristics for ESP applications, design and operating bases for CP, OL, and COL applications, and site parameters for DC applications. The process involves documenting and substantiating all meteorological and air quality conditions used as site characteristics or design bases (SRP 2.3.1, SRP Acceptance Criteria). Reviewers then verify that sufficient information is provided and that the review and calculations support the conclusions in the safety evaluation report, ensuring that the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area have been considered with appropriate margin (SRP 2.3.1, Section IV).

This process supports future combined license (COL) applicants by providing a clear, traceable linkage between site-specific meteorological parameters and their application in safety analyses, as required by 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2. This criterion mandates that SSCs important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, with design bases reflecting the most severe historical data and sufficient margin for data limitations (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2). Additionally, regulatory guidance such as RG 1.76 provides acceptable methods for defining specific meteorological parameters (e.g., design-basis tornado), which must be justified and cross-referenced in the safety analysis (RG 1.76, Section C).

In summary, the NRC process requires applicants to clearly identify and cross-reference all meteorological site parameters to the relevant safety analysis sections, document and substantiate their use, and ensure compliance with regulatory requirements for site-specific natural phenomena. This structured approach facilitates regulatory review and supports COL applicants in demonstrating compliance with site-specific requirements.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for evaluating normal and extreme winter precipitation loads on the roofs of safety-related structures at nuclear power plant sites?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for evaluating normal and extreme winter precipitation loads on the roofs of safety-related structures at nuclear power plant sites are primarily established to ensure that these structures can withstand the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site, as required by 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2 (GDC 2) (see [2]). GDC 2 mandates that structures important to safety must be designed to withstand natural phenomena, including winter precipitation, without loss of safety function, and that the design bases must reflect the most severe historical events with appropriate safety margins.

According to SRP 2.3.1, Section II (see [1]), the evaluation of winter precipitation loads must consider both normal and extreme conditions:
- For normal live loads, the design should be based on the weight of the 100-year snowpack or snowfall (whichever is greater) recorded at ground level.
- For extreme live loads, the design should consider the weight of the 100-year snowpack at ground level plus the weight of the 48-hour probable maximum winter precipitation (PMWP) at ground level for the month corresponding to the selected snowpack. The 48-hour PMWP is defined as the greatest depth of precipitation theoretically possible over a 48-hour period for a 25.9-square-kilometer area at the site during months with the highest historical snowpacks. The weight of the 48-hour PMWP should be determined using NOAA Hydrometeorological Design Studies Center reports.

Applicants may propose alternative methods for defining extreme winter precipitation loads if they can justify, with site-specific analysis, that the 48-hour PMWP could neither fall nor remain on the snowpack or building roofs. The 100-year snowpack data should be sourced from nearby representative climatic stations or appropriate standards, with corrections for local conditions.

These requirements ensure that safety-related structures are robust against both typical and extreme winter precipitation events, consistent with NRC’s regulatory framework for natural phenomena protection (see [2], [1]).

data.query: How should site-specific snow load parameters be identified and compared to design parameters for safety-related structures according to NRC regulatory guidance?
data.answer:
According to NRC regulatory guidance, site-specific snow load parameters for safety-related structures should be identified and compared to design parameters through a systematic process grounded in historical data and established standards. As outlined in SRP 2.3.1 (Section II.6), the winter precipitation loads to be considered in the design should be based on the weight of the 100-year snowpack or snowfall, whichever is greater, recorded at ground level. For extreme live load combinations, the design should use the weight of the 100-year snowpack plus the weight of the 48-hour probable maximum winter precipitation (PMWP) for the month with the highest snowpack. The 48-hour PMWP is defined as the greatest depth of precipitation possible over a 48-hour period for a 25.9-square-kilometer area at the site, and its weight should be determined using NOAA Hydrometeorological Design Studies Center reports.

The 100-year snowpack data should be sourced from nearby representative climatic stations or appropriate standards, with corrections for local conditions as necessary. Applicants may propose alternative methods for defining extreme winter precipitation loads if justified by site-specific meteorological evidence.

This approach aligns with 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2, which requires that safety-related structures be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site, with appropriate margins for data limitations. The design bases must reflect the combination of normal and accident conditions with natural phenomena effects, considering the safety functions to be performed.

In summary, site-specific snow load parameters must be established using historical climatic data and recognized standards, compared to design parameters to ensure that safety-related structures can withstand the most severe credible winter precipitation events, consistent with NRC regulatory requirements (SRP 2.3.1, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A).

data.query: When establishing design parameters for roof snow loads on seismic Category I structures at a nuclear plant, what combined regulatory provisions from general design criteria, review standards, and regulatory guides must be considered to ensure both normal and extreme winter precipitation events are adequately addressed?
data.answer:
When establishing design parameters for roof snow loads on seismic Category I structures at a nuclear plant, several combined regulatory provisions must be considered to ensure both normal and extreme winter precipitation events are adequately addressed. 

First, per 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2 (see [2]), structures important to safety must be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data. This includes appropriate combinations of normal and accident conditions with natural phenomena effects.

The Standard Review Plan (SRP) 2.3.1 (see [1]) provides specific acceptance criteria for winter precipitation loads. For normal live loads, the design should use the weight of the 100-year snowpack or snowfall (whichever is greater) recorded at ground level. For extreme live loads, the design should consider the weight of the 100-year snowpack plus the weight of the 48-hour probable maximum winter precipitation (PMWP) at ground level for the month with the highest snowpack. The 48-hour PMWP is defined as the greatest depth of precipitation possible over a 48-hour period for a 25.9-square-kilometer area, and its weight should be determined using NOAA Hydrometeorological Design Studies Center reports. Alternative methods may be justified if it can be demonstrated that the PMWP could not accumulate on the roof.

Regulatory Guide 1.76 (see [3]) reiterates the requirements of GDC 2 and emphasizes that meteorological characteristics, including extreme precipitation, must be considered in site evaluation and design. For applications after January 10, 1997, 10 CFR 100.20(c)(2) and 100.21(d) require that meteorological characteristics necessary for safety analysis and plant design be evaluated to ensure no undue risk from such physical characteristics.

In summary, the design must reflect the most severe historical snow and precipitation events, using the 100-year snowpack and 48-hour PMWP as specified in SRP 2.3.1, and comply with the general design criteria and regulatory guidance to ensure safety under both normal and extreme winter precipitation conditions.

evidence_chain.section: A. INTRODUCTION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, “Design Bases for Protection Against Natural Phenomena,” of Appendix A, “General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants,” to Title 10, Part 50, of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR Part 50), “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities” (Ref. 1), requires that structures, systems, and components that are important to safety shall be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, such as tornadoes, without loss of capability to perform their safety functions.  GDC 2 also requires that the design bases for these structures, systems, and components shall reflect (1) appropriate consideration of the most severe of the natural phenomena that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated, (2) appropriate combinations of the effects of normal and accident conditions with the effects of the natural phenomena, and (3) the importance of the safety functions to be performed.

GDC 4, “Environmental and Dynamic Effects Design Bases,” of Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50 requires, in part, that structures, systems, and components that are important to safety shall be adequately protected against the effects of missiles resulting from events and conditions outside the plant.

For stationary power reactor site applications submitted before January 10, 1997, paragraph 100.10(c)(2) of 10 CFR Part 100, “Reactor Site Criteria” (Ref. 2), states that meteorological conditions at the site and in the surrounding area should be considered in determining the acceptability of a site for a power reactor.

For stationary power reactor site applications submitted on or after January 10, 1997, paragraph 100.20(c)(2) of 10 CFR Part 100 requires that meteorological characteristics of the site that are necessary for safety analysis or may have an impact upon plant design (such as maximum probable wind speed) must be considered in determining the acceptability of a site for a nuclear power plant.  In addition, paragraph 100.21(d) of 10 CFR Part 100 requires that the physical characteristics of the site, including meteorology, must be evaluated and site parameters established such that potential threats from such physical characteristics will pose no undue risk to the type of facility proposed to be located at the site.

data.query: What is the NRC's regulatory basis for establishing the design basis tornado wind speed for nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC's regulatory basis for establishing the design basis tornado wind speed for nuclear power plants is grounded in several key regulatory requirements and guidance documents. The primary regulatory foundation is 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, which mandates that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety must be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including tornadoes, without loss of safety function. GDC 2 specifically requires that the design bases reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; RG 1.76, Section A).

Additionally, GDC 4 requires SSCs important to safety to be protected against dynamic effects, such as missiles generated by tornadoes (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4; SRP 2.3.1, Section II). Site-specific meteorological characteristics must also be considered per 10 CFR 100.10(c)(2), 100.20(c)(2), and 100.21(d), ensuring that the most severe meteorological conditions are identified and factored into the plant design (SRP 2.3.1, Section II).

For the technical basis, NRC Regulatory Guide 1.76 provides the accepted method for determining design basis tornado wind speeds. It establishes that the design-basis tornado wind speeds should correspond to an exceedance frequency of 10^-7 per year, based on historical tornado data and analysis. The guide specifies maximum wind speeds for different regions of the United States, reflecting observed tornado occurrences and ensuring consistency with the regulatory requirements for safety margins and historical severity (RG 1.76, Section B).

In summary, the NRC's regulatory basis is a combination of GDC 2 and GDC 4 in 10 CFR Part 50, relevant sections of 10 CFR Part 100, and the technical guidance in RG 1.76, all of which ensure that nuclear power plants are designed to withstand the most severe tornado wind speeds appropriate for their location.

data.query: How do NRC requirements for using the best available meteorological data relate to the selection of design basis tornado wind speeds for nuclear facilities?
data.answer:
NRC requirements mandate that the selection of design basis tornado wind speeds for nuclear facilities must be grounded in the best available meteorological data, as outlined in several regulatory documents. General Design Criterion (GDC) 2 of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including tornadoes, by considering the most severe events historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin to account for the limitations in historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; RG 1.76, Section A).

Standard Review Plan (SRP) 2.3.1 further specifies that data on severe weather phenomena, including tornadoes, should be based on standard meteorological records from recognized installations with long periods of data, such as National Weather Service stations. The applicability of these data to the site must be substantiated, ensuring that the meteorological characteristics used for safety analysis accurately represent the expected conditions during the facility's operational period (SRP 2.3.1, Section II).

Regulatory Guide 1.76 provides an accepted method for determining design basis tornado wind speeds, utilizing a comprehensive tornado database (NUREG/CR-4461) that includes decades of recorded tornado events. Applicants may use the tornado parameters from RG 1.76 or propose alternative, technically justified parameters based on site-specific data, provided a thorough technical evaluation is conducted (SRP 2.3.1, Section II; RG 1.76, Section B).

In summary, NRC requirements ensure that the selection of design basis tornado wind speeds is based on the best available, substantiated meteorological data, reflecting the most severe historical phenomena with appropriate safety margins, as required by GDC 2, 10 CFR 100.10(c)(2), 10 CFR 100.20(c)(2), and 10 CFR 100.21(d).

data.query: When determining the design basis tornado wind speed for a new nuclear power plant, how should an applicant reconcile differences between historical regulatory positions and the most current regulatory guidance, considering the requirement to use the best available data and ensure compliance with general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena?
data.answer:
When determining the design basis tornado wind speed for a new nuclear power plant, an applicant must reconcile historical regulatory positions with the most current regulatory guidance by adhering to the requirements set forth in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, and by following the latest NRC guidance, such as Regulatory Guide 1.76 (RG 1.76), unless a justified alternative is proposed.

GDC 2 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in the historical data (10CFR, GDC 2). This means applicants must consider both historical data and the limitations of that data.

The Standard Review Plan (SRP 2.3.1) clarifies that while the SRP and associated regulatory guides (such as RG 1.76) are not regulations themselves, they provide acceptance criteria that are generally considered acceptable for meeting NRC requirements. Applicants are required to identify and justify any differences between their proposed design and the SRP acceptance criteria, demonstrating how their approach still meets the regulatory requirements (SRP 2.3.1, II. Acceptance Criteria; III. Review Procedures).

RG 1.76 provides specific tornado parameter values that are generally acceptable to the NRC staff. If an applicant proposes less-conservative values than those in RG 1.76, a comprehensive technical analysis and justification are required (RG 1.76, C. Regulatory Position). The NRC will evaluate such alternatives to ensure they provide an acceptable method of compliance with GDC 2.

In summary, applicants should use the most current regulatory guidance (e.g., RG 1.76) as the basis for design basis tornado wind speed, unless a technically justified alternative is provided. Any deviations from current guidance must be clearly identified and justified, demonstrating continued compliance with GDC 2 and consideration of the best available data, including historical records and their limitations.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for determining design-basis hurricane wind speeds for nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for determining design-basis hurricane wind speeds for nuclear power plants are primarily established in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, and further detailed in Standard Review Plan (SRP) 2.3.1. GDC 2 requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including hurricanes, without loss of safety function. The design bases must reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2; SRP 2.3.1, II).

SRP 2.3.1 specifies that the basic (straight-line) 100-year return period 3-second gust wind speed should be used, based on appropriate standards and corrected for local conditions. The information should be substantiated using data and practices from authoritative sources such as the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), industry standards, and regulatory guides (SRP 2.3.1, II). Additionally, 10 CFR 100.10(c)(2), 100.20(c)(2), and 100.21(d) require that regional meteorological characteristics, including maximum probable wind speed, be identified and characterized for safety analysis and site acceptability (SRP 2.3.1, II).

Regulatory Guide 1.76 clarifies that it does not address hurricane wind speeds or associated missiles, and notes that tornado wind speeds may not bound hurricane wind speeds for certain coastal regions. In such cases, the NRC evaluates extreme wind conditions, including hurricanes, on a case-by-case basis (RG 1.76, A. INTRODUCTION).

In summary, NRC requirements mandate that design-basis hurricane wind speeds be determined by considering the most severe historically reported events for the site, using a 100-year return period 3-second gust as a basis, and applying appropriate standards and data sources. For regions where hurricane winds may exceed tornado winds, the NRC addresses these conditions individually.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory guides for hurricane wind speeds relate to the general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena at nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory guides for hurricane wind speeds are directly related to the general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena at nuclear power plants, as established in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2. GDC 2 requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena—including hurricanes—without loss of safety function. The design bases must reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; [2]).

Standard Review Plan (SRP) 2.3.1 further clarifies that acceptance criteria for wind speeds, including those from hurricanes, are based on meeting GDC 2 by considering the most severe historical events and using data from sources such as NOAA and industry standards ([1], SRP 2.3.1, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA). The SRP specifies that the basic 100-year return period 3-second gust wind speed should be used, with corrections for local conditions, to ensure that the plant design accounts for severe wind events, including hurricanes.

While Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.76 provides guidance for tornado wind speeds and missiles, it explicitly states that it does not address hurricane wind speeds, noting that tornado wind speeds may not bound hurricane wind speeds in certain coastal areas. Therefore, the NRC addresses hurricane wind speeds on a case-by-case basis, but always within the framework of GDC 2 ([3], RG 1.76, A. INTRODUCTION).

In summary, NRC regulatory guides for hurricane wind speeds are intended to ensure compliance with GDC 2 by requiring that nuclear power plants are designed to withstand the most severe hurricane wind speeds historically reported for the site, using accepted data sources and methodologies, and with appropriate safety margins.

data.query: When establishing design-basis parameters for hurricanes and associated missiles at a nuclear power plant site, how should a reviewer synthesize the requirements from general design criteria, regulatory guides on wind speeds and missiles, and the regulatory review standards for regional climatology to ensure compliance with NRC expectations?
data.answer:
To establish design-basis parameters for hurricanes and associated missiles at a nuclear power plant site, a reviewer should synthesize requirements from general design criteria, regulatory guides, and regulatory review standards as follows:

First, the reviewer must ensure compliance with 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, which requires that safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) are designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; SRP 2.3.1, II. Acceptance Criteria). GDC 4 further requires protection against dynamic effects, including those from missiles generated by natural phenomena (SRP 2.3.1, II. Acceptance Criteria).

The reviewer should use the Standard Review Plan (SRP) 2.3.1 as the primary guide for acceptance criteria, which specifies that tornado and hurricane parameters should be based on established regulatory guides and industry standards, such as Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.76 for tornadoes and tornado-generated missiles. For hurricanes, the 100-year return period 3-second gust wind speed should be determined using appropriate standards and corrected for local conditions (SRP 2.3.1, II. Acceptance Criteria).

RG 1.76 provides NRC-accepted methods for selecting design-basis tornado and missile parameters, including regional parameter values and missile spectra. If an applicant proposes less-conservative parameters than those in RG 1.76, a comprehensive, site-specific technical justification is required (RG 1.76, C. Regulatory Position).

Finally, the reviewer must ensure that the site’s meteorological characteristics are identified and characterized per 10 CFR 100.10(c)(2), 100.20(c)(2), and 100.21(d), and that all data and analyses are substantiated using NOAA data, industry standards, and regulatory guides (SRP 2.3.1, II. Acceptance Criteria).

In summary, the reviewer should integrate the regulatory requirements (GDC 2 and 4), follow SRP 2.3.1 for process and data sources, apply RG 1.76 for tornado and missile parameters, and ensure all site-specific deviations are technically justified and documented.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory expectations for establishing design-basis dry-bulb and wet-bulb temperature values for nuclear power plant sites?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory expectations for establishing design-basis dry-bulb and wet-bulb temperature values for nuclear power plant sites are detailed primarily in SRP 2.3.1, with supporting regulatory basis in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2. According to SRP 2.3.1 (Sections I and II), applicants must identify and substantiate ambient temperature and humidity statistics, including 2% and 1% annual exceedance and 100-year maximum dry bulb temperature and coincident wet bulb temperature, as well as 2% and 1% annual exceedance and 100-year maximum wet bulb temperature (non-coincident), and 98% and 99% annual exceedance and 100-year minimum dry bulb temperature. These statistics are used to establish heat loads for the design of normal plant heat sink systems, post-accident containment heat removal systems, and plant HVAC systems.

The data should be derived from nearby representative climatic stations or appropriate standards, with suitable corrections for local conditions. Reference 23 in SRP 2.3.1 provides a method for estimating 100-year return period extreme temperature values based on annual extremes. The information must be substantiated using acceptable practices and data as promulgated by NOAA, industry standards, and regulatory guides.

Additionally, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2, requires that the design bases for structures, systems, and components important to safety reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in the data. This ensures that the plant is designed to withstand extreme meteorological conditions without loss of safety function.

In summary, the NRC expects applicants to use rigorous, data-driven methods to establish design-basis temperature values, referencing historical extremes, accepted standards, and regulatory guidance, and to provide substantiation for the selected values.

data.query: How do regulatory standards define the methods for determining site-specific design-basis temperature values, and how should these values be characterized to ensure consistency for future applicants?
data.answer:
Regulatory standards define the methods for determining site-specific design-basis temperature values through a combination of historical data analysis, use of recognized meteorological sources, and adherence to established industry and regulatory guidance. According to SRP 2.3.1 (Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA and III. REVIEW PROCEDURES), applicants should base their characterization of site climate and temperature extremes on standard climatic summaries compiled by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and other authoritative sources. Data should be drawn from nearby representative National Weather Service (NWS) or other recognized stations with long-term records, ensuring the data are applicable to the expected period of reactor operation. Specifically, ambient temperature statistics should be derived from these sources or appropriate standards, with corrections for local conditions as needed. Reference 23 in SRP 2.3.1 provides a method for estimating 100-year return period extreme temperature values based on annual extremes, and the historical data should cover a significant time interval to capture cyclical extremes. 

10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2, further requires that design bases reflect the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in the data. This ensures that the design-basis values are conservative and robust. 

To ensure consistency for future applicants, the methods and data sources used should be clearly documented, substantiated, and based on accepted practices and regulatory guidance. This includes using NOAA data, standard meteorological records, and established statistical methods for extreme value estimation, as outlined in SRP 2.3.1. By following these procedures and referencing the same authoritative sources, future applicants can achieve consistent and comparable characterization of design-basis temperature values.

data.query: When establishing envelope site parameter values for dry-bulb and wet-bulb temperatures in a design certification, what combined regulatory guidance and review standards must be considered to ensure that future combined license applicants can appropriately compare their site-specific climatological data to these parameters, particularly regarding the statistical basis and exceedance criteria for temperature values?
data.answer:
When establishing envelope site parameter values for dry-bulb and wet-bulb temperatures in a design certification (DC), regulatory guidance and review standards require that these parameters be statistically robust and allow future combined license (COL) applicants to compare their site-specific climatological data appropriately. According to SRP 2.3.1, the site parameters for ambient temperature and humidity must include statistics such as 2% and 1% annual exceedance values, 100-year maximum dry bulb temperature and coincident wet bulb temperature, and 98% and 99% annual exceedance and 100-year minimum dry bulb temperature. These statistics are used for the design of plant heat sink systems and HVAC systems. The acceptance criteria specify that these values should be derived from data recorded at nearby representative climatic stations or from appropriate standards, with corrections for local conditions. Reference 23 in SRP 2.3.1 provides a method for estimating 100-year return period extreme temperature values based on annual extremes.

For DC applications, per 10 CFR 52.47(a)(1) and as reviewed in SRP 2.3.1, the applicant must provide postulated site parameters that are representative of a reasonable number of potential COL sites and must provide a basis for each parameter. This ensures that future COL applicants can compare their site-specific data to the DC envelope using the same statistical basis and exceedance criteria. The design bases, as defined in 10 CFR 50.2, must reflect values or ranges chosen as reference bounds for design, derived from state-of-the-art practices or analysis of postulated accidents.

While RG 1.76 focuses on wind speeds and tornadoes, it reinforces the principle from GDC 2 that design bases for natural phenomena must consider the most severe historically reported values with sufficient margin, which is analogous to the approach for temperature extremes. In summary, the combined regulatory guidance requires that envelope values for temperature be based on statistically significant exceedance criteria (e.g., 1% and 2% annual exceedance, 100-year extremes), derived from representative data, and justified as bounding for a reasonable range of potential sites, ensuring comparability for future COL applicants.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for establishing design-basis dry-bulb and wet-bulb temperatures for nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for establishing design-basis dry-bulb and wet-bulb temperatures for nuclear power plants are primarily grounded in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, and further detailed in the Standard Review Plan (SRP) 2.3.1. GDC 2 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in the historical data (see [2]).

SRP 2.3.1, Section II, specifies that applicants must provide ambient temperature and humidity statistics, including 2% and 1% annual exceedance and 100-year maximum dry bulb temperature and coincident wet bulb temperature, as well as 2% and 1% annual exceedance and 100-year maximum wet bulb temperature (non-coincident), and 98% and 99% annual exceedance and 100-year minimum dry bulb temperature. These statistics are used to establish heat loads for the design of normal plant heat sink systems, post-accident containment heat removal systems, and plant HVAC systems (see [1]).

The data should be derived from nearby representative climatic stations or appropriate standards, with suitable corrections for local conditions. Reference 23 in SRP 2.3.1 provides a method for estimating 100-year return period extreme temperature values based on annual extremes (see [1]).

Additionally, 10 CFR Part 100 (§100.10(c)(2), §100.20(c)(2), and §100.21(d)) requires consideration of regional meteorological characteristics in site evaluation (see [1]).

In summary, the NRC requires that design-basis dry-bulb and wet-bulb temperatures be established using statistically significant historical data, with appropriate margins and consideration of local and regional meteorological conditions, as detailed in SRP 2.3.1 and required by GDC 2 and 10 CFR Part 100.

data.query: How do NRC regulations for environmental design parameters ensure that both summer and winter temperature extremes are considered in the safety analysis of nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
NRC regulations ensure that both summer and winter temperature extremes are considered in the safety analysis of nuclear power plants through a combination of specific technical requirements and general design criteria. According to SRP 2.3.1, the NRC staff reviews detailed climatic data provided by applicants, including averages and extremes of temperature and humidity. This review specifically requires the consideration of both high (summer) and low (winter) temperature extremes, such as 100-year maximum and minimum dry bulb temperatures, and associated wet bulb temperatures, using statistics like 2% and 1% annual exceedance for maxima and 98% and 99% for minima. These data are used to establish heat loads for critical plant systems, including normal heat sinks, post-accident containment heat removal, and HVAC systems (SRP 2.3.1, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA).

Furthermore, SRP 2.3.1 mandates that the potential for water freezing in ultimate heat sink (UHS) water storage facilities be analyzed, using conservative site characteristics such as the maximum accumulated degree-days below freezing recorded in the region. This ensures that winter extremes are explicitly addressed in the design (SRP 2.3.1, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA).

General Design Criterion 2 of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site, with appropriate margins for data uncertainties (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2). This includes temperature extremes as part of the natural phenomena considered. Regulatory Guide 1.76 and 10 CFR Part 100 further reinforce the requirement to evaluate meteorological characteristics, including temperature extremes, in determining site acceptability and establishing site parameters (RG 1.76, A. INTRODUCTION).

In summary, NRC regulations require a comprehensive evaluation of both summer and winter temperature extremes, using long-term, site-specific meteorological data, to ensure that nuclear power plant safety systems are robust against the full range of environmental conditions.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, “Design Bases for Protection Against Natural Phenomena,” of Appendix A, “General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants,” to Title 10, Part 50, of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR Part 50), “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities” (Ref. 1), requires that structures, systems, and components that are important to safety shall be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, such as tornadoes, without loss of capability to perform their safety functions.  GDC 2 also requires that the design bases for these structures, systems, and components shall reflect (1) appropriate consideration of the most severe of the natural phenomena that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated, (2) appropriate combinations of the effects of normal and accident conditions with the effects of the natural phenomena, and (3) the importance of the safety functions to be performed.

For stationary power reactor site applications submitted on or after January 10, 1997, paragraph 100.20(c)(2) of 10 CFR Part 100 requires that meteorological characteristics of the site that are necessary for safety analysis or may have an impact upon plant design (such as maximum probable wind speed) must be considered in determining the acceptability of a site for a nuclear power plant.  In addition, paragraph 100.21(d) of 10 CFR Part 100 requires that the physical characteristics of the site, including meteorology, must be evaluated and site parameters established such that potential threats from such physical characteristics will pose no undue risk to the type of facility proposed to be located at the site.

data.query: For a new nuclear power plant design, what regulatory guidance and review standards must be used to justify the statistical basis and selection of design-basis non-coincident wet-bulb temperatures, and how should these be applied across diverse geographic and topographic regions?
data.answer:
For a new nuclear power plant design, the regulatory guidance and review standards for justifying the statistical basis and selection of design-basis non-coincident wet-bulb temperatures are primarily outlined in SRP 2.3.1 (Sections II and III) and are grounded in the requirements of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2. 

SRP 2.3.1 specifies that ambient temperature and humidity statistics—including non-coincident wet-bulb temperatures at various exceedance levels (e.g., 2%, 1%, and 100-year maximum)—must be established for use in the design of plant heat sink systems and HVAC systems. The acceptance criteria require that these statistics be derived from data recorded at nearby, representative climatic stations or from appropriate standards, with suitable corrections for local conditions such as topography, terrain elevation, land use, and proximity to large bodies of water. The data should cover a significant time interval to capture cyclical extremes, and the methods used should be substantiated by NOAA data, industry standards, and regulatory guides (SRP 2.3.1, II.6.e, II.7, III).

GDC 2 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) mandates that the design bases for safety-related structures, systems, and components reflect the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in the data. This includes appropriate consideration of the effects of normal and accident conditions combined with natural phenomena (10 CFR Part 50, App. A, GDC 2).

When applying these standards across diverse geographic and topographic regions, SRP 2.3.1 emphasizes the importance of evaluating the representativeness of meteorological data sources, considering local variations, and making corrections as necessary. The review procedures require that proximity, topography, and other local factors be considered to ensure the selected statistics accurately reflect site-specific conditions (SRP 2.3.1, III). 

In summary, the justification for design-basis non-coincident wet-bulb temperatures must be based on long-term, representative meteorological data, adjusted for local conditions, and must meet the regulatory requirements for conservatism and margin as specified in SRP 2.3.1 and GDC 2.

B.  DISCUSSION
Regionalization of Tornado Wind Speeds
Nuclear power plants must be designed so that they remain in a safe condition under severe meteorological events, including those that could result in the most severe tornado that could reasonably be predicted to occur at the site.  The NRC based the original version of Regulatory Guide 1.76, published in April 1974, on WASH-1300 (Ref. 3).  WASH-1300 chose the design-basis tornado wind speeds so that the probability that a tornado exceeding the design basis would occur was on the order of 10^-7 per year per nuclear power plant. ...
The design-basis tornado wind speeds presented in this regulatory guide are based on Revision 2 of NUREG/CR-4461 (Ref. 4).  The tornado database used in that revision of NUREG/CR-4461 includes information recorded for more than 46,800 tornado segments occurring from January 1, 1950, through August 31, 2003. ...
Meteorological and topographic conditions, which vary significantly within the continental United States, influence the frequency of occurrence and intensity of tornadoes.  The NRC staff has determined that the design-basis tornado wind speeds for new reactors should correspond to the exceedance frequency of 10^-7 per year (calculated as a best estimate), thus using the same exceedance frequency as the original version of this regulatory guide.  The results of the analysis indicated that a maximum wind speed of 103 meters per second (m/s) [230 miles per hour (mph)] is appropriate for tornadoes for the central portion of the United States; a maximum wind speed of 89 m/s (200 mph) is appropriate for a large region of the United States along the east coast, the northern border, and western Great Plains; and a maximum wind speed of 72 m/s (160 mph) is appropriate for the western United States.  These geographic wind speed regions are defined by observed tornado occurrences within the two-degree latitude and longitude boxes in the contiguous United States.  Figure 1 shows the three tornado intensity regions for the contiguous United States at the 10^-7 per year probability level, in which the abscissa is the longitude (degrees west) and the ordinate is the latitude (degrees north).

C.  REGULATORY POSITION
The NRC staff has established the following regulatory positions for licensees and applicants to use in selecting the design-basis tornado and design-basis tornado-generated missiles that a nuclear power plant should be designed to withstand to prevent undue risk to the health and safety of the public.
1. Design-Basis Tornado Parameters
Nuclear power plants should be designed to withstand the design-basis tornado.  The parameter values specified in Table 1 for the appropriate regions identified in Figure 1 are generally acceptable to the NRC staff for defining the design-basis tornado for a nuclear power plant.  If a design-basis tornado proposed for a given site is characterized by less-conservative parameter values than the regional values in Table 1, a comprehensive analysis should be provided to justify the selection of the less-conservative design-basis tornado.  Sites located near the general boundaries of adjoining regions may involve additional considerations.  The radius of maximum rotational speed of 45.7 meters (150 feet) is used for all three tornado intensity regions.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for determining the design-basis outdoor air temperature conditions used in the evaluation of nuclear power plant ventilation systems?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for determining the design-basis outdoor air temperature conditions used in the evaluation of nuclear power plant ventilation systems are primarily established by 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, and further detailed in the Standard Review Plan (SRP) 2.3.1. GDC 2 requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including extreme temperatures, without loss of safety function. The design bases must reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin to account for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; SRP 2.3.1, Section II).

SRP 2.3.1 specifies that ambient temperature and humidity statistics should be derived from data recorded at nearby representative climatic stations or obtained from appropriate standards, with suitable corrections for local conditions. It references methods for estimating 100-year return period extreme temperature values based on annual extremes, ensuring that the design-basis conditions are conservative and reflective of rare but credible events (SRP 2.3.1, Section II, Acceptance Criteria 7).

Additionally, 10 CFR Part 100 (§100.10(c)(2), §100.20(c)(2), and §100.21(d)) requires that regional meteorological characteristics necessary for safety analysis or that may impact plant design be identified, characterized, and evaluated to ensure that physical site characteristics, including meteorology, pose no undue risk (SRP 2.3.1, Section II; 10 CFR Part 100).

In summary, the regulatory requirements mandate the use of the most severe historically reported outdoor air temperature conditions, with appropriate statistical and site-specific adjustments, to establish the design-basis for ventilation system evaluations, ensuring safety margins are maintained.

data.query: What is the NRC's regulatory requirement for establishing design-basis dry-bulb and wet-bulb temperature values for nuclear power plant site parameters?
data.answer:
The NRC's regulatory requirement for establishing design-basis dry-bulb and wet-bulb temperature values for nuclear power plant site parameters is grounded in both regulatory criteria and specific technical guidance. According to SRP 2.3.1, Section II, the acceptance criteria are based on 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, which requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in the historical data (SRP 2.3.1 II; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2). Additionally, 10 CFR Part 100 (§100.10(c)(2), §100.20(c)(2), and §100.21(d)) requires consideration of regional meteorological characteristics in site evaluation and parameter establishment (SRP 2.3.1 II; RG 1.76 A).

Specifically, SRP 2.3.1 outlines that ambient temperature and humidity statistics—including 2% and 1% annual exceedance and 100-year maximum dry bulb temperature and coincident wet bulb temperature, as well as 2% and 1% annual exceedance and 100-year maximum wet bulb temperature (non-coincident), and 98% and 99% annual exceedance and 100-year minimum dry bulb temperature—must be established. These values are used for the design of plant heat sink systems, post-accident containment heat removal, and HVAC systems (SRP 2.3.1 I.6.e). The statistics should be derived from data recorded at nearby representative climatic stations or from appropriate standards, with suitable corrections for local conditions. Reference 23 in the SRP provides a method for estimating 100-year return period extreme temperature values (SRP 2.3.1 II.7).

In summary, the NRC requires that design-basis temperature values be established using rigorous statistical analysis of historical meteorological data, ensuring that the most severe credible conditions are considered with appropriate safety margins, as specified in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2, 10 CFR Part 100, and detailed in SRP 2.3.1.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory guides and review standards define the process for determining the exceedance values and duration exclusions when establishing design-basis temperature site parameters for nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The process for determining exceedance values and duration exclusions when establishing design-basis temperature site parameters for nuclear power plants is defined through a combination of regulatory requirements and accepted methodologies as outlined in NRC regulatory guides and review standards.

According to SRP 2.3.1, the NRC requires that ambient temperature and humidity statistics—such as 2% and 1% annual exceedance values, and 100-year maximum and minimum temperatures—be established for use in the design of plant systems (Section I.6.e). These statistics are derived from historical meteorological data recorded at nearby representative climatic stations or from appropriate standards, with corrections for local conditions as necessary (Section II.7). Reference 23 in the SRP provides a method for estimating 100-year return period extreme temperature values based on annual extremes. The data used should cover a significant time interval to capture cyclical extremes, and current literature on regional weather changes should be reviewed to ensure the reasonableness of the methods used.

10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2, further requires that the design bases for structures, systems, and components important to safety reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in the data (Criterion 2).

While RG 1.76 focuses on tornado wind speeds, it illustrates the NRC's approach to exceedance values for natural phenomena: design-basis parameters are set to correspond to specific exceedance frequencies (e.g., 10^-7 per year for tornadoes), and less-conservative values must be justified with comprehensive analysis (Section C).

In summary, NRC regulatory guides and review standards require that exceedance values and duration exclusions for design-basis temperature site parameters be based on long-term, representative meteorological data, established statistical methods (such as 100-year return periods), and consideration of the most severe historical events, with appropriate margins for uncertainty. The process must be substantiated with data and analysis in accordance with accepted standards and regulatory guidance (SRP 2.3.1, 10 CFR Part 50, RG 1.76).

data.query: For a new nuclear power plant design, what combined regulatory provisions from review standards and regulatory guides govern the selection, justification, and consistent application of design-basis dry- and wet-bulb temperature site parameters, including the treatment of historical limits and short-duration peak exclusions?
data.answer:
The selection, justification, and consistent application of design-basis dry- and wet-bulb temperature site parameters for a new nuclear power plant are governed by a combination of regulatory requirements and guidance from 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A (General Design Criterion 2), 10 CFR Part 100, the Standard Review Plan (SRP) 2.3.1, and relevant Regulatory Guides such as RG 1.76.

According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2, the design bases for structures, systems, and components important to safety must reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2). This is reinforced by SRP 2.3.1, which specifies that ambient temperature and humidity statistics should be derived from data recorded at nearby representative climatic stations or from appropriate standards, with suitable corrections for local conditions. The historical data used should cover a significant time interval to capture cyclical extremes, and current literature on regional weather changes should be reviewed to ensure the methods for predicting weather extremes are reasonable (SRP 2.3.1, II. Acceptance Criteria).

SRP 2.3.1 also requires that the information be substantiated in accordance with acceptable practices and data as promulgated by NOAA, industry standards, and regulatory guides. Reference 23 in SRP 2.3.1 provides a method for estimating 100-year return period extreme temperature values, which is an accepted approach for defining design-basis temperature parameters. Exclusion of short-duration peaks or less-conservative parameter values must be justified with a comprehensive analysis, as outlined in RG 1.76, which, while focused on tornado parameters, establishes the principle that less-conservative site-specific values require robust justification (RG 1.76, C. Regulatory Position).

In summary, the regulatory framework requires that design-basis temperature parameters be based on the most severe historical data, with sufficient margin and justification for any exclusions or deviations, using established standards and regulatory guidance.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for estimating short-term atmospheric dispersion factors for accident releases at nuclear power plant sites?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for estimating short-term atmospheric dispersion factors (X/Q values) for accident releases at nuclear power plant sites are grounded in several regulations and guidance documents. Applicants must evaluate the radiological consequences of postulated accidents, including the dispersion of radioactive materials, as required by 10 CFR 50.34(a)(1)(ii)(d) (see [2]) and related site assessment regulations (see SRP 2.3.4, Section II, [1]). The evaluation must consider site meteorology and demonstrate that design features and site characteristics adequately mitigate radiological consequences.

The Standard Review Plan (SRP) 2.3.4 ([1]) specifies that applicants should use meteorological data and dispersion models consistent with NRC-endorsed Regulatory Guides. Regulatory Guide 1.23 ([3]) outlines the requirements for onsite meteorological monitoring, including measurements of wind speed and direction at multiple heights (typically 10 m and 60 m), and vertical temperature difference (ΔT) to determine atmospheric stability (Pasquill stability classes). These data are essential for input to dispersion models.

Regulatory Guide 1.145 ([5]) provides the accepted methodology for calculating atmospheric relative concentration (X/Q) values. It specifies that meteorological data (hourly averages of wind speed, wind direction, and stability class) should be used, with wind direction divided into 16 compass sectors. Stability should be determined by ΔT as described in RG 1.23. X/Q values must be calculated for each significant release point at the minimum distances to the exclusion area boundary (EAB) and low population zone (LPZ) in each sector. For short-term (accident) releases, the relative concentration at the EAB should be determined for the 2-hour period immediately following an accident, using 1-hour average meteorological data conservatively applied to the entire 2-hour period.

In summary, NRC requirements mandate the use of site-specific meteorological data collected per RG 1.23, and the calculation of short-term dispersion factors using the methods in RG 1.145, to conservatively estimate radiological consequences at the EAB and LPZ following postulated accidents.

• a conservative assessment by both the applicant and the regulatory staff of the potential dispersion of radioactive material from, and the radiological consequences of, design-basis accidents to aid in evaluating the acceptability of a site and the adequacy of engineered safety features for a nuclear power plant in accordance with 10 CFR Part 100 criteria

This section describes a suitable onsite program to collect the basic meteorological data needed to determine the environmental impacts of the plant, perform consequence assessments supporting routine release and design-basis accident evaluations, and support emergency preparedness programs and other applications at power reactor sites.
...
2. Meteorological Parameters
This section discusses the criteria for a basic meteorological monitoring system.
2.1 Wind Speed and Direction
Wind speed and direction should be measured on one open-lattice tower or mast measured at heights of approximately 10 meters (33 feet) and 60 meters (197 feet) above ground level. A measurement height other than 60 meters (197 feet) may be appropriate for those plants where the most probable atmospheric release height is other than 60 meters (197 feet). A third measurement height should be implemented at a representative level for stack releases that are 85 meters (279 feet) or higher.
2.2 Vertical Temperature Difference
Vertical temperature difference ()T) should be measured on the same open-lattice tower or mast as wind speed and wind direction between the 10-meter (33-foot) level and 60-meter (197-foot) levels and, if necessary, between the 10-meter (33-foot) level and a higher level that is representative of diffusion conditions from release points that are 85 meters (279 feet) or higher. Table 1 provides a definition of Pasquill stability classes as a function of )T.
Vertical temperature difference is the preferred method for determining Pasquill stability classes at nuclear power plants for licensing purposes because it is an effective indicator for the worst-case stability conditions (e.g., Pasquill stability classes E, F, and G). Also, certain Gaussian plume models endorsed by the NRC (such as the models referenced in Regulatory Guides 1.145 and 1.194, Refs. 9 and 11) are based on empirically derived plume meander factors from field tracer studies that used )T to classify atmospheric stability. Alternative methods may be used to classify atmospheric stability for licensing purposes if appropriate justification is provided. However, the use of alternative methods to classify atmospheric stability may require modifications of the models described in Regulatory Guides 1.145 and 1.194.
Alternative methods may be appropriate for classifying atmospheric stability for emergency response purposes if these methods can be shown to be compatible with the plant’s emergency response dose assessment methodology.

evidence_chain.section: C. STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE, Section 3. Control Room Habitability Evaluation
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
3. Control Room Habitability Evaluation 

When performing a detailed evaluation of CR habitability during a hazardous chemical release using this guidance, the metric applicants and licensees should use for each chemical is the IDLH that can be tolerated without physical incapacitation of a CR operator. In deriving the toxicity level in the CR, the detailed calculations should consider several factors, such as accident type; release characterization (e.g., release rate, duration); atmospheric dispersion characteristics, including prevailing meteorological conditions at the site; and the air exchange rate of the CR.  The checklist for the determinations of the toxicity level (i.e., concentration) in the CR, based on the toxic chemical and CR air quality parameter values, is as follows: (1) name of the most hazardous chemical, (2) type of source (stationary or mobile) during the accidental release; (3) maximum quantity or concentration measured (if available); (4) IDLH values (i.e., ppm or mg/m3); (5) average continuous release rate of hazardous chemical; (6) vapor pressure (torr) of hazardous chemical (at local ambient plant temperature); (7) fraction of chemical flashed and rate of boiloff when spilling occurs; (8) total plume travel distance between the CR and the chemicals; and (9) local meteorological data.

For determining the air quality in the CR for habitability evaluation, the NRC recommends the following 7  considerations: (1) the design height of air intake windows; (2) the volume size of CR; (3) the air-exchange rate of CR; (4) the flow rate as cubic feet per minute of the CR; (5) the unfiltered makeup or inleakage air for the CR; (6) the filtered makeup and recirculated air under normal and emergency operations; and (7) the use of a filtered nuclear air-cleaning system or personal breathing-air supplying device during an emergency.
