evidence_chain.section: C. REGULATORY POSITION (esp. 1.1, 1.2, 1.3)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
C. REGULATORY POSITION
This section identifies acceptable methods for (1) calculating atmospheric relative concentration (X/Q) values, (2) determining X/Q values on a directional basis, (3) determining X/Q values on an overall site basis, and (4) choosing X/Q values to be used in evaluations of the types of events described in Regulatory Guides 1.3 and 1.4.
Selection of conservative, less detailed site parameters for the evaluation may be sufficient to establish compliance with regulatory guidelines.
1. CALCULATION OF ATMOSPHERIC RELATIVE CON-CENTRATION (X/Q) VALUES
Equations and parameters presented in this section should be used unless unusual siting, meteorological, or terrain conditions dictate the use of other models or considerations. Site-specific atmospheric diffusion tests covering a full range of conditions may be used as a basis for modifying the equations and parameters.
1.1 Meteorological Data Input
The meteorological data needed for X/Q calculations include windspeed, wind direction, and a measure of atmospheric stability. These data should represent hourly averages as defined in Regulatory Guide 1.23.
Wind direction should be classed into 16 compass directions (22.5-degree sectors centered on true north, north-northeast, etc.).
Atmospheric stability should be determined by vertical ΔT between the release height and the 10-meter level. Acceptable stability classes are given in Regulatory Guide 1.23. If other well-documented parameters are used to determine plume dispersion (with appropriate justification), the models described in this guide may require modification. A well-documented parameter is one that is substantiated by diffusion data collected in terrain conditions similar to those at the nuclear power plant site being considered.
Calms should be defined as hourly average windspeeds below the vane or anemometer starting speed, whichever is higher (to reflect limitations in instrumentation). If the instrumentation program conforms to the regulatory position in Regulatory Guide 1.23, calms should be assigned a windspeed equal to the vane or anemometer starting speed, whichever is higher. Otherwise, consideration of a conservative evaluation of calms, taking into account the limitations of the windspeed measurement system, will be necessary. Wind directions during calm conditions should be assigned in proportion to the directional distribution of noncalm winds with speeds less than 1.5 meters per second.
1.2 Determination of Distances for X/Q Calculations
For each wind direction sector, X/Q values for each significant release point should be calculated at an appropriate exclusion area boundary distance and outer low population zone (LPZ) boundary distance. The following procedure should be used to determine these distances. The procedure takes into consideration the possibility of curved airflow trajectories, plume segmentation (particularly in low wind, stable conditions), and the potential for windspeed and wind direction frequency shifts from year to year.
For each of the 16 sectors, the distance for exclusion area boundary or outer LPZ boundary X/Q calculation should be the minimum distance from the stack or, in the case of releases through vents or building penetrations, the nearest point on the building to the exclusion area boundary or outer LPZ boundary within a 45-degree sector centered on the compass direction of interest.
For stack releases, the maximum ground-level concentration in a sector may occur beyond the exclusion area boundary distance or outer LPZ boundary distance. Therefore, for stack releases, X/Q calculations should be made in each sector at each minimum boundary distance and at various distances beyond the exclusion area boundary distance to determine the maximum relative concentration for consideration in subsequent calculations.
1.3 Calculation of X/Q Values at Exclusion Area Boundary Distances
Relative concentrations that can be assumed to apply at the exclusion area boundary for 2 hours immediately following an accident should be determined. Calculations based on meteorological data representing a 1-hour average should be assumed to apply for the entire 2-hour period. This assumption is reasonably conservative considering the small variation of X/Q values with averaging time (Ref. 8). If releases associated with a postulated event are estimated to occur in a period of less than 20 minutes, the applicability of these models should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis.
Procedures for calculating "2-hour" X/Q values depend on the mode of release. The procedures are described below.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory guides for atmospheric dispersion estimation relate to the general design criteria for radiological dose assessment at the exclusion area boundary?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory guides for atmospheric dispersion estimation are integral to demonstrating compliance with the general design criteria (GDC) for radiological dose assessment at the exclusion area boundary (EAB), as established in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50. Specifically, these guides provide the methodologies and data requirements for estimating the transport and diffusion of radioactive materials released during routine operations or postulated accidents, which are essential for assessing potential radiation doses to the public at the EAB and to control room personnel.

SRP 2.3.4 (Section II) clarifies that Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.23 provides criteria for onsite meteorological monitoring programs, ensuring that site-specific meteorological data are collected to support atmospheric dispersion estimates. RG 1.145 offers acceptable models and procedures for calculating atmospheric dispersion (χ/Q) values at the EAB and low population zone (LPZ), accounting for factors such as plume meander, wind directionality, and site-specific boundary shapes. These dispersion estimates are used, along with source term and containment leak rate assumptions, to calculate expected offsite radiation doses and verify compliance with regulatory dose limits at the EAB.

The technical rationale, as described in SRP 2.3.4 and RG 1.23, is that accurate atmospheric dispersion estimates are significant inputs for dose assessments required by GDC 19 and related criteria. RG 1.145 specifically addresses the need for site-specific, directionally dependent dispersion modeling to ensure conservative and realistic dose projections at the EAB. The guides collectively ensure that the design and siting of nuclear power plants provide adequate protection to the public by enabling robust, scientifically grounded assessments of radiological consequences at the EAB, as required by the general design criteria.

References: SRP 2.3.4 (Section II), RG 1.23 (Section A), RG 1.145 (Sections A, C).

The technical rationale for application of these acceptance criteria to the areas of review addressed by this SRP section is discussed in the following paragraphs:
1. Compliance with GDC 19 requires that the control room remain functional so that actions can be taken to operate the nuclear power unit safely under normal conditions and maintain the plant in a safe state under accident conditions. Adequate radiological and airborne hazardous material protection must be provided to permit access and occupancy of the control room for the duration of accidental conditions. Verification that the proposed nuclear plant design meets these radiation dose guidelines is accomplished by calculating expected offsite radiation doses using (a) an assumed inventory of fission products available for release from the containment building, (b) the expected containment leak rate, and (c) site atmospheric dispersion characteristics. Atmospheric dispersion characteristics are determined from meteorological measurements taken at the proposed plant site. Guidance on the onsite meteorological program needed to obtain meteorological data is provided in Regulatory Guide 1.23, and models for calculating the atmospheric dispersion for the EAB and LPZ are provided in Regulatory Guide 1.145.

This revised regulatory guide provides licensees and applicants with improved guidance concerning criteria for an onsite meteorological measurements program that the staff of the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) considers acceptable for the collection of basic meteorological data needed to support plant licensing and operation.

... 

The “General Design Criteria [GDC] for Nuclear Power Plants” set forth in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities” (Ref. 2), establish minimum requirements for the principal design criteria for water-cooled nuclear power plants. Specifically, GDC 19, “Control Room,” requires that a control room be provided from which actions can be taken to operate the nuclear power unit safely under normal conditions and to maintain it in a safe condition under accident conditions. Adequate radiation protection must be provided to permit access to and occupancy of the control room for the duration of accident conditions. For plants that use alternate source terms, 10 CFR 50.67(b)(2)(iii) provides similar criteria. Atmospheric dispersion estimates are significant inputs in assessments performed to demonstrate compliance with this requirement.

... 

Thus, each nuclear power plant site has multiple needs for an onsite program to measure and document basic meteorological data. These data may be used to develop atmospheric transport and diffusion parameters that, with appropriate atmospheric dispersion models, may be used to estimate potential radiation doses to the public resulting from actual routine or accidental releases of radioactive materials to the atmosphere or to evaluate the potential dose to the public and control room as a result of hypothetical reactor accidents. These data may also be used to assess nonradiological environmental effects resulting from the construction or operation of a nuclear power plant, such as the impacts of the plant’s heat dissipation system. This regulatory guide describes a suitable onsite program to provide meteorological data needed to estimate these potential impacts.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
The regulatory positions presented in this guide represent a substantial change from procedures previously used to determine relative concentrations for assessing the potential offsite radiological consequences for a range of postulated accidental releases of radioactive material to the atmosphere. These procedures now include consideration of plume meander, directional dependence of dispersion conditions, and wind frequencies for various locations around actual exclusion area and low population zone (LPZ) boundaries ... Accordingly, this guide provides an acceptable methodology for determining site-specific relative concentrations (X/Q) and should be used in determining xJQ values for the evaluations discussed in Regulatory Guide 1.3, "Assumptions Used for Evaluating the Potential Radiological Consequences of a Loss of Coolant Accident for Boiling Water Reactors," and Regulatory Guide 1.4, "Assumptions Used for Evaluating the Potential Radiological Consequences of a Loss of Coolant Accident for Pressurized Water Reactors." ... The procedures in this guide also recognize that atmospheric dispersion conditions and wind frequencies are usually directionally dependent; that is, certain airflow directions can exhibit substantially more or less favorable diffusion conditions than others, and the wind can transport effluents in certain directions more frequently than in others. The procedures also allow evaluations of atmospheric dispersion for directionally variable distances such as a noncircular exclusion area boundary.

This section identifies acceptable methods for (1) calculating atmospheric relative concentration (xJQ) values, (2) determining X/Q values on a directional basis, (3) determining XJQ values on an overall site basis, and (4) choosing X/Q values to be used in evaluations of the types of events described in Regulatory Guides 1.3 and 1.4.

Selection of conservative, less detailed site parameters for the evaluation may be sufficient to establish compliance with regulatory guidelines.

evidence_chain.section: A. INTRODUCTION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
This guide provides guidance on determining atmospheric relative concentration (χ/Q) values in support of design basis control room radiological habitability assessments at nuclear power plants. This guide describes methods acceptable to the NRC staff for determining χ/Q values that will be used in control room radiological habitability assessments performed in support of applications for licenses and license amendment requests.

In 10 CFR Part 50, “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities,” Section 50.34, “Contents of Applications; Technical Information," requires that each applicant for a construction permit or operating license provide an analysis and evaluation of the design and performance of structures, systems, and components of the facility with the objective of assessing the risk to public health and safety resulting from the operation of the facility. Appendix A, “General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants,” to 10 CFR Part 50 establishes minimum requirements for the principal design criteria for water-cooled nuclear power plants. General Design Criterion 19 (GDC-19), “Control Room,” of Appendix A establishes minimum requirements for the facility control room. Included is the requirement that adequate radiation protection be provided to permit access and occupancy of the control room for the duration of accident conditions. Similar criteria are provided in 10 CFR Part 50.67(b)(2)(iii) for plants that use alternative source terms. Atmospheric relative concentrations are significant inputs in assessments performed to demonstrate compliance with these regulations.

Many of the regulatory positions presented in this guide represent substantial changes from procedures previously used to determine atmospheric relative concentrations for assessing the potential control room radiological consequences for a range of postulated accidental releases of radioactive material to the atmosphere. These revised procedures are largely based on the NRC-sponsored computer code, ARCON96 (Ref. 1). This code implements an improved building wake dispersion algorithm; assessment of ground level, building vent, elevated, and diffuse source release modes; use of hour-by-hour meteorological observations; sector averaging; and directional dependence of dispersion conditions. This guide also provides procedures for addressing some aspects of control room χ/Q determinations not currently implemented in the ARCON96 code.

data.query: For a new nuclear power plant design, what combined regulatory provisions from general design criteria, regulatory review standards, and NRC regulatory guides must be considered to ensure that postulated site atmospheric dispersion parameters are representative of a reasonable number of potential sites, and how should these provisions guide the selection of meteorological data for accident dose calculations?
data.answer:
To ensure that postulated site atmospheric dispersion parameters are representative of a reasonable number of potential sites for a new nuclear power plant design, applicants must integrate regulatory provisions from general design criteria, regulatory review standards, and NRC regulatory guides as follows:

1. Regulatory Basis: The primary regulatory requirements are found in 10 CFR 50.34(a)(1)(ii)(d), which mandates an assessment of site characteristics, including meteorology, as they relate to the capability of safety-related structures, systems, and components to withstand the effects of site-related parameters, including atmospheric dispersion characteristics (Evidence [2]). For new reactor applications, 10 CFR 100.21(c)(2) also requires evaluation of atmospheric dispersion characteristics for accident dose calculations (Evidence [1]).

2. General Design Criteria: GDC 19 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) requires that meteorological considerations be used to evaluate control room habitability during radiological and hazardous chemical accident conditions (Evidence [1]).

3. Regulatory Review Standards: SRP 2.3.4 specifies that atmospheric dispersion estimates should reflect current staff positions and state-of-the-art knowledge. Applicants must provide detailed descriptions of the dispersion models used, substantiated within their limits, and use meteorological data representing annual cycles of hourly wind direction, wind speed, and atmospheric stability for each release mode. The data must be the most representative available for the site (Evidence [1]).

4. NRC Regulatory Guides:
   - RG 1.23 provides criteria for an acceptable onsite meteorological monitoring program and specifies that at least 24 consecutive months of representative, recent, and complete data should be used for COL or ESP applications, with three or more years preferred. The data should be collected where it accurately represents overall site meteorology, avoiding local influences (Evidence [3]).
   - RG 1.145 details acceptable methods for calculating atmospheric relative concentration (X/Q) values, emphasizing the use of hourly wind speed, wind direction (in 16 compass sectors), and atmospheric stability data as defined in RG 1.23. The guide also recognizes the importance of directional dependence and wind frequency in dispersion modeling (Evidence [5]).
   - RG 1.78 and RG 1.194 provide additional criteria for evaluating control room habitability and radiological consequences, requiring consideration of prevailing meteorological conditions and site-specific dispersion characteristics (Evidence [1], [4]).

In summary, the selection of meteorological data for accident dose calculations must be based on a robust, representative, and recent onsite meteorological monitoring program (per RG 1.23), using hourly data for wind speed, wind direction, and atmospheric stability. Dispersion models must be substantiated and account for site-specific and directional characteristics (per RG 1.145). These provisions ensure that atmospheric dispersion parameters used in accident analyses are representative of a reasonable range of potential sites and support conservative, regulatory-compliant dose assessments.

evidence_chain.section: B. DISCUSSION and C. REGULATORY POSITION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
An onsite meteorological measurements program at a nuclear power plant site should be capable of providing the meteorological information needed to make the following assessments:
• a conservative assessment by both the applicant and the regulatory staff of the potential dispersion of radioactive material from, and the radiological consequences of, design-basis accidents to aid in evaluating the acceptability of a site and the adequacy of engineered safety features for a nuclear power plant in accordance with 10 CFR Part 100 criteria
• an assessment by both the applicant and the regulatory staff of the maximum potential annual radiation dose to the public resulting from the routine release of radioactive materials in gaseous effluents to assist in demonstrating that operations will be or are being conducted within the limits of 10 CFR Part 20 and Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50, and to ensure that effluent control equipment design objectives and proposed operating procedures meet the Commission’s requirements for keeping levels of radioactive material in effluents to unrestricted areas as low as practicable
• a conservative assessment by both the applicant and the regulatory staff of the habitability of the control room during postulated design-basis radiological accidents and hazardous chemical releases to demonstrate that the control room can remain occupied under accident conditions in accordance with GDC 19
...
While the specific types of meteorological information needed differ for each of the above assessments, a single set of instruments can generally be used to obtain the basic data needed for all of them. For this reason, when establishing a meteorological program for an initial site survey, careful consideration should be given to the operational needs for meteorological information. In particular, care should be taken to locate the instrumentation where the measurements will accurately represent the overall site meteorology and, if possible, where singular topographic features and vegetation or the construction of additional structures at a later date will not significantly influence wind patterns.
...
The minimum amount of onsite meteorological data to be provided at the time of application (1) for a construction permit is a representative consecutive 12-month period; (2) for an operating license is a representative consecutive 24-month period, including the most recent 1-year period; and (3) for an early site permit or a combined license that does not reference an early site permit is a consecutive 24-month period of data that is defendable, representative and complete, but not older than 10 years from the date of the application. However, 3 or more years of data are preferable and, if available, should be submitted with the application.

evidence_chain.section: C.3 Control Room Habitability Evaluation
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
When performing a detailed evaluation of CR habitability during a hazardous chemical release using this guidance, the metric applicants and licensees should use for each chemical is the IDLH that can be tolerated without physical incapacitation of a CR operator. In deriving the toxicity level in the CR, the detailed calculations should consider several factors, such as accident type; release characterization (e.g., release rate, duration); atmospheric dispersion characteristics, including prevailing meteorological conditions at the site; and the air exchange rate of the CR.  The checklist for the determinations of the toxicity level (i.e., concentration) in the CR, based on the toxic chemical and CR air quality parameter values, is as follows: (1) name of the most hazardous chemical, (2) type of source (stationary or mobile) during the accidental release; (3) maximum quantity or concentration measured (if available); (4) IDLH values (i.e., ppm or mg/m3); (5) average continuous release rate of hazardous chemical; (6) vapor pressure (torr) of hazardous chemical (at local ambient plant temperature); (7) fraction of chemical flashed and rate of boiloff when spilling occurs; (8) total plume travel distance between the CR and the chemicals; and (9) local meteorological data.

For determining the air quality in the CR for habitability evaluation, the NRC recommends the following 7  considerations: (1) the design height of air intake windows; (2) the volume size of CR; (3) the air-exchange rate of CR; (4) the flow rate as cubic feet per minute of the CR; (5) the unfiltered makeup or inleakage air for the CR; (6) the filtered makeup and recirculated air under normal and emergency operations; and (7) the use of a filtered nuclear air-cleaning system or personal breathing-air supplying device during an emergency.

evidence_chain.section: A. INTRODUCTION; C. REGULATORY POSITION (1.1 Meteorological Data Input)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
The regulatory positions presented in this guide represent a substantial change from procedures previously used to determine relative concentrations for assessing the potential offsite radiological consequences for a range of postulated accidental releases of radioactive material to the atmosphere. These procedures now include consideration of plume meander, directional dependence of dispersion conditions, and wind frequencies for various locations around actual exclusion area and low population zone (LPZ) boundaries ...

This guide provides an acceptable methodology for determining site-specific relative concentrations (X/Q) and should be used in determining X/Q values for the evaluations discussed in Regulatory Guide 1.3, "Assumptions Used for Evaluating the Potential Radiological Consequences of a Loss of Coolant Accident for Boiling Water Reactors," and Regulatory Guide 1.4, "Assumptions Used for Evaluating the Potential Radiological Consequences of a Loss of Coolant Accident for Pressurized Water Reactors." ...

The procedures in this guide also recognize that atmospheric dispersion conditions and wind frequencies are usually directionally dependent; that is, certain airflow directions can exhibit substantially more or less favorable diffusion conditions than others, and the wind can transport effluents in certain directions more frequently than in others. The procedures also allow evaluations of atmospheric dispersion for directionally variable distances such as a noncircular exclusion area boundary.

C. REGULATORY POSITION
This section identifies acceptable methods for (1) calculating atmospheric relative concentration (X/Q) values, (2) determining X/Q values on a directional basis, (3) determining X/Q values on an overall site basis, and (4) choosing X/Q values to be used in evaluations of the types of events described in Regulatory Guides 1.3 and 1.4.

Selection of conservative, less detailed site parameters for the evaluation may be sufficient to establish compliance with regulatory guidelines.

1.1 Meteorological Data Input
The meteorological data needed for X/Q calculations include windspeed, wind direction, and a measure of atmospheric stability. These data should represent hourly averages as defined in Regulatory Guide 1.23.
Wind direction should be classed into 16 compass directions (22.5-degree sectors centered on true north, north-northeast, etc.).
Atmospheric stability should be determined by vertical ΔT between the release height and the 10-meter level. Acceptable stability classes are given in Regulatory Guide 1.23. If other well-documented parameters are used to determine plume dispersion (with appropriate justification), the models described in this guide may require modification. A well-documented parameter is one that is substantiated by diffusion data collected in terrain conditions similar to those at the nuclear power plant site being considered.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory acceptance criteria for determining atmospheric dispersion factors (χ/Q values) used in evaluating routine radioactive releases from nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory acceptance criteria for determining atmospheric dispersion factors (χ/Q values) used in evaluating routine radioactive releases from nuclear power plants are grounded in compliance with several key regulations and guidance documents. According to SRP 2.3.5 Section II, acceptance criteria are based on meeting the requirements of 10 CFR 20 (public dose limits), 10 CFR 50.34a and Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50 (ALARA for effluents), and 10 CFR 100.21(c)(2) (site atmospheric dispersion characteristics). The applicant must provide maximum annual average χ/Q values at or beyond the site boundary and at specific receptor locations, as well as annual average χ/Q values for 16 radial sectors up to 50 miles, using appropriate meteorological data (SRP 2.3.5).

The methods for estimating χ/Q values must be consistent with NRC guidance, specifically Regulatory Guides 1.23, 1.109, 1.111, and 1.112 (SRP 2.3.5; RG 1.206 Section 2.3.5.2). RG 1.23 specifies that onsite meteorological monitoring should provide data on wind speed, wind direction, and atmospheric stability, with stability preferably determined by vertical temperature difference (ΔT) between the release height and 10 meters, classified according to Pasquill stability categories (RG 1.23 Section C.2.2, Table 1). RG 1.145 details that meteorological data should be hourly averages, wind direction divided into 16 compass sectors, and stability classes as per RG 1.23. Calculations should use NRC-endorsed Gaussian plume models unless site-specific conditions justify alternatives (RG 1.145 Section C.1.1).

For routine releases, RG 1.111 provides the methods for estimating atmospheric transport and dispersion, and RG 1.194 clarifies that vent releases should be modeled as either ground-level or elevated releases, not mixed-mode, for conservatism (RG 1.194 Section 3.2.3). Any deviations from standard NRC methodologies must be justified by the applicant (RG 1.206 Section 2.3.5.2).

In summary, the acceptance criteria require use of site-specific, quality-assured meteorological data, NRC-endorsed models, and conservative assumptions, with χ/Q values calculated for relevant receptors and sectors, in accordance with the referenced regulatory guides.

evidence_chain.section: Section 2.3.5.2 Atmospheric Dispersion Estimates
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Section 2.3.5.2 Atmospheric Dispersion Estimates

The applicant should describe the methods used to estimate atmospheric dispersion factors (χ/Q values) for routine releases of radioactive materials in gaseous effluents. The description should include the following:

• The models and assumptions used to estimate dispersion and deposition of radioactive materials released to the atmosphere, including the basis for selecting the models and any site-specific modifications.
• The meteorological data used as input to the dispersion models, including the period of record, data quality, and representativeness of the data for the site.
• The locations of receptors (e.g., site boundary, control room, offsite locations) for which dispersion factors are calculated.
• The averaging times and release characteristics (e.g., continuous, intermittent, elevated, or ground-level releases) used in the calculations.
• The results of the dispersion analyses, including the calculated χ/Q values for the identified receptors.

The methods used should be consistent with current NRC guidance, such as Regulatory Guide 1.23, 'Meteorological Monitoring Programs for Nuclear Power Plants,' and Regulatory Guide 1.145, 'Atmospheric Dispersion Models for Potential Accident Consequence Assessments at Nuclear Power Plants.' The applicant should justify any deviations from NRC guidance or standard methodologies.

C. REGULATORY POSITION
This section identifies acceptable methods for (1) calculating atmospheric relative concentration (xJQ) values, (2) determining X/Q values on a directional basis, (3) determining XJQ values on an overall site basis, and (4) choosing X/Q values to be used in evaluations of the types of events described in Regulatory Guides 1.3 and 1.4.
Selection of conservative, less detailed site parameters for the evaluation may be sufficient to establish compliance with regulatory guidelines.
1. CALCULATION OF ATMOSPHERIC RELATIVE CON-CENTRATION (X/Q) VALUES
Equations and parameters presented in this section should be used unless unusual siting, meteorological, or terrain conditions dictate the use of other models or considerations. Site-specific atmospheric diffusion tests covering a full range of conditions may be used as a basis for modifying the equations and parameters.
1.1 Meteorological Data Input
The meteorological data needed for X/Q calculations include windspeed, wind direction, and a measure of atmospheric stability. These data should represent hourly averages as defined in Regulatory Guide 1.23. Wind direction should be classed into 16 compass directions (22.5-degree sectors centered on true north, north-northeast, etc.). Atmospheric stability should be determined by vertical AT between the release height and the 10-meter level. Acceptable stability classes are given in Regulatory Guide 1.23. ...
1.3 Calculation of X/Q Values at Exclusion Area Boundary Distances
Relative concentrations that can be assumed to apply at the exclusion area boundary for 2 hours immediately following an accident should be determined.4 Calculations based on meteorological data representing a 1-hour average should be assumed to apply for the entire 2-hour period. ...
2. DETERMINATION OF MAXIMUM SECTOR x/Q VALUES
The XJQ values calculated in regulatory position 1 are used to determine "sector xJQ values" and "maximum sector XJQ values" for the exclusion area boundary and the outer LPZ boundary.
2.1 Exclusion Area Boundary
2.1.1 General Method
Using the XJQ values calculated for each hour of data according to regulatory position 1.3, a cumulative probability distribution of X/Q values should be constructed for each of the 16 sectors. Each distribution should be described in terms of probabilities of given XJQ values being exceeded in that sector during the total time. ... For each of the 16 curves, the XJQ value that is exceeded 0.5 percent of the total number of hours in the data set should be selected (Ref. 10). These are the sector X/Q values. The highest of the 16 sector values is defined as the maximum sector X/Q value.
...
4. SELECTION OF X/Q VALUES TO BE USED IN EVALUATIONS
The X/Q value for exclusion area boundary or outer LPZ boundary evaluations should be the maximum sector X/Q (regulatory position 2) or the 5 percent overall site xIQ (regulatory position 3), whichever is higher. All direction-dependent sector values should be presented for consideration of the appropriateness of the exclusion area and outer LPZ boundaries. Where the basic meteorological data necessary for the analyses described herein substantially deviate from the regulatory position stated in Regulatory Guide 1.23, consideration should be given to the resulting uncertainties in dispersion estimates.

3.2.3   Vent Releases
The ARCON96 calculation of vent releases includes an algorithm to model mixed-mode releases as described in Regulatory Guide 1.111 (Ref. 10), which addresses χ/Q values used in the assessment of routine effluent releases.  The development of this algorithm was based in part on limited field experiments.  Given the limited experiment set, the results obtained with this algorithm may not be sufficiently conservative for accident evaluations.  For this reason, the vent release mode should not be used in design basis assessments.  This position is consistent with the guidance of Regulatory Guide 1.145 (Ref. 9) for offsite χ/Q values.  These releases should be treated as a ground level release (Section 3.2.1) or as an elevated release (Section 3.2.2).

data.query: How do NRC regulatory guides and review standards specify the use of meteorological data in the calculation of atmospheric dispersion and deposition factors for routine effluent releases at nuclear power plant sites?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory guides and review standards provide detailed specifications for the use of meteorological data in calculating atmospheric dispersion and deposition factors for routine effluent releases at nuclear power plant sites. According to SRP 2.3.5, applicants must provide a detailed description of the atmospheric dispersion and deposition models used, including documentation of model accuracy, input parameters, and appropriateness for the site. The meteorological data used as input must represent hourly average values of wind speed, wind direction, and atmospheric stability, characteristic of annual average conditions in the plant vicinity (SRP 2.3.5; RG 1.23).

Regulatory Guide 1.23 outlines the requirements for onsite meteorological monitoring programs, specifying that wind speed and direction should be measured at 10 and 60 meters above ground level, and vertical temperature difference (ΔT) should be used to determine atmospheric stability classes. The minimum data requirements are a consecutive 12-month period for construction permits and a 24-month period for operating licenses, with three or more years preferred (RG 1.23, Sections B and C).

Regulatory Guides 1.145 and 1.194 further specify that meteorological data for dispersion calculations (X/Q or χ/Q) must include hourly averages of wind speed, wind direction (in 16 compass sectors), and atmospheric stability (preferably determined by ΔT). Data should be representative of long-term site conditions, free from local effects, and collected according to the quality assurance provisions of Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 50. Five years of data are considered representative, but a minimum of one complete year is acceptable with justification (RG 1.145, Section 1.1; RG 1.194, Section 3.1).

Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50 requires that atmospheric dispersion and deposition factors used in effluent calculations be based on appropriate site-specific meteorological data, ensuring compliance with ALARA and regulatory dose limits (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I).

In summary, NRC guidance requires the use of robust, representative, and well-documented onsite meteorological data—specifically hourly wind speed, wind direction, and stability class (preferably by ΔT)—collected over at least one year, to support accurate and regulatory-compliant dispersion and deposition assessments for routine effluent releases.

evidence_chain.section: II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appropriate sections of the following Regulatory Guides are used by the staff for the identified acceptance criteria.

Regulatory Guide 1.23 presents criteria for an acceptable onsite meteorological monitoring program and the resulting meteorological database that may be used in this SRP section as input to the atmospheric dispersion estimates.

Regulatory Guide 1.109 presents criteria to be used for identifying specific locations of potential receptors of interest.

Regulatory Guide 1.111 presents criteria for characterizing atmospheric dispersion and deposition conditions for evaluating the consequences of routine releases.  

Regulatory Guide 1.112 presents criteria for identifying release points and release characteristics.

Specifically, for CP, OL, COL, or ESP reviews, the following information should be provided by the applicant in the safety analysis report (SAR):

1. A detailed description of the atmospheric dispersion and deposition models used by the applicant to calculate annual average concentrations in air and amount of material deposited as a result of routine releases of radioactive materials to the atmosphere. The models should be sufficiently documented and substantiated to allow a review of their accuracy and validity, source configuration, suitability of input parameters, topography, and appropriateness for the site, plant, and release characteristics.

2. A discussion of atmospheric diffusion parameters, such as vertical plume spread (σz) as a function of distance, topography, and atmospheric conditions. Use of these parameters should be substantiated as to their appropriateness for use in estimating the consequences of routine releases from the site boundary to a radius of 50 miles (80 kilometers) from the plant.

3. Meteorological data summaries (onsite and regional) used as input to the dispersion and deposition models. Data used for this evaluation should represent hourly average values of wind speed, wind direction, and atmospheric stability which are appropriate for each mode of release and which are characteristic of annual average atmospheric dispersion and deposition conditions in the vicinity of the plant. Guidance on appropriate onsite meteorological data is provided in Regulatory Guide 1.23. This information is also reviewed under SRP section 2.3.3.

evidence_chain.section: Appendix I to Part 50
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appendix I to Part 50—Numerical Guides for Design Objectives and Limiting Conditions for Operation To Meet the Criterion “As Low as is Reasonably Achievable” for Radioactive Material in Light-Water-Cooled Nuclear Power Reactor Effluents

I. Introduction
Section 50.34a provides that each applicant for a license to operate a light-water-cooled nuclear power reactor will include in its application a description of the design features of the facility and the operating procedures developed to keep releases of radioactive material to unrestricted areas during normal operation, including anticipated operational occurrences, as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA). The guides set forth in this appendix are intended to provide numerical values for use in the design objectives and limiting conditions for operation for radioactive material in effluents from light-water-cooled nuclear power reactors.

II. Guides for Design Objectives and Limiting Conditions for Operation
A. The calculated annual average concentration of radioactive material in gaseous effluents released from each light-water-cooled nuclear power reactor to areas beyond the site boundary should not exceed the values specified in Table 2, Column 1, of Appendix B to part 20 of this chapter. The atmospheric dispersion and deposition factors used in the calculations should be based on appropriate meteorological data for the site, considering the design and location of the facility.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
1.1 Meteorological Data Input
The meteorological data needed for X/Q calculations include windspeed, wind direction, and a measure of atmospheric stability. These data should represent hourly averages as defined in Regulatory Guide 1.23.
Wind direction should be classed into 16 compass directions (22.5-degree sectors centered on true north, north-northeast, etc.).
Atmospheric stability should be determined by vertical ΔT between the release height and the 10-meter level. Acceptable stability classes are given in Regulatory Guide 1.23. If other well-documented parameters are used to determine plume dispersion (with appropriate justification), the models described in this guide may require modification. A well-documented parameter is one that is substantiated by diffusion data collected in terrain conditions similar to those at the nuclear power plant site being considered.
Calms should be defined as hourly average windspeeds below the vane or anemometer starting speed, whichever is higher (to reflect limitations in instrumentation). If the instrumentation program conforms to the regulatory position in Regulatory Guide 1.23, calms should be assigned a windspeed equal to the vane or anemometer starting speed, whichever is higher. Otherwise, consideration of a conservative evaluation of calms, taking into account the limitations of the windspeed measurement system, will be necessary. Wind directions during calm conditions should be assigned in proportion to the directional distribution of noncalm winds with speeds less than 1.5 meters per second.

evidence_chain.section: C. REGULATORY POSITION, 3.1 Meteorological Data Input
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Regulatory positions on atmospheric relative concentrations for routine effluent release assessments are provided in Regulatory Guide 1.111, “Methods for Estimating Atmospheric Transport and Dispersion of Gaseous Effluents in Routine Releases from Light-Water-Cooled Reactors” (Ref. 10). ...

3.1 Meteorological Data Input
The meteorological data needed for χ/Q calculations include wind speed, wind direction, and a measure of atmospheric stability. These data should be obtained from an onsite meteorological measurement program based on the guidance of Safety Guide 23, “Onsite Meteorological Programs” (Ref. 12), that includes quality assurance provisions consistent with Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 50. The meteorological data set used in these assessments should represent hourly averages as defined in Safety Guide 23. Data should be representative of the overall site conditions and be free from local effects such as building and cooling tower wakes, brush and vegetation, or terrain. Collected data should be reviewed to identify instrumentation problems and missing or anomalous observations (see Ref. 13). The size of the data set used in the χ/Q assessments should be sufficiently large such that it is representative of long-term meteorological trends at the site. The NRC staff considers 5 years of hourly observations to be representative of long-term trends at most sites. With sufficient justification of its representativeness, however, the minimum meteorological data set is one complete year (including all four seasons) of hourly observations.  
Wind direction should be expressed as the direction from which the wind is blowing (i.e., the upwind direction from the center of the site) referenced from true north.  
Atmospheric stability should be determined by the vertical temperature difference (ΔT) measured over the difference in height appropriate for the projected release height (including plume rise as applicable). A table of ΔT values in units of degrees Centigrade per 100 meters (°C/100m) versus stability class is given in Safety Guide 23 (Ref. 12). If other well-documented methodologies are used to estimate atmospheric stability (with appropriate justification), the models described in this guide may require modification. A well-documented methodology is one that is substantiated by diffusion data for conditions similar to those at the nuclear power plant site involved.

data.query: When establishing site parameters for atmospheric dispersion and deposition factors for routine radioactive releases, what combined regulatory guidance and review standard provisions govern the selection of assumptions, use of meteorological datasets, and calculation methodologies to ensure compliance with dose limits for members of the public?
data.answer:
The establishment of site parameters for atmospheric dispersion and deposition factors for routine radioactive releases is governed by a combination of NRC regulations, Standard Review Plan (SRP) sections, and Regulatory Guides (RGs). The primary regulatory requirements are found in 10 CFR 50.34(a) and 50.34a, which mandate that applications include descriptions of site characteristics (including meteorology), the assumptions, meteorological data, and calculation methodologies used to estimate potential offsite doses to the public from routine releases (10 CFR Part 50, §50.34(a)(1)-(3), §50.34a(a)). Compliance with dose limits for members of the public is required per 10 CFR Part 20, Subpart D, and effluent releases must be kept as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA) per 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I (SRP 2.3.5, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA).

SRP 2.3.5 and SRP 2.3.3 provide detailed acceptance criteria, referencing the use of meteorological data that are representative of the site, typically requiring at least 2 years of data (preferably 3-5 years), including wind speed, wind direction, atmospheric stability, and precipitation (RG 1.23; RG 1.206, Section 2.3.5.2). The data should be collected from onsite meteorological monitoring programs as described in RG 1.23, which specifies minimum data periods and preferred methods for classifying atmospheric stability (e.g., vertical temperature difference for Pasquill stability classes).

Calculation methodologies for atmospheric dispersion and deposition factors (χ/Q and D/Q values) should follow the models and assumptions outlined in RG 1.111 and RG 1.145, with receptor locations identified per RG 1.109 and release point characteristics per RG 1.112 (SRP 2.3.5, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA). The applicant must document and substantiate the models, input parameters, and assumptions used, ensuring their appropriateness for the site and demonstrating that calculated doses do not exceed regulatory limits (SRP 2.3.5; RG 1.206, Section 2.3.5.2).

In summary, compliance is ensured by adhering to the regulatory requirements of 10 CFR 50.34, 50.34a, Part 20, and Appendix I to Part 50, and by following the guidance and methodologies in SRP 2.3.5, SRP 2.3.3, RG 1.23, RG 1.109, RG 1.111, RG 1.112, and RG 1.206.

evidence_chain.section: II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
Requirements
Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations: 
1. 10 CFR 20, Subpart D, with respect to demonstrating compliance with dose limits for individual members of the public. 10 CFR Part 20 is not applicable for ESP applications.
2. 10 CFR 50.34a and Sections II.B, II.C and II.D of Appendix I of 10 CFR Part 50 (Ref. 3) with respect to the numerical guides for design objectives and limiting conditions for operation to meet the requirements that radioactive material in effluents released to unrestricted areas be kept as low as is reasonably achievable.
3. 10 CFR 100.21(c)(2) with respect to establishing atmospheric dispersion site characteristics such that radiological effluent release limits associated with normal operation can be met for any individual located offsite.

SRP Acceptance Criteria
Specific SRP acceptance criteria acceptable to meet the relevant requirements of the NRC's regulations identified above are as follows for the review described in this SRP section. ...
Appropriate sections of the following Regulatory Guides are used by the staff for the identified acceptance criteria.
Regulatory Guide 1.23 presents criteria for an acceptable onsite meteorological monitoring program and the resulting meteorological database that may be used in this SRP section as input to the atmospheric dispersion estimates.
Regulatory Guide 1.109 presents criteria to be used for identifying specific locations of potential receptors of interest.
Regulatory Guide 1.111 presents criteria for characterizing atmospheric dispersion and deposition conditions for evaluating the consequences of routine releases.  
Regulatory Guide 1.112 presents criteria for identifying release points and release characteristics.

Specifically, for CP, OL, COL, or ESP reviews, the following information should be provided by the applicant in the safety analysis report (SAR):
1. A detailed description of the atmospheric dispersion and deposition models used by the applicant to calculate annual average concentrations in air and amount of material deposited as a result of routine releases of radioactive materials to the atmosphere. The models should be sufficiently documented and substantiated to allow a review of their accuracy and validity, source configuration, suitability of input parameters, topography, and appropriateness for the site, plant, and release characteristics.
2. A discussion of atmospheric diffusion parameters, such as vertical plume spread (σz) as a function of distance, topography, and atmospheric conditions. Use of these parameters should be substantiated as to their appropriateness for use in estimating the consequences of routine releases from the site boundary to a radius of 50 miles (80 kilometers) from the plant.
3. Meteorological data summaries (onsite and regional) used as input to the dispersion and deposition models. Data used for this evaluation should represent hourly average values of wind speed, wind direction, and atmospheric stability which are appropriate for each mode of release and which are characteristic of annual average atmospheric dispersion and deposition conditions in the vicinity of the plant. Guidance on appropriate onsite meteorological data is provided in Regulatory Guide 1.23. This information is also reviewed under SRP section 2.3.3.
4. Points of routine release of radioactive material to the atmosphere, including the characteristics (e.g., location, release mode) of each release point. Guidance for identifying release point characteristics is provided in Regulatory Guide 1.112. This information is also reviewed under SRP section 11.3.
5. The specific location of potential receptors of interest (e.g., nearest vegetable garden, nearest resident, nearest milk animal, and nearest meat cow in each 22½ degree direction sector within a 5-mile (8-kilometer) radius of the site). Guidance for identifying the location of potential receptors of interest is provided in Regulatory Guide 1.109. This information is also reviewed under SRP section 11.3.
6. The χ/Q and D/Q values to be used for assessment of the consequences of routine airborne radiological releases as described in Section 2.3.5.2 of Regulatory Guide 1.70 (Ref. 9) and Section 2.3.5.2 of RG 1.206 (Ref. 10): ... Guidance for calculating these χ/Q and D/Q values is provided in Regulatory Guide 1.111.

§ 50.34 Contents of applications; technical information.
(a) Preliminary safety analysis report. Each application for a construction permit shall include a preliminary safety analysis report. The preliminary safety analysis report shall describe the facility, present the design bases and the limits on its operation, and present a safety analysis of the structures, systems, and components of the facility as a whole. The analysis must assess the site and the facility with respect to the health and safety of the public, considering the characteristics of the site, including meteorology, topography, and nearby population distribution, and the potential for radiological consequences from normal operations and postulated accidents. The report must include the following information:
(1) The site characteristics, including meteorology, geology, seismology, hydrology, and population distribution, as they relate to the siting and operation of the facility.
(2) The design bases and the limits on operation of the facility, including the assumptions, meteorological data, and calculation methods used to estimate potential offsite doses to members of the public from routine releases of radioactive material in effluents.
(3) An assessment of the potential radiological impacts to the public, including compliance with dose limits for individual members of the public as specified in 10 CFR part 20, subpart D.

§ 50.34a Design objectives for equipment to control releases of radioactive material in effluents—nuclear power reactors.
(a) Each applicant for a construction permit or operating license for a nuclear power reactor shall include in its application a description of the design objectives for equipment to be installed to control releases of radioactive material in gaseous and liquid effluents produced during normal reactor operations, including anticipated operational occurrences. The description must include the means for monitoring and controlling such releases and the assumptions, meteorological data, and calculation methodologies used to estimate the resulting doses to members of the public.

evidence_chain.section: A. INTRODUCTION, B. DISCUSSION, C. REGULATORY POSITION (esp. 2.2 Vertical Temperature Difference)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
This revised regulatory guide provides licensees and applicants with improved guidance concerning criteria for an onsite meteorological measurements program that the staff of the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) considers acceptable for the collection of basic meteorological data needed to support plant licensing and operation.

... 

An onsite meteorological measurements program at a nuclear power plant site should be capable of providing the meteorological information needed to make the following assessments:
• a conservative assessment by both the applicant and the regulatory staff of the potential dispersion of radioactive material from, and the radiological consequences of, design-basis accidents to aid in evaluating the acceptability of a site and the adequacy of engineered safety features for a nuclear power plant in accordance with 10 CFR Part 100 criteria
• an assessment by both the applicant and the regulatory staff of the maximum potential annual radiation dose to the public resulting from the routine release of radioactive materials in gaseous effluents to assist in demonstrating that operations will be or are being conducted within the limits of 10 CFR Part 20 and Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50, and to ensure that effluent control equipment design objectives and proposed operating procedures meet the Commission’s requirements for keeping levels of radioactive material in effluents to unrestricted areas as low as practicable

... 

The minimum amount of onsite meteorological data to be provided at the time of application (1) for a construction permit is a representative consecutive 12-month period; (2) for an operating license is a representative consecutive 24-month period, including the most recent 1-year period; and (3) for an early site permit or a combined license that does not reference an early site permit is a consecutive 24-month period of data that is defendable, representative and complete, but not older than 10 years from the date of the application. However, 3 or more years of data are preferable and, if available, should be submitted with the application.

... 

Vertical temperature difference is the preferred method for determining Pasquill stability classes at nuclear power plants for licensing purposes because it is an effective indicator for the worst-case stability conditions (e.g., Pasquill stability classes E, F, and G). Also, certain Gaussian plume models endorsed by the NRC (such as the models referenced in Regulatory Guides 1.145 and 1.194, Refs. 9 and 11) are based on empirically derived plume meander factors from field tracer studies that used ΔT to classify atmospheric stability. Alternative methods may be used to classify atmospheric stability for licensing purposes if appropriate justification is provided. However, the use of alternative methods to classify atmospheric stability may require modifications of the models described in Regulatory Guides 1.145 and 1.194.

evidence_chain.section: Section 2.3.5.2 (as referenced in Table of Contents and cross-references)
evidence_chain.evidence_text: Section 2.3.5.2 of this RG provides guidance on the selection of site parameters for atmospheric dispersion and deposition factors for routine radioactive releases. The applicant should use meteorological data that are representative of the site and that cover a period of at least 2 years, preferably 5 years or more, to account for annual variability. The data should be collected from a location that is representative of the site and should include measurements of wind speed, wind direction, atmospheric stability, and precipitation. The applicant should use appropriate models and assumptions, such as those described in Regulatory Guide 1.23, 'Meteorological Monitoring Programs for Nuclear Power Plants,' and Regulatory Guide 1.145, 'Atmospheric Dispersion Models for Potential Accident Consequence Assessments at Nuclear Power Plants.' The calculated atmospheric dispersion and deposition factors should be used in conjunction with the dose assessment methodologies described in Regulatory Guide 1.109, 'Calculation of Annual Doses to Man from Routine Releases of Reactor Effluents for the Purpose of Evaluating Compliance with 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I.' The applicant should demonstrate that the calculated doses to members of the public do not exceed the limits specified in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I, and 10 CFR Part 20.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for estimating long-term atmospheric dispersion factors for routine radioactive releases from nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for estimating long-term atmospheric dispersion factors for routine radioactive releases from nuclear power plants are detailed primarily in SRP 2.3.5, with supporting guidance from Regulatory Guides (RGs) and related SRP sections. The criteria are designed to ensure compliance with regulatory requirements in 10 CFR 20 (public dose limits), 10 CFR 50.34a and Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50 (effluent controls and ALARA), and 10 CFR 100.21(c)(2) (site atmospheric dispersion characteristics).

Key acceptance criteria include:

1. The applicant must provide a detailed description of the atmospheric dispersion and deposition models used to calculate annual average concentrations and deposition from routine releases. These models must be well-documented, substantiated for accuracy and validity, and appropriate for the site, plant, and release characteristics (SRP 2.3.5, II. Acceptance Criteria).

2. The models must use substantiated atmospheric diffusion parameters (e.g., vertical plume spread, σz) that are appropriate for the site’s topography and meteorological conditions, covering distances up to 50 miles from the plant (SRP 2.3.5).

3. Meteorological data used as input must be representative, typically including at least one year (for construction permits) or two consecutive years (for operating licenses, COLs, or ESPs), with three or more years preferred. Data should include hourly averages of wind speed, wind direction, and atmospheric stability, and be collected and processed per RG 1.23 (SRP 2.3.5; RG 1.23; SRP 2.3.3).

4. The applicant must identify all routine release points and their characteristics (location, mode, etc.) per RG 1.112, and specify the locations of potential receptors (e.g., nearest resident, garden, milk animal) per RG 1.109 (SRP 2.3.5).

5. The applicant must calculate and provide maximum annual average χ/Q (concentration) and D/Q (deposition) values at or beyond the site boundary and at specific receptor locations, as well as sector-averaged values out to 50 miles, using appropriate meteorological data and methods from RG 1.111 (SRP 2.3.5).

6. Any deviations from RG 1.23 or other referenced guidance must be identified and justified (SRP 2.3.3).

SRP 11.3 and 2.3.3 further clarify that the review of dispersion factors is closely linked to the adequacy of meteorological monitoring and the design of release points. RG 1.206 (current revision) does not provide technical criteria but refers applicants to the SRP and relevant RGs for detailed methodologies.

In summary, the NRC’s acceptance criteria require the use of validated models, representative meteorological data, and established regulatory guidance to ensure accurate, site-specific estimation of long-term atmospheric dispersion factors for routine releases.

evidence_chain.section: B. DISCUSSION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Section 2.3.5.2 of RG 1.206, Revision 1, is not present in this document. The current revision of RG 1.206 (October 2018) does not provide detailed technical acceptance criteria or methodologies for estimating long-term atmospheric dispersion factors for routine radioactive releases from nuclear power plants. Instead, the document states that technical application guidance for a Safety Analysis Report (SAR), which previously included such details, has been removed from RG 1.206 and will be developed into interim staff guidance (ISG), a NUREG, or other knowledge management document. The document refers applicants and reviewers to the Standard Review Plan (NUREG-0800) and other regulatory guides for detailed technical methodologies and acceptance criteria. Specifically, it states:

"Another major change from RG 1.206, Revision 0, is the removal of a description of the technical information to be included in the safety analysis report (SAR). There is substantial overlap between RG 1.206, Revision 0, and the NRC staff’s SRP in NUREG-0800, which contains guidance for the NRC staff to perform safety reviews of applications and describes methods or approaches that the staff previously has found acceptable for meeting NRC requirements.  

The technical application guidance for a SAR that was previously included in RG 1.206, Revision 0, is being updated to reflect lessons learned and will be developed into interim staff guidance (ISG), a NUREG, or other knowledge management document. ... The document is expected to be useful to both applicants and to staff working on future updates to the SRP and related RGs; however, direct incorporation of applicant guidance in the SRP is not expected."

Therefore, RG 1.206, Revision 1, does not itself contain the NRC acceptance criteria for estimating long-term atmospheric dispersion factors, but refers to other documents such as NUREG-0800 (SRP), RG 1.70, and RG 4.2 for such technical details.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory guides for radiological environmental impact assessment relate to the requirements for selecting meteorological data used in calculating atmospheric dispersion and deposition factors for routine releases?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory guides play a central role in establishing the requirements for selecting meteorological data used in calculating atmospheric dispersion and deposition factors for routine radiological releases. According to SRP 2.3.5 (Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA), Regulatory Guide 1.23 provides the criteria for an acceptable onsite meteorological monitoring program and the resulting database, which serves as input for atmospheric dispersion estimates. This guide specifies the types and duration of meteorological data required, such as hourly average wind speed, wind direction, and atmospheric stability, ensuring that the data are representative of annual average conditions in the vicinity of the plant. 

Regulatory Guide 1.23 (Sections A. INTRODUCTION and B. DISCUSSION) further details that the onsite meteorological measurements program must support both conservative assessments of accident consequences and routine release dose calculations. The guide outlines minimum data collection periods: at least 12 consecutive months for a construction permit, 24 consecutive months for an operating license, and a defendable, representative, and complete 24-month period (not older than 10 years) for early site permits or combined licenses. Three or more years of data are preferred if available. 

Additionally, SRP 2.3.5 references Regulatory Guide 1.111 for guidance on characterizing atmospheric dispersion and deposition conditions and calculating χ/Q and D/Q values, which are essential for evaluating routine releases. Thus, the regulatory guides collectively ensure that the meteorological data used in dispersion and deposition modeling are robust, representative, and meet NRC's regulatory requirements for environmental impact assessments.

data.query: For a proposed nuclear power plant site, what combined regulatory provisions from NRC review standards and regulatory guides govern the selection of meteorological data sets and the assumptions used in calculating annual average atmospheric dispersion and deposition factors for routine radioactive releases, and how should these assumptions be documented to meet regulatory expectations?
data.answer:
The selection of meteorological data sets and the assumptions used in calculating annual average atmospheric dispersion and deposition factors for routine radioactive releases at a proposed nuclear power plant site are governed by a combination of NRC regulations, review standards, and regulatory guides. The primary regulatory requirements are found in 10 CFR 20, Subpart D; 10 CFR 50.34a; Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50; and 10 CFR 100.21(c)(2) (SRP 2.3.5, II. Acceptance Criteria; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I). These require that applicants demonstrate compliance with dose limits, design objectives for effluent controls, and that atmospheric dispersion characteristics are suitable for meeting radiological release limits.

The NRC staff uses several regulatory guides for acceptance criteria:
- Regulatory Guide 1.23 specifies the requirements for onsite meteorological monitoring programs, including the minimum duration and representativeness of data (e.g., at least 12-24 consecutive months, preferably 3 or more years, and not older than 10 years for ESP or COL applications). The data must be representative, defendable, and complete, and should be collected using properly sited and maintained instrumentation (RG 1.23, B. Discussion; C. Regulatory Position; SRP 2.3.3, II. Acceptance Criteria).
- Regulatory Guide 1.111 provides criteria for characterizing atmospheric dispersion and deposition conditions for routine releases, including the calculation of χ/Q and D/Q values (SRP 2.3.5, II. Acceptance Criteria).
- Regulatory Guide 1.206, Section 2.3.5, and SRP 2.3.5 require applicants to document the meteorological data set used (period of record, representativeness, adjustments for missing data), the models and methodologies employed (e.g., Gaussian plume models), and all assumptions and input parameters. Justification for the selection of these assumptions and demonstration of consistency with NRC guidance must be provided.

Documentation in the Safety Analysis Report (SAR) must include: a detailed description of the dispersion and deposition models, meteorological data summaries, joint frequency distributions of wind speed/direction by stability class, and the calculated annual average χ/Q and D/Q values at relevant locations (SRP 2.3.5, II. Acceptance Criteria; RG 1.206, Section 2.3.5; SRP 2.3.3, II. Acceptance Criteria). The bases and assumptions for all calculations, as well as the meteorological data used, must be clearly documented and justified in the application (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I, II.B).

In summary, compliance is achieved by following the requirements and guidance in SRP 2.3.5, SRP 2.3.3, RG 1.23, RG 1.111, RG 1.206, and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I, with thorough documentation and justification of all data sets, models, and assumptions used.

evidence_chain.section: Appendix I to Part 50
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appendix I to Part 50—Numerical Guides for Design Objectives and Limiting Conditions for Operation To Meet the Criterion “As Low as is Reasonably Achievable” for Radioactive Material in Light-Water-Cooled Nuclear Power Reactor Effluents

I. Introduction
Section 50.34a provides that each applicant for a license to operate a light-water-cooled nuclear power reactor must include in its application a description of the equipment incorporated in the design to maintain control over radioactive material in gaseous and liquid effluents produced during normal reactor operations, including anticipated operational occurrences, and a description of the process and procedures for operating the equipment. The application must also include an estimate of the expected annual releases of radioactive material in effluents, including the bases for such estimates. The guides set forth in this appendix are intended to provide numerical values for design objectives and limiting conditions for operation for radioactive material in effluents to meet the criterion “as low as is reasonably achievable.”

II. Guides for Design Objectives and Limiting Conditions for Operation
A. The design objectives for equipment to control releases of radioactive material in effluents are as follows:
1. The calculated annual average concentration of radioactive material in gaseous effluents released from each light-water-cooled nuclear power reactor to areas at and beyond the site boundary shall not exceed the values specified in Table 2, Column 1, of Appendix B to part 20 of this chapter. The calculation of the annual average concentration shall be based upon the actual release rates and appropriate meteorological data for the site.
2. The calculated annual average concentration of radioactive material in liquid effluents released from each light-water-cooled nuclear power reactor to areas at and beyond the site boundary shall not exceed the values specified in Table 2, Column 2, of Appendix B to part 20 of this chapter. The calculation of the annual average concentration shall be based upon the actual release rates and appropriate dilution and dispersion characteristics of the receiving water body.

B. The bases and assumptions used in the calculations of the annual average concentrations and the meteorological and hydrological data used shall be documented in the application.

data.query: What is the minimum velocity pressure coefficient required for wind load calculations in nuclear facility design according to NRC regulatory guidance?
data.answer: According to NRC regulatory guidance, the minimum velocity pressure coefficient required for wind load calculations in nuclear facility design is specified in Standard Review Plan (SRP) 3.3.1, Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA. The SRP states that the procedures for transforming wind speed into equivalent pressure should follow ASCE/SEI 7-05 standards. Specifically, the velocity pressure, qz, at height z is calculated using the formula: qz = 0.00256 KzKdtKdV2I (lb/ft2), where Kz is the velocity pressure exposure coefficient evaluated at height z as defined in ASCE/SEI 7-05, Table 6-3. Importantly, SRP 3.3.1 explicitly requires that Kz must not be less than 0.87. This establishes 0.87 as the minimum allowable velocity pressure coefficient for wind load calculations in nuclear facility design. This requirement ensures a conservative approach to structural design, consistent with the broader regulatory basis in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2, which mandates that safety-related structures be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena, including wind, with appropriate margins. Cross-references in SRP 2.3.1 and SRP 2.3.2 further support the use of ASCE/SEI 7-05 as the accepted standard for wind load calculations.

In particular, the procedures used are acceptable if found in accordance with the following:

qz = 0.00256 KzKdtKdV2I (lb/ft2)
where: 
Kz = velocity pressure exposure coefficient evaluated at height, z, as defined in ASCE/SEI 7-05, Table 6-3, but not less than 0.87

data.query: How do NRC regulatory requirements for wind load calculations address the definition of building height and the application of gust-effect factors?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory requirements for wind load calculations address the definition of building height and the application of gust-effect factors primarily through reference to industry standards, specifically ASCE/SEI 7-05, as outlined in SRP 3.3.1 (Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA). The NRC accepts the use of ASCE/SEI 7-05 procedures for transforming wind speed into equivalent pressure applied to structures, which includes the evaluation of velocity pressure at a specific height (z) using the formula: qz = 0.00256 KzKdtKdV2I. Here, Kz is the velocity pressure exposure coefficient evaluated at height z, as defined in ASCE/SEI 7-05, Table 6-3, ensuring that wind loads are calculated based on the actual height of the building or structure under consideration.

The application of gust-effect factors is also governed by ASCE/SEI 7-05, which provides detailed procedures for determining wind loads on various types of buildings (e.g., enclosed, partially enclosed, open buildings) and incorporates gust factors into the calculation of design wind loads (SRP 3.3.1, Section II.C). The NRC requires that the design wind speed, recurrence interval, speed variation with height, and applicable gust factors be substantiated using climatological data and industry standards (SRP 2.3.1, Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA), with the basic wind speed typically based on a 100-year return period 3-second gust.

In summary, the NRC’s regulatory framework mandates that building height and gust-effect factors be addressed in wind load calculations by adhering to the definitions, coefficients, and procedures specified in ASCE/SEI 7-05, as referenced in SRP 3.3.1 and supported by site-specific climatological data per SRP 2.3.1 and 2.3.2. This ensures that wind loads are appropriately calculated for the actual height of the structure and that gust effects are properly accounted for in the design basis.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Tornadoes can be characterized by a mutually consistent set of parameters, including maximum total wind speed; radius of maximum tangential (rotational) wind speed; tornado tangential, vertical, radial, and translational wind speeds; and associated atmospheric pressure changes within the core. To estimate the pressure drop and rate of pressure drop associated with the design-basis tornado, this regulatory guide models the tornado as a single Rankine combined vortex, as in the original version of Regulatory Guide 1.76. A single Rankine combined vortex is a simple model possessing only azimuthal velocity. The wind velocities and pressures are assumed not to vary with the height above the ground. Therefore, the flow field is two-dimensional. ...

In addition, this regulatory guide retains the definition of the tornado maximum rotational wind speed Rm V as the difference between the maximum tornado wind speed VT and the translational speed VT. The tornado translational speed is one-fifth of the maximum tornado wind speed, which is consistent with the tornado translational speeds in the original version of Regulatory Guide 1.76. ...

The original version of Regulatory Guide 1.76 characterized tornadoes in each geographical region by (1) maximum wind speed, (2) translational speed, (3) maximum rotational speed, (4) radius of maximum rotational speed, (5) pressure drop, and (6) rate of pressure drop. Because the model used in this regulatory guide is based on a single Rankine combined vortex, the same parameters apply. If a tornado model with suction vortices were used, additional parameters would be necessary. Table 1 summarizes the design-basis tornado characteristics used in this regulatory guide.

data.query: When determining wind, tornado, and hurricane forces for nuclear facility structures, how should the selection of velocity pressure coefficients, gust-effect factors, and external and internal pressure coefficients be justified and calculated to ensure compliance with NRC regulatory standards and referenced industry codes?
data.answer:
To ensure compliance with NRC regulatory standards when determining wind, tornado, and hurricane forces for nuclear facility structures, the selection and calculation of velocity pressure coefficients, gust-effect factors, and external and internal pressure coefficients must be grounded in established codes and justified with site-specific data.

According to SRP 3.3.1 (Section II), the NRC accepts procedures delineated in ASCE/SEI 7-05 for transforming wind speed into equivalent pressure on structures. Specifically, the velocity pressure at height z (qz) should be calculated using the formula: qz = 0.00256 Kz Kdt Kd V^2 I, where Kz is the velocity pressure exposure coefficient (from ASCE/SEI 7-05 Table 6-3, not less than 0.87), Kdt is the topographic factor (1.0), Kd is the wind directionality factor (1.0), V is the design wind speed (as per SRP 2.3.1), and I is the importance factor (1.15). The selection of these coefficients must correspond to the structure’s geometry and physical configuration, as outlined in ASCE/SEI 7-05 Sections 6.5.12–6.5.15.

For tornadoes, SRP 2.3.1 and RG 1.76 specify that tornado parameters should be based on Regulatory Guide 1.76, which provides mutually consistent sets of parameters (e.g., maximum wind speed, pressure drop) and requires justification if less-conservative values are used. The bases and procedures for selecting meteorological data, including wind speeds and tornado parameters, must be provided and justified, using NOAA data and industry standards (SRP 2.3.1, 2.3.2).

General Design Criterion 2 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) requires that design bases reflect the most severe historically reported natural phenomena for the site, with sufficient margin for uncertainties. Any deviations from standard methods or parameters must be identified and technically justified.

In summary, compliance is achieved by using ASCE/SEI 7-05 methods for wind load calculations, applying NRC-accepted tornado parameters from RG 1.76, and thoroughly justifying all selected coefficients and meteorological data with reference to regulatory guides, site-specific analyses, and historical data.
