data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for evaluating wind loads on safety-related structures in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for evaluating wind loads on safety-related structures in nuclear power plants are primarily established in 10 CFR 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, which mandates that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety must be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including wind events such as tornadoes and hurricanes, without loss of safety function. The design bases must reflect the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2; [2]).

The Standard Review Plan (SRP) 3.3.1 further specifies that the wind used in design should be the most severe historically reported, with appropriate margin, and that the design wind speed, recurrence interval, speed variation with height, and gust factors should be determined per SRP Sections 2.3.1 and 2.3.2 ([1]). The basic 100-year return period 3-second gust wind speed is recommended as a standard, with corrections for local conditions (SRP 2.3.1, [3]).

Wind loads must be calculated using procedures from ASCE/SEI 7-05, specifically Sections 6.5.12 through 6.5.15, which address different building and structure types ([1]). The transformation of wind speed to equivalent pressure for structural design must follow these standards.

Meteorological data collection and site characterization are also required. SRP 2.3.2 and Regulatory Guide 1.23 specify that wind speed and direction should be measured at multiple heights (e.g., 10 m and 60 m) on an open-lattice tower, sited to avoid obstructions and provide representative data for the site ([4], [5]). Wind roses and joint frequency distributions by atmospheric stability are required for all measurement levels ([4]).

In summary, NRC requirements mandate that safety-related structures be designed for the most severe credible wind loads, using site-specific meteorological data and established engineering standards, with detailed documentation and justification for all parameters and methods used.

2. Meteorological Parameters
This section discusses the criteria for a basic meteorological monitoring system.
2.1 Wind Speed and Direction
Wind speed and direction should be measured on one open-lattice tower or mast measured at heights of approximately 10 meters (33 feet) and 60 meters (197 feet) above ground level. A measurement height other than 60 meters (197 feet) may be appropriate for those plants where the most probable atmospheric release height is other than 60 meters (197 feet). A third measurement height should be implemented at a representative level for stack releases that are 85 meters (279 feet) or higher.
...
3. Siting of Meteorological Instruments
To the extent practical, meteorological measurements should be made in locations that can provide data representative of the atmospheric conditions into which material will be released and transported. The tower or mast should be sited at approximately the same elevation as finished plant grade. Factors to be considered in selecting the appropriate measurement locations and installation of the instruments include the prevailing wind direction, topography, and location of manmade and vegetation obstructions.
Whenever possible, wind measurements should be made at locations and heights that avoid airflow modifications by obstructions such as large structures, trees, and nearby terrain. The sensors should be located over level, open terrain at a distance of at least 10 times the height of any nearby obstruction if the height of the obstruction exceeds one-half the height of the wind measurement.
Wind sensors should be located on top of the measurement tower or mast or extended outward on a boom to reduce airflow modification and turbulence induced by the supporting structure itself.
Because the tower structure can affect downwind measurements, wind sensors on the side of a tower should be mounted at a distance equal to at least twice the longest horizontal dimension of the tower (e.g., the side of a triangular tower). The sensors should be on the upwind side of the mounting object in areas with a dominant prevailing wind direction. In areas with two distinct prevailing wind directions (e.g., mountain valleys), the sensors should be mounted in a direction perpendicular to the primary two directions.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory standards address the selection of velocity pressure coefficients and gust-effect factors when determining wind loads for nuclear facility structures?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory standards address the selection of velocity pressure coefficients and gust-effect factors for determining wind loads on nuclear facility structures primarily by requiring adherence to established industry standards, specifically ASCE/SEI 7-05. According to SRP 3.3.1, Section II (Acceptance Criteria), the procedures for transforming wind speed into equivalent pressure must follow ASCE/SEI 7-05, which includes the use of specific coefficients and factors. The velocity pressure at a given height (qz) is calculated using the formula: qz = 0.00256 Kz Kdt Kd V^2 I, where Kz is the velocity pressure exposure coefficient (as defined in ASCE/SEI 7-05, Table 6-3, but not less than 0.87), Kdt is the topographic factor (set to 1.0), Kd is the wind directionality factor (set to 1.0), V is the design wind speed, and I is the importance factor (set to 1.15 for nuclear safety-related structures). 

SRP 3.3.1 further specifies that design wind loads should be determined in accordance with ASCE/SEI 7-05 Sections 6.5.12 through 6.5.15, which address wind loads on various types of structures. The selection of coefficients and factors, including gust-effect factors, must therefore be consistent with the methodologies and tables provided in ASCE/SEI 7-05. 

Additionally, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2, requires that structures important to safety be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena, including wind, with appropriate consideration of historical data and sufficient safety margin. SRP 2.3.1 and 2.3.2 reinforce the use of ASCE/SEI 7-05 and require that wind speed data and site-specific meteorological conditions be appropriately considered and documented. 

In summary, NRC regulatory standards mandate the use of ASCE/SEI 7-05 for the selection of velocity pressure coefficients and gust-effect factors, ensuring that wind loads are determined using industry-accepted methods and that safety-related structures are robust against extreme wind events.

evidence_chain.section: B. DISCUSSION (Tornado Characteristics, Design-Basis Tornado Characteristics)
evidence_chain.evidence_text: Tornadoes can be characterized by a mutually consistent set of parameters, including maximum total wind speed; radius of maximum tangential (rotational) wind speed; tornado tangential, vertical, radial, and translational wind speeds; and associated atmospheric pressure changes within the core. To estimate the pressure drop and rate of pressure drop associated with the design-basis tornado, this regulatory guide models the tornado as a single Rankine combined vortex, as in the original version of Regulatory Guide 1.76. A single Rankine combined vortex is a simple model possessing only azimuthal velocity. The wind velocities and pressures are assumed not to vary with the height above the ground. Therefore, the flow field is two-dimensional. The flow field of a Rankine combined vortex is equivalent to that of a solid rotating body within the core of radius Rm. data.query: How are external and internal pressure coefficients for building walls determined according to NRC guidance, and what is the relationship between these coefficients and referenced industry standards for wind load calculations?
data.answer:
According to NRC guidance, the determination of external and internal pressure coefficients for building walls is based on procedures outlined in the American Society of Civil Engineers/Structural Engineering Institute (ASCE/SEI) 7-05, specifically in Sections 6.5.12 through 6.5.15. As stated in SRP 3.3.1 (Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA), these sections provide the acceptable methods for calculating design wind loads on various types of buildings and structures, including enclosed, partially enclosed, and open buildings, as well as solid freestanding walls and signs. The NRC staff has reviewed and found the use of ASCE/SEI 7-05 methods acceptable for transforming wind speed into equivalent pressure and for selecting pressure coefficients that correspond to the geometry and physical configuration of the structure. These coefficients are essential for determining the wind-induced loadings on structures, ensuring that the design accounts for the effects of wind as a natural phenomenon.

The relationship between these coefficients and referenced industry standards is direct: NRC guidance explicitly endorses the use of ASCE/SEI 7-05 as the industry standard for wind load calculations, including the selection of pressure coefficients. This approach aligns with the regulatory requirement in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2, which mandates that structures important to safety must be designed to withstand natural phenomena, such as wind, using appropriate and proven engineering methods. Thus, the NRC relies on ASCE/SEI 7-05 to provide the technical basis for determining wind pressures and associated coefficients, ensuring safety and regulatory compliance.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for analyzing the effects of flood and groundwater levels on the structural integrity of safety-related nuclear facility structures?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for analyzing the effects of flood and groundwater levels on the structural integrity of safety-related nuclear facility structures are primarily based on compliance with General Design Criterion (GDC) 2 of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, which requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site, including floods and groundwater effects, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; SRP 3.4.2, Section II; SRP 2.4.3, Section II; SRP 2.4.12, Section II).

Specifically, the acceptance criteria require:
1. The design must consider the highest flood and groundwater levels historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with appropriate margin for data limitations (SRP 3.4.2, II; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2).
2. Hydrostatic and hydrodynamic effects associated with these levels must be evaluated. If the highest flood level is below plant grade, only hydrostatic effects are typically considered, unless drainage or pumping systems relieve the hydrostatic head. Otherwise, hydrostatic pressure must be treated as a structural load on basement walls and foundation slabs. Buoyancy forces must be calculated based on the highest flood or groundwater level, excluding wave action, but wave action must be included for lateral and overturning movement analyses (SRP 3.4.2, II).
3. If the flood level is above plant grade, dynamic loads from wave action must be considered, using procedures equivalent to those in the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' Shore Protection Manual or Coastal Engineering Manual (SRP 3.4.2, II).
4. The effects of groundwater on plant foundations and other safety-related SSCs must be described in sufficient detail to determine any adverse impacts (SRP 2.4.12, II).
5. The applicant must document and justify the design bases for affected facilities if a potential hazard to SSCs important to safety exists, using conservative assumptions for hydrometeorological and hydraulic characteristics (SRP 2.4.3, II).

Alternative methods or analytical techniques may be proposed but must be justified and reviewed on a case-by-case basis (SRP 3.4.2, II).

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for protecting safety-related structures, systems, and components from groundwater intrusion at nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for protecting safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) from groundwater intrusion at nuclear power plants are primarily established in General Design Criterion (GDC) 2 of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A. GDC 2 requires that SSCs important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including floods and groundwater, without loss of capability to perform their safety functions. The design bases must consider the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; SRP 3.4.2 II).

Specifically, the design must account for the highest flood and groundwater levels, including associated static and dynamic effects. If hydrostatic pressure from groundwater is not relieved by drainage or pumping systems, it must be considered as a structural load on basement walls and foundation slabs. The total buoyancy force for uplifting or floating of structures should be based on the highest flood or groundwater level (SRP 3.4.2 II).

Applicants must provide a complete description of the effects of groundwater on plant foundations and other safety-related SSCs, sufficient to determine any adverse impacts (SRP 2.4.12 II.2). If dewatering systems are used to maintain groundwater conditions within design bases, their reliability must be described, including whether they are safety-related and required during plant operation (SRP 2.4.12 II.4).

Additionally, site evaluations must identify and assess hydrological features and flooding hazards, including site drainage and erosion effects, to ensure SSCs are protected (SRP 2.4.3 II; SRP 2.4.12 II). Applicants must document and justify the design bases for affected facilities if potential hazards exist.

In summary, NRC regulations require robust design and documentation to ensure safety-related SSCs are protected from groundwater intrusion, with specific attention to historical site data, structural loads, and the reliability of any dewatering systems.

data.query: How do general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena relate to regulatory guidance on preventing groundwater intrusion into safety-related structures at nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for protection against natural phenomena, specifically GDC 2 as outlined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, require that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety at nuclear power plants be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena such as earthquakes, floods, and high groundwater levels without loss of safety function (10CFR, Appendix A, GDC 2). This requirement is directly related to regulatory guidance on preventing groundwater intrusion into safety-related structures.

Standard Review Plan (SRP) 3.4.2 clarifies that compliance with GDC 2 includes designing structures to withstand the highest historically reported flood and groundwater levels, accounting for both hydrostatic and hydrodynamic effects. If groundwater levels could impose hydrostatic loads on basement walls or foundation slabs, these must be considered unless mitigated by drainage or pumping systems (SRP 3.4.2, Section II). The design must also consider buoyancy and potential for uplifting or floating of structures due to groundwater.

SRP 2.4.12 further elaborates that the effects of groundwater on plant foundations and other safety-related SSCs must be fully described and evaluated to ensure there are no adverse impacts. This includes providing detailed information on site dewatering systems and their reliability to maintain groundwater conditions within the design bases of SSCs important to safety. The rationale is that groundwater levels can significantly affect the seismic and structural design bases of safety-related foundations, often necessitating dewatering systems to minimize dynamic loads (SRP 2.4.12, Section II).

In summary, the general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena establish the regulatory basis for requiring nuclear power plant designs to address groundwater intrusion. Regulatory guidance in the SRPs specifies that applicants must demonstrate, through conservative design and reliable dewatering systems, that safety-related structures will not lose their safety function due to groundwater effects, thereby fulfilling the intent of GDC 2.

data.query: What regulatory requirements govern the protection of Seismic Category I buried structures, such as tunnels, pipes, and duct banks, from the effects of probable maximum flood and groundwater?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements governing the protection of Seismic Category I buried structures—such as tunnels, pipes, and duct banks—from the effects of probable maximum flood (PMF) and groundwater are primarily established in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, and are further detailed in NRC Standard Review Plan (SRP) sections.

GDC 2 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including floods and groundwater, without loss of safety function. The design bases must reflect the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in the data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; SRP 3.4.2, Section II; SRP 2.4.3, Section II; SRP 2.4.12, Section II).

SRP 3.4.2 specifies that the design of Seismic Category I buried structures must consider the highest flood and groundwater levels, including associated static and dynamic effects. Hydrostatic pressure from these levels must be treated as a structural load unless relieved by drainage or pumping systems. Buoyancy forces and the potential for uplifting or floating must be evaluated based on the highest flood or groundwater levels, and wave action must be included for lateral and overturning stability (SRP 3.4.2, Section II).

SRP 2.4.3 and SRP 2.4.12 further require that applicants identify and evaluate hydrological site features, including PMF and groundwater effects, and document the design bases for affected facilities. The effects of erosion, sedimentation, and hydrodynamic forces during flooding must be assessed for their impact on SSCs important to safety. The applicant must provide a complete description of groundwater effects on plant foundations and other safety-related SSCs to demonstrate that the design appropriately accounts for these hazards (SRP 2.4.3, Section II; SRP 2.4.12, Section II).

In summary, compliance with GDC 2 and the associated SRP sections requires robust design and documentation to ensure Seismic Category I buried structures are protected from the most severe credible flood and groundwater conditions at the site.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory requirements for protection against flooding address the need to evaluate dynamic loads, such as wave action, on seismic Category I structures when the flood level may exceed the finished grade elevation?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory requirements for protection against flooding explicitly address the need to evaluate dynamic loads, such as wave action, on seismic Category I structures when the flood level may exceed the finished grade elevation. According to SRP 3.4.2 (Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA), for plants where the flood level is higher than the proposed grade around the plant structures, the dynamic phenomena associated with flooding—including currents, flood waves, and their hydrodynamic effects—must be analyzed. The procedures used to transform both static and dynamic effects of the highest flood and groundwater levels into effective loads on seismic Category I structures are reviewed for compliance with 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2. Specifically, wave action must be included in calculations for lateral and overturning movements of structures, and dynamic loads from wave action should be considered when the flood level is above grade. Acceptable procedures for determining such dynamic loads are those in accordance with or equivalent to the U.S. Army Coastal Engineering Research Center's 'Shore Protection Manual' or the USACE 'Coastal Engineering Manual' (SRP 3.4.2).

GDC 2 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) requires that safety-related structures, systems, and components be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including floods, without loss of safety function. The design bases must reflect the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site, appropriate combinations of normal and accident conditions with natural phenomena, and the importance of the safety functions performed.

SRP 2.4.3 and SRP 2.4.12 further reinforce that the design bases for flooding must conservatively estimate dynamic effects, including wave action and hydrodynamic loads, and document their impact on safety-related structures. These requirements ensure that all relevant dynamic flood loads are considered in the design and safety analysis of seismic Category I structures when flood levels may exceed the finished grade.

data.query: What is the relationship between general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena and the analysis procedures for determining whether wave action loads must be considered for safety-related structures during probable maximum flood events?
data.answer:
The relationship between the general design criteria (GDC) for protection against natural phenomena and the analysis procedures for determining whether wave action loads must be considered for safety-related structures during probable maximum flood (PMF) events is established through regulatory requirements and detailed guidance in NRC documents. 

GDC 2, as stated in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including floods and associated effects such as wave action, without loss of safety function. The design bases must reflect the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site, with sufficient margin for uncertainties (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2).

SRP 3.4.2 clarifies that compliance with GDC 2 requires consideration of both hydrostatic and dynamic loads from flooding. Specifically, if the flood level is above the plant grade, dynamic loads from wave action must be included in the structural analysis. Acceptable procedures for determining these loads are those consistent with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' Shore Protection Manual or Coastal Engineering Manual (SRP 3.4.2, Section II).

SRP 2.4.3 and SRP 2.4.12 further reinforce that the design bases for flooding, including PMF events, must conservatively estimate water surface elevations and dynamic effects (such as wind-waves) on SSCs important to safety. The applicant must document and justify the design bases, including the consideration of wave action if it poses a hazard (SRP 2.4.3, Section II; SRP 2.4.12, Section II).

In summary, the general design criteria mandate that safety-related structures be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena, and the analysis procedures must include wave action loads during PMF events when flood levels are above plant grade, using accepted engineering methods. This ensures compliance with NRC regulations and the protection of safety functions.

data.query: How should analysis procedures account for both static and dynamic effects of maximum flood and groundwater levels when determining loads on safety-related structures in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
Analysis procedures for determining loads on safety-related structures in nuclear power plants must comprehensively account for both static and dynamic effects of maximum flood and groundwater levels, as required by NRC regulations and guidance. According to SRP 3.4.2 (Section II), the procedures must transform the static (e.g., hydrostatic pressure, buoyancy) and dynamic (e.g., wave action, momentum fluxes) effects of the highest historically reported flood and groundwater levels into effective loads on seismic Category I structures. The design must use the most severe historical data, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in data accuracy and completeness, in accordance with GDC 2 of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A.

Static effects include hydrostatic pressures on basement walls and foundation slabs, and buoyancy forces, which must be considered unless mitigated by drainage or pumping systems. Dynamic effects, such as wave action, must be included in calculations for lateral and overturning movements, especially when flood levels exceed plant grade. Acceptable procedures for dynamic load determination are those consistent with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' Shore Protection Manual and Coastal Engineering Manual (SRP 3.4.2).

SRP 2.4.3 and 2.4.12 further require that the design bases for flooding and groundwater-induced loadings be based on conservative hydrometeorologic assumptions and hydraulic characteristics, including velocities and momentum fluxes, to capture dynamic effects. The design must also consider potential future changes in groundwater conditions due to natural or man-made events. Independent calculations and justification of design bases are necessary to ensure adequacy and compliance with regulatory requirements.

In summary, analysis procedures must rigorously evaluate both static and dynamic effects of maximum flood and groundwater levels, using conservative, historically based data and accepted engineering methods, to ensure the safety and integrity of safety-related structures, as mandated by GDC 2 and detailed in SRP 3.4.2, 2.4.3, and 2.4.12.

data.query: How are hydrostatic pressures from design flood levels incorporated into the structural design requirements for seismic Category I structures according to NRC regulatory guidance?
data.answer:
Hydrostatic pressures from design flood levels are incorporated into the structural design requirements for seismic Category I structures in accordance with NRC regulatory guidance by ensuring that these structures are designed to withstand the most severe flood and groundwater levels historically reported for the site, with appropriate safety margins. Specifically, SRP 3.4.2 (Section II) states that unless hydrostatic head from the highest flood and groundwater levels is relieved by drainage or pumping systems, hydrostatic pressure must be considered as a structural load on basement walls and foundation slabs. The total buoyancy force, excluding wave action, is based on the highest flood or groundwater level, and wave action is included for lateral and overturning movement calculations. 

This approach is grounded in General Design Criterion 2 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A), which requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety be designed to withstand natural phenomena, including floods, and that the effects of hydrostatic and hydrodynamic loads from the design basis flood are taken into account. SRP 2.4.3 further clarifies that the design bases for flooding must be based on conservative hydrometeorologic assumptions and must document and justify the design bases for affected facilities. SRP 2.4.12 requires a complete description and review of groundwater-induced loadings on subsurface portions of SSCs important to safety, including independent calculations to ensure adequacy and capability to address potential future changes.

Regulatory Guide 1.29 confirms that seismic Category I SSCs, including their foundations and supports, must be designed to remain functional under these conditions, and quality assurance requirements apply to all safety-related activities. In summary, hydrostatic pressures from design flood levels are explicitly considered as structural loads in the design of seismic Category I structures, consistent with NRC regulations and guidance (SRP 3.4.2, 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A GDC 2, SRP 2.4.3, SRP 2.4.12, RG 1.29).

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for protecting safety-related structures, systems, and components against externally generated missiles at nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for protecting safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) against externally generated missiles at nuclear power plants are primarily established in General Design Criteria (GDC) 2 and 4 of Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, as referenced in SRP 3.5.2. GDC 2 requires that SSCs important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including tornadoes and hurricanes, without loss of their safety functions. This includes appropriate consideration of the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site, with sufficient safety margins, and the potential for missiles generated by such events (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2).

GDC 4 further requires that SSCs important to safety be protected against the effects of missiles resulting from events and conditions outside the nuclear power unit (SRP 3.5.2, Section II). To meet these requirements, the NRC's Standard Review Plan (SRP) 3.5.2 specifies that applicants must:

1. Prevent tornado-generated missiles from compromising the integrity of spent fuel pools (per RG 1.13).
2. Ensure the ultimate heat sink and its conduits can withstand external missiles from natural phenomena (per RG 1.27).
3. Protect essential systems from turbine missiles through orientation or barriers (per RG 1.115).
4. Protect safety-related SSCs from tornado missiles using missile barriers, protected structures, or underground placement (per RG 1.117).
5. Identify all SSCs requiring missile protection, including nonsafety-related SSCs whose failure could prevent safety-related SSCs from performing their functions.

In summary, the design must ensure that all safety-related SSCs, and any nonsafety-related SSCs whose failure could impact safety functions, are protected against externally generated missiles, particularly those from natural phenomena and turbine failures, using a combination of physical barriers, structural design, and appropriate siting, as detailed in the referenced regulatory guides and criteria (SRP 3.5.2, Section II; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2 and 4).

II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
Requirements
Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations:  
1. General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, “Design bases for protection against natural phenomena,” of  Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, requires structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety shall be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena such as tornadoes and hurricanes without loss of capability to perform their safety functions.
2. GDC 4, “ Environmental and dynamic effects design bases,” of Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, requires that SSCs important to safety be appropriately protected against the effects of missiles that may result from events and conditions outside the nuclear power unit. 
...
Acceptance is based on the design meeting the guidelines of Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.13 as to the capability of spent fuel pool systems and structures to withstand the effects of externally-generated missiles and to prevent missiles from contacting stored fuel assemblies; RG 1.27 as to the capability of the ultimate heat sink and connecting conduits to withstand the effects of externally-generated missiles; RG 1.115 as to the protection of important safety-related SSCs from the effects of turbine missiles; and RG 1.117 as to the protection of important safety-related SSCs from the effects of tornado missiles.
...
The applicant has met the requirements of GDCs 2 and 4 for protection of important safety-related SSCs against the effects of externally-generated missiles by:
1. Meeting RG 1.13, Position C.2, "Spent Fuel Storage Facility Design Basis," by preventing missiles generated by tornado winds from causing significant loss of watertight integrity of the fuel storage pool and from contacting fuel within the pool.;
2. Meeting RG 1.27, Positions C.2 and C.3, "Ultimate Heat Sink for Nuclear Power Plants," so that the ultimate heat sink is capable of withstanding the effects of external missiles generated by natural phenomena;
3. Meeting RG 1.115, Position C.2, "Protection Against Low Trajectory Turbine Missiles," so that essential systems are protected from low-trajectory turbine missiles by either proper turbine orientation or missile barriers; 
4. Meeting regulatory Positions C.1, C.2, and C.3 and the Appendix to RG 1.117, "Tornado Design Classification," so that important safety-related SSCs are protected from the effects of missiles generated by the design basis tornado by missile barriers for individual components, by location of independent redundant systems or components in missile-protected structures, or by underground locations at depth sufficient to protect against missiles; and 
5. Identifying all SSCs requiring protection against the effects of externally-generated missiles, including those nonsafety-related SSCs, the failure of which as a result of missiles, may prevent safety-related SSCs from performing their safety-related functions.

evidence_chain.section: Appendix A to Part 50 – General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants, Criterion 2
evidence_chain.evidence_text: Criterion 2—Design bases for protection against natural phenomena. Structures, systems, and components important to safety shall be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena such as earthquakes, tornadoes, hurricanes, floods, tsunami, and seiches without loss of capability to perform their safety functions. The design bases for these structures, systems, and components shall reflect: (1) Appropriate consideration of the most severe of the natural phenomena that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated, (2) appropriate combinations of the effects of normal and accident conditions with the effects of the natural phenomena, and (3) the importance of the safety functions to be performed. Similar criteria shall be applied to structures, systems, and components of the facility which, if they were to fail, could result in loss of capability of safety-related structures, systems, and components to perform their safety functions. The design shall also reflect appropriate consideration of the potential for the safety-related structures, systems, and components to be subject to the effects of missiles (such as those that may result from tornadoes and hurricanes) generated by natural phenomena.

data.query: How do the general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena and external events relate to the requirements for missile protection of risk-significant safety systems at nuclear facilities?
data.answer:
The general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena and external events are directly related to the requirements for missile protection of risk-significant safety systems at nuclear facilities. Specifically, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2 of Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50 requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena such as tornadoes and hurricanes without losing their safety functions (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2). This includes considering the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site, with appropriate safety margins (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2).

GDC 4 further requires that SSCs important to safety be protected against dynamic effects, including those from missiles generated by external events (SRP 3.5.2, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA). This means that the design must account for missiles that could result from natural phenomena (e.g., tornado-generated debris) or other external conditions, ensuring that these SSCs can continue to perform their safety functions, such as maintaining the integrity of the reactor coolant pressure boundary and preventing significant uncontrolled releases of radioactivity (SRP 3.5.2, Technical Rationale).

Regulatory guidance, such as RG 1.138, reinforces that these general design criteria are foundational to the licensing and design of nuclear power plants, ensuring that both natural phenomena and missile hazards are systematically addressed in the protection of risk-significant safety systems (RG 1.138, A. INTRODUCTION).

In summary, the general design criteria establish the regulatory basis for requiring that risk-significant safety systems at nuclear facilities are robustly protected against both the direct effects of natural phenomena and the indirect effects, such as missiles generated by these events.

Applicable Regulations

• Appendix A to Title 10, Part 50, of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR Part 50), “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities” (Ref. 1) governs the licensing of nuclear power plants and provides general design criteria (GDC).

• 10 CFR Part 52 “Licenses, Certifications, and Approvals for Nuclear Power Plants,” (Ref. 2) governs the issuance of early site permits, standard design certifications, combined licenses, standard design approvals, and manufacturing licenses for nuclear power facilities licensed under Section 103 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, as amended (68 Stat.  919), and Title II of the Energy Reorganization Act of 1974 (88 Stat.  1242).    

• 10 CFR Part 100, “Reactor Site Criteria” (Ref. 3), requires the NRC to consider the physical characteristics of a site including seismology and geology in determining the site’s acceptability for a nuclear power reactor.  In particular, 10 CFR 100.20(c), 10 CFR 100.21(d), and 10 CFR 100.23, establish requirements for conducting site investigations for nuclear power plants license applications submitted after January 10, 1997.  The evaluation of a site for seismic response analyses and engineering design requires information about the static and dynamic engineering properties of the site’s soil and rock materials.

data.query: How do general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena relate to the requirements for evaluating site-specific external missile hazards at nuclear facilities?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for protection against natural phenomena, as outlined in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, directly inform the requirements for evaluating site-specific external missile hazards at nuclear facilities. Specifically, GDC 2 mandates that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety must be designed to withstand natural phenomena such as tornadoes and hurricanes without loss of their safety functions (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2). This includes considering the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site, with appropriate safety margins (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2).

GDC 4 further requires that SSCs important to safety be protected against dynamic effects, including missiles generated by events and conditions outside the nuclear unit (SRP 3.5.2, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA). This means that the assessment of external missile hazards—such as those resulting from tornadoes or hurricanes—must be integrated into the design bases for SSCs, ensuring that these components can continue to perform their safety functions even if impacted by such missiles.

The Standard Review Plan (SRP 3.5.2) clarifies that both GDC 2 and GDC 4 are directly applicable to the evaluation of external missile hazards, as these criteria establish the need for SSCs to withstand both the direct effects of natural phenomena and the secondary effects, such as missiles generated by those phenomena. Regulatory Guide 1.138 further emphasizes that site investigations and analyses must be tailored to the specific conditions of each site, with careful consideration of the physical characteristics and potential hazards, including those posed by external missiles (RG 1.138, A. INTRODUCTION and B. DISCUSSION).

In summary, the general design criteria require that site-specific evaluations of external missile hazards be conducted as part of the overall assessment of natural phenomena, ensuring that nuclear facility SSCs are robustly designed to maintain safety under both direct and indirect effects of such events.

evidence_chain.section: A. INTRODUCTION and B. DISCUSSION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Applicable Regulations

• Appendix A to Title 10, Part 50, of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR Part 50), “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities” (Ref. 1) governs the licensing of nuclear power plants and provides general design criteria (GDC).

• 10 CFR Part 52 “Licenses, Certifications, and Approvals for Nuclear Power Plants,” (Ref. 2) governs the issuance of early site permits, standard design certifications, combined licenses, standard design approvals, and manufacturing licenses for nuclear power facilities licensed under Section 103 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, as amended (68 Stat.  919), and Title II of the Energy Reorganization Act of 1974 (88 Stat.  1242).    

• 10 CFR Part 100, “Reactor Site Criteria” (Ref. 3), requires the NRC to consider the physical characteristics of a site including seismology and geology in determining the site’s acceptability for a nuclear power reactor.  In particular, 10 CFR 100.20(c), 10 CFR 100.21(d), and 10 CFR 100.23, establish requirements for conducting site investigations for nuclear power plants license applications submitted after January 10, 1997.  The evaluation of a site for seismic response analyses and engineering design requires information about the static and dynamic engineering properties of the site’s soil and rock materials.

... 

Background

In the course of site investigations and analyses for nuclear power plant facilities, the purpose of a laboratory-testing program is to identify and classify soils and rocks, and to evaluate their physical and engineering properties.  The NRC staff reviews the information obtained from site investigations and laboratory tests and considers the safety aspects of applying the data to the design and construction of nuclear plants.  Consideration of public safety imposes particularly stringent requirements on the design and construction of nuclear power plant facilities.  Therefore, it is essential that investigators carefully plan and carry out all phases of a site investigation program to ensure that the associated field and laboratory testing realistically determine the properties of the soil and rock.   The site and laboratory investigations will depend on actual site conditions, the nature of problems encountered or suspected at the site, site parameters defined by the design of the nuclear power plant to be built on the site, and design requirements for foundations and earthworks.  Therefore, the site investigation program should be flexible and tailored to each site and plant design as the site and laboratory investigations proceed.  Experienced engineers and geologists who have demonstrated competence in the field of soil and rock mechanics testing and familiarity with the site should direct the site investigation program.  Specific testing requirements and details of testing procedures will depend on the nature of the soils and rocks encountered.  Normally, the investigation should follow testing procedures that are generally known and accepted because they are easy to reproduce and their effects on test results are well understood.  Depending on the nature of the soil and rock material, it may be more appropriate and desirable to modify existing standard procedures;  however, it is important to describe such test procedures fully so that other investigators can reproduce the test and verify the results.

data.query: For a new nuclear power plant design, what combined regulatory requirements and guidance must be considered to ensure that safety-related structures, systems, and components are protected from site-specific external missiles that could be more energetic than those defined in the standard design basis?
data.answer:
For a new nuclear power plant design, the combined regulatory requirements and guidance to ensure that safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) are protected from site-specific external missiles—including those more energetic than those defined in the standard design basis—are grounded in both NRC regulations and associated guidance documents. 

According to SRP 3.5.2 Section II (Acceptance Criteria), the primary regulatory requirements are:
1. General Design Criterion (GDC) 2 of Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, which mandates that SSCs important to safety must be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena (such as tornadoes and hurricanes) without loss of safety function. The design bases must consider the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site, with appropriate safety margins (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2).
2. GDC 4 of Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, which requires that SSCs important to safety be appropriately protected against the effects of missiles resulting from external events and conditions.
3. 10 CFR 52.47(b)(1) and 10 CFR 52.80(a), which require that design certification (DC) and combined license (COL) applications include inspections, tests, analyses, and acceptance criteria (ITAAC) to provide reasonable assurance that the plant is constructed and will operate in accordance with NRC regulations.

In addition to these regulations, the design must meet the guidelines of several Regulatory Guides (RGs):
- RG 1.13 (protection of spent fuel pool systems and structures from externally-generated missiles),
- RG 1.27 (protection of the ultimate heat sink and connecting conduits),
- RG 1.115 (protection from turbine missiles), and
- RG 1.117 (protection from tornado missiles).

Therefore, the design must reflect site-specific assessments of external missile hazards, including those more energetic than standard design basis missiles, and demonstrate through ITAAC and adherence to relevant RGs that all safety-related SSCs are adequately protected.

data.query: What are the regulatory acceptance criteria for the use of seismic time history analyses in the design of safety-related structures, systems, and components in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The regulatory acceptance criteria for the use of seismic time history analyses in the design of safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) in nuclear power plants are established to ensure that SSCs can withstand seismic events without loss of safety function. The primary regulatory basis is 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, which requires that SSCs important to safety be designed to withstand the most severe historically reported earthquakes for the site, with appropriate margins (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; SRP 3.7.1, II; SRP 3.7.2, II).

Appendix S to 10 CFR Part 50 further requires that for Safe Shutdown Earthquake (SSE) ground motions, SSCs must remain functional and within applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits, considering soil-structure interaction (SSI) and the expected duration of ground motion (SRP 3.7.1, II; SRP 3.7.2, II).

Specific acceptance criteria for seismic time history analyses include:
- The design ground motion time histories (for both SSE and OBE) must consist of three mutually orthogonal directions (two horizontal, one vertical), and each must be statistically independent (SRP 3.7.1, II.B).
- The response spectra generated from these time histories must generally envelop the design response spectra, and the procedures for generating and comparing these spectra are subject to review (SRP 3.7.1, II.B).
- Either a single set or multiple sets of time histories may be used, with justification and demonstration that the spectra envelop the design spectra and have sufficient power over the frequency range of interest (SRP 3.7.1, II.B).
- Dynamic analyses must consider torsional, rocking, and translational responses, use adequate mass modeling, and include high-frequency mode responses (SRP 3.7.2, II.1.A).
- Appropriate damping values, as specified in RG 1.61, must be used for elastic dynamic analyses, with values depending on material type and earthquake level (SSE or OBE). For ISRS generation, damping values must be compatible with the structural response level (RG 1.61, Section C).

In summary, seismic time history analyses are acceptable if they use statistically independent, three-component ground motions whose response spectra envelop the design spectra, apply appropriate damping values, and comprehensively address dynamic response characteristics, including SSI and high-frequency effects, in accordance with the cited regulations and guidance.

evidence_chain.section: II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

Requirements

Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations:

1. 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, “Design Bases for Protection against Natural Phenomena.” - The design basis shall reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe earthquakes that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which historical data have been accumulated.   

2. 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S is applicable to applications for a DC or COL pursuant to 10 CFR Part 52 or a CP or OL pursuant to 10 CFR Part 50 on or after January 10, 1997.  Appendix S requires that for SSE ground motions, SSCs will remain functional and within applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits.  The required safety functions of SSCs must be assured during and after the vibratory ground motion through design, testing, or qualification methods.  The evaluation must take into account SSI effects and the expected duration of the vibratory motion.  If the OBE is set at one-third or less of the SSE, an explicit analysis or design is not required.  If the OBE is set at a value greater than one-third of the SSE, an analysis and design must be performed to demonstrate that the applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits are satisfied.  Appendix S also requires that the horizontal component of the SSE ground motion in the free-field at the foundation level of the structures must be an appropriate response spectrum with a PGA of at least 0.1g.   

SRP Acceptance Criteria

Specific SRP acceptance criteria acceptable to meet the relevant requirements of the Commission’s regulations identified above are as follows for the review described in this SRP section. ...

B. Design Time Histories.  The SSE and OBE design ground motion time histories can be either real time histories or artificial time histories.  To be acceptable, the design ground motion time histories should consist of three mutually orthogonal directions - two horizontal and one vertical.  For both horizontal and vertical input motions, either a single time history or multiple time histories can be used.  When time histories are used, each of the three ground motion time histories should be shown to be statistically independent from the others.  Each of the response spectra generated from the time histories should generally envelop the design response spectra.  The procedures used to generate response spectra from the artificial time histories and the comparisons of these response spectra with the design response spectra are reviewed.  In addition to the comparison of the response spectra derived from the ground motion time histories with the design response spectra, the frequency intervals at which the spectral values are calculated are also reviewed.  When time history analyses are performed, either of the following options may be considered.  In either case, the time histories may be real or artificial.  Option 1: Single Set of Time Histories.  The justification for the use of the single set of time histories is reviewed.  The approach used to demonstrate that the response spectra generated from the time histories envelop the design response spectra are reviewed.  Depending on the approach used, the application of the requirements to match a target power spectral density (PSD) function compatible with the design response spectra may also be reviewed.  Option 2: Multiple Sets of Time Histories.  In lieu of the use of a single time history, multiple artificial or real ground motion time histories may be used for the seismic analyses and design of the SSCs.  The parameters describing the time histories and the number of time histories are reviewed.  The approach used to demonstrate the adequacy of the set of multiple time histories, in terms of the enveloping criteria and having sufficient power over the frequency range of interest, is reviewed.

evidence_chain.section: Section C. STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
The following regulatory positions provide acceptable damping values to be used in the elastic dynamic seismic analysis and design of SSCs, where energy dissipation is approximated by viscous damping unless otherwise specified. Damping values higher than those provided may be used if documented test data support the higher values. Damping values associated with soil-structure interaction analysis are beyond the scope of this RG.

1. Structural Damping

1.1  Acceptable Structural Damping Values for Containment Structures, Containment Internal Structures, and Other Seismic Category I Structures

1.1.1 Safe-Shutdown Earthquake  
Table 1 provides acceptable damping values for the SSE analysis.  

Table 1 SSE Damping Values

Structural Material Damping (% of Critical Damping)
Reinforced Concrete 7%
Reinforced Masonry 7 %  
Prestressed Concrete 5%
Steel-Plate Composite Walls 5%
Welded Steel or Bolted Steel with Friction Connections 4%
Bolted Steel with Bearing Connections 7%
Note: For steel structures with a combination of different connection types, use the lowest specified damping value, or as an alternative, use a “weighted average” damping value based on the number of connections of each type present in the structure.

1.1.2 Operating-Basis Earthquake

If the design-basis OBE ground acceleration is selected to be less than or equal to one-third of the design-basis SSE ground acceleration, then a separate OBE analysis is not required. However, if the design-basis OBE ground acceleration is selected to be greater than one-third of the design-basis SSE ground acceleration, then a separate OBE analysis should be conducted. Table 2 provides acceptable damping values for the OBE analysis.

Table 2 OBE Damping Values

Structural Material Damping (% of Critical Damping)
Reinforced Concrete 4%
Reinforced Masonry 4 %  
Prestressed Concrete 3%
Steel-Plate Composite Walls 3%
Welded Steel or Bolted Steel with Friction Connections 3%
Bolted Steel with Bearing Connections 5%

1.2  Special Consideration for Generation of In-Structure Response Spectra  

The SSE damping values specified in Table 1 for linear dynamic analysis of structures have been selected based on the expectation that the structural response attributed to load combinations that include the SSE will be close to the applicable code stress limits, as defined in Chapter 3, “Design of Structures, Components, Equipment, and Systems,” of NUREG-0800.

However, in some cases, the predicted structural response to load combinations that include the SSE may be significantly below the applicable code stress limits. Because equivalent viscous damping ratios have been shown to depend on the structural response level, the SSE damping values in Table 1 may be inconsistent with the predicted structural response level.

For structural evaluation, this is not a concern, because the stresses resulting from the use of the damping-compatible structural response will still be less than the applicable code stress limits. However, for ISRS generation, it is necessary to use damping compatible with the structural response stress levels. Consequently, the following additional guidance is provided for analyses used to determine ISRS:

(1) Use the OBE damping values specified in Table 2, which are acceptable to the staff without further review.

(2) In general, for certified standard plant designs where the design-basis ISRS represent the envelope of the in-structure responses obtained from multiple analyses conducted to account for a range of expected site soil conditions associated with the certified seismic design response spectra (CSDRS), the SSE damping values in Table 1 of this RG and cracked concrete properties may be used. Combined license applicants referencing these certified standard plant design cases do not need to address this issue. However, if plant-specific seismic analyses are conducted for Category I structures or for structures not included in the standard plant design, then the applicant should address this issue accordingly.

(3) If a CSDRS is associated with a single site condition, such as the hard-rock high-frequency spectra for a specific site, then the OBE damping values in Table 2 of this RG should be used.

II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

Requirements

Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations:

1. Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2 - The design basis shall reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe earthquakes that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which historical data have been accumulated.

2. 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S is applicable to applications for a DC or COL to 10 CFR Part 52 or a construction permit (CP) or operating license (OL) pursuant to 10 CFR Part 50 on or after January 10, 1997. Appendix S requires that for SSE ground motions, SSCs will remain functional and within applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits. The required safety functions of SSCs must be assured during and after the vibratory ground motion through design, testing, or qualification methods. The evaluation must take into account SSI effects and the expected duration of the vibratory motion. ...

SRP Acceptance Criteria

Specific SRP acceptance criteria acceptable to meet the relevant requirements of the Commission's regulations identified above are as follows for review described in this SRP section. ...

1. Seismic Analysis Methods. The seismic analysis of all seismic Category I SSCs should use either a suitable dynamic analysis method or an equivalent static load analysis method, if justified. The SRP acceptance criteria primarily address linear elastic analysis coupled with allowable stresses near elastic limits of the structures. However, for certain special cases (e.g., stability analyses and evaluation of as-built structures), reliance on limited inelastic/nonlinear behavior is acceptable to the staff when appropriate. Analysis methods incorporating inelastic/nonlinear considerations and the analysis results are reviewed on a case-by-case basis.

A. Dynamic Analysis Method. When calculating seismic responses of seismic Category I structures, dynamic analysis (response spectrum analysis method or time history analysis method) should be performed. To be acceptable, dynamic analyses should consider the following:

i. Use of appropriate methods of analysis (time history analysis method [time domain solution and frequency domain solution]; response spectrum analysis method), accounting for the effects of SSI, if applicable. In general, the response spectrum analysis method is not suitable for SSI analysis.

ii. Seismic analysis should be performed for three orthogonal (two horizontal and one vertical) components of design ground motion.

iii. Consideration of the torsional, rocking, and translational responses of the structures and their foundations (including footings, basemats and buried walls).

iv. Use of an adequate number of discrete mass degrees of freedom in dynamic modeling. ...

v. When using either the response spectrum method or the modal superposition time history method, responses associated with high frequency modes (i.e., f > ZPA [or PGA] frequency) should be included in the total dynamic solution using the guidance and methods described in Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.92, Regulatory Positions C.1.4 and C.1.5.

vi. Consideration of maximum relative displacements between adjacent supports of seismic Category I SSCs.

vii. Inclusion of significant effects such as piping interactions, externally applied structural restraints, hydrodynamic (both mass and stiffness effects) loads, and nonlinear responses.

data.query: How do regulatory requirements ensure that all safety-related structures, systems, and components are designed using appropriate seismic input motions, and what is the relationship between the selection of time history records and the demonstration of compliance with seismic design criteria?
data.answer:
Regulatory requirements ensure that all safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) are designed using appropriate seismic input motions through a combination of site-specific seismic hazard assessment and rigorous design criteria. According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, the design bases for nuclear power plants must include the effects of earthquakes, specifically through the selection of appropriate seismic input motions for the design and qualification of safety-related SSCs. The Safe Shutdown Earthquake Ground Motion (SSE) is determined based on detailed site-specific geologic, seismologic, and geotechnical investigations, and this SSE serves as the seismic input for the design and qualification of safety-related SSCs (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, Section III.2).

The relationship between the selection of time history records and compliance with seismic design criteria is addressed in both SRP 3.7.1 and Appendix S. Time history records used in dynamic analyses must be appropriate for the site-specific SSE and compatible with the design response spectra (Appendix S, Section III.3). SRP 3.7.1 further specifies that acceleration time histories for seismic Category I SSCs are reviewed for their compatibility with the design response spectra. If suitable recorded or specified time histories are unavailable, artificial time histories may be generated from the design response spectra. The response spectra derived from these artificial time histories should generally envelop the design response spectra, ensuring that the seismic input used in analyses is at least as conservative as the design basis (SRP 3.7.1, Areas of Review).

In summary, regulatory requirements mandate that seismic input motions, including time history records, are selected and validated to be representative of site-specific hazards and compatible with design response spectra. This process ensures that safety-related SSCs are robustly designed to withstand seismic events without loss of safety function, thereby demonstrating compliance with seismic design criteria.

evidence_chain.section: I. AREAS OF REVIEW (Design Ground Motion and Design Time Histories)
evidence_chain.evidence_text: For the seismic design of nuclear power plants, it is customary to specify earthquake design ground motions that are exerted on the plant structures and used in soil-structure interaction (SSI) analyses. The design ground motion, also known as the seismic input motion or control motion, is based on the seismicity and geologic conditions at the site and expressed in such a manner that it can be applied to the dynamic analysis of structures, systems, and components (SSCs). ... The seismic free-field ground motions can be developed based on Regulatory Guides (RGs) 1.60, “Design Response Spectra for Seismic Design of Nuclear Power Plants,” or RG 1.208, “A Performance-Based Approach to Define the Site-Specific Earthquake Ground Motion,” and are reviewed under SRP Section 2.5.2. These RGs provide procedures that are acceptable to the staff for defining the design response spectra in the free-field for use in developing the OBE and SSE design ground motion needed for the design of nuclear power plant SSCs. ... Acceleration time histories for computing the response of seismic Category I SSCs are reviewed. The extent to which these time histories are compatible with the design response spectra is reviewed. When an appropriate recorded or specified time history is not available as input ground motion for seismic system analysis, the three spatial components of artificial time histories may be generated from the design response spectra for the purpose of carrying out a time history analysis of the SSCs. ... The response spectra obtained from such artificial time histories of ground motion should generally envelop the design response spectra. The procedures used to generate response spectra from the artificial time histories and the comparisons of these response spectra with the design response spectra are reviewed. ... The approach used to demonstrate that the response spectra generated from the time histories envelop the design response spectra are reviewed. ... The adequacy of time histories used for the nonlinear analyses is reviewed.

evidence_chain.section: Appendix S to Part 50—Earthquake Engineering Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appendix S to Part 50—Earthquake Engineering Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants

I. Introduction

This appendix establishes minimum requirements for earthquake engineering criteria for nuclear power plants. These requirements ensure that nuclear power plants are designed, constructed, and operated to withstand the effects of earthquakes and maintain safety functions. The design bases for nuclear power plants must include consideration of the effects of earthquakes, including the selection of appropriate seismic input motions for the design and qualification of safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs).

II. Definitions

Safe Shutdown Earthquake Ground Motion (SSE): The earthquake ground motion for which certain structures, systems, and components must remain functional.

III. Seismic Design Criteria

1. The design bases for nuclear power plants must include consideration of the effects of earthquakes, including the selection of appropriate seismic input motions for the design and qualification of safety-related SSCs.

2. The Safe Shutdown Earthquake Ground Motion (SSE) must be determined based on site-specific geologic, seismologic, and geotechnical investigations. The SSE is used as the seismic input for the design and qualification of safety-related SSCs.

3. The selection of time history records for use in dynamic analysis must be appropriate for the site-specific SSE. The time history records must be compatible with the design response spectra and must be used to demonstrate compliance with seismic design criteria for safety-related SSCs.

4. The seismic design criteria must ensure that safety-related SSCs are designed to withstand the effects of the SSE without loss of capability to perform their safety functions.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for demonstrating the adequacy of seismic input motions used in soil-structure interaction analyses for nuclear power plant safety-related structures?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for demonstrating the adequacy of seismic input motions used in soil-structure interaction (SSI) analyses for nuclear power plant safety-related structures are grounded in the requirements of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A (GDC 2), and Appendix S, as well as the guidance provided in SRP Sections 3.7.1 and 2.5.2.

According to SRP 3.7.1, the seismic input motions must reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe earthquakes historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data (SRP 3.7.1, II; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2). The design ground motion is established using site-specific free-field input response spectra (FIRS) and performance-based safe shutdown earthquake response spectra (PBSRS), developed per the guidance in SRP 2.5.2. The competent material for defining these motions is generally in-situ material with a minimum shear wave velocity of 1,000 fps, and any soft soil or backfill must be included in the SSI analysis (SRP 3.7.1, II.1.A).

Appendix S to 10 CFR Part 50 requires that the horizontal component of the safe shutdown earthquake (SSE) ground motion at the free-field foundation level must have a peak ground acceleration (PGA) of at least 0.1g, and the associated response spectrum should be a smooth, broadband spectrum (e.g., RG 1.60 or justified alternatives) (SRP 3.7.1, II.1.A; SRP 2.5.2, II.2). The seismic design response spectra must be specified for three mutually orthogonal directions—two horizontal and one vertical—with the two horizontal directions typically assumed to be the same (SRP 3.7.1, II.1.A).

The adequacy of seismic input motions is further supported by site-specific investigations and probabilistic seismic hazard analysis (PSHA) as described in RG 1.208, ensuring that the ground motion response spectrum (GMRS) is appropriate for the site’s geologic and seismologic characteristics (SRP 2.5.2, II).

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria require that seismic input motions for SSI analyses are site-specific, reflect the most severe credible earthquakes with appropriate margin, meet or exceed a minimum PGA of 0.1g for the SSE, use appropriate response spectra, and are developed based on thorough site investigations and hazard analyses.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory guides for seismic analysis relate to the requirements for selecting and justifying deterministic soil profiles in site-specific soil-structure interaction evaluations?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory guides for seismic analysis provide the framework and acceptable methods for selecting and justifying deterministic soil profiles in site-specific soil-structure interaction (SSI) evaluations. According to SRP 3.7.1 (Section II.1.A), seismic free-field ground motions are developed using Regulatory Guides (RGs) such as RG 1.60 and RG 1.208, which define procedures for generating design response spectra and performance-based surface response spectra (PBSRS). These spectra are used to ensure that deterministic soil profiles selected for SSI analyses envelop the probabilistically determined PBSRS, thereby meeting performance requirements. 

10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, mandates that the soil profiles and properties used in SSI analyses must be selected and justified to represent site-specific conditions, considering the range of possible soil properties at the site. The analyses must demonstrate adequacy for this range, and the methods and assumptions must be justified and documented in the safety analysis report (Appendix S, II(1)-(2)). 

SRP 2.5.2 and RG 1.138 further detail the process for site investigations and laboratory testing, emphasizing that soil profiles should be based on representative and statistically meaningful samples, including those with extreme properties to capture variability (RG 1.138, Section C.4). The selection of soil profiles must consider uncertainties in soil properties, layering, and behavior under seismic loading (SRP 3.7.2, Section 4), and the profiles used in deterministic SSI analyses must be shown to envelop the range of site-specific conditions identified through probabilistic analyses (SRP 3.7.1, SRP 3.7.2).

In summary, NRC regulatory guides require that deterministic soil profiles for SSI evaluations be selected and justified based on comprehensive site investigations, laboratory testing, and probabilistic analyses, ensuring that the chosen profiles represent the full range of site-specific conditions and uncertainties, and that the SSI analysis results are compatible with the design ground motions defined by regulatory guidance.

evidence_chain.section: Appendix S to Part 50—Earthquake Engineering Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appendix S to Part 50—Earthquake Engineering Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants

I. Introduction

Every applicant for a construction permit or combined license under this part or part 52 of this chapter shall demonstrate in the safety analysis report required by § 50.34 or § 52.79 of this chapter that the design bases of the structures, systems, and components of the facility reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe earthquake that has been historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated. The design bases for these structures, systems, and components shall also reflect appropriate consideration of the characteristics of the site, including seismology, geology, and soil characteristics.

II. Earthquake Engineering Criteria

(1) The Safe Shutdown Earthquake Ground Motion (SSE) for the site shall be determined based on an evaluation of the maximum earthquake potential considering the regional and local geology and seismology, and the characteristics of subsurface materials, including soil and rock. The evaluation must use current geologic and seismologic knowledge and methods generally accepted and used for such determinations. The SSE shall be characterized by free-field ground motion at the foundation level of the structure. The soil profile and properties used in the soil-structure interaction analyses shall be selected and justified to represent the site-specific conditions, and the analyses shall be performed using appropriate deterministic or probabilistic methods, as applicable. The methods and assumptions used must be justified and documented in the safety analysis report.

(2) The design response spectra and time histories used in the seismic design and soil-structure interaction analyses must be compatible with the SSE and site-specific soil conditions. The selection and justification of soil profiles for these analyses must consider the range of soil properties that could exist at the site, and the analyses must demonstrate that the design is adequate for the range of possible site conditions.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appropriate sections of the following Regulatory Guides (RGs) are used by the staff for the identified acceptance criteria:

RG 1.132, "Site Investigations for Foundations of Nuclear Power Plants," describes programs of site investigations related to geotechnical aspects that would normally meet the needs for evaluating the safety of the site from the standpoint of the performance of foundations and earthworks under anticipated loading conditions, including earthquakes. It provides general guidance and recommendations for developing site-specific investigation programs as well as specific guidance for conducting subsurface investigations, such as borings and sampling.

RG 1.60, "Design Response Spectra for Seismic Design of Nuclear Power Plants,” states that smoothed response spectra are generally used for design purposes. The RG 1.60 standard spectral shape has been frequently used for certified seismic design response spectra (CSDRS). For recent DC applications of plants to be located in the Central and Eastern United States (CEUS), RG 1.60 standard spectra have been modified to account for high frequency motions. Under the COL procedure, the GMRS are used to determine the adequacy of the CSDRS for a site. If adequate, then the CSDRS becomes the SSE for the site. However, for some site-specific structures the SSE could be site-specific SSE and not the CSDRS.

RG 1.138, "Laboratory Investigations of Soils for Engineering Analysis and Design of Nuclear Power Plants," describes laboratory investigations and testing practices acceptable for determining soil and rock properties and characteristics, together with their uncertainties, needed for site geotechnical investigations and evaluations.

RG 1.208, “A Performance-Based Approach to Define the Site-Specific Earthquake Ground Motion," describes acceptable methods to: (1) conduct geological, seismological, geophysical, and geotechnical investigations of the site and region around the site, (2) identify and characterize seismic sources, (3) perform PSHA, (4) perform site response analysis, and (5) determine the GMRS for the site (see SRP Section 2.5.2.6) using the performance-based approach.

The principal geologic and seismic considerations for site suitability are given in 10 CFR 100.23. RG 1.208 provides more detailed guidance on investigations and application of PSHA and development of the GMRS. The GMRS is based on consideration of the regional and local geology and seismology and on the characteristics of the subsurface materials at the site. However, no comprehensive definitive rules can be promulgated regarding the investigations needed to determine the GMRS; the requirements vary from site to site.
