evidence_chain.section: I. AREAS OF REVIEW, 4. Soil-Structure Interaction
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
4. Soil-Structure Interaction.  The design ground motion response spectra at the foundation level (foundation input response spectra (FIRS)) are defined in the free-field, i.e., without the presence of structures, as described in SRP Section 3.7.1, and Interim Staff Guidance (ISG) DC/COL-ISG-01 and DC/COL-ISG-017.  Performance-based free-field surface response spectra (PBSRS) are also defined at the free ground surface to ensure the performance adequacy of the soil columns used in the deterministic SSI analysis.  The FIRS and PBSRS should be developed in a consistent manner.  They are probabilistically determined performance-based spectra generated using the soil columns corresponding to the building.  The properties of the soil columns usually consist of 60 or more randomized sets of properties similar to those used in the probabilistic seismic hazard analysis (PSHA) process.  For sites with soil layers near the surface that will be completely excavated to expose competent material, and replaced with extended compacted backfill layers, the FIRS and PBSRS are determined considering the effect of the backfill layers in the site profiles that will exist after completion of excavation and backfilling.  FIRS at the foundation should also be developed as free-field outcrop motions, not as in-column motions.  Competent material is generally considered to be in-situ material having a minimum shear wave velocity of 1,000 feet/second (fps).

As applicable, the modeling methods (including technical bases) used in the seismic system analysis to account for SSI are reviewed.  The factors to be considered in accepting a particular modeling method include: (1) the extent of embedment, (2) the layering of the soil/rock strata, and (3) the boundary of the soil-structure model.  All SSI analyses should recognize the uncertainties prevalent throughout the phenomenon, and include consideration of the following:

A. The random nature of the soil and rock configuration and material characteristics.

B. Uncertainty in soil constitutive modeling (soil stiffness, damping, etc.).

C. Nonlinear soil behavior.

D. Coupling between the structures and soil.

E. Lack of lateral uniformity in the site soil profile that is usually assumed to be uniformly layered in all horizontal directions in SSI analyses.

F. Effects of the flexibility of soil/rock.

G. Effects of the flexibility of basemat, sidewalls and interior structures.

H. The effect of pore water on structural responses, including the effects of variability of ground-water level with time.

I. Effects of potential separation or loss of contact between the structure (embedded portion of the structure and foundation mat) and the soil during the earthquake.

J. If incoherence effects to reduce high frequency motions are included in the SSI response, consideration of the potential variation of the Coherency Function described in DC/COL-ISG-01 with depth should be included in the evaluation.

The procedures by which strain-dependent soil properties (damping, shear modulus, pore pressure development), layering, and variation of soil properties are incorporated in the analysis are reviewed.  Assumptions for modeling the soil-structure system and computer program validation documents are also reviewed.

4.1. General
a. Undisturbed samples of earth fill should be taken for confirmatory testing during construction and in the testing and re-evaluation of existing structures.
b. Procedures for preparing soil samples for testing should be documented. Details of procedures depend on the nature of the test and the specimen.
For additional information, EM 1110-2-1906 describes procedures for preparing soil samples for testing, and ASTM D4452 can be used to determine the quality of a sample before testing. Regulatory Guide 1.132 discusses methods of determining the in situ density of cohesionless soils.
c. The selection of soil and rock specimens for laboratory testing requires careful examination of records of borings and available samples. To permit establishment of the soil profile, investigators should ensure that test specimens are representative of the soil or rock unit to be tested and should describe them accurately. The number of test specimens should be sufficient to produce statistically meaningful test results. Investigators should identify average test values of material properties as well as the range of values that identify their variability. In addition to the most representative samples, investigators should also test samples that have extreme properties and represent critical zones.
For additional information, Regulatory Guide 1.132 offers guidelines for spacing of borings and frequency of sampling. Additional boring and sampling may be required when laboratory examination of the samples reveals an inadequate number or distribution of suitable samples to meet testing requirements.

data.query: For a new nuclear power plant site, what combined regulatory requirements and guidance govern the demonstration of adequacy for both input ground motion and deterministic soil columns in site-specific soil-structure interaction analyses, including the use of performance-based benchmarks at various depths?
data.answer:
The demonstration of adequacy for both input ground motion and deterministic soil columns in site-specific soil-structure interaction (SSI) analyses for a new nuclear power plant site is governed by a combination of regulatory requirements and guidance documents, primarily 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix S, SRP Sections 2.5.2 and 3.7.1, and Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.208.

According to 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix S (Section II.B.2), SSI analyses must use appropriate site-specific soil profiles and ground motion input, and the adequacy of both must be demonstrated, including the use of performance-based benchmarks at various depths as necessary. The Safe Shutdown Earthquake (SSE) ground motion must be determined based on a comprehensive evaluation of regional and local geology, seismology, and subsurface material characteristics, with consideration of uncertainties (Appendix S, Section II.A.1-2).

SRP Section 2.5.2 (II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA) and SRP Section 3.7.1 (I. AREAS OF REVIEW) specify that the site-specific Ground Motion Response Spectrum (GMRS) is developed using performance-based procedures per RG 1.208, which includes probabilistic seismic hazard analysis (PSHA) and site response analysis. The GMRS, defined at the ground surface or the uppermost competent material, serves as the basis for the SSE and must meet the requirements of 10 CFR 100.23 and Appendix S to 10 CFR Part 50.

For SSI analyses, the Foundation Input Response Spectra (FIRS) is derived from the GMRS and represents the free-field motion at the foundation level. Performance-based surface response spectra (PBSRS) are also developed using randomized soil column properties, and deterministic soil columns used in SSI analyses must produce surface response spectra that envelop the PBSRS, thereby demonstrating their adequacy (SRP 3.7.1, I. AREAS OF REVIEW). Additional guidance on soil column adequacy is provided in SRP 3.7.2 II.4.

In summary, the regulatory framework requires that both the input ground motion and the soil columns used in SSI analyses be justified through performance-based benchmarks (GMRS, FIRS, PBSRS) at relevant depths, following the methodologies and acceptance criteria outlined in 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix S, SRP Sections 2.5.2 and 3.7.1, and RG 1.208.

evidence_chain.section: I. AREAS OF REVIEW (Design Ground Motion, Design Response Spectra, and related subsections)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
The design ground motions for the OBE and SSE should be consistent with the description of the free-field ground motions at the site provided in NUREG-0800, Standard Review Plan (SRP) Section 2.5.2, “Vibratory Ground Motion,” which includes the variation in and distribution of ground motions in the free field, sources and directions of the motion, propagation and transmission of seismic waves, and other site response characteristics.  The seismic free-field ground motions can be developed based on Regulatory Guides (RGs) 1.60, “Design Response Spectra for Seismic Design of Nuclear Power Plants,” or RG 1.208, “A Performance-Based Approach to Define the Site-Specific Earthquake Ground Motion,” and are reviewed under SRP Section 2.5.2.  These RGs provide procedures that are acceptable to the staff for defining the design response spectra in the free-field for use in developing the OBE and SSE design ground motion needed for the design of nuclear power plant SSCs. ...

The GMRS reviewed under SRP Section 2.5.2 are site-specific horizontal and vertical free-field GMRS determined at the ground surface or at the free-field outcrop of the uppermost in-situ competent material using performance-based procedures in accordance with RG 1.208.  The performance-based site-specific GMRS transferred to the foundation level in the free-field is referred to as the foundation input response spectra (FIRS).  Therefore, the FIRS meet the same performance requisite as the GMRS.  Both the GMRS and the FIRS are defined as free-field outcrop response spectra.  The FIRS is the starting point for conducting an SSI analysis and for making a one-to-one comparison of the seismic design capacity of the standard design and the site-specific seismic demand for a site. ...

In addition to the FIRS, free-field performance-based surface response spectra (PBSRS) should be developed using the soil column corresponding to the building for which the performance-based FIRS are also generated.  The properties of the soil column are used to generate 60 or more randomized sets of properties similar to those used in the probabilistic seismic hazard analysis (PSHA) process as described in SRP Section 2.5.2.  The resulting spectra described above are the PBSRS for the horizontal direction.  The PBSRS for the vertical direction can be obtained with the appropriate V/H ratios used to develop the FIRS.  The PBSRS are used to verify and ensure that the soil columns to be used in a deterministic SSI analysis produce surface response spectra which meet the performance requisite by enveloping the corresponding PBSRS.  Additional guidance on demonstrating the adequacy of the soil columns is provided in SRP Section 3.7.2 II.4, “Soil-Structure Interaction,” by the FIRS and PBSRS are associated with subsurface conditions localized to a specific building.  In addition, Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) Part 50, “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities,” Appendix S, “Earthquake Engineering Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants,” is applicable to applications for a DC or COL pursuant to 10 CFR Part 52, “Licenses, Certifications, and Approvals for Nuclear Power Plants,” or a CP or OL pursuant to 10 CFR Part 50 submitted on or after January 10, 1997.  Applications subject to this appendix must:

• Demonstrate that the SSE ground motion in the horizontal direction in the free-field at the FIRS must be an appropriate response spectrum with peak ground acceleration (PGA) of at least 0.1g.   

• Design SSCs to the OBE and SSE loadings.  If the OBE is set at one-third or less of the SSE, an explicit analysis or design is not required.  If the OBE is set at a value greater than one-third of the SSE, an analysis and design must be performed for the OBE to demonstrate that the applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits of the SSCs are satisfied.   

The seismic input motions to the SSI analyses can typically be placed at the free ground surface or at the foundation level using the guidance in this SRP Section 3.7.1, “Seismic Design Parameters,” as supplemented by DC/COL-ISG-017.

evidence_chain.section: Appendix S to Part 50—Earthquake Engineering Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appendix S to Part 50—Earthquake Engineering Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants

I. Introduction
Nuclear power plant structures, systems, and components important to safety must be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena such as earthquakes, tornadoes, hurricanes, floods, tsunami, and seiches without loss of capability to perform their safety functions. The design bases for these structures, systems, and components must reflect: (1) Appropriate consideration of the most severe of the natural phenomena that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated, (2) appropriate combinations of the effects of normal and accident conditions with the effects of the natural phenomena, and (3) the importance of the safety functions to be performed.

II. Earthquakes and Other Dynamic Effects
A. Safe Shutdown Earthquake Ground Motion
1. The Safe Shutdown Earthquake Ground Motion (SSE) for the site shall be determined based on an evaluation of the maximum earthquake potential considering the regional and local geology and seismology, and taking into account the characteristics of subsurface materials. The SSE shall be used to establish the design basis for earthquake-resistant features of the plant.
2. The evaluation must include consideration of the uncertainty in the estimation of the SSE and the potential for surface faulting, soil liquefaction, and other earthquake-induced hazards.

B. Seismic Design Bases
1. Nuclear power plant SSCs important to safety must be designed to withstand the effects of the SSE and remain functional.
2. Soil-structure interaction (SSI) analyses must be performed using appropriate site-specific soil profiles and ground motion input. The adequacy of the input ground motion and soil profiles must be demonstrated, including the use of performance-based benchmarks at various depths, as necessary, to ensure the validity of the SSI analyses.

C. Methodology
1. The methods used to determine the SSE and to perform SSI analyses must be appropriate for the site conditions and must be justified by the applicant. The NRC may require the use of alternative or additional methods if deemed necessary for safety.

III. Implementation
Applicants must provide sufficient information to demonstrate compliance with these criteria, including the technical bases for the selection of input ground motions, soil profiles, and the methodologies used for SSI analyses.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for establishing vertical and horizontal ground motion parameters in the seismic design of nuclear power plant structures?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for establishing vertical and horizontal ground motion parameters in the seismic design of nuclear power plant structures are grounded in regulatory requirements and detailed guidance provided in SRP 3.7.1, SRP 2.5.2, and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A and S.

According to SRP 3.7.1 Section II, the design must comply with 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2, which requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety are designed to withstand the most severe historically reported earthquakes for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; [2]).

Appendix S to 10 CFR Part 50 further specifies that for the Safe Shutdown Earthquake (SSE) ground motions, SSCs must remain functional and within applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits, considering soil-structure interaction (SSI) effects and the expected duration of vibratory motion. The horizontal component of the SSE ground motion at the free-field foundation level must have a peak ground acceleration (PGA) of at least 0.1g and be represented by an appropriate, smooth broadband response spectrum (e.g., RG 1.60 or justified alternatives) ([1], [3]).

The seismic design response spectra must be specified for three mutually orthogonal directions: two horizontal and one vertical. Current practice assumes the two horizontal directions have identical response spectra, including maximum ground accelerations ([1]). The site-specific Foundation Input Response Spectra (FIRS) and Performance-Based Surface Response Spectra (PBSRS) are determined as free-field outcrop motions at the foundation and surface levels, respectively, and are developed using guidance from SRP 2.5.2 ([1], [3]).

In summary, the NRC requires that both vertical and horizontal ground motion parameters be established using site-specific investigations and analyses, with the horizontal SSE PGA at the foundation level not less than 0.1g, and that response spectra be defined for two horizontal and one vertical direction, using appropriate spectral shapes and considering SSI effects (SRP 3.7.1 II, SRP 2.5.2 II, 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A and S).

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

Requirements

Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations:

1. 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, “Design Bases for Protection against Natural Phenomena.” - The design basis shall reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe earthquakes that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which historical data have been accumulated.   

2. 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S is applicable to applications for a DC or COL pursuant to 10 CFR Part 52 or a CP or OL pursuant to 10 CFR Part 50 on or after January 10, 1997.  Appendix S requires that for SSE ground motions, SSCs will remain functional and within applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits.  The required safety functions of SSCs must be assured during and after the vibratory ground motion through design, testing, or qualification methods.  The evaluation must take into account SSI effects and the expected duration of the vibratory motion.  If the OBE is set at one-third or less of the SSE, an explicit analysis or design is not required.  If the OBE is set at a value greater than one-third of the SSE, an analysis and design must be performed to demonstrate that the applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits are satisfied.  Appendix S also requires that the horizontal component of the SSE ground motion in the free-field at the foundation level of the structures must be an appropriate response spectrum with a PGA of at least 0.1g.   

SRP Acceptance Criteria

Specific SRP acceptance criteria acceptable to meet the relevant requirements of the Commission’s regulations identified above are as follows for the review described in this SRP section.  ...

1. Design Ground Motion

A. Design Response Spectra.  The site-specific FIRS and PBSRS reviewed under this SRP section are determined as free-field outcrop motions at the foundation and surface level.  FIRS and associated deterministic soil profiles developed using the PBSRS to meet the performance goal will establish the design basis for the site-specific SSI analysis; this design basis is developed using the guidance reviewed under SRP Section 2.5.2. ...

According to Appendix S to 10 CFR Part 50, the minimum PGA for the horizontal component of the SSE at the foundation level in the free-field should be 0.1g or higher.  The response spectrum associated with this minimum PGA should be a smooth broadband response spectrum (e.g., RG 1.60, or other appropriate shaped spectra, if justified) and is defined as outcrop response spectra at the free-field foundation level.  This response spectrum anchored to 0.1g is referred to in this SRP section as the minimum required response spectrum. ...

To be acceptable, the seismic design response spectra should be specified for three mutually orthogonal directions - two horizontal and one vertical.  Current practice is to assume that the design response spectra (including maximum ground accelerations) in the two horizontal directions are the same.

data.query: How do regulatory requirements for seismic design address the use of vertical-to-horizontal (V/H) spectral ratios when determining ground motion inputs for nuclear facility structures?
data.answer:
Regulatory requirements for seismic design of nuclear facility structures explicitly address the use of vertical-to-horizontal (V/H) spectral ratios when determining ground motion inputs. According to SRP 3.7.1, the site-specific Ground Motion Response Spectra (GMRS) and the Foundation Input Response Spectra (FIRS) are developed for both horizontal and vertical directions. The vertical component of the FIRS is obtained by applying V/H ratios that are appropriate for the specific site. This ensures that the vertical ground motion input used in design reflects the actual seismic hazard at the site, as determined by performance-based procedures in accordance with Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.208 (SRP 3.7.1, Section I.A).

SRP 2.5.2 further clarifies that the GMRS, including both horizontal and vertical components, must be determined using a performance-based approach that considers regional and local geology, seismology, and site-specific geotechnical characteristics. The guidance in RG 1.208, referenced in SRP 2.5.2, provides acceptable methods for conducting the necessary investigations and analyses, including the determination of appropriate V/H ratios for the site.

10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, establishes the regulatory basis by requiring that the design of nuclear power plant structures, systems, and components must consider both horizontal and vertical ground motion components. The vibratory ground motion must be characterized by response spectra that are appropriate for the site, and the methods used to develop these spectra, including the use of V/H ratios, must be justified and suitable for the specific site conditions (Appendix S, Sections I and II).

In summary, the regulatory framework requires that vertical ground motion inputs for seismic design be determined using site-appropriate V/H spectral ratios, as part of a comprehensive, performance-based seismic hazard evaluation. This approach ensures that both horizontal and vertical seismic demands are accurately represented in the design basis for nuclear facility structures.

data.query: For deeply embedded nuclear structures, what regulatory guidance addresses the consideration of uncertainties in vertical-to-horizontal spectral ratios over the depth of the facility, and how should these uncertainties be incorporated into the development of site-specific seismic input motions?
data.answer:
Regulatory guidance addressing the consideration of uncertainties in vertical-to-horizontal (V/H) spectral ratios for deeply embedded nuclear structures is provided in several key documents. Appendix S to 10 CFR Part 50 explicitly requires that, for deeply embedded structures, the effects of embedment on the response to earthquake ground motion must be evaluated, including the uncertainties in V/H spectral ratios at depth. These uncertainties must be incorporated into the development of site-specific seismic input motions for facility design and analysis, and the methods used must be documented and justified in the safety analysis report (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, Section III(2)-(3)).

SRP Section 2.5.2.5 further details that applicants should evaluate the variation of the V/H ratio with depth and incorporate associated uncertainties into the development of site-specific seismic input motions. The staff reviews the applicant’s approach to ensure that uncertainties in the V/H ratio are appropriately characterized and propagated through the site response analysis, ensuring consistency with the site-specific GMRS and regulatory requirements (SRP 2.5.2.5).

SRP 3.7.1 and 3.7.2 reinforce that the foundation input response spectra (FIRS) for the vertical direction should use V/H ratios appropriate for the site, and that the properties of the soil column—including uncertainties—should be represented by multiple randomized sets, as in the PSHA process. SRP 3.7.2 specifically lists the need to recognize and include uncertainties in soil and rock properties, constitutive modeling, and other factors in soil-structure interaction analyses (SRP 3.7.2 I.4).

In summary, regulatory guidance requires that uncertainties in V/H spectral ratios over depth be explicitly evaluated and incorporated into the development of seismic input motions for deeply embedded structures, using probabilistic approaches and thorough documentation, as outlined in Appendix S to 10 CFR Part 50, SRP 2.5.2.5, SRP 3.7.1, and SRP 3.7.2.

4. Soil-Structure Interaction.  The design ground motion response spectra at the foundation level (foundation input response spectra (FIRS)) are defined in the free-field, i.e., without the presence of structures, as described in SRP Section 3.7.1, and Interim Staff Guidance (ISG) DC/COL-ISG-01 and DC/COL-ISG-017.  Performance-based free-field surface response spectra (PBSRS) are also defined at the free ground surface to ensure the performance adequacy of the soil columns used in the deterministic SSI analysis.  The FIRS and PBSRS should be developed in a consistent manner.  They are probabilistically determined performance-based spectra generated using the soil columns corresponding to the building.  The properties of the soil columns usually consist of 60 or more randomized sets of properties similar to those used in the probabilistic seismic hazard analysis (PSHA) process. ... All SSI analyses should recognize the uncertainties prevalent throughout the phenomenon, and include consideration of the following: 

A. The random nature of the soil and rock configuration and material characteristics. 

B. Uncertainty in soil constitutive modeling (soil stiffness, damping, etc.). 

C. Nonlinear soil behavior. 

D. Coupling between the structures and soil. 

E. Lack of lateral uniformity in the site soil profile that is usually assumed to be uniformly layered in all horizontal directions in SSI analyses. 

F. Effects of the flexibility of soil/rock. 

G. Effects of the flexibility of basemat, sidewalls and interior structures. 

H. The effect of pore water on structural responses, including the effects of variability of ground-water level with time. 

I. Effects of potential separation or loss of contact between the structure (embedded portion of the structure and foundation mat) and the soil during the earthquake. 

J. If incoherence effects to reduce high frequency motions are included in the SSI response, consideration of the potential variation of the Coherency Function described in DC/COL-ISG-01 with depth should be included in the evaluation.

evidence_chain.section: Appendix S to Part 50—Earthquake Engineering Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appendix S to Part 50—Earthquake Engineering Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants

I. Introduction

This appendix establishes minimum requirements for earthquake engineering criteria for nuclear power plants. These requirements apply to the design, construction, and operation of nuclear power plants to ensure adequate protection against the effects of earthquakes.

II. Definitions

Safe Shutdown Earthquake Ground Motion (SSE): The earthquake ground motion for which certain structures, systems, and components must remain functional.

III. Requirements

(1) The Safe Shutdown Earthquake Ground Motion (SSE) for the site shall be determined based on an evaluation of the maximum earthquake potential considering the regional and local geology and seismology, and taking into account the uncertainties in the data and methods used in the evaluation. The evaluation shall include consideration of the effects of local site conditions on ground motion, including soil-structure interaction and the potential for amplification or attenuation of seismic waves.

(2) For nuclear power plant structures that are deeply embedded, the effects of embedment on the response of the structure to earthquake ground motion shall be evaluated. The evaluation shall consider the uncertainties in the vertical-to-horizontal spectral ratios of ground motion at depth, and these uncertainties shall be incorporated into the development of site-specific seismic input motions for the design and analysis of the facility.

(3) The methods used to develop the site-specific seismic input motions, including the consideration of uncertainties in ground motion parameters such as vertical-to-horizontal spectral ratios, shall be documented and justified in the safety analysis report.

data.query: What are the regulatory expectations for evaluating the adequacy of finite element modeling in seismic system analysis for nuclear power plant structures?
data.answer:
The regulatory expectations for evaluating the adequacy of finite element modeling (FEM) in seismic system analysis for nuclear power plant structures are clearly outlined in DSRS 3.7.2, with supporting requirements from 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, and cross-referenced guidance in DSRS 3.8.4 and 3.8.5.

According to DSRS 3.7.2 (Section II.3.C.ii), the finite element model is generally used for complex or irregular structures, or where significant three-dimensional effects or soil-structure interaction (SSI) are present. The FEM must adequately represent the mass, stiffness, and damping characteristics of the structure. The mesh size should be chosen to ensure that significant modes of vibration are captured. The adequacy of the FEM must be demonstrated by:

1. Performing a preliminary modal analysis to ensure a sufficient number of modes are included and that mode shapes are reasonably smooth.
2. Performing static analyses to compare FEM results with those from other methods or available test data. If significant discrepancies are found, the model should be refined until satisfactory agreement is achieved.
3. Validating the FEM by comparison with test results or results from other analytical methods, as appropriate.

These expectations are grounded in the regulatory basis of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2, which requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety be designed to withstand the most severe historically reported earthquakes, with sufficient margin for uncertainties (DSRS 3.7.1, II.1).

Additionally, DSRS 3.8.4 and 3.8.5 emphasize the need for compliance with relevant codes (e.g., ACI 349 for concrete, ANSI/AISC N690 for steel), appropriate assumptions on boundary conditions, and validation of computer programs used for analysis (DSRS 3.8.4, I.4.C, and DSRS 3.8.5, II.4.G). Validation of computer programs must follow the procedures in DSRS 3.8.4, II.4.D, which includes providing a design report and, if necessary, a structural audit.

In summary, the NRC expects that finite element models used in seismic analysis are rigorously validated, represent all relevant physical characteristics, and are benchmarked against test data or alternative analytical methods, with any discrepancies resolved through model refinement.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
C. Modeling of Structures.  Two types of structural models are widely used by the nuclear industry:  the lumped-mass stick model and the finite element model.  Either of these two types of modeling techniques is acceptable if the following guidelines are met:

i. Lumped-Mass Stick Model.  The lumped-mass stick model is generally used for modeling buildings and other structures that are essentially regular in plan and elevation.  The model should adequately represent the mass, stiffness, and damping characteristics of the structure.  The number of lumped masses and the location of the masses should be sufficient to represent the dynamic characteristics of the structure, including the significant modes of vibration.

ii. Finite Element Model.  The finite element model is generally used for modeling complex structures, such as irregular buildings, structures with significant three-dimensional effects, or structures with significant interaction with other structures or with the soil.  The finite element model should adequately represent the mass, stiffness, and damping characteristics of the structure.  The mesh size should be selected such that the significant modes of vibration are adequately represented.  The adequacy of the finite element model should be demonstrated by (1) performing a preliminary modal analysis to ensure that a sufficient number of modes are included and that the mode shapes are reasonably smooth, and (2) performing static analyses to compare the results obtained from the finite element model with those obtained from other methods or with available test data.  If significant discrepancies are found, the model should be refined until satisfactory agreement is obtained.  The finite element model should also be validated by comparison with test results or with results from other analytical methods, as appropriate.

General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants
Appendix A to Part 50

CRITERION 2—DESIGN BASES FOR PROTECTION AGAINST NATURAL PHENOMENA
Structures, systems, and components important to safety shall be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena such as earthquakes, tornadoes, hurricanes, floods, tsunami, and seiches without loss of capability to perform their safety functions. The design bases for these structures, systems, and components shall reflect: (1) Appropriate consideration of the most severe of the natural phenomena that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated, (2) appropriate combinations of the effects of normal and accident conditions with the effects of the natural phenomena, and (3) the importance of the safety functions to be performed.

The design bases for these structures, systems, and components shall reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe earthquakes that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated.

2. 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, is applicable to applications for a DC or COL pursuant to 10 CFR Part 52 or a CP or OL pursuant to 10 CFR Part 50 on or after January 10, 1997.  Appendix S requires that, for SSE ground motions, certain SSCs will remain functional and within applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits.  The required safety functions of these SSCs must be assured during and after the vibratory ground motion associated with the SSE ground motion through design, testing, or qualification methods. data.query: How do NRC regulatory standards address the relationship between finite element size, shape, and aspect ratio and the accuracy of seismic analysis results for safety-related structures?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory standards address the relationship between finite element size, shape, and aspect ratio and the accuracy of seismic analysis results for safety-related structures primarily through the guidance provided in DSRS 3.7.2, Section II.3.C. This section specifies that finite element models used in seismic analysis must be sufficiently refined so that the results are not significantly affected by the size, shape, or aspect ratio of the elements. The adequacy of the finite element mesh must be demonstrated through mesh sensitivity studies, which require:

- Refining the mesh until further refinement does not result in significant changes in calculated responses (e.g., displacements, forces, moments) at locations of interest.
- Ensuring that element aspect ratios do not become excessively distorted, as this could adversely affect accuracy.
- Selecting element type and order (e.g., linear, quadratic) appropriate for the structural behavior being modeled.
- Refining the mesh in regions with high stress gradients, such as near supports, connections, and discontinuities.
- Demonstrating mesh adequacy by comparing finite element analysis results with those from alternative modeling approaches (e.g., lumped-mass stick model) or available test data, if applicable.

These requirements are grounded in the broader regulatory basis of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2, which mandates that safety-related structures must be designed to withstand natural phenomena, including earthquakes, with sufficient margin for uncertainties. Cross-references in DSRS 3.7.1, 3.8.4, and 3.8.5 further emphasize the need for compliance with applicable codes and standards (such as ACI 349 and ANSI/AISC N690), and the validation of computer programs used in analysis. In summary, NRC standards require that finite element mesh characteristics be systematically evaluated and justified to ensure seismic analysis accuracy for safety-related structures.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory standards require that seismic analysis methods be validated when comparing results from different analytical models for nuclear power plant structures?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory standards require that seismic analysis methods for nuclear power plant structures be validated through a combination of model adequacy checks, comparison of analytical results, and adherence to established codes and standards. According to DSRS 3.7.2 (Section II.1 and II.12), when comparing results from different analytical models—such as modal response spectrum and time history approaches—the NRC staff reviews the comparison of seismic responses for major seismic Category I structures. The adequacy of dynamic models is confirmed by performing preliminary modal analyses and correlating static analysis results using the dynamic model with those from a distributed mass representation. Specifically, simple 1g static analyses of the dynamic model should be performed in each excitation direction and compared to corresponding results from static analyses with distributed mass. A lack of correlation, especially at support locations, indicates an insufficient number of discrete mass degrees of freedom, signaling the need for model refinement.

Furthermore, DSRS 3.8.4 (Section I.4) and DSRS 3.8.5 (Section II.4.G) require that computer programs used for seismic analysis be validated according to procedures outlined in DSRS 3.8.4 II.4.D, which includes compliance with relevant industry codes (e.g., ACI 349 for concrete, ANSI/AISC N690 for steel) and NRC regulatory guides. The review also encompasses assumptions on boundary conditions, load transmission, and the expected behavior under seismic loads. These requirements ensure that the analytical methods and models used are robust, validated, and capable of accurately predicting the seismic response of safety-related structures, as mandated by 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2.

In summary, NRC standards require rigorous validation of seismic analysis methods by comparing analytical results from different models, ensuring model adequacy, and verifying compliance with established codes and NRC guidance (DSRS 3.7.2 II.1, II.12; DSRS 3.8.4 I.4; DSRS 3.8.5 II.4.G; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2).

data.query: What regulatory expectations exist for ensuring that the loads used in the design of support structures for safety-related components are conservative when multiple seismic analysis methods are employed?
data.answer: Regulatory expectations for ensuring that loads used in the design of support structures for safety-related components are conservative, particularly when multiple seismic analysis methods are employed, are clearly outlined in DSRS 3.7.2 and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2. DSRS 3.7.2 specifies that seismic Category I structures, systems, and components (SSCs) must be analyzed using suitable dynamic analysis methods, such as response spectrum or time history analysis. When these methods are used, all relevant seismic responses, including those from high-frequency modes, must be included in the total dynamic solution, following the guidance in RG 1.92 (DSRS 3.7.2, II.1.A.v). If an equivalent static load method is used, it is only acceptable if it can be justified that the method produces conservative results. Specifically, a factor of 1.5 must be applied to the peak spectral acceleration unless a lower factor is justified (DSRS 3.7.2, II.1.B.iii). Furthermore, the design must reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe natural phenomena, with sufficient margin to account for uncertainties in historical data and analysis methods (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2). In summary, the regulatory expectation is that, regardless of the analysis method chosen, the loads used must be demonstrably conservative, with explicit factors or justifications required to ensure safety-related structures can withstand seismic events without loss of safety function.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for comparing seismic analysis results obtained from different analytical methods for nuclear power plant structures?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for comparing seismic analysis results obtained from different analytical methods for nuclear power plant structures are primarily outlined in DSRS 3.7.2 and supported by the general design criteria in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A. According to DSRS 3.7.2, Section I (Areas of Review, item 12), the NRC staff reviews the comparison of seismic responses for major seismic Category I structures when both modal response spectrum and time history approaches are used. This comparison ensures that the analytical methods yield consistent and reliable results for safety-related structures. 

Section II (Acceptance Criteria, item 1.A.v) of DSRS 3.7.2 specifies that dynamic analysis methods, such as the response spectrum method or the modal superposition time history method, must be used for seismic Category I structures. When comparing results from these methods, it is required that responses associated with high-frequency modes (frequencies greater than or equal to the zero period acceleration (ZPA) or peak ground acceleration (PGA) frequency) are included in the total dynamic solution. The guidance and methods described in Regulatory Guide 1.92 must be followed for combining modal responses and spatial components in seismic response analysis.

Additionally, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2, establishes the regulatory basis by requiring that structures, systems, and components important to safety are designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including earthquakes, with appropriate consideration of the most severe historical events and sufficient safety margins. This criterion underpins the need for robust and validated seismic analysis methods and their comparison to ensure safety functions are maintained.

In summary, the NRC requires that when different seismic analysis methods are used, their results must be compared, high-frequency responses must be included, and NRC-endorsed guidance (such as RG 1.92) must be followed to ensure the adequacy and consistency of seismic design for safety-related structures.

data.query: How do NRC review standards address the conservatism of loads used in the design of support structures for safety-related components under seismic conditions?
data.answer:
NRC review standards address the conservatism of loads used in the design of support structures for safety-related components under seismic conditions through a combination of regulatory requirements and detailed acceptance criteria. According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2, safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) must be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena, including earthquakes, with sufficient margin to account for uncertainties in historical data (10CFR [2]). This regulatory basis is reflected in the DSRS, which requires that seismic design loads and combinations be conservatively specified.

DSRS 3.7.2 specifies that when using the equivalent static load method, a factor of 1.5 must be applied to the peak spectral acceleration to ensure conservatism, unless a lower factor is justified (DSRS 3.7.2 [1]). The method must also account for relative motion between supports and kinematic interaction effects. The NRC reviews the conservatism of any approximate methods, including those used to account for torsional effects and accidental torsion.

DSRS 3.7.1 further requires that the design basis reflect the most severe historically reported earthquakes, with sufficient margin for data uncertainties, and that the design response spectra be specified for three orthogonal directions (DSRS 3.7.1 [3]). The minimum required response spectrum must be anchored to a peak ground acceleration (PGA) of at least 0.1g.

For load combinations, DSRS 3.8.4 and 3.8.5 require that all relevant loads (dead, live, seismic, wind, flood, etc.) and their combinations be considered per ACI 349 and RG 1.142, with additional NRC guidance (DSRS 3.8.4 [4], DSRS 3.8.5 [5]). Seismic Category I foundations must be checked against sliding and overturning using conservative load combinations, and the analysis must consider simultaneous action of seismic forces in all three directions. For nonlinear time history analyses, the seismic input may be increased by the factor of safety to demonstrate adequate stability (DSRS 3.8.5 [5]).

In summary, NRC review standards ensure conservatism in seismic load specification and analysis through regulatory requirements for margin, explicit load factors, comprehensive load combinations, and rigorous review of analysis methods.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory expectations for the use of damping values in the seismic analysis of safety-related structures, systems, and components in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory expectations for the use of damping values in the seismic analysis of safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) in nuclear power plants are clearly outlined in several regulatory documents. According to DSRS 3.7.2, the NRC reviews the procedures used to account for different critical damping values in various elements of the structural model, emphasizing that the stiffness, mass, and damping characteristics must be adequately incorporated into analytical models (DSRS 3.7.2, I. AREAS OF REVIEW, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA). The NRC expects that the effects of parameter variations, including damping, on floor response spectra and response time histories are considered.

DSRS 3.7.1 further specifies that the percentage of critical damping values used for seismic Category I SSCs must be reviewed for both the Operating Basis Earthquake (OBE) and Safe Shutdown Earthquake (SSE). Damping values should reflect the total energy dissipation of the system, including both material and system damping, and should be based on experimental observations where possible. If damping values differ from those recommended in Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.61, the basis for such deviations must be justified and reviewed (DSRS 3.7.1, 2. Percentage of Critical Damping Values).

Additionally, the NRC requires that the analytical modeling procedures incorporate strain-dependent soil properties, including damping, and that the modeling assumptions and validation are reviewed (DSRS 3.7.2). For stability evaluations and dynamic analyses, the mathematical model must adequately represent the dynamic characteristics, including damping, to capture the relevant vibration modes (DSRS 3.8.5, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA, 4. Design and Analysis Procedures).

These expectations are grounded in the regulatory basis of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2, which requires that SSCs important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including earthquakes, with appropriate consideration of uncertainties and sufficient margin.

In summary, the NRC expects that damping values used in seismic analysis are technically justified, consistent with regulatory guidance (such as RG 1.61), and appropriately incorporated into analytical models to ensure the safety-related SSCs can perform their intended functions during and after seismic events.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
2. Percentage of Critical Damping Values.  The percentage of critical damping values used for the seismic analysis of seismic Category I SSCs is reviewed for both the OBE and the SSE.  Critical damping is the amount of damping that would completely eliminate free vibration and is an important measure of the damping capacity of a structure.

Vibrating SSCs have energy losses that depend on numerous factors, such as material characteristics, stress levels, and geometric configurations.  This dissipation of energy, or damping effect, occurs because a part of the excitation input is transformed into heat, sound waves, and other energy forms.  The response of a system to dynamic loads is a function of the amount and type of damping inherent in the system.  Knowledge of appropriate values to represent this characteristic is essential for obtaining realistic results in any dynamic analysis.

In practical seismic analysis, which usually employs linear methods of analysis, damping is also used to account for many nonlinear effects such as changes in boundary conditions, joint slippage, concrete cracking, gaps, and other effects that tend to alter response amplitudes.  In real structures, it is often impossible to separate “true” material damping from system damping, which is the measure of the total energy dissipation.  Overall structural damping used in design is normally determined by observing experimentally the total response of the structure.

Damping values assigned to members of seismic Category I SSCs, including material damping and system damping, are reviewed.  When applicable, the basis for any damping values that differ from those given in RG 1.61, “Damping Values for Seismic Design of Nuclear Power Plants,” is reviewed.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory standards address the selection of damping values and the use of composite modal damping or modal synthesis techniques in the seismic analysis of safety-related structures?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory standards address the selection of damping values and the use of composite modal damping or modal synthesis techniques in the seismic analysis of safety-related structures through detailed review and acceptance criteria. According to DSRS 3.7.2, the NRC staff reviews the procedures used to account for different critical damping values in various elements of the structural model (DSRS 3.7.2, Section I.13). The staff also examines how variations in structural properties, including critical damping values, affect floor response spectra and response time histories (DSRS 3.7.2, Section I.9). Analytical modeling procedures are scrutinized for their treatment of damping, ensuring that the modeling of damping is consistent with the physical characteristics of the structure and its components (DSRS 3.7.2, Section I.3).

When employing the response spectrum or modal superposition time history methods, the NRC requires that responses from high-frequency modes be included in the total dynamic solution, following the guidance in Regulatory Guide 1.92 (DSRS 3.7.2, Section I.v). This ensures that the effects of all relevant modes, including those potentially influenced by different damping assumptions, are properly considered.

These requirements are grounded in the regulatory basis provided by 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2, which mandates that safety-related structures, systems, and components be designed to withstand seismic events, with design bases that appropriately consider the effects of natural phenomena and the importance of safety functions (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2). Thus, the NRC’s standards ensure that the selection and application of damping values, as well as the use of composite modal damping or modal synthesis techniques, are rigorously reviewed to maintain the seismic safety of nuclear power plant structures.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for seismic system analysis in nuclear power plant structures?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for seismic system analysis in nuclear power plant structures are established to ensure that safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) can withstand the effects of earthquakes without loss of safety function. According to DSRS 3.7.2 Section II and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2, the key requirements are as follows:

1. The design basis must reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe earthquakes historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2; DSRS 3.7.2 II.1).

2. Appendix S to 10 CFR Part 50 requires that, for Safe Shutdown Earthquake (SSE) ground motions, certain SSCs remain functional and within applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits during and after the vibratory ground motion. The evaluation must account for soil-structure interaction (SSI) effects and the expected duration of the motion. The horizontal component of the SSE ground motion at the foundation level must have a peak ground acceleration (PGA) of at least 0.1g (DSRS 3.7.2 II.2).

3. For the Operating Basis Earthquake (OBE), if it is set at more than one-third of the SSE, analysis must demonstrate that SSCs necessary for continued operation remain functional and within limits when subjected to OBE and normal operating loads (DSRS 3.7.2 II.2).

4. Seismic analysis of all seismic Category I SSCs should use suitable dynamic analysis methods (such as response spectrum or time history analysis) or justified equivalent static load methods. Analyses must consider three orthogonal components of ground motion (two horizontal, one vertical), torsional, rocking, and translational responses, and use adequate modeling detail (DSRS 3.7.2 II.1.A).

5. The design must include appropriate margins to account for uncertainties and ensure reliability of safety functions (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2).

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria require robust seismic analysis methods, consideration of site-specific seismic hazards, demonstration of SSC functionality under seismic loads, and incorporation of sufficient safety margins.

Appendix S requires that, for SSE ground motions, certain SSCs will remain functional and within applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits. The required safety functions of these SSCs must be assured during and after the vibratory ground motion associated with the SSE ground motion through design, testing, or qualification methods. The evaluation must take into account SSI effects and the expected duration of the vibratory motion. If the OBE is set at one-third or less of the SSE, an explicit response or design analysis is not required. If the OBE is set at a value greater than one-third of the SSE, an analysis and design must be performed to demonstrate that, when subjected to the effects of the OBE in combination with normal operating loads, all SSCs of the nuclear power plant (NPP) necessary for continued operation without undue risk to the health and safety of the public remain functional and within applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits. ... 

DSRS Acceptance Criteria

Specific DSRS acceptance criteria acceptable to meet the relevant requirements of the NRC’s regulations identified above are set forth below. ...

1. Seismic Analysis Methods. The seismic analysis of all seismic Category I SSCs should use either a suitable dynamic analysis method or an equivalent static load analysis method, if justified. The DSRS acceptance criteria primarily address linear elastic analysis coupled with allowable stresses near elastic limits of the structures. However, for certain special cases (e.g., stability analyses and evaluation of as-built structures), reliance on limited inelastic/nonlinear behavior is acceptable to the staff when appropriate. iii. Consideration of the torsional, rocking, and translational responses of the structures and their foundations (including footings, basemats, and buried walls).

iv. Use of an adequate number of discrete mass degrees of freedom in dynamic modeling.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory guides for seismic instrumentation relate to the acceptance criteria for seismic analysis of nuclear power plant structures?
data.answer: NRC regulatory guides for seismic instrumentation, such as Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.92 referenced in DSRS 3.7.2, provide detailed technical guidance on acceptable methods for conducting seismic analysis of nuclear power plant structures, systems, and components (SSCs). These guides are directly related to the acceptance criteria for seismic analysis as outlined in DSRS 3.7.2, Section II, which specifies that seismic analysis methods must be consistent with NRC regulations, including Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50 (General Design Criteria, GDC 2) and Appendix S to 10 CFR Part 50. Specifically, DSRS 3.7.2 requires that seismic Category I SSCs be analyzed using suitable dynamic or justified static methods, and that high-frequency mode responses be included in the total dynamic solution using the guidance in RG 1.92. This ensures that the seismic analysis appropriately accounts for the effects of severe earthquakes, as required by GDC 2, and that SSCs remain functional within stress, strain, and deformation limits during and after seismic events, as required by Appendix S. Thus, NRC regulatory guides for seismic instrumentation serve as the technical basis for demonstrating compliance with the regulatory acceptance criteria for seismic analysis of nuclear power plant structures.

data.query: For nuclear power plant designs that may operate with fewer than the full complement of modules, what combined regulatory provisions from NRC review standards and regulatory guides govern the evaluation of seismic demands at critical building locations, and how should applicants ensure that all potential operating configurations remain within design basis seismic limits?
data.answer:
For nuclear power plant designs that may operate with fewer than the full complement of modules, the evaluation of seismic demands at critical building locations is governed by a combination of NRC regulations, review standards, and regulatory guides. The primary regulatory basis is found in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2, which requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety be designed to withstand the most severe historically reported earthquakes for the site, with appropriate safety margins (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2). Additionally, Appendix S to 10 CFR Part 50 mandates that SSCs remain functional and within applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits during and after the Safe Shutdown Earthquake (SSE), considering soil-structure interaction (SSI) effects (DSRS 3.7.2, II. Acceptance Criteria; DSRS 3.7.1).

The DSRS 3.7.2 provides detailed acceptance criteria for seismic analysis, requiring dynamic analysis methods (such as response spectrum or time history analysis) that account for SSI, three orthogonal ground motion components, and the inclusion of high-frequency modes per RG 1.92. Analytical modeling must consider the designation of systems versus subsystems and the appropriate mass degrees of freedom. DSRS 3.7.1 further specifies that site-specific seismic input (FIRS and PBRS) must be established at relevant depths, and the design basis for SSI analysis must be developed accordingly.

For modular plants, DSRS 3.8.4 and 3.8.5 require that the design and analysis of structures and foundations account for all possible combinations and locations of modules (NPMs) over the plant's life. This includes reviewing loads and load combinations for various module configurations, ensuring that all potential operating scenarios remain within design basis seismic limits. Applicants must demonstrate, through analysis, that the structures and foundations can accommodate the seismic demands for any number and arrangement of modules, using the load combinations and analysis methods specified in DSRS 3.8.4 (II.3) and 3.8.5 (II.3), and referencing the seismic analysis procedures in DSRS 3.7.1 and 3.7.2.

In summary, applicants must ensure that all potential operating configurations, including fewer than the full complement of modules, are analyzed for seismic demands using NRC-accepted methods and load combinations, and that the resulting stresses and deformations remain within the design basis limits established by the applicable regulations and review standards.

data.query: What are the regulatory expectations for accounting for accidental torsion effects in the seismic analysis of nuclear safety-related structures?
data.answer:
The regulatory expectations for accounting for accidental torsion effects in the seismic analysis of nuclear safety-related structures are clearly defined in NRC guidance and regulations. According to DSRS 3.7.2, the methods used to account for torsional effects in seismic Category I structures must be reviewed for conservatism, including the consideration of accidental torsion in calculating structural responses (DSRS 3.7.2, I.11). Acceptance criteria require that dynamic analysis methods (such as response spectrum or time history analysis) explicitly consider torsional, rocking, and translational responses of the structures and their foundations (DSRS 3.7.2, II.1.A.iii).

DSRS 3.8.4 further specifies that seismic loads must include the effects of accidental torsion, eccentric mass distribution, and variations in dynamic characteristics. Accidental torsion effects should be accounted for by assuming a minimum eccentricity of 5 percent of the building dimension perpendicular to the direction of loading, unless a more exact analysis is performed. These torsional effects must be combined with translational motion effects for each load combination (DSRS 3.8.4, II.3.A).

These expectations are grounded in the regulatory basis of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2, which requires that safety-related structures be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including earthquakes, with appropriate consideration of the most severe historical events and sufficient safety margin (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; DSRS 3.7.1, II.1).

In summary, the NRC expects that seismic analyses of safety-related structures explicitly account for accidental torsion by applying a minimum eccentricity (typically 5% of the building dimension) unless a more precise method is justified, and that these effects are combined with other seismic responses to ensure the structures can perform their safety functions during and after seismic events.

The evaluation must take into account SSI effects and the expected duration of the vibratory motion. If the OBE is set at a value greater than one-third of the SSE, an analysis and design must be performed to demonstrate that, when subjected to the effects of the OBE in combination with normal operating loads, all SSCs of the nuclear power plant necessary for continued operation without undue risk to the health and safety of the public remain functional and within applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits. 3. Loads and Load Combinations.  The specified loads and load combinations are acceptable if found to be in accordance with the guidance given below:

A. Concrete Structures

All loads and load combinations are to be in accordance with ACI 349 with additional guidance provided by RG 1.142.  Supplemental criteria on the use of loads and load combinations are presented below.

Dead loads include hydrostatic loads and, for equipment supports, include static and dynamic head and fluid flow effects.

Live loads include any movable equipment loads and other loads which vary with intensity and occurrence, such as soil pressure.  The dynamic effects of lateral soil pressure should be accounted for in accordance with the provisions of Subsection II.4.H of this DSRS section.

Seismic loads include the effects of the safe-shutdown earthquake (SSE) and the operating-basis earthquake (OBE).  The effects of accidental torsion, as well as the effects of eccentric mass distribution and the variation in the dynamic characteristics of the structure, should be considered in the seismic analysis.  The accidental torsion effects should be accounted for by assuming a minimum eccentricity of 5 percent of the building dimension perpendicular to the direction of loading, unless a more exact analysis is performed.  The effects of torsion should be combined with the effects of translational motion in each direction for each load combination.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory standards require the effects of accidental torsion to be incorporated into seismic system analysis, and what is the relationship between these requirements and the use of combination methods such as SRSS for element forces?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory standards require that the effects of accidental torsion be explicitly incorporated into the seismic system analysis of seismic Category I structures. According to DSRS 3.7.2, Section I (Areas of Review, item 11), the NRC reviews the methods used to account for torsional effects, including the conservatism of any approximate methods and the consideration of accidental torsion in calculating structural responses. This ensures that the seismic analysis adequately captures the impact of torsional effects, which may arise from mass or stiffness eccentricities during an earthquake.

Section II (Acceptance Criteria, item 1.A.v) of DSRS 3.7.2 further specifies that dynamic analysis methods, such as the response spectrum or modal superposition time history methods, must be used for seismic analysis. These methods should include the responses from high-frequency modes, and the combination of modal responses must follow the guidance in Regulatory Guide 1.92, which addresses combining modal responses and spatial components—commonly using methods such as the Square Root of the Sum of the Squares (SRSS) for element forces.

The regulatory basis for these requirements is found in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2, which mandates that safety-related structures, systems, and components be designed to withstand natural phenomena, including earthquakes, with appropriate consideration of all relevant effects and combinations of loading conditions. This includes the combined effects of normal, accident, and seismic loads, ensuring the safety functions are preserved.

In summary, NRC standards require that accidental torsion be considered in seismic analysis, and the combination of element forces—such as through SRSS—is an integral part of ensuring all relevant modal and spatial effects, including torsion, are conservatively and comprehensively addressed in accordance with regulatory guidance.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating the seismic analysis of safety-related structures, systems, and components in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating the seismic analysis of safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) in nuclear power plants are grounded in the requirements of Appendix A and Appendix S to 10 CFR Part 50, as well as detailed guidance in DSRS 3.7.2. 

Per 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2, SSCs important to safety must be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including earthquakes, without loss of safety function. The design basis must consider the most severe historically reported earthquakes for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2).

Appendix S to 10 CFR Part 50 further requires that, for Safe Shutdown Earthquake (SSE) ground motions, safety-related SSCs remain functional and within applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits during and after the seismic event. The evaluation must account for soil-structure interaction (SSI) effects and the expected duration of ground motion. If the Operating Basis Earthquake (OBE) is set above one-third of the SSE, explicit analysis is required to demonstrate continued functionality of SSCs under combined OBE and normal operating loads. Appendix S also specifies that the horizontal component of SSE ground motion at the foundation level must have a peak ground acceleration (PGA) of at least 0.1g (DSRS 3.7.2, Section II).

DSRS 3.7.2 outlines specific acceptance criteria for seismic analysis methods. Seismic Category I SSCs should be analyzed using suitable dynamic analysis methods (e.g., response spectrum or time history analysis), considering three orthogonal components of ground motion, SSI effects, torsional and translational responses, and adequate modeling of mass degrees of freedom. High-frequency modal responses must be included per RG 1.92. The analysis must also consider maximum relative displacements, piping interactions, hydrodynamic effects, and nonlinear responses where appropriate. Limited inelastic/nonlinear behavior may be accepted in special cases, subject to NRC review (DSRS 3.7.2, Section II).

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria require robust seismic analysis methods that ensure safety-related SSCs can perform their safety functions during and after the most severe credible seismic events, with explicit consideration of regulatory requirements and technical guidance.

Appendix S also requires that the horizontal component of the SSE ground motion in the free field at the foundation level of the structures must be an appropriate response spectrum with a peak ground acceleration (PGA) of at least 0.1g.

... 

DSRS Acceptance Criteria

Specific DSRS acceptance criteria acceptable to meet the relevant requirements of the NRC’s regulations identified above are set forth below. ...

1. Seismic Analysis Methods. The seismic analysis of all seismic Category I SSCs should use either a suitable dynamic analysis method or an equivalent static load analysis method, if justified. The DSRS acceptance criteria primarily address linear elastic analysis coupled with allowable stresses near elastic limits of the structures. However, for certain special cases (e.g., stability analyses and evaluation of as-built structures), reliance on limited inelastic/nonlinear behavior is acceptable to the staff when appropriate. Analysis methods incorporating inelastic/nonlinear considerations and the analysis results are reviewed on a case-by-case basis.

A. Dynamic Analysis Method. When calculating seismic responses of seismic Category I structures, dynamic analysis (response spectrum analysis method or time history analysis method) should be performed. To be acceptable, dynamic analyses should consider the following:

i. Use of appropriate methods of analysis (time history analysis method (time domain solution and frequency domain solution); response spectrum analysis method) to account for the effects of SSI, if applicable. In general, the response spectrum analysis method is not suitable for SSI analysis.

ii. Seismic analysis should be performed for three orthogonal (two horizontal and one vertical) components of design ground motion.

iii. Consideration of the torsional, rocking, and translational responses of the structures and their foundations (including footings, basemats, and buried walls).

iv. Use of an adequate number of discrete mass degrees of freedom in dynamic modeling. ...

v. When using either the response spectrum method or the modal superposition time history method, responses associated with high-frequency modes (i.e., f ≥ ZPA (or PGA) frequency) should be included in the total dynamic solution using the guidance and methods described in RG 1.92, “Combining Modal Responses and Spatial Components in Seismic Response Analysis.”

vi. Consideration of maximum relative displacements between adjacent supports of seismic Category I SSCs.

vii. Inclusion of significant effects such as piping interactions, externally applied structural restraints, hydrodynamic (both mass and stiffness effects) loads, and nonlinear responses.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory guides for seismic system analysis relate to the requirements for ensuring that standard design safety-related structures, systems, and components can accommodate site-specific seismic demands?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory guides for seismic system analysis are directly related to the requirements for ensuring that standard design safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) can accommodate site-specific seismic demands. According to DSRS 3.7.2, the acceptance criteria for seismic analysis are grounded in the requirements of Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, and Appendix S to 10 CFR Part 50. GDC 2 mandates that SSCs important to safety must be designed to withstand the effects of the most severe earthquakes historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin to account for uncertainties in historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2).

DSRS 3.7.2 further specifies that seismic analyses of all seismic Category I SSCs should employ suitable dynamic or justified static analysis methods. The evaluation must ensure that SSCs remain functional and within applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits during and after the safe shutdown earthquake (SSE) ground motion, considering soil-structure interaction (SSI) effects and the expected duration of seismic motion. The DSRS also references Regulatory Guide 1.92 for combining modal responses and spatial components in seismic response analysis, ensuring that high-frequency modes are appropriately included in the total dynamic solution.

In summary, NRC regulatory guides provide the technical methods and criteria for seismic analysis that must be used to demonstrate compliance with the regulatory requirements for safety-related SSCs to accommodate site-specific seismic demands, as established in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A (GDC 2), and Appendix S.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory requirements for seismic system analysis address the use of fixed-base boundary conditions when modeling nuclear facility structures with spring elements?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory requirements for seismic system analysis specifically address the use of fixed-base boundary conditions when modeling nuclear facility structures with spring elements, particularly in the context of soil-structure interaction (SSI) analyses. According to DSRS 3.7.2, Section II.3.C, when spring elements are used to represent the flexibility of the foundation or other structural elements, the boundary conditions at the base of the springs must realistically represent the actual site conditions. The use of fixed-base boundary conditions—where the base of the springs is assumed to be immovable—is not appropriate for modeling SSI effects unless it can be demonstrated that the foundation is supported on competent rock with negligible flexibility. For most SSI analyses, the boundary conditions should reflect the flexibility of the supporting soil or rock strata, and the soil domain included in the model should be extensive enough to minimize boundary effects on the calculated structural response (DSRS 3.7.2, II.3.C).

This approach is consistent with the broader regulatory framework, which requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety be designed to withstand seismic events, taking into account SSI effects (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S; DSRS 3.7.1, II.2; SRP 2.5.2, II). The supporting media for seismic Category I structures, including soil and foundation characteristics, must be thoroughly described and considered in the SSI analysis (DSRS 3.7.1, I.3; SRP 3.7.1, I.3). The design basis for SSI analysis is established using site-specific seismic response spectra and soil profiles, ensuring that any remaining soft soil or backfill is included in the analysis (DSRS 3.7.1, II.A; SRP 3.7.1, II.1.A).

In summary, NRC requirements do not permit the use of fixed-base boundary conditions at the base of spring elements for SSI analyses unless the foundation is on competent rock with negligible flexibility. Otherwise, boundary conditions must reflect the actual flexibility of the supporting strata to ensure realistic seismic response modeling.

C. Modeling of Structures.  Two types of structural models are widely used by the nuclear industry:  the lumped-mass stick model and the finite element model.  Either of these two types of modeling techniques is acceptable if the following guidelines are met: 

i. Lumped-Mass Stick Model.  The lumped-mass stick model is generally used for modeling the overall dynamic response of a structure.  The model should adequately represent the mass and stiffness distribution of the structure, including the effects of major structural discontinuities.  The use of spring elements to represent the flexibility of the foundation or other structural elements is acceptable, provided that the stiffness values are appropriately justified.  When spring elements are used to model the foundation, the boundary conditions at the base of the springs should be selected to realistically represent the actual site conditions.  The use of fixed-base boundary conditions (i.e., assuming the base of the springs is fixed) is not appropriate for modeling soil-structure interaction (SSI) effects, unless it can be demonstrated that the foundation is supported on competent rock with negligible flexibility.  For SSI analyses, the boundary conditions should reflect the flexibility of the supporting soil or rock strata, and the extent of the soil domain included in the model should be sufficient to minimize the influence of the boundaries on the calculated structural response.
