data.query: What is the regulatory basis for justifying the adequacy of seismic analyses that use a single time history and soil type, in the context of general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena and regulatory expectations for seismic input variability?
data.answer:
The regulatory basis for justifying the adequacy of seismic analyses that use a single time history and soil type is grounded in the requirements of Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, General Design Criteria (GDC) 2, and the detailed acceptance criteria in DSRS 3.7.2. GDC 2 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2) mandates that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety must be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena, including earthquakes, with sufficient margin to account for uncertainties in historical data. This includes appropriate consideration of the effects of natural phenomena and the importance of the safety functions to be performed.

DSRS 3.7.2 further specifies that seismic analyses of seismic Category I SSCs should employ suitable dynamic analysis methods, such as time history analysis, and must account for soil-structure interaction (SSI) effects and the expected duration of ground motion. While DSRS 3.7.2 allows for the use of a single time history and soil type if justified, it emphasizes that the analysis must demonstrate that the chosen input is representative of the design basis earthquake and that the results provide sufficient margin to account for uncertainties. For multiple time history analyses, DSRS 3.7.2 requires procedures to account for uncertainties by varying parameters and justifying the statistical relationship between input and output responses. Thus, if only a single time history and soil type are used, the applicant must provide a robust justification that these choices adequately envelope the design basis and account for the variability and uncertainties inherent in seismic input, consistent with the intent of GDC 2 and the acceptance criteria in DSRS 3.7.2.

data.query: How are boundary conditions for soil-structure interaction models defined in seismic system analysis, particularly regarding the treatment of exterior surfaces of backfill soil elements?
data.answer:
Boundary conditions for soil-structure interaction (SSI) models in seismic system analysis are defined to accurately represent the actual field conditions and to ensure that the model does not introduce artificial constraints or freedoms that could distort the seismic response. According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, Section IV, the boundary conditions used in SSI analysis must be selected to represent the actual field conditions as closely as practicable. Specifically, for the treatment of exterior surfaces of backfill soil elements, the model must avoid artificially restraining or freeing soil movement at these boundaries. The extent of the soil model should be sufficient so that the structural response is not significantly affected by the model boundaries.

DSRS 3.7.2 further emphasizes that the criteria for determining the location of the bottom and side boundaries of the soil-structure system model are reviewed, and that excitation or forcing functions applied at the model boundaries must simulate the design ground motion such that the free-field response matches the design ground motion. This ensures that the SSI analysis reflects the actual seismic demand on the structure.

Additionally, SRP 3.7.1 and DSRS 3.7.1 clarify that the site profiles used in SSI analysis must include the effects of any backfill, and any remaining soft soil or backfill material must be considered in the analysis. For sites where surface soil is excavated and replaced with compacted backfill, the profiles used for SSI analysis should reflect this replacement, and the boundary conditions should be set at distances sufficiently far from the structure to avoid influencing the response within the frequency range of interest.

In summary, boundary conditions for SSI models must: (1) closely represent actual field conditions, (2) avoid artificial restraint or freedom at the exterior surfaces of backfill soil elements, and (3) ensure the soil model is extensive enough that boundary effects do not significantly impact the structural response. (References: 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, Section IV; DSRS 3.7.2, Section I.4; DSRS 3.7.1, Section I.1 and II.1.A; SRP 3.7.1, Areas of Review & Acceptance Criteria)

data.query: What regulatory guidance addresses the consideration of friction between contacting surfaces in seismic analysis of nuclear power plant structures, and how should the coefficient of friction be determined if it is included?
data.answer:
Regulatory guidance addressing the consideration of friction between contacting surfaces in the seismic analysis of nuclear power plant structures is primarily found in DSRS 3.7.2 (Section I, item 14; Section II, item 3) and SRP 3.7.2 (Section II, item 14; item 3.C). These documents require that the NRC staff review the methods and procedures used to determine seismic overturning moments, sliding forces, structure-to-soil pressures, and frictional forces for all seismic Category I structures. Specifically, the analysis must include consideration of potential sliding and separation effects, as well as soil friction, and the applicant must describe and justify the methods used for these determinations.

However, neither DSRS 3.7.2 nor SRP 3.7.2 prescribes a specific regulatory guidance document or a fixed value for the coefficient of friction. Instead, the determination of the coefficient of friction, if it is included in the analysis, is expected to be justified and described by the applicant. The NRC staff then reviews this justification for adequacy. The analytical modeling procedures must adequately represent the mass, stiffness, and damping characteristics of the structure, and include the effects of soil-structure interaction, if applicable (DSRS 3.7.2, Section II.3.C; SRP 3.7.2, Section II.3.C).

In summary, while the regulatory guidance requires the consideration and review of frictional forces in seismic analysis, it does not mandate a specific value or method for determining the coefficient of friction. The applicant is responsible for providing a technical basis for the chosen coefficient, which is then subject to NRC review (DSRS 3.7.2, SRP 3.7.2).

data.query: How do NRC regulatory standards address the consideration of soil-structure interaction effects in the seismic analysis of nuclear power plant structures, particularly when evaluating hard rock site conditions?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory standards require comprehensive consideration of soil-structure interaction (SSI) effects in the seismic analysis of nuclear power plant structures, including those sited on hard rock. According to DSRS 3.7.2, the foundation input response spectra (FIRS)—the ground motion response spectra at the foundation level—must be defined in the free field, without the presence of structures, and developed using probabilistic, performance-based methods consistent with the site-specific geologic and seismic conditions (DSRS 3.7.2; DSRS 3.7.1). For deeply embedded structures, performance-based response spectra (PBRS) are also defined at the ground surface and intermediate depths to ensure the adequacy of the soil columns used in deterministic SSI analysis and to capture kinematic interaction effects over the facility depth.

The NRC review of SSI modeling methods considers factors such as the extent of embedment, soil/rock layering, and model boundaries. Analyses must account for uncertainties in soil and rock properties, constitutive modeling, nonlinear soil behavior, structure-soil coupling, lateral non-uniformity, and the flexibility of both soil/rock and structural elements. For hard rock sites, competent material is defined as in situ material with a minimum shear wave velocity of 1,000 fps (DSRS 3.7.2; DSRS 3.7.1). If soil layers are excavated and replaced with backfill, the effects of backfill must be included in the site profiles for FIRS and PBRS development.

For deeply embedded or fully buried structures, additional considerations include the significance of kinematic interaction, the importance of non-vertically propagating shear waves, the accuracy of impedance functions, nonlinear behavior (such as separation between structure and soil), and variation in vertical-to-horizontal (V/H) spectral ratios with depth (DSRS 3.7.2). The seismic input for SSI analyses should be specified at the foundation level as FIRS, especially for deeply embedded structures (DSRS 3.7.1).

These requirements are grounded in the general design criterion that safety-related structures must withstand the effects of earthquakes and other natural phenomena without loss of safety function (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2). Site investigations must use state-of-the-art techniques to characterize subsurface materials and ensure that SSI analyses are based on accurate, site-specific data (SRP 2.5.4). The seismic probabilistic risk assessment (PRA) and seismic margin assessment (SMA) must also reflect these considerations (SRP 19.0).

evidence_chain.section: I. AREAS OF REVIEW, 4. Soil-Structure Interaction
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
4. Soil-Structure Interaction.  Foundation input response spectra (FIRS) which is the ground motion response spectra at the foundation level are defined in the free field (i.e., without the presence of structures) as described in DSRS Section 3.7.1, DC/COL-ISG-01, “Interim Staff Guidance on Seismic Issues Associated with High Frequency Ground Motion in Design Certification and Combined License Applications,” and DC/COL-ISG-017, “Interim Staff Guidance on Ensuring Hazard-Consistent Seismic Input for Site Response and Soil Structure Interaction Analyses.”  For a deeply embedded structure, performance-based response spectra (PBRS) are also defined in the free field at the ground surface and appropriate intermediate depth(s) to ensure the adequacy of the soil columns used in the deterministic SSI analysis and to determine the potential magnitude of kinematic interaction effects on the structure over the depth of the facility.  The FIRS and PBRS determined at the foundation level, surface, and intermediate depth(s) should be developed in a consistent manner.  They are probabilistically determined performance-based spectra generated using the soil column corresponding to the building.  The properties of the soil columns usually consist of 60 or more randomized sets of properties similar to those used in the probabilistic seismic hazard analysis (PSHA) process.  For sites with soil layers near the surface that will be completely excavated to expose competent material and replaced with extended compacted backfill layers, the FIRS and PBRS are determined by considering the effect of the backfill layers in the site profiles.  FIRS at the foundation and PBRS at intermediate levels should also be developed as free field outcrop motions, not as in-column motions.  Competent material is generally considered to be in situ material having a minimum shear wave velocity of 1,000 fps.

As applicable, the staff reviews the modeling methods (including technical bases) used in the seismic system analysis to account for SSI.  The factors to be considered in accepting a particular modeling method include (1) the extent of embedment, (2) the layering of the soil/rock strata, and (3) the boundary of the soil-structure model.  All SSI analyses should recognize the uncertainties prevalent throughout the phenomenon and include consideration of the following:

A. The random nature of the soil and rock configuration and material characteristics.

B. Uncertainty in soil constitutive modeling (soil stiffness, damping, etc.).

C. Nonlinear soil behavior.

D. Coupling between the structures and soil.

E. Lack of lateral uniformity in the site soil profile that is usually assumed to be uniformly layered in all horizontal directions in SSI analyses.

F. Effects of the flexibility of soil/rock.

G. Effects of the flexibility of basemat, sidewalls, and interior structures.

H. The effect of pore water on structural responses, including the effects of variability of ground water level with time.

I. Effects of potential separation or loss of contact between the structure (embedded portion of the structure and foundation mat) and the soil during the earthquake.

J. For deeply embedded or fully buried structures, (1) the effect of deep embedment on the relative significance of kinematic interaction, (2) the extent to which nonvertically propagating shear waves may be more important for deeply embedded structures than for those with shallow embedment depth, (3) the impact of deep embedment on the accuracy of sidewall impedance functions calculated with standard methods, (4) the effect of nonlinear behavior (e.g., separation of structure and soil, and soil material properties) on wall pressure and SSI calculations, and (5) the variation of V/H (vertical to horizontal) spectral ratios on ground motion over the depth of the facility.

The seismic free-field ground motions can be developed based on Regulatory Guides (RGs) 1.60, “Design Response Spectra for Seismic Design of Nuclear Power Plants,” or 1.208, “A Performance-Based Approach to Define the Site-Specific Earthquake Ground Motion” and are reviewed under SRP Section 2.5.2. The performance-based site-specific GMRS transferred to the foundation level in the free field is referred to as the foundation input response spectra (FIRS). Therefore, the FIRS satisfy the same performance criteria as the GMRS. Both the GMRS and the FIRS are defined as free-field outcrop response spectra. The FIRS is the starting point for conducting an SSI analysis and for making a one-to-one comparison of the seismic design capacity of the standard design and the site-specific seismic demand for a site. The FIRS for the vertical direction is obtained with the vertical to horizontal (V/H) ratios appropriate for the site. If noncompetent material is present, any excavation and/or backfilling should not alter the development or location of the GMRS; however, the development of the FIRS uses the site profiles, including the effect of backfill. The remaining soft soil or backfill material needs to be considered in the SSI or other analyses. Further information on the development of the GMRS and FIRS is provided in DC/COL-ISG-01, “Interim Staff Guidance on Seismic Issues Associated with High Frequency Ground Motion in Design Certification and Combined License Applications,” and DC/COL-ISG-17, “Interim Staff Guidance on Ensuring Hazard-Consistent Seismic Input for Site Response and Soil Structure Interaction Analyses.”

In these situations, the seismic input should be specified only at the foundation level as FIRS.

data.query: What regulatory guidance is provided for estimating water pressure effects due to seismic events in safety-related pools, and how should fluid-structure interaction be accounted for in this context?
data.answer:
Regulatory guidance for estimating water pressure effects due to seismic events in safety-related pools is primarily provided in DSRS 3.7.2 and DSRS 3.8.4, with the regulatory basis established by 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2. According to DSRS 3.7.2 (Section I, items 1, 3, and 4; Section II, item 1.A.vii), seismic analyses must account for significant effects such as hydrodynamic effects, including both mass and stiffness contributions from the pool water. The staff reviews the modeling criteria and procedures, ensuring that hydrodynamic effects and fluid-structure interaction (FSI) are appropriately included in the seismic system analyses. This includes the modeling of hydrodynamic loads, the effect of pore water on structural responses, and the variability of groundwater levels over time.

DSRS 3.8.4 (Section II.3; I.4) further specifies that all relevant loads and load combinations, including hydrostatic and hydrodynamic loads, must be considered in accordance with ACI 349 and RG 1.142. For seismic Category I structures, such as reactor and spent fuel pools, the review encompasses hydrostatic loads and hydrodynamic loads induced by seismic events (e.g., operating-basis earthquake and safe-shutdown earthquake). The analysis must address the behavior of structures under these loads and the methods by which forces are transmitted through the structure, including the interaction between multiple non-fuel pool modules (NPMs) and the pool water.

General Design Criterion 2 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) requires that safety-related structures be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena, including earthquakes, with appropriate consideration of combined effects and sufficient safety margins.

In summary, regulatory guidance requires that seismic analyses of safety-related pools explicitly account for water pressure effects through hydrodynamic modeling and fluid-structure interaction, using accepted codes and standards (ACI 349, RG 1.142), and that these effects be included in the load combinations for design and analysis to ensure structural integrity under seismic events.

3. Loads and Load Combinations.  The specified loads and load combinations are acceptable if found to be in accordance with the guidance given below:

A. Concrete Structures

All loads and load combinations are to be in accordance with ACI 349 with additional guidance provided by RG 1.142.  Supplemental criteria on the use of loads and load combinations are presented below.

Dead loads include hydrostatic loads and, for equipment supports, include static and dynamic head and fluid flow effects.

Live loads include any movable equipment loads and other loads which vary with intensity and occurrence, such as soil pressure.  The dynamic effects of lateral soil pressure should be accounted for in accordance with the provisions of Subsection II.4.H of this DSRS section.

Hydrodynamic loads, if applicable (e.g., safety relief valve actuation and loss-of-coolant accidents (LOCAs)), which could generate building vibration inertial loads, including floor response spectra, direct loads on structures, and elevated temperatures.

data.query: What are the regulatory expectations for considering soil-structure interaction effects in the seismic analysis of nuclear power plant structures, particularly when the site is characterized by hard rock conditions?
data.answer:
The regulatory expectations for considering soil-structure interaction (SSI) effects in the seismic analysis of nuclear power plant structures, particularly at sites characterized by hard rock conditions, are clearly outlined in several NRC documents. According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, Section III.3, the seismic analysis must account for SSI effects as appropriate to the site conditions. Specifically, for sites founded on hard rock, the analysis must consider the response of plant structures to ground motion at the rock surface, and the potential for SSI effects must be evaluated. If SSI effects are determined to be negligible due to hard rock conditions, this must be demonstrated through appropriate analysis or justification (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, Section III.3).

DSRS 3.7.2 further elaborates that the foundation input response spectra (FIRS) should be defined at the foundation level in the free field, and the modeling methods for SSI must consider factors such as the extent of embedment, layering of soil/rock strata, and the boundaries of the soil-structure model. Even in hard rock conditions, uncertainties in material properties, soil/rock configuration, and potential nonlinear behavior must be addressed in the analysis (DSRS 3.7.2, I.4). The DSRS also requires that the flexibility of the rock, potential separation between structure and rock, and the effects of embedment be considered, especially for deeply embedded or fully buried structures.

DSRS 3.7.1 supports this by stating that for structures with shallow or surface foundations, seismic input motions can be placed at the free ground surface or foundation level, but for deeply embedded structures, input should be specified at the foundation level as FIRS. The adequacy of the soil (or rock) columns used in SSI analysis must be verified, and for sites with uniform shear wave velocity profiles (as is typical for hard rock), the development of PBRS at the surface and intermediate depths is generally sufficient (DSRS 3.7.1, I).

In summary, even for hard rock sites, SSI effects must be evaluated and, if negligible, justified with analysis. The seismic analysis must use appropriate, site-specific methods and address uncertainties and potential nonlinearities in the rock-structure system, as detailed in DSRS 3.7.2, DSRS 3.7.1, and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S.

evidence_chain.section: I. AREAS OF REVIEW, 4. Soil-Structure Interaction
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
4. Soil-Structure Interaction.  Foundation input response spectra (FIRS) which is the ground motion response spectra at the foundation level are defined in the free field (i.e., without the presence of structures) as described in DSRS Section 3.7.1, DC/COL-ISG-01, “Interim Staff Guidance on Seismic Issues Associated with High Frequency Ground Motion in Design Certification and Combined License Applications,” and DC/COL-ISG-017, “Interim Staff Guidance on Ensuring Hazard-Consistent Seismic Input for Site Response and Soil Structure Interaction Analyses.”  For a deeply embedded structure, performance-based response spectra (PBRS) are also defined in the free field at the ground surface and appropriate intermediate depth(s) to ensure the adequacy of the soil columns used in the deterministic SSI analysis and to determine the potential magnitude of kinematic interaction effects on the structure over the depth of the facility.  The FIRS and PBRS determined at the foundation level, surface, and intermediate depth(s) should be developed in a consistent manner.  They are probabilistically determined performance-based spectra generated using the soil column corresponding to the building.  The properties of the soil columns usually consist of 60 or more randomized sets of properties similar to those used in the probabilistic seismic hazard analysis (PSHA) process.  For sites with soil layers near the surface that will be completely excavated to expose competent material and replaced with extended compacted backfill layers, the FIRS and PBRS are determined by considering the effect of the backfill layers in the site profiles.  FIRS at the foundation and PBRS at intermediate levels should also be developed as free field outcrop motions, not as in-column motions.  Competent material is generally considered to be in situ material having a minimum shear wave velocity of 1,000 fps.

As applicable, the staff reviews the modeling methods (including technical bases) used in the seismic system analysis to account for SSI.  The factors to be considered in accepting a particular modeling method include (1) the extent of embedment, (2) the layering of the soil/rock strata, and (3) the boundary of the soil-structure model.  All SSI analyses should recognize the uncertainties prevalent throughout the phenomenon and include consideration of the following:

A. The random nature of the soil and rock configuration and material characteristics.

B. Uncertainty in soil constitutive modeling (soil stiffness, damping, etc.).

C. Nonlinear soil behavior.

D. Coupling between the structures and soil.

E. Lack of lateral uniformity in the site soil profile that is usually assumed to be uniformly layered in all horizontal directions in SSI analyses.

F. Effects of the flexibility of soil/rock.

G. Effects of the flexibility of basemat, sidewalls, and interior structures.

H. The effect of pore water on structural responses, including the effects of variability of ground water level with time.

I. Effects of potential separation or loss of contact between the structure (embedded portion of the structure and foundation mat) and the soil during the earthquake.

J. For deeply embedded or fully buried structures, (1) the effect of deep embedment on the relative significance of kinematic interaction, (2) the extent to which nonvertically propagating shear waves may be more important for deeply embedded structures than for those with shallow embedment depth, (3) the impact of deep embedment on the accuracy of sidewall impedance functions calculated with standard methods, (4) the effect of nonlinear behavior (e.g., separation of structure and soil, and soil material properties) on wall pressure and SSI calculations, and (5) the variation of V/H (vertical to horizontal) spectral ratios on ground motion over the depth of the facility.

data.query: How do NRC review standards address the evaluation of hydrodynamic effects, such as vertical water pressure, in the seismic analysis of safety-related pools, and what technical bases are expected for methods used to account for fluid-structure interaction?
data.answer:
NRC review standards require that hydrodynamic effects, such as vertical water pressure, be explicitly addressed in the seismic analysis of safety-related pools (e.g., spent fuel pools, suppression pools, reactor cavities). According to DSRS 3.7.2 and SRP 3.7.2 (Sections I and II), the NRC staff reviews the analytical modeling to ensure that hydrodynamic effects—including both mass and stiffness contributions—are adequately incorporated. This includes the modeling of vertical water pressure, sloshing, and fluid-structure interaction. The technical bases for the methods used to account for these effects must be provided and justified. Acceptable methods may include added mass approaches, coupled fluid-structure analyses, or other appropriate techniques. The modeling should capture both impulsive and convective (sloshing) components of the fluid response. The adequacy of the chosen analytical approach must be demonstrated through comparison with test data, published literature, or other suitable means (SRP 3.7.2, II.3.D).

Furthermore, seismic analyses must consider three orthogonal components of ground motion (two horizontal and one vertical), as specified in SRP 3.7.1 and DSRS 3.7.2, ensuring that vertical hydrodynamic effects are not neglected. The overall design must comply with the general design criteria in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2, which requires that safety-related structures withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including earthquakes, with appropriate consideration of all relevant loads and interactions.

In summary, NRC review standards require a technically justified, comprehensive approach to modeling hydrodynamic effects in seismic analyses of safety-related pools, with explicit consideration of vertical water pressure and fluid-structure interaction, supported by technical bases such as test data or literature comparisons.

To be acceptable, the seismic design response spectra should be specified for three mutually orthogonal directions - two horizontal and one vertical. Current practice is to assume that the design response spectra (including maximum ground accelerations) in the two horizontal directions are the same.

B. Design Time Histories. The SSE and OBE design ground motion time histories can be either real time histories or artificial time histories. To be acceptable, the design ground motion time histories should consist of three mutually orthogonal directions - two horizontal and one vertical. For both horizontal and vertical input motions, either a single time history or multiple time histories can be used. When time histories are used, each of the three ground motion time histories should be shown to be statistically independent from the others. Each of the three time histories should be compatible with the corresponding design response spectrum for the appropriate direction. The procedures used to generate response spectra from the artificial time histories and the comparisons of these response spectra with the design response spectra are reviewed.

... The seismic system analysis which utilizes the design ground motion developed in this SRP section is reviewed under SRP Section 3.7.2.

... The required safety functions of SSCs must be assured during and after the vibratory ground motion through design, testing, or qualification methods. The evaluation must take into account SSI effects and the expected duration of the vibratory motion.

evidence_chain.section: II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA, 4. Design and Analysis Procedures
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
4. Design and Analysis Procedures.  The design and analysis procedures used for seismic Category I foundations are acceptable if found to be in accordance with the following:

A. The design should consider the soil-structure interaction (SSI), hydrodynamic effect, and dynamic soil pressure.

...

In addition to the above, the design and analysis procedures for the following details are reviewed on a case-by-case basis:

A. Appropriateness of the method for determination of the bending moments and shear forces in the mat foundation for seismic loads.

B. Adequacy of the sliding analysis method and the analysis results to account for potential mat foundation liftoff effects.  The staff should also review the calculation of the factor of safety against sliding.  If sliding resistance is the sum of shear friction along the basemat and contribution of soil lateral pressure up to the full passive pressure capacity induced by embedment effects, the adequacy of the analysis to consider these effects is addressed using a consistent lateral displacement criterion.  This involves the use of static versus dynamic coefficient of friction consistent with the use of partial versus full passive pressure.  The reviewer should also consider whether the selection of the coefficient of friction used in the sliding stability analysis considers the various sliding interfaces (e.g., soil shear failure, concrete to soil, waterproofing to soil, concrete basemat to concrete mudmat).

If the stability evaluation is performed based on a pseudo-static approach, using the maximum seismic demand loads (e.g., maximum forces in the two horizontal directions and one vertical direction), then the factors of safety for sliding and overturning can be determined by the ratio of capacity to demand loads.  

However, if a linear time history analysis approach is utilized, then the factor of safety can be calculated at each time step throughout the time history.  The minimum value of the factors of safety calculated in this manner should be compared against the acceptance criteria for that load combination.  For the pseudo-static and time history analysis methods, all three directional demand forces should be considered to act simultaneously.  Therefore, the resultant seismic forces (horizontal resultant force for sliding from the two horizontal forces and similarly the resultant overturning moment for overturning stability) should be considered.  In the case of the sliding evaluation, if instead of using the resultant horizontal force with the vertical force, each pair of horizontal force and vertical force is evaluated separately, then the frictional resistance in the horizontal directions should be apportioned considering the existence of the two horizontal forces.

If the stability evaluation is performed using a nonlinear time history analysis that includes foundation sliding and uplift, the analysis should consider the following criteria:  

i. The development of the set of time histories should follow the guidance described in SRP Section 3.7.1.  This includes identification of the number of time histories needed to perform the nonlinear time history analyses and the development of each of the individual time histories.  In this case, the guidance in SRP 3.7.1 II.B, Option 2, for multiple sets of time histories is applicable.

ii. To demonstrate an adequate factor of safety, the seismic input time histories should be increased by a factor equal to the factor of safety for the applicable load combination (e.g., increase the seismic input time history amplitudes by a factor of 1.1 for load combination C).  No, or minimal sliding, and no overturning should be demonstrated for each of the time history analyses.

iii. The mathematical model should include the effects of sliding and uplift between the foundation and the soil media using appropriate finite elements that can simulate sliding once the frictional limit is reached and can simulate contact surfaces that can transmit compression but not tension.

iv. The sliding and overturning stability evaluation should consider the various significant parameters that were evaluated in the design basis seismic SSI analysis (e.g., range of soil profiles, concrete stiffness variation).

v. If the input motion applied at the foundation of a structural model without the soil is developed from the response of the linear SSI analysis, justification is needed to demonstrate that any minimal sliding or uplift would not affect the assumed seismic input motion taken from the SSI analysis that does not consider any sliding and uplift.  Alternatively, the structural model could be coupled with the soil model and a nonlinear SSI analysis performed.

vi. The mathematical model should adequately represent the dynamic characteristics of the structure and capture the vibration modes important for the sliding and overturning stability analysis.

vii. If some minimal sliding does occur, the justification for incurring a small magnitude of sliding needs to be provided.  In this case, the magnitude of sliding should be based on the envelope of the values obtained from the individual time history analyses.  In addition, the magnitude of sliding/overturning plus the SSI building displacements need to be evaluated for adequate seismic gaps between structures, and the design adequacy of commodities attached to the structures (e.g., piping and conduit between adjacent structures above grade; buried piping, conduit, and tunnels) need to be evaluated.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating the effects of soil-structure interaction in seismic system analysis for nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating the effects of soil-structure interaction (SSI) in seismic system analysis for nuclear power plants are grounded in the requirements of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A (General Design Criterion 2) and Appendix S, as well as detailed guidance in the DSRS and SRP sections (DSRS 3.7.2, DSRS 3.7.1, SRP 2.5.2, SRP 3.7.1).

Key criteria include:

1. The design basis must reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe earthquakes historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; DSRS 3.7.2, Section II; SRP 2.5.2, Section II).

2. For safe shutdown earthquake (SSE) ground motions, safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) must remain functional and within applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits during and after the vibratory ground motion. The evaluation must explicitly account for SSI effects and the expected duration of the motion (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S; DSRS 3.7.2, Section II; SRP 2.5.2, Section II).

3. Seismic analysis of seismic Category I SSCs should use suitable dynamic analysis methods (such as time history or response spectrum analysis), with dynamic analysis preferred for SSI. The response spectrum analysis method is generally not suitable for SSI unless justified (DSRS 3.7.2, Section II.1.A.i).

4. SSI modeling must consider factors such as the random nature of soil, uncertainty in soil constitutive modeling, nonlinear soil behavior, coupling, lack of lateral uniformity, flexibility of soil/rock and basemat, pore water effects, separation/loss of contact, deep embedment effects, and incoherence (DSRS 3.7.2, Section II.1.A.i).

5. The design ground motion for SSI analysis is established using site-specific free-field input response spectra (FIRS) and performance-based response spectra (PBRS), with a minimum required peak ground acceleration (PGA) of 0.1g for the horizontal component at the foundation level (DSRS 3.7.1, Section II; SRP 3.7.1, Section II; SRP 2.5.2, Section II).

6. If the operating basis earthquake (OBE) is set at one-third or less of the SSE, explicit SSI analysis is not required. If OBE exceeds one-third of SSE, analysis must demonstrate that SSCs remain within applicable limits under combined OBE and normal loads (DSRS 3.7.1, Section II; SRP 2.5.2, Section II).

In summary, the NRC requires that SSI effects be rigorously evaluated using appropriate dynamic analysis methods, with consideration of site-specific soil conditions and uncertainties, to ensure that safety-related SSCs maintain their safety functions during and after seismic events, in accordance with regulatory requirements and acceptance criteria outlined in the referenced documents.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

Requirements

Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations:

1. Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, GDC 2—The design basis shall reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe earthquakes that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which historical data have been accumulated.

2. Appendix S, “Earthquake Engineering Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants,” to 10 CFR Part 50, is applicable to applications for a DC or COL under 10 CFR Part 52, “Licenses, Certifications, and Approvals for Nuclear Power Plants,” or a CP or OL pursuant to 10 CFR Part 50, “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities,” on or after January 10, 1997. Appendix S requires that, for SSE ground motions, certain SSCs will remain functional and within applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits. The required safety functions of these SSCs must be assured during and after the vibratory ground motion associated with the SSE ground motion through design, testing, or qualification methods. The evaluation must take into account SSI effects and the expected duration of the vibratory motion. ...

DSRS Acceptance Criteria

Specific DSRS acceptance criteria acceptable to meet the relevant requirements of the NRC’s regulations identified above are set forth below. ...

Appendix S requires that, for SSE ground motions, certain SSCs will remain functional and within applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits.  The required safety functions of these SSCs must be assured during and after the vibratory ground motion associated with the SSE ground motion through design, testing, or qualification methods.  The evaluation must take into account SSI effects and the expected duration of the vibratory motion.  If the OBE is set at one-third or less of the SSE, an explicit response or design analysis is not required.  If the OBE is set at a value greater than one-third of the SSE, an analysis and design must be performed to demonstrate that, when subjected to the effects of the OBE in combination with normal operating loads, all SSCs of the nuclear power plant necessary for continued operation without undue risk to the health and safety of the public remain functional and within applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits.  Appendix S also requires that the horizontal component of the SSE ground motion in the free field at the foundation level of the structures must be an appropriate response spectrum with a PGA of at least 0.1g.

... 

DSRS Acceptance Criteria

Specific DSRS acceptance criteria acceptable to meet the relevant requirements of the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s (NRC’s) regulations identified above are set forth below.  The DSRS is not a substitute for the NRC’s regulations, and compliance with it is not required.  

1. Design Ground Motion

A. Design Response Spectra.  The site-specific FIRS and PBRS reviewed under this DSRS section are determined as free-field outcrop motions at the foundation level, the surface, and other appropriate intermediate depths.  FIRS and associated deterministic soil profiles developed using the PBRS to meet the performance goal will establish the design basis for the site-specific SSI analysis; this design basis is developed using the guidance provided in SRP Section 2.5.2.

For sites with soil layers near the surface that will be completely excavated (defined as excavations to distances sufficiently far from the structures to be considered infinitely far from the facility over the frequency range of interest) and replaced with compacted backfill, the FIRS and PBRS are determined using the site profiles including the replacement backfill.  The competent material is generally considered to be in situ material having a minimum shear wave velocity of 1,000 fps.  Any remaining soft soil or backfill material needs to be considered in the SSI or other analyses.

According to Appendix S to 10 CFR Part 50, the minimum PGA for the horizontal component of the SSE at the foundation level in the free field should be 0.1g or higher.  The response spectrum associated with this minimum PGA should be a smooth broadband response spectrum (e.g., RG 1.60, or other appropriate shaped spectra, if justified) and is defined as outcrop response spectra at the free-field foundation level.  This response spectrum anchored to 0.1g is referred to in this DSRS section as the minimum required response spectrum.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory requirements for seismic system analysis address the consideration of different soil types, including hard rock, when evaluating soil-structure interaction effects?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory requirements for seismic system analysis explicitly address the consideration of different soil types, including hard rock, when evaluating soil-structure interaction (SSI) effects. According to DSRS 3.7.2, the foundation input response spectra (FIRS) and performance-based response spectra (PBRS) are developed using site-specific soil columns that represent the actual subsurface conditions, including soil layering and properties. These spectra are probabilistically determined using randomized sets of soil and rock properties, reflecting the variability and uncertainty inherent in site conditions (DSRS 3.7.2, Section I.4; DSRS 3.7.1, Section I.1.A).

The NRC requires that the SSI analysis account for the random nature of soil and rock configurations, uncertainties in material characteristics, nonlinear soil behavior, and the coupling between soil and structures. The analysis must also consider the flexibility of both soil and rock, and any lack of lateral uniformity in the site profile (DSRS 3.7.2, Section I.4). For sites where surface soils are excavated to expose competent material (defined as in situ material with a minimum shear wave velocity of 1,000 fps), or where backfill is used, the effects of these layers must be included in the SSI analysis (DSRS 3.7.2, Section I.4; DSRS 3.7.1, Section I.1.A).

SRP 2.5.2 and RG 1.138 further require detailed site investigations and laboratory testing to characterize the engineering properties of both soils and rocks, including wave propagation characteristics, shear and compressional wave velocities, and dynamic moduli and damping ratios (SRP 2.5.2, Section II; RG 1.138, Sections C.4 and C.4.5). These properties are essential inputs for dynamic SSI analyses. The regulatory framework ensures that the seismic response of structures is evaluated using site-specific data that reflect the full range of possible soil and rock conditions, including hard rock, and their interaction with the structure.

In summary, NRC requirements mandate a comprehensive, site-specific approach to SSI analysis that rigorously considers the effects of different soil types, including hard rock, through probabilistic modeling, laboratory testing, and detailed site characterization (DSRS 3.7.2, DSRS 3.7.1, SRP 2.5.2, RG 1.138).

evidence_chain.section: I. AREAS OF REVIEW, 4. Soil-Structure Interaction
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
4. Soil-Structure Interaction.  Foundation input response spectra (FIRS) which is the ground motion response spectra at the foundation level are defined in the free field (i.e., without the presence of structures) as described in DSRS Section 3.7.1, DC/COL-ISG-01, “Interim Staff Guidance on Seismic Issues Associated with High Frequency Ground Motion in Design Certification and Combined License Applications,” and DC/COL-ISG-017, “Interim Staff Guidance on Ensuring Hazard-Consistent Seismic Input for Site Response and Soil Structure Interaction Analyses.”  For a deeply embedded structure, performance-based response spectra (PBRS) are also defined in the free field at the ground surface and appropriate intermediate depth(s) to ensure the adequacy of the soil columns used in the deterministic SSI analysis and to determine the potential magnitude of kinematic interaction effects on the structure over the depth of the facility.  The FIRS and PBRS determined at the foundation level, surface, and intermediate depth(s) should be developed in a consistent manner.  They are probabilistically determined performance-based spectra generated using the soil column corresponding to the building.  The properties of the soil columns usually consist of 60 or more randomized sets of properties similar to those used in the probabilistic seismic hazard analysis (PSHA) process.  For sites with soil layers near the surface that will be completely excavated to expose competent material and replaced with extended compacted backfill layers, the FIRS and PBRS are determined by considering the effect of the backfill layers in the site profiles.  FIRS at the foundation and PBRS at intermediate levels should also be developed as free field outcrop motions, not as in-column motions.  Competent material is generally considered to be in situ material having a minimum shear wave velocity of 1,000 fps.

As applicable, the staff reviews the modeling methods (including technical bases) used in the seismic system analysis to account for SSI.  The factors to be considered in accepting a particular modeling method include (1) the extent of embedment, (2) the layering of the soil/rock strata, and (3) the boundary of the soil-structure model.  All SSI analyses should recognize the uncertainties prevalent throughout the phenomenon and include consideration of the following:

A. The random nature of the soil and rock configuration and material characteristics.

B. Uncertainty in soil constitutive modeling (soil stiffness, damping, etc.).

C. Nonlinear soil behavior.

D. Coupling between the structures and soil.

E. Lack of lateral uniformity in the site soil profile that is usually assumed to be uniformly layered in all horizontal directions in SSI analyses.

F. Effects of the flexibility of soil/rock.

evidence_chain.section: I. AREAS OF REVIEW, 1. Design Ground Motion, A. Design Response Spectra
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
The GMRS reviewed under SRP Section 2.5.2 are site-specific horizontal and vertical free-field ground motion response spectra determined at the ground surface or at the free-field outcrop of the uppermost in situ competent material using performance-based procedures in accordance with RG 1.208. The performance-based site-specific GMRS transferred to the foundation level in the free field is referred to as the foundation input response spectra (FIRS). Therefore, the FIRS satisfy the same performance criteria as the GMRS. Both the GMRS and the FIRS are defined as free-field outcrop response spectra. The FIRS is the starting point for conducting an SSI analysis and for making a one-to-one comparison of the seismic design capacity of the standard design and the site-specific seismic demand for a site. The FIRS for the vertical direction is obtained with the vertical to horizontal (V/H) ratios appropriate for the site. GMRS are those derived from the global understanding of the site soil layers above the rock condition as determined from the site exploration activities and, therefore, are unique to a particular site.

Competent material is generally considered to be in situ material having a minimum shear wave velocity of 1,000 feet per second (fps). If noncompetent material is present, any excavation and/or backfilling should not alter the development or location of the GMRS; however, the development of the FIRS uses the site profiles, including the effect of backfill. The remaining soft soil or backfill material needs to be considered in the SSI or other analyses. Further information on the development of the GMRS and FIRS is provided in DC/COL-ISG-01, “Interim Staff Guidance on Seismic Issues Associated with High Frequency Ground Motion in Design Certification and Combined License Applications,” and DC/COL-ISG-17, “Interim Staff Guidance on Ensuring Hazard-Consistent Seismic Input for Site Response and Soil Structure Interaction Analyses.”

In addition to the FIRS, additional performance-based response spectra (PBRS) need to be developed at one or more intermediate depths between the foundation and ground surface. The PBRS need to be probabilistically determined using procedures that are consistent with the development of the FIRS. The PBRS are performance-based free-field outcrop response spectra generated using the soil column corresponding to the building for which the performance-based FIRS are also generated. The properties of the soil column are used to generate 60 or more randomized sets of properties similar to those used in the probabilistic seismic hazard analysis (PSHA) process as described in SRP Section 2.5.2. The resulting PBRS described above are the PBRS for the horizontal direction and may be established at various elevations in the free field. The PBRS developed at the ground surface is referred to as the performance-based surface response spectra (PBSRS) as described in DC/COL-ISG-017. The PBRS for the vertical direction can be obtained with the appropriate V/H ratios used to develop the FIRS. In addition, the methodology for developing V/H ratios for deep soil site conditions is reviewed on a case-by-case basis. The PBRS are used to verify and ensure that the soil columns to be used in a deterministic SSI analysis produce response spectra at the surface and other locations in the free field, which envelope the corresponding PBRS. Additional guidance for demonstrating the adequacy of the soil columns is provided in Design-Specific Review Standard (DSRS) Section 3.7.2 II.4. The FIRS and PBRS are associated with subsurface conditions localized to a specific building.

evidence_chain.section: Section C.4 and C.4.5 (Selection and Preparation of Test Specimens; Laboratory Testing Program)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
4. Selection and Preparation of Test Specimens
4.1. General
a. Undisturbed samples of earth fill should be taken for confirmatory testing during construction and in the testing and re-evaluation of existing structures.
b. Procedures for preparing soil samples for testing should be documented. Details of procedures depend on the nature of the test and the specimen.
For additional information, EM 1110-2-1906 describes procedures for preparing soil samples for testing, and ASTM D4452 can be used to determine the quality of a sample before testing. Regulatory Guide 1.132 discusses methods of determining the in situ density of cohesionless soils.
c. The selection of soil and rock specimens for laboratory testing requires careful examination of records of borings and available samples. To permit establishment of the soil profile, investigators should ensure that test specimens are representative of the soil or rock unit to be tested and should describe them accurately. The number of test specimens should be sufficient to produce statistically meaningful test results. Investigators should identify average test values of material properties as well as the range of values that identify their variability. In addition to the most representative samples, investigators should also test samples that have extreme properties and represent critical zones.

...

4.5. Laboratory Testing Program

a. The study of soil and rock mechanics covers the investigation, description, classification, testing, and analysis of soil and rock to determine their interaction with structures built in, upon, or with them. The physical properties of soils and rocks should be determined by carrying out tests on samples of soil in a laboratory. These tests fall into two main categories: classification tests and engineering properties tests. Classification tests indicate the general type of soil and the engineering category to which it belongs. Specific tests to determine engineering properties require careful consideration of field conditions, various design loading conditions, material properties, and possible problems at the site. The focus of laboratory investigations should depend on the design requirements and nature of problems encountered or suspected at the site.
b. In addition to the usual geotechnical engineering considerations, the investigation and evaluation of sites for nuclear power plants requires an evaluation of the site’s response to earthquake loading and other dynamic loading conditions. Such analyses include the evaluation of wave propagation characteristics of subsurface materials with interaction effects of structures, analysis of the potential for soil liquefaction, settlement under dynamic loading, and analysis of the effects of earthquake loading on the stability of slope and embankments.
c. The basic parameters required as input for dynamic response analyses of soils include total mass density, relative density, Poisson’s ratio, static soil strength, initial stress conditions, shear and compressional wave velocities, and the dynamic shear modulus and damping ratio. Such analyses also need the variation of strength, moduli, and damping with strain.

data.query: In the context of seismic system analysis for nuclear power plants, what regulatory guidance governs the selection and justification of correction factors for soil-structure interaction effects when the boundary conditions of fixed-base and flexible-base models are similar, particularly for hard rock sites? Additionally, what are the regulatory expectations for technically justifying approaches to account for fluid-structure interaction effects on vertical water pressure estimation in safety-related pools?
data.answer:
The regulatory guidance governing the selection and justification of correction factors for soil-structure interaction (SSI) effects, particularly when the boundary conditions of fixed-base and flexible-base models are similar (such as at hard rock sites), is primarily found in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, Section III.3. This section requires that, for structures founded on rock, the analysis must consider the potential for amplification or deamplification of seismic motions due to the structure and rock properties. Specifically, it states that where the boundary conditions of fixed-base and flexible-base models are similar, the use of correction factors must be technically justified. This means that any deviation from standard modeling approaches, such as applying correction factors, must be supported by a robust technical basis that addresses the specific site conditions and modeling assumptions.

Further, DSRS 3.7.2 (Section I.4 and II.1.B) reinforces that all SSI analyses should recognize uncertainties and include consideration of the flexibility of soil/rock, the extent of embedment, and the boundary of the soil-structure model. The NRC staff reviews the technical bases for modeling methods and any justification for not using an SSI analysis or for using alternative approaches, such as equivalent static load factors. For example, a factor less than the standard 1.5 may be used if adequately justified.

Regarding fluid-structure interaction (FSI) effects on vertical water pressure estimation in safety-related pools, Appendix S, Section III.4, requires that the effects of interaction between the structure and contained fluids must be considered in the design and analysis of safety-related pools and tanks. The estimation of vertical water pressures and other hydrodynamic effects must be based on technically justified approaches that account for the dynamic response of both the fluid and the structure. DSRS 3.7.2 (II.1.B.vii) also expects inclusion of significant effects such as hydrodynamic loads in the analysis. DSRS 3.8.4 (II.4.B) further specifies that the approach used to analyze and develop loads, including those from fluid interaction in reactor pools, must be reviewed for adequacy.

In summary, the NRC expects that any correction factors or modeling approaches for SSI and FSI effects must be supported by a thorough technical justification, particularly when standard assumptions do not apply or are modified due to site-specific conditions such as hard rock foundations or complex fluid-structure interactions.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory standards address the consideration of soil-structure interaction correction factors when analyzing seismic responses for nuclear power plant structures founded on hard rock?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory standards require that soil-structure interaction (SSI) be thoroughly considered in the seismic analysis of nuclear power plant structures, including those founded on hard rock. According to DSRS 3.7.2, Section I.4, the NRC staff reviews the modeling methods used for SSI, focusing on factors such as the extent of embedment, layering of soil/rock strata, and the boundaries of the soil-structure model. The analysis must account for uncertainties in soil and rock properties, nonlinear soil behavior, coupling between soil and structure, and the flexibility of both the soil/rock and the structure itself. For structures founded on hard rock, the flexibility of the rock and any remaining soft soil or backfill must be considered (DSRS 3.7.1, Section II.1). The NRC also requires that strain-dependent soil properties, layering, and property variations be incorporated into the analysis, and that the technical bases and validation of modeling assumptions be reviewed.

Correction factors, such as those for damping and amplification, are addressed through the use of standardized response spectra (e.g., RG 1.60) and, where appropriate, site-specific procedures reviewed on a case-by-case basis (DSRS 3.7.1, Section II.1). For hard rock sites, the competent material is defined by a minimum shear wave velocity, and any remaining softer materials must be included in the SSI analysis. The overall regulatory basis, as stated in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2, requires that structures be designed to withstand seismic events with appropriate consideration of uncertainties and margins, ensuring safety functions are maintained. Thus, NRC standards require explicit consideration of SSI correction factors, including those relevant to hard rock foundations, to ensure seismic responses are accurately analyzed and safety is maintained.

data.query: What are the regulatory expectations for accounting for fluid-structure interaction effects when estimating vertical water pressures in safety-related pools during seismic events?
data.answer:
The regulatory expectations for accounting for fluid-structure interaction (FSI) effects, specifically hydrodynamic effects, when estimating vertical water pressures in safety-related pools during seismic events are clearly outlined in NRC guidance and regulations. According to DSRS 3.7.2 (Section I, Areas of Review and Section II, Acceptance Criteria), the NRC staff reviews seismic analyses of safety-related (seismic Category I) structures to ensure that significant effects—including hydrodynamic effects—are properly modeled. This includes the consideration of both mass and stiffness effects of the fluid, as well as nonlinear responses that may arise during seismic events. The modeling must account for the interaction between the fluid (water) and the structure, which directly affects the estimation of vertical water pressures during seismic loading.

Furthermore, the acceptance criteria in DSRS 3.7.2 (II.1.A.vii, 3) require that the procedures for modeling hydrodynamic effects are reviewed, ensuring that the analysis captures the impact of fluid-structure interaction on structural responses. This is consistent with the broader regulatory basis in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2, which mandates that safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) be designed to withstand natural phenomena, including earthquakes, without loss of safety function. The design must consider appropriate combinations of normal, accident, and natural phenomena effects, which includes hydrodynamic loads from water in pools.

Additionally, SRP 2.5.2 and SRP 3.7.1 reinforce that soil-structure interaction (SSI) and hydrodynamic effects must be included in the seismic analysis to ensure that SSCs remain functional during and after seismic events. The evaluation must use site-specific seismic input motions and soil profiles, and must demonstrate that stress, strain, and deformation limits are not exceeded, taking into account the duration and characteristics of the seismic motion.

In summary, NRC regulatory expectations require that seismic analyses for safety-related pools explicitly account for fluid-structure interaction effects, including hydrodynamic pressures, using appropriate modeling techniques. These analyses must demonstrate that the structures can withstand the combined effects of seismic and hydrodynamic loads, ensuring continued safety function as required by DSRS 3.7.2, 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A, and supporting SRP sections.

data.query: How are soil-structure interaction effects considered in the seismic analysis of nuclear power plant structures, and what is the regulatory basis for applying correction factors when hard rock site conditions are present?
data.answer:
Soil-structure interaction (SSI) effects are a critical consideration in the seismic analysis of nuclear power plant structures. According to DSRS 3.7.2, SSI analysis involves defining the foundation input response spectra (FIRS) at the foundation level in the free field, which serves as the seismic input for the analysis. The FIRS is developed based on site-specific ground motion response spectra (GMRS) and accounts for the characteristics of the soil and rock strata, including layering, extent of embedment, and boundary conditions of the soil-structure model. The analysis must consider uncertainties in SSI phenomena, such as the flexibility of soil or rock, and ensure that safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) remain functional within stress, strain, and deformation limits during and after seismic events (DSRS 3.7.2, Section II; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S).

For sites with hard rock conditions (shear wave velocity greater than 2.5 km/sec), 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S explicitly requires that the seismic input motion be appropriately modified to account for the reduced SSI effects. This may involve the application of correction factors or alternative methodologies, which must be justified and documented in the seismic analysis. The regulatory basis for this requirement is found in Appendix S, which mandates that the methods used to account for SSI effects, including correction factors for hard rock sites, be consistent with current engineering practice and be described and justified in the safety analysis report (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, Section II).

In summary, SSI effects are incorporated into seismic analyses through the development of site-specific input motions and detailed modeling of soil and structural interactions. For hard rock sites, regulatory guidance requires the use of justified correction factors to reflect the diminished SSI effects, ensuring that the seismic design remains robust and consistent with regulatory expectations.

I. Introduction

Nuclear power plant structures, systems, and components important to safety must be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena such as earthquakes without loss of capability to perform their safety functions. data.query: What regulatory guidance addresses the estimation of vertical water pressure due to seismic effects in pools, and how should fluid-structure interaction be incorporated into this calculation?
data.answer:
The regulatory guidance addressing the estimation of vertical water pressure due to seismic effects in pools, and the incorporation of fluid-structure interaction (FSI) into this calculation, is primarily found in DSRS 3.7.2 and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S.

DSRS 3.7.2 explicitly requires that seismic system analyses for nuclear facilities consider hydrodynamic effects, which include the vertical water pressure induced by seismic events in pools. The guidance specifies that analytical modeling must account for hydrodynamic effects and fluid-structure interaction (FSI), both in the modeling of mass and stiffness and in the dynamic analysis methods used (DSRS 3.7.2, I. AREAS OF REVIEW; II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA). The review process includes evaluating the criteria and procedures for modeling these effects, ensuring that both mass and stiffness contributions from the contained fluid are included in the seismic response analysis. The acceptance criteria further require that dynamic analyses (such as response spectrum or time history methods) incorporate significant effects, including hydrodynamic loads and FSI (DSRS 3.7.2, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA).

10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, Section IV, reinforces this requirement by mandating that the seismic design and analysis of safety-related structures must consider the dynamic effects of the safe-shutdown earthquake (SSE), including the interaction of the structure with contained fluids (FSI). The regulation specifies that both vertical and horizontal components of ground motion must be included, and that the analysis must estimate forces and deformations resulting from FSI for use in design (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, IV.2 and IV.3).

In summary, both DSRS 3.7.2 and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, require that vertical water pressure due to seismic effects in pools be estimated by incorporating hydrodynamic effects and fluid-structure interaction into the seismic analysis using appropriate dynamic modeling methods.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory standards address the consideration of soil-structure interaction effects when performing seismic system analysis for nuclear power plant structures founded on hard rock?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory standards require that soil-structure interaction (SSI) effects be considered in the seismic system analysis of nuclear power plant structures, including those founded on hard rock. According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, Section II.1, the dynamic analysis of safety-related structures must include SSI effects, except for structures founded on competent rock where such effects are negligible. For structures on hard rock, a fixed-base response analysis may be used, but only if its adequacy is demonstrated through appropriate engineering evaluation (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, II.1(b)).

DSRS 3.7.2 further clarifies that the foundation input response spectra (FIRS) should be defined at the foundation level in the free field, and the modeling methods for SSI analysis must consider factors such as the extent of embedment, layering of soil/rock strata, and model boundaries. The analysis should account for uncertainties in soil and rock properties, nonlinear soil behavior, coupling between structure and soil, and the flexibility of both the soil/rock and the structure itself (DSRS 3.7.2, I.4). For sites where the foundation is on competent material (shear wave velocity ≥ 1,000 fps), and SSI effects are shown to be negligible, a fixed-base assumption may be justified (DSRS 3.7.1, I; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S).

However, the NRC requires that the assumption of negligible SSI effects for hard rock foundations be supported by engineering evaluation. If SSI effects are not negligible, a full SSI analysis must be performed, considering the specific site conditions and uncertainties (DSRS 3.7.2, I.4; SRP 2.5.2, II). The FIRS and performance-based response spectra (PBRS) must be developed consistently, and the analysis must ensure that safety-related structures, systems, and components remain functional within stress, strain, and deformation limits during and after seismic events (SRP 2.5.2, II; DSRS 3.7.1, I).

In summary, NRC standards allow for a fixed-base analysis for structures founded on hard rock only if it is demonstrated that SSI effects are negligible; otherwise, a comprehensive SSI analysis is required, with careful consideration of site-specific conditions and uncertainties.

evidence_chain.section: I. AREAS OF REVIEW, 4. Soil-Structure Interaction
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
4. Soil-Structure Interaction.  Foundation input response spectra (FIRS) which is the ground motion response spectra at the foundation level are defined in the free field (i.e., without the presence of structures) as described in DSRS Section 3.7.1, DC/COL-ISG-01, “Interim Staff Guidance on Seismic Issues Associated with High Frequency Ground Motion in Design Certification and Combined License Applications,” and DC/COL-ISG-017, “Interim Staff Guidance on Ensuring Hazard-Consistent Seismic Input for Site Response and Soil Structure Interaction Analyses.”  For a deeply embedded structure, performance-based response spectra (PBRS) are also defined in the free field at the ground surface and appropriate intermediate depth(s) to ensure the adequacy of the soil columns used in the deterministic SSI analysis and to determine the potential magnitude of kinematic interaction effects on the structure over the depth of the facility.  The FIRS and PBRS determined at the foundation level, surface, and intermediate depth(s) should be developed in a consistent manner.  They are probabilistically determined performance-based spectra generated using the soil column corresponding to the building.  The properties of the soil columns usually consist of 60 or more randomized sets of properties similar to those used in the probabilistic seismic hazard analysis (PSHA) process.  For sites with soil layers near the surface that will be completely excavated to expose competent material and replaced with extended compacted backfill layers, the FIRS and PBRS are determined by considering the effect of the backfill layers in the site profiles.  FIRS at the foundation and PBRS at intermediate levels should also be developed as free field outcrop motions, not as in-column motions.  Competent material is generally considered to be in situ material having a minimum shear wave velocity of 1,000 fps.

As applicable, the staff reviews the modeling methods (including technical bases) used in the seismic system analysis to account for SSI.  The factors to be considered in accepting a particular modeling method include (1) the extent of embedment, (2) the layering of the soil/rock strata, and (3) the boundary of the soil-structure model.  All SSI analyses should recognize the uncertainties prevalent throughout the phenomenon and include consideration of the following:

A. The random nature of the soil and rock configuration and material characteristics.

B. Uncertainty in soil constitutive modeling (soil stiffness, damping, etc.).

C. Nonlinear soil behavior.

D. Coupling between the structures and soil.

E. Lack of lateral uniformity in the site soil profile that is usually assumed to be uniformly layered in all horizontal directions in SSI analyses.

F. Effects of the flexibility of soil/rock.

G. Effects of the flexibility of basemat, sidewalls, and interior structures.

H. The effect of pore water on structural responses, including the effects of variability of ground water level with time.

I. Effects of potential separation or loss of contact between the structure (embedded portion of the structure and foundation mat) and the soil during the earthquake.

J. For deeply embedded or fully buried structures, (1) the effect of deep embedment on the relative significance of kinematic interaction, (2) the extent to which nonvertically propagating shear waves may be more important for deeply embedded structures than for those with shallow embedment depth, (3) the impact of deep embedment on the accuracy of sidewall impedance functions calculated with standard methods, (4) the effect of nonlinear behavior (e.g., separation of structure and soil, and soil material properties) on wall pressure and SSI calculations, and (5) the variation of V/H (vertical to horizontal) spectral ratios on ground motion over the depth of the facility.

data.query: What is the regulatory basis for accounting for fluid-structure interaction effects in the estimation of vertical water pressure loads during seismic events in nuclear facility safety-related pools?
data.answer:
The regulatory basis for accounting for fluid-structure interaction (FSI) effects in the estimation of vertical water pressure loads during seismic events in nuclear facility safety-related pools is established through both the Design-Specific Review Standard (DSRS) 3.7.2 and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criteria (GDC) 2. 

DSRS 3.7.2, Sections I and II, specifies that the NRC staff reviews seismic analysis methods for seismic Category I structures, which includes the modeling of hydrodynamic effects—explicitly referencing both mass and stiffness effects. The review encompasses the procedures and criteria used in modeling hydrodynamic effects as part of the dynamic system analysis, ensuring that the interaction between the fluid (water) and the structure is appropriately considered. This includes the impact of pore water on structural responses and the variability of groundwater levels, which are essential for accurately estimating vertical water pressure loads during seismic events. The DSRS further requires that dynamic analyses for seismic Category I structures include significant effects such as hydrodynamic loads and nonlinear responses, thereby mandating the consideration of FSI in the safety analysis of pools.

Additionally, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2, requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including earthquakes, without loss of safety function. The design bases must reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe natural phenomena, including the combination of normal, accident, and natural event effects. This regulatory criterion underpins the requirement to account for all relevant physical interactions, such as FSI, to ensure the integrity and safety function of safety-related pools during seismic events.

In summary, the regulatory basis is grounded in DSRS 3.7.2's explicit requirements for hydrodynamic modeling in seismic analysis and GDC 2's mandate for robust design against natural phenomena, collectively ensuring that FSI effects are properly accounted for in the estimation of vertical water pressure loads during seismic events.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for defining the pressure boundary of a steel containment vessel in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for defining the pressure boundary of a steel containment vessel in nuclear power plants are grounded in compliance with specific regulatory requirements, codes, and standards. According to DSRS 3.8.2 (Section II), the primary regulatory basis includes 10 CFR 50.55a, 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A (notably General Design Criteria 1, 2, 4, 16, 50, and 53), and 10 CFR 50.44. These regulations require that the steel containment vessel meets quality, design, and testing standards to ensure structural integrity under all design-basis conditions.

The applicable codes and standards are primarily the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, Section III, Division 1, Subsection NE (Class MC Components), as mandated by 10 CFR 50.55a(b)(2). This code governs the design, materials, fabrication, erection, inspection, testing, and inservice surveillance of steel containment vessels. Additionally, ASME BPV Code Section XI, Subsection IWE, covers inservice inspection requirements.

Design limits for the pressure boundary are specified in RG 1.57, which requires that total stresses from the most adverse combination of loadings must remain within the limits defined by ASME BPV Code, Section III, Articles NE-3221.1 through NE-3221.4. Buckling effects under earthquake, thermal, and pressure loads must be evaluated, with complex cases addressed per ASME Code Case N-284-2 (RG 1.57).

For demonstrating containment pressure capacity above the design pressure, RG 1.216 (Regulatory Position 1) specifies that a nonlinear finite element analysis is typically required, and for cylindrical steel containments, the pressure capacity may be based on a maximum global membrane (hoop) strain of 1.5% away from discontinuities.

Weld fabrication and repair must comply with ASME Code Sections III and IX, with additional qualification and monitoring requirements as outlined in RG 1.71.

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria for defining the pressure boundary of a steel containment vessel require compliance with ASME BPV Code Section III (Class MC), adherence to design stress and strain limits, evaluation of buckling, and demonstration of adequate pressure capacity, all as detailed in DSRS 3.8.2, 10 CFR 50.55a, RG 1.57, RG 1.216, and RG 1.71.

The NRC also reviews the design to ensure it accommodates ISI of critical areas, including provisions for physical access, alternative means for identifying degradation in inaccessible areas, and remote visual monitoring in high-radiation zones (DSRS 3.8.2, Area of Review 7). Any special testing or surveillance requirements for new or untried designs are also subject to NRC review. In summary, the NRC mandates adherence to ASME BPV Code Section XI for ISI of containment welds, with additional requirements for accessibility and monitoring as necessary to ensure ongoing structural integrity.
