data.query: How do NRC regulatory guides for nondestructive examination relate to the acceptance criteria for materials and welds used in containment nozzles and associated pressure boundary components?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory guides for nondestructive examination (NDE) are closely related to the acceptance criteria for materials and welds used in containment nozzles and associated pressure boundary components through their integration with the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code requirements, as mandated by NRC regulations. According to DSRS 3.8.2, Section 6, the quality control program for containment vessel fabrication must emphasize compliance with Articles NB-2000, NB-4000, and NB-5000 of ASME BPV Code, Section III, Division 1, Subsection NB. This includes the nondestructive examination of materials and welds to determine their physical properties and ensure structural integrity. 

10 CFR 50.55a further requires that components of the reactor coolant pressure boundary, which include containment nozzles and associated pressure boundary components, be designed, fabricated, constructed, tested, and inspected to quality standards commensurate with their safety function. These standards are typically those of the ASME BPV Code, which incorporates NDE methods and acceptance criteria for materials and welds. The NRC may also require the use of additional regulatory guides or impose further requirements as necessary to ensure public health and safety (§ 50.55a(h)). 

In summary, NRC regulatory guides for NDE support and supplement the ASME BPV Code requirements, which are incorporated by reference in NRC regulations, to establish the acceptance criteria for materials and welds in containment nozzles and pressure boundary components. Compliance with these guides and codes is essential for demonstrating that the components meet the required quality and safety standards.

data.query: For welded and bolted connections forming part of the containment pressure boundary, what combined NRC regulatory provisions address inservice inspection, fabrication nondestructive examination, and periodic leakage testing to ensure ongoing structural and leakage integrity?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory provisions addressing inservice inspection, fabrication nondestructive examination, and periodic leakage testing for welded and bolted connections forming part of the containment pressure boundary are comprehensively established through a combination of requirements in 10 CFR 50.55a, the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (BPV Code), and NRC guidance documents.

For fabrication, 10 CFR 50.55a(c)(1) requires that the construction of components, including welded and bolted connections, must include nondestructive examination (NDE) methods as specified in ASME BPV Code, Section III. DSRS 3.8.2 further clarifies that the NRC reviews the quality control program for containment fabrication, emphasizing compliance with Articles NB-2000, NB-4000, and NB-5000 of ASME BPV Code, Section III, Division 1, Subsection NB, which cover material properties, welding procedures, and NDE of materials and welds.

For inservice inspection, 10 CFR 50.55a(g) mandates that licensees comply with ASME BPV Code, Section XI, for periodic inservice inspection (ISI) and testing of components. DSRS 3.8.2 specifies that components constructed to ASME BPV Code, Section III, Division 1, Subsection NB, should be subject to periodic examination in accordance with Section XI, Subsection IWB, ensuring ongoing structural integrity.

For periodic leakage testing, 10 CFR 50.55a(h) requires that primary reactor containment undergo periodic leakage rate testing as specified in Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50. DSRS 3.8.2 also notes that the NRC reviews pre-operational structural test programs and periodic surveillance to ensure compliance with Article NB-6000 of ASME BPV Code, Section III.

In summary, the NRC ensures the structural and leakage integrity of welded and bolted containment pressure boundary connections through: (1) fabrication NDE per ASME BPV Code, Section III (10 CFR 50.55a(c)), (2) periodic ISI per ASME BPV Code, Section XI (10 CFR 50.55a(g)), and (3) periodic leakage testing per Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50 (10 CFR 50.55a(h)), as reinforced by DSRS 3.8.2.

In summary, the NRC mandates that ISI methods for welds in steel containment penetrations follow the ASME BPV Code, Section XI, Subsection IWE, as referenced in 10 CFR 50.55a, and that the containment design facilitates effective inspection and surveillance of these welds.

Furthermore, components relied upon for containment structural integrity that are constructed in accordance with ASME BPV Code, Section III, Division 1, Subsection NB, are also subject to periodic inservice examination in accordance with ASME BPV Code, Section XI, Subsection IWB, as required by 10 CFR 50.55a(g) and referenced in DSRS 3.8.2, Areas of Review, 7. This ensures ongoing structural integrity through both initial fabrication NDE and subsequent inservice inspections.

In summary, NRC regulatory standards mandate that containment nozzle welds, as part of the reactor coolant pressure boundary, undergo NDE during fabrication in accordance with the applicable ASME BPV Code provisions (Section III, Subsection NB), and are subject to periodic inservice examination per Section XI, as incorporated by 10 CFR 50.55a.

data.answer:
The combined NRC regulatory requirements governing the inservice inspection, fabrication non-destructive examination, and periodic testing provisions for welded and bolted connections, including pressure-retaining seals, in a steel containment system with penetrations forming part of the reactor coolant pressure boundary are established primarily through 10 CFR 50.55a and the referenced ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code provisions.

According to 10 CFR 50.55a (§ 50.55a(a)-(d)), components of the reactor coolant pressure boundary and containment penetrations—including welded and bolted connections and pressure-retaining seals—must comply with the applicable editions and addenda of the ASME BPV Code and the ASME Code for Operation and Maintenance of Nuclear Power Plants (OM Code), as incorporated by reference. These requirements encompass design, fabrication, installation, examination, testing, inspection, and repair/replacement activities. DSRS 3.8.2 further clarifies that the NRC reviews the quality control program for containment fabrication, emphasizing compliance with ASME BPV Code, Section III, Division 1, Subsection NB (Articles NB-2000, NB-4000, NB-5000) for nondestructive examination, welding procedures, and erection tolerances. Pre-operational and periodic testing must comply with Article NB-6000 of Section III, and inservice inspection of critical areas must follow Section XI, Subsection IWB. The design must also accommodate ISI, including provisions for access and alternative monitoring methods for inaccessible or high-radiation areas.

In summary, the regulatory framework is based on 10 CFR 50.55a and the incorporated ASME BPV Code and OM Code requirements, as detailed in DSRS 3.8.2, covering all aspects of fabrication, examination, testing, and periodic inspection for welded and bolted connections and pressure-retaining seals in steel containment penetrations.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for inservice inspection methods to ensure the structural integrity of containment nozzle welds in steel containments?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for inservice inspection (ISI) methods to ensure the structural integrity of containment nozzle welds in steel containments are grounded in compliance with the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, as incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a. Specifically, steel containments and their integral attachments, including nozzle welds, must be designed and constructed in accordance with ASME BPV Code Section III, Division 1, Subsection NE (10 CFR 50.55a(g)(1)). For inservice inspection and testing, the requirements of ASME BPV Code Section XI, Division 1, Subsection IWE apply (10 CFR 50.55a(g)(4)).

The NRC requires that ISI methods, such as visual examinations of containment surfaces (including nozzle welds), be performed by personnel qualified and trained per IWA-2300, as modified by NRC regulations (10 CFR 50.55a(g)(4)(i)). The NRC staff also reviews whether the design accommodates ISI of critical areas, ensuring sufficient physical access or alternative means for identifying degradation in inaccessible areas (DSRS 3.8.2, Area of Review 7). Any special testing or surveillance requirements for new or untried designs must be reviewed for adequacy.

In summary, the acceptance criteria are: (1) adherence to ASME BPV Code Section III for construction and Section XI, Subsection IWE for ISI; (2) visual examinations performed by qualified personnel; and (3) design provisions that facilitate effective ISI of critical welds, including nozzle welds, to ensure ongoing structural integrity.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for defining the pressure boundary of a steel containment vessel in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for defining the pressure boundary of a steel containment vessel in nuclear power plants are grounded in compliance with specific regulatory requirements, codes, and guidance documents. According to DSRS 3.8.2 (Section II), the criteria are based on meeting the requirements of 10 CFR 50.55a and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criteria (GDCs) 1, 2, 4, 16, 50, and 53, as well as 10 CFR 50.44 regarding combustible gas loads. The primary codes and standards referenced are the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, Section III, Division 1, Subsection NE (Class MC Components), and Section XI, Subsection IWE, for inservice inspection.

RG 1.57 provides detailed guidance on design limits and loading combinations for metal containment system components. It specifies that the pressure boundary includes the containment vessel, penetration assemblies, access openings, and attached piping up to isolation valves. The design must consider all relevant loads (dead, live, pressure, thermal, seismic, etc.) and their combinations, as outlined in RG 1.57, and ensure that total stresses remain within the limits defined by ASME BPV Code Section III, Articles NE-3221.1 to NE-3221.4. Buckling effects under pressure, thermal, and seismic loads must also be evaluated, potentially using nonlinear analysis per ASME Code Case N-284-2.

RG 1.216 further requires that the pressure capacity of the steel containment be demonstrated to exceed the design-basis accident pressure, typically through nonlinear finite element analysis. The analysis should incrementally increase internal pressure until a failure criterion is reached, such as a maximum global membrane strain of 1.5% for cylindrical steel containments. The stress-strain relationship used must be based on ASME Code-specified minimum yield strength at the design-basis accident temperature.

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria for the steel containment pressure boundary require adherence to ASME BPV Code Section III (Subsection NE), compliance with relevant GDCs, consideration of all applicable loads and load combinations, evaluation of buckling, and demonstration of adequate pressure capacity above design pressure, as detailed in DSRS 3.8.2, RG 1.57, and RG 1.216.

evidence_chain.section: C. REGULATORY POSITION, 1. Prediction of Containment Internal Pressure Capacity above Design Pressure
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Regulatory Position 1 of this regulatory guide identifies methods acceptable to the staff for demonstrating that a concrete or steel containment possesses a significant internal pressure capacity above the containment design pressure.

1.  Prediction of Containment Internal Pressure Capacity above Design Pressure

The purpose of this evaluation is to assess the pressure capacity of the containment at which the structural integrity is retained, and a failure leading to a significant release of fission products does not occur.  This analysis is intended to address the containment structural capacity and not to evaluate the potential effects of containment structural response on other connected components, such as attached piping and other equipment.  An applicant for a DC or COL should submit the details of this containment capacity analysis with its application.   

To estimate the pressure capacity of the containment structure, typically, a nonlinear finite element analysis will be needed to examine the overall response.  Large penetrations are usually included in the finite element model; smaller penetrations and penetration closure components are typically analyzed using a separate finite element model, test data, or both.   

For cylindrical containment structures and axisymmetric components of the containment, it may be feasible to use closed-form solutions or semiempirical methods to estimate the pressure capacity; in such cases, the applicant should provide an adequate technical justification for all simplifications.  Test results may also be used; however, the applicant should provide sufficient information to demonstrate the applicability of the test results to the particular containment design and loading condition.

The information submitted should be sufficient for the staff to make a determination of the safety margin above the design-basis accident pressure.

In determining the containment internal pressure capacity, and also in the interpretation and evaluation of results, the applicant should consider the following staff expectations:

a. The use of a three-dimensional finite element model is acceptable.  Axisymmetric or partial (e.g., half model or wedge) finite element models can be used, if a sufficient technical basis is provided.

b. For the purpose of estimating the safety margin above the design-basis accident pressure, a static analysis is acceptable.  However, if dynamic response effects are important, the static pressure capacity may need to be reduced to account for such effects.  One acceptable approach to determine the reduced pressure capacity is a nonlinear dynamic analysis.  The NRC will review, on a case-by-case basis, alternative approaches provided by the applicant; for example, the use of an appropriate dynamic amplification factor.

c. The initial condition for the nonlinear analysis of the containment structure should be the linear elastic response caused by dead load and design pressure, at the design temperature.  The internal pressure is incrementally increased until a specified failure criterion is reached (e.g., deflection limit; strain limit; solution divergence).  When performing this analysis, the applicant should record the pressure(s) corresponding to initial yielding of the liner, reinforcing steel, prestressing tendon (if applicable), and steel components not backed by concrete (e.g., closure head, hatch) for concrete containments; it should record the pressure(s) corresponding to initial yielding of the steel shell and yielding of other steel components (e.g., closure head, hatch) for steel containments.

d. The nonlinear stress-strain curve for steel materials (steel liner, reinforcing steel, prestressing tendons, steel components, steel shell) should be based on the ASME Code-specified minimum yield strength for the specific grade of steel and a stress-strain relationship beyond yield that is representative of the specific grade of steel.  The stress-strain curve used in the analysis should correspond to the design-basis accident temperature.

...

f. The following are acceptable simplified methods for determining the pressure capacity of cylindrical containments:

(4) For cylindrical steel containments, the pressure capacity analysis may be based on attaining a maximum global membrane strain away from discontinuities (i.e., the hoop membrane strain in a cylinder) of 1.5 percent.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory requirements for seismic analysis address the use of damping values in the evaluation of steel containment structures?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory requirements for seismic analysis of steel containment structures address the use of damping values primarily through incorporation by reference of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, Section III, Division 1, Subsection NE, as mandated by 10 CFR 50.55a (see [2]). The NRC does not specify explicit damping values in its regulations or regulatory guides; instead, it requires that seismic analyses, including the selection of damping values, conform to the methods and parameters accepted in the ASME BPV Code and NRC practice (see [3], RG 1.57, Section C). Specifically, DSRS 3.8.2 and RG 1.57 emphasize that the dynamic effects of seismic loads must be considered in the analysis of steel containment structures, and that the analysis procedures—including the treatment of damping—must be consistent with the ASME Code and referenced regulatory guidance ([1], [3]). 

Additionally, RG 1.84 clarifies that NRC-approved ASME Code Cases may be used as voluntary alternatives, provided they do not conflict with regulatory requirements ([4]). Therefore, the use of damping values in seismic analysis is governed by the provisions and methodologies specified in the ASME BPV Code, Section III, Division 1, Subsection NE, and any applicable NRC-endorsed Code Cases. The NRC’s regulatory framework ensures that damping values and other dynamic analysis parameters are selected in accordance with established industry standards and accepted engineering practice, as referenced in the applicable codes and regulatory guides.

data.query: In the context of nuclear containment design, how do general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena relate to the acceptance criteria for stress intensities under seismic loading conditions?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for protection against natural phenomena, specifically GDC 2 as outlined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, require that nuclear containment structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena such as earthquakes without loss of their safety functions (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; RG 1.57, Section A; RG 1.29, Section A). This requirement is operationalized in the acceptance criteria for stress intensities under seismic loading conditions through specific load combinations and design limits.

According to DSRS 3.8.2 and RG 1.57, the acceptance criteria for containment structures under seismic loading are based on combinations of normal, accident, and seismic loads (such as the Operating Basis Earthquake [OBE] and Safe Shutdown Earthquake [SSE]). For each load combination, the containment must meet defined service limits (Level B for operational conditions and Level C for safe shutdown scenarios) (DSRS 3.8.2, II.3; RG 1.57, C.I, B). The structural acceptance criteria require that stress intensities (including primary, secondary, and peak stresses) remain within the allowable limits specified in the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section III, Division 1, Subsection NB (DSRS 3.8.2, II.5; RG 1.57, C. Design Limits).

Thus, the general design criteria establish the overarching requirement for seismic protection, while the acceptance criteria translate this into specific, code-based stress limits for containment structures under defined seismic load combinations. This ensures that containment structures maintain their safety functions during and after seismic events, in compliance with regulatory requirements.

data.query: What are the regulatory acceptance criteria for leakage in steel containment structures, specifically regarding gasketed joints?
data.answer:
The regulatory acceptance criteria for leakage in steel containment structures, specifically regarding gasketed joints, are established through a combination of requirements from the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code and NRC regulations. According to 10 CFR 50.55a (§ 50.55a Codes and standards), steel containment structures and their associated penetrations and gasketed joints must comply with the applicable provisions of the ASME BPV Code, Section III, Division 1, as incorporated by reference. For Class MC components, this includes adherence to Subsection NB for construction and Subsection NE for pressure-retaining components and their attachments. 

Furthermore, 10 CFR 50.55a(b)(2)(ix) specifies that containment leakage testing must be performed in accordance with 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J. Appendix J establishes the performance criteria for leakage rates, including those at gasketed joints, to ensure that the containment maintains its integrity under design-basis accident conditions. The DSRS 3.8.2 (Section I.7) reinforces that the NRC staff reviews pre-operational and inservice test programs for compliance with these codes and standards, with particular attention to the acceptance criteria for leakage as defined in Article NB-6000 of the ASME BPV Code and the requirements of Appendix J. 

In summary, the acceptance criteria for leakage at gasketed joints in steel containment structures are those specified by the ASME BPV Code (Section III, Division 1, Subsections NB and NE) and the leakage rate limits and testing protocols of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, as required by 10 CFR 50.55a.

data.query: How do the general design criteria for containment integrity relate to the regulatory requirements for pressure testing of containment structures, particularly in regard to exemptions for bolts and gaskets?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for containment integrity, as outlined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, specifically GDC 16, require that the reactor containment and associated systems provide an essentially leak-tight barrier to prevent the uncontrolled release of radioactivity. This includes ensuring that the containment, its penetrations, and isolation systems can withstand the pressure and temperature conditions resulting from any loss-of-coolant accident without exceeding the design leakage rate. GDC 16 also emphasizes the need for periodic inspection and testing of the containment and containment isolation systems to assure their ongoing integrity (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 16).

The regulatory requirements for pressure testing of containment structures are directly linked to these design criteria. According to DSRS 3.8.2, the acceptance criteria for containment integrity are based on compliance with GDC 16 and related criteria. The staff reviews pre-operational structural test programs and inservice surveillance programs to ensure that containment structures and components meet the requirements of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, as incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a. This includes periodic examinations and pressure testing to verify structural integrity and leak-tightness (DSRS 3.8.2, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA, item 7).

Regarding exemptions for bolts and gaskets, while the provided evidence does not explicitly mention specific exemptions, it does state that the review includes the extent of compliance with the ASME BPV Code and any special testing or surveillance requirements for new or untried designs. This suggests that any exemptions, such as for bolts and gaskets, would need to be justified within the context of the ASME Code and NRC regulations, and would be subject to NRC review to ensure that containment integrity is not compromised (DSRS 3.8.2, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA, item 7).

In summary, the general design criteria establish the fundamental requirement for containment integrity, and the regulatory requirements for pressure testing operationalize this by mandating periodic testing and inspection, with any exemptions subject to rigorous review to maintain the required level of safety.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for defining and documenting the pressure boundary of a steel containment vessel in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for defining and documenting the pressure boundary of a steel containment vessel in nuclear power plants are established through a combination of NRC regulations, guidance documents, and referenced industry codes. 

According to DSRS 3.8.2 (Sections I and II), the containment description must include detailed plans and sections that define all primary structural aspects and elements relied upon for the containment function. This includes the cylindrical shell, top and bottom closure heads, all penetrations, access openings, and attachments (DSRS 3.8.2, I.B). The documentation must be sufficient to establish the pressure boundary, encompassing all components that perform a containment function, such as the vessel, penetration assemblies, access openings, and piping systems up to isolation valves (RG 1.57, Section B).

The design, fabrication, erection, construction, testing, and inspection of the containment pressure boundary must comply with the requirements of 10 CFR 50.55a, which mandates adherence to the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (BPV Code), Section III, Division 1, Subsection NE for Class MC components, and applicable portions of Section XI for inservice inspection (10 CFR 50.55a(c); DSRS 3.8.2, II.2).

Applicants must provide a design specification that stipulates the design requirements, including mechanical and operational loadings, and must document the design limits and load combinations per ASME Code and NRC guidance (RG 1.57, Section B; RG 1.216, C.1). The documentation should include engineering drawings, analysis details, modeling assumptions, material properties, loading sequences, failure modes, and acceptance criteria for leakage and structural integrity (RG 1.216, C.1.k). The evaluation must address all major penetrations and demonstrate that leakage is within acceptable limits under design and accident conditions (RG 1.216, C.1.g, j).

All information should be presented in the FSAR or DCD, specifically in Section 3.8.2 for steel containments, consistent with the guidance in RG 1.206 (RG 1.216, C.1.k.8).

evidence_chain.section: Section B. DISCUSSION (pp. 5-6)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
The design conditions and functional requirements of components that provide a pressure boundary for the primary reactor containment function should be reflected in the application of appropriate design limits (e.g., stress or strain limits) for the most adverse combination of loadings to which these components might be subjected. For components constructed in accordance with Subsection NE of the Code (Code Class MC), the NRC requires provision of a design specification, which stipulates the design requirements (e.g., the mechanical and operational loadings) for the components.

In Appendix B to the Code, entitled “Owner’s Design Specifications,” Paragraph B-2125, “Load Combinations,” states, “In order to provide a complete definition of service loads, the combination of specific events must be considered. Since these combinations are a function of specific systems which make up a part of a specific type of nuclear facility, this section does not directly address service loads other than to provide different stress limits for various loadings.”

To further provide a consistent basis for the design of metal containment system components, this guide delineates acceptable design limits for appropriate combinations of loadings. The intent is to address only the most adverse combinations of loadings resulting from those events or conditions identified herein (e.g., those combinations of loadings that result in the limiting or controlling design condition). These loadings are associated either with conditions for which the containment function is required in combination with specified seismic events producing possible mechanisms for failure that could affect the function and/or integrity of structures, systems, and components important to safety. ...

The approach set forth in this guide is directly related to Section III of the Code. Design limits as specified in Section III are adopted to provide assurance of maintaining the pressure-retaining integrity of the primary reactor containment. The primary reactor containment system of metal construction includes all components that perform a containment function, such as (1) the containment vessel(s), (2) penetration assemblies and access openings, and (3) piping systems attached to the containment vessel nozzles or penetration assemblies out to and including all pumps and valves required to isolate the containment.

data.query: How do NRC regulations address the inclusion of penetrations and valve assemblies as part of the containment vessel pressure boundary, and what documentation standards apply to their depiction in design submittals?
data.answer:
NRC regulations explicitly address the inclusion of penetrations and valve assemblies as integral parts of the containment vessel pressure boundary. According to DSRS 3.8.2 (Section I.B), the review of the containment shell encompasses all penetrations, access openings, and attachments to both the shell and closure heads. The descriptive information in the safety analysis report (SAR) must meet the criteria of RG 1.206 Section 3.8.2.1, ensuring that all features, including penetrations and valve assemblies, are adequately described for regulatory review.

Regulatory Guide 1.206 (Appendix A and Section C.1.2) further clarifies documentation standards. It requires that the FSAR section on 'Steel Containment' describe the design, materials, fabrication, erection, inspection, and testing of the containment structure, explicitly including the main shell, heads, penetrations, access openings, and the basis for their design. The documentation must also cover the design, construction, and testing of containment penetrations (such as piping and electrical penetrations, airlocks, and other access openings) and containment isolation valves and valve assemblies. The SAR must provide sufficient detail—such as drawings, specifications, and descriptions—to allow NRC staff to evaluate the adequacy of the design, including all pressure boundary components.

10 CFR 50.55a establishes the regulatory basis for these requirements. It mandates that components of the containment vessel and its penetrations, including access openings and containment isolation valves, meet the applicable ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code requirements (Class 2 or Class 3, as appropriate). Design submittals must include sufficient information to demonstrate compliance, including identification and justification of the codes and standards used and the bases for their selection.

In summary, NRC regulations require that penetrations and valve assemblies be treated as part of the containment vessel pressure boundary, and that their design, construction, and testing be thoroughly documented in design submittals, following the standards set forth in RG 1.206 and 10 CFR 50.55a.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory requirements define the extent of the containment pressure boundary for steel containment structures, particularly in relation to penetrations and associated valve assemblies?
data.answer: NRC regulatory requirements define the extent of the containment pressure boundary for steel containment structures to include not only the main containment vessel (the cylindrical shell and closure heads) but also all penetrations, access openings, and attachments to the inside and outside surfaces of the shell and heads (DSRS 3.8.2, Areas of Review). Specifically, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 16, requires that the containment structure and its internal pressure boundary—including access openings, penetrations, and isolation valves—be designed to withstand accident conditions without exceeding the design leakage rate. Regulatory Guide 1.57 further clarifies that the primary reactor containment system of metal construction encompasses all components that perform a containment function, including the containment vessel, penetration assemblies, access openings, and piping systems attached to the containment vessel nozzles or penetration assemblies out to and including all pumps and valves required to isolate the containment. Penetration assemblies are specifically defined as parts or appurtenances that permit piping, mechanical devices, and electrical connections to pass through the containment vessel shell or head while maintaining leak-tight integrity. Thus, the containment pressure boundary extends from the steel containment vessel itself through all penetrations and includes associated valve assemblies required for containment isolation, as these are essential to maintaining the leak-tight barrier function (DSRS 3.8.2; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 16; RG 1.57, Section B).

data.query: What is the relationship between the regulatory requirements for containment integrity and the inclusion of safety system components, such as emergency core cooling system solenoid valve assemblies, within the containment pressure boundary?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for containment integrity are closely linked to the inclusion of safety system components, such as emergency core cooling system (ECCS) solenoid valve assemblies, within the containment pressure boundary. According to DSRS 3.8.2, the review of containment integrity encompasses all penetrations, access openings, and attachments to the containment vessel shell, including the effects of containment internals attached to the shell. This means that safety system components located within or attached to the containment pressure boundary must be considered in the structural integrity review and must meet the same regulatory requirements for containment integrity, including applicable codes, standards, and inservice inspection requirements (DSRS 3.8.2, I. AREAS OF REVIEW and II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA).

General Design Criterion (GDC) 16 in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, requires that the containment and associated systems provide an essentially leak-tight barrier against the uncontrolled release of radioactivity and be capable of accommodating accident conditions, such as those resulting from a loss-of-coolant accident (LOCA), without exceeding design leakage and pressure limits. This includes ensuring that penetrations and access openings, as well as systems important to safety (such as ECCS components), are designed to maintain containment integrity and are subject to periodic inspection and testing (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 16).

Regulatory Guide 1.57 further clarifies that all components performing a containment function—including penetration assemblies, piping, pumps, and valves required to isolate the containment—are considered part of the primary containment system. These components must be constructed in accordance with the appropriate ASME Code class (Class MC, 1, or 2) depending on their function and location, and must be designed to withstand specified loads and load combinations as outlined in the ASME Code (RG 1.57, B. DISCUSSION and C. STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE).

In summary, safety system components such as ECCS solenoid valve assemblies, if included within or attached to the containment pressure boundary, are subject to the same regulatory requirements for containment integrity as the containment structure itself. This includes compliance with design codes, structural integrity reviews, and periodic inspection and testing to ensure ongoing containment integrity, as mandated by GDC 16 and detailed in DSRS 3.8.2 and RG 1.57.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for identifying and defining the entire pressure boundary of a steel containment vessel in a nuclear power plant?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for identifying and defining the entire pressure boundary of a steel containment vessel in a nuclear power plant are established through a combination of descriptive, design, and quality assurance criteria. According to DSRS 3.8.2, the safety analysis report (SAR) must provide sufficient descriptive information, including plans and sections, to clearly define the primary structural aspects and elements of the containment vessel relied upon for containment function. This includes detailed geometry, sketches showing plan views at various elevations, and sections in at least two orthogonal directions. The SAR must specifically describe the cylindrical portion of the shell, all penetrations, access openings, attachments, and the top and bottom closure heads, including bolting, welding details, and any reinforcement at junctions (DSRS 3.8.2, I.A-B).

The acceptance criteria for these descriptions are based on compliance with 10 CFR 50.55a and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criteria (GDC) 1, 2, 4, 16, 50, and 53, which require that containment structures be designed, fabricated, erected, constructed, tested, and inspected to quality standards commensurate with their safety function (DSRS 3.8.2, II; 10 CFR 50.55a(a)). Specifically, 10 CFR 50.55a(b) requires that the steel containment vessel meet the requirements for Class 1 components in Section III of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, and the applicable code edition must be identified in the SAR (10 CFR 50.55a(b)(2)).

Furthermore, the primary reactor containment and other pressure-retaining components must be subject to periodic testing and inspection to ensure the integrity of the pressure boundary (10 CFR 50.55a(g)). If the containment has new or unique features not specifically covered by RG 1.206, adequate information must be provided to demonstrate equivalence in function and compliance with applicable requirements (DSRS 3.8.2, I.B).

In summary, the NRC requires a comprehensive, detailed definition of the entire pressure boundary in the SAR, adherence to ASME Code requirements, and ongoing testing and inspection to ensure integrity, as outlined in DSRS 3.8.2, 10 CFR 50.55a, and related guidance.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for evaluating the ultimate pressure capacity of steel containment vessels in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for evaluating the ultimate pressure capacity of steel containment vessels in nuclear power plants are grounded in compliance with the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, Section III, Division 1, as incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a (see [2]). The design and analysis procedures must emphasize conformance with Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.57 and consider unique design features, such as the effects of radiation exposure and fracture toughness, as outlined in DSRS 3.8.2, Section I.4 (see [1]).

Specifically, the evaluation must address:
- Treatment of nonaxisymmetric and localized loads, local buckling effects, cyclic fatigue, and effects of submergence and dynamic fluid-structure interaction (DSRS 3.8.2, I.4).
- The steel containment vessel and reactor pressure vessel (RPV) should be analyzed as coupled structures for seismic and other relevant loads, including interaction forces at supports (DSRS 3.8.2, I.4).

RG 1.57 provides detailed guidance on acceptable loading combinations and design limits for Code Class MC containment vessels. For ultimate pressure capacity, the vessel must withstand specified load combinations, including accident pressures (e.g., hydrogen release and post-accident inerting), with minimum combined pressures not less than 310 kPa (45 psig) for certain scenarios (RG 1.57, C.B.(c)-(v)). Total stresses under these combinations must remain within the limits defined by ASME Code Articles NE-3221.1 through NE-3221.4 (RG 1.57, C.C).

Buckling effects under earthquake, thermal, and pressure loads must be considered. For complex geometries and loading conditions, buckling should be evaluated per ASME Code Case N-284-2 (or the latest acceptable revision, such as N-284-4, as listed in RG 1.84, Table 1), using nonlinear analysis as an acceptable approach (RG 1.57, C.D; RG 1.84, Table 1).

In summary, the ultimate pressure capacity evaluation must follow ASME BPV Code Section III, Division 1, as required by 10 CFR 50.55a, and adhere to NRC guidance in RG 1.57 and RG 1.84, ensuring all relevant load combinations, design limits, and buckling criteria are addressed.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory guides address the impact of changes to containment vessel reinforcement or support structures on the ultimate pressure and buckling analyses for steel containment?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory guides address the impact of changes to containment vessel reinforcement or support structures on ultimate pressure and buckling analyses for steel containment by requiring compliance with the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code and associated regulatory guidance. According to DSRS 3.8.2, the design and analysis procedures for steel containment must emphasize compliance with ASME BPV Code, Section III, Division 1, Subsection NB, as incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a, and conformance with Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.57. The review specifically focuses on the treatment of local buckling effects and the ultimate capacity of the steel containment, including the interaction forces at the containment vessel supports (DSRS 3.8.2, Section I.4).

RG 1.57 provides further guidance, stating that buckling effects under earthquake, thermal, and pressure loads must be considered, especially for shells with complex geometries or loading conditions. For such cases, the criteria in ASME Code Case N-284-2 (and by extension, N-284-4 as accepted in RG 1.84) should be used, and nonlinear analysis is recommended (RG 1.57, Section I.D; RG 1.84, Table 1). Design limits for combined loads must remain within the stress limits defined in the ASME Code (RG 1.57, Section I.C).

10 CFR 50.55a mandates that Class MC pressure-retaining components and their supports meet the requirements of the ASME BPV Code, Section III, Division 1, Subsection NE, ensuring that any changes to reinforcement or supports are analyzed for their impact on structural integrity, including buckling and ultimate pressure capacity (10 CFR 50.55a(b)(1)).

In summary, NRC regulatory guides require that any changes to containment vessel reinforcement or support structures be evaluated using ASME BPV Code methods, with explicit consideration of buckling and ultimate pressure capacity, and that these analyses conform to the latest accepted Code Cases and regulatory guidance (DSRS 3.8.2; RG 1.57; RG 1.84; 10 CFR 50.55a).

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory expectations for the methods used in the structural analysis of steel containment structures?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory expectations for the methods used in the structural analysis of steel containment structures are grounded in compliance with the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, Section III, Division 1, as incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a (see [2]). Specifically, the design and analysis procedures must conform to Subsection NB for Class 1 components and to the requirements for Class MC components, as applicable (see [1], [3]). The NRC expects that the analysis methods address a comprehensive set of loadings and load combinations, including dead and live loads, test and operating pressures and temperatures, seismic loads (including both operating-basis and safe-shutdown earthquakes), accident-induced loads (e.g., pipe breaks, hydrodynamic effects), and post-accident conditions such as hydrogen generation and flooding (see RG 1.57, Section C, [3]).

The analysis must explicitly consider nonaxisymmetric and localized loads, local buckling, cyclic fatigue, submergence effects, and dynamic fluid-structure interaction under seismic loading. For unique designs, such as the NuScale steel containment, the vessel and reactor pressure vessel (RPV) should be analyzed as coupled structures for seismic and other relevant loads, including interaction forces at supports (see [1]).

Computer programs used for structural analysis must be validated and benchmarked against hand calculations, published analytical results, experimental tests, or previously accepted programs, with detailed documentation provided (see SRP 3.9.1, [4]). If experimental stress analysis methods are used, they must meet the provisions of Appendix II to the ASME BPV Code and be sufficiently detailed to demonstrate compliance with design specifications (see [4]).

Buckling analysis must address complex geometries and loading conditions, potentially using nonlinear analysis as described in ASME Code Case N-284-2 (see [3]). All stress calculations must remain within the limits defined by the relevant ASME Code articles (e.g., NE-3221.x) for the applicable load combinations (see [3]).

In summary, NRC expects structural analysis methods for steel containment structures to rigorously follow ASME BPV Code requirements, address all relevant loadings and combinations, validate computational tools, and provide detailed documentation to demonstrate compliance (see [1], [2], [3], [4]).

4. Design and Analysis Procedures.  The design and analysis procedures used for the steel containment are reviewed, with emphasis on the extent of compliance with ASME BPV Code, Section III, Division 1, Subsection NB, as incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a, and conformance with RG 1.57.  The unique design features of the NuScale steel containment require consideration of the effects of radiation exposure on the material properties and fracture toughness.  This is reviewed in SRP Section 6.2.7.

The review will place particular emphasis on the following subjects:

A. treatment of nonaxisymmetric and localized loads

B. treatment of local buckling effects

C. consideration of cyclic fatigue

D. effects of submergence in the reactor pool (i.e., normal operating external pressure loading, dynamic fluid-structure interaction under seismic loading)

E. computer programs used in the design and analysis (other than those addressed in SRP Section 3.9.1)

F. ultimate capacity of steel containment

Because of the unique design of the NuScale RPV/steel containment module, the steel containment vessel and the RPV should be analyzed as coupled structures for seismic loading, and potentially also for other loads (e.g., hydrodynamic loads, thermal loads) applied to either the containment vessel or to the RPV.  Interaction forces at the RPV-to-containment vessel supports must be included in the structural assessment of the containment vessel.

evidence_chain.section: C. STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
C.  STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE 

I. Code Class MC vessels, electrical and mechanical penetration assemblies, and other penetration assemblies (excluding bellows-type expansion joints) that are parts or appurtenances of the vessel.  

Code Class MC components of primary metal containment systems that are completely enclosed within Seismic Category I structures should be designed to withstand the following loads and loading combinations within the specified design limits.
A. Loads
D Dead loads.
L Live loads, including all loads resulting from platform flexibility and deformation and from crane loading, if applicable.
Pt Test pressure.
Tt Test temperature.
To Thermal effects and loads during startup, normal operating, or shutdown conditions, based on the most critical transient or steady-state condition.
Ro Pipe reactions during startup, normal operating, or shutdown conditions based on the most critical transient or steady-state condition.
Po External pressure loads resulting from pressure variation either inside or outside containment.
E Loads generated by the operating-basis earthquake including sloshing effects, if applicable.
E’ Loads generated by the SSE, including sloshing effects.
Pa Pressure load generated by the postulated pipe break accident (including pressure generated by postulated small-break or intermediate-break pipe ruptures), pool swell, and subsequent hydrodynamic loads.
Ta Thermal loads under thermal conditions generated by the postulated pipe break accident, pool swell, and subsequent hydrodynamic reaction loads.
Ra Pipe reactions under thermal conditions generated by the postulated pipe break accident, pool swell, and subsequent hydrodynamic reaction loads.
Ps All pressure loads that are caused by the actuation of safety relief valve (SRV) discharge, including pool swell and subsequent hydrodynamic loads.
Ts All thermal loads that are generated by the actuation of SRV discharge, including pool swell and subsequent hydrodynamic thermal loads.
Rs All pipe reaction loads that are generated by the actuation of SRV discharge, including pool swell and subsequent hydrodynamic reaction loads.
Yr Equivalent static load on the structure generated by the reaction on the broken pipe during the design-basis accident.
Yj Jet impingement equivalent static load on the structure generated by the broken pipe during the design-basis accident.
Ym Missile impact equivalent static load on the structure generated by or during the design-basis accident, such as pipe whipping.
FL Load generated by the post-LOCA flooding of the containment, if any.
Pg1 Pressure resulting from an accident that releases hydrogen generated from 100% fuel clad metal-water reaction.
Pg2 Pressure resulting from uncontrolled hydrogen burning.
Pg3 Pressure resulting from post-accident inerting, assuming carbon dioxide is the inerting agent. See Regulatory Guide 1.7 “Control of Combustible Gas Concentrations in Containment,” for additional guidance about the pressure load Pg3 due to combustible gas concentration.
B. Loading Combinations and Design Limits
The specified loads and load combinations are acceptable if found to be in accordance with the following guidance. The following load combinations include all loading combinations for which the containment might be designed for or subjected to during the expected life of the plant:
1. Testing Condition
This includes the testing condition of the containment to verify its leak integrity. In this case, the loading combination includes: D + L + Tt + Pt
2. Design Conditions
These include all design loadings for which the containment vessel or portions thereof might be designed for during the expected life of the plant. Such loads include design pressure, design temperature, and the design mechanical loads generated by the design-basis accident. In this case, the loading combination includes: D + L + Pa + Ta + Ra
3. Service Conditions
The load combinations in these cases correspond to and include Level A service limits, Level B service limits, Level C service limits, Level D service limits and the post-flooding condition. The loads may be combined by their actual time history of occurrence, taking into consideration their dynamic effect upon the structure. ...
C. Design Limits
Total stresses for the combination of loads delineated in Regulatory Position 1.2 (above) are acceptable if found to be within the limits defined by Articles NE-3221.1, NE-3221.2, NE-3221.3 and NE-3221.4 of the Code.
D. Treatment of Buckling Effects
Earthquake, thermal, and pressure loads require consideration of buckling of the shell. Buckling of shells with more complex geometries and loading conditions than those covered by Article NE-3133 of the Code should be considered in accordance with the criteria described in ASME Code Case N-284-2. An acceptable approach to this problem is to perform a nonlinear analysis.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
This guide describes a method that the staff of the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) considers acceptable for implementing the agency’s requirements regarding the control of welding for nuclear components, as they relate to light-water-cooled and gas-cooled reactors.  In particular, General Design Criterion 1, “Quality Standards and Records,” as specified in Appendix A, “General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants,” to Title 10, Part 50, of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR Part 50), “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities” (Ref. 1) requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety shall be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with the importance of the safety functions to be performed.
To augment that requirement, Appendix B, “Quality Assurance Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants and Fuel Reprocessing Plants,” to 10 CFR Part 50 requires the establishment of measures to ensure the control of materials and special processes such as welding, as well as proper welder qualification. Moreover, 10 CFR 50.55a, “Codes and Standards,” requires, in part, that components of the reactor coolant pressure boundary must be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested in accordance with the standards in Section III, “Nuclear Power Plant Components,” of the Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (Ref. 2) promulgated by the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME), or equivalent quality standards.
...
Weld fabrication and repair should comply with the fabrication standards specified in Sections III and IX of the ASME Code, supplemented by the following:
(1) Performance qualification should provide for testing the welder or welding operator under simulated access, and visibility limitations when physical conditions restrict the welder’s access to a production weld to less than 30 centimeters (12 inches) in any direction from the joint and which would affect electrode manipulation, or bead progression, or require an indirect means of weld pool observation (such as a mirror).
(2) Requalification should be necessary when (a) the use of an indirect means is required to view the weld pool (such as a mirror) during production welding and the welder or welding operator did not qualify for welding in areas of limited accessibility using that indirect means of weld pool observation, or (b) any of the essential welding variables for welders (QW-350) or welding operators (QW-360) listed in Section IX change, or (c) the qualification expires per QW-320.
(3) Production welding and adherence to welding qualification criteria should be monitored.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory guides for containment analysis methods relate to the general requirements for design certification applications?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory guides for containment analysis methods provide detailed, acceptable approaches for meeting the general requirements for design certification applications, particularly those related to the structural integrity and safety of containment systems. According to DSRS 3.8.2 (Section II), regulatory guides such as RG 1.57 and RG 1.216 are specifically referenced as acceptable guidance for the design, analysis, and evaluation of steel containment structures. These guides supplement the requirements of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, which is mandated by 10 CFR 50.55a as part of the licensing basis for nuclear facilities.

RG 1.57 outlines acceptable methods for designing metal primary reactor containment system components, including design limits and loading combinations, and ties these methods directly to the requirements of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A (General Design Criteria) and 10 CFR Part 52, which governs design certification applications (RG 1.57, Sections A and B). RG 1.216 provides methods for predicting internal pressure capacity above design-basis accident pressures and for demonstrating containment structural integrity in the context of severe accidents and combustible gas control, as required by 10 CFR 52.47 and 52.79 for design certification and combined license applications (RG 1.216, Section A).

These regulatory guides are used by NRC staff to evaluate whether design certification applications meet the technical and safety requirements specified in the regulations, including those in 10 CFR Part 50 and Part 52. The guides ensure that containment structures are designed to withstand postulated accident conditions and maintain their safety functions, as required by the general design criteria and the technical content requirements for design certification applications (DSRS 3.8.2; RG 1.57; RG 1.216; 10 CFR 50.55a).

The approach set forth in this guide is directly related to Section III of the Code.  Design limits as specified in Section III are adopted to provide assurance of maintaining the pressure-retaining integrity of the primary reactor containment.  The primary reactor containment system of metal construction includes all components that perform a containment function, such as (1) the containment vessel(s), (2) penetration assemblies and access openings, and (3) piping systems attached to the containment vessel nozzles or penetration assemblies out to and including all pumps and valves required to isolate the containment.

evidence_chain.section: A. INTRODUCTION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
This guide describes methods that the staff of the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) considers acceptable for (1) predicting the internal pressure capacity for containment structures above the design-basis accident pressure, (2) demonstrating containment structural integrity related to combustible gas control, and (3) demonstrating containment structural integrity through an analysis that specifically addresses the Commission’s performance goals related to the prevention and mitigation of severe accidents.  It provides guidance on methods for satisfying requirements in Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) Part 52, “Licenses, Certifications, and Approvals for Nuclear Power Plants” (Ref. 1).  Requirements in 10 CFR 52.47, “Contents of Applications; Technical Information,” and in 10 CFR 52.79, “Contents of Applications; Technical Information in Final Safety Analysis Report [FSAR],” relate to the structural integrity of containments under internal pressurization that pertain to the containment structural capacity above design-basis pressures, to combustible gas control, and to the prevention and mitigation of severe accidents.  This guidance is intended to be consistent with the Commission’s goals and other related guidance, as discussed in the remainder of this section.  This regulatory guide does not address requirements and guidance for the structural evaluation of containments for design-basis pressure.

Prediction of Containment Internal Pressure Capacity Above Design-Basis Pressure:  10 CFR 50, Appendix A, General Design Criteria (GDC) 50, “Containment Design Basis,” requires that the reactor containment structure and its internal compartments can accommodate, without exceeding the design leakage rate and with sufficient margin, the calculated pressure and temperature conditions caused by a loss of coolant accident (LOCA).  According to 10 CFR 52.47(a)(9), for design certification (DC) applications, and 10 CFR 52.79(a)(41), for combined license (COL) applications, applications for light water-cooled nuclear power plants shall include an evaluation of the facility against NUREG-0800, “Standard Review Plan for the Review of Safety Analysis Reports for Nuclear Power Plants” (hereafter referred to as the Standard Review Plan (SRP)) (Ref.2).  In sections 3.8.1 and 3.8.2 of the SRP, the need for the determination of the internal pressure capacity as a measure of the safety margin above the design-basis accident pressure is described. This regulatory guide addresses methods acceptable to the staff for estimating the margin by predicting the internal pressure capacity for containment structures above the internal pressure for the design-basis LOCA.  The internal pressure capacity in this estimation is an internal pressure capacity at which the structural integrity is retained and a failure leading to a significant release of fission products does not occur.

§ 50.55a Codes and standards.

data.query: When evaluating the acceptability of analysis methods for steel containment structures in a new nuclear power plant design, what combined regulatory guidance and review standards must be considered to ensure compliance with NRC requirements for both analysis methodology and documentation in a design certification application?
data.answer:
When evaluating the acceptability of analysis methods for steel containment structures in a new nuclear power plant design, both regulatory requirements and NRC-endorsed guidance must be considered to ensure compliance in a design certification application. The primary regulatory basis is found in 10 CFR 50.55a, which requires that containment structures meet the design, fabrication, construction, testing, and performance standards set forth in the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, Section III, Division 1, as incorporated by reference (10 CFR Part 50, §50.55a(a)(1)). The application must identify the applicable codes and standards, their editions, and any exceptions or alternatives, and must describe the quality assurance program (10 CFR 50.55a(c)).

Design and analysis procedures must demonstrate compliance with General Design Criteria (GDC) in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, including GDC 1 (quality standards), GDC 2 (protection against natural phenomena), GDC 4 (environmental and dynamic effects), GDC 16, GDC 50, and GDC 53 (DSRS 3.8.2, II. Acceptance Criteria). For design certification applications, 10 CFR 52.47(b)(1) requires inclusion of proposed Inspections, Tests, Analyses, and Acceptance Criteria (ITAAC) necessary to provide reasonable assurance of compliance (DSRS 3.8.2).

The NRC’s Design-Specific Review Standard (DSRS) 3.8.2 and Standard Review Plan (SRP) 3.8.2 provide detailed review criteria, emphasizing compliance with ASME BPV Code Section III, Subsections NB and NE, and conformance with Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.57 for design limits and loading combinations. Additional guidance includes RG 1.216 for evaluating containment structural integrity above design-basis pressures, and RG 1.71 for welding quality standards. The application should document analysis methods, including treatment of nonaxisymmetric and localized loads, local buckling, cyclic fatigue, dynamic fluid-structure interaction, and computer program validation (DSRS 3.8.2, I. Areas of Review).

Documentation must clearly explain how the analysis addresses each regulatory requirement and performance goal, especially if a single analysis is used for multiple requirements (RG 1.216, C. REGULATORY POSITION). The application should reference and justify the use of NRC-endorsed codes, standards, and regulatory guides, and provide sufficient detail to demonstrate compliance with all applicable NRC regulations and guidance.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
This guide describes a method that the staff of the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) considers acceptable for implementing the agency’s requirements regarding the control of welding for nuclear components, as they relate to light-water-cooled and gas-cooled reactors.  In particular, General Design Criterion 1, “Quality Standards and Records,” as specified in Appendix A, “General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants,” to Title 10, Part 50, of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR Part 50), “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities” (Ref. 1) requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety shall be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with the importance of the safety functions to be performed. To augment that requirement, Appendix B, “Quality Assurance Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants and Fuel Reprocessing Plants,” to 10 CFR Part 50 requires the establishment of measures to ensure the control of materials and special processes such as welding, as well as proper welder qualification. Moreover, 10 CFR 50.55a, “Codes and Standards,” requires, in part, that components of the reactor coolant pressure boundary must be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested in accordance with the standards in Section III, “Nuclear Power Plant Components,” of the Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (Ref. 2) promulgated by the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME), or equivalent quality standards.

Weld fabrication and repair should comply with the fabrication standards specified in Sections III and IX of the ASME Code, supplemented by the following:
(1) Performance qualification should provide for testing the welder or welding operator under simulated access, and visibility limitations when physical conditions restrict the welder’s access to a production weld to less than 30 centimeters (12 inches) in any direction from the joint and which would affect electrode manipulation, or bead progression, or require an indirect means of weld pool observation (such as a mirror).
(2) Requalification should be necessary when (a) the use of an indirect means is required to view the weld pool (such as a mirror) during production welding and the welder or welding operator did not qualify for welding in areas of limited accessibility using that indirect means of weld pool observation, or (b) any of the essential welding variables for welders (QW-350) or welding operators (QW-360) listed in Section IX change, or (c) the qualification expires per QW-320.
(3) Production welding and adherence to welding qualification criteria should be monitored.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for the structural design of seismic Category II structures in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for the structural design of seismic Category II structures in nuclear power plants are grounded in several regulatory requirements and guidance documents. According to DSRS 3.8.4 Section II, the acceptance criteria are based on compliance with 10 CFR 50.55a and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criteria (GDC) 1, 2, 4, and 5, as well as Appendix B for quality assurance. These criteria require that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function (GDC 1), and be able to withstand the most severe natural phenomena, including earthquakes, with appropriate load combinations (GDC 2).

For seismic Category II structures, which are typically not safety-related but may house important systems such as radwaste management, Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.143 provides additional specific guidance. Section 6 of RG 1.143 states that such structures should be evaluated for natural phenomena and man-induced hazards using the demand definitions, load combinations, and capacity criteria specified in Tables 2, 3, and 4 of the guide. For buildings housing radwaste systems (RW-IIb and RW-IIc classifications), the foundation and walls up to the spill height must meet at least the seismic base shear requirements of the 1997 Uniform Building Code (UBC), with further guidance from ASCE 7-95.

The acceptability of the design is evaluated based on the requirements of the applicable codes and standards listed in Table 1 of RG 1.143, using the capacity criteria in Table 4. In summary, seismic Category II structures must be designed to withstand seismic and other natural phenomena loads as specified in RG 1.143, using recognized building codes (UBC 1997, ASCE 7-95) and must meet the NRC’s general quality and safety requirements as outlined in 10 CFR 50.55a and the DSRS.

data.query: How do general design criteria for quality assurance and seismic protection interact when evaluating the placement and restraint of non-seismic Category I structures adjacent to seismic Category I safety-related structures?
data.answer:
The interaction between general design criteria for quality assurance and seismic protection is critical when evaluating the placement and restraint of non-seismic Category I structures adjacent to seismic Category I safety-related structures. According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 1 (Evidence [2]), all structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety must be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function, and a quality assurance program must be implemented to ensure satisfactory performance.

DSRS 3.8.4 (Evidence [1]) specifies that the NRC staff reviews the relationship between adjacent structures, including the separation or structural ties, to assess the potential impact on the safety-related structure’s performance under design loads, including seismic events. The review includes examining seismic gaps and the arrangement of adjacent buildings to ensure that non-seismic Category I structures do not adversely affect the seismic Category I structure.

RG 1.29 (Evidence [5]) provides further guidance, stating that non-seismic Category I SSCs whose failure could impact the safety function of seismic Category I SSCs should be designed and constructed so that a Safe Shutdown Earthquake (SSE) would not cause such failure. Where practical, these non-seismic structures should be separated or relocated to eliminate the risk of interaction. At interfaces, seismic analysis requirements for Category I should be extended into the non-seismic system up to the first anchor point or a sufficient distance to maintain the validity of the seismic analysis.

Additionally, RG 1.143 (Evidence [3]) and SRP 3.9.2 (Evidence [4]) reinforce the need for quality assurance and appropriate dynamic analysis at interfaces, ensuring that non-seismic structures do not compromise the integrity or function of seismic Category I structures. Quality assurance programs, as referenced in RG 1.143, must be sufficient to ensure compliance with design, construction, and testing provisions, with records maintained to demonstrate implementation.

In summary, the placement and restraint of non-seismic Category I structures adjacent to seismic Category I structures must be evaluated to prevent adverse seismic interactions, ensure adequate separation or restraint, and maintain quality assurance standards, as required by GDC 1 and detailed in DSRS 3.8.4, RG 1.29, RG 1.143, and SRP 3.9.2.

data.query: In the context of refueling operations at a nuclear power plant, what combined regulatory requirements from general design criteria, seismic structural review standards, and relevant regulatory guides must be considered to ensure that temporary or movable structures, such as bioshields and inspection racks, do not adversely interact with seismic Category I safety-related structures during seismic events?
data.answer:
To ensure that temporary or movable structures, such as bioshields and inspection racks, do not adversely interact with seismic Category I safety-related structures during seismic events in the context of refueling operations, several combined regulatory requirements must be considered:

1. General Design Criteria (GDC):
- GDC 1 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) requires that all structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function. This includes maintaining appropriate records and implementing a quality assurance program (Evidence [2]).
- GDC 2 and GDC 4 require that SSCs important to safety withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including seismic events, without losing their safety function (Evidence [1], [5]).

2. Seismic Structural Review Standards:
- DSRS 3.8.4 mandates a review of the relationship between seismic Category I structures and adjacent or internal structures, including temporary or removable sections like bioshields. The review focuses on the arrangement, separation (seismic gaps), and potential interactions to ensure that design boundary conditions and structural behavior under seismic loads are not compromised (Evidence [1]).
- Compliance with ACI 349 (for concrete) and ANSI/AISC N690 (for steel), as supplemented by RG 1.142, is required for seismic Category I structures (Evidence [1]).

3. Regulatory Guides:
- RG 1.143 provides criteria for evaluating structures for natural phenomena, including seismic loads, and references codes and standards for design and capacity criteria (Evidence [3]).
- RG 1.160 requires monitoring the performance and condition of SSCs, including during maintenance and refueling, to ensure continued capability to fulfill safety functions. Before maintenance activities, the licensee must assess and manage any increased risk, including the potential for temporary structures to impact safety-related SSCs (Evidence [4]).
- RG 1.221 emphasizes the need to protect safety-related SSCs from the effects of natural phenomena, including wind- or missile-generated impacts, which is analogous to ensuring that temporary structures cannot become hazards during seismic events (Evidence [5]).

In summary, the combined requirements dictate that temporary or movable structures used during refueling must be evaluated for their potential to interact with seismic Category I structures under seismic loads. This includes ensuring adequate separation, structural integrity, and risk assessment per the referenced codes, standards, and regulatory guides. The design and placement of such structures must not compromise the safety function of seismic Category I SSCs during seismic events.

evidence_chain.section: B. DISCUSSION (Hurricane-Generated Missiles)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
In accordance with GDC 2 and 4, structures, systems, and components that are important to safety must be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena without losing the ability to perform their safety function. Hurricane missiles (i.e., objects moving under the action of aerodynamic forces induced by the hurricane wind) are among the most extreme effects of credible natural phenomena that can occur at nuclear power plant sites subject to hurricanes.

To ensure the safety of nuclear power plants in the event of a hurricane strike, NRC regulations require that nuclear power plant designs consider the impact of hurricane-generated missiles, in addition to the direct action of the hurricane wind. Hurricanes are capable of generating missiles from objects lying within the path of the hurricane wind and from the debris of nearby damaged structures. The two basic approaches used to characterize hurricane-generated missiles are (1) a standard spectrum of hurricane missiles, and (2) a site-specific probabilistic assessment of the hurricane hazard. No definitive guidance has been developed for use in applying hazard probability methods to characterize site-dependent hurricane-generated missiles. Damage to safety-related structures by hurricanes or other wind-generated missiles implies that a sequence of random events has occurred. That event sequence typically includes an occurrence of a hurricane in the plant vicinity, existence and availability of missiles in the area, injection of missiles into the wind field, suspension and flight of those missiles, impact of the missiles on safety-related structures, and resulting damage to critical equipment. Given defense-in-depth considerations, the uncertainties in these events preclude the use of a probabilistic assessment as the sole basis for assessing how well the plant is protected against hurricane missile damage.

Protection from a spectrum of missiles (ranging from a massive missile that deforms on impact to a rigid penetrating missile) provides assurance that the necessary structures, systems, and components will be available to mitigate the potential effects of a hurricane on plant safety. Given that the design-basis hurricane windspeed has a very low frequency of occurrence, to be credible, the representative missiles must be common items around the plant site and must have a reasonable probability of becoming airborne within the hurricane wind field.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for the structural design of seismic Category I steel structures?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for the structural design of seismic Category I steel structures are primarily established through compliance with specific codes, standards, and regulatory requirements. According to DSRS 3.8.4, Section II (Acceptance Criteria), the design, materials, fabrication, erection, inspection, and testing of seismic Category I steel structures must comply with ANSI/AISC N690-1994, including Supplement 2 (2004), which is the 'Specification for the Design, Fabrication and Erection of Steel Safety-Related Structures for Nuclear Facilities.' The design should also adhere to the applicable portions of the AISC Specification for Structural Steel Buildings (AISC 360), as referenced by AISC N690. The NRC reviews the use of more recent codes on a case-by-case basis for adequacy.

The acceptance criteria include: (1) ensuring that all loads and load combinations are in accordance with ANSI/AISC N690-1994 (DSRS 3.8.4, II.3.B); (2) imposing design limits on stresses, strains, gross deformations, and factors of safety against structural failure, with allowable limits compared to those delineated in the DSRS (DSRS 3.8.4, II.5); and (3) ensuring that the structures are designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, such as earthquakes, without loss of safety function, as required by 10 CFR 50.55a(b).

Additionally, 10 CFR 50.55a(a) requires that structures important to safety meet quality standards commensurate with their safety function and be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site, with sufficient margin for uncertainties. RG 1.143 further supports the use of AISC N690 and related standards for steel structures, emphasizing that acceptability evaluations should be based on these codes and their capacity criteria.

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria for seismic Category I steel structures are grounded in compliance with ANSI/AISC N690-1994 (with Supplement 2), AISC 360 as referenced, and the requirements of 10 CFR 50.55a, ensuring adequate safety margins and structural integrity under seismic and other natural phenomena loads.
