data.query: How are acceptance criteria for foundation settlement reconciled with general design criteria for quality assurance in nuclear power plant construction?
data.answer:
Acceptance criteria for foundation settlement in nuclear power plant construction are reconciled with general design criteria for quality assurance through a structured regulatory framework that integrates both technical and quality assurance requirements. According to SRP 3.8.5 Section II, acceptance criteria for foundation settlement are established to meet the requirements of 10 CFR 50.55a and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 1, which mandate that safety-related structures be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety functions. Additionally, Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 50 sets forth quality assurance criteria, including Criterion III—Design Control, which requires measures to ensure that regulatory requirements and design bases are correctly translated into specifications, drawings, procedures, and instructions (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, Criterion III).

The review process described in SRP 3.8.5 includes assessment of materials, quality control, and special construction techniques for seismic Category I foundations, ensuring that quality control programs address fabrication and construction, including nondestructive examination and erection tolerances. These technical acceptance criteria are directly linked to the quality assurance program, which is reviewed under SRP Chapter 17 and must comply with Appendix B requirements.

Furthermore, 10 CFR 50.55a(b) requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed and constructed to quality standards, and that codes and standards used must be evaluated for adequacy and supplemented as necessary. Regulatory Guide 1.206 reinforces that Appendix B quality assurance requirements apply to all phases of plant construction, ensuring that both technical and quality assurance criteria are integrated and reconciled throughout the design and construction process.

In summary, acceptance criteria for foundation settlement are reconciled with general design criteria for quality assurance by requiring that both sets of criteria be met through coordinated design control, quality control, and quality assurance programs, as mandated by 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A and B, and as implemented through the SRP and associated regulatory guidance.

evidence_chain.section: A. INTRODUCTION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
• 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, “General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants.” The General Design Criteria (GDC) establish minimum requirements for the principal design criteria for water-cooled nuclear power plants similar in design and location to plants for which construction permits have been issued by the Commission. The NRC issued RG 1.232, “Guidance for Developing Principal Design Criteria for Non-Light-Water Reactors” (Ref. 12), to provide guidance on how the GDC in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, may be adapted for non-LWR designs.

• 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, “Quality Assurance Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants and Fuel Processing Plants.” Appendix B sets forth the requirements for quality assurance programs for nuclear power plants and is applicable to applications for ESPs, DCs, and COLs as per 10 CFR 52.17(a)(1)(xi), 10 CFR 52.47(a)(19) and 10 CFR 52.79(a)(25) and 10 CFR 52.79(a)(27).

Purpose of Regulatory Guides

The NRC issues RGs to describe to the public methods that the staff considers acceptable for use in implementing specific parts of the agency’s regulations, to explain techniques that the staff uses in evaluating specific problems or postulated events, and to provide guidance to applicants. Regulatory guides are not substitutes for regulations and compliance with them is not required. Methods and solutions that differ from those set forth in RGs will be deemed acceptable if they provide a basis for the findings required for the issuance or continuance of a permit or license by the Commission.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory requirements address the consideration of buoyancy forces in the structural analysis of nuclear power plant foundations, and how should these requirements be applied to ensure consistency in the analysis methodology?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory requirements explicitly address the consideration of buoyancy forces in the structural analysis of nuclear power plant foundations to ensure safety under various natural phenomena, including floods. According to SRP 3.8.5 (Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA), buoyancy (denoted as F') due to design-basis floods must be included in specific load combinations (e.g., D + F'), alongside other loads such as dead load (D), lateral earth pressure (H), and environmental loads (E, W, Wt). The SRP requires that the analysis for seismic Category I foundations consider soil-structure interaction, hydrodynamic effects, and dynamic soil pressure, and that the adequacy of sliding and overturning analyses—including the effects of buoyancy—be reviewed on a case-by-case basis. The analysis must use consistent criteria for lateral displacement and coefficients of friction, reflecting the nature of the sliding interface and the extent of passive pressure mobilization.

SRP 3.7.2 further reinforces that the analysis must account for buoyancy, groundwater, and pore water pressure, including their variability over time, when evaluating seismic overturning moments, sliding forces, and soil-structure interaction. The staff reviews whether the applicant’s analysis appropriately considers these effects, as well as the potential for separation or loss of contact between the structure and the soil during seismic events.

10 CFR 50.55a establishes the regulatory basis, requiring that structures important to safety be designed to withstand natural phenomena, including floods, and that appropriate combinations of normal, accident, and natural phenomena effects be considered. The design must reflect the most severe historical conditions with sufficient margin.

To ensure consistency in analysis methodology, the SRP emphasizes the use of accepted load combinations, consistent application of coefficients and criteria, and cross-referencing with related SRP sections (e.g., SRP 3.7.1 and 2.5.4) to ensure technical consistency across reviews. Thus, buoyancy forces must be systematically included in foundation stability analyses, with methodologies and assumptions clearly justified and consistently applied as per SRP and regulatory requirements.

evidence_chain.section: II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
In addition to the load combinations referenced above, the combinations used to check against sliding and overturning attributable to earthquakes, winds, tornadoes, hurricanes, and against flotation because of floods are acceptable if found to be in accordance with the following:

A. D + H + E 
B. D + H + W 
C. D + H + E' 
D. D + H + Wt 
E. D + F' 

Where D, E, W, E', and Wt are as referenced in Subsection II.3 of SRP Section 3.8.4, where H is the lateral earth pressure, and F' is the buoyant force of the design-basis flood. In load combination D, the higher of Wt or hurricane should be used. Justification should be provided for including live loads or portions thereof in these combinations.

... The design and analysis procedures used for seismic Category I foundations are acceptable if found to be in accordance with the following:

A. The design should consider the soil-structure interaction (SSI), hydrodynamic effect, and dynamic soil pressure.

... In addition to the above, the design and analysis procedures for the following details are reviewed on a case-by-case basis:

... B. Adequacy of the sliding analysis method and the analysis results to account for potential mat foundation liftoff effects. The staff should also review the calculation of the factor of safety against sliding. If sliding resistance is the sum of shear friction along the basemat and contribution of soil lateral pressure up to the full passive pressure capacity induced by embedment effects, the adequacy of the analysis to consider these effects is addressed using a consistent lateral displacement criterion. This involves the use of static versus dynamic coefficient of friction consistent with the use of partial versus full passive pressure. The reviewer should also consider whether the selection of the coefficient of friction used in the sliding stability analysis considers the various sliding interfaces (e.g., soil shear failure, concrete to soil, waterproofing to soil, concrete basemat to concrete mudmat).

... For the pseudo-static and time history analysis methods, all three directional demand forces should be considered to act simultaneously. Therefore, the resultant seismic forces (horizontal resultant force for sliding from the two horizontal forces and similarly the resultant overturning moment for overturning stability) should be considered.

data.query: What is the relationship between general design criteria for structural integrity and the treatment of external hydrostatic pressures, such as buoyancy, in the design and analysis of nuclear facility basemats?
data.answer:
The relationship between the general design criteria for structural integrity and the treatment of external hydrostatic pressures, such as buoyancy, in the design and analysis of nuclear facility basemats is established through regulatory requirements and detailed guidance on load combinations and analytical modeling. 

According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A (GDC 1, 2, 4), structures important to safety, including basemats, must be designed to withstand natural phenomena (such as floods) and environmental effects without loss of safety function (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criteria 1, 2, 4). This includes consideration of the most severe historical natural phenomena and appropriate combinations of normal, accident, and natural event loads (Evidence [2]).

SRP 3.8.5 specifies that the design of seismic Category I foundations must include load combinations that account for buoyant forces due to external hydrostatic pressures, such as those from design-basis floods (load combination D + F'). These combinations are used to check against flotation, sliding, and overturning, ensuring the structural integrity of the basemat under such conditions (Evidence [1]). The inclusion of the buoyant force (F') directly addresses the impact of external hydrostatic pressures on the basemat.

Further, SRP 3.7.2 and 3.7.1 reinforce that analytical modeling for seismic Category I structures must consider the effects of groundwater (pore water), variability of groundwater level, and potential separation or loss of contact between the basemat and soil, all of which are influenced by external hydrostatic pressures (Evidence [4], [5]). These requirements ensure that the basemat is evaluated for both structural integrity and stability under the combined effects of seismic and hydrostatic loads.

In summary, the general design criteria require that basemats be designed to maintain structural integrity under all credible load combinations, including those involving external hydrostatic pressures (buoyancy). The SRP provides specific guidance on how to incorporate these pressures into the design and analysis, ensuring compliance with the regulatory basis established in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A.

data.query: How do general design criteria for structural integrity and the requirements for foundation analysis address the consideration of buoyancy effects in nuclear power plant basemat design?
data.answer:
The general design criteria for structural integrity and foundation analysis in nuclear power plant basemat design explicitly address the consideration of buoyancy effects, particularly in the context of flood conditions. According to SRP 3.8.5 (Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA), the design must include load combinations that account for flotation due to floods, with the buoyant force (F') of the design-basis flood specifically included in the load combinations (e.g., D + F'). These combinations are used to check against sliding, overturning, and flotation, ensuring that the basemat remains stable under various loading scenarios, including those induced by buoyancy during flooding events. The review process also includes verification of adequate safety margins against overturning and sliding, further ensuring structural integrity under buoyant forces.

Additionally, SRP 3.7.2 (Section I.4) and SRP 3.7.1 (Section I, II) emphasize the importance of soil-structure interaction (SSI) analysis, which must consider the effects of pore water, variability of groundwater levels, and potential separation or loss of contact between the foundation and soil. These factors are critical in assessing how buoyancy and groundwater conditions affect the structural response and stability of the basemat.

The regulatory basis for these requirements is found in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A (Criterion 1), which mandates that structures important to safety be designed and constructed to quality standards that ensure their safety functions are maintained. RG 1.206 further clarifies that the General Design Criteria (GDC) in Appendix A establish the minimum requirements for principal design criteria, and the Standard Review Plan (NUREG-0800) provides acceptable methods for meeting these requirements.

In summary, the NRC’s general design criteria and foundation analysis requirements comprehensively address buoyancy effects by mandating explicit load combinations for flotation, requiring SSI analysis that considers groundwater and pore water effects, and enforcing quality standards to ensure structural integrity under all relevant loading conditions (SRP 3.8.5, SRP 3.7.2, SRP 3.7.1, 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A, RG 1.206).

data.query: What is the relationship between regulatory requirements for load combinations and the treatment of buoyancy forces in the structural analysis of nuclear power plant foundations?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for load combinations in the structural analysis of nuclear power plant foundations explicitly mandate the inclusion and proper treatment of buoyancy forces. According to SRP 3.8.5, Section II.3, the design of seismic Category I foundations must use specified load combinations that are consistent with those described in SRP Sections 3.8.1 and 3.8.4. Importantly, these combinations must include not only typical loads such as dead load (D), lateral earth pressure (H), and seismic (E) or wind (W) loads, but also the buoyant force (F') associated with the design-basis flood. For example, one of the required load combinations is D + F', which directly addresses the need to consider buoyancy in the analysis, particularly for checking against flotation due to floods.

This requirement is reinforced by 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, Section IV.A.2-3, which states that the design of Seismic Category I structures must consider the effects of seismic events in combination with other loads, and specifically requires that the design account for the effects of buoyancy and hydrodynamic forces resulting from groundwater or other sources during and after seismic events. This ensures that the foundation's stability is maintained under all credible loading scenarios, including those where buoyancy could compromise structural integrity.

In summary, regulatory requirements establish a direct relationship between load combinations and the treatment of buoyancy forces: buoyancy must be explicitly included in the load combinations used for the structural analysis of nuclear power plant foundations to ensure safety against flotation and other buoyancy-related hazards, as mandated by both SRP 3.8.5 and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory requirements for structural analysis methods ensure that the modeling approach for nuclear power plant basemats is consistent with general design criteria for quality assurance?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory requirements for structural analysis methods ensure that the modeling approach for nuclear power plant basemats is consistent with general design criteria for quality assurance through a combination of regulatory mandates and detailed acceptance criteria. Specifically, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 1 (see [2]), requires that safety-related structures, such as basemats, be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety functions. This includes the use of recognized codes and standards, which must be evaluated for applicability and adequacy, and the establishment of a quality assurance program to ensure satisfactory performance.

SRP 3.8.5 (see [1]) operationalizes these requirements by specifying that design and analysis procedures for basemats must comply with 10 CFR 50.55a, GDC 1, and Appendix B (quality assurance criteria). The SRP acceptance criteria require that modeling approaches, including the use of computer programs, be validated according to established procedures (referencing SRP 3.8.1). The design must consider critical factors such as soil-structure interaction, hydrodynamic effects, and dynamic soil pressure, and must follow industry standards like ACI 349 and guidance in RG 1.142. Analytical methods for determining bending moments, shear forces, and sliding stability are reviewed for adequacy, ensuring that all relevant interfaces and effects are properly considered.

Furthermore, SRP 3.7.2 (see [3]) and SRP 3.7.1 (see [4]) reinforce that analytical models must accurately represent the stiffness, mass, and damping characteristics of the basemat and associated structures, and that the effects of basemat flexibility are explicitly considered. These SRPs require applicants to identify and justify any deviations from the SRP criteria, ensuring transparency and regulatory oversight.

In summary, the NRC’s regulatory framework, as detailed in the cited documents, ensures that structural analysis methods for basemats are rigorously controlled, validated, and consistent with the overarching quality assurance requirements of GDC 1, thereby supporting the safety and reliability of nuclear power plant foundations.

data.query: What is the relationship between NRC expectations for modeling techniques in seismic analysis and the acceptance criteria for foundation design in nuclear facilities?
data.answer:
The NRC's expectations for modeling techniques in seismic analysis are closely linked to the acceptance criteria for foundation design in nuclear facilities, as both are grounded in regulatory requirements and detailed guidance to ensure safety under seismic events.

According to SRP 3.8.5 (Section II.4), acceptable design and analysis procedures for seismic Category I foundations must consider soil-structure interaction (SSI), hydrodynamic effects, and dynamic soil pressure. The modeling techniques—whether pseudo-static, linear time history, or nonlinear time history analysis—must be robust enough to capture the dynamic characteristics of the structure and foundation, including all three directional seismic forces acting simultaneously. The choice of modeling technique directly affects how factors of safety for sliding and overturning are calculated and compared to acceptance criteria. For example, in time history analyses, the minimum factor of safety over the time history must meet the acceptance criteria for the relevant load combination.

SRP 3.7.2 and SRP 3.7.1 further clarify that seismic analysis methods must use suitable dynamic or equivalent static load analysis, with a preference for dynamic analysis (response spectrum or time history methods) that account for SSI and the three orthogonal components of ground motion. The acceptance criteria require that the analysis methods be capable of demonstrating that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) remain functional and within stress, strain, and deformation limits during and after seismic events, as mandated by 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2, and Appendix S.

SRP 2.5.2 and referenced Regulatory Guides (e.g., RG 1.132, RG 1.208) provide additional expectations for site investigations and ground motion characterization, which inform the modeling inputs and acceptance criteria for foundation design.

In summary, the NRC expects that modeling techniques in seismic analysis must be sufficiently rigorous and validated to demonstrate compliance with acceptance criteria for foundation design, ensuring that nuclear facility foundations can withstand seismic demands as required by regulatory standards (SRP 3.8.5, SRP 3.7.2, SRP 3.7.1, SRP 2.5.2, 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A and S).

data.query: How do NRC regulations define the acceptable methods for modeling nuclear power plant foundations to ensure structural integrity under design basis loads?
data.answer:
NRC regulations define acceptable methods for modeling nuclear power plant foundations to ensure structural integrity under design basis loads through a combination of regulatory requirements, codes, standards, and detailed technical guidance. The primary requirements are set forth in 10 CFR Part 50, including § 50.55a, which mandates that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety must be designed to withstand natural phenomena such as earthquakes, using appropriate codes and standards (e.g., ASME, ACI, ANSI/AISC) and reflecting the most severe historical site-specific events (10 CFR Part 50, § 50.55a(h); SRP 2.5.2 II.1).

For modeling foundations, the Standard Review Plan (SRP) provides detailed acceptance criteria. SRP 3.8.5 II.4 specifies that design and analysis procedures must account for soil-structure interaction (SSI), hydrodynamic effects, and dynamic soil pressure. For concrete foundations, ACI 349 and RG 1.142 are referenced; for steel foundations, ANSI/AISC N690-1994 applies. Containment foundations must follow SRP 3.8.1 II.4. Analytical modeling must consider sliding, overturning, and uplift, with stability evaluated using either pseudo-static or time history analysis methods. For nonlinear time history analyses, the model must simulate sliding and uplift using appropriate finite elements, and seismic input time histories must be scaled by the required safety factor (SRP 3.8.5 II.4).

SRP 3.7.2 II.3 further clarifies that both lumped-mass stick models and finite element models are acceptable if they accurately represent the stiffness, mass, and damping of the structure and foundation, including torsion, rocking, and translation effects. The adequacy of the model must be demonstrated by comparison with static analysis results and by ensuring smooth mode shapes.

Additionally, SRP 3.7.1 and SRP 2.5.2 require that SSI effects, site-specific soil properties, and the full range of design ground motions (in three orthogonal directions) be incorporated into the analysis. Regulatory Guides (e.g., RG 1.132, RG 1.138) provide further guidance on site and laboratory investigations to support the modeling and analysis of foundation behavior under design basis loads.

In summary, NRC regulations require that foundation modeling for nuclear power plants use validated analytical methods, incorporate SSI and site-specific geotechnical data, and follow established codes and standards to ensure structural integrity under design basis loads.

iii. The mathematical model should include the effects of sliding and uplift between the foundation and the soil media using appropriate finite elements that can simulate sliding once the frictional limit is reached and can simulate contact surfaces that can transmit compression but not tension.

3. Procedures Used for Analytical Modeling.  A nuclear power plant (NPP) facility consists of very complex structural systems.  To be acceptable, the stiffness, mass, and damping characteristics of the structural systems should be adequately incorporated into the analytical models.  Specifically, the following items should be considered in analytical modeling:

A. Designation of Systems Versus Subsystems.  Seismic Category I structures that are considered in conjunction with the foundation and its supporting media are defined as "seismic systems."  Other seismic Category I SSCs that are not designated as "seismic systems" should be considered as "seismic subsystems."

...

C. Modeling of Structures.  Two types of structural models are widely used by the nuclear industry: lumped-mass stick model and finite element model.  Either of these two types of modeling techniques is acceptable if the following guidelines are met:

i. Lumped-Mass Stick Model

For a lumped-mass model, the eccentricities between the centroid (the neutral axis for axial and bending deformation), the center of rigid mass, and the center of gravity of the mass at each floor or mass station should be considered.  The model should include the effects of torsion, rocking, and translation.  The number of lumped masses should be sufficient to ensure that the mode shapes are reasonably smooth and that the frequencies of interest are adequately represented.

ii. Finite Element Model

For a finite element model, the mesh should be fine enough to represent the significant modes of vibration and to provide reasonably accurate results for the frequencies and mode shapes of interest.  The model should include the effects of torsion, rocking, and translation, and should adequately represent the stiffness and mass distribution of the structure, including the foundation and supporting media.

The adequacy of the model should be demonstrated by comparison with static analysis results and by ensuring that the mode shapes are reasonably smooth for all modes included in the dynamic analysis.

data.query: What is the relationship between general design criteria for quality standards and the regulatory expectations for analytical methods used in the structural analysis of nuclear facility basemats?
data.answer:
The general design criteria for quality standards, as established in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, require that structures, systems, and components important to safety—such as nuclear facility basemats—be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety functions. This regulatory expectation extends to the analytical methods used in the structural analysis of basemats. Specifically, Criterion 1 mandates the use of generally recognized codes and standards, which must be identified, evaluated for applicability and adequacy, and supplemented as necessary to ensure a quality product (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1).

SRP 3.8.5 further clarifies that the acceptance criteria for basemat structural analysis are based on compliance with these general design criteria. The SRP specifies that analytical methods and design procedures must align with recognized standards such as ACI 349 for concrete foundations and ANSI/AISC N690 for steel foundations, and must consider factors like soil-structure interaction and dynamic effects. The SRP also requires that any deviations from these methods be justified by the applicant, demonstrating that alternative approaches still meet the underlying regulatory requirements (SRP 3.8.5, Section II).

Regulatory Guides (e.g., RG 1.206) provide acceptable methods for meeting these requirements but are not mandatory; alternative methods may be used if they provide an adequate basis for regulatory findings. Thus, the relationship is that the general design criteria set the overarching quality expectations, and the regulatory framework—including SRP and RGs—translates these into specific expectations for analytical methods, ensuring that the structural analysis of basemats is performed to standards that guarantee safety-related performance.

data.query: How do general design criteria for quality assurance apply to the modeling and analysis of nuclear power plant foundations using finite element methods?
data.answer:
The general design criteria for quality assurance, as outlined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 1, require that structures, systems, and components important to safety—including nuclear power plant foundations—be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety functions (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 1). This mandate is implemented through a quality assurance (QA) program established and maintained in accordance with Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 50, which specifies 18 quality criteria (SRP 17.5, Section II; SRP 3.8.5, II.1, II.5).

For the modeling and analysis of nuclear power plant foundations using finite element methods (FEM), these QA requirements apply to both the analytical process and the supporting software tools. SRP 3.8.5 (II.4.H) specifies that computer programs used for design and analysis, such as FEM software, must be validated according to established procedures (referencing SRP 3.8.1, II.4.E). The QA program must ensure that modeling and analysis activities are performed under controlled conditions, using appropriate equipment and procedures, and that special controls and verification methods are in place (SRP 17.5, II.B.6, II.B.8).

Additionally, the QA program must document all activities, including the selection and validation of codes and standards (e.g., ACI 349 for concrete, ANSI/AISC N690 for steel), and maintain records throughout the life of the facility (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 1; SRP 3.8.5, II.6.A). Regulatory Guide 1.28 endorses the use of ASME NQA-1 standards (including Subpart 2.5 for foundations), which provide detailed QA requirements for design, analysis, and construction activities, including the use of FEM (RG 1.28, Section C.6).

In summary, the general design criteria for quality assurance require that finite element modeling and analysis of nuclear power plant foundations be performed within a documented QA program, using validated software, recognized codes and standards, and under controlled conditions, with comprehensive records maintained to demonstrate compliance and support the safety function of the foundations.

data.query: What are the regulatory expectations for the selection and justification of element types (such as solid or shell elements) in the structural analysis of nuclear power plant basemats?
data.answer:
The regulatory expectations for the selection and justification of element types (such as solid or shell elements) in the structural analysis of nuclear power plant basemats are clearly outlined in NRC guidance documents. According to SRP 3.7.2, Section II.3.C, when using finite element models for basemats, the type of elements (e.g., beam, shell, solid) must be explicitly justified. The selection of element type, mesh size, and modeling assumptions should be made to adequately represent the stiffness, mass, and boundary conditions of the basemat. Specifically, the use of shell or solid elements for modeling thick slabs like basemats requires justification, and the mesh must be sufficiently refined to capture significant modes of vibration and stress distributions. The adequacy of the model should be demonstrated through sensitivity studies or by comparison with analytical solutions or test data, if available. Furthermore, the modeling must account for soil-structure interaction and the flexibility of the basemat (SRP 3.7.2, II.3.C).

SRP 3.8.5, Section II.4, reinforces that the appropriateness of the method for determining bending moments and shear forces in the mat foundation for seismic loads is reviewed on a case-by-case basis, emphasizing the need for a sound technical basis for the chosen modeling approach. Additionally, the design and analysis procedures must comply with relevant codes and standards (e.g., ACI 349, RG 1.142) and consider all pertinent load effects, including seismic and soil-structure interaction.

These expectations are grounded in the regulatory requirement that safety-related structures must be designed to withstand natural phenomena, as stated in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2. This criterion mandates that the design bases reflect appropriate consideration of severe natural events and ensure the continued performance of safety functions.

In summary, the NRC expects that the selection and justification of element types in basemat analysis be technically justified, adequately documented, and demonstrated to accurately represent the physical behavior of the structure under all relevant loading conditions.

evidence_chain.section: II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA, 3. Procedures Used for Analytical Modeling
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
C. Modeling of Structures.  Two types of structural models are widely used by the nuclear industry: lumped-mass stick model and finite element model.  Either of these two types of modeling techniques is acceptable if the following guidelines are met:

i. Lumped-Mass Stick Model

For a lumped-mass model, the eccentricities between the centroid (the neutral axis for axial and bending deformation), the center of rigid mass, and the center of gravity of the mass at each floor or mass level should be considered.  The stick model should be capable of representing the significant dynamic characteristics of the structure, including the effects of torsion, rocking, and translation.  The stick model should be validated by comparison with a more refined model or by comparison with test data, if available.

ii. Finite Element Model

For a finite element model, the type of elements (e.g., beam, shell, solid) used to represent the structure should be justified.  The element type, mesh size, and modeling assumptions should be selected to adequately represent the stiffness, mass, and boundary conditions of the structure.  The adequacy of the finite element model should be demonstrated by sensitivity studies or by comparison with analytical solutions or test data, if available.  The use of shell or solid elements to model thick slabs (such as basemats) should be justified.  The mesh should be sufficiently refined to capture the significant modes of vibration and stress distributions.  The modeling of the basemat should consider the interaction with the supporting soil or rock, and the flexibility of the basemat should be represented in the model.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory requirements for seismic analysis of nuclear power plant foundations ensure that all relevant structural elements, such as basemats, walls, and pilasters, are appropriately modeled and evaluated for seismic demands?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory requirements for seismic analysis of nuclear power plant foundations ensure that all relevant structural elements—such as basemats, walls, and pilasters—are appropriately modeled and evaluated for seismic demands through a combination of detailed review criteria, modeling guidelines, and quality assurance standards.

According to SRP 3.8.5 (Sections I and II.4), the NRC review encompasses all seismic Category I foundation elements, including basemats and the junctions with sidewalls, to confirm that sufficient descriptive and analytical information is provided. The design must consider soil-structure interaction (SSI), hydrodynamic effects, and dynamic soil pressures. The mathematical model is required to adequately represent the dynamic characteristics of the structure, capturing vibration modes critical for sliding and overturning stability analyses. The appropriateness of methods for determining bending moments and shear forces in the mat foundation under seismic loads is reviewed on a case-by-case basis.

SRP 3.7.2 (Section II) further specifies that analytical models must incorporate the stiffness, mass, and damping characteristics of all significant structural elements, including basemats, walls, and pilasters. Both lumped-mass stick models and finite element models are acceptable if they include all significant masses and stiffnesses and account for the flexibility of basemats, sidewalls, and interior structures, as well as their interaction with supporting soil or rock. The procedures must also address seismic overturning moments, sliding forces, and soil pressures beneath and along the foundation walls.

10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, establishes the regulatory basis by requiring that all structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function, and that appropriate records be maintained.

In summary, NRC requirements ensure comprehensive seismic modeling and evaluation of all relevant foundation elements by mandating detailed analytical procedures, robust modeling of all significant structural components, and adherence to quality assurance standards (SRP 3.8.5, SRP 3.7.2, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1).

When time history analyses are performed, either of the following options may be considered. In either case, the time histories may be real or artificial.  

Option 1:  Single Set of Time Histories.  The justification for the use of the single set of time histories is reviewed.  The approach used to demonstrate that the response spectra generated from the time histories envelop the design response spectra are reviewed.  Depending on the approach used, the application of the requirements to match a target power spectral density (PSD) function compatible with the design response spectra may also be reviewed.   

Option 2:  Multiple Sets of Time Histories.  In lieu of the use of a single time history, multiple artificial or real ground motion time histories may be used for the seismic analyses and design of the SSCs.  The parameters describing the time histories and the number of time histories are reviewed.  The approach used to demonstrate the adequacy of the set of multiple time histories, in terms of the enveloping criteria and having sufficient power over the frequency range of interest, is reviewed.   

In some instances, a nonlinear analysis of the SSCs may be appropriate (e.g., stability analysis and evaluation of existing structures).  Multiple time history analyses using artificial or real earthquake time histories may be used when such analyses are proposed.  The adequacy of time histories used for the nonlinear analyses is reviewed.

data.query: What is the relationship between general design criteria for structural integrity and the NRC's expectations for the use of different structural analysis models in the design of nuclear power plant foundations?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for structural integrity, as outlined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A (specifically GDC 1, 2, and 4), establish the foundational regulatory expectations for the design, fabrication, erection, and testing of nuclear power plant structures, including foundations. These criteria require that safety-related structures be designed to quality standards commensurate with their safety functions (GDC 1), be capable of withstanding severe natural phenomena (GDC 2), and be protected against dynamic effects (GDC 4) (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1).

SRP 3.8.5 Section II further clarifies the NRC's expectations for the use of structural analysis models in meeting these criteria. The NRC requires that the design and analysis procedures for seismic Category I foundations explicitly consider factors such as soil-structure interaction, hydrodynamic effects, and dynamic soil pressure. The use of specific codes and standards (e.g., ACI 349 for concrete, ANSI/AISC N690-1994 for steel) is mandated, with additional guidance from regulatory guides as appropriate. The NRC reviews the appropriateness of analysis methods (e.g., for bending moments, shear forces, sliding, and overturning) on a case-by-case basis, ensuring that the chosen models and methods are consistent with the required safety functions and quality standards.

Furthermore, the NRC expects that the selection and application of structural analysis models (such as pseudo-static or linear time history analysis) are justified and that the factors of safety are determined in a manner consistent with the load combinations and acceptance criteria. The analysis must account for all relevant forces and interactions, and the adequacy of the models is evaluated against the regulatory acceptance criteria to ensure structural integrity under all design-basis conditions (SRP 3.8.5, Section II).

In summary, the relationship is that the general design criteria set the high-level requirements for structural integrity, while the NRC's expectations for structural analysis models ensure that these requirements are met through the use of appropriate, code-compliant, and rigorously justified analysis procedures.

Requirements

Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations:

2. GDC 2, as it relates to the design of the safety-related structures that are capable of withstanding the most severe natural phenomena, such as wind, tornadoes, hurricanes, floods, and earthquakes and the appropriate combination of all loads.

3. GDC 4, as it relates to appropriately protecting safety-related structures against dynamic effects, including the effects of missiles, pipe whipping, and discharging fluids, that may result from equipment failures and from events and conditions outside the nuclear power unit.

...

4. Design and Analysis Procedures.  The design and analysis procedures used for seismic Category I foundations are acceptable if found to be in accordance with the following:

A. The design should consider the soil-structure interaction (SSI), hydrodynamic effect, and dynamic soil pressure.

B. For seismic Category I concrete foundations other than the containment foundations, the procedures are in accordance with the ACI 349, with additional guidance provided by RG 1.142.

C. For seismic Category I steel foundations, the procedures are in accordance with ANSI/AISC N690-1994 including Supplement 2 (2004).

D. For the containment foundation, if in accordance with the design and analysis procedures referenced in SRP Section 3.8.1, Subsection II.4.

...

In addition to the above, the design and analysis procedures for the following details are reviewed on a case-by-case basis:

A. Appropriateness of the method for determination of the bending moments and shear forces in the mat foundation for seismic loads.

B. Adequacy of the sliding analysis method and the analysis results to account for potential mat foundation liftoff effects.  The staff should also review the calculation of the factor of safety against sliding.  If sliding resistance is the sum of shear friction along the basemat and contribution of soil lateral pressure up to the full passive pressure capacity induced by embedment effects, the adequacy of the analysis to consider these effects is addressed using a consistent lateral displacement criterion.  This involves the use of static versus dynamic coefficient of friction consistent with the use of partial versus full passive pressure.  The reviewer should also consider whether the selection of the coefficient of friction used in the sliding stability analysis considers the various sliding interfaces (e.g., soil shear failure, concrete to soil, waterproofing to soil, concrete basemat to concrete mudmat).

If the stability evaluation is performed based on a pseudo-static approach, using the maximum seismic demand loads (e.g., maximum forces in the two horizontal directions and one vertical direction), then the factors of safety for sliding and overturning can be determined by the ratio of capacity to demand loads.  

However, if a linear time history analysis approach is utilized, then the factor of safety can be calculated at each time step throughout the time history.  The minimum value of the factors of safety calculated in this manner should be compared against the acceptance criteria for that load combination.  For the pseudo-static and time history analysis methods, all three directional demand forces should be considered to act simultaneously.  Therefore, the resultant seismic forces (horizontal resultant force for sliding from the two horizontal forces and similarly the resultant overturning moment for overturning stability) should be considered.

data.query: How do general design criteria for quality assurance and structural integrity apply to the modeling of soil-structure interaction for nuclear power plant foundations?
data.answer:
The general design criteria for quality assurance and structural integrity, as outlined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A (GDC 1 and GDC 2), directly inform the modeling of soil-structure interaction (SSI) for nuclear power plant foundations. GDC 1 requires that safety-related structures be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety functions, and that a quality assurance program be implemented (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1; SRP 2.5.4). This means that all aspects of SSI modeling—including site investigations, laboratory testing of soils, and analytical methods—must adhere to rigorous quality assurance protocols, with appropriate records maintained throughout the plant’s life (SRP 2.5.4; RG 1.28, RG 1.132, RG 1.138).

GDC 2 requires that safety-related structures be capable of withstanding the most severe natural phenomena, including earthquakes, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2; SRP 3.7.1, SRP 3.7.2, SRP 3.8.5). This necessitates that SSI modeling incorporates the effects of seismic ground motions, soil layering, embedment, and dynamic soil-structure coupling. The modeling must account for uncertainties in soil properties, nonlinear soil behavior, and potential loss of contact between the structure and soil during seismic events (SRP 3.7.2). The design ground motion for SSI analysis is established using free-field response spectra at the foundation level, considering site-specific soil profiles (SRP 3.7.1).

Furthermore, SRP 3.8.5 specifies that design and analysis procedures for seismic Category I foundations are acceptable if they consider SSI, hydrodynamic effects, and dynamic soil pressure, and if they are consistent with quality assurance and structural integrity requirements. The adequacy of methods for determining foundation responses (e.g., bending moments, shear forces, sliding stability) is reviewed on a case-by-case basis, ensuring that all relevant interfaces and failure modes are addressed.

In summary, the general design criteria mandate that SSI modeling for nuclear power plant foundations be performed using high-quality, validated methods that ensure structural integrity under severe natural phenomena, with comprehensive quality assurance and documentation throughout the process.

Requirements

Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations:

Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2 - The design basis shall reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe earthquakes that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which historical data have been accumulated.

2. 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S is applicable to applications for a DC or COL to 10 CFR Part 52 or a construction permit (CP) or operating license (OL) pursuant to 10 CFR Part 50 on or after January 10, 1997. Appendix S requires that for SSE ground motions, SSCs will remain functional and within applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits. The required safety functions of SSCs must be assured during and after the vibratory ground motion through design, testing, or qualification methods. The evaluation must take into account SSI effects and the expected duration of the vibratory motion. ...

SRP Acceptance Criteria

Specific SRP acceptance criteria acceptable to meet the relevant requirements of the Commission's regulations identified above are as follows for review described in this SRP section. ...

1. Seismic Analysis Methods. The seismic analysis of all seismic Category I SSCs should use either a suitable dynamic analysis method or an equivalent static load analysis method, if justified. The SRP acceptance criteria primarily address linear elastic analysis coupled with allowable stresses near elastic limits of the structures. ...

A. Dynamic Analysis Method. When calculating seismic responses of seismic Category I structures, dynamic analysis (response spectrum analysis method or time history analysis method) should be performed. To be acceptable, dynamic analyses should consider the following:

i. Use of appropriate methods of analysis (time history analysis method ...; response spectrum analysis method), accounting for the effects of SSI, if applicable. In general, the response spectrum analysis method is not suitable for SSI analysis.

...

4. Soil-Structure Interaction. The design ground motion response spectra at the foundation level (foundation input response spectra (FIRS)) are defined in the free-field, i.e., without the presence of structures, as described in SRP Section 3.7.1, and Interim Staff Guidance (ISG) DC/COL-ISG-01 and DC/COL-ISG-017. ... As applicable, the modeling methods (including technical bases) used in the seismic system analysis to account for SSI are reviewed. The factors to be considered in accepting a particular modeling method include: (1) the extent of embedment, (2) the layering of the soil/rock strata, and (3) the boundary of the soil-structure model. All SSI analyses should recognize the uncertainties prevalent throughout the phenomenon, and include consideration of the following:

A. The random nature of the soil and rock configuration and material characteristics.

B. Uncertainty in soil constitutive modeling (soil stiffness, damping, etc.).

C. Nonlinear soil behavior.

D. Coupling between the structures and soil.

E. Lack of lateral uniformity in the site soil profile that is usually assumed to be uniformly layered in all horizontal directions in SSI analyses.

F. Effects of the flexibility of soil/rock.

G. Effects of the flexibility of basemat, sidewalls and interior structures.

H. The effect of pore water on structural responses, including the effects of variability of ground-water level with time.

I. Effects of potential separation or loss of contact between the structure (embedded portion of the structure and foundation mat) and the soil during the earthquake.

J. If incoherence effects to reduce high frequency motions are included in the SSI response, consideration of the potential variation of the Coherency Function described in DC/COL-ISG-01 with depth should be included in the evaluation.

The procedures by which strain-dependent soil properties (damping, shear modulus, pore pressure development), layering, and variation of soil properties are incorporated in the analysis are reviewed. Assumptions for modeling the soil-structure system and computer program validation documents are also reviewed.

data.query: What regulatory guidance addresses the treatment of soil stiffness reductions in the analysis of foundation settlements for nuclear facility structures?
data.answer:
The regulatory guidance addressing the treatment of soil stiffness reductions in the analysis of foundation settlements for nuclear facility structures is primarily found in several sections of the Standard Review Plan (SRP) and Regulatory Guide 1.138 (RG 1.138). SRP Section 3.8.5 (I. AREAS OF REVIEW) specifies that the modeling of soil stiffness for various loading conditions, including seismic loading, is coordinated with reviews under SRP Sections 2.5.4 and 3.7.2. SRP Section 2.5.4.2 requires that state-of-the-art methods be used to determine both static and dynamic engineering properties of foundation soils, including their consolidation behavior and strength, and that these properties be quantitatively characterized for use in safety analyses. SRP Section 3.7.2 (I.4) further emphasizes that soil-structure interaction (SSI) analyses must account for uncertainties in soil constitutive modeling, including soil stiffness and its nonlinear, strain-dependent behavior. The procedures for incorporating strain-dependent soil properties, such as reductions in shear modulus (stiffness) and increases in damping with strain, are explicitly reviewed.

Regulatory Guide 1.138, Section C.6.1, provides accepted methods for determining dynamic soil properties. It states that the reduction in soil stiffness (shear modulus) with increasing strain should be determined for site soils, and that laboratory test data should be used to develop modulus reduction and damping curves for use in dynamic response analyses. The laboratory test program must cover the full range of strains expected under design loading conditions, and results should be validated against field measurements.

In summary, the treatment of soil stiffness reductions is addressed through coordinated review and analysis requirements in SRP Sections 3.8.5, 2.5.4, and 3.7.2, with specific testing and analytical guidance provided in RG 1.138 Section C.6.1.

evidence_chain.section: Section C.6.1, Testing Procedures for Determining Dynamic Soil Properties
evidence_chain.evidence_text: 6. Testing Procedures for Determining Dynamic Soil Properties  6.1. General To ensure a realistic assessment of soil properties, it is important that the laboratory tests represent field conditions as closely as is practical. Before performing dynamic tests, laboratory personnel should determine the initial state of stress in the soil and perform a series of static consolidated-drained and/or consolidated-undrained tests to establish the stress-strain behavior of the soil. The dynamic properties of soils, such as shear modulus and damping ratio, are strain-dependent and decrease with increasing strain amplitude. The reduction in soil stiffness (shear modulus) with increasing strain should be determined for the soils at the site. The laboratory test data should be used to develop modulus reduction and damping curves for use in dynamic response analyses. The selection of appropriate laboratory test methods (e.g., resonant column, cyclic triaxial, cyclic simple shear) should be based on the soil type, anticipated strain levels, and the specific requirements of the engineering analyses. The laboratory test program should be designed to provide data for the full range of strains expected under design loading conditions, including both small-strain and large-strain behavior. The laboratory test results should be compared with available field measurements, such as shear wave velocity profiles obtained from in situ tests, to ensure consistency and reliability of the data used in engineering analyses.

data.query: How are variations in foundation soil stiffness, such as stiff and soft spots, expected to be addressed in the evaluation of basemat support for seismic Category I structures according to NRC regulatory review standards?
data.answer:
According to NRC regulatory review standards, variations in foundation soil stiffness, such as stiff and soft spots, must be systematically identified, characterized, and incorporated into the evaluation of basemat support for seismic Category I structures. SRP 3.8.5 specifies that the review of basemat design must consider the effects of stiff or soft spots in the underlying soil, as these can influence bending, shear, and settlement behavior of the foundation (SRP 3.8.5, Area 4). This review is coordinated with SRP 2.5.4, which requires a detailed, quantitative assessment of subsurface material properties, including spatial variability (both horizontal and vertical) and the use of multiple testing methods to capture the range of soil parameters (SRP 2.5.4.2). The applicant must demonstrate that all critical soil parameters, including those representing extreme (soft or stiff) zones, are adequately sampled, tested, and used in safety analyses.

SRP 3.7.2 further requires that soil-structure interaction (SSI) analyses account for the random nature and variability of soil properties, including lack of lateral uniformity and the presence of soft or stiff zones (SRP 3.7.2, I.4.E). The SSI analysis must incorporate uncertainties in soil stiffness and layering, and the procedures for including strain-dependent and variable soil properties are subject to review.

10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, Section IV, mandates that seismic design must explicitly consider site-specific soil and foundation properties, including variations in soil stiffness or strength, and ensure that the structure can withstand differential settlement or movements resulting from such variations. The analysis must be based on best-estimate and range-of-property values, including soft or stiff zones.

Regulatory Guide 1.138 reinforces that sampling and testing must be sufficient to capture both average and extreme values of soil properties, ensuring that critical zones (such as soft or stiff spots) are represented in the data used for design and analysis (RG 1.138, C.4).

In summary, NRC standards require a comprehensive, site-specific approach to identifying and addressing variations in soil stiffness, ensuring that both the design and analysis of basemat support for seismic Category I structures are robust against the effects of stiff and soft spots in the foundation soils.

data.query: What is the relationship between the consideration of soil-structure interaction and the treatment of non-uniform foundation conditions in the seismic design of nuclear power plant structures?
data.answer:
The consideration of soil-structure interaction (SSI) and the treatment of non-uniform foundation conditions are closely interrelated in the seismic design of nuclear power plant structures. Regulatory guidance and requirements emphasize that both aspects must be addressed to ensure the safety and performance of seismic Category I structures.

According to SRP 3.8.5 (Section I, Areas of Review; Section II, Acceptance Criteria), the design and analysis of foundations must account for factors such as uneven settlement, mat flexibility, and the presence of stiff or soft spots in the underlying soil. These non-uniform foundation conditions directly influence the structural response during seismic events and must be incorporated into the SSI analysis. The review process specifically evaluates how bending moments and shear forces in the mat foundation are determined under seismic loads, considering the effects of non-uniform soil properties and construction sequences.

SRP 3.7.2 (Section I.4) further clarifies that SSI analyses must recognize uncertainties in soil and rock configurations, including the lack of lateral uniformity in the site soil profile. The modeling methods for SSI should account for the random nature of soil properties, layering, and the flexibility of both the soil and the structure. This ensures that the effects of non-uniform foundation conditions—such as variable soil stiffness or the presence of backfill—are reflected in the seismic response predictions.

SRP 2.5.4 (Section 2.5.4.2) underscores the importance of thorough site investigations to establish accurate soil profiles and engineering properties, which are essential inputs for both SSI and the assessment of non-uniform foundation conditions.

10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2, explicitly requires that the design bases for safety-related structures reflect appropriate consideration of both SSI and the effects of non-uniform foundation conditions, particularly for extreme events like the design basis earthquake.

In summary, the seismic design process integrates SSI analysis with a detailed evaluation of non-uniform foundation conditions. Accurate characterization of subsurface materials and explicit modeling of soil variability are essential to ensure that the seismic response of nuclear power plant structures is reliably predicted and that safety functions are maintained under seismic loading.

evidence_chain.section: I. AREAS OF REVIEW, 1. Design Ground Motion (pages 3.7.1-2 to 3.7.1-3)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
The seismic input motions to the SSI analyses can typically be placed at the free ground surface or at the foundation level using the guidance in this SRP Section 3.7.1, “Seismic Design Parameters,” as supplemented by DC/COL-ISG-017.

The GMRS reviewed under SRP Section 2.5.2 are site-specific horizontal and vertical free-field GMRS determined at the ground surface or at the free-field outcrop of the uppermost in-situ competent material using performance-based procedures in accordance with RG 1.208. The performance-based site-specific GMRS transferred to the foundation level in the free-field is referred to as the foundation input response spectra (FIRS). Therefore, the FIRS meet the same performance requisite as the GMRS. Both the GMRS and the FIRS are defined as free-field outcrop response spectra. The FIRS is the starting point for conducting an SSI analysis and for making a one-to-one comparison of the seismic design capacity of the standard design and the site-specific seismic demand for a site. The FIRS for the vertical direction is obtained with the vertical to horizontal (V/H) ratios appropriate for the site. GMRS are those derived from the global understanding of the site soil layers above the rock condition as determined from the site exploration activities, and therefore, are unique to a particular site.

Competent material is generally considered to be in-situ material having a minimum shear wave velocity of 1,000 feet/second (fps). If non-competent material is present, any excavation and/or backfilling should not alter the development or location of the GMRS. The development of the FIRS should use the site profiles including the effect of backfill. The remaining soft soil or backfill material should be considered in the SSI or other analyses.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory requirements for nuclear power plant foundations address the specification and evaluation of reinforcement patterns to ensure structural stability?
data.answer: NRC regulatory requirements for nuclear power plant foundations address the specification and evaluation of reinforcement patterns primarily through the review of materials, quality control, and construction techniques as outlined in SRP 3.8.5, Section I.6. The NRC reviews the use of reinforcing bars and mechanical splices as major materials in seismic Category I foundations, ensuring that their specification and placement contribute to structural stability. The review process includes assessing the quality control program for fabrication and construction, which covers nondestructive examination of materials, concrete placement, and erection tolerances. For seismic Category I foundations (other than containment), compliance with ACI 349 (as supplemented by RG 1.142) is required for concrete, which includes detailed requirements for reinforcement patterns, spacing, and anchorage to ensure structural integrity. If welding of reinforcing bars is used, the design must comply with the relevant sections of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section III, Division 2, with any exceptions requiring justification. Thus, NRC requirements ensure that reinforcement patterns are specified and evaluated according to established codes and standards, with a focus on quality control and compliance to maintain structural stability.

data.query: In the context of nuclear power plant foundation design, how are reinforcement detailing requirements integrated with general criteria for stability under seismic and static loads?
data.answer:
Reinforcement detailing requirements for nuclear power plant foundations are integrated with general criteria for stability under seismic and static loads through a combination of material standards, quality control programs, and design and analysis procedures, as outlined in NRC regulatory guidance and federal regulations.

According to SRP 3.8.5, the review of seismic Category I foundations includes an assessment of materials (such as reinforcing bars and mechanical splices) and the associated quality control programs. These programs must comply with recognized codes and standards, specifically ACI 349 for concrete (with additional guidance from RG 1.142) and ANSI/AISC N690-1994 for steel. If welding of reinforcing bars is used, compliance with the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section III, Division 2, is required, and any exceptions must be justified (SRP 3.8.5, I.6).

For design and analysis, SRP 3.8.5 (II.4) requires that procedures address soil-structure interaction, hydrodynamic effects, and dynamic soil pressure. The design must ensure that reinforcement detailing supports the foundation’s ability to withstand both seismic and static loads, including the determination of bending moments, shear forces, and sliding stability. The adequacy of these analyses is reviewed on a case-by-case basis, considering factors such as the coefficient of friction at various interfaces and the effects of embedment.

These requirements are grounded in the general design criteria of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, which mandates that structures important to safety be designed, fabricated, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety functions. Recognized codes and standards must be identified, evaluated, and supplemented as necessary to ensure a quality product, and a quality assurance program must be implemented and documented throughout the plant’s life.

In summary, reinforcement detailing is closely tied to the overall stability criteria through adherence to established codes, rigorous quality control, and comprehensive analysis procedures, ensuring that foundations meet both seismic and static load requirements (SRP 3.8.5; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1).

data.query: How do NRC regulatory standards address the consideration of both vertical and horizontal ground motion components in the seismic design and evaluation of nuclear power plant foundations?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory standards require that both vertical and horizontal ground motion components be explicitly considered in the seismic design and evaluation of nuclear power plant foundations. According to SRP 3.8.5, the review of foundation design emphasizes the transfer of horizontal shears caused by earthquakes and requires that analysis procedures for seismic Category I foundations account for all three directional demand forces (two horizontal and one vertical) acting simultaneously. The resultant seismic forces, including sliding and overturning moments, must be evaluated using methods described in SRP Section 3.7.2 (SRP 3.8.5, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA).

SRP 3.7.2 further specifies that seismic analysis for all seismic Category I structures, systems, and components (SSCs) must consider three orthogonal components of design ground motion—two horizontal and one vertical—using either dynamic or justified equivalent static analysis methods (SRP 3.7.2, II.1.A.ii). The dynamic analysis should use response spectra or time history methods, and the statistical independence of the three components must be reviewed if time histories are used (SRP 3.7.2, I.6).

SRP 3.7.1 reinforces this requirement by stating that the seismic design response spectra and time histories must be specified for three mutually orthogonal directions (two horizontal, one vertical), and that the horizontal components are typically assumed to be the same (SRP 3.7.1, II.1.A and B).

The site-specific ground motion response spectra (GMRS), which serve as the basis for the seismic design, are defined to include both horizontal and vertical components (SRP 2.5.2, I. AREAS OF REVIEW). These spectra are developed using performance-based procedures and must meet the requirements of Appendix S to 10 CFR Part 50 and 10 CFR 100.23.

In summary, NRC standards require that seismic design and evaluation of nuclear power plant foundations address both vertical and horizontal ground motion components through comprehensive analysis methods, ensuring the safety and stability of the structures under seismic loading.

The modeling of soil stiffness for seismic loading is coordinated with the review under SRP Section 3.7.2. ... The specified loads and load combinations used in the design of seismic Category I foundations are acceptable if found to be in accordance with those combinations described in Subsection II.3 of SRP Section 3.8.1 for the containment foundation and with those combinations listed in Subsection II.3 of SRP Section 3.8.4 for all other seismic Category I foundations. ... Methods for determining the sliding forces and overturning moment attributable to an earthquake should be in accordance with the methods described in SRP Section 3.7.2. ... For the pseudo-static and time history analysis methods, all three directional demand forces should be considered to act simultaneously. Therefore, the resultant seismic forces (horizontal resultant force for sliding from the two horizontal forces and similarly the resultant overturning moment for overturning stability) should be considered.

data.query: What is the regulatory basis for evaluating the potential impact of horizontal seismic ground motion on the uplift behavior of nuclear power plant structures?
data.answer:
The regulatory basis for evaluating the potential impact of horizontal seismic ground motion on the uplift behavior of nuclear power plant structures is grounded in several key NRC regulations and guidance documents. The primary regulatory requirement is found in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, which mandates that safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) must be designed to withstand the effects of the most severe natural phenomena, including earthquakes, without loss of safety function (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; SRP 3.8.5, II; SRP 3.7.2, II; SRP 2.5.1, II). This includes appropriate consideration of horizontal seismic ground motions and their effects, such as sliding, overturning, and uplift.

SRP 3.8.5 specifies that the review of containment base slab design must emphasize methods for transferring horizontal shears from earthquakes to the foundation, and the determination of overturning moments attributable to earthquakes, referencing SRP 3.7.2 for detailed analysis methods. The acceptance criteria require that the mathematical model for stability evaluation includes the effects of sliding and uplift between the foundation and soil, using finite elements that can simulate sliding and contact surfaces that transmit compression but not tension (SRP 3.8.5, II.4.G.iii).

SRP 3.7.2 further details the review of seismic overturning moments, sliding forces, and structure-to-soil pressures, including potential sliding and separation effects. It requires that the evaluation of seismic Category I structures accounts for the horizontal component of the Safe Shutdown Earthquake (SSE) ground motion, with a minimum peak ground acceleration (PGA) of 0.1g at the foundation level (SRP 3.7.2, II.2).

Additionally, SRP 2.5.1 and 10 CFR 100.23 require thorough investigation of geologic and seismic site characteristics to support estimates of SSE ground motion and ensure adequate engineering solutions for seismic effects, including those from horizontal ground motion (SRP 2.5.1, II.4).

In summary, the regulatory basis is established by 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A (GDC 2), 10 CFR 100.23, and detailed in SRP Sections 3.8.5, 3.7.2, and 2.5.1, which collectively require that the design and analysis of nuclear power plant structures explicitly address the impact of horizontal seismic ground motion on uplift and related stability behaviors.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory standards address the consideration of buoyancy forces when evaluating the uplift resistance of nuclear power plant foundations?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory standards explicitly require the consideration of buoyancy forces when evaluating the uplift resistance of nuclear power plant foundations. According to SRP 3.8.5, Section II.3, the NRC mandates that load combinations used to assess sliding, overturning, and flotation (uplift) must include the buoyant force resulting from design-basis floods. Specifically, load combination 'E. D + F'' is identified, where 'D' represents dead load and 'F'' is the buoyant force of the design-basis flood. This ensures that the potential for flotation due to buoyancy is directly addressed in the structural evaluation of foundations.

Further, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, Section II.2, reinforces this requirement by stating that the design of safety-related structures must account for the effects of natural phenomena, including flooding and groundwater, and must include consideration of the effects of buoyancy and other forces that may result from these sources. This regulatory basis ensures that the uplift resistance of foundations is evaluated against the most severe credible site-related natural events, including those that could induce significant buoyant forces.

While RG 1.206 discusses the evolution of technical guidance and its relationship to the SRP, it does not provide additional specific requirements regarding buoyancy. Instead, it points to the SRP as the primary source of accepted methods for meeting NRC requirements in this area.

In summary, NRC standards require that buoyancy forces from groundwater or flooding be explicitly included in the load combinations used to evaluate the uplift resistance of nuclear power plant foundations, as detailed in SRP 3.8.5 and supported by the regulatory basis in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S.

data.query: What is the relationship between the requirements for dead load calculations and the treatment of buoyancy effects in the seismic and structural analysis of nuclear facility foundations?
data.answer:
The requirements for dead load calculations and the treatment of buoyancy effects are closely related in the seismic and structural analysis of nuclear facility foundations, as both are fundamental components of the load combinations that ensure the safety and integrity of seismic Category I structures.

According to SRP 3.8.5 (Section II.3), the design of seismic Category I foundations must consider specified loads and load combinations, which explicitly include dead load (D) and buoyant force (F'). These combinations are used to evaluate the foundation's resistance to sliding, overturning, and flotation under various scenarios, such as earthquakes, floods, and wind events. For example, load combinations such as D + H + E (dead load, lateral earth pressure, and earthquake load) and D + F' (dead load and buoyant force) are required to ensure that both the weight of the structure and the upward force from buoyancy are properly accounted for in the analysis.

10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S (Section II.2.b) further mandates that the design bases for safety-related structures must account for static and dynamic loads, including dead load, live load, and the effects of buoyancy, in combination with earthquake ground motion. This regulatory requirement ensures that the combined effects of these loads are considered to maintain structural integrity during seismic events and other natural phenomena.

SRP 3.7.2 (Areas of Review 14 and II.3.H) also emphasizes the need to consider the effects of pore water (which relates to buoyancy) and the variability of groundwater levels in the structural response analysis, particularly during seismic events. This highlights the importance of integrating buoyancy effects with dead load calculations in the overall assessment of foundation stability.

In summary, regulatory guidance requires that dead load and buoyancy effects be explicitly included and properly combined in the structural and seismic analysis of nuclear facility foundations to ensure safety against sliding, overturning, and flotation. These requirements are grounded in SRP 3.8.5, SRP 3.7.2, and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for evaluating the potential for horizontal sliding of nuclear power plant foundations during seismic events?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for evaluating the potential for horizontal sliding of nuclear power plant foundations during seismic events are primarily detailed in SRP 3.8.5, with cross-references to SRP 3.7.2 and 3.7.1, and are grounded in the requirements of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A and S.

SRP 3.8.5 (Section II) specifies that the review must include factors of safety against sliding to ensure adequate safety margins. The design must consider specified loads and load combinations, including those induced by seismic events, as described in SRP Sections 3.8.1 and 3.8.4. For sliding and overturning attributable to earthquakes, acceptable load combinations include D + H + E, where D is dead load, H is lateral earth pressure, and E is earthquake load (SRP 3.8.5, II.3).

The methods for determining sliding forces and overturning moments due to earthquakes should follow SRP 3.7.2. The analysis must account for all three directional seismic forces (two horizontal, one vertical) acting simultaneously. The factor of safety against sliding is calculated as the ratio of capacity to demand loads, using either a pseudo-static approach (maximum seismic demand loads) or a linear time history analysis (minimum factor of safety over the time history). The analysis must consider the appropriate coefficients of friction for different sliding interfaces and the contribution of soil lateral pressure, with attention to whether static or dynamic coefficients are used (SRP 3.8.5, II.4.G).

SRP 3.7.2 further requires that the evaluation of sliding forces, structure-to-soil pressures, and frictional forces for seismic Category I structures must reflect the most severe historical earthquakes for the site, with sufficient margin (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; SRP 3.7.2, II). Appendix S to 10 CFR Part 50 requires that safety-related structures remain functional and within stress, strain, and deformation limits during and after the seismic event, considering soil-structure interaction (SSI) effects.

Additionally, SRP 3.7.1 requires that seismic input motions for analysis be specified for three orthogonal directions, with a minimum horizontal peak ground acceleration (PGA) of 0.1g at the foundation level (SRP 3.7.1, II.1).

In summary, the evaluation must use NRC-accepted load combinations, consider all relevant seismic forces and soil-structure interactions, apply appropriate coefficients of friction, and demonstrate adequate safety margins against sliding, as detailed in SRP 3.8.5, SRP 3.7.2, SRP 3.7.1, and 10 CFR Part 50 Appendices A and S.
