evidence_chain.evidence_text:
The review includes factors of safety against overturning and sliding to ensure adequate safety margins. ...

3. Loads and Load Combinations.  The specified loads and load combinations used in the design of seismic Category I foundations are acceptable if found to be in accordance with those combinations described in Subsection II.3 of SRP Section 3.8.1 for the containment foundation and with those combinations listed in Subsection II.3 of SRP Section 3.8.4 for all other seismic Category I foundations.  Also to be included are loads that are induced by the construction sequence and by the differential settlements of the soil under and to the sides of the structures. 

In addition to the load combinations referenced above, the combinations used to check against sliding and overturning attributable to earthquakes, winds, tornadoes, hurricanes, and against flotation because of floods are acceptable if found to be in accordance with the following: 

A. D + H + E 
B. D + H + W 
C. D + H + E' 
D. D + H + Wt      
E. D + F' 

Where D, E, W, E', and Wt are as referenced in Subsection II.3 of SRP Section 3.8.4, where H is the lateral earth pressure, and F' is the buoyant force of the design-basis flood. ...

4. Design and Analysis Procedures.  ...

G. Methods for determining the sliding forces and  overturning moment attributable to an earthquake should be in accordance with the methods described in SRP Section 3.7.2. ...

B. Adequacy of the sliding analysis method and the analysis results to account for potential mat foundation liftoff effects.  The staff should also review the calculation of the factor of safety against sliding.  If sliding resistance is the sum of shear friction along the basemat and contribution of soil lateral pressure up to the full passive pressure capacity induced by embedment effects, the adequacy of the analysis to consider these effects is addressed using a consistent lateral displacement criterion.  This involves the use of static versus dynamic coefficient of friction consistent with the use of partial versus full passive pressure.  The reviewer should also consider whether the selection of the coefficient of friction used in the sliding stability analysis considers the various sliding interfaces (e.g., soil shear failure, concrete to soil, waterproofing to soil, concrete basemat to concrete mudmat). 

If the stability evaluation is performed based on a pseudo-static approach, using the maximum seismic demand loads (e.g., maximum forces in the two horizontal directions and one vertical direction), then the factors of safety for sliding and overturning can be determined by the ratio of capacity to demand loads.  

However, if a linear time history analysis approach is utilized, then the factor of safety can be calculated at each time step throughout the time history.  The minimum value of the factors of safety calculated in this manner should be compared against the acceptance criteria for that load combination.  For the pseudo-static and time history analysis methods, all three directional demand forces should be considered to act simultaneously.  Therefore, the resultant seismic forces (horizontal resultant force for sliding from the two horizontal forces and similarly the resultant overturning moment for overturning stability) should be considered.  In the case of the sliding evaluation, if instead of using the resultant horizontal force with the vertical force, each pair of horizontal force and vertical force is evaluated separately, then the frictional resistance in the horizontal directions should be apportioned considering the existence of the two horizontal forces.

evidence_chain.section: Appendix A to Part 50 – General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants, Criterion 1
evidence_chain.evidence_text: Criterion 1—Quality standards and records. Structures, systems, and components important to safety shall be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with the importance of the safety functions to be performed. Where generally recognized codes and standards are used, they shall be identified and evaluated to determine their applicability, adequacy, and sufficiency and shall be supplemented or modified as necessary to assure a quality product in keeping with the required safety function. data.query: How do NRC regulatory standards address the relationship between seismic analysis methods and the acceptance criteria for foundation sliding in nuclear power plant structures?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory standards establish a clear relationship between seismic analysis methods and the acceptance criteria for foundation sliding in nuclear power plant structures. According to SRP 3.8.5, the NRC reviews the analysis procedures used for seismic Category I foundations, focusing on the applicability of the underlying theories and the adequacy of methods for determining seismic-induced sliding forces and overturning moments (SRP 3.8.5, II.4, G). The acceptance criteria require that the specified loads and load combinations, including those attributable to earthquakes, conform to the combinations described in SRP Sections 3.8.1 and 3.8.4. For sliding analysis, the NRC expects the use of methods consistent with SRP Section 3.7.2, which details the determination of seismic overturning moments and sliding forces, including structure-to-soil pressures and frictional forces (SRP 3.7.2, I.14).

The NRC requires that the factor of safety against sliding be calculated using either a pseudo-static approach (using maximum seismic demand loads) or a linear time history analysis (calculating the factor of safety at each time step). In both cases, all three directional demand forces (two horizontal, one vertical) must be considered simultaneously, and the minimum factor of safety from the time history analysis must be compared to the acceptance criteria for the relevant load combination (SRP 3.8.5, II.4, G). The analysis must also account for the characteristics of sliding interfaces and the appropriate coefficients of friction, considering whether static or dynamic values are justified based on the analysis method and interface conditions.

These requirements are grounded in the general design criteria of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, which mandates quality standards and assurance for safety-related structures, and in Appendix S, which requires that safety-related structures, systems, and components remain functional during and after seismic events (SRP 3.7.2, II). The NRC's Standard Review Plan (SRP) and related guidance documents, such as RG 1.206, provide the accepted methods and review criteria for ensuring that seismic analysis methods and acceptance criteria for foundation sliding are robust and consistent with regulatory expectations.

data.query: How should the effects of buoyancy forces be considered in the regulatory evaluation of nuclear power plant foundation uplift analyses?
data.answer:
The effects of buoyancy forces must be explicitly considered in the regulatory evaluation of nuclear power plant foundation uplift analyses. According to SRP 3.8.5, Section II.3, buoyancy forces (denoted as F') are included in the required load combinations for evaluating sliding, overturning, and flotation due to floods. Specifically, the load combination 'D + F'' (where D is dead load and F' is the buoyant force of the design-basis flood) is required to assess the potential for flotation. Other combinations also include lateral earth pressure (H) and various environmental loads (E for earthquake, W for wind, etc.), ensuring comprehensive evaluation under different scenarios. Justification is required if live loads are included in these combinations.

Furthermore, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, Section II, mandates that the design of safety-related structures must account for the effects of foundation uplift and buoyancy forces, in addition to other geotechnical hazards. This regulatory basis requires that the geologic, seismologic, and engineering characteristics of the site be investigated in sufficient detail to permit adequate evaluation and engineering solutions for these effects. The design must ensure that structures, systems, and components important to safety can withstand these forces without loss of safety function.

While RG 1.206 notes that technical guidance for safety analysis reports is being updated, it affirms that the SRP provides acceptable methods for meeting NRC requirements. Therefore, the evaluation of buoyancy effects should follow the load combinations and criteria specified in SRP 3.8.5 and be consistent with the regulatory requirements of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S.

data.query: What is the relationship between the treatment of dead weight and buoyancy forces in the regulatory acceptance criteria for evaluating the stability of nuclear power plant foundations under dynamic loading conditions?
data.answer:
The regulatory acceptance criteria for evaluating the stability of nuclear power plant foundations under dynamic loading conditions explicitly address the treatment of dead weight (D) and buoyancy forces (F') as key components in load combinations used to assess sliding, overturning, and flotation stability. According to SRP 3.8.5, Section II ('3. Loads and Load Combinations' and '4. Design and Analysis Procedures'), dead weight (D) is included in all relevant load combinations, reflecting its stabilizing effect, while buoyancy (F') is specifically included in combinations addressing flotation due to floods, reflecting its destabilizing effect. For example, the load combination 'D + F'' is used to evaluate flotation, ensuring that the foundation's dead weight is sufficient to counteract the upward buoyant force during flood conditions. Other combinations (e.g., 'D + H + E') include dead weight alongside lateral earth pressure (H) and dynamic loads (E for earthquake, W for wind, etc.) to assess sliding and overturning stability.

The acceptance criteria require that these forces be considered simultaneously, especially under dynamic loading such as seismic events, and that factors of safety against sliding and overturning be calculated using the combined effects. The minimum factor of safety, determined either by pseudo-static or time history analysis, must meet the acceptance criteria for the relevant load combination (SRP 3.8.5, Section II.4).

This approach is consistent with the broader regulatory basis in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criteria 1 and 2, which require that structures important to safety be designed to withstand natural phenomena (including earthquakes and floods) by considering appropriate combinations of normal, accident, and natural phenomena loads. SRP 3.7.2 further reinforces the need to account for effects such as pore water and potential loss of contact between structure and soil, which can influence both dead weight effectiveness and buoyancy during dynamic events.

In summary, the regulatory framework requires that dead weight and buoyancy forces be explicitly and appropriately combined in stability evaluations, with dead weight providing resistance and buoyancy representing a destabilizing force, particularly under flood conditions. The adequacy of these combinations is verified through factors of safety and compliance with NRC acceptance criteria.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory requirements for foundation stability address the evaluation of sliding, overturning, and flotation for safety-related building basemats in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory requirements for foundation stability of safety-related building basemats in nuclear power plants address the evaluation of sliding, overturning, and flotation through a combination of regulatory criteria, technical guidance, and acceptance criteria. According to SRP 3.8.5 (Section II.3, II.4, II.5), the NRC review ensures that foundations can safely transmit structural loads to the soil with appropriate safety margins. The evaluation specifically includes factors of safety against overturning, sliding, and flotation, considering load combinations that account for dead load (D), lateral earth pressure (H), earthquake (E), wind (W), tornado (Wt), and buoyant force from flooding (F'). The adequacy of sliding analysis must consider mat foundation liftoff, the calculation of safety factors, and the contributions of shear friction and soil lateral pressure, with attention to the interfaces involved (e.g., soil to concrete, waterproofing). Both static and dynamic coefficients of friction are considered, depending on the analysis method.

For seismic events, the NRC requires that all three directional demand forces (two horizontal, one vertical) be considered simultaneously, and that the resultant forces and moments be used in stability checks. Nonlinear time history analyses, if used, must include foundation sliding and uplift, and consider parameters such as soil profiles and concrete stiffness variations, as evaluated in the seismic soil-structure interaction (SSI) analysis.

These requirements are grounded in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criteria (GDC) 1 and 2, which mandate quality standards and consideration of the most severe natural phenomena, and Appendix S, which requires that safety-related structures remain functional during and after seismic events, accounting for SSI effects (SRP 3.7.1, 3.7.2). The NRC’s Standard Review Plan (SRP) and related guidance documents (e.g., RG 1.206) provide the accepted methods for demonstrating compliance with these regulatory requirements.

data.query: What is the relationship between the general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena and the acceptance criteria for seismic stability analyses of nuclear facility foundations?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for protection against natural phenomena, as established in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A (specifically GDC 1 and GDC 2), provide the regulatory foundation for the seismic stability analyses of nuclear facility foundations. GDC 1 requires that safety-related structures be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety functions, while GDC 2 mandates that these structures be capable of withstanding the most severe natural phenomena, including earthquakes, without loss of safety function (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criteria 1 and 2 [2]).

The acceptance criteria for seismic stability analyses, as detailed in SRP 3.8.5, are directly derived from these GDCs. Specifically, SRP 3.8.5 Section II states that acceptance criteria are based on compliance with GDC 1 and GDC 2, ensuring that seismic Category I foundations are designed to withstand specified load combinations that include seismic (earthquake) loads, as well as other natural phenomena such as wind and flood (SRP 3.8.5, II [1]). The acceptance criteria require that the design basis for seismic loads reflects the most severe historical events with appropriate safety margins, as required by GDC 2.

Further, SRP 3.7.1 and SRP 2.5.2 reinforce that the seismic stability analyses must demonstrate that safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) remain functional and within applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits during and after the design-basis earthquake (SSE), as required by Appendix S to 10 CFR Part 50 (SRP 3.7.1, II; SRP 2.5.2, II [4][5]). The acceptance criteria also require consideration of soil-structure interaction and site-specific ground motion response spectra anchored to a minimum peak ground acceleration (PGA) of 0.1g at the foundation level (SRP 3.7.1, II; SRP 2.5.2, II [4][5]).

In summary, the acceptance criteria for seismic stability analyses operationalize the general design criteria by specifying the technical requirements and analytical methods necessary to demonstrate compliance with the regulatory basis for protection against natural phenomena. The acceptance criteria ensure that the intent of the GDCs—robust protection of safety-related structures against seismic and other natural hazards—is met through detailed engineering analyses and design practices.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
GENERAL DESIGN CRITERIA FOR NUCLEAR POWER PLANTS

Criterion 1—Quality standards and records. Structures, systems, and components important to safety shall be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with the importance of the safety functions to be performed. Where generally recognized codes and standards are used, they shall be identified and evaluated to determine their applicability, adequacy, and sufficiency and shall be supplemented or modified as necessary to assure a quality product in keeping with the required safety function. A quality assurance program shall be established and implemented in order to provide adequate assurance that these structures, systems, and components will satisfactorily perform their safety functions. Appropriate records of the design, fabrication, erection, and testing of structures, systems, and components important to safety shall be maintained by or under the control of the nuclear power unit licensee throughout the life of the unit.

Criterion 2—Design bases for protection against natural phenomena. Structures, systems, and components important to safety shall be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena such as earthquakes, tornadoes, hurricanes, floods, tsunami, and seiches without loss of capability to perform their safety functions. The design bases for these structures, systems, and components shall reflect: (1) Appropriate consideration of the most severe of the natural phenomena that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated, (2) appropriate combinations of the effects of normal and accident conditions with the effects of the natural phenomena, and (3) the importance of the safety functions to be performed. The design shall also reflect appropriate consideration of the potential for the occurrence and magnitude of natural phenomena that may be associated with the site, whether such phenomena are mentioned in this criterion or not.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating the fatigue life of mechanical components subjected to cyclic loading in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating the fatigue life of mechanical components subjected to cyclic loading in nuclear power plants are primarily outlined in SRP 3.9.1 and SRP 3.9.3, with regulatory basis in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criteria (GDC) 1. According to SRP 3.9.1 (Section II), applicants must provide a comprehensive list of all transients used in the design and fatigue analysis of Code Class 1 components and related structures within the reactor coolant pressure boundary. This includes specifying the number of events for each transient, the number of load and stress cycles per event, and the combination of events. The selected transient conditions must be based on conservative estimates of the magnitude and frequency of temperature and pressure variations, considering all operational and accident scenarios, including startup, shutdown, power changes, malfunctions, operator errors, hydrostatic tests, seismic events, and other design-basis events. Environmental factors, such as coolant chemistry, must also be considered to minimize material degradation.

SRP 3.9.3 (Section II) further requires that the design and service loading combinations, including system operating transients and associated stress limits, be clearly defined for all Code Class 1, 2, and 3 components and supports. The acceptability of these combinations and stress limits is judged by comparison with the positions stated in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50 and with recognized codes and standards. Where no code criteria exist, the design must ensure structural integrity and the continued performance of safety-related functions.

GDC 1 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) mandates that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function, using recognized codes and standards as appropriate. A quality assurance program and appropriate records must be maintained throughout the unit's life.

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria require a conservative, comprehensive fatigue analysis based on all relevant transients and load cycles, adherence to recognized codes and standards, and assurance of structural integrity and safety function over the plant's service life (SRP 3.9.1 II, SRP 3.9.3 II, 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A, GDC 1).

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for considering cyclic loading and fatigue analysis of mechanical components in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for considering cyclic loading and fatigue analysis of mechanical components in nuclear power plants are primarily established in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criteria (GDC), and further detailed in the Standard Review Plan (SRP) Sections 3.9.1 and 3.9.3.

GDC 1 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety functions. This includes the use of recognized codes and standards, supplemented as necessary, and the maintenance of appropriate records (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1).

SRP 3.9.1 specifies that to meet GDCs 1, 2, 14, and 15, applicants must provide a comprehensive list of transients for the design and fatigue analysis of all Code Class 1 components and related structures. This list must include the number of events for each transient, the number of load and stress cycles per event, and combinations thereof. All relevant transients—such as startup/shutdown, power changes, malfunctions, operator errors, inservice tests, seismic events, and design-basis events—must be considered. The selection of these transients should be based on conservative estimates of their magnitude and frequency, and should provide a complete basis for fatigue evaluation over the plant's service life (SRP 3.9.1, Section II).

SRP 3.9.3 further requires that the design and service loading combinations, including system operating transients and associated stress limits, be sufficiently defined for all Code Class 1, 2, and 3 components and supports. Fatigue strength must be evaluated, particularly for components like snubbers used as shock and vibration arresters, considering factors such as movement amplitude, force, vibration frequency, and number of load cycles. Fatigue evaluation may be omitted for snubbers if the number of load cycles is small (<2500) or if motion does not exceed the snubber's dead band (SRP 3.9.3, Section II).

In summary, regulatory requirements mandate a thorough and conservative fatigue analysis based on all credible cyclic loading scenarios, in accordance with applicable codes and standards, to ensure the structural integrity and safety function of mechanical components throughout the plant's operational life.

data.query: How are seismic event cycles, such as those from operating basis earthquakes, incorporated into the fatigue analysis requirements for nuclear plant mechanical components?
data.answer:
Seismic event cycles, including those from operating basis earthquakes (OBE), are explicitly incorporated into the fatigue analysis requirements for nuclear plant mechanical components through regulatory and design processes. According to SRP 3.9.1 (Section II), applicants must provide a comprehensive list of all transients, including seismic events as determined by Appendix S to 10 CFR Part 50, for use in the design and fatigue analysis of Code Class 1 components and related structures. This includes specifying the number of events, load and stress cycles per event, and their combinations, ensuring that the fatigue evaluation is based on conservative estimates of magnitude and frequency of the resulting temperature and pressure conditions.

SRP 3.7.2 further clarifies that seismic events such as the OBE and Safe Shutdown Earthquake (SSE) are considered in the design review. If the OBE is greater than one-third of the SSE, explicit analysis and design are required to demonstrate that stress, strain, and deformation limits are satisfied, as mandated by Appendix S to 10 CFR Part 50. This ensures that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) remain functional and within limits during and after seismic events.

Additionally, SRP 3.9.3 (Sections I and II) requires that loading combinations for Code Class 1, 2, and 3 components—including those from seismic events—are reviewed to ensure compliance with applicable stress and deformation criteria. These requirements are grounded in the quality standards and records provisions of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, which mandates that SSCs important to safety are designed and maintained to perform their safety functions under all expected conditions, including seismic transients.

In summary, seismic event cycles, including those from OBE, are incorporated into fatigue analysis by requiring their explicit inclusion in the list of design transients, quantification of their frequency and magnitude, and demonstration of compliance with stress and deformation limits as specified in NRC regulations and guidance documents.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for the number of postulated design transients that mechanical components important to safety must be designed to withstand during the plant's design life?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for the number of postulated design transients that mechanical components important to safety must be designed to withstand during the plant's design life are outlined primarily in SRP 3.9.1, Section II. The applicant is required to provide a comprehensive list of transients for use in the design and fatigue analysis of all Code Class 1 components, supports, reactor core support structures, and reactor vessel internal components within the reactor coolant pressure boundary. This list must include the number of events for each transient, as well as the number of load and stress cycles per event and in combination. The transients to be considered encompass a wide range of operational and abnormal conditions, such as startup and shutdown, power changes, emergency and recovery conditions (including natural convection cooldown for new applications), switching operations, system or component malfunctions, operator errors, inservice hydrostatic tests, seismic events (per Appendix S to 10 CFR Part 50), and other design-basis events specified in the component design specifications.

The selection of these transients and their frequencies must be based on conservative estimates of the magnitude and frequency of the temperature and pressure conditions they cause, relying on engineering judgment and experience. The NRC staff will evaluate whether the number of transients specified is appropriate for the plant's design life. The design and service loading combinations, including these transients, must provide a complete basis for the design of the reactor coolant pressure boundary for all expected service lifetime conditions (SRP 3.9.1, Section II; SRP 3.9.3, Section II). These requirements are grounded in the regulatory basis provided by 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, which mandates that safety-important components be designed and tested to quality standards that ensure their safety functions throughout the plant's life.

In summary, the NRC does not prescribe a fixed number of transients but requires a justified, conservative, and comprehensive accounting of all relevant transients and their frequencies, ensuring that mechanical components important to safety can withstand all postulated events over the plant's design life.

data.query: What are the NRC requirements for including environmental effects in the fatigue evaluation of Class 1 mechanical components in nuclear power plants?
data.answer: The NRC requires that environmental effects be considered in the fatigue evaluation of Class 1 mechanical components in nuclear power plants. According to SRP 3.9.1, the applicant’s Safety Analysis Report (SAR) must include a conservative estimate of the magnitude and frequency of temperature and pressure conditions caused by transients, and environmental conditions such as coolant water chemistry must be considered to minimize material degradation due to corrosion (SRP 3.9.1, Section II). SRP 3.9.3 further clarifies that, in accordance with General Design Criterion (GDC) 4, components important to safety must be designed to accommodate and be compatible with environmental conditions associated with normal operation, maintenance, testing, and postulated accidents, including loss-of-coolant accidents (LOCA). This includes consideration of loading effects and resulting stresses expected during the plant’s life, ensuring that the design and service loading combinations and associated stress limits are sufficiently defined for all conditions (SRP 3.9.3, Section II). Additionally, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards that ensure their safety function, and that recognized codes and standards be supplemented as necessary to assure quality (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1). In summary, NRC requirements mandate that environmental effects, including those from coolant chemistry and operational transients, be explicitly considered in the fatigue evaluation of Class 1 components to ensure their integrity and safety function throughout the plant’s service life.

data.query: How do general design criteria for reactor protection systems relate to the requirements for mechanical components to withstand postulated transients during power changes?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for reactor protection systems, as outlined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, directly relate to the requirements for mechanical components to withstand postulated transients during power changes by establishing the foundational safety and quality standards that must be met. Specifically, GDC 1 requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety are designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety functions (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1; SRP 3.9.1; SRP 3.9.3). This includes the use of recognized codes and standards, and the implementation of a quality assurance program to ensure continued performance throughout the plant's life.

GDC 14 and GDC 15 further specify that the reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) and reactor coolant system (RCS), along with associated auxiliary, control, and protection systems, must be designed with sufficient margin to ensure that design conditions are not exceeded during any normal operation or anticipated operational occurrences, including power changes (SRP 3.9.1; SRP 3.9.3). This means that mechanical components must be capable of withstanding all postulated transients—such as startup, shutdown, power level changes, and system malfunctions—without loss of function or integrity.

To comply with these criteria, applicants must provide a comprehensive list of transients for use in the design and fatigue analysis of all Code Class 1 components and supports, including the number and combination of load and stress cycles expected (SRP 3.9.1). The design must ensure that the mechanical components remain functional under all anticipated conditions, including those resulting from power changes, thereby providing reasonable assurance of safety as required by the GDCs.

In summary, the GDCs establish the regulatory basis for ensuring that reactor protection systems and mechanical components are robustly designed to withstand the full range of postulated transients, including those associated with power changes, through rigorous quality standards, design margins, and comprehensive analysis of operational scenarios.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for vibration testing of reactor internals and components?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for vibration testing of reactor internals and components are established to ensure structural integrity and safety under operational and accident conditions. According to SRP 3.9.2, the test program must specify acceptance criteria, allowable vibration and stress limits, and corrective actions if excessive vibration or thermal motion restraint is detected. The NRC reviews calculated vibration and stress levels, ensuring adequate safety margins (e.g., a margin of safety of 2.0 has been acceptable in past reviews), and requires that acceptance criteria be justified and documented. For components with a history of adverse flow-induced vibration (FIV) effects, measurements are required, and test results must be compared with analytical predictions, with plans for updating analyses as needed (SRP 3.9.2, I.3, I.4).

Regulatory Guide 1.20, Section C.2.1.3.2 and C.2.1.3.3, further specifies that acceptance criteria should ensure vibratory stresses do not exceed fatigue endurance limits for the expected number of cycles, as defined by the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, Section III, Division 1, Subsection NG, Article NG-3226. The criteria must also prevent unacceptable motion (e.g., impacting, fretting, excessive displacement), loose parts, cracking, or significant wear. If predicted stresses exceed endurance limits, design modifications or operational restrictions are required. The basis for acceptance criteria must be documented, referencing applicable codes, standards, and operating experience.

10 CFR 50.55a mandates that reactor internals and safety-related components meet the design, fabrication, construction, testing, and performance requirements of the ASME BPV Code and the ASME OM Code, or equivalent standards. Inservice inspection and testing must also comply with these codes.

In summary, NRC acceptance criteria for vibration testing require that: (1) vibratory stresses remain below fatigue endurance limits per ASME BPV Code; (2) vibration does not cause unacceptable motion, loose parts, or wear; (3) acceptance criteria are justified and documented; and (4) corrective actions are defined if limits are exceeded. These requirements are grounded in SRP 3.9.2, RG 1.20 (Sections C.2.1.3.2 and C.2.1.3.3), and 10 CFR 50.55a.

evidence_chain.section: Section C.2.1.3.2 and C.2.1.3.3 (Stress Convergence and High-Cycle Fatigue Evaluation; Operational Vibration and Stress Acceptance Criteria)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
2.1.3.2 Stress Convergence and High-Cycle Fatigue Evaluation

The applicant or licensee should demonstrate that the computed stresses in the reactor internals have converged and are not unduly sensitive to mesh refinement or other modeling parameters. The applicant or licensee should evaluate the potential for high-cycle fatigue (HCF) failure of reactor internals due to vibratory loads. The evaluation should be based on the computed vibratory stresses and the applicable fatigue curves (e.g., those in the ASME BPV Code, Section III, Division 1, Subsection NG, Article NG-3226). The applicant or licensee should demonstrate that the predicted vibratory stresses are below the fatigue endurance limits for the expected number of cycles during the service life of the component. If the predicted vibratory stresses exceed the endurance limits, the applicant or licensee should propose design modifications or operational restrictions to ensure the structural integrity of the reactor internals.

2.1.3.3 Operational Vibration and Stress Acceptance Criteria

The applicant or licensee should establish acceptance criteria for operational vibration and stress levels for reactor internals. The acceptance criteria should be based on the following considerations:

• The vibratory response of reactor internals should not result in stresses that exceed the applicable fatigue endurance limits for the expected number of cycles during the service life of the component.
• The vibratory response should not result in unacceptable motion, such as impacting or fretting between components, or excessive displacement that could impair the safety function of the reactor internals.
• The vibratory response should not result in the generation of loose parts, cracking, or significant wear of reactor internals.

The applicant or licensee should document the basis for the acceptance criteria, including the applicable codes, standards, and operating experience. The acceptance criteria should be used to evaluate the results of the vibration measurement and inspection programs.

data.query: How do general design criteria for dynamic effects and regulatory guidance for vibration assessment interact in establishing requirements for the vibration testing of safety-related components?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) established in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, particularly GDC 1, GDC 2, and GDC 4, set the foundational regulatory requirements for the design, fabrication, erection, and testing of safety-related components to ensure their structural and functional integrity under dynamic effects, including vibration (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criteria 1, 2, 4; RG 1.20, Section A; RG 1.100, Section A). These criteria require that safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) be designed and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety functions and be able to withstand environmental and dynamic effects such as seismic events and operational vibrations.

Regulatory guidance, such as SRP 3.9.2 and RG 1.20, provides the detailed methodologies and acceptable practices for implementing these criteria. SRP 3.9.2 outlines the review areas and testing procedures to ensure compliance with the GDCs, emphasizing the need for dynamic analyses and vibration testing of SSCs under vibratory loadings, including flow-induced and seismic excitations. It references RG 1.20 as the accepted method for developing a Comprehensive Vibration Assessment Program (CVAP), which integrates predictive analysis, measurement, and inspection to verify the structural integrity of reactor internals (SRP 3.9.2, Section I; RG 1.20, Section C).

RG 1.20 further details the process for vibration assessment, requiring predictive analyses to establish expected vibration levels, measurement programs to confirm these predictions during preoperational and startup testing, and inspection programs to verify results. This approach ensures that all potential vibration mechanisms—flow-induced, acoustic, and mechanical—are adequately assessed and that the requirements of the GDCs are met in practice (RG 1.20, Section C).

In summary, the GDCs provide the regulatory basis for vibration testing requirements, while regulatory guidance such as SRP 3.9.2 and RG 1.20 operationalize these requirements by specifying acceptable methods for vibration assessment and testing. This interaction ensures that safety-related components are robustly evaluated for dynamic effects, with vibration testing programs designed to demonstrate compliance with the GDCs.

data.query: How do general design criteria for dynamic testing of reactor internals relate to the NRC's requirements for verifying the structural integrity of systems, structures, and components subjected to operational vibration loads?
data.answer:
The general design criteria for dynamic testing of reactor internals are closely aligned with the NRC's requirements for verifying the structural integrity of systems, structures, and components (SSCs) subjected to operational vibration loads. According to SRP 3.9.2, dynamic testing and analysis are required to ensure that reactor internals and related SSCs can withstand vibratory loadings from sources such as flow-induced excitations and seismic events. These requirements are grounded in compliance with 10 CFR 50.55a and the General Design Criteria (GDC) in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, specifically GDC 1, 2, and 4, which mandate quality standards, protection against natural phenomena, and consideration of environmental and dynamic effects.

SRP 3.9.2 further specifies that dynamic testing, including vibration monitoring and analysis, must confirm that SSCs are adequately designed to withstand anticipated steady-state and transient operational conditions without excessive vibration or structural damage. The analyses must verify the structural integrity of reactor internals for various vibration mechanisms, including flow-induced vibration (FIV), acoustic resonance (AR), acoustic-induced vibration (AIV), and mechanical-induced vibration (MIV).

Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.20 provides an acceptable method for implementing a Comprehensive Vibration Assessment Program (CVAP) for reactor internals. This program integrates predictive analysis, measurement, and inspection to verify structural integrity throughout the reactor's service life. Predictive analysis offers theoretical verification, the measurement program confirms these predictions and identifies unforeseen vibration mechanisms, and the inspection program provides both quantitative and qualitative verification of results (RG 1.20, Section C).

Additionally, 10 CFR 50.55a requires that SSCs important to safety meet applicable codes and standards, including those addressing vibration loads and dynamic effects, and be designed, constructed, and tested to ensure structural integrity and operational reliability under all operational conditions. RG 1.29 further clarifies that reactor internals are designated as seismic Category I SSCs and must meet seismic and dynamic analysis requirements to ensure continued functionality during seismic events.

In summary, the NRC's general design criteria and associated regulatory guidance require a comprehensive approach—encompassing analysis, testing, and inspection—to verify the structural integrity of reactor internals and other SSCs under operational vibration loads, ensuring safety and compliance with regulatory standards.

data.query: What is the relationship between regulatory guidance on vibration assessment and the acceptance criteria for preoperational testing of reactor core support structures?
data.answer:
The relationship between regulatory guidance on vibration assessment and the acceptance criteria for preoperational testing of reactor core support structures is established through a structured framework that integrates predictive analysis, measurement, and inspection, as outlined in NRC guidance and regulations.

SRP 3.9.2 (Sections I.3 and I.4) specifies that analyses of dynamic responses (including vibration from flow, acoustic, and mechanical sources) for reactor internals must be consistent with the approach in RG 1.20. These analyses are intended to verify the structural integrity of reactor internals, including core support structures, under preoperational and startup conditions. The NRC reviews both the analytical predictions and the actual test results, ensuring that acceptance criteria are defined and that any discrepancies between as-designed and as-built conditions are addressed during the ITAAC process. The vibration monitoring program during preoperational testing must confirm that no excessive vibrations or structural damage occur, with test results compared against analytical predictions and acceptance criteria (SRP 3.9.2, I.4).

RG 1.20 provides the accepted method for implementing a Comprehensive Vibration Assessment Program (CVAP), which includes predictive analysis, measurement, and inspection programs. The predictive analysis establishes the basis for selecting monitoring locations and components, while the measurement program confirms the analysis results and is sensitive enough to detect unanticipated vibration mechanisms. The inspection program provides both quantitative and qualitative verification (RG 1.20, Section C).

Regulatory basis for these requirements is found in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, which mandates that structures important to safety (including core support structures) be tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function, and that appropriate records be maintained. RG 1.68 and RG 1.29 further clarify that a graded approach to testing is appropriate, with more stringent requirements for safety-significant structures such as seismic Category I components, which include reactor core and vessel internals (RG 1.29, Section C; RG 1.68, pp. 3-4, 7).

In summary, regulatory guidance requires that vibration assessment for reactor core support structures be integrated into preoperational testing, with acceptance criteria derived from predictive analyses and confirmed by measurement and inspection, all within a quality assurance framework commensurate with the safety significance of the structures.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating crack initiation in components that are not accessible for visual inspection?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating crack initiation in components that are not accessible for visual inspection are grounded in the requirements for maintaining structural integrity and ensuring safety-related functions, as outlined in several regulatory documents. According to RG 1.20, Section C.2.3, when direct visual inspection is not possible, the applicant or licensee must propose alternative inspection methods or monitoring techniques—such as remote visual inspection, ultrasonic testing, eddy current testing, or other nondestructive examination methods. These alternatives must be justified as capable of providing assurance of structural integrity equivalent to that provided by direct visual inspection. The acceptance criteria for such inspection programs require that there be no evidence of loose parts, cracking, unacceptable motion, or significant wear. If any of these conditions are detected, the licensee must evaluate the significance and take appropriate corrective actions, which may include additional inspections, analyses, or modifications to ensure continued structural integrity (RG 1.20, Section C.2.3).

Additionally, 10 CFR 50.55a(b) mandates that inservice inspection and testing be performed in accordance with Section XI of the ASME BPV Code, which allows for alternative examination methods or augmented requirements where visual inspection is not possible. The NRC staff reviews the adequacy of these methods to ensure they meet the quality standards commensurate with the safety functions of the components (10 CFR 50.55a(a), (b)).

In summary, the NRC requires that for components not accessible for visual inspection, alternative nondestructive examination methods must be used and justified, with acceptance criteria focused on the absence of cracking and other signs of degradation, and with corrective actions required if such conditions are found. (RG 1.20, Section C.2.3; 10 CFR 50.55a(b)).

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
§ 50.55a Codes and standards.
(a) Each nuclear power plant to which this part applies must be designed, fabricated, erected, constructed, tested, and inspected to quality standards commensurate with the importance of the safety functions to be performed. Where codes and standards are used, they must be identified and evaluated to determine their applicability, adequacy, and sufficiency and shall be supplemented or modified as necessary to assure a quality product in keeping with the required safety function. The structures, systems, and components to which this section applies are those that are safety related. This includes those structures, systems, and components that are part of the reactor coolant pressure boundary, those that are relied upon to shut down the reactor and maintain it in a safe shutdown condition, or those that are relied upon to prevent or mitigate the consequences of accidents which could result in potential offsite exposures comparable to the guidelines set forth in § 50.34(a)(1), § 50.67(b)(2), or § 100.11 of this chapter, as applicable.

(b) The structures, systems, and components of boiling and pressurized water-cooled nuclear power reactors must meet the requirements for Class 1, 2, and 3 components in Section III of the American Society of Mechanical Engineers Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (ASME BPV Code), and the applicable addenda and Code Cases, as endorsed in the regulations. Inservice inspection and testing must be performed in accordance with Section XI of the ASME BPV Code and applicable addenda, subject to the limitations and modifications listed in the regulations. Where visual inspection is not possible, alternative examination methods or augmented requirements may be required as specified by the ASME Code or as determined by the Commission.

2.3 Inspection Program

The inspection program should address both quantitative and qualitative verification of the predictive analysis and measurement program results. The inspection program should include the following elements:

If any of these conditions are identified, the applicant or licensee should evaluate the significance of the findings and take appropriate corrective actions, including additional inspections, analyses, or modifications, as necessary to ensure the continued structural integrity of the reactor internals.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating the seismic response of mechanical systems and components in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating the seismic response of mechanical systems and components in nuclear power plants are established to ensure the structural and functional integrity of safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) under seismic events. According to SRP 3.9.2, the review encompasses the criteria, testing procedures, and dynamic analyses used to demonstrate that piping systems, mechanical equipment, reactor internals, and their supports can withstand vibratory loadings, including those from postulated seismic events. The seismic analysis must consider appropriate methods (such as response spectra, time history, or equivalent static load), selection of significant modes, adequate degrees of freedom, evaluation of maximum relative displacements, and effects such as hydrodynamic forces and nonlinear response. The analysis must also account for all three components of earthquake motion and use appropriate damping criteria (SRP 3.9.2, Areas of Review A, D, L).

Regulatory requirements in 10 CFR 50.55a mandate that mechanical systems and components important to safety meet the design, fabrication, construction, testing, and performance requirements of the applicable ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code or equivalent standards. Seismic and dynamic qualification must be demonstrated by testing, analysis, or a combination thereof, in accordance with ASME and IEEE standards referenced in the regulation (10 CFR 50.55a(h)).

Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.29 specifies that seismic Category I SSCs must be designed to remain functional during the Safe Shutdown Earthquake (SSE), and the quality assurance requirements of Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 50 apply to all activities affecting their safety-related functions (RG 1.29, Section C). RG 1.100 further endorses the use of ASME QME-1-2017 for the functional qualification of active mechanical equipment and IEEE Std 344-2013 for seismic qualification, both by analysis, testing, or combined methods, with NRC-specified exceptions and clarifications (RG 1.100, Section C).

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria require that seismic Category I mechanical systems and components be qualified through rigorous analysis and/or testing per endorsed ASME and IEEE standards, considering all relevant dynamic effects, and that they remain functional under design-basis seismic events, in compliance with 10 CFR 50.55a and associated regulatory guidance.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for selecting damping values in the seismic analysis of nuclear power plant structures and components?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for selecting damping values in the seismic analysis of nuclear power plant structures and components are grounded in a combination of regulatory requirements, technical guidance, and review procedures. According to SRP 3.9.2, the NRC reviews the criteria used for damping in systems, components, equipment, and their supports, with particular attention to the adequacy of any structural damping assumptions, especially when values greater than 1% are used (SRP 3.9.2, I.2.L, 3.A(ii)). The resonance frequencies and mode shapes from simulations and measurements should be compared to establish model accuracy, and the effects of variable or uncertain boundary conditions on structural vibration must be assessed.

Regulatory Guide 1.20 (Section C.2.1.1.2) provides accepted methods for selecting damping values. Damping values should be based on the best available information, including test data, technical literature, and engineering judgment. Where possible, measured damping values from similar components or in-plant measurements should be used; otherwise, values from literature or engineering judgment may be used if justified. The selected values must be appropriate for the expected vibration modes and frequency ranges, and sensitivity studies should be performed to assess the impact of damping variations on predicted responses. All assumptions, uncertainties, and the basis for selected values must be clearly documented, and the NRC staff will review this justification as part of their evaluation.

Additionally, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed and analyzed to quality standards commensurate with their safety functions, using recognized codes and standards as appropriate, and maintaining adequate records.

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria require that damping values be justified, documented, consistent with similar applications, and supported by sensitivity analyses, with particular scrutiny for values exceeding 1%. The selection process must be transparent and based on quality standards as outlined in the referenced regulatory documents.

evidence_chain.evidence_text: Criterion 1—Quality standards and records. Structures, systems, and components important to safety shall be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with the importance of the safety functions to be performed. Where generally recognized codes and standards are used, they shall be identified and evaluated to determine their applicability, adequacy, and sufficiency and shall be supplemented or modified as necessary to assure a quality product in keeping with the required safety function. A quality assurance program shall be established and implemented in order to provide adequate assurance that these structures, systems, and components will satisfactorily perform their safety functions. Appropriate records of the design, fabrication, erection, and testing of structures, systems, and components important to safety shall be maintained by or under the control of the nuclear power unit licensee throughout the life of the unit.

evidence_chain.section: C.2.1.1.2 Vibration Damping
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
2.1.1.2 Vibration Damping

The applicant or licensee should select damping values for use in the vibration and stress analysis program based on the best available information, including test data, technical literature, and engineering judgment. The selected damping values should be justified and documented. The applicant or licensee should consider the following in selecting damping values:

• Damping values should be consistent with those used in the design and analysis of similar reactor internals or components, unless differences in design, materials, or operating conditions warrant otherwise.
• Where available, measured damping values from tests on similar components or from in-plant measurements should be used. If measured values are not available, values from the technical literature or engineering judgment may be used, provided they are justified.
• The selected damping values should be appropriate for the expected vibration modes and frequency ranges of interest. For example, damping may vary with frequency, mode shape, material, and boundary conditions.
• Sensitivity studies should be performed to assess the effect of variations in damping values on the predicted vibration response and stress levels.
• The basis for the selected damping values, including any assumptions or uncertainties, should be clearly documented in the analysis report.

The NRC staff will review the justification for the selected damping values as part of its evaluation of the vibration and stress analysis program.

data.query: How do general design criteria for dynamic loading and regulatory guidance on damping values interact when determining acceptable methods for seismic analysis of reactor vessel internals and containment structures?
data.answer:
The interaction between general design criteria for dynamic loading and regulatory guidance on damping values is central to determining acceptable seismic analysis methods for reactor vessel internals and containment structures. General Design Criteria (GDC) from 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A (see [2]), such as GDC 1 (Quality Standards and Records), GDC 2 (Design Bases for Protection against Natural Phenomena), and GDC 4 (Environmental and Dynamic Effects Design Bases), require that safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs)—including reactor vessel internals and containment—be designed and analyzed to withstand seismic and other dynamic loads, using quality standards and records commensurate with their safety functions.

SRP 3.9.2 ([1]) operationalizes these criteria by specifying that dynamic analyses, including those for seismic events, must ensure the structural and functional integrity of SSCs. The SRP requires that the criteria used for damping in seismic analysis be reviewed, and any use of damping values greater than 1% must be specifically justified and assessed for adequacy. This ensures that the dynamic response of reactor internals and containment structures is not underestimated due to non-conservative damping assumptions.

Regulatory guidance, such as RG 1.20 ([4]), further clarifies that damping values used in vibration and stress analyses must be justified with the best available information—such as test data, operating experience, or published literature. If such data are unavailable, conservative values consistent with similar applications should be used. The NRC evaluates the acceptability of these values on a case-by-case basis, considering the justification provided and the potential effects of aging or wear.

In summary, the general design criteria establish the requirement for robust seismic analysis, while regulatory guidance on damping ensures that the methods and assumptions used—particularly regarding damping—are technically justified and conservative. This integrated approach provides reasonable assurance that reactor vessel internals and containment structures will maintain their integrity under seismic loading, as required by NRC regulations and guidance (see [1], [2], [3], [4]).

data.query: How do general design criteria for dynamic effects and regulatory guidance on damping values inform the selection of appropriate damping values for seismic analysis of reactor vessel internals and containment structures?
data.answer:
The selection of appropriate damping values for seismic analysis of reactor vessel internals and containment structures is informed by both general design criteria and specific regulatory guidance. According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 4, structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety must be designed to accommodate dynamic effects, including those from seismic events, and must consider the most severe postulated conditions at the site. This establishes the regulatory basis for ensuring that seismic analyses, including damping assumptions, are robust and conservative (10CFR, Appendix A, Criterion 4).

Regulatory guidance further clarifies how damping values should be selected and justified. SRP 3.9.2 specifies that the criteria for damping in systems, components, and their supports must be reviewed, with particular attention to the adequacy of any damping values greater than 1%. The review process includes comparing simulated and measured vibration characteristics, and assessing uncertainties due to differences between modeled and as-built conditions (SRP 3.9.2, Sections 2.L and 3.A). Reference is made to RG 1.20 for further details.

RG 1.20, Section C.2.1.1.2, provides accepted methods for selecting damping values, stating that these should be justified using the best available information, such as test data, operating experience, or published literature. The technical basis for the selected values must consider the type of structure, mode of vibration, frequency range, and operating environment. If direct data are unavailable, conservative values from literature or codes may be used, and all assumptions must be documented for NRC review.

Additionally, RG 1.29 identifies reactor vessel internals and containment structures as seismic Category I SSCs, which must be designed to withstand the Safe Shutdown Earthquake (SSE) and remain functional. The seismic analysis requirements, including damping, must be applied to these SSCs and extended as necessary to ensure the validity of the analysis at interfaces with non-seismic Category I systems (RG 1.29, Section C).

In summary, the general design criteria establish the need for robust seismic design, while regulatory guidance provides detailed expectations for the selection, justification, and documentation of damping values in seismic analyses of reactor vessel internals and containment structures.

data.query: What regulatory guidance exists for justifying the use of higher damping values in seismic analysis, and how can testing data or in-service inspection requirements be used to support such justification?
data.answer:
Regulatory guidance for justifying the use of higher damping values in seismic analysis is provided primarily in Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.61, RG 1.20, and the Standard Review Plan (SRP) 3.9.2. RG 1.61 (Section C) establishes acceptable damping values for seismic analysis of structures, systems, and components (SSCs), but explicitly allows for the use of higher damping values if they are supported by documented test data. RG 1.20 (Section C.2.1.1.2) further details the requirements for such justification: applicants or licensees must provide a technical basis for higher damping values, supported by test data or in-service inspection results. This technical basis should include a description of the test program or inspection results, address the similarity of test or inspection conditions to actual plant conditions, the representativeness of test specimens or components, and the adequacy of instrumentation and data acquisition methods. Additionally, the potential variability of damping values due to changes in plant conditions (such as temperature, pressure, and aging) must be considered. The NRC staff evaluates the acceptability of proposed higher damping values on a case-by-case basis, considering the technical justification provided.

SRP 3.9.2 (Areas of Review 2.L and 3.A) reinforces that any use of greater than 1% damping should be assessed for adequacy, and that both simulated and measured frequency response functions (FRFs) from modal or shaker testing should be examined to validate the assumptions. The resonance frequencies and mode shapes from simulations and measurements should be compared to establish model accuracy. RG 1.29 and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, further require that quality standards and records be maintained, and that any alternative methods (such as higher damping values) must be justified with sufficient technical basis to demonstrate compliance with regulatory requirements.

In summary, higher damping values may be justified if supported by robust test data or in-service inspection results, with comprehensive documentation and technical analysis as outlined in RG 1.20, RG 1.61, and SRP 3.9.2.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for dynamic testing and analysis of piping systems in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for dynamic testing and analysis of piping systems in nuclear power plants are grounded in a combination of regulatory requirements, industry codes, and NRC-endorsed guidance. According to 10 CFR 50.55a (§ 50.55a Codes and standards), dynamic testing and analysis of piping systems must conform to the requirements of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (BPV Code), Section III, and other standards as specified by the Commission. This includes design, fabrication, construction, testing, and performance criteria for safety-related systems, structures, and components (SSCs).

The Standard Review Plan (SRP) 3.9.2 specifies that the test program must detail acceptance criteria, allowable limits, and corrective actions if excessive vibration or thermal motion restraint is detected. The calculated vibration and stress levels must be reviewed with their safety margins and acceptance criteria, including justification for vibration and stress limits. The SRP also references RG 1.20, which provides acceptable methods for developing and implementing a comprehensive vibration assessment program (CVAP) for reactor internals, including predictive analysis, measurement, and inspection programs. These programs must verify structural integrity under steady-state and transient vibratory loads, and measurements must be sensitive enough to detect significant excitation mechanisms not previously evaluated.

Additionally, RG 1.100 endorses the use of IEEE Std 344-2013 and ASME QME-1-2017 for seismic and functional qualification of equipment, including dynamic restraints and active mechanical equipment, through analysis, testing, or combined methods. For seismic Category I SSCs, RG 1.29 requires that dynamic analysis requirements extend to interfaces with non-seismic systems to ensure the validity of the seismic analysis.

In summary, NRC acceptance criteria require conformance to ASME BPV Code Section III, detailed test programs with specified acceptance criteria and corrective actions, justification of vibration and stress limits, and the use of NRC-endorsed methods for analysis and testing as described in SRP 3.9.2, RG 1.20, RG 1.29, and RG 1.100.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
C. STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE
The NRC staff considers the guidance in this RG to provide an acceptable method for developing and implementing a CVAP for reactor internals at nuclear power plants. In particular, the applicant or licensee should apply the classifications identified in Section C.1 to categorize reactor internals according to design, operating parameters, and operating experience. The applicant or licensee should establish an appropriate CVAP using the guidance in Sections C.2, C.3, and C.4, as they relate to the specific classifications of the applicable reactor internals.

This RG describes acceptable methods for evaluating the potential adverse effects from FIV, AR, AIV, and MIV. Section C.2 of this RG provides detailed information for these vibration mechanisms. These vibration excitation mechanisms need to be assessed for reactor internals in BWR, PWR, and SMR nuclear power plants.  

Consistent with RG 1.68, “Initial Test Program for Water-Cooled Nuclear Power Plant” (Ref. 4), the term “preoperational testing,” as used in this guide, consists of testing before fuel loading, and “startup testing” refers to testing after fuel loading.  

Reactor internals are designed to accommodate steady-state and transient vibratory loads throughout the service life of the reactor. The overall program includes predictive analysis, a measurement program, and an inspection program. The term “comprehensive” appears in the title of the overall program to emphasize that these individual elements are used together to verify structural integrity of the reactor internals (including BWR steam dryers): 

• The predictive analysis provides theoretical verification of structural integrity and the basis for the choice of components and specific locations to be monitored in the measurement and inspection programs.  

• The measurement program confirms the results of the predictive analyses. However, the measurements (i.e., data acquisition, reduction, and interpretation processes) need to be sufficiently flexible and sensitive to permit identification and definition of any significant excitation mechanisms and vibration that are present but were not evaluated in the predictive program.

• The inspection program addresses both quantitative and qualitative verification of the predictive analysis and measurement program results.

1.1 Regulatory Positions on IEEE Std 344-2013

1.1.1 General NRC Staff Positions

IEEE Std 344-2013 is, in general, acceptable to the NRC staff for the seismic qualification of (1) electrical equipment in new NPPs and (2) new or replacement electrical equipment in operating NPPs, subject to the following provisions:

a. Rigorous seismic qualification by analysis, testing, or combined analysis and testing, as described in Clauses 7, 8, and 9 of IEEE Std 344-2013, are acceptable methods for the seismic qualification of electrical equipment.

b. The NRC staff will review the use of experience data (earthquake or test experience data) for the seismic qualification of electrical equipment. The licensee or applicant may submit the information, perhaps as a technical report (TR), to the NRC for approval. The staff’s review will include areas such as (1) the credibility and completeness of the compilation of the experience database, (2) the inclusion and exclusion rules (termed “prohibited features” in IEEE Std 344-2013) of equipment in the database, (3) the similarity between equipment in the database and the equipment in NPPs, and (4) the adequacy of the experience data to demonstrate the required performance of the equipment.

1.2 Regulatory Positions on ASME QME-1-2017

ASME QME-1-2017 is, in general, acceptable to the NRC staff for the functional qualification of active mechanical equipment used in nuclear facilities, subject to the exceptions and clarifications provided in this section. The standard provides requirements and guidelines for qualifying active mechanical equipment, including pumps, valves, dynamic restraints, and nonmetallic parts, for use in nuclear facilities. The NRC staff endorses the use of the methods described in ASME QME-1-2017, including the use of analysis, testing, or combined analysis and testing, as acceptable methods for the functional qualification of active mechanical equipment.

data.query: How do general design criteria for reactor protection and engineered safety features relate to the requirements for vibration testing of piping during initial startup?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for reactor protection and engineered safety features, as outlined in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, establish the foundational requirements for the design, fabrication, erection, and testing of structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety, including piping systems. Specifically, GDC 1 (Quality Standards and Records), GDC 2 (Design Bases for Protection against Natural Phenomena), and GDC 4 (Environmental and Dynamic Effects Design Bases) require that SSCs be designed and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety functions and be capable of withstanding environmental and dynamic effects, such as vibration (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A; RG 1.100, Section A).

SRP 3.9.2 further clarifies that compliance with these GDCs necessitates dynamic testing and analysis of SSCs, including vibration testing of piping, during initial startup. The purpose of such testing is to confirm that piping systems, restraints, components, and supports are adequately designed to withstand flow-induced dynamic loadings and operational transients, and that normal thermal motion is not improperly restrained. The startup test program must specify flow modes, inspection locations, acceptance criteria, and corrective actions for excessive vibration or thermal restraint (SRP 3.9.2, Section I).

Additionally, RG 1.29 and RG 1.100 emphasize that safety-related SSCs, such as those classified as seismic Category I, must meet the quality assurance and testing requirements of Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 50, ensuring their functionality under postulated accident and seismic conditions. Thus, the GDCs provide the regulatory basis for requiring vibration testing of piping during initial startup as part of the overall assurance that reactor protection and engineered safety features will perform their intended safety functions.

data.query: For a nuclear power plant, what combined regulatory requirements from general design criteria, dynamic testing standards, and regulatory guides must be met when incorporating piping vibration testing into the initial startup test program?
data.answer:
When incorporating piping vibration testing into the initial startup test program for a nuclear power plant, several combined regulatory requirements must be met, drawing from general design criteria, dynamic testing standards, and regulatory guides:

1. General Design Criteria: Compliance with 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, specifically General Design Criteria (GDC) 1, 2, 4, 14, and 15, is required. These criteria mandate quality standards, protection against natural phenomena (including seismic events), and consideration of environmental and dynamic effects on the reactor coolant pressure boundary and system design (SRP 3.9.2; 10 CFR 50.55a).

2. Codes and Standards: Piping systems must meet the requirements of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (BPV Code) Section III for design, fabrication, construction, and testing, as well as the ASME Code for Operation and Maintenance (OM Code) for inservice inspection and testing (10 CFR 50.55a(b), (h)). Alternatives may be used if they provide an acceptable level of quality and safety (10 CFR 50.55a(i)).

3. Dynamic Testing: Startup testing must include piping vibration, safety relief valve vibration, thermal expansion, and dynamic effects testing for ASME BPV Code Class 1, 2, and 3 systems, high-energy piping inside seismic Category I structures, and other specified systems (SRP 3.9.2). The test program should specify flow modes, inspection locations, acceptance criteria, and corrective actions for excessive vibration or thermal restraint.

4. Seismic and Dynamic Analysis: Seismic Category I SSCs (as defined in RG 1.29) must be designed and tested to withstand safe-shutdown earthquake (SSE) effects and remain functional (RG 1.29; SRP 3.7.2). Dynamic analysis methods, including response spectrum or time history analysis, must be used, considering high-frequency modes, relative displacements, and piping interactions (SRP 3.7.2).

5. Regulatory Guides and Standards: The NRC endorses IEEE Std 344-2013 for seismic qualification of electrical equipment and ASME QME-1-2017 for functional qualification of active mechanical equipment, including dynamic restraints, with specified exceptions and clarifications (RG 1.100).

In summary, the initial startup test program must integrate requirements from 10 CFR Part 50 (including GDCs and Appendix B), ASME BPV and OM Codes, NRC-endorsed standards (IEEE 344, ASME QME-1), and NRC regulatory guides (RG 1.29, RG 1.100), ensuring that piping systems are dynamically tested and analyzed to confirm their integrity and functionality under operational and seismic conditions.

Compliance with the specific criteria guidance in subsection II of this SRP section will provide reasonable assurance of appropriate dynamic testing and analysis of structures, systems, and components (SSCs) within the scope of this SRP section in conformance with Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) 50.55a, “Codes and Standards,” 10 CFR Part 50, “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities,” Appendix A, “General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants,” General Design Criterion (GDC) 1, “Quality Standards and Records,” GDC 2, “Design Bases for Protection against Natural Phenomena,” GDC 4, “Environmental and Dynamic Effects Design Bases,” GDC 14, “Reactor Coolant Pressure Boundary,” and GDC 15, “Reactor Coolant System Design,” 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, “Quality Assurance Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants and Fuel Reprocessing Plants,” and 10 CFR 52.47(b) and 10 CFR 52.80(a).

A. American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (BPV Code) Class 1, 2, and 3 systems,  
B. other high-energy piping systems inside seismic Category I structures (“seismic Category I” is defined in Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.29, “Seismic Design Classification”)  
C. high-energy portions of systems whose failure could reduce the functioning of any seismic Category I SSCs to an unacceptable safety level, and  
D. seismic Category I portions of moderate-energy piping systems located outside containment.

The supports and restraints necessary for operation during the life of the nuclear power plant are considered to be part of the piping system.

The purpose of these tests is to confirm that these piping systems, restraints, components, and supports have been adequately designed to withstand flow-induced dynamic loadings under the steady-state and operational transient conditions anticipated during service and to confirm that normal thermal motion is not restrained. Requirements
