data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating the primary stress limits of reactor pressure vessels during dynamic loading events?
data.answer: The NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating the primary stress limits of reactor pressure vessels during dynamic loading events are grounded in the requirements of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (BPV Code), Section III, as endorsed by 10 CFR 50.55a. According to Regulatory Guide 1.20, Section C.2.1.3.2, applicants must perform stress analyses using appropriate finite element models that account for all significant dynamic loads, including flow-induced vibration, acoustic resonance, acoustic-induced vibration, and mechanical-induced vibration. The primary and secondary stress limits must be evaluated in accordance with the provisions of ASME BPV Code, Section III, which specifies allowable stress values for the relevant materials and service conditions. The acceptance criteria for primary stress are thus the allowable stress values defined in the Code for the specific material and service class. Additionally, the analysis must demonstrate that the cumulative usage factor for fatigue, as calculated using the Code's fatigue design curves, does not exceed the allowable value at any location subject to significant vibratory loading. The Standard Review Plan (SRP) 3.9.2 further emphasizes the need to justify vibration and stress limits, ensure stress convergence, and benchmark analysis methodologies. The regulatory basis for these requirements is found in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, which mandates the use of recognized codes and standards and the implementation of a quality assurance program to ensure safety-related structures and components meet their intended safety functions.

evidence_chain.section: I. AREAS OF REVIEW, Item 3.C (Results of vibration and stress calculations)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
The calculated vibration and stress levels of reactor internal structures are reviewed with their safety margins and acceptance criteria. The procedures for combining the vibration and stress response models (Item 3.A above) with the forcing functions (Item 3.B above) to compute overall vibration and stress response are also reviewed. The results for structures and components with a history of failures from adverse flow effects (such as steam dryers excited by flow instabilities over the openings of valve standoff pipes) are evaluated in greater detail. In particular, the following items are reviewed:
(i) Chosen locations for vibration and stress calculations, and any locations where instrumentation will be installed for subsequent power ascension testing; along with the choice of analysis approach (time or frequency domain) and the acceptability of damping modeling (such as the Rayleigh damping method used for time domain calculations).
(ii) Benchmarking of analysis methodologies, particularly end-to-end benchmarking using previous testing on valid prototypes.
(iii) Stress convergence and high-cycle fatigue evaluation, particularly structural model development, application of dynamic loads to the structural model, and fatigue analysis of two-sided fillet welds.
(iv) Vibration and stress limits and their justification.
For further details, refer to RG 1.20, Revision 4, Section C.2.1.3.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
2.1.3.2 Stress Convergence and High-Cycle Fatigue Evaluation

The applicant or licensee should demonstrate that the stress analysis is sufficiently converged to provide reliable estimates of the maximum stresses in the reactor internals. The stress analysis should be performed using appropriate finite element models and should include all significant sources of loading, including those from flow-induced vibration (FIV), acoustic resonance (AR), acoustic-induced vibration (AIV), and mechanical-induced vibration (MIV). The applicant or licensee should evaluate the primary and secondary stress limits in accordance with the applicable provisions of Section III of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (BPV Code), as endorsed in 10 CFR 50.55a. The acceptance criteria for primary stress limits should be based on the allowable stress values specified in the ASME BPV Code, Section III, for the applicable materials and service conditions. The applicant or licensee should also evaluate the potential for high-cycle fatigue failure due to vibratory loads, using the fatigue design curves and cumulative usage factors specified in the ASME BPV Code, Section III. The analysis should demonstrate that the cumulative usage factor for each location subject to significant vibratory loading does not exceed the allowable value specified in the Code.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory requirements address the frequency of in-service inspection for reactor vessel internal components that are susceptible to flow-induced vibration, and what relationship exists between vibration assessment program findings and inspection intervals?
data.answer: NRC regulatory requirements address the frequency of in-service inspection for reactor vessel internal components susceptible to flow-induced vibration (FIV) through a risk-informed, performance-based approach that is closely tied to the findings of the vibration assessment program. According to Regulatory Guide 1.20, Section C.2.3, the inspection program must verify the absence of adverse vibration effects and confirm the results of vibration and stress analyses. Inspections are required at appropriate intervals during preoperational, startup, and subsequent in-service periods. Critically, the frequency and extent of in-service inspections are determined by the results of the vibration assessment program, which includes both predictive analysis and measurement data. If the assessment shows that reactor internals are not susceptible to adverse vibration effects, inspection intervals may be reduced. Conversely, if susceptibility is identified, inspection intervals must be increased to ensure continued structural integrity. Additional inspections are mandated if significant vibration or adverse conditions are detected during operation. This approach is consistent with the quality assurance principles outlined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, which requires that safety-related components be designed, tested, and maintained to standards commensurate with their safety function, and that records be kept throughout the plant’s life. The Standard Review Plan (SRP 3.9.2, Section I.4) further emphasizes the importance of vibration monitoring and the need to update analyses and inspection plans based on monitoring results. Thus, there is a direct relationship between vibration assessment findings and inspection intervals: the greater the demonstrated susceptibility to FIV, the more frequent and extensive the required inspections.

evidence_chain.section: I. AREAS OF REVIEW, Item 4
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
The NRC staff will review the plans for vibration monitoring of reactor internals conducted during the preoperational and startup test program. General guidance for preoperational and initial startup testing for prototypes, limited prototypes, and non-prototypes is identical to that for the analyses described in Section I.3. Components that should be considered for instrumentation in preoperational and initial startup testing are listed in Section I.3. However, new reactor internals designs may include additional components not listed in Section I.3 which also need to be evaluated.

For components with no prior history of adverse effects due to FIV, AR, AIV, or MIV; and which have been shown by analysis to have a high margin of safety against such effects (for example, a margin of safety of 2.0 has been acceptable in past reviews), no on-structure instrumentation or measurements are necessary. Measurements need to be performed, however, on systems and components that have been adversely affected by FIV, AR, AIV and MIV in the past (such as BWR steam dryers). Instrumentation should also be considered for new components that have no operating experience. Less instrumentation and measurements are needed for limited prototypes. Additional guidance for limited prototypes is found in RG 1.20, Revision 4, Section C.3.2, and for nonprototypes in Section C.4.2.

The purpose of vibration monitoring is to confirm and complement the analyses to demonstrate that adverse flow, mechanical, and acoustic excitation mechanisms expected during all steady state and anticipated transient conditions that correspond to preoperational, startup test, and normal operating conditions will not cause excessive vibrations or structural damage. The NRC staff reviews the test program description to ensure it includes all potential plant operating conditions (such as pressures, flow rates, and temperatures), potential flow-induced resonance behavior, mechanical and acoustic sources, sensor types and locations (and how the locations are connected to key response regions identified by the analyses), a description of test procedures and methods to be used to process and interpret the measured data including bias errors and uncertainties, a description of the visual inspections to be made, planned comparisons of the test results with the analytical predictions along with acceptability criteria, and plans for updating and correcting the analyses based on the monitoring results.

evidence_chain.section: C.2.3 Inspection Program
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
2.3 Inspection Program

The inspection program should be designed to verify the absence of adverse vibration effects and to confirm the results of the vibration and stress analysis and measurement programs. The inspection program should include both quantitative and qualitative inspections of reactor internals and should be performed at appropriate intervals during preoperational and startup testing, as well as during subsequent inservice inspections. The frequency and extent of inservice inspections should be based on the results of the vibration assessment program, including the predictive analysis and measurement program. If the results of the vibration assessment program indicate that the reactor internals are not susceptible to adverse vibration effects, the frequency of inservice inspections may be reduced. Conversely, if the vibration assessment program identifies components that are susceptible to flow-induced vibration or other adverse effects, the inspection intervals should be adjusted accordingly to ensure continued structural integrity. The inspection program should also provide for additional inspections if significant vibration or other adverse conditions are identified during operation.

data.query: What regulatory guidance is provided for establishing long-term inspection plans for reactor control rod drive shafts and steam generator inlet flow restrictors, particularly in the context of components identified as susceptible to vibration-induced wear?
data.answer:
Regulatory guidance for establishing long-term inspection plans for reactor control rod drive shafts and steam generator inlet flow restrictors, particularly for components susceptible to vibration-induced wear, is provided primarily in SRP 3.9.2, Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.20, and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1.

SRP 3.9.2 (Section I.4) emphasizes the need for vibration monitoring and inspection plans during preoperational and startup testing, especially for components with a history of flow-induced vibration (FIV) issues or those lacking operational experience. The guidance requires that the inspection and monitoring program address all relevant plant operating conditions and include procedures for visual inspections, data interpretation, and updating analyses based on test results.

RG 1.20 (Section C.2.3) provides detailed expectations for the inspection program. It states that inspections should focus on components identified as susceptible to vibration-induced wear, such as control rod drive shafts and steam generator inlet flow restrictors. The program should include visual inspections, nondestructive examinations, and other appropriate techniques to detect signs of vibration-induced damage. Inspections should be scheduled after preoperational and startup testing and at periodic intervals during plant operation. The results must be documented and used to update predictive analyses and measurement programs to ensure continued structural integrity. The inspection plan should be tailored to the specific design and operating conditions of the components and integrated into the overall long-term inspection plan for reactor internals.

10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, establishes the regulatory basis, requiring that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed, tested, and maintained to quality standards, with a quality assurance program and appropriate records maintained throughout the unit's life.

2.3 Inspection Program

The inspection program should be designed to provide both quantitative and qualitative verification of the predictive analysis and measurement program results. The inspection program should include the following elements:

• Preoperational and startup inspections of reactor internals and other components identified as susceptible to vibration-induced wear, including those with a history of vibration problems or those with significant design or operational changes.

• Inspections should focus on locations where the predictive analysis and measurement program indicate the potential for adverse vibration effects, such as high-stress regions, locations of maximum vibration amplitude, and areas where wear or fatigue damage is most likely to occur.

• The inspection program should include visual inspections, nondestructive examinations (NDE), and other appropriate techniques to detect cracking, wear, loose parts, or other signs of vibration-induced damage.

• The inspection program should be scheduled to coincide with key phases of plant operation, such as after preoperational and startup testing, and at periodic intervals during plant operation, as appropriate.

• The results of the inspection program should be documented and used to update the predictive analysis and measurement program, as necessary, to ensure continued structural integrity of reactor internals and other susceptible components.

The inspection program should be sufficiently comprehensive to provide assurance that vibration-induced wear or damage will be detected in a timely manner, and that corrective actions can be implemented before structural integrity is compromised. For components such as control rod drive shafts and steam generator inlet flow restrictors, which may be susceptible to vibration-induced wear, the inspection program should be tailored to address their specific design and operating conditions, and should be integrated into the overall long-term inspection plan for reactor internals.

data.query: How do regulatory requirements for protection against dynamic effects from postulated pipe ruptures address the conversion of fluid acceleration to mechanical loading on system components during transient events?
data.answer:
Regulatory requirements for protection against dynamic effects from postulated pipe ruptures specifically address the conversion of fluid acceleration to mechanical loading on system components during transient events through a combination of analysis, modeling, and qualification programs. According to SRP 3.9.2 (Section I, items 1, 3, and 3.A/B/C), the NRC reviews whether piping systems, restraints, components, and supports are designed to withstand flow-induced dynamic loadings, including those arising from operational transients and postulated events such as pipe ruptures. The analyses must define input-forcing functions and estimate the resulting vibration and alternating stress levels, considering mechanisms like vortex-induced vibration and acoustic resonance, which can amplify dynamic loads.

Regulatory Guide 1.20 (Section C.2.1) further details that applicants should perform structural, hydraulic, and acoustic modeling to predict the response of reactor internals to vibratory loads, explicitly including those from postulated pipe ruptures. The analysis must identify and characterize forcing functions, such as fluid acceleration, and assess how these are converted into mechanical loads on system components during transients. The computed responses, including frequency response functions and stress evaluations, must demonstrate that components can accommodate these dynamic effects within acceptable limits.

These requirements are grounded in the general design criteria of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, which mandates that safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) be designed and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function. Additionally, RG 1.100 and RG 1.29 provide guidance on the qualification and dynamic analysis of active mechanical equipment and seismic Category I SSCs, ensuring that dynamic effects, including those from fluid acceleration during transients, are adequately addressed through functional qualification and dynamic analysis up to appropriate system boundaries.

In summary, the regulatory framework requires detailed modeling and analysis to ensure that the conversion of fluid acceleration to mechanical loading during transient events, such as postulated pipe ruptures, is fully evaluated and that system components are qualified to withstand these dynamic effects.

data.query: What are the regulatory expectations for modeling the transmission of forces from fluid acceleration to structural elements when evaluating the effects of high-energy line breaks in nuclear power plant systems?
data.answer:
The regulatory expectations for modeling the transmission of forces from fluid acceleration to structural elements, particularly when evaluating the effects of high-energy line breaks in nuclear power plant systems, are clearly defined in several NRC documents. According to SRP 3.9.2 (Section I, items 1 and 3, and 3.A), analyses must confirm that piping systems, restraints, components, and supports are adequately designed to withstand flow-induced dynamic loadings, including those from fluid acceleration. The analyses should assess vibration behavior, define input-forcing functions, and estimate resulting vibration and alternating stress levels. All analytic and numerical modeling procedures must be reviewed, including models of fluid hydraulic and acoustic behavior and their coupling to structural models, with particular attention to fluid-structure interaction effects.

10 CFR 50.55a requires that components important to safety meet the design, fabrication, construction, testing, and performance requirements of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section III, or equivalent standards. This includes requirements for the transmission of forces and loads, such as those from fluid acceleration, to structural elements.

Regulatory Guide 1.20 (Section C.2.1.1) further specifies that applicants should develop structural, hydraulic, and acoustic models capable of predicting the vibratory response of reactor internals to excitation mechanisms, including fluid acceleration. The models must represent geometry, mass, stiffness, damping, and boundary conditions, and must explicitly couple the fluid and structural domains to account for force transmission (fluid-structure interaction). The adequacy of these models should be justified by benchmarking against test data or operating experience.

In summary, the NRC expects comprehensive modeling of fluid-structure interactions, adherence to ASME Code requirements, and validation of models through benchmarking, to ensure that structural elements can withstand forces transmitted from fluid acceleration during high-energy events such as line breaks.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating the dynamic response of reactor coolant system piping and connected structures to postulated pipe breaks?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating the dynamic response of reactor coolant system (RCS) piping and connected structures to postulated pipe breaks are grounded in a combination of regulatory requirements, codes, and detailed technical guidance. According to SRP 3.9.2 (Items 1 and 3.C), the evaluation must include a test program specifying acceptance criteria for vibration and stress, corrective actions for excessive vibration, and detailed analysis of locations with a history of adverse flow effects. The procedures must combine vibration and stress response models with forcing functions to compute overall response, and the acceptability of analysis methods (e.g., time or frequency domain, damping modeling) must be justified. Benchmarking against previous valid prototypes and convergence of stress and fatigue analyses are required, with particular attention to high-cycle fatigue and welds.

Regulatory Guide 1.20 (Sections C.2.1.3.2 and C.2.1.3.3) further specifies that the stress analysis must be refined to ensure convergence and that fatigue usage factors, calculated using ASME BPV Code Section III, Division 1 fatigue curves, must be less than 1.0 at all locations of interest. The acceptance criteria must ensure that vibratory responses do not result in unacceptable stresses, excessive vibration, or fatigue damage during all operational and postulated events. Justification for the selected criteria, including any deviations from code requirements, must be provided.

Additionally, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety be designed, fabricated, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety functions, using recognized codes and standards as appropriate. RG 1.29 clarifies that the reactor coolant pressure boundary and connected piping up to specified isolation points must be designed to withstand seismic and dynamic loads, including those from postulated pipe breaks, and must meet quality assurance requirements.

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria require demonstration, through analysis and testing, that RCS piping and connected structures will not experience unacceptable vibration, stress, or fatigue under postulated pipe break conditions, with all evaluations based on applicable codes (notably the ASME BPV Code), validated methodologies, and documented justification for all criteria used (SRP 3.9.2; RG 1.20 C.2.1.3.2, C.2.1.3.3; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A; RG 1.29).

The applicant or licensee should demonstrate that the stress analysis is sufficiently refined to ensure that the calculated stresses are converged and that the results are not unduly sensitive to mesh size or other numerical parameters. The applicant or licensee should evaluate the potential for high-cycle fatigue (HCF) failure of reactor internals due to vibratory loads. The evaluation should include the following:

data.query: How do general design criteria for protection against dynamic effects relate to the requirements for analyzing pressure waves resulting from postulated breaks in reactor coolant system injection lines?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for protection against dynamic effects, as outlined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A (specifically GDC 1, 2, 4, 14, and 15), establish the regulatory foundation for ensuring that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety are designed, fabricated, and tested to withstand dynamic loads, including those resulting from postulated breaks in reactor coolant system injection lines. SRP 3.9.2 clarifies that compliance with these criteria requires dynamic testing and analysis of SSCs to confirm their ability to withstand flow-induced dynamic loadings, such as pressure waves and vibrations that may result from abnormal flow conditions, including postulated pipe breaks. This analysis is necessary to provide reasonable assurance that the design bases for environmental and dynamic effects are met, as required by GDC 4, and that the reactor coolant pressure boundary and system design (GDC 14 and 15) maintain their integrity under such conditions.

Furthermore, RG 1.29 specifies that the reactor coolant pressure boundary and associated systems (including injection lines) are classified as seismic Category I SSCs, which must be designed to withstand not only seismic events but also other dynamic effects, such as those from pressure waves due to postulated breaks. The guidance emphasizes that the system boundary for safety analysis includes all portions required to accomplish the safety function, ensuring that dynamic effects from non-seismic portions do not compromise the integrity of seismic Category I SSCs. Thus, the general design criteria directly inform the requirements for analyzing and testing for pressure waves and other dynamic effects resulting from postulated breaks in reactor coolant system injection lines, ensuring the continued safety and functionality of critical plant systems.

References: SRP 3.9.2, Section I; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 1, 2, 4, 14, 15; RG 1.29, Section C.

data.query: How do general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena relate to the selection of damping values for seismic analysis of safety-related components in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena, specifically as outlined in General Design Criterion (GDC) 2 of 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A, require that structures, systems, and components important to safety in nuclear power plants be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena such as earthquakes without loss of their safety functions. This criterion mandates that the design bases must consider the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site, include appropriate safety margins, and account for combinations of normal, accident, and natural phenomena effects (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2).

SRP 3.9.3 further clarifies that, to comply with GDC 2, the NRC staff reviews the loading combinations, stresses, and stress limits for safety-related components, ensuring these are evaluated under the combined effects of normal, accident, and natural phenomena conditions, including seismic events. The selection of damping values for seismic analysis is a critical aspect of this evaluation, as damping directly affects the calculated stresses and dynamic response of components during an earthquake. By ensuring that appropriate damping values are used in seismic analysis, the design can demonstrate that safety-related components will maintain their functional capability under seismic loading, as required by GDC 2 (SRP 3.9.3, Section II).

In summary, the general design criteria establish the regulatory basis for ensuring that seismic analyses—including the selection of damping values—are performed in a manner that provides reasonable assurance of safety-related components' ability to withstand natural phenomena without loss of safety function.

data.answer: The regulatory guidance that addresses the consideration of buoyancy forces and support conditions when evaluating the potential for uplift of reactor modules during seismic events is found in Standard Review Plan (SRP) 3.9.3, specifically in Section II, Acceptance Criteria. This section emphasizes that component support designs must provide adequate margins of safety under all combinations of loadings, which would include seismic events and associated forces such as buoyancy. The SRP requires that the combination of loadings considered for each component support, including system operating transients, must meet the criteria outlined in Appendix A, Regulatory Guides 1.124 and 1.130, and Subsection NF of the Code. Furthermore, the SRP specifies that possible movements of the support base structures must be taken into account when establishing allowable equipment deformations. This implies that uplift due to buoyancy forces during seismic events, as well as the adequacy of support conditions to resist such uplift, should be evaluated as part of the seismic qualification and functionality assurance program for reactor modules. Therefore, SRP 3.9.3 provides the primary regulatory guidance for addressing these considerations.

data.query: How are dynamic loads, such as those from earthquakes and relief-valve actuation, required to be considered in the design and analysis of ASME Code Class 1, 2, and 3 piping systems?
data.answer:
Dynamic loads, such as those from earthquakes and relief-valve actuation, are required to be explicitly considered in the design and analysis of ASME Code Class 1, 2, and 3 piping systems. According to SRP 3.9.3, the design must address loading combinations that include both operational transients and dynamic events, such as seismic loads and relief valve discharges. The design and service stress limits and deformation criteria must comply with the applicable ASME Code requirements and the criteria in Appendix A of SRP 3.9.3. Specifically, the design must account for the most severe combinations of internal fluid weight, momentum, pressure, dead weight, thermal loads, steady-state and transient valve operation, reaction forces from valve discharges (including thrust, bending, and torsion), seismic forces, and dynamic forces from events like BWR safety relief valve discharge into suppression pools. The structural response of the piping and its supports must be evaluated using dynamic or time-history analyses to ensure appropriate support and restraint under these dynamic loadings.

SRP 3.9.2 further requires that startup testing confirm the adequacy of the piping systems, restraints, and supports to withstand flow-induced dynamic loadings and seismic effects. Analytical procedures for seismic analysis must consider differential support movements, hydrodynamic effects, and nonlinear responses. RG 1.29 and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, reinforce that seismic Category I systems (including piping and supports) must be designed to withstand the Safe Shutdown Earthquake (SSE) and remain functional, with seismic dynamic analysis requirements extending to interfaces with non-seismic systems as necessary to maintain validity. All these requirements are subject to quality assurance provisions to ensure safety functions are preserved.

References: SRP 3.9.3 (I.1, I.2), SRP 3.9.2 (I.1, I.2.A, I.2.F), RG 1.29 (C.1, C.3), 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A (Criterion 1).

data.query: What regulatory requirements govern the use of elastic response spectrum analysis, including peak broadening and damping values, when calculating dynamic moments for safety-related piping systems?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements governing the use of elastic response spectrum analysis, including peak broadening and damping values, for calculating dynamic moments in safety-related piping systems are primarily established through the incorporation of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section III, Division 1, as mandated by 10 CFR 50.55a (see 10 CFR Part 50, § 50.55a(a), (b)(1), and (b)(2)). This Code sets forth the detailed technical criteria for the design, analysis, and testing of piping and other safety-related components. While 10 CFR 50.55a itself does not specify the technical details of elastic response spectrum analysis, it requires compliance with the ASME Code, which addresses the methods, including the use of elastic response spectrum analysis, and prescribes requirements for parameters such as damping values and peak broadening.

Additionally, SRP 3.9.3 Section II (Acceptance Criteria) reinforces that the acceptability of analysis methods—including elastic response spectrum analysis—must be demonstrated by adherence to the ASME Code and relevant Regulatory Guides (e.g., RG 1.124 and RG 1.130). The SAR (Safety Analysis Report) must describe the calculational procedures, including the treatment of dynamic effects such as changes in momentum, and demonstrate that stress computations and limits conform to the Code. The combination of loadings and the selection of appropriate stress limits must also meet the criteria in Appendix A and referenced standards.

In summary, the regulatory framework requires that elastic response spectrum analysis for safety-related piping systems be performed in accordance with the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section III, Division 1, as incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a, and as further clarified by SRP 3.9.3. The specific technical requirements for peak broadening and damping values are found within the ASME Code itself.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for the physical arrangement and support of reactor vessel internals to ensure their retention and alignment within the reactor pressure vessel?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for the physical arrangement and support of reactor vessel internals are established to ensure their retention and alignment within the reactor pressure vessel (RPV) under all operating and postulated accident conditions. According to SRP 3.9.5 (Sections I and II), the NRC reviews the design arrangements of all reactor internals, focusing on their positioning, securing, and the provision for axial and lateral retention and support. The design must accommodate dimensional changes due to thermal and other effects. 

The acceptance criteria are grounded in several General Design Criteria (GDC) from 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, including:
- GDC 1 and 10 CFR 50.55a: Internals must be designed, fabricated, erected, tested, and inspected to quality standards commensurate with their safety function (see also 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1).
- GDC 2: Internals must withstand natural phenomena (e.g., earthquakes) and accident conditions without loss of safety function.
- GDC 4: Internals must be compatible with environmental conditions from normal operation, maintenance, testing, and postulated pipe ruptures, including LOCA.
- GDC 10: Internals must have sufficient margin to ensure fuel design limits are not exceeded during normal and anticipated operational occurrences.

SRP 3.9.5 further requires that core support structures comply with ASME BPV Code Section III, Subsection NG, as incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a. Other internals must meet the guidelines of NG-3000 and not adversely affect core support structure integrity (NG-1122). Deformation limits must be established and justified in the safety analysis report, ensuring stresses do not exceed specified limits.

SRP 3.9.3 and SRP 3.9.2 emphasize that loading combinations, including operational transients and dynamic effects (e.g., flow-induced vibration), must be analyzed to verify structural integrity. RG 1.20 provides guidance for a comprehensive vibration assessment program (CVAP), requiring predictive analysis, measurement, and inspection to confirm that internals remain retained and aligned under all relevant conditions.

In summary, NRC requirements mandate robust physical arrangements, quality standards, and analytical verification to ensure reactor internals are retained and aligned within the RPV, as detailed in SRP 3.9.5, 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A, SRP 3.9.3, SRP 3.9.2, and RG 1.20.

data.answer:
The NRC’s general design criteria for quality standards and design control, as articulated in 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A, Criterion 1 (GDC 1), directly inform the expectations for the positioning and securing of reactor vessel internals within the reactor pressure vessel (RPV). GDC 1 requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety—including reactor internals—be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with the importance of their safety functions (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1; SRP 3.9.5, II). This means that the physical arrangement, retention, and support of internals must ensure their ability to withstand operational, environmental, and accident conditions, including thermal effects and vibratory loads (SRP 3.9.5, I; RG 1.20, C; SRP 3.9.2, I).

The NRC expects that the design of reactor internals includes provisions for both axial and lateral retention and support, accommodating dimensional changes due to thermal and other effects, and ensuring that these components remain properly positioned and secured under all anticipated conditions (SRP 3.9.5, I). The application of recognized codes and standards is required, and where such standards are not sufficient, they must be supplemented to assure a quality product (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1).

Furthermore, the NRC requires a comprehensive vibration assessment program (CVAP) as described in RG 1.20, which includes predictive analysis, measurement, and inspection programs to verify the structural integrity and secure positioning of reactor internals under steady-state and transient vibratory loads (RG 1.20, C; SRP 3.9.2, I). Acceptance criteria for these aspects are based on compliance with GDC 1 and 10 CFR 50.55a, ensuring that the design and securing of reactor internals do not impair safety-related functions (SRP 3.9.5, II; SRP 3.9.3, II).

In summary, the NRC’s general design criteria require that the positioning and securing of reactor vessel internals be accomplished through robust quality standards, design control, and verification programs, ensuring their integrity and functionality throughout the plant’s operational life.

The physical or design arrangements of all reactor internals structures, components, assemblies, and systems, are evaluated including the positioning and securing of such items within the RPV, the provision for axial and lateral retention and support of the internals assemblies and components, and the accommodation of dimensional changes due to thermal and other effects. ... Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations: 1. GDC 1 and 10 CFR 50.55a require that reactor internals be designed, fabricated, erected, tested, and inspected to quality standards commensurate with the importance of the safety functions performed. ... The technical rationale for application of these acceptance criteria ... GDC 1 and 10 CFR 50.55a require that SSCs important to safety be designed to quality standards commensurate with the importance of the safety functions performed. The reactor internals include SSCs performing safety functions and SSCs whose failure can affect the performance of other SSC safety functions, including reactivity monitoring and control, core cooling, and fission product confinement (within both the fuel cladding and the primary reactor coolant system). Application of this requirement to the reactor internals provides assurance that established design practices of proven or demonstrated effectiveness achieve a high likelihood that these safety functions will be performed.

Applicable Regulations

• CFR, Title 10, “Energy,” Part 50, “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities,” (10 CFR 50).

o 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, “General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants,” General Design Criterion (GDC) 1, “Quality Standards and Records,” requires that reactor internals be designed, fabricated, and tested to quality standards commensurate with the importance of the safety functions to be performed.

o 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4, “Environmental and Dynamic Effects Design Bases,” requires reactor internals to be designed to accommodate the effects of, and to be compatible with, the environmental conditions associated with normal operations, maintenance and testing.

o 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, “Quality Assurance Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants,” requires reactor internals to be designed and tested according to appropriate quality standards.

...

C. STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE
The NRC staff considers the guidance in this RG to provide an acceptable method for developing and implementing a CVAP for reactor internals at nuclear power plants. In particular, the applicant or licensee should apply the classifications identified in Section C.1 to categorize reactor internals according to design, operating parameters, and operating experience. The applicant or licensee should establish an appropriate CVAP using the guidance in Sections C.2, C.3, and C.4, as they relate to the specific classifications of the applicable reactor internals.

This RG describes acceptable methods for evaluating the potential adverse effects from FIV, AR, AIV, and MIV. Section C.2 of this RG provides detailed information for these vibration mechanisms. These vibration excitation mechanisms need to be assessed for reactor internals in BWR, PWR, and SMR nuclear power plants.

...

Reactor internals are designed to accommodate steady-state and transient vibratory loads throughout the service life of the reactor. The overall program includes predictive analysis, a measurement program, and an inspection program. The term “comprehensive” appears in the title of the overall program to emphasize that these individual elements are used together to verify structural integrity of the reactor internals (including BWR steam dryers):

• The predictive analysis provides theoretical verification of structural integrity and the basis for the choice of components and specific locations to be monitored in the measurement and inspection programs.

• The measurement program confirms the results of the predictive analyses. However, the measurements (i.e., data acquisition, reduction, and interpretation processes) need to be sufficiently flexible and sensitive to permit identification and definition of any significant excitation mechanisms and vibration that are present but were not evaluated in the predictive program.

• The inspection program addresses both quantitative and qualitative verification of the predictive analysis and measurement program results.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating core bypass flow in reactor pressure vessel internals?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating core bypass flow in reactor pressure vessel internals are grounded in ensuring the structural integrity and safety function of reactor internals under all operating conditions, including those affected by core bypass flow. According to SRP 3.9.5 (Section II), the design and construction of core support structures should comply with Subsection NG of the ASME BPV Code as incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a, though use of Subsection NG is not mandated but considered an acceptable method for meeting NRC requirements, specifically 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 1. Applicants must identify and justify any deviations from these criteria.

The acceptance criteria require that:
- The design criteria, loading conditions, and analyses for reactor internals must meet the guidelines of NG-3000 and not adversely affect the integrity of core support structures (SRP 3.9.5, Item 3).
- Deformation limits for reactor internals must be established and justified by the applicant, ensuring that stresses from displacements do not exceed specified limits (SRP 3.9.5, Item 4).
- The design must accommodate asymmetric loads, such as those from postulated pipe ruptures, and demonstrate that these loads do not exceed code and standard limits (SRP 3.9.5, Item 5).

SRP 3.9.3 further specifies that loading combinations, system operating transients, and stress limits must be defined for core support structures, and their acceptability is judged by comparison with NRC positions and appropriate standards (SRP 3.9.3, II.1).

Dynamic response analyses, including those for flow-induced vibration (FIV) and other flow excitation mechanisms relevant to core bypass flow, must be performed as described in SRP 3.9.2 and RG 1.20. These analyses must verify that vibration and stress levels remain within justified safety margins and acceptance criteria (SRP 3.9.2, Item 3; RG 1.20, Section C).

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria for core bypass flow evaluation require compliance with quality standards (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 1), adherence to ASME BPV Code guidance (Subsection NG), establishment and justification of deformation and stress limits, and comprehensive dynamic analyses to ensure structural integrity under all relevant loading conditions.

evidence_chain.section: II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
SRP Acceptance Criteria
Specific SRP acceptance criteria acceptable to meet the relevant requirements of the NRC’s regulations identified above are as follows for the review described in this SRP section.  The SRP is not a substitute for the NRC’s regulations, and compliance with it is not required.  However, an applicant is required to identify differences between the design features, analytical techniques, and procedural measures proposed for its facility and the SRP acceptance criteria and evaluate how the proposed alternatives to the SRP acceptance criteria provide acceptable methods of compliance with the NRC regulations.  
1. Provisions for loads, loading combinations, and limits applicable to those portions of reactor internals constructed to Subsection NG, “Core Support Structures,” of the ASME BPV Code as incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a are discussed in SRP Section 3.9.3.   
2. The design and construction of the core support structures should comply with the provisions of Subsection NG of the ASME BPV Code as incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a.  In the Federal Register notice providing the final rule to amend the regulations to incorporate by reference the ASME BPV Codes and new and revised ASME BPV Code cases dated June 21, 2011 (76 FRN 36323), the NRC clarified that Subsection NG is incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a, but is not mandated.  Therefore, Subsection NG is not an NRC requirement.  Rather, the NRC considers Subsection NG to be approved for use by applicants and licensees of nuclear power plants by virtue of the NRC’s overall approval of Section III, Division 1 rules without condition.  In this manner, approval of Subsection NG is similar to regulatory guidance provided in RGs in that it provides an acceptable method for meeting NRC requirements and, in this particular case, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 1.  An applicant may propose means other than those specified by the provisions in Subsection NG for meeting the applicable regulations.   
3. The design criteria, loading conditions, and analyses that provide the bases for the design of reactor internals other than the core support structures should meet the guidelines of NG-3000 and be constructed not to affect the integrity of the core support structures adversely (NG-1122).  If other guidelines (e.g., manufacturer standards or empirical methods based on field experience and testing) are the bases for the stress, deformation, and fatigue criteria, those guidelines should be identified and their use justified.
4. Deformation limits for reactor internals should be established by the applicant and presented in the safety analysis report.  The basis for these limits should be included.  The stresses induced by these displacements should not exceed the specified limits.  The provisions for dynamic analysis of these components are addressed in SRP Section 3.9.2.
5. The reactor internals should be designed to accommodate asymmetric blowdown loads from postulated pipe ruptures.  The applicant's evaluation of such loads should demonstrate that they do not exceed the limits imposed by the applicable codes and standards.  Where double-ended guillotine break of reactor coolant piping is postulated, criteria for evaluating loading transients and structural components are specified in NUREG-0609.  SRP Section 3.6.2 provides additional guidance on transient and dynamic loading effects from postulated pipe ruptures.

evidence_chain.section: I. AREAS OF REVIEW, Item 3 (Dynamic Response Analysis of Reactor Internals)
evidence_chain.evidence_text: 3. Analyses of dynamic responses of structural components within the reactor vessel caused by steady-state and operational flow transient conditions, including all fluctuating loading induced by flow, acoustic, or mechanical sources, are reviewed to confirm that they are consistent with the approach described in RG 1.20, “Comprehensive Vibration Assessment Program for Reactor Internals during Preoperational and Initial Startup Testing,” Revision 4. For example, reviews are conducted of analyses required for prototype, limited prototype, and nonprototype plants and components (such as steam dryers in boiling water reactor [BWR] nuclear power plants), and for operating plants requesting a power uprate, or replacing a reactor internal component. ... The purpose of the analyses is to assess the vibration behavior of the components, including the definition of the input-forcing functions, and estimation of the consequent vibration and alternating stress levels. The analyses should verify the structural integrity of reactor internals for flow-induced vibration (FIV), acoustic resonance (AR), acoustic-induced vibration (AIV), and mechanical-induced vibration (MIV). Flow excitation mechanisms such as vortex-induced vibration, flow-excited acoustic resonance, fluid-elastic instability, and turbulence buffeting as well as other flow excitations of flow separation, reattachment, and impinging flow instabilities should be considered. ... The following areas related to the dynamic response analysis are reviewed along with their bias errors and uncertainties. For more details on NRC guidance to applicants, refer to RG 1.20, Revision 4, Section C.2. ... C. Results of vibration and stress calculations. The calculated vibration and stress levels of reactor internal structures are reviewed with their safety margins and acceptance criteria. The procedures for combining the vibration and stress response models (Item 3.A above) with the forcing functions (Item 3.B above) to compute overall vibration and stress response are also reviewed. The results for structures and components with a history of failures from adverse flow effects (such as steam dryers excited by flow instabilities over the openings of valve standoff pipes) are evaluated in greater detail. In particular, the following items are reviewed: (i) Chosen locations for vibration and stress calculations, and any locations where instrumentation will be installed for subsequent power ascension testing; along with the choice of analysis approach (time or frequency domain) and the acceptability of damping modeling (such as the Rayleigh damping method used for time domain calculations). (ii) Benchmarking of analysis methodologies, particularly end-to-end benchmarking using previous testing on valid prototypes. (iii) Stress convergence and high-cycle fatigue evaluation, particularly structural model development, application of dynamic loads to the structural model, and fatigue analysis of two-sided fillet welds. (iv) Vibration and stress limits and their justification. For further details, refer to RG 1.20, Revision 4, Section C.2.1.3.

data.query: How do general design criteria for structural integrity and protection against natural phenomena apply to the design and function of reactor pressure vessel internals, specifically regarding the transfer of mechanical and seismic loads?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for structural integrity and protection against natural phenomena, as specified in 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A (GDC 1, 2, and 4), require that reactor pressure vessel (RPV) internals be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety functions (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1; SRP 3.9.5; RG 1.20). Specifically, GDC 2 mandates that these components be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena such as earthquakes, while GDC 4 requires accommodation of environmental and dynamic effects, including those from normal operation, maintenance, testing, and postulated accidents (SRP 3.9.5; RG 1.20).

In application, these criteria mean that the design of RPV internals must account for all relevant mechanical and seismic loads, including those from normal operation, anticipated operational occurrences, adverse flow effects, postulated accidents (e.g., loss-of-coolant accidents), and seismic events (SRP 3.9.5; SRP 3.9.2; SRP 3.9.3). The NRC review process evaluates the physical arrangement, retention, and support of internals, as well as their ability to accommodate dimensional changes due to thermal and other effects (SRP 3.9.5). All combinations of design and service loadings must be identified and analyzed, with stresses compared against code-allowable limits (SRP 3.9.5; SRP 3.9.3).

Dynamic analyses, including those for flow-induced, acoustic, and mechanical vibrations, are required to verify that the internals can withstand vibratory and seismic loads without loss of function (SRP 3.9.2; RG 1.20). These analyses must confirm the adequacy of the structural design under combined accident and seismic conditions (e.g., LOCA plus safe-shutdown earthquake) (SRP 3.9.2). The use of recognized codes and standards, such as the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, is required, and where such codes do not exist, alternative criteria must ensure structural integrity and safety function (SRP 3.9.3).

In summary, the GDC ensure that RPV internals are robustly designed to transfer and withstand mechanical and seismic loads, maintaining structural integrity and safety functions under all credible conditions, as verified through predictive analysis, measurement, and inspection programs (SRP 3.9.5; RG 1.20).

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) regulations in Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) Part 50, “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities,” Appendix A, “General Design Criteria (GDC) for Nuclear Plants,” GDC 1, “Quality Standards and Records,” GDC 2, “Design Bases for Protection against Natural Phenomena,” GDC 4, "Environmental and Dynamic Effects Design Bases," and GDC 10, "Reactor Design,"; 10 CFR 50.55a, “General Provisions”; and 10 CFR Part 52, “Licenses, Certifications, and Approvals for Nuclear Power Plants”; require that structures and components important to safety be constructed and tested to quality standards commensurate with the importance of the safety functions performed and designed with appropriate margins to withstand effects of anticipated operational occurrences and normal operation, natural phenomena such as earthquakes, postulated accidents including loss-of-coolant accidents (LOCAs), and events and conditions outside the nuclear power unit.

... The staff’s review includes consideration of the design input parameters and the design basis loads and load combinations for plant components for normal operation, upset, emergency, and faulted conditions. The review also addresses the analytical methodologies, assumptions, the code, and code edition for the evaluation of the plant components. The review also includes a comparison of stresses against code allowable limits. The specific areas of review are as follows:

1. The physical or design arrangements of all reactor internals structures, components, assemblies, and systems, are evaluated including the positioning and securing of such items within the RPV, the provision for axial and lateral retention and support of the internals assemblies and components, and the accommodation of dimensional changes due to thermal and other effects.
2. The basis for the reactor internals’ design loading conditions for normal operation, anticipated operational occurrences, potential adverse flow effects, postulated accidents, and seismic events are evaluated. All combinations of design and service loadings (e.g., operating differential pressure and thermal effects, adverse flow effects, seismic loads, and transient pressure loads of postulated LOCAs) addressed in the design of the reactor internals should be listed. The distribution of the design and service loadings acting on the internal components and structures should be described. The analytical or experimental methods for determining the loading conditions and their validation should be described along with their random uncertainties and bias errors.

data.query: What are the regulatory expectations for the nomenclature and identification of core support structures, such as core plates and core support plates, in the context of reactor pressure vessel internal design reviews?
data.answer:
The regulatory expectations for the nomenclature and identification of core support structures, such as core plates and core support plates, in the context of reactor pressure vessel (RPV) internal design reviews are grounded in several key NRC documents and referenced codes. According to SRP 3.9.5, 'reactor internals' explicitly include core support structures and other internal elements within the RPV for BWRs, PWRs, and SMRs. The design and construction of these core support structures must comply with Subsection NG of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, as incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a. The nomenclature and identification of these structures should be consistent with the definitions provided in Article NG-1120 of Section III of the ASME BPV Code (SRP 3.9.5; RG 1.20, Section B).

Regulatory guidance (RG 1.20, SRP 3.9.2) provides specific examples of core support structures, such as the 'core plate' for BWRs and 'upper core support assembly' and 'lower core support assembly' for PWRs. These terms are used consistently across NRC documents and are expected to be used by applicants in their Safety Analysis Reports (SARs) to ensure clarity and traceability. The NRC staff reviews the configuration and general arrangement of all mechanical and structural internal elements, comparing them to those of previously licensed plants to ensure consistency in nomenclature and identification (SRP 3.9.5).

Furthermore, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety—including core support structures—be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards, with appropriate records maintained. This includes clear identification and documentation of all core support structures throughout the life of the unit. SRP 3.9.3 reinforces that the design and service limits for core support structures must be clearly defined and documented, and that the nomenclature used should align with the ASME Code and NRC guidance to facilitate regulatory review and ensure compliance.

In summary, regulatory expectations require that core support structures be clearly identified and named in accordance with ASME BPV Code definitions and NRC guidance, with consistent terminology used in all design and licensing documentation to support effective review and compliance.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for the structural support and deadweight loading of reactor pressure vessel internals during maintenance and refueling operations?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for the structural support and deadweight loading of reactor pressure vessel internals during maintenance and refueling operations are grounded in several regulatory and guidance documents. According to SRP 3.9.5 (Section II), the design and construction of core support structures should comply with Subsection NG of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, as incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a, though its use is not mandated but considered an acceptable method for meeting NRC requirements (SRP 3.9.5, II.2). For reactor internals other than core support structures, the design criteria, loading conditions, and analyses should meet the guidelines of NG-3000 and ensure they do not adversely affect the integrity of the core support structures (SRP 3.9.5, II.3). If alternative guidelines are used, their basis and justification must be provided.

Deformation limits for reactor internals must be established by the applicant, justified, and documented in the safety analysis report, ensuring that stresses from deadweight and other loads do not exceed specified limits (SRP 3.9.5, II.4). The acceptance criteria also require that loading combinations, including deadweight and maintenance/refueling loads, and associated stress limits, are defined and justified for all conditions (SRP 3.9.3, II.1). These criteria are judged against the requirements of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 1 and 4, which mandate quality standards and the ability to accommodate environmental and operational effects, including those during maintenance and refueling (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1; RG 1.20, Section A).

In summary, the NRC expects applicants to (1) define and justify all relevant loads and stress limits, (2) ensure compliance with or provide justification for alternatives to ASME BPV Code Subsection NG, (3) establish and justify deformation limits, and (4) demonstrate, through analysis and documentation, that the structural integrity of reactor internals is maintained during maintenance and refueling operations.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
SRP Acceptance Criteria
Specific SRP acceptance criteria acceptable to meet the relevant requirements of the NRC’s regulations identified above are as follows for the review described in this SRP section.  The SRP is not a substitute for the NRC’s regulations, and compliance with it is not required.  However, an applicant is required to identify differences between the design features, analytical techniques, and procedural measures proposed for its facility and the SRP acceptance criteria and evaluate how the proposed alternatives to the SRP acceptance criteria provide acceptable methods of compliance with the NRC regulations.  
1. Provisions for loads, loading combinations, and limits applicable to those portions of reactor internals constructed to Subsection NG, “Core Support Structures,” of the ASME BPV Code as incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a are discussed in SRP Section 3.9.3.   
2. The design and construction of the core support structures should comply with the provisions of Subsection NG of the ASME BPV Code as incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a.  In the Federal Register notice providing the final rule to amend the regulations to incorporate by reference the ASME BPV Codes and new and revised ASME BPV Code cases dated June 21, 2011 (76 FRN 36323), the NRC clarified that Subsection NG is incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a, but is not mandated.  Therefore, Subsection NG is not an NRC requirement.  Rather, the NRC considers Subsection NG to be approved for use by applicants and licensees of nuclear power plants by virtue of the NRC’s overall approval of Section III, Division 1 rules without condition.  In this manner, approval of Subsection NG is similar to regulatory guidance provided in RGs in that it provides an acceptable method for meeting NRC requirements and, in this particular case, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 1.  An applicant may propose means other than those specified by the provisions in Subsection NG for meeting the applicable regulations.   
3. The design criteria, loading conditions, and analyses that provide the bases for the design of reactor internals other than the core support structures should meet the guidelines of NG-3000 and be constructed not to affect the integrity of the core support structures adversely (NG-1122).  If other guidelines (e.g., manufacturer standards or empirical methods based on field experience and testing) are the bases for the stress, deformation, and fatigue criteria, those guidelines should be identified and their use justified.
4. Deformation limits for reactor internals should be established by the applicant and presented in the safety analysis report.  The basis for these limits should be included.  The stresses induced by these displacements should not exceed the specified limits.  The provisions for dynamic analysis of these components are addressed in SRP Section 3.9.2.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for allowable stress limits applied to reactor pressure vessel internals under service level D conditions?
data.answer: The NRC acceptance criteria for allowable stress limits applied to reactor pressure vessel internals under Service Level D (faulted) conditions are grounded in the requirements of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, Section III, Subsection NG, as referenced in 10 CFR 50.55a and detailed in NRC guidance documents. Specifically, for core support structures, the allowable stress limits under Service Level D conditions are those specified in ASME BPV Code, Section III, Subsection NG-3225 (RG 1.20, Section C.2.1.3.2; SRP 3.9.5, II.1-3). The applicant or licensee must demonstrate that computed stresses do not exceed these limits and that the analysis methodology is robust, including stress convergence and high-cycle fatigue evaluation (RG 1.20, C.2.1.3.2; SRP 3.9.2, II.C). For reactor internals other than core support structures, the design criteria should meet the guidelines of NG-3000 and not adversely affect the integrity of the core support structures (SRP 3.9.5, II.3). If alternative guidelines or methods are used, their basis and justification must be provided (SRP 3.9.5, II.3). The NRC considers compliance with Subsection NG an acceptable method for meeting regulatory requirements, but alternatives may be proposed if justified (SRP 3.9.5, II.2; 10 CFR 50.55a(b)(4)). In summary, the acceptance criteria require that allowable stress limits for Service Level D are those in ASME BPV Code, Section III, Subsection NG-3225 for core support structures, with supporting fatigue evaluations per NG-3222.4(e), and that any deviations or alternative methods be justified and documented.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory requirements for service level categorization relate to the selection of allowable stress limits for reactor pressure vessel internals during postulated reactivity accidents?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory requirements for service level categorization are directly related to the selection of allowable stress limits for reactor pressure vessel internals during postulated reactivity accidents. According to SRP 3.9.5 (Section II), the acceptance criteria for reactor internals are based on compliance with General Design Criterion (GDC) 1 and 10 CFR 50.55a, which require that reactor internals be designed and constructed to quality standards commensurate with their safety function importance. Specifically, for core support structures, the design must comply with Subsection NG of the ASME BPV Code as referenced in 10 CFR 50.55a, and the applicable loads, loading combinations, and stress limits are discussed in SRP 3.9.3.

SRP 3.9.3 (Section II) further clarifies that the design and service loading combinations, including those from postulated reactivity accidents, must be defined for each component and its supports. The appropriate service level categorization (e.g., Service Levels A, B, C, D) determines the allowable stress limits for each loading combination, and these are judged by comparison with the positions stated in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50 and with recognized codes and standards. Where no specific code criteria exist for certain internal parts, the design criteria must ensure structural integrity so that safety-related functions are not impaired.

In summary, the NRC requires that the service level categorization of reactor internals, which reflects the severity and frequency of postulated events (such as reactivity accidents), be used to select the appropriate allowable stress limits as defined by applicable codes (e.g., ASME BPV Code) and regulatory guidance. This ensures that the internals maintain their safety functions under all postulated loading conditions, including those arising from reactivity accidents, in accordance with the quality standards and safety significance outlined in GDC 1 and 10 CFR 50.55a.

data.query: When evaluating the structural integrity of reactor pressure vessel internals during a rod ejection accident, how do NRC regulatory provisions from general design criteria, review standards, and regulatory guides collectively determine the appropriate service level classification and corresponding allowable stress limits?
data.answer:
The evaluation of the structural integrity of reactor pressure vessel internals during a rod ejection accident is governed by a combination of NRC general design criteria, review standards, and regulatory guides, which collectively determine the appropriate service level classification and corresponding allowable stress limits.

General Design Criteria (GDC) from 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, specifically GDC 1, 2, 4, and 10, require that reactor internals be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety functions, and be capable of withstanding normal, upset, emergency, and faulted conditions, including postulated accidents such as rod ejection (SRP 3.9.5, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1). These criteria mandate the use of recognized codes and standards, such as the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (BPV Code), and require that the adequacy of these codes be evaluated for applicability and sufficiency (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1).

The Standard Review Plan (SRP) Sections 3.9.3 and 3.9.5 provide detailed acceptance criteria for load combinations and stress limits. They specify that each combination of design and service loadings must be categorized by allowable design or service limits as defined in the ASME BPV Code (SRP 3.9.5, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA; SRP 3.9.3, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA). For a rod ejection accident, which is considered a faulted condition, the relevant service level is typically Service Level D, corresponding to faulted conditions in the ASME BPV Code. The stress limits for this service level are those specified in the Code for such conditions, ensuring that the structural integrity of the internals is maintained and safety functions are not impaired (SRP 3.9.5; SRP 3.9.3).

Regulatory Guide 1.20 and SRP 3.9.2 further require dynamic analyses to confirm that reactor internals can withstand accident-induced loads, including those from rod ejection, without loss of function. These analyses must demonstrate compliance with the vibration and stress limits justified by the ASME BPV Code and NRC guidance (RG 1.20, C.1; SRP 3.9.2, I. AREAS OF REVIEW).

In summary, NRC regulatory provisions require that the service level classification for a rod ejection accident be based on the ASME BPV Code (typically Service Level D for faulted conditions), and that allowable stress limits be those defined in the Code for such conditions, as verified through dynamic analysis and comparison with NRC acceptance criteria (SRP 3.9.5, SRP 3.9.3, RG 1.20, 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A).

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for deformation limits of reactor pressure vessel internals to ensure safety functions are maintained under all service level conditions?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for deformation limits of reactor pressure vessel internals are established to ensure that safety functions are maintained under all service level conditions. According to SRP 3.9.5, Section II, applicants must define deformation limits for reactor internals in the safety analysis report, providing the basis for these limits. The induced stresses from such deformations must not exceed specified limits, and the applicant must demonstrate that deflections will not interfere with the function of related components (e.g., control rods, standby cooling systems), with stresses remaining below the limits for core support structures (SRP 3.9.5, Section III.4).

The regulatory basis, as outlined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed and tested to quality standards that ensure the required safety functions are maintained. This includes the use of recognized codes and standards, such as the ASME BPV Code, and the implementation of a quality assurance program.

RG 1.20, Sections C.2.1.3.2 and C.2.1.3.3, further specify that computed stresses in reactor internals must be within allowable limits for all service level conditions, as defined by the ASME BPV Code, Section III. For high-cycle fatigue, the cumulative usage factor at each location must be less than 1.0, per ASME BPV Code requirements. Vibration and stress levels must not exceed allowable limits, and vibration amplitudes must be low enough to prevent impact, fretting, or wear that could compromise safety functions.

Cross-references in SRP 3.9.2 and 3.9.3 reinforce that vibration and stress calculations, including deformation limits, must be justified and benchmarked, and that deformation limits for component supports must be compatible with operational readiness requirements and incorporated into the functionality assurance and seismic qualification program.

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria require that deformation limits for reactor pressure vessel internals be established based on analysis, justified against applicable codes (primarily ASME BPV Code), and demonstrated not to impair safety functions under all service level conditions.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for the classification and design requirements of reactor pressure vessel internal supports?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for the classification and design requirements of reactor pressure vessel internal supports are grounded in several regulatory requirements and guidance documents. According to SRP 3.9.5 (Section II), reactor internals, including internal supports, must be designed, fabricated, erected, tested, and inspected to quality standards commensurate with their safety function importance, as required by General Design Criterion (GDC) 1 and 10 CFR 50.55a. The design must ensure the ability to withstand natural phenomena (GDC 2), accommodate environmental and accident conditions (GDC 4), and maintain appropriate margins to prevent exceeding fuel design limits during normal and anticipated operational occurrences (GDC 10).

For core support structures, compliance with Subsection NG of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, as referenced in 10 CFR 50.55a, is required (SRP 3.9.5, SRP 3.9.3). Other reactor internals must meet the guidelines of NG-3000 and not adversely affect the integrity of core support structures (NG-1122). Where alternative guidelines are used, their basis must be identified and justified.

Dynamic response analyses must be performed to assess vibration and stress levels, ensuring structural integrity under flow-induced, acoustic, and mechanical vibration mechanisms (SRP 3.9.2; RG 1.20, Section C.2). data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for the classification and design standards of reactor pressure vessel internals?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for the classification and design standards of reactor pressure vessel (RPV) internals are primarily established in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criteria (GDC), and 10 CFR 50.55a, as well as detailed in the Standard Review Plan (SRP) Sections 3.9.3 and 3.9.5.

RPV internals, which include all structural and mechanical elements inside the reactor vessel, must be designed, fabricated, erected, tested, and inspected to quality standards commensurate with the importance of their safety functions (SRP 3.9.5; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 1; 10 CFR 50.55a). The design must ensure that these components can withstand the effects of normal operation, anticipated operational occurrences, natural phenomena (such as earthquakes), and postulated accidents, including loss-of-coolant accidents (LOCAs), without loss of safety function (SRP 3.9.5; GDC 2, GDC 4).

Specifically, core support structures within the RPV internals must comply with Subsection NG, 'Core Support Structures,' of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code as incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a (SRP 3.9.5). Other RPV internals should meet the guidelines of NG-3000 and must not adversely affect the integrity of the core support structures (SRP 3.9.5). If alternative standards or empirical methods are used, their applicability and adequacy must be justified (SRP 3.9.5).

The classification of components (Code Class 1, 2, or 3) and the associated design and service stress limits must be defined for all conditions, and the acceptability of loading combinations and stress limits is judged by comparison with NRC positions and recognized standards (SRP 3.9.3). A quality assurance program must be established and maintained throughout the life of the unit, with appropriate records kept (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 1).

In summary, NRC regulations require that RPV internals be classified and designed according to their safety significance, using recognized codes and standards (primarily the ASME BPV Code), and be capable of performing their safety functions under all credible conditions.
