data.query: When qualifying nonmetallic parts of active mechanical equipment for safety-related functions in nuclear power plants, how should regulatory requirements for environmental qualification, general design criteria, and NRC-endorsed industry standards be integrated to ensure compliance in both harsh and mild environments?
data.answer:
To ensure compliance when qualifying nonmetallic parts of active mechanical equipment for safety-related functions in nuclear power plants, regulatory requirements for environmental qualification (EQ), general design criteria, and NRC-endorsed industry standards must be integrated as follows:

1. General Design Criteria: Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, specifically General Design Criterion (GDC) 4, requires that safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) be designed to withstand the most severe environmental and dynamic effects postulated for their location, including temperature, pressure, humidity, radiation, chemical effects, and submergence (10 CFR Part 50, App. A, GDC 4).

2. Environmental Qualification: For equipment in harsh environments, compliance with GDC 4 is demonstrated by showing that nonmetallic parts can perform their safety functions under postulated design-basis environmental conditions. For mild environments, compliance is achieved by incorporating all relevant environmental conditions into the design and equipment specifications (DSRS 3.11, Sections I & II).

3. Quality Assurance: Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 50 requires a QA program to ensure that all safety-related SSCs, including nonmetallic parts, are designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function (DSRS 3.11; 10 CFR Part 50, App. B).

4. NRC-Endorsed Industry Standards: NRC Regulatory Guides (RGs) endorse specific industry standards as acceptable methods for meeting regulatory requirements. For nonmetallic parts of active mechanical equipment, RG 1.100 endorses ASME QME-1-2017, including Nonmandatory Appendix QR-B, which provides guidance for qualification of nonmetallic parts. Use of these standards, as endorsed in RGs, is considered acceptable for demonstrating compliance (RG 1.100, Section C; DSRS 3.11).

5. Integration: Licensees should use NRC-endorsed standards (e.g., ASME QME-1-2017 per RG 1.100) to guide qualification activities, ensuring that all environmental and functional requirements from GDC 4 and QA requirements from Appendix B are met. If a standard is not endorsed, its use must be justified and consistent with regulatory practice (DSRS 3.11; RG 1.53).

In summary, compliance is achieved by designing and qualifying nonmetallic parts per GDC 4 and QA requirements, using NRC-endorsed standards such as ASME QME-1-2017, and ensuring all relevant environmental conditions are addressed for both harsh and mild environments.

data.query: What are the NRC requirements for establishing an environmental qualification operational program for mechanical and electrical equipment in nuclear power plants?
data.answer: The NRC requires nuclear power plant licensees to establish an environmental qualification (EQ) operational program for both mechanical and electrical equipment important to safety, ensuring these items can perform their safety functions under all normal, anticipated, and accident environmental conditions. According to DSRS 3.11, the program must demonstrate that all safety-important equipment (mechanical, electrical, and I&C, including digital) is capable of functioning during normal operation, anticipated operational occurrences, and postulated accidents, in accordance with the environmental design-basis requirements of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 4. For electrical equipment in harsh environments, 10 CFR 50.49 specifically requires licensees to: (1) identify safety-important electric equipment in harsh environments; (2) establish and maintain an EQ program that documents qualification, maintains qualification, ensures replacement with qualified equipment, and maintains records; and (3) ensure equipment remains functional to maintain reactor coolant pressure boundary integrity, safe shutdown capability, and accident mitigation. For mechanical equipment, compliance with GDC 4 is generally demonstrated by showing nonmetallic parts are suitable for design-basis environmental conditions. The EQ program must be described in the FSAR and implemented as part of the plant’s operational programs, with milestones tracked per FSAR Section 13.4. Additionally, Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 50 requires a quality assurance program to ensure SSCs perform their safety functions satisfactorily. For accident monitoring instrumentation, RG 1.97 provides acceptable methods for qualification, referencing IEEE Std. 497-2016 for accident monitoring variables, and requires documentation of the program’s basis and any updates or modifications. In summary, the NRC’s requirements are grounded in 10 CFR 50.49, GDC 4, Appendix B, and associated regulatory guidance, and require a documented, maintained, and quality-assured EQ operational program for both mechanical and electrical safety equipment.

data.query: How should surveillance and preventive maintenance activities be determined for environmentally qualified equipment according to NRC regulatory standards, and how do these activities relate to maintaining equipment qualification over time?
data.answer:
According to NRC regulatory standards, surveillance and preventive maintenance activities for environmentally qualified (EQ) equipment must be determined and implemented as part of a comprehensive program to maintain equipment qualification throughout its installed life. Specifically, 10 CFR 50.49(e) requires that each item of electric equipment important to safety, which has been environmentally qualified, must be maintained in its qualified state during its operational life. To achieve this, licensees are required to establish a program that includes: (i) a schedule for periodic inspections, tests, or preventive maintenance to ensure the equipment remains capable of performing its safety function under design basis accident conditions; (ii) provisions for replacement or refurbishment of equipment as necessary to maintain qualification; (iii) review of operating experience, including failures, malfunctions, and degradations, to assess if qualification has been compromised; and (iv) maintenance of records of qualification and maintenance activities for the installed life of the equipment (10 CFR 50.49(e)).

The DSRS 3.11 further clarifies that these requirements are grounded in the quality assurance provisions of Appendix A and Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 50, which mandate that safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards, and that a QA program be established to ensure ongoing performance of safety functions. Regulatory Guide 1.89 and IEEE Std. 323-1974 provide additional guidance on implementing these requirements, emphasizing that environmental qualification is only acceptable when it can be demonstrated that these ongoing maintenance and surveillance activities are effectively performed.

In summary, surveillance and preventive maintenance activities must be systematically scheduled and documented to ensure that EQ equipment continues to meet its qualification requirements, thereby maintaining its ability to perform safety functions over time.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for maintaining environmental qualification of mechanical and electrical equipment throughout their installed lifetime in a nuclear power plant?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for maintaining environmental qualification (EQ) of mechanical and electrical equipment throughout their installed lifetime in a nuclear power plant are established primarily in 10 CFR Part 50, including Appendix A (General Design Criteria) and 10 CFR 50.49, as well as associated regulatory guidance documents.

According to DSRS 3.11 and 10 CFR 50.49, licensees must establish and maintain an EQ program for electric equipment important to safety that is located in a 'harsh' environment. This program must:
- Identify all electric equipment important to safety in harsh environments (10 CFR 50.49(a)(1)).
- Document the qualification of this equipment, including qualification methods, test results, analyses, and other relevant information (10 CFR 50.49(a)(2)).
- Maintain the qualified status of equipment throughout its installed life by ensuring replacement equipment is qualified, qualified life is not exceeded, and significant aging effects are managed (10 CFR 50.49(a)(3)).
- Control design changes, modifications, and repairs to ensure continued qualification (10 CFR 50.49(a)(4)).
- Maintain records sufficient to demonstrate compliance (10 CFR 50.49(a)(5)).

For both mechanical and electrical equipment important to safety, Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50 requires that such equipment be capable of performing its safety functions under all anticipated operational occurrences and accident environments for the required duration (DSRS 3.11, Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50). Appendix B requires a quality assurance program to ensure these requirements are met.

Regulatory guides such as RG 1.97 and RG 1.100 endorse industry standards (e.g., IEEE Std. 497-2016, IEEE Std. 344-2013, ASME QME-1-2017) as acceptable methods for qualification and ongoing assurance of equipment performance under environmental and seismic conditions. These standards provide detailed methods for qualification testing, analysis, and documentation, as well as requirements for maintaining qualification through the equipment’s operational life (RG 1.100, Section C).

In summary, NRC regulations require that safety-related mechanical and electrical equipment be qualified for their environment, that qualification be maintained throughout their installed life, and that adequate records and quality assurance measures be in place to demonstrate ongoing compliance.

data.query: How do NRC regulations require the integration of vendor recommendations and operating experience into the surveillance and preventive maintenance activities for environmentally qualified equipment?
data.answer:
NRC regulations explicitly require the integration of vendor recommendations and operating experience into the surveillance and preventive maintenance activities for environmentally qualified (EQ) equipment. According to 10 CFR 50.49(e), licensees must establish and implement a program to ensure that the qualified condition of electric equipment important to safety is maintained throughout its installed life. This program must include provisions for maintenance, inspection, and testing, as well as the evaluation of changes in equipment design, qualification methods, or plant environmental conditions. Critically, section 50.49(e)(2)(iv) specifically mandates that vendor recommendations and operating experience be considered in the development and implementation of maintenance and surveillance activities necessary to ensure the qualified condition of the equipment.

Additionally, DSRS 3.11 reinforces the importance of incorporating operating experience into the EQ process. It references IEEE Std. 323-1974, which requires consideration of the service environment and installed configuration as part of qualification. The DSRS cites operating experience (e.g., NRC Information Notice 89-63) to illustrate how real-world events, such as water intrusion into electrical enclosures, must inform preventive measures and qualification requirements. This demonstrates that both vendor input and lessons learned from operating experience are integral to maintaining the qualified status of EQ equipment, as required by NRC regulations.

In summary, NRC regulations require that both vendor recommendations and operating experience are systematically integrated into the maintenance and surveillance programs for EQ equipment to ensure ongoing qualification and safety.

IEEE Std. 323 requires that the service environment, including the installed configuration of the equipment, be considered as part of the qualification process. data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for evaluating thermal stresses in piping systems connected to the reactor coolant system to ensure structural integrity?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for evaluating thermal stresses in piping systems connected to the reactor coolant system (RCS) are detailed in SRP 3.12, Section II.C, and are grounded in the quality standards of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 1. Applicants must identify and evaluate any unisolable piping connected to the RCS that could be subjected to temperature stratification or oscillation, as outlined in NRC Bulletin 88-08. If such susceptibility exists, the application must describe a program that meets the criteria of BL 88-08 to ensure ongoing assurance that unacceptable thermal stresses do not occur. 

For feedwater lines, if the design is susceptible to thermal fatigue cracking due to thermal stratification (as identified in BL 79-13), the applicant must describe an inspection program consistent with BL 79-13, Revision 2. For the pressurizer surge line, as per BL 88-11, the applicant must demonstrate that fatigue and stresses from thermal stratification and thermal striping are considered in piping analyses to ensure compliance with applicable code limits. Additionally, a monitoring program must be described to verify that thermal stratification, thermal striping, and piping deflections remain within design expectations and do not result in adverse consequences.

These requirements are underpinned by General Design Criterion 1, which mandates that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards appropriate to their safety function, with a quality assurance program and maintenance of appropriate records throughout the unit's life.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for considering friction forces in the design of piping supports in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for considering friction forces in the design of piping supports in nuclear power plants are explicitly addressed in Standard Review Plan (SRP) 3.12, Section II.D.x. This section requires that the design of sliding-type supports, such as guides or box supports, must include an evaluation of the friction loads induced by the pipe on the support, particularly during thermal expansion of the piping. The applicant is required to provide the friction coefficients used in these evaluations. This ensures that the effects of friction are properly accounted for in the structural integrity and functionality of the piping support system.

Additionally, SRP 3.9.3, Section II.3, reinforces that component support designs must provide adequate safety margins under all combinations of loadings, including those arising from system operating transients. The combination of loadings considered for each support must meet the criteria outlined in Appendix A, relevant Regulatory Guides (RG 1.124 and RG 1.130), and Subsection NF of the applicable code. This comprehensive approach ensures that all relevant forces, including those due to friction, are considered in the design and qualification of piping supports.

Furthermore, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, establishes the overarching requirement that structures, systems, and components important to safety must be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety functions. This includes the use of recognized codes and standards, supplemented as necessary to ensure quality and safety, and the maintenance of appropriate records.

In summary, the regulatory framework requires explicit evaluation and documentation of friction forces in the design of sliding-type piping supports, the use of appropriate friction coefficients, and the integration of these considerations into the overall safety and quality assurance program for nuclear power plant piping systems.

data.query: How do regulatory standards address the treatment of friction forces arising from deadweight and thermal loads versus those from dynamic or cyclic loads in the analysis of piping supports?
data.answer:
Regulatory standards distinguish between friction forces arising from deadweight and thermal loads versus those from dynamic or cyclic loads in the analysis of piping supports by requiring explicit consideration and evaluation of each type within the design process. According to SRP 3.12, Section II.D, the design of sliding-type supports (such as guides or box supports) must include evaluation of friction loads induced by the pipe on the support, particularly during thermal expansion. The applicant is required to provide the friction coefficients used in these evaluations, ensuring that friction forces from deadweight and thermal loads are properly accounted for in the support design.

Furthermore, SRP 3.12 and cross-referenced SRP 3.9.3 emphasize that piping system supports must maintain adequate safety margins under all combinations of loadings, which include both static (deadweight, thermal) and dynamic or cyclic loads (such as those from system operating transients, LOCA, and SSE events). SRP 3.9.3 further clarifies that component support designs must provide adequate margins of safety under all load combinations and that the appropriate service stress limits for each loading combination must be met, referencing applicable codes and regulatory guides.

Dynamic or cyclic loads are specifically addressed through the use of devices such as snubbers, which do not transmit loads during normal operations but act as rigid supports during dynamic events. The analysis of these supports must consider factors such as snubber end fitting clearance and load sharing, especially under dynamic loading conditions.

The regulatory basis for these requirements is established in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, which mandates that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed and tested to quality standards that ensure their safety functions are maintained under all relevant loading conditions.

In summary, regulatory standards require that friction forces from both deadweight/thermal and dynamic/cyclic loads be explicitly evaluated and incorporated into the design and analysis of piping supports, with appropriate safety margins and adherence to recognized codes and standards (SRP 3.12, SRP 3.9.3, 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A).

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for establishing limiting conditions for operation related to reactor coolant system flow rates in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for establishing limiting conditions for operation (LCOs) related to reactor coolant system (RCS) flow rates in nuclear power plants are grounded in several key documents. According to DSRS 4.4 (Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA), technical specifications must ensure safe plant operation under all expected combinations of system parameters, including coolant flow rate. Safety limits and limiting safety settings must be established for each parameter, or combinations thereof, to meet specific acceptance criteria. Uncertainties in process parameters such as coolant flow rate must be addressed with at least a 95-percent probability at the 95-percent confidence level, considering uncertainties from fabrication, computation, and measurement. The methodology for combining these uncertainties must be clearly described, and instrumentation uncertainties must be included. For example, to meet the criterion for critical heat flux (CHF) correlations, there should be a 95-percent probability at the 95-percent confidence level that the hottest fuel rod does not experience a boiling crisis during normal operation or anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs). Additionally, coolant flow should be monitored every 24 hours.

10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 10, further requires that the reactor core and associated coolant systems be designed with appropriate margin to ensure that specified acceptable fuel design limits are not exceeded during normal operation or AOOs. This includes limiting power density so the core can be adequately cooled in the event of a loss of coolant or flow. The design must also provide means for detecting and, where practical, identifying the location of coolant leakage, and the reactor coolant pressure boundary must be robust against leakage and failure.

Regulatory guidance (RG 1.68 and RG 1.29) emphasizes that systems, structures, and components (SSCs) important to safety, including the reactor coolant pressure boundary, must be tested and classified appropriately (e.g., seismic Category I) and subject to quality assurance requirements. Testing and documentation should be commensurate with the safety significance of the SSCs, and a graded approach is recommended.

In summary, LCOs for RCS flow rates must be established with rigorous consideration of uncertainties, regular monitoring, and robust design and testing requirements as specified in DSRS 4.4, 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A, RG 1.68, and RG 1.29.

data.query: What is the regulatory requirement for establishing limiting conditions for operation to ensure reactor coolant system flow rates are maintained within safety analysis bounds?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirement for establishing limiting conditions for operation (LCOs) to ensure reactor coolant system (RCS) flow rates are maintained within safety analysis bounds is grounded in both regulatory criteria and accepted methods. According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 10, the reactor core and associated coolant systems must be designed with appropriate margins to ensure that specified acceptable fuel design limits are not exceeded during normal operation and anticipated operational occurrences. This is achieved by specifying limiting conditions for operation of the reactor coolant system, including flow rates, as necessary to maintain these safety margins (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 10).

DSRS 4.4 further clarifies that technical specifications must ensure safe plant operation under all expected combinations of system parameters, including coolant flow rate. Safety limits and limiting safety settings must be established for each parameter, and uncertainties in process parameters (such as coolant flow rate) must be addressed with at least a 95-percent probability at the 95-percent confidence level. The methodology for combining uncertainties (statistical or deterministic) must be clearly described, and the origin of each uncertainty (fabrication, computational, or measurement) must be identified (DSRS 4.4, Section II).

Additionally, RG 1.68 and RG 1.160 emphasize the need for ongoing monitoring, testing, and maintenance of structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety, including those related to the RCS. Licensees are required to monitor the performance of these SSCs against established goals to provide reasonable assurance that they fulfill their intended safety functions, and to take corrective action if performance goals are not met (RG 1.160, quoting 10 CFR 50.65). Testing and documentation should be commensurate with the safety significance of the SSC (RG 1.68, Section B).

In summary, the regulatory framework requires that LCOs for RCS flow rates be established in technical specifications, account for uncertainties, and be supported by ongoing monitoring and maintenance to ensure compliance with safety analysis bounds (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 10; DSRS 4.4; RG 1.68; RG 1.160).

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for establishing conservative safety limits for critical heat flux correlations used in thermal and hydraulic design of nuclear reactors?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for establishing conservative safety limits for critical heat flux (CHF) correlations in the thermal and hydraulic design of nuclear reactors are primarily grounded in ensuring that fuel design limits are not exceeded during normal operation and anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs). According to DSRS 4.4, Section II, the specific criterion is that there must be at least a 95-percent probability at the 95-percent confidence level that the hottest fuel rod in the core does not experience a boiling crisis (i.e., departure from nucleate boiling or CHF) during these conditions. This statistical assurance must account for uncertainties in process parameters (such as reactor power, coolant flow rate, inlet temperature and pressure), core design parameters, calculational methods, and instrumentation. Each source of uncertainty—whether statistical or deterministic—must be identified, and the methodology for combining these uncertainties must be clearly described.

This approach is consistent with the regulatory basis provided by 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 10, which requires that the reactor core and associated systems be designed with appropriate margin to ensure that specified acceptable fuel design limits are not exceeded during any condition of normal operation, including AOOs. The design must ensure core cooling capability and prevent core damage during operational transients.

Additionally, RG 1.68 and SRP 14.2 emphasize that acceptance criteria and test procedures must be established and justified, with controls in place to ensure that test objectives, methods, and acceptance limits are consistent with regulatory requirements and the safety significance of the systems, structures, and components (SSCs) involved. The defense-in-depth concept requires that adequate safety margins are maintained, and that all relevant uncertainties are systematically addressed in the establishment of CHF correlations and their associated safety limits.

References: DSRS 4.4 Section II; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 10; SRP 14.2 Section II; RG 1.68 Section A.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory requirements address the impact of secondary side conditions and changes in axial flux shape on natural circulation characteristics in reactor thermal-hydraulic design?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory requirements address the impact of secondary side conditions and changes in axial flux shape on natural circulation characteristics in reactor thermal-hydraulic design through a combination of analytical, empirical, and testing-based approaches. According to DSRS 4.4 (Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA), the NRC review ensures that the thermal-hydraulic design uses acceptable analytical methods and provides adequate safety margins against fuel damage during normal operation and anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs). The analysis must account for local coolant conditions, critical heat flux (CHF), and thermal-hydraulic stability, with CHF correlations being updated to reflect changes in fuel assembly design and axial power distributions. Subchannel hydraulic analysis codes, validated by experimental data, are required to accurately model local fluid conditions, including the effects of axial power (flux) distributions and secondary side conditions such as flow and pressure losses through components like the riser and steam generator.

General Design Criterion 10 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) mandates that the reactor core and associated systems be designed with sufficient margin to ensure fuel design limits are not exceeded under all normal and anticipated conditions, implicitly requiring consideration of factors such as secondary side conditions and axial flux shape.

Furthermore, RG 1.68 and SRP 14.2 require that initial test programs (ITP) and startup testing validate analytical models and confirm that the plant responds as predicted to transients and postulated accidents. These tests must verify the adequacy of design features, including those affecting natural circulation and thermal-hydraulic performance, under a range of operating conditions. For new or unique design features, functional testing requirements and acceptance criteria must be submitted for NRC review and approval, ensuring that the impact of secondary side conditions and axial flux shape on natural circulation is adequately addressed and verified.

In summary, NRC requirements ensure that the effects of secondary side conditions and axial flux shape on natural circulation are addressed through rigorous analysis, validated by empirical data and comprehensive testing, to maintain safety margins and design integrity (DSRS 4.4, 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A GDC 10, RG 1.68, SRP 14.2).

6. Verify by trial use, to the extent practical, that the facility operating procedures and emergency procedures are adequate.   

The ITP may include system and component tests, monitoring of SSC performance, and inspection and surveillance test activities for plant SSCs.  An ITP satisfying these objectives should provide the necessary assurance that the facility can be operated in accordance with design requirements and in a manner that will not endanger the health and safety of the public.

As previously noted, the ITP consists of preoperational and initial startup tests.  “Preoperational testing,” as used in this regulatory guide, consists of those tests conducted following completion of construction inspections and tests, but before fuel loading, to demonstrate, to the extent practical, the capability of SSCs to meet the performance requirements to satisfy the design criteria.  

Initial startup testing, as used in this regulatory guide, consists of equipment performance tests completed during and after fuel loading.  These performance tests are normally completed during fuel loading, pre-critical, initial criticality, low power and power ascension phases to confirm the design bases and demonstrate, to the extent practical, that the plant will operate in accordance with design and that it is capable of responding to anticipated transients and postulated accidents as specified in the FSAR.

data.query: What is the relationship between regulatory requirements for limiting conditions for operation and the need to monitor parameters that affect energy stored in the reactor coolant system during a loss-of-coolant accident?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for limiting conditions for operation (LCOs) are closely linked to the need to monitor parameters that affect energy stored in the reactor coolant system during a loss-of-coolant accident (LOCA). According to DSRS 4.4, technical specifications must ensure safe plant operation under all expected system parameter combinations, with safety limits and settings established for each relevant parameter. Instrumentation must be provided to unambiguously indicate critical conditions, such as core cooling status, and must meet design requirements specified in the TMI Action Plan and 10 CFR 50.34(f)(2)(xviii). This instrumentation is essential for monitoring thermal-hydraulic parameters that are important to safety, including those affecting energy storage in the reactor coolant system.

General Design Criteria (GDC) 10 and 12 in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, require that the reactor core and associated systems be designed with sufficient margin to prevent exceeding fuel design limits during normal and anticipated operational occurrences, and to detect and suppress power oscillations. These criteria necessitate monitoring of parameters that could influence energy storage and release during accidents such as LOCA.

Regulatory Guides 1.68 and 1.160 further reinforce the need for monitoring. RG 1.68 states that operations, testing, and monitoring of structures, systems, and components (SSCs) must be consistent with technical specifications and 10 CFR 50.65, ensuring SSCs important to safety perform as intended during accidents. RG 1.160, quoting 10 CFR 50.65, requires monitoring the performance or condition of SSCs to provide reasonable assurance that they can fulfill their intended safety functions, including maintaining the integrity of the reactor coolant pressure boundary and mitigating accident consequences.

In summary, regulatory requirements for LCOs mandate the monitoring of parameters that affect energy stored in the reactor coolant system, as this is critical for ensuring that safety limits are not exceeded during a LOCA. This monitoring supports the detection, prevention, and mitigation of accident conditions, as required by technical specifications, general design criteria, and maintenance rules (DSRS 4.4; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 10 and 12; RG 1.68; RG 1.160).

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for the functional design of control rod drive systems in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for the functional design of control rod drive systems (CRDS) in nuclear power plants are established to ensure compliance with specific General Design Criteria (GDC) in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, as well as additional regulatory requirements. According to SRP 4.6, Section II, the CRDS must:

1. Remain functional and provide reactor shutdown capabilities under adverse environmental conditions and after postulated accidents, in accordance with GDC 4 (SRP 4.6 II.1; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4).
2. Be designed to fail in an acceptable condition under adverse conditions, preventing fuel cladding damage and excessive reactivity changes during failure, as required by GDC 23 (SRP 4.6 II.2).
3. Ensure that a single malfunction of the CRDS does not result in exceeding acceptable fuel design limits, per GDC 25 (SRP 4.6 II.3).
4. Provide sufficient operational control and reliability during reactivity changes in normal operation and anticipated operational occurrences, as required by GDC 26 (SRP 4.6 II.4).
5. In combination with the emergency core cooling system, reliably control reactivity changes to assure the capability to cool the core under accident conditions, per GDC 27 (SRP 4.6 II.5).
6. Be designed with appropriate limits on the amount and rate of reactivity increase to prevent damage to the reactor coolant pressure boundary and significant impairment of core coolability, as required by GDC 28 (SRP 4.6 II.6).
7. Ensure an extremely high probability of functioning during anticipated operational occurrences, in accordance with GDC 29 (SRP 4.6 II.7).
8. For BWRs, include an alternate rod injection system that is diverse and independent from the reactor trip system, with redundant scram air header exhaust valves, as specified in 10 CFR 50.62(c)(3) (SRP 4.6 II.8).

These criteria collectively ensure that the CRDS is robust, reliable, and capable of maintaining reactor safety under a wide range of operational and accident conditions.

evidence_chain.section: II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
Requirements
Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations: 
1. GDC 4 found in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, as it relates to the structures, systems, and components important to safety that shall be designed to accommodate the effects of and to compatible with the environmental conditions during normal plant operation as well as during postulated accidents. 
2. GDC 23, as it relates to the protection system failure modes such that the system shall fail into a safe state or into a state demonstrated to be acceptable on some other defined basis if conditions such as disconnection of system, loss of energy, or postulated adverse environment are experienced. 
3. GDC 25, as it relates to the fuel design such that the specified limits are not exceeded for any single malfunction of the reactivity control system. 
4. GDC 26, as it relates to the reactivity control system redundancy and capability such that two independent reactivity control systems of different design principles shall be provided and capable of reliably controlling reactivity changes under conditions of normal operation, including anticipated operational occurrences to assure acceptable fuel design limits are not exceeded. In addition, one of the systems must be capable of holding the reactor core subcritical under cold conditions.
5. GDC 27, as it relates to the combined reactivity control systems capability such that the reactivity control system design shall have a combined capability, in conjunction with poison addition by the emergency core cooling system to reliably control  reactivity changes to assure that under postulated accident conditions the capability to cool the core is maintained. 
6. GDC 28, as it relates to reactivity limits such that reactivity control systems shall be designed with appropriate limits on the potential amount and rate of reactivity increase to assure that the effects of postulated reactivity accidents can neither result in damage to the reactor coolant boundary nor disturb the core and its supports structures to impair significant capability to cool the core. 
7. GDC 29, as it relates to protecting system against anticipated operational occurrences such that the design of the protection and reactor control systems should assure an extremely high probability of accomplishing their safety functions in the event of anticipated operational  occurrences. 
8. 10 CFR 50.62(c)(3), as it relates to those requirements that impact the CRDS functional design.  Specifically for BWRs, the alternate rod injection system must be diverse and independent (from the reactor trip system) and must have redundant scram air header exhaust valves.

SRP Acceptance Criteria
Specific SRP acceptance criteria acceptable to meet the relevant requirements of the NRC’s regulations identified above are as follows for the review described in this SRP section.  The SRP is not a substitute for the NRC’s regulations, and compliance with it is not required. 
However, an applicant is required to identify differences between the design features, analytical techniques, and procedural measures proposed for its facility and the SRP acceptance criteria and evaluate how the proposed alternatives to the SRP acceptance criteria provide acceptable methods of compliance with the NRC regulations.   
1. To meet the requirements of GDC 4, the CRDS should remain functional and provide reactor shutdown capabilities under adverse environmental conditions and after postulated accidents.
2. To meet the requirements of GDC 23, the CRDS should fail in an acceptable condition, even under adverse conditions, that prevents damage to the fuel cladding and excessive reactivity changes during failure.  
3. To meet the requirements of GDC 25, the design of the reactivity control systems should assure that a single malfunction of the CRDS will not result in exceeding acceptable fuel design limits. 
4. To meet the requirements of GDC 26, the CRDS should be capable of providing sufficient operational control and reliability during reactivity changes during normal operation and anticipated operational occurrences. 
5. To meet the requirements of GDC 27, the combined capability of CRDS and emergency core cooling system should reliably control the reactivity changes to assure the capability to cool the core under accident conditions.
6. To meet the requirements of GDC 28, the CRDS should be designed to assure that reactivity accidents do not result in damage to the reactor coolant pressure boundary, or result in sufficient damage to the core or support structures so as to significantly impair coolability. 
7. The CRDS should be designed to ensure an extremely high probability of functioning during anticipated operational occurrences to in conformance is GDC, 29.
8. To meet the requirements of 10 CFR 50.62(c)(3), BWR plants should have an alternate rod injection system that is diverse and independent from the reactor trip system and should have redundant scram air header exhaust valves.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for control rod drop time during initial testing of the control rod drive system?
data.answer: The NRC acceptance criteria for control rod drop time during initial testing of the control rod drive system are that the measured drop time must not exceed the value assumed in the plant's safety analysis report (SAR) and technical specifications. According to RG 1.68, Appendix A, Section 5.2.4, the control rod drive system should be tested under conditions as close as practical to those expected during normal operation, including temperature, pressure, and flow conditions. The acceptance criterion is that the control rods must insert within the time assumed in the SAR for the most limiting condition. SRP 4.6 further emphasizes that required scram times must be clearly identified and consistent with technical specifications and SRP Sections 14 and 15. SRP 14.2 requires that the initial test program (ITP) include detailed acceptance criteria for control rod drop time, consistent with RG 1.68 and the SAR. Therefore, the NRC does not specify a universal numerical value for drop time; rather, the acceptance criterion is plant-specific and must match the value used in the plant's licensing basis documents (SAR and technical specifications), verified under representative operating conditions during initial testing.

data.query: How do regulatory requirements for control rod position indication accuracy relate to the acceptance criteria for control rod drive system performance during initial testing?
data.answer:
Regulatory requirements for control rod position indication accuracy are closely linked to the acceptance criteria for control rod drive system (CRDS) performance during initial testing. According to SRP 4.6, Section III (Review Procedures) and II (Acceptance Criteria), the NRC reviewers assess the functional tests of the CRDS, including rod insertion, withdrawal, and scram operations, under all required thermal-hydraulic and postulated operating conditions. The acceptance criteria are grounded in several General Design Criteria (GDC) from Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, notably GDC 4, 23, 25, and 26.

Specifically, GDC 4 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety, such as the CRDS, be designed to function under normal and accident conditions, including environmental and dynamic effects. Accurate control rod position indication is essential to verify that the CRDS can reliably perform its safety functions under these conditions.

SRP 4.6 further clarifies that acceptance criteria for initial testing must demonstrate that the CRDS meets system requirements, such as required scram times and operational reliability, consistent with technical specifications and other SRP sections. The CRDS must provide sufficient operational control and reliability during reactivity changes (GDC 26), and the position indication system must support this by accurately reflecting rod positions to ensure that fuel design limits are not exceeded (GDC 25) and that the system can fail safely (GDC 23).

In summary, control rod position indication accuracy is a critical aspect of the acceptance criteria for CRDS performance during initial testing, as it underpins the system's ability to meet regulatory requirements for safety, reliability, and operational control as specified in SRP 4.6 and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A.

When establishing acceptance criteria for the initial testing of the control rod drive system (CRDS), a licensee must integrate requirements for control rod insertion and withdrawal speeds, position indication accuracy, and individual control rod drop times by ensuring that these criteria are consistent with both regulatory requirements and technical specifications. According to SRP 4.6, Section II, acceptance criteria should be based on meeting the relevant General Design Criteria (GDC) found in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, specifically GDC 4, 23, 25, 26, 27, 28, and 29. The test program must include functional tests that verify the system's ability to meet required scram (rapid insertion) times, as well as accurate position indication and proper operation under all thermal-hydraulic and postulated operating conditions. The reviewers ensure that the system requirements, such as scram times and position indication accuracy, are clearly identified and consistent with the technical specifications and other relevant SRP sections. Experimental verification should also address single failure scenarios, such as stuck rods or accumulator leakage, to demonstrate compliance with the GDCs.

GDC 4 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) specifically requires that safety-related structures, systems, and components, including the CRDS, be designed to accommodate environmental and dynamic effects during normal and accident conditions. This underscores the need for robust acceptance criteria that ensure the CRDS will perform its safety functions under all required conditions.

In summary, the licensee should establish acceptance criteria for initial CRDS testing that explicitly verify compliance with the relevant GDCs by demonstrating required insertion and withdrawal speeds, position indication accuracy, and drop times under all applicable conditions, including single failure scenarios and environmental challenges, as outlined in SRP 4.6 and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for materials used in reactor coolant pressure boundary components?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for materials used in reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) components are established to ensure the integrity, quality, and safety of these components. The criteria are grounded in several regulatory requirements and guidance documents:

1. Regulatory Basis: The primary requirements are found in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criteria (GDC) 1, 4, 14, 30, and 31, and Appendix B, Criterion XIII, as well as 10 CFR 50.55a and Appendix G to Part 50 (SRP 5.2.3, Section II; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 1).

2. Material Specifications: Materials must comply with the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, Section III, and applicable Code Cases as described in Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.84. Acceptable materials are those listed in ASME Section III, Appendix I, or detailed in Section II, Parts A, B, and C. Code Cases must be NRC-approved and implemented per 10 CFR 50.55a (SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.84).

3. Fracture Toughness: Ferritic materials must meet fracture toughness requirements per Appendix G to 10 CFR Part 50 and Article NB-2300 of ASME Section III. This includes Charpy V-notch impact tests with acceptance standards specified in Table NB-2332(a)-1 for piping, pumps, and valves, and NB-2333 for bolting materials (SRP 5.2.3).

4. Austenitic Stainless Steels: Unstabilized austenitic stainless steels must be solution heat treated, verified for nonsensitization (ASTM A262), and protected against contaminants. Additional requirements apply to materials exposed to sensitizing temperatures, with controls on carbon content and retesting as specified in RG 1.44.

5. Weld Fabrication: Welds in low-alloy steel components must comply with ASME Sections III and IX, with specific controls on preheat and interpass temperatures, postweld heat treatment, and monitoring, as detailed in RG 1.50.

In summary, NRC acceptance criteria require RCPB materials to meet ASME Code standards, NRC-approved Code Cases, fracture toughness and corrosion resistance requirements, and specific fabrication and testing controls to ensure safety and reliability (SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.44; RG 1.50; RG 1.84; 10 CFR Part 50).

evidence_chain.section: C. REGULATORY POSITION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
C.  REGULATORY POSITION

Unstabilized, austenitic stainless steel of the AISI Type 3XX series used for components that are part of (1) the reactor coolant pressure boundary, (2) systems required for reactor shutdown, (3) systems required for emergency core cooling, and (4) reactor vessel internals that are relied on to permit adequate core cooling for any mode of normal operation or under credible postulated accident conditions should meet the following criteria:

1. Material should be suitably cleaned and suitably protected against contaminants capable of causing stress-corrosion cracking during fabrication, shipment, storage, construction, testing, and operation of components and systems.

2. Material from which components and systems are to be fabricated should be solution heat treated to produce a nonsensitized condition in the material.

3. Nonsensitization of the material should be verified using ASTM A262, Practices A or E, or another method that can be demonstrated to show nonsensitization in austenitic stainless steel. Test specimens should be selected from material subjected to each different heat treatment practice and from each heat.

4. Material subjected to sensitizing temperature in the range of 427 to 816 degrees C (800 to 1,500 degrees F), subsequent to solution heat treating in accordance with Regulatory Position 2 above and testing in accordance with Regulatory Position 3 above, should be L Grade material; that is, it should not have a carbon content greater than 0.03 percent. Exceptions are the following:

a. material exposed to pressurized water reactor coolant that has a controlled concentration of typically less than 0.020 parts per million, with a limiting value of 0.10 parts per million dissolved oxygen at all temperatures above 90 degrees C (200 degrees F) during normal operation; or

b. material in the form of castings or weld metal with a ferrite content of at least 5 percent; or

c. piping in the solution annealed condition whose exposure to temperatures in the range of 427 to 816 degrees C (800 to 1,500 degrees F) has been limited to welding operations, provided it is of sufficiently small diameter so that in the event of a credible postulated failure of the piping during normal reactor operation, the reactor can be shut down and cooled down in an orderly manner, assuming makeup is provided by the reactor coolant makeup system only.

5. Material subjected to sensitizing temperatures in the range of 427 to 816 degrees C (800 to 1,500 degrees F) during heat treating or processing other than welding, subsequent to solution heat treating in accordance with Regulatory Position 2 above and testing in accordance with Regulatory Position 3 above, should be retested in accordance with Regulatory Position 3 to demonstrate that it is not susceptible to intergranular attack, except that retest is not required for the following:

a. cast metal or weld metal with a ferrite content of 5 percent or more; or

b. material with a carbon content of 0.03 percent or less that is subjected to temperatures in the range of 427 to 816 degrees C (800 to 1,500 degrees F) for less than one hour; or

c. material exposed to special processing, provided that the processing is properly controlled to  develop a uniform product, and provided that adequate documentation exists of service experience and/or test data to demonstrate that the processing will not result in increased susceptibility to intergranular stress corrosion.

6. Welding practices and, if necessary, material composition should be controlled to avoid excessive sensitization of base metal heat-affected zones of weldments. Controls to prevent sensitization of the material during welding include maintaining low heat input and limiting the interpass temperature.

7.   An intergranular corrosion test, such as specified in Regulatory Position 3 above, should be performed for each welding procedure to be used for welding material having a carbon content greater than 0.03 percent.

evidence_chain.section: C. REGULATORY POSITION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Weld fabrication for low-alloy steel (P Nos. 3, 4, and 5A) components should comply with the fabrication requirements specified in Sections III and IX of the ASME B&PV Code, supplemented by the regulatory positions below.

1. The Welding Procedure Specification should specify a maximum interpass temperature and a minimum preheat temperature that are equal to the maximum interpass temperature and minimum preheat temperature used during procedure qualification.   

2. For production welds, the preheat temperature should be maintained until final postweld heat treatment or a post weld hydrogen bakeout is performed between 200 and 400ºC (400 and 750ºF) for a minimum of four hours after which the component may be slowly cooled to ambient temperature prior to the performance of the final post weld heat treatment. .  The postweld hydrogen bakeout temperature and soak time should be based on the materials being welded, the geometry, and the welding process used.

3. Production welding should be monitored to verify that the limits on preheat and interpass temperatures are maintained.

4. If Regulatory Positions 1, 2, and 3 above are not met, the weld is subject to rejection.  However, the soundness of the weld may be demonstrated by an acceptable examination procedure meeting the acceptance criteria specified in Section III of the ASME B&PV Code.

data.query: How do general design criteria for quality assurance and environmental compatibility apply to the selection of materials for reactor coolant pressure boundary components?
data.answer:
The general design criteria for quality assurance and environmental compatibility are fundamental to the selection of materials for reactor coolant pressure boundary components. According to SRP 5.2.3 (Section II), the relevant requirements are primarily derived from General Design Criteria (GDC) 1, 4, and 30 in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50. 

GDC 1 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A; RG 1.84; RG 1.44) mandates that structures, systems, and components important to safety—including reactor coolant pressure boundary components—must be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function. This includes the use of recognized codes and standards, such as the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section III, and the application of NRC-endorsed Code Cases (SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.84). A quality assurance program must be established to ensure these standards are met, and appropriate records must be maintained throughout the unit’s life (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 1).

GDC 4 requires that components be compatible with environmental conditions, including those associated with normal operation, maintenance, testing, and postulated accident conditions (SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.44). For material selection, this means ensuring materials are resistant to environmental degradation mechanisms such as stress corrosion cracking. For example, unstabilized austenitic stainless steels used in pressure boundary components must be solution heat treated to avoid sensitization, verified by appropriate testing (e.g., ASTM A262), and protected from contaminants (RG 1.44, Section C). Welding and fabrication processes must also be controlled to prevent sensitization and intergranular attack.

GDC 30 further emphasizes that reactor coolant pressure boundary components must be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to the highest quality standards practical (RG 1.84).

In summary, the selection of materials for reactor coolant pressure boundary components must comply with stringent quality assurance and environmental compatibility requirements as specified in GDC 1, 4, and 30, implemented through adherence to the ASME Code, NRC regulatory guides, and robust quality assurance programs.

data.query: For reactor coolant pressure boundary check valves, what are the combined regulatory requirements and acceptance standards regarding the specification of material types and grades, including corrosion resistance, as established by design criteria, regulatory review standards, and regulatory guides?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements and acceptance standards for specifying material types and grades, including corrosion resistance, for reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) check valves are established through a combination of NRC regulations, design criteria, regulatory review standards, and regulatory guides.

According to SRP 5.2.3 (Sections I and II), material specifications for RCPB components, including check valves, must be reviewed for adequacy and suitability, focusing on ferritic materials, nonferrous metals, and austenitic stainless steels. The compatibility of these materials with the reactor coolant, including resistance to general and stress corrosion cracking, is a key review area. Acceptance criteria are based on compliance with:
- General Design Criteria (GDC) 1 and 30 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A), which require the use of high-quality standards for design, fabrication, erection, and testing, and selection of materials to minimize environmentally assisted cracking.
- GDC 4, which requires compatibility with environmental conditions.
- 10 CFR 50.55a, which mandates compliance with ASME BPV Code, Section III, for Class 1 components (see also RG 1.84).

Material specifications must comply with the ASME Code, Section III (including Appendix I and Section II, Parts A, B, and C), and may use NRC-approved Code Cases as described in Regulatory Guide 1.84. For corrosion resistance, ferritic and carbon steels are typically clad with austenitic stainless steel, or conservative corrosion allowances must be provided if cladding is not used (SRP 5.2.3, II.2).

For austenitic stainless steels, Regulatory Guide 1.44 provides specific requirements to prevent stress corrosion cracking, including:
- Use of solution heat-treated, nonsensitized material (RG 1.44, C.2-3),
- Verification of nonsensitization (ASTM A262 or equivalent),
- Use of L Grade material (≤0.03% carbon) if exposed to sensitizing temperatures, with certain exceptions (RG 1.44, C.4),
- Retesting after exposure to sensitizing temperatures unless specific exceptions apply (RG 1.44, C.5).

In summary, the combined requirements mandate the use of ASME Code-listed materials and NRC-approved Code Cases, with additional controls for corrosion resistance and prevention of sensitization in stainless steels, as detailed in SRP 5.2.3, 10 CFR Part 50 (GDC 1, 4, 30), RG 1.84, and RG 1.44.

Means shall be provided for detecting and, to the extent practical, identifying the location of the source of reactor coolant leakage. The reactor coolant pressure boundary shall be designed with sufficient margin to assure that under operating, maintenance, testing, and postulated accident conditions, the boundary behaves in a nonbrittle manner and the probability of rapidly propagating fracture is minimized. The materials of the boundary shall be selected to minimize the likelihood of environmentally assisted cracking.

evidence_chain.section: C. REGULATORY POSITION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
C.  REGULATORY POSITION

Unstabilized, austenitic stainless steel of the AISI Type 3XX series used for components that are part of (1) the reactor coolant pressure boundary, (2) systems required for reactor shutdown, (3) systems required for emergency core cooling, and (4) reactor vessel internals that are relied on to permit adequate core cooling for any mode of normal operation or under credible postulated accident conditions should meet the following criteria:

1. Material should be suitably cleaned and suitably protected against contaminants capable of causing stress-corrosion cracking during fabrication, shipment, storage, construction, testing, and operation of components and systems.

2. Material from which components and systems are to be fabricated should be solution heat treated to produce a nonsensitized condition in the material.

3. Nonsensitization of the material should be verified using ASTM A262, Practices A or E, or another method that can be demonstrated to show nonsensitization in austenitic stainless steel. Test specimens should be selected from material subjected to each different heat treatment practice and from each heat.

4. Material subjected to sensitizing temperature in the range of 427 to 816 degrees C (800 to 1,500 degrees F), subsequent to solution heat treating in accordance with Regulatory Position 2 above and testing in accordance with Regulatory Position 3 above, should be L Grade material; that is, it should not have a carbon content greater than 0.03 percent. Exceptions are the following:

a. material exposed to pressurized water reactor coolant that has a controlled concentration of typically less than 0.020 parts per million, with a limiting value of 0.10 parts per million dissolved oxygen at all temperatures above 90 degrees C (200 degrees F) during normal operation; or

b. material in the form of castings or weld metal with a ferrite content of at least 5 percent; or

c. piping in the solution annealed condition whose exposure to temperatures in the range of 427 to 816 degrees C (800 to 1,500 degrees F) has been limited to welding operations, provided it is of sufficiently small diameter so that in the event of a credible postulated failure of the piping during normal reactor operation, the reactor can be shut down and cooled down in an orderly manner, assuming makeup is provided by the reactor coolant makeup system only.

5. Material subjected to sensitizing temperatures in the range of 427 to 816 degrees C (800 to 1,500 degrees F) during heat treating or processing other than welding, subsequent to solution heat treating in accordance with Regulatory Position 2 above and testing in accordance with Regulatory Position 3 above, should be retested in accordance with Regulatory Position 3 to demonstrate that it is not susceptible to intergranular attack, except that retest is not required for the following:

a. cast metal or weld metal with a ferrite content of 5 percent or more; or

b. material with a carbon content of 0.03 percent or less that is subjected to temperatures in the range of 427 to 816 degrees C (800 to 1,500 degrees F) for less than one hour; or

c. material exposed to special processing, provided that the processing is properly controlled to  develop a uniform product, and provided that adequate documentation exists of service experience and/or test data to demonstrate that the processing will not result in increased susceptibility to intergranular stress corrosion.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for the selection and qualification of materials used in the reactor coolant pressure boundary to ensure they are suitable for their intended safety function?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for the selection and qualification of materials used in the reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) are established to ensure that materials are suitable for their intended safety function. These requirements are grounded in several NRC regulations and guidance documents:

1. General Design Criteria (GDC) 1 and 30 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) require that RCPB components be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to the highest quality standards practical, using recognized codes and standards (such as the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code), and that a quality assurance program be implemented (SRP 5.2.3; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 1; RG 1.84).

2. Material specifications must comply with ASME Code, Section III, and acceptable Code Cases as described in Regulatory Guide 1.84. Materials must be those identified in ASME Code, Section III, Appendix I, or Section II, Parts A, B, and C (SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.84).

3. For ferritic materials, fracture toughness requirements are specified in Appendix G to 10 CFR Part 50 and Article NB-2300 of ASME Code, Section III. These include Charpy V-notch impact test standards and specific requirements for piping, pumps, and valves (SRP 5.2.3).

4. Austenitic stainless steels must be solution heat treated to avoid sensitization, verified by ASTM A262 or equivalent tests, and protected from contaminants that could cause stress corrosion cracking. Additional requirements for carbon content and retesting after exposure to sensitizing temperatures are detailed in Regulatory Guide 1.44 (SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.44).

5. Weld fabrication for low-alloy steels must comply with ASME Code Sections III and IX, with additional controls on preheat and interpass temperatures, postweld heat treatment, and monitoring as described in Regulatory Guide 1.50 (RG 1.50).

6. All fabrication, cleaning, and processing must be controlled per Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 50, Criterion XIII, and environmental compatibility must be ensured per GDC 4 (SRP 5.2.3).

In summary, the NRC requires strict adherence to ASME Code provisions, NRC-endorsed Code Cases, and supplemental regulatory guidance to ensure that RCPB materials are selected, processed, and qualified to maintain integrity and safety under all operating conditions.

evidence_chain.section: C. REGULATORY POSITION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Weld fabrication for low-alloy steel (P Nos. 3, 4, and 5A) components should comply with the fabrication requirements specified in Sections III and IX of the ASME B&PV Code, supplemented by the regulatory positions below.

1. The Welding Procedure Specification should specify a maximum interpass temperature and a minimum preheat temperature that are equal to the maximum interpass temperature and minimum preheat temperature used during procedure qualification.   

2. For production welds, the preheat temperature should be maintained until final postweld heat treatment or a post weld hydrogen bakeout is performed between 200 and 400ºC (400 and 750ºF) for a minimum of four hours after which the component may be slowly cooled to ambient temperature prior to the performance of the final post weld heat treatment. .  The postweld hydrogen bakeout temperature and soak time should be based on the materials being welded, the geometry, and the welding process used.

3. Production welding should be monitored to verify that the limits on preheat and interpass temperatures are maintained.

4. If Regulatory Positions 1, 2, and 3 above are not met, the weld is subject to rejection.  However, the soundness of the weld may be demonstrated by an acceptable examination procedure meeting the acceptance criteria specified in Section III of the ASME B&PV Code.

data.query: How do the general design criteria for quality standards interact with the requirements for fabrication, inspection, and repair of small diameter components in the reactor coolant pressure boundary?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for quality standards, particularly GDC 1 and GDC 30 from Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, establish the foundational requirements that all structures, systems, and components important to safety—including small diameter components in the reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB)—must be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1; RG 1.84, Section A). These criteria require the use of generally recognized codes and standards, such as the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (B&PV) Code, and mandate that these codes be evaluated for applicability and supplemented as necessary to ensure a quality product (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1; RG 1.84, Section A).

For fabrication, inspection, and repair of small diameter RCPB components, these general criteria are operationalized through specific requirements:
- Fabrication and welding must comply with ASME Code Sections III and IX, as well as NRC-endorsed Regulatory Guides (SRP 5.2.3, II.1; RG 1.50, Section C; RG 1.71, Section C).
- For areas of limited accessibility (such as small diameter components), welder qualification must address restricted access conditions. If access is less than 30-35 cm (12-14 inches) from the joint, special performance qualification is required, or alternatively, 100% radiographic and/or ultrasonic examination of the weld may be performed (SRP 5.2.3, II.3.B.3; RG 1.71, Section C).
- All fabrication, inspection, and repair activities must be documented and records maintained throughout the life of the unit, as required by GDC 1 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1).

In summary, the general design criteria for quality standards provide the regulatory basis for the detailed requirements governing the fabrication, inspection, and repair of small diameter RCPB components. These requirements are implemented through compliance with the ASME Code and NRC Regulatory Guides, ensuring that even components with challenging access are fabricated and inspected to the highest practical quality standards (SRP 5.2.3, RG 1.50, RG 1.71, RG 1.84).

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for selecting weld filler materials used in the reactor coolant pressure boundary to ensure compatibility with low alloy steel base metals?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for selecting weld filler materials used in the reactor coolant pressure boundary, specifically to ensure compatibility with low alloy steel base metals, are grounded in compliance with ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (B&PV) Code requirements and supplemented by NRC regulatory guides. According to SRP 5.2.3, Section II, the fabrication and processing of ferritic (low alloy) materials must adhere to quality standards as required by General Design Criteria (GDC) 1 and 30, and 10 CFR 50.55a, which mandate the use of recognized codes and standards (see 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1).

Specifically, weld fabrication for low-alloy steel components must comply with ASME B&PV Code Sections III and IX, as supplemented by Regulatory Guide 1.50 (RG 1.50, Section C). The Welding Procedure Specification (WPS) must specify maximum interpass and minimum preheat temperatures consistent with those used during procedure qualification. For production welds, the preheat temperature must be maintained until postweld heat treatment or a hydrogen bakeout is performed, as detailed in RG 1.50. Production welding must be monitored to ensure these temperature limits are maintained; failure to do so subjects the weld to rejection unless soundness can be demonstrated by examination per ASME Code acceptance criteria.

Additionally, for stainless steel weld cladding on low-alloy steel, Regulatory Guide 1.43 provides criteria to prevent underclad cracking, requiring that materials susceptible to such cracking not be weld clad by high-heat-input processes unless qualified to demonstrate resistance (SRP 5.2.3). For electroslag welds, Regulatory Guide 1.34 specifies acceptable solidification patterns and impact test limits.

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria require that weld filler materials and procedures for the reactor coolant pressure boundary be qualified and controlled per ASME Code and NRC regulatory guides to ensure compatibility and integrity of low alloy steel base metals.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
3. Fabrication and Processing of Ferritic Materials
B. The acceptance criteria for control of ferritic steel welding are based upon the following regulatory guides and ASME Code provisions to satisfy the quality standards requirements of GDC 1, GDC 30, and § 50.55a:
(1) The amount of specified preheat must be in accordance with the requirements of the Code, Section III, Appendix D, Paragraph D-1210. These requirements are supplemented by positions described in Regulatory Guide 1.50, “Control of Preheat Temperature for Welding of Low Alloy Steel.”
The supplemental acceptance criteria for control of preheat temperature are as follows:
(a) According to the welding procedure qualification minimum preheat and maximum interpass temperatures should be specified and the welding procedure should be qualified at the minimum preheat temperature. For production welds, the preheat temperature should be maintained until a post-weld heat treatment has been performed.
(b) Production welding should be monitored to verify that the limits on preheat and interpass temperatures are maintained. In the event that the above criteria are not met, the weld is subject to rejection.
(2) The acceptance criteria for electroslag welds are presented in Regulatory Guide 1.34, “Control of Electroslag Weld Properties.” These criteria specify acceptable solidification patterns and impact test limits (for qualification of welds in Class 1 and Class 2 components) and the criteria for verifying conformance during production welding.
(4) Regulatory Guide 1.43, “Control of Stainless Steel Weld Cladding of Low-Alloy Steel Components,” provides criteria to limit the occurrence of underclad cracking in low-alloy steel safety-related components clad with stainless steel. According to these criteria, material known to have susceptibility to underclad cracking should not be weld clad by high-heat-input welding processes and should be qualified for use to demonstrate that underclad cracking is not induced.

data.query: How do general design criteria for quality assurance and material compatibility apply to the selection of weld filler materials for low alloy steel components in the reactor coolant pressure boundary?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for quality assurance and material compatibility directly inform the selection of weld filler materials for low alloy steel components in the reactor coolant pressure boundary. GDC 1 and GDC 30 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A; [2]) require that such components be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to the highest quality standards practical, with a quality assurance program in place to ensure safety functions are met. GDC 4 further requires that components be compatible with the environmental conditions they will encounter during normal operation and postulated accidents.

To meet these criteria, NRC guidance (SRP 5.2.3, Section II; [1]) specifies that material specifications, including weld filler materials, must comply with the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, Section III, and applicable Code Cases as endorsed in Regulatory Guide 1.84 ([3]). This ensures that the selected weld filler materials are of adequate quality and are compatible with the base materials and service environment. For ferritic (low alloy) steel welding, additional requirements are provided in Regulatory Guide 1.50 ([4]), which mandates control of preheat and interpass temperatures during welding, as well as postweld heat treatment or hydrogen bakeout to prevent weld defects such as cracking. Production welding must be monitored to ensure these parameters are maintained, and failure to comply may result in weld rejection unless soundness can be demonstrated by examination per ASME Code acceptance criteria.

Furthermore, for stainless steel cladding of low-alloy steel, Regulatory Guide 1.43 (referenced in [1]) provides criteria to limit underclad cracking, emphasizing the importance of material compatibility and process qualification. In summary, the selection and use of weld filler materials for low alloy steel components in the reactor coolant pressure boundary must adhere to rigorous quality assurance and compatibility standards as established by NRC regulations and endorsed codes and guides.
