data.query: For Class 1 piping welds in the reactor coolant pressure boundary, what combined regulatory provisions from general design criteria, NRC review standards, and regulatory guides govern the minimum surface area and quality required for ultrasonic preservice examination to ensure reliable flaw detection?
data.answer:
The minimum surface area and quality required for ultrasonic preservice examination (UT PSE) of Class 1 piping welds in the reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) are governed by a combination of regulatory provisions from general design criteria, NRC review standards, and regulatory guides, all of which require adherence to the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (B&PV) Code, Section III.

General Design Criteria (GDC) 1 and 30 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) mandate that RCPB components be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to the highest quality standards practical, using recognized codes and standards (Evidence [2], [3]). NRC Standard Review Plan (SRP) 5.2.3 further specifies that compliance with GDC 1, GDC 30, and 10 CFR 50.55a is achieved by meeting the applicable provisions of the ASME Code, Section III, particularly Paragraphs NB-2550 through NB-2570, which detail nondestructive examination (NDE) requirements for ferritic steel tubular products (Evidence [1]).

Regulatory Guides (RG) 1.84, 1.50, and 1.71 reinforce that weld fabrication, including preservice examination, must comply with ASME Code Sections III and IX, and that any deviation from prescribed fabrication or examination procedures must be justified by demonstrating weld soundness through acceptable examination procedures meeting ASME Section III acceptance criteria (Evidence [3], [4], [5]).

In summary, the minimum surface area and quality for UT PSE are those required by ASME Section III, NB-2550 through NB-2570, as incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a and endorsed by NRC regulatory guides. These provisions ensure that the entire weld and adjacent base material are examined to the extent necessary to detect flaws reliably, and that examination quality meets the highest standards practical for safety-related components.

evidence_chain.section: A. INTRODUCTION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Purpose

 This regulatory guide (RG) lists the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, Section III, Division 1, “Rules for Construction of Nuclear Power Plant Components” (Ref. 1), Code Cases that the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has approved for use as voluntary alternatives to the mandatory ASME BPV Code provisions that are incorporated by reference into Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR), Part 50, “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities” (Ref. 2).

Applicability  

  This RG applies to reactor licensees and applicants subject to 10 CFR Part 50, Section 50.55a, “Codes and standards.”

Applicable Regulations

• General Design Criterion (GDC) 1, “Quality Standards and Records,” of Appendix A, “General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants,” to 10 CFR Part 50 requires, in part, that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with the importance of the safety function to be performed. Where generally recognized codes and standards are used, GDC 1 requires that they be identified and evaluated to determine their applicability, adequacy, and sufficiency and be supplemented or modified as necessary to ensure a quality product in keeping with the required safety function.

• 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 30, “Quality of Reactor Coolant Pressure Boundary,” requires, in part, that components that are part of the reactor coolant pressure boundary be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to the highest quality standards practical. 

• 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, “Quality Assurance Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants and Fuel Processing Plants,” requires, in part, that measures be established for the control of special processing of materials and that proper testing be performed.

• 10 CFR 50.55a(c) requires, in part, that components of the reactor coolant pressure boundary must be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested in accordance with the requirements for the Class 1 components of ASME BPV Code, Section III, or equivalent quality standards.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for materials used in the reactor coolant pressure boundary, specifically regarding weld filler materials?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for materials used in the reactor coolant pressure boundary, specifically regarding weld filler materials, are grounded in compliance with quality standards and codes, primarily the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (B&PV) Code, as supplemented by NRC regulatory guides and requirements. According to SRP 5.2.3, Section II, acceptance criteria for ferritic steel welding—including weld filler materials—are based on ASME Code Section III, Appendix D, and are supplemented by Regulatory Guides such as RG 1.50, RG 1.34, RG 1.43, and RG 1.71. 

Key criteria include:
- The welding procedure must specify and maintain minimum preheat and maximum interpass temperatures as established during procedure qualification (SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.50, C.1).
- For production welds, preheat temperature must be maintained until post-weld heat treatment or a hydrogen bakeout is performed, with specific temperature and soak time requirements based on material and process (SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.50, C.2).
- Production welding must be monitored to ensure compliance with preheat and interpass temperature limits; noncompliance may result in weld rejection unless soundness is demonstrated by examination per ASME Section III (SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.50, C.3-4).
- For electroslag welds, acceptance criteria include solidification patterns and impact test limits as per RG 1.34 (SRP 5.2.3).
- For stainless steel weld cladding on low-alloy steel, materials susceptible to underclad cracking must not be used with high-heat-input processes unless qualified to demonstrate no underclad cracking (SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.43).
- Welder qualification, especially in areas of limited accessibility, must follow ASME Section IX and RG 1.71, with requalification required if essential variables change or if indirect means of weld pool observation are used (SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.71).

These criteria are established to satisfy the quality standards requirements of General Design Criteria (GDC) 1 and 30 in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, ensuring that all materials and welds in the reactor coolant pressure boundary meet stringent safety and quality assurance standards.

For production welds, the preheat temperature should be maintained until a post-weld heat treatment has been performed.
(b) Production welding should be monitored to verify that the limits on preheat and interpass temperatures are maintained. In the event that the above criteria are not met, the weld is subject to rejection.
(2) The acceptance criteria for electroslag welds are presented in Regulatory Guide 1.34, “Control of Electroslag Weld Properties.” These criteria specify acceptable solidification patterns and impact test limits (for qualification of welds in Class 1 and Class 2 components) and the criteria for verifying conformance during production welding.
(3) Regulatory Guide 1.71, “Welder Qualification for Areas of Limited Accessibility,” provides the following criteria for requalification of welders: the performance qualification should require testing of the welder when conditions of accessibility to a production weld are less than 30 to 35 cm (12-14 inches) in any direction from the joint; and requalification is required for different restricted accessibility conditions or when any of the essential variables listed in the Code, Section IX, “Welding and Brazing Qualifications” are changed.
Qualification of the welder or welding operators for limited accessibility may be waived provided that 100% radiographic and/or ultrasonic examination of the completed welded joint is performed. Examination procedures and acceptance standards should meet the requirements of the ASME Section III of the Code. Records of the examination reports and radiographs should be retained and made part of the Quality Assurance Documentation for the completed weld.
(4) Regulatory Guide 1.43, “Control of Stainless Steel Weld Cladding of Low-Alloy Steel Components,” provides criteria to limit the occurrence of underclad cracking in low-alloy steel safety-related components clad with stainless steel. According to these criteria, material known to have susceptibility to underclad cracking should not be weld clad by high-heat-input welding processes and should be qualified for use to demonstrate that underclad cracking is not induced.

data.query: How do general design criteria for quality assurance and reactor coolant pressure boundary integrity relate to the selection and qualification of weld filler materials?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for quality assurance (GDC 1) and reactor coolant pressure boundary integrity (GDC 30) directly inform the selection and qualification of weld filler materials for nuclear power plant components. GDC 1 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1) requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards appropriate to their safety function, using recognized codes and standards (such as the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code) that are evaluated for applicability and adequacy (Evidence: [2], [3]). GDC 30 further requires that reactor coolant pressure boundary components be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to the highest quality standards practical (Evidence: [3]).

To meet these criteria, NRC acceptance criteria (SRP 5.2.3) specify that material specifications for weld filler materials must comply with the ASME Code, Section III and II, and may use NRC-approved Code Cases as described in Regulatory Guide 1.84 (Evidence: [1], [3]). The selection of weld filler materials is thus limited to those identified in the ASME Code or approved Code Cases, ensuring their suitability for nuclear service.

Additionally, fabrication and processing requirements, such as control of preheat and interpass temperatures, are established to ensure weld quality and integrity, as detailed in Regulatory Guide 1.50 and referenced in SRP 5.2.3 (Evidence: [1], [4]). These requirements are designed to prevent weld defects and ensure that the welds meet the quality standards mandated by GDC 1 and GDC 30. For example, the welding procedure specification must match the conditions used during procedure qualification, and production welding must be monitored for compliance (Evidence: [4]).

In summary, the general design criteria require that weld filler materials be selected and qualified according to stringent quality standards, using recognized codes and NRC-approved alternatives, and that fabrication processes are controlled to ensure the integrity of the reactor coolant pressure boundary.

data.query: When evaluating weld filler materials for the reactor coolant pressure boundary in a new nuclear plant, what combined regulatory requirements from general design criteria, regulatory review standards, and relevant regulatory guides must be considered to ensure material acceptability and long-term integrity?
data.answer:
When evaluating weld filler materials for the reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) in a new nuclear plant, a comprehensive set of regulatory requirements must be met to ensure material acceptability and long-term integrity. These requirements are derived from the General Design Criteria (GDC) in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, NRC Standard Review Plan (SRP) 5.2.3, and relevant Regulatory Guides (RGs).

First, GDC 1 and GDC 30 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A; RG 1.84) require that RCPB components be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to the highest quality standards practical, using recognized codes and standards such as the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, Section III. The applicability and adequacy of these codes must be evaluated, and a quality assurance program must be implemented (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B).

GDC 4 requires compatibility of materials with environmental conditions, which is addressed by compliance with ASME Code provisions and RG 1.44 for austenitic stainless steels, ensuring materials are non-sensitized and resistant to stress-corrosion cracking (SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.44).

GDC 14 and GDC 31 require minimizing the probability of rapidly propagating fracture and gross rupture. This is achieved by meeting fracture toughness requirements in Appendix G to 10 CFR Part 50 and by following fabrication and welding controls for ferritic materials as outlined in RG 1.50 (SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.50).

Specific acceptance criteria include:
- Use of ASME BPV Code, Section III, and NRC-approved Code Cases (RG 1.84) for material specifications and welding procedures.
- Control of welding parameters (preheat, interpass temperature) and postweld treatments for ferritic steels (RG 1.50).
- Verification of non-sensitization for austenitic stainless steels using ASTM A262 or equivalent methods, and control of welding practices to avoid sensitization (RG 1.44).
- Additional controls for cleaning, protection against contaminants, and documentation of fabrication processes (SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.44).

In summary, compliance with the ASME Code as endorsed and supplemented by NRC regulatory guides (RG 1.84, RG 1.44, RG 1.50), adherence to GDCs 1, 4, 14, 30, and 31, and implementation of a robust quality assurance program are required to ensure the acceptability and long-term integrity of weld filler materials for the RCPB.

evidence_chain.section: C. REGULATORY POSITION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
C.  REGULATORY POSITION

Unstabilized, austenitic stainless steel of the AISI Type 3XX series used for components that are part of (1) the reactor coolant pressure boundary, (2) systems required for reactor shutdown, (3) systems required for emergency core cooling, and (4) reactor vessel internals that are relied on to permit adequate core cooling for any mode of normal operation or under credible postulated accident conditions should meet the following criteria:

1. Material should be suitably cleaned and suitably protected against contaminants capable of causing stress-corrosion cracking during fabrication, shipment, storage, construction, testing, and operation of components and systems.

2. Material from which components and systems are to be fabricated should be solution heat treated to produce a nonsensitized condition in the material.

3. Nonsensitization of the material should be verified using ASTM A262, Practices A or E, or another method that can be demonstrated to show nonsensitization in austenitic stainless steel. Test specimens should be selected from material subjected to each different heat treatment practice and from each heat.

4. Material subjected to sensitizing temperature in the range of 427 to 816 degrees C (800 to 1,500 degrees F), subsequent to solution heat treating in accordance with Regulatory Position 2 above and testing in accordance with Regulatory Position 3 above, should be L Grade material; that is, it should not have a carbon content greater than 0.03 percent. Exceptions are the following:

a. material exposed to pressurized water reactor coolant that has a controlled concentration of typically less than 0.020 parts per million, with a limiting value of 0.10 parts per million dissolved oxygen at all temperatures above 90 degrees C (200 degrees F) during normal operation; or

b. material in the form of castings or weld metal with a ferrite content of at least 5 percent; or

c. piping in the solution annealed condition whose exposure to temperatures in the range of 427 to 816 degrees C (800 to 1,500 degrees F) has been limited to welding operations, provided it is of sufficiently small diameter so that in the event of a credible postulated failure of the piping during normal reactor operation, the reactor can be shut down and cooled down in an orderly manner, assuming makeup is provided by the reactor coolant makeup system only.

5. Material subjected to sensitizing temperatures in the range of 427 to 816 degrees C (800 to 1,500 degrees F) during heat treating or processing other than welding, subsequent to solution heat treating in accordance with Regulatory Position 2 above and testing in accordance with Regulatory Position 3 above, should be retested in accordance with Regulatory Position 3 to demonstrate that it is not susceptible to intergranular attack, except that retest is not required for the following:

a. cast metal or weld metal with a ferrite content of 5 percent or more; or

b. material with a carbon content of 0.03 percent or less that is subjected to temperatures in the range of 427 to 816 degrees C (800 to 1,500 degrees F) for less than one hour; or

c. material exposed to special processing, provided that the processing is properly controlled to develop a uniform product, and provided that adequate documentation exists of service experience and/or test data to demonstrate that the processing will not result in increased susceptibility to intergranular stress corrosion.

6. Welding practices and, if necessary, material composition should be controlled to avoid excessive sensitization of base metal heat-affected zones of weldments. Controls to prevent sensitization of the material during welding include maintaining low heat input and limiting the interpass temperature.

7. An intergranular corrosion test, such as specified in Regulatory Position 3 above, should be performed for each welding procedure to be used for welding material having a carbon content greater than 0.03 percent.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for materials used in the reactor coolant pressure boundary, specifically regarding weld filler materials?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for materials used in the reactor coolant pressure boundary, specifically regarding weld filler materials, are grounded in compliance with quality standards and codes to ensure safety and reliability. According to SRP 5.2.3 Section II, the acceptance criteria for ferritic steel welding are based on ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (B&PV) Code, Section III and IX, and are supplemented by several Regulatory Guides (RGs) to satisfy General Design Criteria (GDC) 1 and 30, and 10 CFR 50.55a. 

Key requirements include:
- The welding procedure must specify and maintain minimum preheat and maximum interpass temperatures as per ASME Code Section III, Appendix D, Paragraph D-1210, and RG 1.50 (SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.50, C.1, C.2, C.3).
- For production welds, preheat temperature must be maintained until post-weld heat treatment or a hydrogen bakeout is performed (RG 1.50, C.2).
- Production welding must be monitored to ensure temperature limits are maintained; failure to meet these criteria subjects the weld to rejection unless soundness is demonstrated by examination per ASME Section III (SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.50, C.4).
- Electroslag welds must meet the criteria in RG 1.34, including acceptable solidification patterns and impact test limits (SRP 5.2.3).
- Welder qualification, especially in areas of limited accessibility, must follow RG 1.71 and ASME Section IX, with requalification required if essential variables change or if indirect means of weld pool observation are used (SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.71, C.1-C.3).
- For stainless steel weld cladding of low-alloy steel, RG 1.43 provides criteria to prevent underclad cracking (SRP 5.2.3).

All weld fabrication and repair must comply with ASME Code Sections III and IX, and be supplemented by NRC regulatory positions to ensure quality and safety (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1; SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.50; RG 1.71).

3. Fabrication and Processing of Ferritic Materials

(1) The amount of specified preheat must be in accordance with the requirements of the Code, Section III, Appendix D, Paragraph D-1210. These requirements are supplemented by positions described in Regulatory Guide 1.50, “Control of Preheat Temperature for Welding of Low Alloy Steel.”
The supplemental acceptance criteria for control of preheat temperature are as follows:
(a) According to the welding procedure qualification minimum preheat and maximum interpass temperatures should be specified and the welding procedure should be qualified at the minimum preheat temperature. For production welds, the preheat temperature should be maintained until a post-weld heat treatment has been performed.
(b) Production welding should be monitored to verify that the limits on preheat and interpass temperatures are maintained. In the event that the above criteria are not met, the weld is subject to rejection.
(2) The acceptance criteria for electroslag welds are presented in Regulatory Guide 1.34, “Control of Electroslag Weld Properties.” These criteria specify acceptable solidification patterns and impact test limits (for qualification of welds in Class 1 and Class 2 components) and the criteria for verifying conformance during production welding.
(3) Regulatory Guide 1.71, “Welder Qualification for Areas of Limited Accessibility,” provides the following criteria for requalification of welders: the performance qualification should require testing of the welder when conditions of accessibility to a production weld are less than 30 to 35 cm (12-14 inches) in any direction from the joint; and requalification is required for different restricted accessibility conditions or when any of the essential variables listed in the Code, Section IX, “Welding and Brazing Qualifications” are changed.
Qualification of the welder or welding operators for limited accessibility may be waived provided that 100% radiographic and/or ultrasonic examination of the completed welded joint is performed. Examination procedures and acceptance standards should meet the requirements of the ASME Section III of the Code. Records of the examination reports and radiographs should be retained and made part of the Quality Assurance Documentation for the completed weld.
(4) Regulatory Guide 1.43, “Control of Stainless Steel Weld Cladding of Low-Alloy Steel Components,” provides criteria to limit the occurrence of underclad cracking in low-alloy steel safety-related components clad with stainless steel. According to these criteria, material known to have susceptibility to underclad cracking should not be weld clad by high-heat-input welding processes and should be qualified for use to demonstrate that underclad cracking is not induced.

data.query: How do general design criteria for quality assurance and reactor coolant pressure boundary integrity relate to the selection and qualification of weld filler materials in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for quality assurance (GDC 1) and reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) integrity (GDC 30) directly inform the selection and qualification of weld filler materials in nuclear power plants by establishing rigorous quality standards and requiring adherence to recognized codes and standards. According to SRP 5.2.3, compliance with GDC 1 and GDC 30 is achieved by following the applicable provisions of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (B&PV) Code and by using materials and processes qualified through acceptable Code Cases, as outlined in Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.84. These criteria ensure that material specifications, including weld filler materials, meet the necessary quality standards for safety-related components.

GDC 1 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) mandates that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function, and that a quality assurance program be implemented (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1; RG 1.84, Section A). GDC 30 further requires that RCPB components be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to the highest quality standards practical (RG 1.84, Section A).

For weld filler materials, this means that their selection and qualification must comply with ASME Code requirements (SRP 5.2.3, II.1; RG 1.84), and that special processes such as welding are controlled and monitored as part of the quality assurance program (RG 1.50, Section A). Specific acceptance criteria for welding, including preheat and interpass temperature controls, postweld heat treatment, and monitoring, are detailed in RG 1.50 and must be followed to ensure weld integrity. Failure to meet these criteria can result in weld rejection unless soundness is demonstrated by examination per ASME Code (RG 1.50, Section C).

In summary, the general design criteria require that weld filler materials for safety-related components, especially those forming part of the RCPB, be selected and qualified according to stringent quality standards, recognized codes (ASME), and regulatory guidance to ensure structural integrity and safety.

data.query: For a new nuclear plant design, what combined regulatory requirements from general design criteria, regulatory review standards, and relevant regulatory guides must be met to ensure the selection, qualification, and documentation of weld filler materials used in the reactor coolant pressure boundary?
data.answer:
To ensure the selection, qualification, and documentation of weld filler materials used in the reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) for a new nuclear plant design, a combination of regulatory requirements from general design criteria, regulatory review standards, and relevant regulatory guides must be met. 

First, the General Design Criteria (GDC) 1 and 30 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) require that structures, systems, and components important to safety, including the RCPB, be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to the highest quality standards practical, with appropriate records maintained throughout the life of the unit (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1; [2]). 

Compliance with 10 CFR 50.55a is required, mandating that RCPB components meet the requirements for ASME BPV Code, Section III, Class 1 components or equivalent standards ([3]). Material specifications for weld filler materials must conform to those identified in ASME Code, Section III, Appendix I, and Section II, Parts A, B, and C, or be covered by NRC-approved Code Cases as described in Regulatory Guide 1.84 ([1], [3]). 

Fabrication and processing of welds must follow ASME Code requirements, supplemented by NRC regulatory guides. For ferritic materials, preheat and interpass temperatures must be controlled per ASME Code Section III, Appendix D, and Regulatory Guide 1.50 ([1], [4]). Electroslag welds and stainless steel cladding must meet the criteria in Regulatory Guides 1.34 and 1.43, respectively ([1]). Welder qualification, especially in areas of limited accessibility, must follow ASME Code Sections III and IX, with additional requirements for performance and requalification as detailed in Regulatory Guide 1.71 ([1], [5]). 

All these requirements are reviewed and enforced through the Standard Review Plan (SRP) 5.2.3, which integrates the above regulations and guides to ensure that weld filler materials for the RCPB are properly selected, qualified, and documented.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Purpose

 This regulatory guide (RG) lists the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, Section III, Division 1, “Rules for Construction of Nuclear Power Plant Components” (Ref. 1), Code Cases that the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has approved for use as voluntary alternatives to the mandatory ASME BPV Code provisions that are incorporated by reference into Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR), Part 50, “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities” (Ref. 2).

Applicability  

  This RG applies to reactor licensees and applicants subject to 10 CFR Part 50, Section 50.55a, “Codes and standards.”

Applicable Regulations

• General Design Criterion (GDC) 1, “Quality Standards and Records,” of Appendix A, “General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants,” to 10 CFR Part 50 requires, in part, that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with the importance of the safety function to be performed. Where generally recognized codes and standards are used, GDC 1 requires that they be identified and evaluated to determine their applicability, adequacy, and sufficiency and be supplemented or modified as necessary to ensure a quality product in keeping with the required safety function.

• 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 30, “Quality of Reactor Coolant Pressure Boundary,” requires, in part, that components that are part of the reactor coolant pressure boundary be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to the highest quality standards practical.

• 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, “Quality Assurance Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants and Fuel Processing Plants,” requires, in part, that measures be established for the control of special processing of materials and that proper testing be performed.

• 10 CFR 50.55a(c) requires, in part, that components of the reactor coolant pressure boundary must be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested in accordance with the requirements for the Class 1 components of ASME BPV Code, Section III, or equivalent quality standards.

• 10 CFR 52.79(a)(11) (Ref. 3) requires the final safety analysis report to include “a description of the program(s), and their implementation, necessary to ensure that the systems and components meet the requirements of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code and the ASME Code for Operation and Maintenance of Nuclear Power Plants in accordance with 50.55a of this chapter.”

Purpose of this Regulatory Guide

The NRC incorporated this RG into 10 CFR 50.55a by reference. The RG contains new Code Cases and revisions to existing Code Cases that the staff has approved for use, as listed in Tables 1 and 2 of this guide. The RG also states the requirements that govern the use of Code Cases. Licensees may voluntarily use Code Cases approved by the NRC as an alternative to compliance with the ASME Code provisions that have been incorporated by reference into 10 CFR 50.55a. Because the status of Code Cases continually changes, the staff plans to periodically update 10 CFR 50.55a and this guide to accommodate new Code Cases and any revisions to existing Code Cases.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for materials used in the reactor coolant pressure boundary, specifically regarding weld filler materials?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for materials used in the reactor coolant pressure boundary, specifically regarding weld filler materials, are grounded in compliance with quality standards and codes to ensure safety and integrity. According to SRP 5.2.3 Section II, acceptance criteria for ferritic steel welding are based on ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (Sections III and IX), supplemented by NRC Regulatory Guides (RGs) and specific regulatory positions to satisfy General Design Criteria (GDC) 1 and 30, and 10 CFR 50.55a. 

Key requirements include:
- The welding procedure must specify and maintain minimum preheat and maximum interpass temperatures as qualified (SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.50, C.1). Production welds must be monitored to ensure these temperatures are maintained until post-weld heat treatment or hydrogen bakeout is performed (SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.50, C.2-3).
- If these temperature controls are not met, the weld is subject to rejection unless soundness can be demonstrated by examination procedures meeting ASME Section III acceptance criteria (SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.50, C.4).
- For electroslag welds, acceptance criteria include solidification patterns and impact test limits as per RG 1.34 (SRP 5.2.3).
- For welds in areas of limited accessibility, welder qualification must address access limitations, and requalification is required if essential variables change (SRP 5.2.3; RG 1.71, C.1-2). Monitoring of production welding and adherence to qualification criteria is required (RG 1.71, C.3).
- For stainless steel weld cladding of low-alloy steel, materials susceptible to underclad cracking must not be used with high-heat-input processes unless qualified to demonstrate no underclad cracking (SRP 5.2.3).

All fabrication, including weld filler materials, must comply with ASME Code requirements and be supplemented as necessary to assure quality commensurate with safety significance (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 1). Records of design, fabrication, and testing must be maintained throughout the unit's life (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 1).

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Weld fabrication for low-alloy steel (P Nos. 3, 4, and 5A) components should comply with the fabrication requirements specified in Sections III and IX of the ASME B&PV Code, supplemented by the regulatory positions below.

1. The Welding Procedure Specification should specify a maximum interpass temperature and a minimum preheat temperature that are equal to the maximum interpass temperature and minimum preheat temperature used during procedure qualification.   

2. For production welds, the preheat temperature should be maintained until final postweld heat treatment or a post weld hydrogen bakeout is performed between 200 and 400ºC (400 and 750ºF) for a minimum of four hours after which the component may be slowly cooled to ambient temperature prior to the performance of the final post weld heat treatment. .  The postweld hydrogen bakeout temperature and soak time should be based on the materials being welded, the geometry, and the welding process used.

3. Production welding should be monitored to verify that the limits on preheat and interpass temperatures are maintained.

4. If Regulatory Positions 1, 2, and 3 above are not met, the weld is subject to rejection.  However, the soundness of the weld may be demonstrated by an acceptable examination procedure meeting the acceptance criteria specified in Section III of the ASME B&PV Code.

data.query: How do general design criteria for quality assurance and reactor coolant pressure boundary integrity relate to the selection and qualification of weld filler materials in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for quality assurance and reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) integrity directly inform the selection and qualification of weld filler materials in nuclear power plants by establishing rigorous quality standards and requiring adherence to recognized codes and standards. Specifically, GDC 1 (Quality Standards and Records) and GDC 30 (Quality of Reactor Coolant Pressure Boundary), as outlined in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, mandate that structures, systems, and components important to safety—including welds in the RCPB—be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to the highest quality standards practical (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criteria 1 and 30; RG 1.84, Section A).

To meet these criteria, the NRC requires compliance with the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, Section III, for material specifications and welding processes (SRP 5.2.3, II. Acceptance Criteria; RG 1.84, Section A). The selection and qualification of weld filler materials must therefore conform to the applicable ASME Code provisions, and any use of Code Cases must be consistent with NRC-endorsed guidance (SRP 5.2.3, II.1; RG 1.84).

Furthermore, Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 50 requires that special processes such as welding are controlled and properly monitored, ensuring that weld filler materials and welding procedures are qualified and that process parameters (e.g., preheat and interpass temperatures) are maintained during production (RG 1.50, Sections A, B, C; SRP 5.2.3, II.3.B). Additional regulatory guides (e.g., RG 1.43, RG 1.34) provide criteria to prevent weld defects such as underclad cracking and to ensure the mechanical integrity of welds, further supporting the GDC requirements for RCPB integrity (SRP 5.2.3, II.3.B.4).

In summary, the general design criteria for quality assurance and RCPB integrity require that weld filler materials be selected and qualified according to the highest quality standards, as defined by the ASME Code and NRC regulatory guidance, to ensure the safety and reliability of nuclear power plant components.

data.query: For the selection and qualification of weld filler materials used in the reactor coolant pressure boundary, what combined regulatory provisions from general design criteria, NRC review standards, and relevant regulatory guides must be met to ensure compliance with NRC requirements?
data.answer:
To ensure compliance with NRC requirements for the selection and qualification of weld filler materials used in the reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB), a combination of regulatory provisions from general design criteria, NRC review standards, and relevant regulatory guides must be met:

1. General Design Criteria (GDC):
- GDC 1 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety, including the RCPB, be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function. Recognized codes and standards (such as the ASME BPV Code) must be identified, evaluated, and supplemented as necessary (Evidence [2], [3]).
- GDC 30 requires RCPB components to be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to the highest quality standards practical (Evidence [3]).

2. NRC Review Standards (SRP 5.2.3):
- Compliance with GDC 1, 4, 14, 30, and 31, as well as 10 CFR 50.55a and Appendix B, is required (Evidence [1]).
- Material specifications must comply with ASME BPV Code Section III and NRC-accepted Code Cases as described in Regulatory Guide 1.84 (Evidence [1], [3]).
- Additional requirements for ferritic and austenitic stainless steel welding are specified, including preheat and interpass temperature controls (Regulatory Guide 1.50), electroslag weld properties (Regulatory Guide 1.34), welder qualification (Regulatory Guide 1.71), and control of stainless steel weld cladding (Regulatory Guide 1.43) (Evidence [1]).
- Measures to avoid sensitization in austenitic stainless steels are required, with testing and qualification methods described in Regulatory Guide 1.44 and NUREG-0313 (Evidence [1]).

3. Regulatory Guides and ASME Code:
- Regulatory Guide 1.84 lists NRC-approved ASME Code Cases that may be used as alternatives to mandatory ASME BPV Code provisions, provided they do not conflict with regulatory requirements (Evidence [3]).
- Regulatory Guide 1.50 provides supplemental requirements for preheat and interpass temperature control during welding of low-alloy steels (Evidence [4]).
- Regulatory Guide 1.71 addresses welder qualification for areas of limited accessibility and requalification criteria (Evidence [5]).

In summary, compliance is achieved by meeting the requirements of GDC 1 and 30, 10 CFR 50.55a, and Appendix B, using ASME BPV Code Section III (and NRC-accepted Code Cases per RG 1.84), and following supplemental guidance in RGs 1.50, 1.71, 1.34, 1.43, and 1.44, as applicable. These provisions collectively ensure the selection and qualification of weld filler materials meet NRC quality and safety standards for the RCPB.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for inservice inspection of reactor coolant pressure boundary piping in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for inservice inspection (ISI) of reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) piping in nuclear power plants are established primarily by 10 CFR 50.55a, which mandates that ISI programs for these components comply with the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section XI, or an equivalent standard acceptable to the NRC (10 CFR 50.55a(b); RG 1.147, Section B). Specifically, all Code Class 1 components of the RCPB, as defined in ASME Section III, must meet the inspection requirements set forth in ASME Section XI (DSRS 5.2.4, Section II). 

The ISI program must ensure that components are designed and provided with access to permit periodic inspection and testing to assess their structural and leaktight integrity (DSRS 5.2.4, Section II). The required examinations and pressure tests must be completed during each ten-year inspection interval, as specified in Article IWA-2000 of ASME Section XI (DSRS 5.2.4, Section II). 

Additionally, 10 CFR 50.55a(g) requires that Class 1, 2, 3, metal containment, and concrete containment components and their supports meet the requirements of ASME Section XI or equivalent standards (RG 1.147, Section B). Licensees may use NRC-approved ASME Code Cases as voluntary alternatives to the mandatory ASME Code provisions, provided they implement the most recent version incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a (RG 1.147, Sections A and B). 

In summary, ISI of RCPB piping must be performed in accordance with ASME Section XI requirements as incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a, including periodic inspections and pressure tests every ten years, with the option to use NRC-approved Code Cases as alternatives.

data.query: How do general design criteria for reactor coolant pressure boundary integrity relate to the inservice inspection requirements for small-diameter piping in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) integrity, specifically GDC 32, directly inform the inservice inspection requirements for all RCPB components, including small-diameter piping in nuclear power plants. According to DSRS 5.2.4 and Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, GDC 32 mandates that RCPB components must be designed to allow for periodic inspection and testing of important areas and features to assess their structural and leak-tight integrity. This requirement ensures that aging effects or incipient degradation can be detected early, allowing for preventive measures to maintain the integrity of the RCPB (DSRS 5.2.4, Section II; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 32).

The implementation of these criteria is operationalized through 10 CFR 50.55a, which incorporates by reference ASME Section XI. ASME Section XI specifies the intervals, scope, and methods for inservice inspection of Code Class 1 components, which include small-diameter piping if it is part of the RCPB. The code details the inspection sample, methodology, and acceptance criteria for flaws, ensuring that the structural and leak-tight integrity of all RCPB components, regardless of size, is maintained at a level comparable to initial installation (DSRS 5.2.4, Section II).

In summary, the general design criteria require that small-diameter piping, as part of the RCPB, be designed for inspectability and subject to periodic inservice inspection per ASME Section XI. This linkage ensures ongoing assurance of boundary integrity and compliance with NRC regulations (DSRS 5.2.4; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 30, 31, 32).

evidence_chain.section: II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA and Technical Rationale
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Requirements

Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations:

1. General Design Criteria (GDC) 32 found in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, as it relates to periodic inspection and testing of the RCPB;

2. 10 CFR 50.55a, as it relates to the requirements for testing and inspecting Code Class 1 components of the RCPB as specified in ASME Section XI;

...

The technical rationale for application of these acceptance criteria to the areas of review addressed by this DSRS section is discussed in the following paragraphs:

1. General Design Criterion 32 requires, in part, that all components that are part of the RCPB be designed to permit periodic inspection and testing of important areas and features to assess structural and leak-tight integrity. DSRS Section 5.2.4 is the primary DSRS section assessing compliance with GDC 32. Meeting the requirements of General Design Criterion 32 assures that an effective periodic inspection program can be performed on the RCPB, so that aging effects or other incipient degradation phenomena may be identified and preventive measures promptly taken to preclude potential loss of reactor coolant or impairment of reactor core cooling.

2. According to 10 CFR 50.55a, “Codes and Standards," structures, systems, and components (SSCs) must be designed, fabricated, erected, constructed, tested, and inspected to quality standards commensurate with the importance of the safety function they are intended to perform. Section 50.55a incorporates by reference Section XI of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code. ASME Section XI defines, for each Code Class, the intervals between inservice inspections, the scope of the inspection activity, the inspection sample, the sample selection methodology, the method of inspection, the acceptance criteria for various types and sizes of material flaws identified during the inspection, and various other related technical details required for properly performing the inservice inspection activity. Performing a periodic inspection program based on the requirements of 10 CFR 50.55a and ASME Section XI is the means of maintaining the structural integrity of the RCPB at a level of reliability comparable to that at which it was initially installed and of ensuring the structural and leak-tight integrity of the RCPB.

General Design Criterion 32—Inspection of reactor coolant pressure boundary. Components which are part of the reactor coolant pressure boundary shall be designed to permit (a) periodic inspection and testing of important areas and features to assess their structural and leaktight integrity, and (b) an appropriate material surveillance program for the reactor pressure vessel.

General Design Criterion 31—Fracture prevention of reactor coolant pressure boundary. The reactor coolant pressure boundary shall be designed with sufficient margin to assure that, when stressed under operating, maintenance, testing, and postulated accident conditions, (a) the boundary behaves in a nonbrittle manner and (b) the probability of rapidly propagating fracture is minimized. The design shall reflect consideration of service temperatures and other conditions of the boundary material under operating, maintenance, testing, and postulated accident conditions and the uncertainties in determining (1) material properties, (2) the effects of irradiation on material properties, (3) residual, steady state, and transient stresses, and (4) size of flaws.

General Design Criterion 30—Quality of reactor coolant pressure boundary. Components which are part of the reactor coolant pressure boundary shall be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to the highest quality standards practical. Means shall be provided for detecting and, to the extent practical, identifying the location of the source of reactor coolant leakage.

data.query: For nuclear power plant designs that use code exemptions for inservice inspection of small-diameter reactor coolant pressure boundary piping, what combined regulatory provisions from general design criteria, inservice inspection standards, and regulatory guides must be considered to ensure an extremely low probability of abnormal leakage or failure?
data.answer:
For nuclear power plant designs that utilize code exemptions for inservice inspection of small-diameter reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) piping, several combined regulatory provisions must be considered to ensure an extremely low probability of abnormal leakage or failure. 

First, General Design Criterion (GDC) 32 in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50 requires that RCPB components be designed to permit periodic inspection and testing of important areas, such as welds, and to provide the capability to detect, characterize, and locate flaws or failures. The design must support an extremely low probability of abnormal leakage or rapidly propagating failure (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 32; [2]).

Second, 10 CFR 50.55a mandates that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) be designed, fabricated, erected, constructed, tested, and inspected to quality standards commensurate with their safety function, specifically referencing ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section XI ([1], [3]). ASME Section XI, Subsubarticle IWB-1220, allows for certain code exemptions for components deemed exempt from examination, such as small-diameter piping, provided the criteria in IWB-1220 are met ([1]). Any exemptions taken must be clearly listed in the licensee’s program and justified per the ASME Code.

Third, Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.147 provides NRC-approved ASME Code Cases that may be used as alternatives to the mandatory ASME Code provisions incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a. Licensees must ensure that the use of any Code Case does not conflict with regulatory requirements or licensee commitments ([3]). Code Cases not specifically referenced in RG 1.147 require case-by-case NRC review and acceptance ([1]).

In summary, compliance with GDC 32, 10 CFR 50.55a (including ASME Section XI and its exemptions), and RG 1.147 (for Code Cases) is required. These provisions collectively ensure that even when code exemptions are used for small-diameter RCPB piping, the design and inspection program maintain an extremely low probability of abnormal leakage or failure, consistent with NRC safety objectives.

data.query: How do regulatory requirements for inservice inspection of Class 1 piping welds ensure the structural integrity and leak tightness of the reactor coolant pressure boundary?
data.answer:
Regulatory requirements for inservice inspection (ISI) of Class 1 piping welds are designed to ensure the structural integrity and leak tightness of the reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) through a comprehensive framework grounded in federal regulations and industry codes. According to DSRS 5.2.4, components that are part of the RCPB must be designed with access for periodic inspection and testing to assess their structural and leaktight integrity. The ISI programs are mandated by 10 CFR 50.55a, which requires compliance with the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section XI, 'Rules for Inservice Inspection of Nuclear Power Plant Components.' Specifically, all Class 1 pressure-containing components and their supports must meet the inspection requirements detailed in ASME Section XI (DSRS 5.2.4; 10 CFR 50.55a(g)).

ASME Section XI, Article IWB-2000, specifies examination categories and methods for these inspections, ensuring that every area subject to examination is covered and inspected to the extent required. Acceptance standards for examination results are provided in Article IWB-3000, and pressure-retaining component leakage and hydrostatic pressure tests are governed by Article IWB-5000. These requirements collectively ensure that the RCPB maintains a level of reliability and integrity comparable to its initial installation (DSRS 5.2.4).

Furthermore, 10 CFR 50.55a(g)(4) explicitly states that the ISI program must be established to ensure the structural integrity and leak tightness of the RCPB. The NRC may also impose additional requirements if necessary (10 CFR 50.55a(g)(7)). Regulatory Guide 1.147 provides guidance on the use of NRC-approved ASME Code Cases as acceptable alternatives, provided they do not conflict with regulatory requirements (RG 1.147).

In summary, the regulatory requirements mandate periodic, systematic inspections and tests based on ASME Section XI, as incorporated into federal regulations, to detect and address any degradation in Class 1 piping welds, thereby ensuring the ongoing structural integrity and leak tightness of the reactor coolant pressure boundary.

data.query: How do general design criteria for reactor coolant pressure boundary integrity relate to the sampling requirements for weld inspections in Class 1 piping systems?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) integrity, specifically GDC 32 in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, establish the foundational requirement that RCPB components must be designed to allow for periodic inspection and testing to assess their structural and leaktight integrity (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 32). This includes ensuring that important areas and features of the RCPB, such as Class 1 piping systems, are accessible for inspection and that means are provided for detecting and locating coolant leakage.

These design criteria directly relate to the sampling requirements for weld inspections in Class 1 piping systems by mandating that the design must facilitate the inspection of pressure-retaining components and their welds. The implementation of these requirements is governed by 10 CFR 50.55a, which incorporates by reference the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, Section XI. Specifically, DSRS 5.2.4 states that all Class 1 pressure-containing components, including piping welds, must meet the inspection requirements of ASME Section XI, Article IWB-2000. This article defines the examination categories, methods, and extent of sampling (i.e., which welds and how many must be inspected) for Class 1 piping welds.

Therefore, the general design criteria ensure that the plant is designed to permit the required sampling and inspection of welds, while the specific sampling requirements—such as which welds are inspected and how frequently—are detailed in ASME Section XI, as required by 10 CFR 50.55a and referenced in DSRS 5.2.4. The NRC Regulatory Guide 1.147 further clarifies that licensees may use NRC-approved ASME Code Cases as alternatives, provided they meet the regulatory requirements. In summary, the GDC provide the high-level requirement for inspectability, and the sampling requirements for weld inspections in Class 1 piping systems are the practical implementation of this requirement through ASME Section XI and NRC regulations.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for accessibility of reactor coolant pressure boundary nozzles for inservice inspection?
data.answer: The regulatory requirements for accessibility of reactor coolant pressure boundary nozzles for inservice inspection are established primarily through 10 CFR 50.55a and the associated ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (BPV Code), Section XI. According to 10 CFR 50.55a(g)(1), components that must be accessible for inservice inspection—including reactor coolant pressure boundary nozzles—must be designed and arranged to provide access for these activities in accordance with the applicable provisions of ASME BPV Code, Section XI. Specifically, DSRS 5.2.4 references Subarticle IWA-1500, 'Accessibility,' of ASME Section XI, which sets the criteria for adequate clearance and access. The design must ensure that sufficient clearance is provided for inspection, as outlined in Article IWB-2000, 'Examination and Inspection,' of ASME Section XI. Furthermore, for components affected by radiation fields after plant startup, such as reactor vessel nozzle interior surfaces, provisions must be made for remote inspection. The feasibility of using remote inspection devices for periodic inservice inspections must be demonstrated during the preservice baseline inspection program. The NRC reviewer verifies compliance with these requirements by reviewing descriptive information in the Safety Analysis Report (SAR) and ensuring that the design meets the DSRS acceptance criteria and ASME Section XI standards (DSRS 5.2.4, Section II.2 and III; 10 CFR 50.55a(g)(1)).

data.query: How do the requirements for inservice inspection accessibility relate to the methods of nozzle attachment to the reactor vessel and head?
data.answer:
The requirements for inservice inspection (ISI) accessibility are directly related to the methods of nozzle attachment to the reactor vessel and head, as these methods influence the ability to perform required inspections. According to DSRS 5.2.4, the design and arrangement of system components, including nozzle attachments, must provide adequate clearance for inspection in accordance with ASME Section XI, Subarticle IWA-1500, 'Accessibility.' This ensures that the geometry and configuration of nozzle attachments do not impede the ability to conduct preservice and inservice inspections, particularly for critical areas such as nozzle welds and interior surfaces. The DSRS further emphasizes that any interferences due to design, geometry, or materials of construction must be eliminated during the design stage to enable performance of ISI examinations as required by regulations (DSRS 5.2.4, Acceptance Criteria 2 and 8).

10 CFR 50.55a(b) reinforces this by requiring that reactor coolant pressure boundary components, including nozzle welds, be designed and constructed to permit periodic inspection and detection of flaws. The regulation mandates compliance with ASME Section XI for ISI, unless alternatives are authorized (10 CFR 50.55a(g), (z)). Thus, the method of nozzle attachment must not hinder accessibility for ISI, and any limitations must be addressed in the design phase to avoid the need for relief requests. In summary, nozzle attachment methods must facilitate, not obstruct, the accessibility required for ISI in accordance with ASME Section XI and NRC regulations.

data.query: How do NRC regulations address the use of alternative inspection or testing methods for components within the reactor coolant pressure boundary, and what is the relationship between these alternatives and the requirements for inservice inspection programs?
data.answer:
NRC regulations allow for the use of alternative inspection or testing methods for components within the reactor coolant pressure boundary, particularly within the context of inservice inspection (ISI) programs. According to 10 CFR 50.55a(z), alternatives to the requirements of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, Section XI, as incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a, may be used if authorized by the NRC. To obtain such authorization, the applicant or licensee must demonstrate that the proposed alternative either provides an acceptable level of quality and safety or that compliance with the existing requirements would result in hardship or unusual difficulty without a compensating increase in quality and safety (10 CFR 50.55a(z)(1); DSRS 5.2.4, II.14).

The relationship between these alternatives and the requirements for ISI programs is that alternatives, including risk-informed ISI programs or NRC-approved ASME Code Cases, can be used in place of the standard ASME Section XI provisions if they meet the criteria outlined above. Regulatory Guide 1.147 details that NRC-approved ASME Code Cases provide voluntary alternatives to the mandatory ASME Code provisions, and licensees may use these Code Cases as long as they are listed in the NRC's guidance and incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a. If a licensee wishes to use a Code Case not yet endorsed by the NRC, they must request authorization under 10 CFR 50.55a(z).

In summary, NRC regulations provide a structured process for the use of alternative inspection or testing methods within ISI programs, requiring demonstration of equivalent or improved safety and quality, and formal NRC authorization. These alternatives are closely tied to the regulatory framework governing ISI, ensuring that any deviations from standard requirements maintain the necessary safety standards (10 CFR 50.55a(z); DSRS 5.2.4, II.14; RG 1.147, Sections A and B).

evidence_chain.section: A. INTRODUCTION; B. DISCUSSION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Purpose

This regulatory guide (RG) lists the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, Section XI, “Rules for Inservice Inspection of Nuclear Power Plant Components” (Ref. 1), Code Cases that the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has approved for use as voluntary alternatives to the mandatory ASME BPV Code provisions that are incorporated by reference into Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) Part 50, “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities” (Ref. 2).

... 

The NRC incorporated this RG into 10 CFR 50.55a by reference. The RG contains new Code Cases and revisions to existing Code Cases that the NRC staff has approved for use, as listed in Tables 1 and 2 of this guide. The RG also states the requirements governing the use of Code Cases. Licensees may voluntarily use Code Cases approved by the NRC as an alternative to compliance with the ASME Code provisions that have been incorporated by reference into 10 CFR 50.55a. Because the status of Code Cases continually changes, the staff plans to periodically update 10 CFR 50.55a and this guide to accommodate new Code Cases and any revisions of existing Code Cases.

... 

Background

Provisions of the ASME BPV Code have been used since 1971 as one part of the framework to establish the necessary design, fabrication, construction, testing, and performance requirements for structures, systems, and components important to safety in nuclear power plants. Among other things, ASME standards committees develop improved methods for the construction and inservice inspection (ISI) of ASME Class 1, 2, 3, MC, and CC nuclear power plant components. ...

ASME publishes a new edition of the BPV Code, which includes Section XI, every 2 years. In 10 CFR 50.55a(a)(1)(ii), the NRC references the latest edition of Section XI, that the agency has approved for use. ASME also publishes Code Cases quarterly. Code Cases provide alternatives developed and approved by ASME. This RG identifies the Code Cases that the NRC has determined to be acceptable alternatives to applicable parts of Section XI. Under 10 CFR 50.55a(z), a licensee or applicant may request authorization to use Section XI Code Cases that the NRC has not yet endorsed. In 10 CFR 50.55a(z), the NRC permits the use of alternatives to the Code requirements referenced in 10 CFR 50.55a provided that the proposed alternatives result in an acceptable level of quality and safety and their use is authorized by the Director of the Office of Nuclear Reactor Regulation.

The NRC incorporated the ASME BPV Code by reference into 10 CFR 50.55a. NRC approved Code Cases provide an acceptable voluntary alternative to the mandatory ASME Code provisions. The regulation at 10 CFR 50.55a(b)(5) provides requirements related to the implementation of ASME Section XI Code Cases. When a licensee initially applies a Code Case listed in Table 1 or 2 of this guide, it must implement the most recent version of that Code Case incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a.

data.query: What is the regulatory process for requesting approval to use alternatives to code requirements for inservice inspection or testing of reactor coolant pressure boundary components, and how must these requests comply with NRC regulations?
data.answer:
The regulatory process for requesting approval to use alternatives to code requirements for inservice inspection (ISI) or testing of reactor coolant pressure boundary components is governed primarily by 10 CFR 50.55a(z). According to 10 CFR 50.55a(z)(1), an applicant or licensee may propose alternatives to the requirements of 10 CFR 50.55a(b)-(h) if they can demonstrate either: (i) the proposed alternative provides an acceptable level of quality and safety, or (ii) compliance with the specified requirements would result in hardship or unusual difficulty without a compensating increase in quality and safety. Such requests must be submitted and authorized by the Director, Office of Nuclear Reactor Regulation, or the Director, Office of New Reactors, prior to implementation (10 CFR 50.55a(z)(1)).

The request must include: (A) the specific requirement(s) for which the alternative is sought, (B) the proposed alternative(s), and (C) the basis for seeking authorization (DSRS 5.2.4, II.14). The NRC may impose conditions on the use of the alternative to ensure acceptable quality and safety (10 CFR 50.55a(z)(2)). Requests must be submitted in accordance with 10 CFR 50.4(a), and records of alternatives and their justifications must be maintained and available for NRC inspection (10 CFR 50.55a(z)(3)-(4)).

Additionally, when using ASME Section XI Code Cases not yet endorsed by the NRC, the applicant must ensure that the provisions do not conflict with regulatory requirements or licensee commitments (RG 1.147, B. DISCUSSION). The NRC only permits alternatives that meet the criteria outlined above and may require the use of the most recent version of a Code Case incorporated by reference (RG 1.147, B. DISCUSSION).

In summary, the process requires a detailed, justified request demonstrating compliance with NRC regulations, with NRC authorization required before implementation.

data.query: What is the NRC regulatory requirement for achieving 'essentially 100 percent' inspection coverage of the reactor coolant pressure boundary during inservice inspection programs?
data.answer: The NRC regulatory requirement for achieving 'essentially 100 percent' inspection coverage of the reactor coolant pressure boundary during inservice inspection programs is grounded in compliance with the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section XI, as mandated by 10 CFR 50.55a. Specifically, 10 CFR 50.55a(b)(2)(xxvi) requires licensees to perform inservice inspection of the reactor coolant pressure boundary in accordance with Section XI of the ASME Code, unless specific relief is granted by the Commission. Section XI, Article IWB-2000, as referenced in DSRS 5.2.4, establishes the examination categories and methods, requiring that every area subject to examination falls within one or more of these categories and is examined to at least the extent specified. For high-energy fluid system piping between containment isolation valves, DSRS 5.2.4 further clarifies that the inservice examination should provide 100% volumetric examination of circumferential and longitudinal pipe welds. Alternatives to these requirements may be authorized by the NRC if the applicant demonstrates an acceptable level of quality and safety or undue hardship without a compensating increase in safety, as per 10 CFR 50.55a(z). Therefore, the regulatory requirement is to achieve 100% inspection coverage as specified by ASME Section XI, unless a justified alternative is approved by the NRC.

data.query: How do NRC requirements for inservice inspection coverage of the reactor coolant pressure boundary relate to the acceptance criteria for inspection methods and techniques?
data.answer:
NRC requirements for inservice inspection (ISI) coverage of the reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) are closely linked to the acceptance criteria for inspection methods and techniques through a framework of regulatory and code-based standards. According to DSRS 5.2.4, acceptance criteria for ISI are based on compliance with General Design Criterion (GDC) 32 in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, which mandates that RCPB components be designed to allow periodic inspection and testing to assess their structural and leaktight integrity. This requirement ensures that inspection methods and techniques must be capable of effectively evaluating these aspects (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 32).

The NRC further requires, via 10 CFR 50.55a, that ISI of Code Class 1 components of the RCPB be performed in accordance with ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, Section XI. Specifically, DSRS 5.2.4 and RG 1.147 clarify that examination categories, methods, techniques, and procedures must align with ASME Section XI, Articles IWA-2000 and IWB-2000, which detail the required examination and inspection practices. The acceptance standards for the results of these inspections are set forth in ASME Section XI, Article IWB-3000. If defects are found, repair or replacement activities must comply with Article IWA-4000.

Additionally, RG 1.147 notes that NRC-approved ASME Code Cases may be used as voluntary alternatives, provided they do not conflict with regulatory requirements or licensee commitments. The use of these Code Cases is governed by 10 CFR 50.55a(b)(5), which requires implementation of the most recent NRC-approved version.

In summary, NRC requirements ensure that ISI coverage and acceptance criteria for inspection methods and techniques are directly tied to the ability to perform effective inspections as required by GDC 32, and must conform to the detailed standards and acceptance criteria of ASME Section XI, as incorporated by reference in NRC regulations.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
General Design Criterion 32—Inspection of reactor coolant pressure boundary. Components which are part of the reactor coolant pressure boundary shall be designed to permit (a) periodic inspection and testing of important areas and features to assess their structural and leaktight integrity, and (b) an appropriate material surveillance program for the reactor pressure vessel.

This criterion establishes that the design of the reactor coolant pressure boundary must allow for periodic inspection and testing to assess structural and leaktight integrity. The acceptance criteria for inspection methods and techniques are thus directly related to the ability to perform these inspections effectively, as required by the design criterion.

data.query: What are the NRC requirements for the inservice inspection of the reactor coolant pressure boundary?
data.answer:
The NRC requirements for the inservice inspection (ISI) of the reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) are primarily established in 10 CFR 50.55a, which mandates that ISI and testing of the RCPB be performed in accordance with the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section XI, as incorporated by reference (10 CFR 50.55a(a)(2), (g)(1)). These requirements apply to Code Class 1 components, as defined in ASME Section III, and include both the components and their supports (DSRS 5.2.4, II. Acceptance Criteria; 10 CFR 50.55a(g); RG 1.147, B. Discussion).

The ISI program must ensure that RCPB components are designed and arranged to allow periodic inspection and testing of important areas to assess structural and leaktight integrity (DSRS 5.2.4, II. Acceptance Criteria). Adequate clearance for access must be provided in accordance with ASME Section XI, Subarticle IWA-1500. The required examinations and pressure tests must be completed during each ten-year inspection interval, as specified in ASME Section XI, Article IWA-2000 (DSRS 5.2.4, II. Acceptance Criteria).

The examination categories and methods must align with ASME Section XI, Article IWB-2000, and the program must comply with the scheduling and interval provisions of Article IWA-2000 (DSRS 5.2.4, II. Acceptance Criteria). Licensees may use NRC-approved ASME Code Cases as alternatives to the mandatory ASME Code provisions, provided they do not conflict with regulatory requirements or licensee commitments (RG 1.147, B. Discussion).

In summary, the NRC requires that ISI of the RCPB be conducted in accordance with ASME Section XI, as incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a, including provisions for accessibility, inspection intervals, and examination methods, with the option to use NRC-approved Code Cases as alternatives.

data.query: How do the requirements for inservice inspection of the reactor coolant pressure boundary relate to the use of specific editions and addenda of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code?
data.answer:
The requirements for inservice inspection (ISI) of the reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) are directly tied to the use of specific editions and addenda of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, as mandated by NRC regulations. According to 10 CFR 50.55a, components of the RCPB must comply with the requirements of ASME BPV Code Section III (for construction) and Section XI (for inservice inspection), using the editions and addenda specifically incorporated by reference in the regulation (10 CFR 50.55a(a)(1)). The selection of the applicable edition and addenda is further governed by the conditions and intervals specified in 10 CFR 50.55a(b), (c), and (f).

DSRS 5.2.4 reinforces that ISI programs must meet the inspection requirements of ASME Section XI for all Class 1 pressure-containing components, with examination categories and methods aligning with Article IWB-2000 and scheduling per Article IWA-2000. The required examinations and pressure tests must be completed during each ten-year inspection interval, and the program must use the code of record (the edition and addenda in effect at the start of the interval, as required by 10 CFR 50.55a(g)(4)).

Regulatory Guide 1.147 provides further guidance on the use of ASME Code Cases as alternatives to the mandatory code provisions. Only those Code Cases listed in RG 1.147 and incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a may be used, and licensees must implement the most recent version of a Code Case at the time of application. If a Code Case is annulled by ASME and subsequently removed from NRC approval, it cannot be newly implemented, though ongoing use is permitted through the end of the current ISI code of record interval.

In summary, the ISI requirements for the RCPB are governed by the specific editions and addenda of the ASME BPV Code incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a, and any use of Code Cases must comply with NRC-approved versions as detailed in RG 1.147.

data.query: For the first 120-month inspection interval of a nuclear power plant, what combined regulatory provisions from general design criteria, NRC regulations, and regulatory guides govern the selection and implementation of ASME Code requirements for inservice inspection of the reactor coolant pressure boundary, including any conditions imposed on the use of specific code editions and addenda?
data.answer:
For the first 120-month (10-year) inspection interval of a nuclear power plant, the selection and implementation of ASME Code requirements for inservice inspection of the reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) are governed by a combination of general design criteria, NRC regulations, and regulatory guides. 

General Design Criterion (GDC) 32 in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50 requires that RCPB components be designed to permit periodic inspection and testing to assess their structural and leaktight integrity, as well as to support a material surveillance program for the reactor pressure vessel (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 32). This is implemented through compliance with ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section XI, as referenced in NRC regulations (DSRS 5.2.4; 10 CFR 50.55a).

10 CFR 50.55a(g) specifically requires that Class 1 components of the RCPB meet the requirements of ASME Section XI for inservice inspection. The inspection interval is defined as a ten-year period, and the examinations and pressure tests must be completed within each interval, following the scheduling provisions of Article IWA-2000 of ASME Section XI (DSRS 5.2.4).

The NRC imposes conditions on the use of specific ASME Code editions and addenda through 10 CFR 50.55a, which specifies which editions and addenda are acceptable and may include additional requirements or exceptions (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 32; RG 1.147). When using ASME Code Cases as alternatives to mandatory Code provisions, only those Code Cases listed in NRC Regulatory Guide 1.147 and incorporated by reference in 10 CFR 50.55a may be used, and the most recent version must be implemented (RG 1.147). Any Code Case not referenced in RG 1.147 requires case-by-case NRC review and approval (DSRS 5.2.4).

In summary, the regulatory framework for the first 120-month inspection interval requires compliance with GDC 32, 10 CFR 50.55a, ASME Section XI (with NRC-specified editions/addenda), and NRC-approved Code Cases per RG 1.147, with additional NRC conditions as specified in these documents.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory expectations for leakage detection methods used to monitor the reactor coolant pressure boundary in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory expectations for leakage detection methods used to monitor the reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) in nuclear power plants are grounded in compliance with General Design Criteria (GDC) 2, 14, and 30 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A; DSRS 5.2.5). These criteria require that leakage detection systems be designed to withstand natural phenomena, maintain the integrity of the RCPB, and ensure quality in safety-related functions. 

Specifically, NRC guidance (DSRS 5.2.5; RG 1.45) expects leakage detection systems to:
- Detect and, to the extent practical, identify the source of reactor coolant leakage.
- Monitor and collect leakage from both identifiable and unidentifiable sources separately.
- Provide adequate indicators and alarms in the main control room, allowing operators to interpret leak rates.
- Demonstrate sufficient capability, sensitivity, response time, and diversity in detection methods.

RG 1.45 outlines acceptable methods for monitoring leakage, recommending a combination of instruments and techniques to ensure effective detection and source identification. These include monitoring changes in tank/sump levels or flow rates, airborne particulate and gaseous radioactivity, containment humidity, pressure, temperature, and condensate flow from air coolers. Additional methods for source identification include humidity sensors, acoustic emission monitoring, and video surveillance within containment.

Instrumentation used for leakage detection must be designed as seismic Category I (RG 1.29), ensuring operability during seismic events, and must meet quality assurance requirements (Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 50). Accident monitoring instrumentation should follow the guidance in RG 1.97, which endorses IEEE Std. 497-2016, requiring sufficient range, accuracy, and spatial distribution of measurement points to support normal, emergency, and severe accident conditions.

In summary, NRC expects a diverse, sensitive, and reliable set of leakage detection methods, with robust instrumentation and clear operator interfaces, to promptly detect, quantify, and help locate RCPB leakage, in accordance with regulatory and guidance documents (DSRS 5.2.5, RG 1.45, RG 1.29, RG 1.97, 10 CFR Part 50).
