evidence_chain.section: Methods for Monitoring Leakage and Identifying Its Source (Section B, pages 3-4)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Effective methods for monitoring (including detecting) any leakage and locating its source are important because leakage may have the following implications: 

• It may indicate that a component no longer has adequate structural integrity. 
• It may cause degradation or corrosion of a component (other than the leaking component) as a result of the interaction between the leaking coolant and the other component. 
• It may indicate that there is an accumulation of chemical compounds (e.g., boric acid) that could invalidate various design assumptions. 
• It may contaminate work surfaces. 
• It may affect the capability of other instruments (including leakage monitoring instruments) or components.

Various instruments and methods are available for monitoring RCS leakage. The capabilities of these instruments and methods differ in terms of their response time, sensitivity, and accuracy. In addition, some instruments and methods continuously monitor for leakage, while others are for periodic use only. An effective leakage monitoring strategy will include a combination of leakage monitoring instruments and methods. Monitoring changes in the following parameters can be useful for detecting a leak, as well as quantifying the flow rate:

$ level or flow rate to tanks and sumps,
$ airborne particulate radioactivity,
$ airborne gaseous radioactivity,
$ containment atmosphere humidity,
$ containment atmosphere pressure and temperature, and
$ condensate flow rate from air coolers.

Because of the need to identify the source of leakage to assess its safety significance, plants should install monitoring systems to assist in locating the source of leakage during reactor operation. Plants can accomplish this, in part, by installing a number of instruments throughout containment and monitoring the response of each of these instruments to leakage. An instrument that is closer to a leak is likely to respond sooner than an instrument that is further away, assuming that the two instruments have similar capabilities (e.g., sensitivity). The following examples illustrate some other methods for identifying the source of leakage:

$ humidity sensors mounted on specific component surfaces,
$ acoustic emission monitoring systems mounted on specific component surfaces, and
$ online surveillance via radiation-resistant video cameras throughout the containment.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory guides for leakage detection instrumentation relate to the requirements for leak-before-break applications in main steam and feedwater piping within containment?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory guides for leakage detection instrumentation are closely linked to the requirements for leak-before-break (LBB) applications in main steam and feedwater piping within containment. According to DSRS 5.2.5, when leakage detection systems are used to support LBB, the NRC reviewer verifies compliance with SRP Section 3.6.3, focusing on the leakage detection limit, detector sensitivity, and capability. Specifically, for LBB, the detection system must demonstrate a margin of 10 for sensitivity and capability, which may be more stringent than the general requirements in RG 1.45 (DSRS 5.2.5, item 12).

RG 1.45 further clarifies that, for LBB applications, the leakage monitoring system’s response time and sensitivity must be sufficient to support the LBB analysis. In some cases, especially for smaller diameter pipes, the system specifications may need to exceed the quantitative criteria outlined in RG 1.45 to ensure timely and reliable detection (RG 1.45, Capability, Operability, and Availability of Monitoring Instruments).

Additionally, RG 1.29 designates portions of the main steam and feedwater systems within containment as seismic Category I, requiring them to remain functional during seismic events. This includes accident monitoring instrumentation, which must meet the criteria in RG 1.97 (RG 1.29, C.1). RG 1.97, in turn, endorses IEEE Std. 497-2016, specifying that accident monitoring instrumentation must have sufficient range and margin to cover normal, accident, and severe accident conditions (RG 1.97, C. STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE).

In summary, NRC regulatory guides require that leakage detection instrumentation for LBB applications in main steam and feedwater piping within containment meet enhanced sensitivity, response time, and reliability criteria, potentially exceeding standard guidance, and be robust against seismic and accident conditions as outlined in RG 1.45, RG 1.29, and RG 1.97.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for welding procedures and inspections of reactor coolant pressure boundary components?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for welding procedures and inspections of reactor coolant pressure boundary components are grounded in a combination of ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (B&PV) Code requirements, NRC regulatory guides, and quality assurance standards. According to DSRS 5.3.1 (Section II), only welding processes qualified per ASME Code Sections III and IX may be used, with records maintained as required by NB-4300 of Section III. For ferritic steels, ASME Code criteria are supplemented by RG 1.50, which requires welding procedure specifications to define maximum interpass and minimum preheat temperatures, with production welding monitored to ensure these limits are maintained. Failure to meet these requirements may result in weld rejection unless soundness is demonstrated by ASME Code-compliant examination (RG 1.50, Section C).

For austenitic stainless steels, ASME Code requirements are supplemented by RG 1.31 (control of ferrite content), RG 1.34 (electroslag weld properties), and RG 1.44 (control of sensitization). RG 1.44 specifies that welding practices must avoid excessive sensitization by controlling heat input and interpass temperature, and requires intergranular corrosion testing (e.g., ASTM A-262) for procedures involving material with carbon content greater than 0.03%. Additionally, RG 1.28 and ASME NQA-1 standards require quality assurance controls for cleaning and contamination prevention to avoid stress corrosion cracking.

All welding and inspection activities must be performed under a quality assurance program meeting Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 50 and General Design Criterion 1 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A), ensuring that all records are maintained throughout the plant's life. The NRC recognizes ASME accreditation for QA programmatic aspects but requires effective implementation by suppliers (RG 1.28).

In summary, NRC acceptance criteria require compliance with ASME Code Sections III and IX, supplemented by specific NRC regulatory guides (RGs 1.28, 1.31, 1.34, 1.43, 1.44, 1.50), and implementation of a robust QA program per Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 50.

data.query: How do NRC requirements for welding controls interact with inspection requirements for components that form part of the reactor coolant pressure boundary?
data.answer:
NRC requirements for welding controls and inspection of components forming part of the reactor coolant pressure boundary are closely integrated to ensure the integrity and safety of these critical components. Welding controls are established to ensure that welds meet stringent quality standards, as required by General Design Criterion 1 (GDC 1) in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, which mandates that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function. 

According to DSRS 5.3.1, welding processes for ferritic and austenitic steels must comply with the qualification requirements of ASME Code Sections III and IX. Only those welding processes capable of producing welds in accordance with these requirements may be used, and detailed records must be maintained as specified in NB-4300 of Section III. Special attention is given to the welding of dissimilar metal joints and controls for abrasive work to prevent contamination and excessive cold-working.

Inspection requirements, particularly nondestructive examination (NDE), are also governed by ASME Code Section III (e.g., NB-2580 and NB-5000), and must be performed according to these standards, supplemented by NRC regulatory guidance such as RG 1.65. The adequacy of welding controls is directly linked to inspection requirements: if welding controls (such as preheat and interpass temperature limits) are not met, the weld may be subject to rejection unless its soundness can be demonstrated by acceptable examination procedures meeting ASME Code acceptance criteria (RG 1.50, Regulatory Position 4).

Furthermore, NRC-endorsed quality assurance programs (e.g., NQA-1 as referenced in RG 1.28) require that both welding and inspection activities be planned, controlled, and documented to ensure compliance with regulatory and code requirements throughout the component's life. Thus, NRC requirements for welding controls and inspection are mutually reinforcing, with compliance to both being necessary to assure the quality and safety of reactor coolant pressure boundary components.

evidence_chain.section: Regulatory Position (Section C), and Discussion (Section B)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
All welding processes will result in some carbide precipitation in the weld metal and in the base metal heat-affected zone of stainless steel welds, but significant sensitization does not normally result when typical welding procedures and material chemistry are used and when no further heating of material occurs. However, there is evidence that atypical welding methods using very high heat input could result in stress-corrosion cracking in the heat-affected zone of the weld. To avoid this, the welding procedures and material chemistry (if necessary) should be controlled to prevent undue sensitization of the heat-affected zones of the weldments. Controls to prevent sensitization of the material during welding may include the following:

a. avoiding welding practices that result in the generation of high heat;  
b. maintaining low heat input by controlling current, voltage, and travel speed;  
c. limiting interpass temperature;  
d. using stringer bead techniques and avoiding excessive weaving; and  
e. limiting the carbon level of the material where section thickness makes the material more prone to sensitization.

In addition, welding procedures should be qualified by passing a suitable intergranular corrosion test in all cases where the procedure is used for welding stainless steel having a carbon level greater than 0.03 percent. The qualification test should be performed using base material with the maximum carbon content anticipated and the minimum and maximum thicknesses anticipated.

At minimum, the qualification test should control the variables of heat input, interpass temperature, and welding techniques for specific section thicknesses.

data.query: In the context of reactor vessel materials, what regulatory provisions and review standards must be considered to ensure that construction and preservice inspection requirements for non-standard components, such as threaded inserts and their seal welds, provide an equivalent level of assurance as required for other reactor coolant pressure boundary components?
data.answer:
To ensure that construction and preservice inspection requirements for non-standard reactor vessel components, such as threaded inserts and their seal welds, provide an equivalent level of assurance as required for other reactor coolant pressure boundary components, several regulatory provisions and review standards must be considered:

1. General Design Criteria (GDC) 1 and 30, and 10 CFR 50.55a, require that quality standards be met by compliance with the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section III (DSRS 5.3.1, II.A). Acceptable materials and fabrication processes are those identified in Section III, Appendix I, and must also meet 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix G, where applicable. For materials or components not specified in the Code, their suitability must be evaluated individually, with supporting data on mechanical properties, weldability, and physical changes, per Section III, Appendix IV-1000 (DSRS 5.3.1, II.B).

2. All reactor vessel components, including non-standard items, must be fabricated and installed in accordance with ASME Code Section III, Paragraph NB-4100, and certified per Article NCA-8000 (DSRS 5.3.1). Nondestructive examination acceptance criteria are specified in Section III, NB-5000.

3. 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, requires that all safety-related components be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function. Recognized codes and standards must be evaluated for adequacy and supplemented as necessary. A quality assurance program per Appendix B must be established and maintained (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1).

4. Regulatory Guide 1.44 provides additional criteria for austenitic stainless steel components, including requirements for material cleaning, heat treatment, verification of nonsensitization, welding controls, and intergranular corrosion testing to prevent stress-corrosion cracking (RG 1.44, C. REGULATORY POSITION).

5. Regulatory Guide 1.28 endorses the use of ASME NQA-1 standards for quality assurance during design and construction, and recognizes ASME accreditation as evidence of a compliant QA program, provided effective implementation is ensured (RG 1.28, C. STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE).

In summary, non-standard components must be evaluated and qualified to the same standards as Code-listed items, with appropriate documentation, QA, and inspection processes to ensure equivalent assurance of safety and integrity.

This regulatory guide (RG) describes methods that the staff of the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) considers acceptable for complying with the provisions of Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) Part 50, “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities”, and 10 CFR Part 52, “Licenses, Certifications, and Approvals for Nuclear Power Plants”, which refer to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, “Quality Assurance Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants and Fuel Reprocessing Plants,” for establishing and implementing a quality assurance (QA) program for the design and construction of nuclear power plants and fuel reprocessing plants.

... 

The NRC staff endorses the Part I and Part II requirements included in NQA-1-2017, NQA-1-2019, and NQA-1-2022 for the implementation of a QA program during the design and construction phases of nuclear power plants and fuel reprocessing plants. They provide an adequate basis for complying with the requirements of Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 50, subject to the exceptions and clarifications of NQA-1-2017, NQA-1-2019, and NQA-1-2022 identified below. ...

Note: The NRC recognizes the ASME Accreditation Program and associated certificates of authorization as evidence that the holder of the certificate of authorization has a documented QA program that meets the requirements of Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 50. However, recognition of the ASME Accreditation Program applies only to the programmatic aspects of the QA programs. Applicants and licensees or their subcontractors should ensure that the suppliers are effectively implementing their approved QA programs.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for the mechanical properties of reactor vessel internal components such as threaded inserts?
data.answer: The NRC regulatory requirements for the mechanical properties of reactor vessel internal components, such as threaded inserts, are primarily based on compliance with quality standards and material specifications as outlined in several regulatory documents. According to DSRS 5.3.1, the material specifications for reactor vessel attachments and appurtenances—including components like threaded inserts—are reviewed for adequacy based on their mechanical and physical properties, effects of irradiation, corrosion resistance, and fabricability. The acceptance criteria require that these materials meet the relevant requirements of General Design Criteria (GDC) 1 and 30 from Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, as well as 10 CFR 50.55a, by complying with the provisions of the ASME Code, Section III. Specifically, acceptable materials are those identified in ASME Code, Section III, Appendix I, and, where applicable, must also meet the requirements of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix G. If materials not specified in the Code are used, their suitability must be evaluated individually, with supporting data on mechanical properties, weldability, and physical changes submitted per Code Section III, Appendix IV-1000 and, where applicable, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix G. Furthermore, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, requires that all structures, systems, and components important to safety—including reactor vessel internals—be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function, with appropriate records maintained throughout the life of the unit. In summary, the NRC requires that the mechanical properties of reactor vessel internal components such as threaded inserts be demonstrated to meet the applicable ASME Code standards and NRC regulations to ensure safety and reliability.

data.query: How do NRC regulations ensure that reactor vessel threaded inserts are designed to withstand mechanical loads during both normal and emergency core cooling system actuation conditions?
data.answer:
NRC regulations ensure that reactor vessel threaded inserts (fasteners) are designed to withstand mechanical loads during both normal and emergency core cooling system actuation conditions through a combination of material selection, design, fabrication, testing, and quality assurance requirements. According to DSRS 5.3.1, Section II, the NRC reviews the mechanical properties of fasteners, including fracture toughness, to ensure adequacy under service and shutdown conditions. Acceptance criteria are established by Appendix G to 10 CFR Part 50 and Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.65, which reference the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code Section III. Specifically, suitable materials (e.g., SA-540, SA-193, SA-194, SA-320 grades) are identified, and limits are set on ultimate tensile strength (not exceeding 1170 MPa) and yield strength (not exceeding 1034 MPa per RG 1.65).

Fracture toughness testing and nondestructive examination are required per ASME BPV Code Section III, NB-2300 and NB-2580, to verify the integrity of the fasteners. Surface treatments and lubricants must be compatible and stable at operating temperatures to prevent degradation such as stress-corrosion cracking. The design and fabrication of threaded inserts must comply with ASME BPV Code Section III, articles NB-3000 (Design) and NB-4000 (Fabrication and Installation), as well as EPRI NP-6316 guidelines (RG 1.65, Section C).

General Design Criterion 1 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) further requires that all safety-related components, including reactor vessel fasteners, be designed, fabricated, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function, and that appropriate records be maintained. Collectively, these requirements ensure that reactor vessel threaded inserts are capable of withstanding mechanical loads during both normal operation and emergency conditions, such as actuation of the emergency core cooling system.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for the design and installation of threaded inserts used in the reactor coolant pressure boundary to ensure structural integrity?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for the design and installation of threaded inserts used in the reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) to ensure structural integrity are grounded in several regulatory requirements and guidance documents. According to DSRS 5.3.1 (Section II), the criteria for reactor vessel fasteners—which include threaded inserts—are established by paragraph IV.A of Appendix G to 10 CFR Part 50 and the recommendations of Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.65. These criteria are intended to satisfy the quality standards of General Design Criteria (GDC) 1 and 30, as well as the fracture prevention requirements of GDC 31 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A).

Specifically, RG 1.65 (Section C) requires that the design of threaded fasteners comply with Section III, Article NB-3000 (Design) of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel (BPV) Code, and their fabrication and installation comply with Article NB-4000 (Fabrication and Installation) of the same code. Materials must meet the requirements of Section II of the ASME Code, with suitable grades specified (e.g., SA-540 Grades B-23/B-24, SA-193 Grade B-7, etc.), and must not exceed an ultimate tensile strength of 1170 MPa (170 ksi). Fracture toughness testing and acceptance levels per NB-2333 are also required.

Surface treatments, plating, or lubricants must be compatible with the materials and stable at operating temperatures. Nondestructive examination must be performed per Section III, Subsubarticle NB-2580 of the ASME Code, with additional recommendations from RG 1.65. Furthermore, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, requires that all structures, systems, and components important to safety—including threaded inserts—be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function, with appropriate records maintained throughout the unit's life.

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria for threaded inserts in the RCPB require compliance with ASME BPV Code Section III (NB-3000 and NB-4000), use of qualified materials, fracture toughness and nondestructive testing, compatibility of surface treatments, and adherence to quality standards and recordkeeping as outlined in 10 CFR Part 50 and RG 1.65.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for residual heat removal systems regarding the removal of decay heat following a reactor shutdown?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for residual heat removal (RHR) systems, which are responsible for removing decay heat following a reactor shutdown, are grounded in several key regulations and guidance documents. According to DSRS 5.4.7, the RHR system must meet the requirements of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criteria (GDC), specifically GDC 34, which mandates that a system be provided to remove residual heat from the reactor core so that specified fuel design limits and reactor coolant pressure boundary conditions are not exceeded. The operation of the RHR must be coordinated with other safety systems to ensure adequate heat removal rates (DSRS 5.4.7, Section II). 

Additionally, GDC 1 requires that RHR systems be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function, with a quality assurance program in place and appropriate records maintained (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1). Regulatory Guide 1.26 further specifies that RHR system components should meet ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section III, Class 2 standards (Quality Group B), ensuring robust construction and reliability (RG 1.26, Table 1). 

Furthermore, Regulatory Guide 1.29 designates RHR systems as seismic Category I, meaning they must be capable of withstanding the Safe Shutdown Earthquake (SSE) and remain functional to ensure continued removal of decay heat under seismic conditions (RG 1.29, Section C). These requirements collectively ensure that the RHR system is capable of reliably removing decay heat after shutdown, maintaining core and containment integrity, and protecting public health and safety.

data.query: How do regulatory requirements for residual heat removal systems address the need to consider limiting initial conditions, such as maximum allowable pool temperature, in safety analyses?
data.answer: Regulatory requirements for residual heat removal (RHR) systems explicitly address the need to consider limiting initial conditions, such as the maximum allowable pool temperature, in safety analyses. According to DSRS 5.4.7, the review of the decay heat removal (DHR) function must encompass all conditions from shutdown at normal reactor coolant system (RCS) power operating pressure and temperature to safe shutdown. This includes a detailed evaluation of the DHR heat exchanger's cooling capacity for all anticipated operating conditions. The DSRS further specifies that the organization responsible for evaluating the reactor building pool must review the pool support systems that establish the initial conditions of the ultimate heat sink (UHS), which includes the maximum pool temperature. The acceptance criteria in DSRS 5.4.7 require that the DHR system conform to General Design Criterion (GDC) 5, particularly regarding the determination of maximum pool temperature in scenarios involving multiple unit shutdowns or a combination of shutdowns and a loss of coolant accident. This ensures that the RHR system is capable of maintaining safe conditions even under the most limiting initial conditions. Additionally, operation of the DHR system must be coordinated with the emergency core cooling system (ECCS) to ensure that residual heat is removed at a rate that prevents exceeding specified fuel design limits and reactor coolant pressure boundary design conditions, as required by GDC 34. GDC 5 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) further reinforces that any sharing of safety-related systems must not impair their ability to perform safety functions, including under limiting initial conditions. Thus, regulatory requirements mandate that safety analyses for RHR systems explicitly consider and address limiting initial conditions such as maximum allowable pool temperature.

data.query: What are the NRC requirements for the capability of residual heat removal systems to withstand a single failure and continue to perform their safety function?
data.answer:
The NRC requires that residual heat removal (RHR) systems, also referred to as decay heat removal (DHR) systems, be capable of withstanding a single failure and continue to perform their safety function. According to DSRS 5.4.7, the review of the DHR function must ensure that the system can accomplish cooldown from normal reactor coolant system (RCS) operating conditions to safe shutdown, even in the event of a single failure. This is achieved by providing suitable redundancy in components and features, as specified in DSRS Branch Technical Position (BTP) 5-4 (Functional Requirement Item B). The DHR system must also meet the functional, isolation, pressure relief, and test requirements outlined in DSRS BTP 5-4 and General Design Criterion (GDC) 1.

GDC 1, as found in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, further requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety—including the RHR system—be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function. A quality assurance program must be established to ensure these systems will satisfactorily perform their safety functions, and appropriate records must be maintained throughout the life of the unit.

In summary, NRC requirements mandate that the RHR system be designed with sufficient redundancy to ensure it can perform its safety function in the presence of a single failure, and that it adheres to rigorous quality standards and assurance programs as specified in DSRS 5.4.7 and GDC 1 of 10 CFR Part 50.

data.query: How do the general design criteria for residual heat removal systems address the use of non-safety related components, such as isolation valves, in ensuring system reliability during postulated accidents?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for residual heat removal (RHR) systems address the use of non-safety related components, such as isolation valves, by establishing rigorous requirements to ensure system reliability during postulated accidents. According to DSRS 5.4.7, the design of the RHR system must conform to several GDCs (including GDC 1, 2, 4, 5, 14, 19, 34, 54, and 57) as outlined in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50. Specifically, GDC 1 requires that all structures, systems, and components important to safety—including isolation valves—be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function, and that a quality assurance program be implemented (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1).

For containment penetrations, DSRS 6.2.4 clarifies that the GDCs generally require two isolation valves in series to maintain the isolation function, even in the event of a single active failure. However, a single isolation valve may be acceptable if it can be demonstrated that system reliability is greater, the system is closed outside containment, and a single active failure can be accommodated. In such cases, the closed system must meet stringent design standards (e.g., seismic Category I, Group B quality, appropriate temperature and pressure ratings) and be protected from external hazards. Leak testing or demonstration of system integrity during normal operations is also required. Additionally, sealed-closed barriers (such as blind flanges or sealed-closed isolation valves) may be used in place of automatic isolation valves, provided they are under strict administrative control to prevent inadvertent opening.

In summary, the GDCs and associated DSRS guidance ensure that even if non-safety related components like isolation valves are used, their design, quality assurance, and administrative controls must collectively ensure the reliability of the RHR system during postulated accidents (DSRS 5.4.7; DSRS 6.2.4; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1).

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for residual heat removal systems to ensure removal of post-shutdown decay heat in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for residual heat removal (RHR) systems, also referred to as decay heat removal (DHR) systems, are established to ensure the safe removal of post-shutdown decay heat in nuclear power plants. These requirements are primarily grounded in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criteria (GDC), and are further detailed in NRC guidance documents.

Key requirements include:

1. Quality Standards and Records (GDC 1): RHR systems must be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function. A quality assurance program must be implemented, and appropriate records maintained throughout the plant's life (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 1; [2]). Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.26 specifies that RHR system components should meet ASME BPV Code, Section III, Class 2 standards (Quality Group B) for pressure vessels, piping, pumps, and valves ([3], Table 1).

2. Protection Against Natural Phenomena (GDC 2): RHR systems must be capable of withstanding natural events such as earthquakes, tornadoes, hurricanes, and floods. RG 1.29 designates RHR systems as seismic Category I, requiring them to remain functional during and after a safe shutdown earthquake (SSE) ([1], [4]).

3. Environmental and Dynamic Effects (GDC 4): Design features and procedures must prevent damage from environmental and dynamic effects, such as water hammer ([1]).

4. Independence and Sharing (GDC 5): Safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) performing RHR functions must not be shared between modules unless it can be demonstrated that sharing does not impair safety ([1]).

5. Control and Operation (GDC 19): Operators must be able to control RHR from the control room and an alternate shutdown location ([1]).

6. Functional Requirements (GDC 34): The RHR system must remove residual heat at a rate that prevents exceeding fuel design limits and reactor coolant pressure boundary conditions ([1]).

7. Containment Penetrations (GDC 54): Piping systems penetrating containment must have leak detection, isolation, and containment capabilities ([1]).

Additionally, compliance with requirements for automatic initiation during anticipated transients without scram (10 CFR 50.62) and for station blackout (10 CFR 50.63) is required ([1]).

In summary, NRC regulations require RHR systems to be robust, seismically qualified, constructed to high quality standards, and capable of reliably removing decay heat under a range of post-shutdown conditions, with appropriate controls, testing, and containment features.

data.query: How do general design criteria for core cooling and residual heat removal address scenarios where the system may be required to remove both decay heat and ongoing fission power during certain transients?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for core cooling and residual heat removal (RHR) address scenarios where the system may be required to remove both decay heat and ongoing fission power during certain transients by mandating robust, redundant, and quality-assured systems capable of handling a range of operating and accident conditions. According to DSRS 5.4.7, the Decay Heat Removal System (DHR) is designed to provide secondary-side cooling during non-LOCA design basis events, such as loss of main feedwater, and is required to function from normal operating conditions through safe shutdown. The DHR, in coordination with the Emergency Core Cooling System (ECCS), must be capable of removing heat at a rate that ensures fuel design limits and reactor coolant pressure boundary conditions are not exceeded, as required by GDC 34 (DSRS 5.4.7).

DSRS 6.3 further clarifies that the ECCS must have sufficient capacity and capability to assure core cooling during anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs) and postulated accidents, including scenarios where both decay heat and residual fission power are present (GDC 17, 27, 35). The ECCS and DHR systems must be able to withstand single failures and provide long-term cooling, with acceptance criteria based on 10 CFR 50.46 and GDC 35, 36, and 37. These criteria ensure that the systems can transfer heat from the core to prevent fuel and clad damage, maintain coolable core geometry, and provide long-term cooling (DSRS 6.3).

Regulatory Guide 1.82 and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, reinforce these requirements by specifying that long-term core cooling must be assured (10 CFR 50.46(b)(5)), and that emergency core cooling and containment heat removal systems must be provided and evaluated for both LOCA and certain non-LOCA events (GDC 35, 38). The design must address challenges such as debris, hydraulic effects, and pump operability during long-term recirculation (RG 1.82).

In summary, the GDCs and associated regulatory guidance require that core cooling and RHR systems be designed to remove both decay heat and ongoing fission power during transients, ensuring safety margins are maintained under all anticipated conditions.

evidence_chain.section: A. INTRODUCTION and B. DISCUSSION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Applicable Regulations

• 10 CFR Part 50 provides regulations for licensing production and utilization facilities.  

o 10 CFR 50.46(b)(5) requires that licensees of nuclear power plants provide long-term cooling of the reactor core. 

...

o 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 35, “Emergency core cooling,” requires that systems be provided to perform emergency core cooling following any loss of reactor coolant.   

o 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 38, “Containment heat removal,” requires that a system be provided to perform containment heat removal following any loss of coolant accident.

...

Background
Long-term recirculation cooling raises four primary safety concerns following a LOCA: 
(1)  LOCA-generated and pre-LOCA debris materials may be transported to the ECCS strainers, the downstream components in the ECCS, the containment spray system (CSS), and the reactor core, resulting in adverse heat transfer, blockage, or wear effects, or some combination of all three,  
(2)  There may be post-LOCA hydraulic effects, particularly air ingestion (e.g., through vortexing or deaeration) and flashing. Gas that may exist in system piping downstream of the strainers could be a concern when recirculation is initiated. Activities in response to Generic Letter (GL) 2008-01, “Managing Gas Accumulation in Emergency Core Cooling, Decay Heat Removal, and Containment Spray Systems,” dated January 11, 2008 (Ref. 5), address this issue. 
(3)  The combination of Items (1) and (2) may affect long-term recirculation pump operability (i.e., it may affect NPSH available at the pump inlet).  
(4)  CAP may be used in determining the NPSH margin for the ECCS and containment heat removal pumps.  
These ECCS safety concerns extend to the CSSs for plants with containment designs in which the CSS draws suction from the water supply used for long-term recirculation. In some plant designs (e.g., PWR sub-atmospheric containments), the CSS draws from the recirculation sump much earlier than the ECCS. In other plant designs, the CSS switches the pump suction to the recirculation sump after the ECCS pumps are switched. Some designs provide CSS through the residual heat removal (RHR) system, either directly or by supplying the CSS pumps from the RHR pump discharge.  
For some plant designs, high-energy line breaks (HELBs) that are not LOCAs, such as main steamline breaks, require recirculation from the long-term water source. For these plants, non-LOCA HELBs that require recirculation should be evaluated using the same criteria and methodology (as appropriate for the HELB conditions, duration, and consequences) as those for pipe breaks that result in a LOCA.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for demonstrating the capability of residual heat removal systems to perform their safety function in as-built nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for demonstrating the capability of residual heat removal (RHR) systems to perform their safety function in as-built nuclear power plants are grounded in multiple regulations and criteria. According to DSRS 5.4.7 (Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA), the review of the RHR (or DHR) function must encompass all operational conditions from shutdown at normal reactor coolant system (RCS) pressure and temperature to safe shutdown. The cooling capacity of the RHR heat exchanger must be evaluated for all anticipated operating conditions. 

The design and demonstration of RHR system capability must conform to the General Design Criteria (GDCs) in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, specifically GDCs 1, 2, 4, 5, 14, 19, 34, 44, 45, 46, 54, and 57. These criteria address quality standards, protection against natural phenomena, environmental and dynamic effects, sharing of systems, reactor coolant pressure boundary, control room requirements, residual heat removal, cooling water systems, inspection and testing, containment penetrations, and isolation valves. 

Additionally, compliance with 10 CFR 50.62 (ATWS events), 10 CFR 50.63 (station blackout), and 10 CFR 20.1406 (minimization of contamination and waste) is required. For as-built plants, 10 CFR 52.47(b)(1) and 10 CFR 52.80(a) require that inspections, tests, analyses, and acceptance criteria (ITAACs) be established and met to provide reasonable assurance that the plant is constructed and will operate in accordance with the licensing basis and NRC regulations. 

Furthermore, as per 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1, RHR systems must be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function, with a quality assurance program in place and appropriate records maintained throughout the plant's life. 

In summary, demonstrating RHR system capability requires meeting detailed design, quality, testing, and operational criteria as specified in the referenced regulations and GDCs, with comprehensive documentation and verification through ITAACs and quality assurance records.

data.query: How do NRC regulations address the verification of as-built residual heat removal system performance through testing, and how does this relate to the general design criteria for decay heat removal?
data.answer:
NRC regulations require that the as-built performance of the residual heat removal (RHR) system—also known as the decay heat removal (DHR) system—be verified through a structured program of inspections, tests, analyses, and acceptance criteria (ITAAC). According to DSRS 5.4.7, the NRC staff reviews the applicant’s proposed ITAAC for the DHR system to ensure that all safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) are identified and addressed, as outlined in SRP Section 14.3. The review includes ensuring that preoperational and initial startup test programs will demonstrate the DHR system’s ability to remove core residual heat, as required by General Design Criterion (GDC) 34 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A).

GDC 34 specifically mandates that the RHR system must be capable of transferring sufficient heat from the reactor core after shutdown and under accident conditions, ensuring that fuel design limits and reactor coolant pressure boundary conditions are not exceeded. The criterion also requires that the system be designed for periodic inspection and testing to assure its integrity and capability to perform its required function.

DSRS 14.2 further details that preoperational tests must demonstrate the capability of SSCs to meet performance requirements and design criteria. Applicants must provide test abstracts describing objectives, methods, monitored parameters, and acceptance criteria to verify the functional adequacy of the DHR system. For new or unique design features, specific functional testing requirements and acceptance criteria must be submitted for NRC review and approval.

Additionally, RG 1.26 and 10 CFR 50.55a require that safety-related SSCs be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function, referencing the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code for applicable standards. This ensures that the DHR system is constructed and tested to recognized codes and standards, supporting the general design criteria for decay heat removal.

In summary, NRC regulations require verification of as-built DHR system performance through ITAAC and preoperational testing, directly supporting the general design criteria for decay heat removal by ensuring the system’s capability, integrity, and compliance with quality standards (DSRS 5.4.7, DSRS 14.2, 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A GDC 34, RG 1.26).

data.query: What are the regulatory acceptance criteria for residual heat removal systems in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The regulatory acceptance criteria for residual heat removal (RHR) systems in nuclear power plants are established to ensure that these systems can reliably perform their safety-related functions under all conditions, including normal operation, shutdown, and accident scenarios. According to DSRS 5.4.7 Section II, the acceptance criteria are based on compliance with several key requirements from 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criteria (GDC), and related regulations:

1. Quality Standards: RHR systems must be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards appropriate to their safety function, as required by GDC 1 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1) and supported by a quality assurance program with comprehensive records (see also [2]).
2. Protection Against Natural Phenomena: The system must withstand natural events such as earthquakes, tornadoes, hurricanes, and floods (GDC 2).
3. Environmental and Dynamic Effects: Design features and procedures must prevent damage from environmental and dynamic effects, such as water hammer (GDC 4).
4. Independence: Safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) should not be shared between modules unless it can be demonstrated that sharing does not impair safety functions (GDC 5).
5. Reactor Coolant Pressure Boundary: The system must demonstrate an extremely low failure probability for the reactor coolant pressure boundary (GDC 14).
6. Control Room Access: Operators must be able to control the RHR system from the control room and an alternate shutdown location (GDC 19).
7. Heat Removal Capability: The RHR system must remove residual heat at a rate that prevents exceeding fuel design limits and pressure boundary conditions (GDC 34).
8. Cooling Water and Containment: The system must meet requirements for cooling water supply, inspection, testing, and containment penetration, including leak detection and isolation (GDC 44, 45, 46, 54, 57).
9. Additional Requirements: The system must address automatic initiation during anticipated transients without scram (10 CFR 50.62), station blackout recovery (10 CFR 50.63), and minimization of contamination and radioactive waste (10 CFR 20.1406).

These criteria are further detailed in DSRS Branch Technical Position 5-4 and require applicants to demonstrate compliance through inspections, tests, analyses, and acceptance criteria as specified in 10 CFR 52.47(b)(1) and 52.80(a).

DSRS Acceptance Criteria

Specific DSRS acceptance criteria acceptable to meet the relevant requirements of the NRC’s regulations identified above are set forth below.  The DSRS is not a substitute for the NRC’s regulations, and compliance with it is not required.  As an alternative, and as described in more detail below, an applicant may identify the differences between a DSRS section and the design features (DC and COL applications only), analytical techniques, and procedural measures proposed in an application and discuss how the proposed alternative provides an acceptable method of complying with the NRC regulations that underlie the DSRS acceptance criteria.

1. The DHR should satisfy the functional, isolation, pressure relief, and test requirements specified in DSRS Branch Technical Position (BTP) 5-4 and GDC 1.

2. The DHR should be capable of withstanding the effects of natural phenomena like earthquakes, tornadoes, hurricanes, and floods to meet the requirements of GDC 2.

3. To meet the requirements of GDC 4, Design features and operating procedures should be provided to prevent damaging water hammer caused by such mechanisms as voided lines.

4. To meet the requirements of GDC 5, SSCs performing a safety function must not be shared between modules of a multi-module  site, unless it can be shown that such sharing will not significantly impair the ability of the SSCs to perform their safety functions.

5. Extremely low failure probability of the reactor coolant pressure boundary must be demonstrated to meet the requirements of GDC 14.

6. Controls should be available to the operator to provide for DHR from the control room and an alternate shutdown location outside the control room during normal and shutdown operations as required by GDC 19.

7. Operation of the DHR should be coordinated with the operation of the ECCS passive decay heat removal system to provide for RHR from the reactor core at a rate such that specified fuel design limits and design conditions of the reactor coolant pressure boundary are not exceeded as required by GDC 34.

data.query: How do general design criteria for decay heat removal and requirements for post-accident testing interact to ensure the safety function of residual heat removal systems?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for decay heat removal (DHR) and the requirements for post-accident testing interact to ensure the safety function of residual heat removal systems through a comprehensive framework of design, quality assurance, and verification testing. According to DSRS 5.4.7, the DHR system must be designed to function under all conditions from normal shutdown to safe shutdown, with its design conforming to multiple GDCs in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, including GDC 1 (Quality Standards and Records), GDC 34 (Residual Heat Removal), and GDC 46 (Testing of Cooling Water System), among others. These criteria require that the DHR system be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to standards commensurate with its safety importance (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 1).

The interaction is operationalized through rigorous preoperational and initial startup testing, as outlined in DSRS 14.2 and RG 1.68. Preoperational tests, conducted before fuel loading, and initial startup tests, conducted during and after fuel activities, are designed to demonstrate that the DHR system and related SSCs can meet their performance requirements and design criteria under both normal and post-accident conditions. These tests must include objectives, methods, monitored parameters, and acceptance criteria sufficient to establish the functional adequacy of the DHR system (DSRS 14.2). Furthermore, Criterion XI of Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 50 requires a test program to ensure all safety-related SSCs are tested according to written procedures that reflect design requirements (RG 1.68).

In summary, the GDCs establish the foundational safety and quality requirements for DHR systems, while post-accident testing requirements ensure these systems are verified to perform their safety functions under all relevant conditions, thereby providing reasonable assurance of plant safety.

data.query: For a passive safety system designed to remove decay heat, what combined regulatory requirements from design criteria, review standards, and regulatory guides govern the verification of as-built system thermal performance through pre-operational testing?
data.answer:
The verification of as-built thermal performance for a passive safety system designed to remove decay heat is governed by a combination of regulatory requirements from design criteria, review standards, and regulatory guides. The primary regulatory basis is found in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, specifically General Design Criteria (GDC) 1, 34, and 46, which require that safety-related systems be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function, including provisions for residual heat removal and testing of cooling water systems (DSRS 5.4.7; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A).

Pre-operational testing requirements are further detailed in Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.68, which specifies that preoperational tests must demonstrate, to the extent practical, the capability of structures, systems, and components (SSCs) to meet performance requirements and satisfy design criteria before fuel loading. The Initial Test Program (ITP) must include suitable testing of all SSCs important to safety, with a graded approach based on safety significance. For first-of-a-kind (FOAK) or passive systems, specific in-plant functional testing requirements must be identified early and incorporated into the ITP (RG 1.68, Section B).

Design-Specific Review Standard (DSRS) 14.2 and 5.4.7 require that the applicant’s test programs conform to RG 1.68 and that the pre-operational and startup test programs demonstrate the decay heat removal (DHR) function. The NRC reviews these programs to ensure they meet the requirements of 10 CFR 52.47(b)(1) and 52.80(a), which mandate that inspections, tests, and analyses (including those for emergency planning) are sufficient to provide reasonable assurance that the facility is constructed and will operate in accordance with the license and NRC regulations. For advanced or passive designs, 10 CFR 50.43(e) requires that performance of safety features be demonstrated through analysis, test programs, or experience (DSRS 14.2).

In summary, verification of as-built system thermal performance through pre-operational testing is governed by:
- 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A (GDC 1, 34, 46)
- 10 CFR 52.47(b)(1), 52.80(a), and 50.43(e)
- DSRS 5.4.7 and 14.2
- RG 1.68
These collectively require a quality-assured, graded, and comprehensive pre-operational test program that demonstrates the passive system’s ability to remove decay heat as designed.

evidence_chain.section: B. DISCUSSION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
As previously noted, the ITP consists of preoperational and initial startup tests.  “Preoperational testing,” as used in this regulatory guide, consists of those tests conducted following completion of construction inspections and tests, but before fuel loading, to demonstrate, to the extent practical, the capability of SSCs to meet the performance requirements to satisfy the design criteria.

... The ITP should be designed to demonstrate the performance of SSCs and design features that will be used during normal facility operations, as well as the performance of standby systems and features that must function to maintain the plant in a safe condition in the event of malfunctions or accidents.  The startup tests should be sequenced so that plant safety is never entirely dependent on the performance of untested SSCs.

As mentioned in the introduction to this regulatory guide, the ITP is required to include suitable testing of all SSCs important to safety.  Both Appendices A and B to 10 CFR Part 50 recognize that some SSCs are more important to safety than others. ... Thus, the NRC does not intend that the same test requirements be established for all SSCs important to safety.  Rather, applicants should implement a graded approach to testing in order to provide reasonable assurance, considering the importance to safety of the item, that the item will perform satisfactorily while, at the same time, accomplishing the testing in a cost-effective manner.  Documentation (such as procedures and records) associated with testing also should be commensurate with the importance to safety of the item being tested.

If the facility is using first-of-a-kind (FOAK) SSCs that are new, unique, or special design feature in the facility, then the in-plant functional testing requirements needed to verify their performance should be identified at an early date to permit the test requirements to be appropriately accounted for in the final test design.  For example, some new plant designs licensed under 10 CFR Part 52 have new passive plant design features and FOAK tests for systems that are safety-related or important to safety.  Consequently, each new DC, SDA, ML, COL, or OL applicant for an advanced plant should identify new FOAK tests in the given plant.  For DC and COL applicants, the NRC will verify that applicable FOAK tests proposed by the applicant are included in the ITP.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for the limiting temperature of the ultimate heat sink in relation to containment heat removal capability?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for the limiting temperature of the ultimate heat sink, as it relates to containment heat removal capability, are grounded in ensuring that the containment structure can withstand the pressure and temperature conditions resulting from postulated accidents such as a loss-of-coolant accident (LOCA), steam line, or feedwater line break. According to DSRS 6.2.1 Section II, the containment must maintain its functional integrity and remain a low-leakage barrier for as long as accident conditions require. The design and sizing of containment systems are based on the pressure and temperature conditions that result from such accidents, with specific requirements outlined in General Design Criteria (GDC) 4, 16, and 50 in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, and in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix K.

GDC 4 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety, including those for heat removal, be designed to accommodate environmental conditions associated with postulated accidents. Furthermore, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix K.I.D.2 specifies that the containment pressure used for evaluating cooling effectiveness during reflood and spray cooling must not exceed a conservatively calculated value. This ensures that the ultimate heat sink temperature does not compromise the containment heat removal capability, and that the containment remains within its design limits for pressure and temperature during accident scenarios. The acceptance criteria are further detailed in the relevant SRP and DSRS sections referenced in DSRS 6.2.1.

data.query: What is the regulatory requirement for establishing limiting initial conditions in the functional design of containment systems for nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirement for establishing limiting initial conditions in the functional design of containment systems for nuclear power plants is grounded in several key regulations and guidance documents. According to DSRS 6.2.1, the containment structure must be designed to withstand, without loss of function, the pressure and temperature conditions resulting from postulated accidents such as loss-of-coolant accidents (LOCA), steam line, or feedwater line breaks. The design basis for containment must consider the effects of stored energy in the reactor coolant system, decay energy, and other energy sources, including those from secondary systems and metal-water reactions. The containment must maintain its integrity as a low-leakage barrier for as long as accident conditions require.

The basic functional design requirements are specified in General Design Criteria (GDC) 4, 16, and 50 in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, as well as in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix K. Specifically, GDC 4 requires that safety-related structures, systems, and components be designed to accommodate environmental conditions associated with both normal operation and postulated accidents, including LOCA. The design must also account for dynamic effects such as missiles and pipe whipping, unless analyses demonstrate an extremely low probability of such events.

Furthermore, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix K.I.D.2 mandates that the containment pressure used for evaluating cooling effectiveness during reflood and spray cooling must not exceed a conservatively calculated value. Appendix K.I.A details the required and acceptable sources of energy to be included in determining mass and energy releases from LOCAs and secondary system pipe ruptures. These requirements ensure that the limiting initial conditions used in containment design are conservative and encompass all credible accident scenarios, thereby providing adequate safety margins.

References: DSRS 6.2.1 (Areas of Review); 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A (GDC 4); 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix K.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for materials used in containment vessel bolting to ensure corrosion resistance and structural integrity?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for materials used in containment vessel bolting to ensure corrosion resistance and structural integrity are grounded in several regulatory requirements and guidance documents. According to DSRS 6.2.1, the basic functional design requirements for containment, including bolting, are established in General Design Criteria (GDC) 4, 16, and 50 of Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50. Specifically, GDC 4 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 4) requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety, such as containment vessel bolting, must be designed to accommodate and be compatible with the environmental conditions associated with normal operation, maintenance, testing, and postulated accidents, including loss-of-coolant accidents. This includes ensuring that materials are appropriately protected against environmental and dynamic effects, such as corrosion and mechanical stresses, and are qualified to perform their safety functions under the most severe postulated service conditions.

SRP 3.9.3 further clarifies that acceptance criteria for bolting and threaded fasteners are based on compliance with 10 CFR 50.55a and GDC 1, which require that such components be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function. The SRP acceptance criteria specify that the design and service loading combinations and associated stress limits for bolting must be defined and must comply with applicable codes and standards (such as ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code). Where no specific code criteria exist, the design must ensure structural integrity so that no safety-related functions are impaired.

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria require that containment vessel bolting materials be selected and qualified to withstand all environmental and loading conditions, including corrosion, as specified in GDC 4, and that their structural integrity is assured through adherence to applicable codes and standards, as outlined in SRP 3.9.3 and DSRS 6.2.1.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for the design and installation of containment structural components to ensure their integrity during service?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for the design and installation of containment structural components are established to ensure that the containment structure maintains its integrity and functionality during service, particularly under accident conditions. According to DSRS 6.2.1, the containment must withstand the pressure and temperature conditions resulting from postulated accidents such as loss-of-coolant accidents (LOCA), steam line breaks, or feedwater line breaks, without loss of function. It must also maintain long-term integrity as a low-leakage barrier to prevent the uncontrolled release of fission products for the duration required by postulated accident scenarios. 

The regulatory basis for these criteria is found in General Design Criteria (GDC) 4, 16, and 50 in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, and in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix K. GDC 4 requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed to accommodate environmental and dynamic effects from normal operation, maintenance, testing, and postulated accidents, including protection against dynamic effects such as missiles, pipe whipping, and discharging fluids. The design must also consider the need for high-quality fabrication and inspection to minimize the probability of abnormal leakage or failure. GDC 16 establishes the requirement for the containment to be essentially leak-tight to prevent uncontrolled radioactivity release. GDC 50 and Appendix K further require conservative assessment of containment design margins, including the use of conservatively calculated containment pressures for evaluating cooling effectiveness during accident conditions.

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria require that containment structural components be designed and installed to withstand all credible accident conditions, maintain leak-tightness, and be robust against environmental and dynamic effects, as specified in DSRS 6.2.1 and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A (GDC 4, 16, 50), and Appendix K.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for preservice inspection of containment vessel welds to ensure structural integrity?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for preservice inspection of containment vessel welds to ensure structural integrity are grounded in several key regulations and guidance documents. General Design Criteria (GDC) 4, 16, and 50 in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50 establish the fundamental requirements for containment structures, including the need for a leak-tight barrier and consideration of environmental and dynamic effects (DSRS 6.2.1; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 4). Specifically, GDC 4 requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed to accommodate environmental and dynamic effects, and that the integrity of the reactor coolant pressure boundary be ensured through control of material properties and inspection of welds (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 4).

Regulatory Guide 1.71 provides further detail, stating that weld fabrication and repair should comply with the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Sections III and IX. This includes performance qualification of welders under simulated access and visibility limitations, requalification when essential welding variables change, and monitoring of production welding and adherence to qualification criteria (RG 1.71, Section C). Additionally, all welding constituting the pressure boundary must be performed in accordance with ASME Section IX (RG 1.143, Regulatory Position 4.3).

Inspection and testing provisions must be incorporated to enable periodic evaluation of operability and functional performance (RG 1.143, Regulatory Position 4.5). Pressure-retaining components, including welds, should be hydrostatically tested in accordance with applicable ASME or ANSI codes, with pneumatic testing as an alternative in specific cases (RG 1.143, Regulatory Position 4.4).

In summary, NRC requirements mandate that containment vessel welds be fabricated, inspected, and tested in accordance with ASME Code standards, with specific attention to welder qualification, weld accessibility, and comprehensive pressure testing, all to ensure the structural integrity and leak-tightness of the containment vessel.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
This regulatory guide (RG) describes a method that the staff of the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) considers acceptable in complying with regulations for design basis accident (DBA) dose consequence analysis using an alternative source term (AST). This guidance for light-water reactor (LWR) designs includes the scope, nature, and documentation of associated analyses and evaluations; consideration of impacts on analyzed risk; and content of submittals. ...

Applicable Regulations

• 10 CFR Part 50 provides regulations for licensing production and utilization facilities.

o 10 CFR 50.67, “Accident source term,” allows applicable licensees to voluntarily revise the accident source term used in design basis radiological consequence analyses. A licensee that seeks to revise its current accident source term shall apply for a license amendment under 10 CFR 50.90, “Application for amendment of license, construction permit, or early site permit.” The regulation in 10 CFR 50.90 also allows the NRC to issue these amendments if the applicant’s analysis demonstrates with reasonable assurance that certain dose reference values are met. In accordance with 10 CFR 50.67, a holder of an operating license issued before January 10, 1997, can voluntarily revise the accident source term used in design basis radiological consequence analyses. data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for the mechanical design requirements of containment penetrations and associated components during normal and off-normal operations?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for the mechanical design requirements of containment penetrations and associated components during normal and off-normal operations are grounded in the General Design Criteria (GDC) 4, 16, and 50 of Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, as well as 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix K. Specifically, GDC 4 requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety—including containment penetrations and associated components—must be designed to withstand and be compatible with the environmental conditions of normal operation, maintenance, testing, and postulated accidents (such as loss-of-coolant accidents). These SSCs must also be protected against dynamic effects, including those from missiles, pipe whipping, and discharging fluids resulting from equipment failures or external events. The design must account for dynamically and thermally induced stresses due to rapid changes in temperature and pressure, as well as dynamic loads from pipe ruptures (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4; [2]).

Additionally, GDC 16 requires that containment be designed as an essentially leak-tight barrier to prevent uncontrolled release of radioactivity (DSRS 6.2.1; [1]). GDC 50 emphasizes the need to consider degraded engineered safety features, limitations in accident phenomena definitions, and conservatism in calculation models and input parameters to ensure adequate containment design margins (DSRS 6.2.1; [1]).

Therefore, the acceptance criteria are met when the design and design bases for containment penetrations and associated components conform to these regulatory requirements, ensuring mechanical integrity and leak-tightness under both normal and off-normal (accident) conditions.

data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for the functional design of containment penetrations are established to ensure that the containment structure, including its penetrations, can withstand the pressure and temperature conditions resulting from postulated accidents such as loss-of-coolant accidents (LOCA), steam line breaks, or feedwater line breaks, without loss of function (DSRS 6.2.1, Section I). The containment must maintain its integrity as a low-leakage barrier against the release of fission products for as long as accident conditions persist.

GDC 4 requires that all structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety—including containment penetrations—be designed to accommodate environmental and dynamic effects from normal operation and postulated accidents. This includes protection against dynamic effects such as missiles, pipe whipping, and discharging fluids, and requires that penetrations be designed, fabricated, and tested to the highest quality standards practical. The design must also provide for inspection, testing, and maintenance to assure integrity throughout the plant’s life (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4).

Additionally, GDC 16 requires the containment to be essentially leak-tight, and GDC 50 requires consideration of degraded engineered safety features and conservatism in design margins. Appendix K.I.D.2 further specifies that the containment pressure used for evaluating cooling effectiveness during accident conditions must be calculated conservatively. 

In summary, containment penetrations must maintain mechanical integrity under design pressure conditions, be resistant to environmental and dynamic effects, and be inspectable and maintainable to ensure long-term functional integrity (DSRS 6.2.1; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4).

data.query: How do general design criteria for containment heat removal and regulatory guidance on inspection programs together establish requirements for periodic inspection of containment heat removal surfaces in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The requirements for periodic inspection of containment heat removal surfaces in nuclear power plants are established through a combination of general design criteria (GDC) and regulatory guidance on inspection programs. Specifically, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 38 mandates that a system be provided for containment heat removal following any loss of coolant accident (LOCA), while GDC 39 requires that the containment heat removal system be designed to permit appropriate periodic inspection of important components (RG 1.82, Section A; DSRS 6.2.2, Section II). GDC 40 further requires that the system be designed to allow for periodic testing to ensure its integrity and operability.

The DSRS 6.2.2 clarifies that compliance with GDC 39 means the design must provide for periodic inspection and inservice testing (IST) of system components, including ensuring accessibility for inspection and accounting for potential fouling of containment surfaces. This is reinforced by referencing 10 CFR 50.55a, which governs inservice inspection (ISI) and IST programs, ensuring that the design provisions facilitate such inspections (DSRS 6.2.2, Section III).

Regulatory guides, such as RG 1.82, provide acceptable methods for implementing these requirements, offering guidance on how to meet the inspection and testing provisions of the GDCs. While compliance with regulatory guides is not mandatory, following their guidance is considered an acceptable means of demonstrating compliance with NRC regulations (RG 1.82, Section A).

In summary, the GDCs establish the regulatory basis for periodic inspection and testing of containment heat removal systems, and NRC guidance documents, such as the DSRS and RGs, provide detailed methods and staff expectations for implementing these requirements in inspection programs.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating the performance of containment heat removal systems following a loss-of-coolant accident?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating the performance of containment heat removal systems following a loss-of-coolant accident (LOCA) are grounded in several regulatory requirements and guidance documents. According to DSRS 6.2.2 (Section II), the criteria are based on compliance with General Design Criteria (GDC) 5, 38, 39, and 40 from 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, as well as 10 CFR 50.46(b)(5). Key acceptance criteria include:

1. Redundancy and Single Failure: The containment heat removal systems must meet redundancy and power source requirements for engineered safety features, ensuring the system can withstand a single failure without loss of function (DSRS 6.2.2, GDC 38).

2. Heat Removal Capability: Analyses must demonstrate that the system can remove heat from the containment, accounting for potential surface fouling (both interior and exterior) over the plant’s life. Provisions must be made to prevent or account for fouling in establishing heat removal capability. The system’s ability to transfer heat passively to the environment must also be analyzed (DSRS 6.2.2).

3. Long-Term Cooling and Sump Design: The containment emergency sump must provide a reliable, long-term water source for the ECCS, with adequate water level (head) above the recirculation return valves (RRVs). The design must consider hydraulic performance, LOCA-generated and latent debris, chemical products, and their effects on system performance, including potential blockage (DSRS 6.2.2, RG 1.82).

4. Debris and Chemical Effects: The evaluation must include the effects of debris and chemical reaction products on strainer head loss, with prototypical testing to determine total head loss. All debris and chemical products transportable to the ECCS strainer must be considered, and the design must ensure adequate net positive suction head (NPSH) for pumps under all postulated accident conditions (RG 1.82, Section C.1.1.1).

5. System Integrity: The design must prevent impairment of safety functions due to sharing of structures, systems, or components among units, unless specifically reviewed and approved (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 5).

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria require robust, redundant, and tested containment heat removal systems that maintain long-term cooling capability, account for debris and chemical effects, and ensure reliable sump performance following a LOCA, as detailed in DSRS 6.2.2, 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A, and RG 1.82.

evidence_chain.section: Section C. STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE (esp. 1.1.1 and related discussion in Section B)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Section C. STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE

1. General

1.1 Regulatory Positions Common to All Water-Cooled Reactors

1.1.1 Emergency Core Cooling System Sumps, Suppression Pools, Suction Strainers, and Debris Interceptors

The ECCS and containment heat removal systems must be capable of performing their safety functions following a LOCA. The following criteria and methodology are acceptable to the NRC staff for evaluating the adequacy of water sources for long-term recirculation cooling:

• The design should ensure that the ECCS and containment heat removal pumps have adequate net positive suction head (NPSH) under all postulated accident conditions, including the effects of debris and chemical reaction products on strainer head loss.
• The calculation of NPSH margin should include head loss caused by debris, by subtracting the total debris-laden strainer head loss from the available hydraulic head. The total debris-laden strainer head loss, including chemical reaction products, should be determined by prototypical strainer testing.
• The analyses and testing for head loss effects should include all debris and chemical reaction products that are transportable to the ECCS strainer. Fine debris that is small enough to pass through the strainer should be included for head loss effects if it can be filtered by the debris bed on the strainer.
• ECCS components and flow restrictions inside the reactor vessel should be evaluated for erosion, wear, and blockage that may be caused by the debris and chemical precipitates that penetrate the strainers.
• The size of the openings in the strainer should be appropriate for any physical restrictions in the systems supplied with coolant from the ECCS sump, including openings in the containment spray nozzles, coolant channel openings in the core fuel assemblies, fuel assembly inlet debris screens, small clearances within system flowpaths (e.g., high-pressure safety injection (HPSI) throttle valves), and pump component clearances such as seals, bearings, and impeller running clearances.
• The effects of debris blockage of ECCS strainers, sump outlet configurations, and post-LOCA hydraulic conditions (e.g., air ingestion) should be considered in an integrated manner.
• Small amounts of ingested gas during steady-state pump operation will not lead to severe pumping degradation if the NPSHr from the pump manufacturer’s curve is increased to account for the air ingestion. Thus, it is important to use the combined results of all post-LOCA effects to estimate NPSH margin at the pump inlet.

Appendix A to this guide provides information on estimating NPSH margins in ECCS strainer designs in which estimated levels of air or gas ingestion are low (2 percent or less).
