data.query: When a nuclear plant applicant requests an exemption from containment combustible gas control requirements, what regulatory provisions must be considered to ensure that the exemption is authorized by law and does not present an undue risk to public health and safety, and how should risk assessments for multi-module small modular reactors be incorporated into this evaluation?
data.answer:
When a nuclear plant applicant requests an exemption from containment combustible gas control requirements, the regulatory provisions that must be considered are primarily outlined in 10 CFR 50.44(c). According to 10 CFR 50.44(c), the NRC may grant exemptions if they are authorized by law, do not present an undue risk to public health and safety, and are consistent with the common defense and security. The applicant must demonstrate that the exemption meets these criteria.

For multi-module small modular reactors (SMRs), 10 CFR 50.44(d) allows applicants to propose risk-informed alternatives to the standard requirements. The Commission will evaluate these alternatives on a case-by-case basis, provided the applicant demonstrates that the proposed approach provides an adequate level of safety and aligns with NRC regulations and guidance.

Risk assessments for multi-module SMRs should be incorporated into the exemption evaluation by following the guidance in DSRS 6.2.5 and SRP 19.0. DSRS 6.2.5 references the use of risk insights to enhance the safety focus of SMR reviews, as directed by the Commission in SRM-COMGBJ-10-0004/COMGEA-10-0001. SRP 19.0 further specifies that the applicant’s probabilistic risk assessment (PRA) and severe accident evaluation should be coordinated with the review of containment performance under severe accident conditions, ensuring that risk-important human actions and containment performance goals are addressed.

Additionally, Regulatory Guide 1.216 provides acceptable methods for demonstrating containment structural integrity, including analysis of hydrogen generation and burning scenarios, and references the use of analytical techniques and load combinations as defined in Regulatory Guides 1.7, 1.57, and 1.136. The applicant must show that systems necessary to ensure containment integrity can perform their functions under these conditions.

In summary, the exemption request must be justified under 10 CFR 50.44(c), incorporate risk-informed approaches as allowed by 10 CFR 50.44(d) for SMRs, and be supported by robust risk assessments and containment performance analyses as described in DSRS 6.2.5, SRP 19.0, and RG 1.216.

evidence_chain.section: § 50.44 Combustible gas control for nuclear power reactors
evidence_chain.evidence_text: (a) General. Each holder of or applicant for an operating license under this part, a combined license under part 52 of this chapter, or a manufacturing license under part 52 of this chapter for a nuclear power reactor shall comply with the requirements of this section. (b) Combustible gas control. (1) Each boiling or pressurized light-water nuclear power reactor fueled with uranium oxide pellets within cylindrical zircaloy or ZIRLOTM cladding must have the capability to control the concentration of combustible gases in the containment atmosphere following an accident to ensure that containment integrity is maintained. (2) The requirements of paragraph (b)(1) of this section do not apply to: (i) An applicant for or holder of an operating license or combined license for a nuclear power reactor that is not a light-water reactor; (ii) An applicant for or holder of an operating license or combined license for a light-water reactor that does not use uranium oxide fuel within cylindrical zircaloy or ZIRLOTM cladding; or (iii) An applicant for or holder of an operating license or combined license for a light-water reactor that demonstrates that the reactor design can accommodate the generation and control of combustible gases following an accident without loss of containment integrity. (c) Exemptions. The Commission may, upon application by any interested person or upon its own initiative, grant such exemptions from the requirements of this section as it determines are authorized by law and will not present an undue risk to the public health and safety and are consistent with the common defense and security. (d) Risk-informed alternatives for multi-module small modular reactors. For multi-module small modular reactors, the applicant may propose risk-informed alternatives to the requirements of this section. The Commission will consider such alternatives on a case-by-case basis, provided that the applicant demonstrates that the proposed alternatives provide an adequate level of safety and are consistent with the Commission's regulations and guidance.

evidence_chain.section: Section A. INTRODUCTION and Section C. REGULATORY POSITION (2. Combustible Gas Control Inside Containment)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
As required by 10 CFR 50.44(c)(5), an applicant must perform an analysis that demonstrates containment structural integrity. This demonstration must use an analytical technique that is acceptable to the NRC, and the analysis must address an accident that releases hydrogen generated from a 100-percent fuel clad-coolant reaction, accompanied by hydrogen burning. Applicants must also demonstrate that systems necessary to ensure containment integrity are able to perform their functions under these conditions. Regulatory Guide 1.7 specifically addresses requirements in 10 CFR 50.44(c)(5) to demonstrate containment structural integrity.

... 

In accordance with the regulatory guidance described above, the containment should be evaluated for (1) the pressure arising from the fuel cladding-water reaction, hydrogen burning, and post-accident inerting (if applicable), or (2) 45 pounds per square inch gauge, whichever is higher. Regulatory Guides 1.57 and 1.136 define the pressures associated with the fuel cladding-water reaction, hydrogen burning, and post-accident inerting, as well as the load combinations to be considered for the structural integrity assessment.

In addition to the guidance in Regulatory Guides 1.7, 1.57, and 1.136, the analysis to demonstrate the structural integrity of the containment should take into account the following items:   

a. The development of a mathematical finite element model of the containment using the approach described under Regulatory Position 1, subject to the limitations discussed below, is acceptable.

(1) ASME Code-specified material properties should be used.  These should correspond to the metal temperature(s) resulting from the hydrogen-generation event.

(2) For steel containment elements, linear elastic material properties may be used.  For concrete containments, the tensile strength of concrete should be neglected while for the concrete in compression the nonlinear stress-strain relationship should be used or justification should be provided for an equivalent linear stress-strain model.  The staff will review the justification for an equivalent linear stress-strain model on a case-by-case basis.

(3) The potential structural dynamic amplification effects caused by the pressure transient loading associated with hydrogen gas generation or the burning of hydrogen, if significant, should be included in calculating the response of the containment.

b. The accident sequence used to determine the pressure load should address the hydrogen mass and energy releases generated from a 100-percent fuel clad-coolant reaction accompanied by the burning of hydrogen.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for controlling combustible gas concentrations within containment during and following an accident?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for controlling combustible gas concentrations within containment during and following an accident are primarily established in 10 CFR 50.44 and are further detailed in DSRS 6.2.5 and Regulatory Guide 1.216. The key requirements are as follows:

1. Mixed Atmosphere: Containments must have the capability to ensure a mixed atmosphere during design-basis and significant beyond design-basis accidents to prevent local hydrogen accumulation (DSRS 6.2.5, II.A; 10 CFR 50.44(d)).

2. Hydrogen Concentration Limits: For new water-cooled reactor containments, hydrogen concentrations must be limited to less than 10 percent by volume during and following an accident that releases an amount of hydrogen equivalent to a 100 percent fuel clad-coolant reaction, unless the containment is inerted (DSRS 6.2.5, II.B; 10 CFR 50.44(c)(2); RG 1.216, A).

3. Equipment Survivability: Systems and components necessary for safe shutdown and containment integrity must be capable of performing their functions during and after exposure to environmental conditions created by hydrogen burning, including local detonations unless such events are shown to be unlikely (DSRS 6.2.5, II.C; RG 1.216, A).

4. Monitoring: Equipment for monitoring hydrogen in containment must be functional, reliable, and capable of continuously measuring hydrogen concentration following a significant accident for accident management and emergency planning (DSRS 6.2.5, II.D).

5. Structural Analysis: Applicants must perform an analysis, using NRC-accepted techniques, to demonstrate containment structural integrity under conditions of hydrogen release and burning from a 100 percent fuel clad-coolant reaction. Systems necessary to ensure containment integrity must be shown to perform their functions under these conditions (DSRS 6.2.5, II.E; 10 CFR 50.44(c)(5); RG 1.216, A).

In summary, NRC regulations require robust design and analysis to ensure that combustible gas concentrations, particularly hydrogen, are controlled to prevent loss of containment integrity during and after accidents, with specific limits, monitoring, and survivability criteria.

The analysis must address an accident that releases hydrogen generated from 100 percent fuel clad-coolant reaction accompanied by the hydrogen burning. Systems necessary to ensure containment integrity must also be demonstrated to perform their function under these conditions.

data.query: How do NRC regulations for combustible gas control in containment relate to the requirements for maintaining containment structural integrity during post-accident conditions?
data.answer:
NRC regulations for combustible gas control in containment are directly linked to the requirements for maintaining containment structural integrity during post-accident conditions. According to 10 CFR 50.44, each light-water nuclear power reactor must have systems capable of controlling the concentration of combustible gases, such as hydrogen, in the containment atmosphere following a postulated loss-of-coolant accident (LOCA). The regulations specifically require that these systems prevent an uncontrolled increase in combustible gas generation that could threaten the integrity of the containment or lead to a loss of containment function (10 CFR 50.44(a)).

The systems must be designed to handle the hydrogen generated from a 100 percent fuel-clad metal-water reaction, assuming all fuel in the core is involved, and must control hydrogen concentrations to ensure containment integrity is not compromised (10 CFR 50.44(b)(2)). These systems must also remain operable under accident conditions, including loss of offsite power (10 CFR 50.44(b)(3)).

DSRS 6.2.5 further clarifies that acceptance criteria for combustible gas control are based on demonstrating that containment structural integrity can be maintained during and after exposure to environmental conditions created by hydrogen burning, including local detonations unless shown unlikely. Applicants must perform structural analyses addressing accidents involving hydrogen generated from a full fuel-clad reaction and subsequent burning, demonstrating that containment and necessary systems can perform their functions under these conditions (DSRS 6.2.5, II.C, II.E). The analysis must use NRC-accepted techniques and provide sufficient justification that the containment response to structural loads is adequately described (DSRS 6.2.5, II.6).

In summary, NRC regulations require that combustible gas control systems are integral to maintaining containment structural integrity during post-accident conditions by preventing hydrogen concentrations from reaching levels that could compromise containment, and by ensuring that containment and its systems remain functional under the most severe postulated accident scenarios.

data.query: How do regulatory requirements for combustible gas control in containment address the survivability of containment penetrations and equipment during hydrogen combustion events, including potential detonations?
data.answer:
Regulatory requirements for combustible gas control in containment, as specified in 10 CFR 50.44 and detailed in DSRS 6.2.5, directly address the survivability of containment penetrations and equipment during hydrogen combustion events, including potential detonations. According to 10 CFR 50.44(a), equipment and systems for hydrogen control must be capable of performing their safety functions during and after exposure to environmental conditions resulting from postulated accidents, which include the effects of hydrogen burning and, unless shown to be not credible, hydrogen detonation. The design must ensure that containment structural integrity and the ability to achieve and maintain safe shutdown are not compromised by such events.

DSRS 6.2.5 further clarifies that acceptance criteria require containments to maintain safe shutdown and structural integrity with systems and components that can perform their functions during and after hydrogen burning. The environmental conditions considered must include those caused by local detonations of hydrogen, unless such detonations are demonstrated to be unlikely. The analysis must assume hydrogen generation equivalent to a 100 percent fuel clad-coolant reaction. Structural analysis must demonstrate that containment and necessary systems, including penetrations and equipment, can withstand the loads and environmental conditions from hydrogen combustion, referencing accepted analytical techniques such as those in the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (DSRS 6.2.5, II.E).

In summary, the regulations require robust analysis and design to ensure that containment penetrations and equipment necessary for safety remain functional and that containment integrity is preserved during and after hydrogen combustion events, including potential detonations, unless such events are shown to be unlikely.

data.query: What is the relationship between equipment qualification temperature limits for containment systems and the regulatory expectations for maintaining containment integrity during postulated hydrogen combustion events?
data.answer:
The equipment qualification temperature limits for containment systems are directly related to the regulatory expectations for maintaining containment integrity during postulated hydrogen combustion events. According to 10 CFR 50.44(c) and the guidance in DSRS 6.2.5, equipment, systems, and components that are necessary for achieving and maintaining safe shutdown and containment structural integrity must be capable of performing their safety functions during and after exposure to the environmental conditions created by hydrogen burning. This includes the temperature and pressure transients resulting from hydrogen combustion events, such as those that could occur following a fuel clad-coolant reaction involving 100 percent of the fuel cladding. 

Therefore, the qualification temperature limits for containment equipment must be set at levels that reflect the maximum environmental conditions (including temperature) expected during and after hydrogen combustion. The equipment must be demonstrated to survive and function under these postulated conditions to ensure that containment integrity is maintained, as required by 10 CFR 50.44(c) and as described in DSRS 6.2.5 (Section II). If equipment is not qualified for these conditions, it may fail to perform its safety function, potentially compromising containment integrity during a hydrogen combustion event.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory requirements for combustible gas control in containment address the impact of water inventory on available containment free volume during severe accidents?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory requirements for combustible gas control in containment address the impact of water inventory on available containment free volume during severe accidents by requiring that analyses supporting combustible gas control explicitly consider the containment free volume, which is directly affected by water inventory. According to DSRS 6.2.5, while the section does not explicitly mention water inventory, it requires that applicants demonstrate, through analysis, that the containment can safely accommodate hydrogen generated by a 100 percent fuel clad-coolant reaction, maintaining hydrogen concentrations below regulatory limits and ensuring containment structural integrity. This implicitly requires consideration of any reduction in containment free volume, such as that caused by increased water inventory during severe accidents.

Regulatory Guide 1.216 provides more explicit guidance, stating that the analysis should consider the containment free volume available for gas mixing and pressure rise, and that this volume should be based on the minimum water inventory that could be present during the postulated accident sequence. This approach maximizes the pressure rise for a given mass of hydrogen, ensuring a conservative analysis. The applicant must provide a technical basis for the assumed water inventory and resulting free volume, and must also consider the effects of water vapor, steam, condensation, and heat transfer on the containment atmosphere during the accident sequence (RG 1.216, Section C.2).

Additionally, RG 1.57 specifies that the analysis of containment structural integrity must include load combinations that account for post-LOCA flooding (i.e., increased water inventory) and its impact on containment pressure boundary components. The guidance requires that the most adverse combination of loadings, including those resulting from flooding, be considered in the design and analysis (RG 1.57, Section C).

In summary, NRC requirements ensure that the impact of water inventory on containment free volume is addressed in combustible gas control analyses by mandating that applicants justify their assumptions regarding water inventory and demonstrate containment integrity under the most limiting conditions, including those with reduced free volume due to water accumulation.

data.answer:
Based on the provided evidence, regulatory expectations for containment pressure calculations during post-accident conditions focus primarily on demonstrating containment structural integrity and the safe control of combustible gases, such as hydrogen, rather than specifying assumptions about the presence of condensed water in containment. 

DSRS 6.2.5 (Section II. Acceptance Criteria) requires applicants to analyze and demonstrate that the containment can safely accommodate hydrogen generated by a 100 percent fuel clad-coolant reaction, while maintaining containment structural integrity under post-accident conditions. The analysis must address the containment response to structural loads, including those from hydrogen burning, and demonstrate compliance with applicable ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code criteria (DSRS 6.2.5, II.6; RG 1.7, Rev. 3, Section C.5). However, the DSRS does not explicitly discuss or require specific assumptions regarding the presence or role of condensed water in containment for these calculations.

Similarly, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 41, establishes that systems must be provided to control hydrogen or oxygen concentrations and to clean up the containment atmosphere following postulated accidents, ensuring system safety during and after conditions of increased containment pressure and temperature. This criterion emphasizes the capability of systems to function under post-accident pressure and temperature, but does not prescribe modeling parameters related to condensed water.

In summary, while regulatory requirements mandate robust analyses of containment pressure and structural integrity under post-accident conditions, they do not explicitly address or require assumptions about condensed water in containment for these calculations.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for controlling combustible gas concentrations in containment during and following a postulated accident?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for controlling combustible gas concentrations in containment during and following a postulated accident are primarily established in 10 CFR 50.44 and are further detailed in DSRS 6.2.5. The regulations require that each boiling or pressurized light-water nuclear power reactor must have the capability to control the concentration of combustible gases, such as hydrogen, in the containment atmosphere after an accident to ensure containment integrity is maintained (10 CFR 50.44(a)(1); DSRS 6.2.5 II.A). Additionally, the containment must be equipped with systems to rapidly mix the atmosphere to prevent localized hydrogen concentrations that could threaten containment integrity (10 CFR 50.44(a)(2); DSRS 6.2.5 II.A).

Containments must limit hydrogen concentrations to less than 10 percent by volume during and following an accident that releases an amount of hydrogen equivalent to that generated from a 100 percent fuel clad-coolant reaction, assuming uniform distribution (DSRS 6.2.5 II.B). The hydrogen control system must be capable of accommodating this amount of hydrogen (10 CFR 50.44(b)(2)).

Furthermore, equipment for monitoring hydrogen in containment must be functional, reliable, and capable of continuously measuring hydrogen concentration following a significant beyond design-basis accident for accident management and emergency planning (DSRS 6.2.5 II.D). The containment and its systems must also be analyzed and demonstrated to maintain structural integrity under conditions created by hydrogen burning, including local detonations unless such events are shown to be unlikely (DSRS 6.2.5 II.C, II.E).

In summary, the NRC requires robust systems for hydrogen control, mixing, monitoring, and structural analysis to ensure containment integrity during and after postulated accidents involving combustible gas generation.

data.query: How do NRC regulations for combustible gas control in containment address both the initial hydrogen release from fuel-clad reactions and the potential for continued gas generation during prolonged accident scenarios?
data.answer:
NRC regulations for combustible gas control in containment address both the initial hydrogen release from fuel-clad reactions and the potential for continued gas generation during prolonged accident scenarios through a combination of requirements for containment design, monitoring, and mitigation systems. According to DSRS 6.2.5 and 10 CFR 50.44, after an accident, hydrogen is generated primarily from the reaction between fuel cladding and reactor coolant, as well as from radiolytic decomposition of emergency coolant. The regulations require that containment systems must be capable of limiting hydrogen concentrations to less than 10 percent by volume during and following an accident that releases an amount of hydrogen equivalent to a 100 percent fuel clad-coolant reaction (DSRS 6.2.5, II.1.B; RG 1.216, A). This ensures that even in the worst-case scenario of complete fuel-clad reaction, containment integrity is maintained.

Additionally, the regulations require the capability to mix the containment atmosphere to prevent local high concentrations of combustible gases, continuous monitoring of hydrogen concentrations, and the ability to reduce hydrogen concentrations by suitable means (DSRS 6.2.5, I.2-4). For new water-cooled reactors, if an inerted atmosphere is not used, systems must be in place to control hydrogen so that containment structural integrity is not lost (RG 1.216, A). Applicants must also perform structural analyses to demonstrate that containment and essential systems can withstand the environmental conditions created by hydrogen burning, including those resulting from both initial and ongoing hydrogen generation (DSRS 6.2.5, II.1.E; RG 1.216, A).

In summary, NRC regulations require a comprehensive approach that addresses both the initial and ongoing generation of combustible gases by mandating containment design features, monitoring, mixing, and mitigation systems, as well as robust structural analyses to ensure containment integrity under all credible accident conditions.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
After an accident, combustible gas is predominantly generated within the containment because of the reaction between the fuel cladding and the reactor coolant. Hydrogen and oxygen are also generated because of radiolytic decomposition of the post-accident emergency coolant.

If a sufficient amount of combustible gas is generated, it may react with any oxygen present in the containment at a rate rapid enough to breach the containment or cause a leakage rate in excess of technical specification limits. Additionally, the associated pressure and temperature increase could damage systems and components essential to continued control of the post-accident conditions. This review includes the following general areas:

1. the production and accumulation of combustible gases within the containment following a beyond-design-basis accident

2. the capability to mix the combustible gases within the containment and prevent high concentrations of combustible gases in local areas

3. the capability to monitor combustible gas concentrations within containment

4. the capability to reduce combustible gas concentrations within containment by suitable means, as required

...

1. Regulations in 10 CFR 50.44 state:

A. Mixed atmosphere: Containments must have a capability for ensuring a mixed atmosphere during design-basis and significant beyond design-basis accidents.

B. Combustible gas control: Containments must limit hydrogen concentrations in containment during and following an accident that releases an equivalent amount of hydrogen as would be generated from a 100 percent fuel clad-coolant reaction, uniformly distributed, to less than 10 percent (by volume).

C. Equipment Survivability. Containments must be able to establish and maintain safe shutdown and containment structural integrity with systems and components capable of performing their functions during and after exposure to the environmental conditions created by the burning of hydrogen. Environmental conditions caused by local detonations of hydrogen must also be included, unless such detonations can be shown unlikely to occur. The amount of hydrogen to be considered must be equivalent to that generated from a fuel clad-coolant reaction involving 100 percent of the fuel cladding surrounding the active fuel region.

D. Monitoring. Equipment provided for monitoring hydrogen in the containment must be functional, reliable, and capable of continuously measuring the concentration of hydrogen in the containment atmosphere following a significant beyond design-basis accident for accident management, including emergency planning.

E. Structural analysis. An applicant must perform an analysis that demonstrates containment structural integrity. The analysis must address an accident that releases hydrogen generated from 100 percent fuel clad-coolant reaction accompanied by the hydrogen burning. Systems necessary to ensure containment integrity must also be demonstrated to perform their function under these conditions.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory guides for containment leakage testing relate to the general requirements for documenting regulatory guidance in safety analysis reports?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory guides for containment leakage testing, such as Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.163, provide detailed methods and acceptable practices for implementing the requirements of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, which governs primary reactor containment leakage testing for water-cooled power reactors. These guides are directly related to the general requirements for documenting regulatory guidance in safety analysis reports (SARs).

According to DSRS 6.2.6, the reactor containment leakage rate testing program must be described in the SAR or design certification document (DCD) and must conform to the requirements of Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50. The SAR must detail the test methods, frequency, and acceptance criteria, and demonstrate compliance with either Option A or Option B of Appendix J. Option B allows for performance-based testing programs, provided they follow methods approved by the NRC and endorsed in a regulatory guide, such as RG 1.163 (DSRS 6.2.6, Section II; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section I.C).

Appendix J further specifies that the SAR must describe the containment leakage testing program in a manner consistent with the appendix and any applicable regulatory guides (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section I.C). Documentation of test results, procedures, conditions, and evaluations must be sufficient to permit independent assessment (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section I.B).

RG 1.163 endorses NEI 94-01, Revision 3-A, and ANSI/ANS-56.8 standards as acceptable methods for performing leakage tests under Option B of Appendix J. It also outlines specific documentation and submittal requirements, such as providing a schedule of inspections and addressing areas susceptible to degradation in license amendment requests (RG 1.163, Section C).

In summary, NRC regulatory guides for containment leakage testing provide the detailed, NRC-accepted methods and documentation expectations that must be reflected in the SAR to demonstrate compliance with the general regulatory requirements of Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50.

Appendix J to Part 50—Primary Reactor Containment Leakage Testing for Water-Cooled Power Reactors

I. Introduction
A. The primary reactor containment for a water-cooled power reactor is an essential barrier against the uncontrolled release of radioactivity to the environment. The integrity of this barrier must be maintained to ensure that the containment can perform its safety function. To provide assurance of this integrity, the containment must be subjected to periodic testing to measure leakage rates and to demonstrate that leakage is within allowable limits specified in the technical specifications for the plant.

B. The results of the tests must be documented and reported as required by § 50.4 and § 50.36a of this part. The documentation must include a summary of the test results, the test procedures used, the test conditions, and an evaluation of the results. The documentation must be sufficient to permit independent assessment of the test and its results.

C. The safety analysis report required by § 50.34 must describe the containment leakage testing program, including the test methods, frequency, and acceptance criteria. The program must be consistent with the requirements of this appendix and any applicable regulatory guides or standards endorsed by the Commission.

data.query: What is the relationship between the NRC's guidance on containment leakage rate testing and the general procedures for referencing regulatory guidance in licensing documents?
data.answer:
The NRC’s guidance on containment leakage rate testing is closely linked to the general procedures for referencing regulatory guidance in licensing documents. According to DSRS 6.2.6, the containment leakage rate testing program must conform to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, and relevant General Design Criteria (GDCs). Conformance with either Option A or Option B of Appendix J, as well as the provisions of Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.163, is considered an acceptable basis for meeting these requirements. However, the DSRS itself is not a substitute for NRC regulations, and applicants may propose alternatives if they demonstrate compliance with the underlying regulations (DSRS 6.2.6, Section II).

Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50 establishes the regulatory basis for containment leakage rate testing, specifying that tests must ensure leakage does not exceed allowable rates and that the integrity of the containment is maintained. Appendix J also references § 50.34, which requires that licensing applications include descriptions and safety analyses demonstrating compliance with applicable regulations, such as Appendix J (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section I.C).

Regulatory Guide 1.163 provides detailed guidance on acceptable performance-based leak-test programs and methods for complying with Option B of Appendix J. It endorses specific industry standards and risk-informed methodologies, and clarifies that licensees wishing to adopt these methods must submit a license amendment request (LAR) to update their Technical Specifications. If a licensee chooses to deviate from NRC-endorsed methods, the submittal must include justification and supporting analysis (RG 1.163, Sections A and B).

In summary, NRC guidance on containment leakage rate testing is referenced in licensing documents by demonstrating conformance to Appendix J and, where applicable, RG 1.163. The general procedure requires applicants to describe their testing program, reference applicable regulatory guidance, and justify any deviations, ensuring compliance with NRC regulations.

The general procedures for referencing regulatory guidance in licensing documents are established in § 50.34, which requires that applications for construction permits and operating licenses include a description and safety analysis of the structures, systems, and components of the facility, including the containment, and demonstrate compliance with applicable regulations, such as this appendix.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for instrumentation used during containment integrated leakage rate testing in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for instrumentation used during containment integrated leakage rate testing (CILRT) in nuclear power plants are established primarily in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section III, and further detailed in NRC guidance documents such as DSRS 6.2.6 and Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.163.

According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section III, the test methods for measuring containment leakage rates must be capable of measuring the leakage rate with sufficient accuracy to demonstrate compliance with the allowable leakage rate specified in the plant's technical specifications. The methods must include a description of the instrumentation used, its calibration, and the measurement procedures. Importantly, the accuracy of the test instrumentation and the measurement method must be established and documented, with the overall measurement uncertainty required to be less than or equal to 0.25 times the allowable leakage rate. All test instrumentation must be calibrated prior to the test, and this calibration must be traceable to a recognized standard (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section III.B).

DSRS 6.2.6 further clarifies that instrumentation lines penetrating containment should not be isolated from the containment atmosphere during the CILRT unless they are locally leakage rate tested. If such lines are isolated and locally tested, their measured leakage rates must be added to the CILRT result. Provisions must also be made to restore these lines to operable status after testing. All leakage rate tests, whether pneumatic or hydrostatic, must be able to quantify leakage rates explicitly or by a conservative bounding method to satisfy Appendix J and technical specification acceptance criteria (DSRS 6.2.6, Section II).

RG 1.163 endorses the use of NEI 94-01 and ANSI/ANS-56.8 standards for technical methods and techniques, with the condition that the performance leakage rate definition from NEI 94-01, Revision 3-A, be used for Type A tests (RG 1.163, Section C).

In summary, the instrumentation used for CILRT must be accurate, calibrated, and documented, with measurement uncertainty tightly controlled, and must follow the technical methods described in referenced standards and regulatory guidance.

Appendix J, Option A, Section III.A.1(a), requires no repairs or adjustments be made to the containment before the performance of the CILRT so the containment can be tested in as close to the “as is” condition as practical. Under Option B, RG 1.163 endorses Nuclear Energy Institute (NEI) 94-01, Revision 0 (with certain exceptions), which provides similar guidance in Sections 8.0 and 9.0. Instrumentation lines that penetrate containment; however, are sometimes isolated for the CILRT. To ensure that they are included in the test, the following should be done. Leakage rate testing of instrumentation lines that penetrate containment may be done in conjunction with either the LLRTs or the CILRT. Instrumentation lines that are not locally leakage rate tested should not be isolated from the containment atmosphere during the performance of the CILRT. The measured leakage rates from instrumentation lines that are locally leakage rate tested, and also isolated during CILRTs, should be added to the CILRT result. Provisions should be made to ensure that instrumentation lines isolated during the CILRT are restored to their operable status following the test.

All leakage rate tests, performed by either pneumatic or hydrostatic means, should have the capability to quantify the leakage rates either explicitly or by a conservative bounding method to satisfy test acceptance criteria in Appendix J and the TS.

data.query: How do general design criteria for containment integrity relate to the requirements for instrumentation placement and performance during integrated leakage rate testing?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for containment integrity, particularly GDC 52 as outlined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, require that the reactor containment and associated equipment be designed to allow for periodic integrated leakage rate testing (ILRT or CILRT) at the containment design pressure. This includes providing means for measuring the leakage rate and ensuring that the design accommodates the placement and performance of necessary instrumentation under test conditions, such as temperature, pressure, humidity, and radiation (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 52).

DSRS 6.2.6 further clarifies that compliance with Appendix J (Option A or B) and Regulatory Guide 1.163 is an acceptable basis for meeting these GDCs. Specifically, instrumentation lines that penetrate containment must be considered during leakage rate testing. If these lines are not locally leakage rate tested (LLRT), they should not be isolated during the CILRT to ensure their contribution to overall leakage is measured. If they are locally tested and isolated during the CILRT, their measured leakage rates must be added to the CILRT results. Provisions must also be made to restore these lines to operable status after testing (DSRS 6.2.6, Section II).

Regulatory Guide 1.163 endorses NEI 94-01 and ANSI/ANS-56.8 for technical methods, emphasizing that the containment leakage testing program (including ILRTs and LLRTs) and inservice inspection programs are intended to ensure ongoing containment integrity. Visual inspections of containment surfaces are also required to identify any structural deterioration that could affect leak-tightness, supporting the overall objective of the GDCs (RG 1.163, Sections B and C).

In summary, the general design criteria for containment integrity directly inform the requirements for instrumentation placement and performance during integrated leakage rate testing by mandating that the containment design supports effective measurement, inspection, and restoration of all relevant systems and penetrations, including instrumentation lines, to ensure accurate and comprehensive leakage rate assessments.

data.query: What is the NRC acceptance criterion for containment hydrostatic testing with respect to allowable leakage?
data.answer: The NRC acceptance criterion for containment hydrostatic testing with respect to allowable leakage is that the measured integrated leakage rate for the primary reactor containment, as determined from the Type A (integrated leakage rate) test, must not exceed the allowable leakage rate specified in the plant's technical specifications (TS). This requirement is established in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Sections IV and VI, which state that both the integrated leakage rate (Type A) and the sum of local leakage rates from penetrations and valves (Types B and C) must not exceed the allowable rates specified in the TS. DSRS 6.2.6 further clarifies that the minimum acceptable design containment leakage rate should not be less than 0.1 percent per day, which provides adequate margin above typically measured rates and aligns with current test methods and acceptance criteria. Regulatory Guide 1.163 endorses the use of NEI 94-01, Revision 3-A, and ANSI/ANS-56.8 standards for performing these tests, with the performance leakage rate definition in NEI 94-01, Revision 3-A, being preferred for Type A tests. In summary, the acceptance criterion is that the measured leakage rate during hydrostatic (or pneumatic) testing must be quantified and shown to be at or below the allowable leakage rate specified in the plant's technical specifications, with a minimum design value of 0.1 percent per day as a reference point. (References: DSRS 6.2.6 Section II; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Sections IV and VI; RG 1.163 Sections B and C)

data.query: How do NRC requirements for periodic containment leakage testing relate to the need for instrumentation accuracy in detecting unknown leakage pathways over time?
data.answer:
NRC requirements for periodic containment leakage testing, as outlined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, are closely linked to the need for instrumentation accuracy in detecting unknown leakage pathways over time. Appendix J mandates that the primary reactor containment must not exceed allowable leakage rates specified in plant technical specifications, and that periodic Type A (integrated), Type B (local), and Type C (penetration and isolation valve) tests be performed to ensure containment integrity (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Sections I.A–I.B). Instrumentation used for these tests must be of sufficient accuracy to determine leakage rates within regulatory limits, and its accuracy must be verified prior to each test, with verification results included in the test report (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section I.C).

DSRS 6.2.6 further clarifies that all leakage rate tests, whether pneumatic or hydrostatic, must be capable of quantifying leakage rates explicitly or by a conservative bounding method to satisfy Appendix J and technical specification acceptance criteria. Special attention is given to instrumentation lines penetrating containment; if these are not locally tested, they must not be isolated during the integrated test, and any measured leakage from locally tested and isolated lines must be added to the overall result. This ensures that all potential leakage pathways, including those through instrumentation lines, are accounted for in the periodic testing (DSRS 6.2.6, Section II).

Regulatory Guide 1.163, which endorses NEI 94-01 for performance-based testing, notes that while the frequency of Type A tests may be extended due to the low risk impact, the effectiveness of the testing program still depends on the ability to detect and quantify leakage, particularly from pathways not identified by local tests. Thus, accurate instrumentation is essential for reliably detecting unknown or emerging leakage pathways over time, supporting the overall objective of maintaining containment integrity and public safety.

In summary, NRC requirements for periodic containment leakage testing are fundamentally dependent on the accuracy of instrumentation to ensure that all leakage, including from unknown pathways, is detected and quantified within regulatory limits, thereby supporting the integrity of the containment structure over time.

I. Introduction
A. The primary reactor containment of all water-cooled power reactors, subject to the provisions of this part, must meet the containment leakage test requirements set forth in this appendix to ensure that leakage through the containment or systems and components penetrating the containment does not exceed allowable leakage rate values as specified in the technical specifications for the plant.

C. Instrumentation used for the measurement of containment leakage rates must be of sufficient accuracy to assure that the containment leakage rate can be determined within the limits required by this appendix and the plant technical specifications. evidence_chain.section: B. DISCUSSION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50 requires the following types of containment leakage tests: 

• Type A tests: integrated leakage rate tests (ILRTs)
• Type B tests: leakage tests across each pressure-containing or leakage-limiting boundary for specified primary reactor containment penetrations including seals, gaskets, and expansion bellows
• Type C tests: leakage tests of containment isolation valves

Type B and C tests are also referred to as local leakage rate tests (LLRTs).

Maximum allowable leakage rates (La) are calculated in accordance with 10 CFR Part 100, “Reactor Site Criteria,” (Ref. 7), except where alternates have been granted and are specified in licensee site specific TS.  

Appendix J has two options to determine test frequencies: Option A (prescriptive) and Option B (performance-based). Under Option A, three Type A tests are to be performed at approximately equal intervals during each inservice inspection period. The Option B performance-based requirements, issued in 1995, allow licensees to replace prescriptive testing requirements with testing requirements based on leakage rate performance and a supporting plant-specific risk impact assessment. Option B also introduced a requirement for visual inspection of accessible portions of the containment before each Type A test and at a periodic interval between tests. Licensees usually satisfy this requirement through the containment inservice inspection program conducted in accordance with American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (BPV Code), Section XI, Subsections IWE and IWL (Ref. 8 and Ref. 9), as incorporated by reference and conditioned in 10 CFR 50.55a, “Codes and standards.”

NUREG-1493 is a detailed study of the impacts, costs, and risk of the Appendix J requirements and provided the methodology used to determine the acceptability of extended testing intervals. Sensitivity analyses in NUREG-1493 and other studies show that light-water reactor accident risk is relatively insensitive to the containment leakage rate because the risk is dominated by accident sequences that result in failure or bypass of containment. Reducing the frequency of Type A tests over extended periods, including up to 15 years, was found to lead to an imperceptible increase in risk. The estimated increase in risk is very small because (1) ILRTs identify only a few potential containment leakage paths that cannot be identified by Type B and Type C testing, and (2) the leaks that have been found by Type A tests have been only marginally above existing requirements. Given the insensitivity of risk to the containment leakage rate and the small fraction of leakage paths detected solely by Type A testing, increasing the interval between ILRTs is possible with minimal impact on risk to the public.

The performance-based, “Option B,” containment leak test program is characterized by three areas (1) leakage rate testing, (2) containment inspections, and (3) risk impact.  The following subsections provide the technical basis for each of these focus areas.

data.query: For a novel containment design where standard Type A testing criteria may not be directly applicable due to temperature and pressure variations, what alternative approaches are recognized by NRC regulatory standards and guidance to demonstrate compliance with containment leakage rate requirements?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory standards recognize several alternative approaches for demonstrating compliance with containment leakage rate requirements when standard Type A testing criteria may not be directly applicable due to unique containment designs or varying temperature and pressure conditions. According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section I.B, for reactors with a containment design where the prescribed test methods, procedures, or acceptance criteria are not applicable, the applicant is required to propose and justify alternative test methods, procedures, and acceptance criteria appropriate for the specific containment design. These alternatives must be submitted to the NRC for approval. Furthermore, exemptions from Appendix J requirements may be granted under 10 CFR 50.12 if adequately justified and found to be in the public interest (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section I.A).

DSRS 6.2.6 further clarifies that compliance can be achieved either by meeting the requirements of Option A or Option B of Appendix J. Under Option B, applicants may use methods approved by the NRC and endorsed in Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.163, or propose other implementation documents with supporting analyses, provided these are justified to the NRC staff and cited in the technical specifications (DSRS 6.2.6, II.6.B). RG 1.163 endorses NEI 94-01, Revision 3-A, and ANSI/ANS-56.8-2020 as acceptable industry standards for technical methods and techniques for performing leakage rate tests, and explicitly allows for the use of alternative testing methods approved by the NRC (RG 1.163, Section C).

In summary, NRC standards allow for alternative approaches to containment leakage rate testing for novel designs, provided the applicant proposes, justifies, and obtains NRC approval for methods, procedures, and acceptance criteria that are appropriate for the specific containment design and demonstrate compliance with regulatory requirements.

data.query: What is the NRC regulatory definition of standard cubic feet per hour (SCFH) and standard cubic feet per minute (SCFM) as they apply to containment leakage testing?
data.answer: The NRC regulatory definition of standard cubic feet per hour (SCFH) and standard cubic feet per minute (SCFM) as they apply to containment leakage testing is provided in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section II. According to this section, a 'standard cubic foot' is defined as a cubic foot of gas at standard conditions of temperature and pressure, specifically at 75 °F and 29.92 inches Hg absolute. 'Standard cubic feet per hour (SCFH)' and 'standard cubic feet per minute (SCFM)' are defined as the number of standard cubic feet of gas passing a given point in one hour or one minute, respectively. These definitions are used in the context of quantifying containment leakage rates during required leakage rate tests, as referenced in DSRS 6.2.6 and further supported by Regulatory Guide 1.163, which endorses the use of these standard conditions and measurement units for containment leakage testing. Therefore, for NRC regulatory purposes, SCFH and SCFM are explicitly tied to the passage of gas at the specified standard conditions, ensuring consistency and comparability in leakage rate measurements across nuclear power plants.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for containment leakage testing methods, including the use of remote tools or automation, during periodic surveillance of nuclear power plant containments?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for containment leakage testing methods during periodic surveillance of nuclear power plant containments are primarily established in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, and further detailed in NRC guidance documents such as DSRS 6.2.6 and Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.163.

Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50 mandates periodic integrated (Type A) and local (Types B and C) leakage rate testing to ensure that leakage does not exceed the allowable rates specified in the plant's technical specifications (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section I.A). The test methods used must be capable of detecting and measuring leakage rates with sufficient accuracy to demonstrate compliance with these limits (Appendix J, Section III.A). While Appendix J does not explicitly address the use of remote tools or automation, it requires that any method employed must meet the accuracy and detection requirements.

DSRS 6.2.6 clarifies that leakage rate tests may be performed by pneumatic or hydrostatic means, and the results must be quantified explicitly or by a conservative bounding method to satisfy Appendix J and technical specification criteria. Licensees may choose between Option A (prescriptive) or Option B (performance-based) approaches in Appendix J. Under Option B, licensees must use NRC-approved methods, such as those endorsed in RG 1.163, and incorporate these into their technical specifications.

RG 1.163 endorses the use of NEI 94-01, Revision 3-A, and references ANSI/ANS-56.8-2002 or ANSI/ANS-56.8-2020 for detailed technical methods, which include provisions for using commercially available non-destructive examination (NDE) techniques (e.g., boroscopes, guided wave techniques) for inspecting inaccessible areas. The guidance allows for the use of such remote or automated tools, provided they are viable, commercially available, and capable of supporting plant-specific evaluations (RG 1.163, Section C).

In summary, containment leakage testing methods must be accurate and capable of quantifying leakage rates as required by Appendix J and technical specifications. The use of remote tools or automation is permissible if these methods meet the regulatory requirements for accuracy and detection, and are consistent with NRC-endorsed standards and guidance.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
APPENDIX J TO PART 50—PRIMARY REACTOR CONTAINMENT LEAKAGE TESTING FOR WATER-COOLED POWER REACTORS

I. Introduction
A. The primary reactor containment of all water-cooled power reactors, subject to the provisions of this appendix, must be subject to periodic integrated leakage rate testing and to periodic local leakage rate testing, as specified in this appendix, to assure that leakage through the primary reactor containment and systems and components penetrating primary containment does not exceed allowable leakage rates specified in the technical specifications. ...

II. Definitions
A. "Type A Test" means an overall integrated leakage rate test of the primary reactor containment.
B. "Type B Test" means a leakage rate test to determine the leakage through pressure-containing or leakage-limiting boundaries, other than the primary reactor containment, that enclose the primary reactor containment.
C. "Type C Test" means a leakage rate test to determine the leakage through containment isolation valves.

III. Test Methods
A. The test methods used must be those that will detect and measure the leakage rates as specified in this appendix. The methods must be capable of measuring the leakage rates with sufficient accuracy to assure that the allowable leakage rates specified in the technical specifications are not exceeded.
B. The use of remote tools or automation is not explicitly addressed in the appendix, but the requirement is that the methods used must be capable of detecting and measuring leakage rates with sufficient accuracy.

IV. Test Schedules
A. Type A tests must be conducted at a frequency as specified in the technical specifications, but at least once per 10 years, unless a performance-based schedule is approved.
B. Type B and C tests must be conducted at intervals specified in the technical specifications, but not to exceed 30 months for Type B and C tests, unless a performance-based schedule is approved.

data.query: How do NRC regulations address the acceptance criteria for visual inspections and leak testing of containment flanges and seals during containment reassembly after maintenance activities?
data.answer:
NRC regulations address the acceptance criteria for visual inspections and leak testing of containment flanges and seals during containment reassembly after maintenance activities primarily through the requirements of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, and associated regulatory guidance.

According to DSRS 6.2.6 (Section II), acceptance criteria are based on compliance with either Option A or Option B of Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50, and, for Option B, the provisions of Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.163. These requirements ensure that containment leakage rate testing meets the General Design Criteria (GDC) for containment integrity, inspection, and leakage rate determination.

Appendix J (Sections IV and V) specifies that the measured leakage rates for Type A (integrated), Type B, and Type C (local) tests must not exceed the allowable rates defined in the plant’s technical specifications. Specifically, Section IV.B states that the measured leakage rates for Type B and C tests (which include flanges and seals) must not exceed the allowable leakage rates for each component, and the sum of these rates must be less than the total allowable leakage rate for the containment system. Section V requires a general visual inspection of accessible containment surfaces, including seals and gaskets, prior to the Type A test to identify any deficiencies (such as degraded seals or loose bolts) that could affect integrity. Any deficiencies found must be evaluated and corrected before leakage rate testing.

RG 1.163 endorses NEI 94-01 and ANSI/ANS-56.8 for detailed testing methods. It also clarifies that after major modifications or repairs, a Type A test is required to verify both structural and leak-tight integrity before returning the containment to service. For minor modifications, a local leakage rate test (LLRT) is sufficient to verify the integrity of affected areas.

In summary, NRC regulations require that after maintenance activities involving containment flanges and seals, visual inspections must confirm the absence of conditions that could compromise integrity, and leak testing must demonstrate that leakage rates are within technical specification limits. These requirements are detailed in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J (Sections IV and V), DSRS 6.2.6, and RG 1.163.

data.query: How do regulatory requirements for containment leakage testing ensure that local leak rate tests accurately reflect the total allowable containment leakage rate for operability determinations?
data.answer:
Regulatory requirements for containment leakage testing ensure that local leak rate tests (LLRTs) accurately reflect the total allowable containment leakage rate for operability determinations through a combination of integrated and local testing, explicit summation of results, and strict adherence to technical specifications. According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J (Section I.B), the measured integrated leakage rate from Type A tests (CILRT/ILRT) and the sum of the measured leakage rates from Type B and C tests (LLRTs) must not exceed the allowable leakage rate specified in the plant's technical specifications. This ensures that all sources of potential leakage, including those from penetrations, valves, and other boundaries, are accounted for in the total leakage assessment.

DSRS 6.2.6 (Section II) further clarifies that instrumentation lines penetrating containment, which may be isolated during the CILRT, must have their leakage rates measured via LLRTs and these values must be added to the CILRT result. This prevents underestimation of total leakage by ensuring that all penetrations, whether tested locally or as part of the integrated test, are included in the total leakage calculation. The guidance also requires that all leakage rate tests, whether pneumatic or hydrostatic, must be capable of quantifying leakage rates explicitly or by a conservative bounding method to meet Appendix J and technical specification acceptance criteria.

Regulatory Guide 1.163 (Section B) supports this approach by endorsing NEI 94-01, which provides detailed guidance on the performance-based Option B program. This includes requirements for continual monitoring, staggered performance of LLRTs, and the summation of local leakage rates to ensure that the total does not exceed the allowable limit. The performance-based approach allows for extended test intervals only if acceptable performance history is demonstrated, ensuring ongoing reliability of leakage rate determinations.

In summary, the regulatory framework requires that LLRTs are performed in a manner that their results, when combined with integrated test results, provide a comprehensive and accurate assessment of total containment leakage, directly supporting operability determinations as specified in technical specifications (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J; DSRS 6.2.6; RG 1.163).

data.query: How are general design criteria for containment integrity applied in the context of local leak rate testing to ensure that all potential leakage paths, including those associated with bolted flanges, are adequately addressed?
data.answer:
General design criteria (GDC) for containment integrity, specifically GDC 52, 53, and 54, are applied to ensure that all potential leakage paths—including those associated with bolted flanges—are adequately addressed through a comprehensive containment leakage rate testing program. According to DSRS 6.2.6 (Sections II and III), the NRC reviews the applicant’s leakage rate testing program for conformance with 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, which prescribes requirements for both integrated and local leakage rate testing. GDC 52 requires that the containment and its penetrations be designed to accommodate periodic integrated leakage rate testing at design pressure, while GDC 53 and 54 require provisions for inspection, surveillance, and the capability to test penetrations and isolation valves for leakage.

Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50, as referenced in DSRS 6.2.6 and RG 1.163, mandates three types of tests: Type A (integrated leakage rate tests), Type B (local leakage rate tests of penetrations, including seals, gaskets, and expansion bellows), and Type C (local leakage rate tests of isolation valves). Type B and C tests—collectively known as local leak rate tests (LLRTs)—specifically address potential leakage paths such as bolted flanges by requiring direct testing of these boundaries. RG 1.163 further clarifies that acceptable methods for performing these tests are detailed in ANSI/ANS-56.8, which includes procedures for testing bolted flanges and other penetrations.

The NRC’s review ensures that all potential leakage paths, including those bypassing containment or leading directly to the atmosphere, are identified and tested. The total allowable bypass leakage must be specified and included in technical specifications (TS). For any modifications or repairs to pressure-retaining boundaries, such as bolted flanges, leakage integrity must be verified by an LLRT (RG 1.163, Section C). Thus, the application of GDCs through Appendix J and associated regulatory guidance ensures that all potential leakage paths, including those associated with bolted flanges, are systematically tested and controlled to maintain containment integrity.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for containment leakage testing methods, specifically regarding allowable leakage rates?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for containment leakage testing methods, specifically regarding allowable leakage rates, are established primarily in Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50 and further clarified in DSRS 6.2.6 and Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.163. 

Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50 requires that the measured leakage rates from containment and its penetrations must not exceed the allowable leakage rates specified in the plant's technical specifications (TS) (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Sections I.A and II.A-B). The three types of required tests are:
- Type A: Integrated Leakage Rate Test (ILRT) for the entire containment structure at peak accident pressure.
- Type B: Local Leakage Rate Tests (LLRTs) for containment penetrations (e.g., airlocks, hatches).
- Type C: LLRTs for containment isolation valves.

For all these tests, the measured leakage rates must be within the allowable limits set in the TS (Appendix J, II.A.2, II.B.3). The minimum acceptable design containment leakage rate is 0.1% of containment air weight per day (DSRS 6.2.6, II.A), which provides adequate margin above typical measured rates and aligns with current test methods.

Under Option B of Appendix J, as endorsed by RG 1.163, licensees may use performance-based methods (e.g., NEI 94-01, Revision 3-A) for leakage rate testing, provided these methods are referenced in the TS and are consistent with NRC-approved standards such as ANSI/ANS-56.8-2002 or ANSI/ANS-56.8-2020 (RG 1.163, C.1). The maximum allowable leakage rate (La) is calculated per 10 CFR Part 100, unless an alternate is specified in the TS (RG 1.163, B).

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria require that containment leakage rates, as measured by approved methods, do not exceed the allowable rates specified in the plant's TS, with a minimum design leakage rate of 0.1% per day. Compliance with either Option A or Option B of Appendix J, as described in DSRS 6.2.6 and RG 1.163, is required.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for pressure conditions to be used during containment leakage testing of nuclear power plant containments?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for pressure conditions during containment leakage testing of nuclear power plant containments are established primarily in Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50, as referenced in DSRS 6.2.6 and Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.163. 

For the integrated leakage rate test (Type A), Appendix J (Section II.A.1) requires that the test be conducted at the calculated peak containment internal pressure (Pa) related to the design basis accident (DBA), as specified in the plant's technical specifications. The test pressure must not be less than this peak calculated pressure, and the test should be performed under conditions as close as practical to the DBA conditions of pressure, temperature, and humidity (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section II.A.1; DSRS 6.2.6, Section II).

For local leakage rate tests (Types B and C), which include tests of penetrations, seals, gaskets, expansion bellows, and containment isolation valves, Appendix J (Section II.B.1) specifies that these tests must also be conducted at a pressure not less than Pa, unless otherwise specified in the technical specifications or approved by the NRC. DSRS 6.2.6 further clarifies that the test pressures for these components should be stated in the test program and technical specifications, and are acceptable if they correspond to the calculated peak containment internal pressure related to the DBA.

RG 1.163 endorses the use of NEI 94-01 and ANSI/ANS-56.8 for technical methods, but the pressure requirements remain those specified in Appendix J: testing at or above the DBA peak pressure (Pa), unless otherwise justified and approved.

In summary, containment leakage testing must be performed at pressures at least equal to the calculated peak internal pressure for the design basis accident (Pa), as specified in the plant's technical specifications, and under conditions as close as practical to those expected during a DBA.

data.query: How do regulatory standards ensure that the pressure applied during a Type B containment leak test is representative of the internal design pressure used in a Type A test?
data.answer:
Regulatory standards ensure that the pressure applied during a Type B containment leak test is representative of the internal design pressure used in a Type A test through explicit requirements and acceptance criteria outlined in both regulatory guidance and federal regulations. According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section II, the test pressure for Type A (integrated leakage rate) tests must be equal to the calculated peak containment internal pressure associated with the design basis accident (DBA), as specified in the technical specifications. For Type B (local leakage rate) tests, the regulation requires that the test pressure be determined so as to be representative of the containment design basis accident conditions, and it must be at least equal to the containment DBA pressure unless a lower pressure is justified and approved by the NRC (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section II.B.1).

DSRS 6.2.6 further reinforces this by stating that test pressures for containment penetrations (Type B tests) should be specified in the test program and technical specifications, and are acceptable if they correspond to the calculated peak containment internal pressure related to the DBA loss-of-coolant accident (LOCA). This ensures consistency between the pressures used in both Type A and Type B tests, making the Type B test pressure representative of the internal design pressure used in the Type A test.

Additionally, Regulatory Guide 1.163 endorses the use of NEI 94-01 and ANSI/ANS-56.8 standards, which provide detailed methodologies for performing these tests in accordance with Appendix J requirements. This regulatory framework ensures that the pressure conditions during Type B tests accurately reflect those expected during a design basis accident, thereby validating the integrity of containment penetrations under realistic accident conditions.

References: 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Sections I and II; DSRS 6.2.6, Sections II and III; RG 1.163, Section C.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for leakage testing of all bolted flanges in containment systems, regardless of pipe size?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for leakage testing of all bolted flanges in containment systems, regardless of pipe size, are primarily governed by Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50 and supporting guidance documents. According to Appendix J, Section III.A.1, all containment penetrations subject to possible leakage, including those with resilient seals, gaskets, or other sealing mechanisms, must be tested using Type B or Type C local leakage rate tests (LLRTs). This includes bolted flanges that serve as pressure-containing or leakage-limiting boundaries. The tests are to be performed at the containment design basis accident pressure unless a lower pressure is justified (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section III.A.1).

However, DSRS 6.2.6 and referenced industry standards (NEI 94-01, ANSI/ANS-56.8) provide specific exceptions. Type B or C tests are not required for containment boundaries that do not constitute potential atmospheric leakage pathways during and after a design-basis LOCA, boundaries sealed with a qualified seal system, or for test connections, vents, and drains that are 1 inch or less in size, administratively secured closed, and have a double barrier (DSRS 6.2.6, II. Acceptance Criteria). For qualified seal systems, periodic leakage rate testing using the sealing liquid as the test medium is required to ensure limits are maintained.

Regulatory Guide 1.163 further clarifies that the NRC accepts the methodologies in ANSI/ANS-56.8-2002 and -2020 for performing these tests, and that leakage integrity of affected areas should be verified by LLRT following modifications (RG 1.163, Section B and C).

In summary, all bolted flanges in containment systems that are potential leakage pathways must undergo Type B LLRTs unless they meet specific exemption criteria outlined in DSRS 6.2.6 and referenced standards.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
NEI 94-01, Revision 0 (Section 6.0), and ANSI/ANS-56.8-1994 (Section 3.3.1) state that Type B or Type C tests are not required for the following cases:

1. containment boundaries that do not constitute potential containment atmospheric leakage pathways during and following a design-basis loss-of-coolant accident (DB LOCA)

2. containment boundaries sealed with a qualified seal system

3. test connections, vents, and drains between containment isolation valves that:

A. are 1 inch or less in size

B. administratively secured closed

C. consist of a double barrier (e.g., two valves in series, one valve with a nipple and cap, one valve and a blind flange)

This guidance may be applied to either Option A or Option B of Appendix J.

For Case No. 2, a qualified seal system is defined in ANSI/ANS-56.8-1994 as a system that is capable of sealing the leakage with a liquid at a pressure no less than 1.1 Pa, (calculated containment peak accident pressure), for at least 30 days following the DB LOCA. The staff’s position is the analysis of the sealing capability includes the assumption of the most limiting single failure of any active component. Also, unless there is a virtually unlimited supply of sealing liquid (such as from a suppression pool or recirculation sump), limits for liquid leakage rate should be assigned to these valves based on analysis and included in the plant TS. Periodic leakage rate testing, using the sealing liquid as the test medium, is then needed to ensure that the limits are maintained.

For Case No. 3, to ensure that containment integrity is restored after testing, the test, vent, and drain connections that are used to facilitate local leakage rate testing and the performance of the CILRT should be under administrative control and should be subject to periodic surveillance, to ensure their integrity and to verify the effectiveness of administrative controls.

data.query: How do NRC regulations address the calculation and verification of stud preload for containment vessel bolted flanges as part of leakage testing programs?
data.answer:
NRC regulations address the calculation and verification of stud preload for containment vessel bolted flanges as part of leakage testing programs primarily through requirements for containment integrity and leakage rate testing, rather than prescribing specific preload calculation methods. According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J (Section VI), the containment and its penetrations, including bolted connections, must be inspected and maintained to assure their integrity and capability to meet leakage rate requirements. Leakage rate tests (Types A, B, and C) must be performed using methods capable of accurately measuring leakage to ensure compliance with allowable limits specified in technical specifications (Appendix J, Sections III and IV).

DSRS 6.2.6 further clarifies that the leakage rate testing program must conform to Appendix J and relevant General Design Criteria (GDCs), and that test pressures for containment penetrations (including bolted flanges) should be stated in the test program and technical specifications. The test pressure is typically the calculated peak containment internal pressure related to the design-basis loss-of-coolant accident (DB LOCA).

Regulatory Guide 1.163 endorses the use of NEI 94-01 and ANSI/ANS-56.8 standards for technical methods and techniques in leakage testing. These standards, referenced in RG 1.163, provide detailed procedures for performing leakage rate tests, which would include ensuring that bolted flanges are properly assembled and preloaded to maintain containment integrity during testing. However, the NRC regulations and guidance do not specify the exact calculation or verification method for stud preload; rather, they require that bolted connections be maintained and tested to demonstrate compliance with leakage rate limits.

In summary, NRC regulations require that stud preload for containment vessel bolted flanges be sufficient to maintain integrity during leakage testing, with verification achieved through successful performance of the required leakage rate tests as outlined in Appendix J, DSRS 6.2.6, and RG 1.163.

data.query: How is the allowable integrated containment leakage rate determined for demonstrating containment operability, and how does this relate to the quantification of leakage contributions from Type A testing?
data.answer:
The allowable integrated containment leakage rate, referred to as La, is determined based on the requirements of Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50 and is specified in the plant's technical specifications. La represents the maximum leakage rate, at the calculated peak containment pressure associated with the design basis loss-of-coolant accident, that is assumed in the safety analysis for establishing containment acceptance criteria (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Sections I.A and II.A; DSRS 6.2.6, Section II). The measured integrated leakage rate from the Type A test (also known as the Containment Integrated Leakage Rate Test, or CILRT) must not exceed La, with margin, to demonstrate containment operability (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section I.A).

Type A testing quantifies the overall leakage rate through all potential leakage paths, including penetrations and isolation valves (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section II.A). The results of the Type A test are compared directly to La to demonstrate that the total leakage rate does not exceed the allowable limit (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section III.A). If certain penetrations, such as instrumentation lines, are isolated during the Type A test and are not locally leakage rate tested, their leakage must be included in the total measured leakage rate for comparison to La (DSRS 6.2.6, Section II).

The design leakage rate should not be less than 0.1 percent per day, providing adequate margin above typically measured rates and aligning with current test methods and acceptance criteria (DSRS 6.2.6, Section II). Both prescriptive (Option A) and performance-based (Option B) approaches to testing are acceptable, with Option B allowing for extended test intervals based on performance and risk assessment, as endorsed by Regulatory Guide 1.163 (RG 1.163, Section B).

In summary, the allowable integrated containment leakage rate (La) is a safety analysis-derived value specified in technical specifications, and the measured leakage from Type A testing must be quantified and shown not to exceed La to demonstrate containment operability.
