Nuclear power plant leakage rate testing experience shows a design leakage rate of 0.1 percent per day provides adequate margin above typically measured containment leakage rates and is compatible with current leakage rate test methods and test acceptance criteria. Therefore, the minimum acceptable design containment leakage rate should not be less than 0.1 percent per day.

... Appendix J, Option A, Section III.A.1(a), requires no repairs or adjustments be made to the containment before the performance of the CILRT so the containment can be tested in as close to the “as is” condition as practical. Under Option B, RG 1.163 endorses Nuclear Energy Institute (NEI) 94-01, Revision 0 (with certain exceptions), which provides similar guidance in Sections 8.0 and 9.0. Instrumentation lines that penetrate containment; however, are sometimes isolated for the CILRT. To ensure that they are included in the test, the following should be done. Leakage rate testing of instrumentation lines that penetrate containment may be done in conjunction with either the LLRTs or the CILRT. Instrumentation lines that are not locally leakage rate tested should not be isolated from the containment atmosphere during the performance of the CILRT. Provisions should be made to ensure that instrumentation lines isolated during the CILRT are restored to their operable status following the test.

All leakage rate tests, performed by either pneumatic or hydrostatic means, should have the capability to quantify the leakage rates either explicitly or by a conservative bounding method to satisfy test acceptance criteria in Appendix J and the TS.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
APPENDIX J TO PART 50—PRIMARY REACTOR CONTAINMENT LEAKAGE TESTING FOR WATER-COOLED POWER REACTORS

I. Introduction
A. The primary reactor containment of all water-cooled power reactors, subject to the provisions of this appendix, must be subject to periodic integrated leakage rate testing and to periodic local leakage rate testing, as specified in this appendix, to assure that leakage through the primary reactor containment and systems and components penetrating primary containment does not exceed allowable leakage rates specified in the technical specifications. The measured integrated leakage rate must not exceed the allowable leakage rate (La) with margin, as specified in the technical specifications. The allowable leakage rate (La) is the maximum leakage rate, at the calculated peak containment pressure related to the design basis loss-of-coolant accident, that is assumed in the safety analysis for establishing the containment acceptance criteria. The contribution from Type A tests (integrated leakage rate tests) to the total leakage rate must be quantified and compared to the allowable leakage rate (La) to demonstrate containment operability.

II. Definitions
A. Type A Test—An integrated leakage rate test to measure the overall leakage rate through all potential leakage paths, including penetrations and isolation valves, of the primary reactor containment.

B. Type B and Type C Tests—Local leakage rate tests to measure leakage across specific containment penetrations and isolation valves.

III. Test Requirements
A. The containment leakage testing program must include both integrated and local leakage rate tests. The results of the Type A test must be used to demonstrate that the total leakage rate does not exceed the allowable leakage rate (La) specified in the technical specifications.

evidence_chain.section: B. DISCUSSION (Background)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50 requires the following types of containment leakage tests: 

• Type A tests: integrated leakage rate tests (ILRTs)
• Type B tests: leakage tests across each pressure-containing or leakage-limiting boundary for specified primary reactor containment penetrations including seals, gaskets, and expansion bellows
• Type C tests: leakage tests of containment isolation valves

Type B and C tests are also referred to as local leakage rate tests (LLRTs).

Maximum allowable leakage rates (La) are calculated in accordance with 10 CFR Part 100, “Reactor Site Criteria,” (Ref. 7), except where alternates have been granted and are specified in licensee site specific TS.  

Appendix J has two options to determine test frequencies: Option A (prescriptive) and Option B (performance-based). Under Option A, three Type A tests are to be performed at approximately equal intervals during each inservice inspection period. The Option B performance-based requirements, issued in 1995, allow licensees to replace prescriptive testing requirements with testing requirements based on leakage rate performance and a supporting plant-specific risk impact assessment. Option B also introduced a requirement for visual inspection of accessible portions of the containment before each Type A test and at a periodic interval between tests. Licensees usually satisfy this requirement through the containment inservice inspection program conducted in accordance with American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (BPV Code), Section XI, Subsections IWE and IWL (Ref. 8 and Ref. 9), as incorporated by reference and conditioned in 10 CFR 50.55a, “Codes and standards.”

NUREG-1493 is a detailed study of the impacts, costs, and risk of the Appendix J requirements and provided the methodology used to determine the acceptability of extended testing intervals. Sensitivity analyses in NUREG-1493 and other studies show that light-water reactor accident risk is relatively insensitive to the containment leakage rate because the risk is dominated by accident sequences that result in failure or bypass of containment. Reducing the frequency of Type A tests over extended periods, including up to 15 years, was found to lead to an imperceptible increase in risk. The estimated increase in risk is very small because (1) ILRTs identify only a few potential containment leakage paths that cannot be identified by Type B and Type C testing, and (2) the leaks that have been found by Type A tests have been only marginally above existing requirements. Given the insensitivity of risk to the containment leakage rate and the small fraction of leakage paths detected solely by Type A testing, increasing the interval between ILRTs is possible with minimal impact on risk to the public.

data.query: What is the relationship between the technical specification limit for containment leakage and the acceptance criteria for integrated leakage rate testing in regulatory review standards?
data.answer:
The technical specification (TS) limit for containment leakage and the acceptance criteria for integrated leakage rate testing are directly related and must be consistent with each other. According to Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50 (Evidence [2]), each plant's TS must specify the maximum allowable leakage rate for the primary reactor containment, as measured during the integrated leakage rate test (Type A test). The acceptance criteria for this test must align with the TS limit, ensuring that the measured leakage rate does not exceed the value specified in the TS. This relationship ensures that the containment's leak tightness is maintained within regulatory limits, thereby supporting the containment's safety function and compliance with offsite dose requirements (10 CFR Part 100).

DSRS 6.2.6 (Evidence [1]) further clarifies that acceptance criteria for leakage rate tests are based on meeting the requirements of Appendix J and that all leakage rate tests must be capable of quantifying leakage rates to satisfy both Appendix J and TS acceptance criteria. Meeting Appendix J requirements provides assurance that containment leakage will remain within TS values.

Regulatory Guide 1.163 (Evidence [3]) supports this by stating that maximum allowable leakage rates (La) are calculated per 10 CFR Part 100 and specified in the TS. The guide also describes acceptable methods for performing and evaluating integrated leakage rate tests, ensuring that the test results are compared against the TS-specified limits. Thus, the acceptance criteria for integrated leakage rate testing serve as the operational means to demonstrate compliance with the TS containment leakage limit.

A. The primary reactor containment for a water-cooled power reactor is subject to potential leakage of air, steam, and radioactive materials. The technical specifications for each operating license issued under this part must specify the maximum allowable leakage rate for the primary reactor containment, as measured under the conditions of an integrated leakage rate test. The acceptance criteria for the integrated leakage rate test must be consistent with the maximum allowable leakage rate specified in the technical specifications. The test program must be designed to ensure that the containment leakage rate does not exceed the allowable value, thereby providing assurance that the containment will perform its intended safety function.

II. Types of Tests
A. The test program consists of:
1. An integrated leakage rate test (Type A test), which measures the overall leakage rate of the primary reactor containment.
2. Local leakage rate tests (Type B and C tests), which measure the leakage rates of containment penetrations and isolation valves.

III. Test Requirements
A. The integrated leakage rate test must be conducted at the containment design basis pressure and must demonstrate that the measured leakage rate does not exceed the maximum allowable leakage rate specified in the technical specifications.

B. The results of the integrated leakage rate test must be used to determine compliance with the acceptance criteria established in the technical specifications.

data.query: What are the NRC requirements for demonstrating the acceptability of Type A containment leakage testing for nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC requirements for demonstrating the acceptability of Type A containment leakage testing for nuclear power plants are established in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, and further clarified in regulatory guidance documents. Licensees must implement a reactor containment leakage rate testing program that conforms to Appendix J, which provides two compliance options: Option A (Prescriptive Requirements) and Option B (Performance-Based Requirements) (DSRS 6.2.6, II. Acceptance Criteria; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, I.A).

Type A tests are defined as integrated leakage rate tests that measure the overall leakage rate of the primary containment structure (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, II.A). These tests must be performed at intervals and under conditions specified in Appendix J and the plant's technical specifications. The test methods must be capable of measuring the minimum leakage rates specified in the technical specifications with an accuracy of ±0.25 times the allowable leakage rate at a 95% confidence level (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, III.B).

Under Option A, licensees must meet the prescriptive requirements for preoperational and periodic leakage rate testing as stated in Appendix J. Under Option B, licensees may adopt a performance-based approach, provided they comply with the requirements of Appendix J Option B and the provisions of Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.163, which endorses NEI 94-01, Revision 3-A, and ANSI/ANS-56.8-2002 or ANSI/ANS-56.8-2020 for technical methods (DSRS 6.2.6; RG 1.163, Section C.1).

For Type A test intervals, the normal interval should be less than 15 years. Extensions beyond 15 years require a license amendment request (LAR) and justification based on unforeseen emergent conditions (RG 1.163, Section C.5). When seeking to extend the interval to 15 years, licensees must demonstrate that the risk increase is small, using a PRA of sufficient quality (at least Capability Category I per RG 1.200) and quantitatively evaluating the risk impact, particularly on large early release frequency (LERF), as described in EPRI Report No. 1009325, Revision 2-A and RG 1.174 (RG 1.163, Sections C.7 and C.8).

In summary, acceptability is demonstrated by compliance with Appendix J (either Option A or B), adherence to technical specifications, use of NRC-endorsed methods, and, for extended intervals, a risk-informed justification as outlined in RG 1.163.

evidence_chain.section: Appendix J to Part 50—Primary Reactor Containment Leakage Testing for Water-Cooled Power Reactors
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appendix J to Part 50—Primary Reactor Containment Leakage Testing for Water-Cooled Power Reactors

I. Introduction
A. The primary reactor containment for a water-cooled power reactor is subject to potential leakage. The purpose of the tests described in this appendix is to assure that leakage through the primary reactor containment and systems and components penetrating primary containment shall not exceed allowable leakage rates specified in the technical specifications or associated bases. These tests are intended to ensure that the containment, as a barrier against the uncontrolled release of radioactivity to the environment, will perform its function as assumed in the safety analysis for the plant.

B. The requirements of this appendix apply to all water-cooled power reactors, except as provided in paragraph III.A of this appendix. The tests required by this appendix are:
1. Type A tests—integrated leakage rate tests to measure the overall leakage rate of the primary containment;
2. Type B tests—local leakage rate tests to measure the leakage across each pressure-containing or leakage-limiting boundary, other than those tested by Type A or Type C tests;
3. Type C tests—local leakage rate tests to measure the leakage across each containment isolation valve.

II. Definitions
A. "Type A test" means an overall integrated leakage rate test of the primary containment structure.
B. "Type B test" means a test to determine leakage rates for containment penetrations, such as airlocks, hatches, and other penetrations, except those tested by Type C tests.
C. "Type C test" means a test to determine leakage rates for containment isolation valves.

III. Performance of Tests
A. Each licensee shall perform Type A, B, and C tests, as applicable, at the intervals and under the conditions specified in this appendix and in accordance with the technical specifications for the plant.
B. The methods used for measuring leakage rates must be capable of measuring the minimum leakage rates specified in the technical specifications with an accuracy of at least plus or minus 0.25 times the allowable leakage rate at a 95 percent confidence level.

C.  STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE

NEI 94-01, Revision 3-A, provides methods acceptable to the NRC staff for complying with the provisions of Option B in Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50, subject to the following regulatory positions.  Licensees wishing to use this RG should follow the regulatory positions identified in Section C of this RG in addition to the “Limitations and Conditions” identified in the safety evaluation appended to NEI 94-01, Revision 3-A.

1. NEI 94-01, Revision 3-A, references ANSI/ANS-56.8-2002, “Containment System Leakage Testing Requirements” (Ref. 17), for detailed descriptions of the technical methods and techniques used for performing Types A, B, and C tests under Option B of Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50. The NRC staff agrees with the methodology used in ANSI/ANS-56.8-2002 as well as the most recent methodology used in ANSI/ANS-56.8-2020 and accepts these as references for how licensees should perform the tests. ANSI/ANS-56.8-2020 as approved by this RG may be used in lieu of ANSI/ANS 56.8-2002 without a LAR if (1) the licensee’s TS incorporate NEI 94-01, Revision 3-A and (2) the licensee’s TS do not explicitly reference the 2002 ANSI/ANS standard and there is no other license provision that would necessitate a LAR to use ANSI/ANS-56.8-2020.1. The NRC staff has one condition for licensees referencing these standards. Specifically, for calculating the Type A leakage rate, the licensee should use the performance leakage rate definition in NEI 94-01, Revision 3-A, in lieu of that in ANSI/ANS-56.8-2002 or ANSI/ANS-56.8-2020.  The definition contained in NEI 94-01, Revision 3-A, is more inclusive because it considers excessive leakage in the performance determination.

5. The normal Type A test interval should be less than 15 years. If a licensee desires to use the provision of Section 9.1 of NEI 94-01, Revision 3-A, related to extending the ILRT interval beyond 15 years, the licensee should demonstrate in a LAR that the extension is necessary due to an unforeseen emergent condition (see Regulatory Issue Summary 2008–27, “Staff Position on Extension of the Containment Type A Test Interval Beyond 15 Years Under Option B of Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50,” dated December 8, 2008 (Ref. 19)).

7. When using the methodology in EPRI Report No. 1009325, Revision 2-A to permanently extend the ILRT interval to 15 years, the licensee should submit documentation indicating that the technical adequacy of the PRA used to support its performance-based Appendix J program is consistent with the guidance in RG 1.200, “Acceptability of Probabilistic Risk Assessment Results for Risk-Informed Activities,” (Ref. 20), relevant to the ILRT extension application. RG 1.200 describes one acceptable approach for determining whether a base PRA, in total or the parts that are used to support an application, is sufficient to provide confidence in the results, such that the PRA can be used in regulatory decision-making for light-water reactors. A minimum of Capability Category I of the ASME PRA standard should be applied as the standard for assessing PRA quality for ILRT extension applications, since approximate values of core damage frequency (CDF) and large early release frequency (LERF) and their distribution among release categories are sufficient to support the evaluation of changes to ILRT frequencies. The assessment of external events may be taken from existing analyses, previously submitted to, and approved by the NRC staff, or from another alternate method of assessing an order of magnitude estimate for the contribution of the external event to the impact of the changed interval.

8.  When using the methodology in EPRI Report No. 1009325, Revision 2-A to permanently extend the ILRT interval to 15 years, the licensee should submit documentation indicating that the estimated risk increase associated with extending the ILRT surveillance interval to 15 years is small. The methodology should quantitatively evaluate the risk impact of the ILRT extension. The most relevant risk metric is LERF, since the Type A test does not generally impact CDF.  RG 1.174, “An Approach for Using Probabilistic Risk Assessment in Risk-Informed Decisions on Plant-Specific Changes to the Licensing Basis,” (Ref. 21) provides guidance for determining the risk impact of plant-specific changes to the licensing basis.  Additional risk metrics—including the increase in population dose and the increase in conditional containment failure probability—are also evaluated in EPRI Report No. 1009325, Revision 2-A to help ensure that the key safety principles in RG 1.174 are met.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory guides for risk-informed containment leakage testing relate to the general requirements for containment leak rate testing frequencies?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory guides for risk-informed containment leakage testing, specifically Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.163, provide an acceptable method for implementing the performance-based requirements of Option B in Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50. Appendix J establishes the general requirements for containment leak rate testing, including the types of tests (Type A, B, and C), their purposes, and the required frequencies. Under Option A of Appendix J, test frequencies are prescriptive (e.g., Type C tests every 24 months), and deviations require exemptions (DSRS 6.2.6; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J).

Option B, as described in Appendix J and endorsed by RG 1.163, allows for a performance-based, risk-informed approach to determining test intervals. This approach enables licensees to extend test intervals (e.g., Type A up to 15 years, Type C up to 75 months) if they demonstrate adequate performance history and a plant-specific risk assessment shows that the risk increase is small (RG 1.163, Section B; DSRS 6.2.6). The performance-based approach requires compliance with methods approved by the NRC and inclusion of these requirements in the plant's technical specifications (DSRS 6.2.6).

In summary, NRC regulatory guides such as RG 1.163 provide the framework and criteria for licensees to adopt risk-informed, performance-based containment leakage testing programs under Option B of Appendix J, allowing for extended test intervals beyond the prescriptive frequencies of Option A, provided that safety and risk criteria are met and NRC approval is obtained.

data.query: In the context of siting criteria for nuclear power plants, how are the requirements for evaluating postulated fission product release integrated with the demonstration of containment leak rate acceptability, and what regulatory guidance supports the use of risk-informed methods to extend leak rate testing intervals?
data.answer:
The requirements for evaluating postulated fission product release are directly integrated with the demonstration of containment leak rate acceptability through regulatory frameworks that link containment performance to offsite dose calculations and site acceptability. According to DSRS 6.2.6, the containment leakage rate is a critical parameter in accident analyses used to determine whether offsite radiation doses remain within the reference values specified in 10 CFR Part 100, which governs reactor site criteria. The measured or assumed containment leakage rate is used in conjunction with postulated fission product releases to evaluate the potential offsite dose consequences of design basis accidents (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, I.A).

To ensure that the containment leakage rate remains within acceptable limits, periodic leakage rate testing is required. These tests verify that the actual leakage rate does not exceed the values assumed in accident analyses, thereby supporting the acceptability of the exclusion area, low population zone, and population center distances (DSRS 6.2.6; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, I.A).

Regulatory guidance supports the use of risk-informed methods to extend leak rate testing intervals. Appendix J, Option B, allows for performance-based testing intervals, provided that licensees demonstrate, through plant-specific risk assessments, that the risk from extending the intervals is small (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, I.B). Regulatory Guide 1.163 endorses NEI 94-01 (Revision 3-A), which allows for Type A test intervals up to 15 years and Type C intervals up to 75 months, contingent on acceptable performance history and a plant-specific probabilistic risk assessment (RG 1.163, Section B). EPRI Report 1009325, endorsed by RG 1.163, provides a risk-informed methodology for justifying such extensions, and studies such as NUREG-1493 have shown that the risk increase from extending test intervals is minimal.

In summary, the integration is achieved by ensuring that the containment leakage rate used in fission product release evaluations is periodically verified through testing, and risk-informed regulatory guidance allows for extended testing intervals when justified by performance and risk assessments.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for visual inspection of containment vessel surfaces during leakage testing?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for visual inspection of containment vessel surfaces during leakage testing are established primarily in Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50, as referenced in DSRS 6.2.6 and Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.163. Prior to conducting a Type A (Integrated Leak Rate Test, ILRT), a visual inspection must be performed on accessible interior and exterior surfaces of the containment system. This inspection is intended to identify structural deterioration, loose or missing bolts, evidence of leakage, or other deficiencies that could affect the integrity or leak-tightness of the containment (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section II.A.1). Any deficiencies discovered must either be corrected before the test or evaluated and found acceptable by the licensee, with the evaluation documented in the test report (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section II.A.1).

For licensees following Option B (performance-based approach), RG 1.163 specifies that a general visual inspection must be performed before each Type A test and at periodic intervals between tests, with the frequency based on containment performance. For plants with extended Type A test intervals (up to 15 years), a general visual inspection should be conducted prior to each Type A test and during at least three other outages before the next test. These inspections should be coordinated with ASME BPV Code, Section XI, Subsections IWE and IWL inspections (RG 1.163, Section B).

In summary, the acceptance criteria require that visual inspections identify and address any conditions that could compromise containment integrity or leak-tightness, with deficiencies either corrected or formally evaluated and justified prior to leakage testing.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for performing leakage tests on containment bolted closures using local pressurization at peak accident pressure during reactor shutdowns for refueling?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for performing leakage tests on containment bolted closures using local pressurization at peak accident pressure during reactor shutdowns for refueling are established primarily in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, and further detailed in NRC guidance documents such as DSRS 6.2.6 and Regulatory Guide 1.163.

Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50 requires periodic leakage rate testing of containment penetrations (Type B tests) to ensure that leakage does not exceed allowable rates specified in the plant technical specifications (TS). Type B tests, which include bolted closures, must be performed using local pressurization at the calculated peak containment internal pressure related to the design basis accident (DBA), as specified in the TS (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section II.B and IV.A). The test methods and acceptance criteria must conform to those in Appendix J and the TS, and the test pressure must be the DBA peak pressure unless otherwise specified (DSRS 6.2.6, Section III; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section IV.A).

The frequency for Type B tests is generally not to exceed 30 months, unless a longer interval is justified and approved (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section III.A). These tests are typically performed during reactor shutdowns for refueling, as part of the periodic containment leakage testing program (DSRS 6.2.6, Section II; RG 1.163, Section C).

The NRC accepts the technical methods described in ANSI/ANS-56.8-2002 (and later versions) for performing these tests, as referenced in NEI 94-01, Revision 3-A (RG 1.163, Section C). The tests must be capable of quantifying leakage rates to demonstrate compliance with acceptance criteria (DSRS 6.2.6, Section III).

In summary, local leakage rate tests on containment bolted closures during refueling shutdowns must be performed at the calculated peak accident pressure, using NRC-accepted methods, at intervals specified in the TS (not to exceed 30 months), and must demonstrate that leakage does not exceed allowable rates as required by 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
APPENDIX J TO PART 50—PRIMARY REACTOR CONTAINMENT LEAKAGE TESTING FOR WATER-COOLED POWER REACTORS

I. Introduction
A. The primary reactor containment of all water-cooled power reactors, subject to the provisions of this part, must be subject to periodic integrated leakage rate testing and to periodic leakage rate testing of containment penetrations and isolation valves to assure that leakage through these barriers does not exceed allowable leakage rates as specified in the technical specifications. The test methods, procedures, and acceptance criteria must be in accordance with the requirements of this appendix, as supplemented or modified by plant technical specifications.

II. Types of Tests
A. Type A Test—Integrated Leakage Rate Test. The test must measure the leakage rate from all containment penetrations and isolation valves, including those that are normally open during reactor operation, at the calculated peak containment internal pressure related to the design basis accident as specified in the technical specifications.
B. Type B and C Tests—Local Leakage Rate Tests. Type B tests are intended to measure leakage rates for containment penetrations, and Type C tests are intended to measure leakage rates for containment isolation valves. These tests must be conducted at the containment design basis accident pressure, except as otherwise specified in the technical specifications.

III. Test Schedules
A. Type A tests must be conducted at a frequency of at least once per 10 years, based upon acceptable performance history, as specified in the technical specifications. Type B and C tests must be performed at intervals specified in the technical specifications, but not to exceed 30 months for Type B tests and not to exceed 24 months for Type C tests, unless a longer interval is justified by performance history and approved by the Commission.

IV. Test Methods
A. The methods used for performing the tests must be those specified in the technical specifications or those approved by the Commission. The test pressure must be the calculated peak containment internal pressure related to the design basis accident, as specified in the technical specifications.

data.query: How do the requirements for examination and inspection of containment flange bolting relate to the overall containment leakage testing program, and what regulatory provisions govern the frequency and methods for inspecting flange bolts when they are removed?
data.answer:
The requirements for examination and inspection of containment flange bolting are integral to the overall containment leakage testing program, as governed by 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J. Appendix J establishes the regulatory framework for both preoperational and periodic leakage-rate testing of the primary reactor containment and its penetrations, including flanged connections (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Sections III and IV).

Specifically, Type B tests are required to detect and measure leakage across pressure-containing or leakage-limiting boundaries, such as flanges (Appendix J, III.B.1). The frequency of these tests is performance-based but must occur at least once every 30 months unless otherwise specified (Appendix J, III.B.2). For flanged connections that are disassembled and reassembled during service, a leakage test must be performed before the containment is returned to service, using a method capable of detecting leakage across the pressure boundary (Appendix J, III.D.1-2).

Additionally, Appendix J, Section IV requires that the containment leakage testing program include provisions for inspection and maintenance of penetrations, including flange bolting, to ensure containment integrity. When bolted connections are disassembled, bolts and sealing surfaces must be visually inspected for defects, and corrective actions taken as necessary before reassembly (Appendix J, IV.B).

Regulatory guidance (DSRS 6.2.6; RG 1.163) further clarifies that these requirements are part of a broader program that includes both leakage rate testing (Types A, B, and C) and inservice inspection per ASME BPV Code, Section XI. The NRC accepts technical methods described in ANSI/ANS-56.8 for performing these tests (RG 1.163, Section C).

In summary, the inspection and testing of containment flange bolting are directly linked to the containment leakage testing program, with specific regulatory provisions in Appendix J governing the frequency, methods, and inspection requirements when flange bolts are removed and reassembled.

data.query: What regulatory criteria must be met to ensure that carbon steel used beneath stainless steel cladding in containment vessels remains protected from corrosion and leakage if the cladding is degraded?
data.answer:
To ensure that carbon steel used beneath stainless steel cladding in containment vessels remains protected from corrosion and leakage, especially if the cladding is degraded, several regulatory criteria must be met. According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J (Section III.A), the containment structure—including the carbon steel base metal beneath the stainless steel cladding—must be maintained in a condition that precludes corrosion and leakage. If the cladding is degraded, the underlying carbon steel must be protected to prevent loss of containment integrity. The test program must include periodic integrated and local leakage rate tests (Type A, B, and C tests) at intervals specified in the technical specifications, with provisions for corrective action if unacceptable leakage or corrosion is detected (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section III.B).

DSRS 6.2.6 (Section II) further clarifies that compliance with Appendix J and Regulatory Guide 1.163 (RG 1.163) is required to meet General Design Criteria (GDC) 52, 53, and 54, which relate to containment design, inspection, surveillance, and leakage rate testing. RG 1.163 (Section B) specifies that licensees must perform general visual inspections of accessible interior and exterior surfaces of the containment system for structural deterioration that may affect leak-tight integrity. These inspections are to be performed before each Type A test and at periodic intervals, coordinated with ASME BPV Code, Section XI, Subsections IWE and IWL inspections as required by 10 CFR 50.55a. Visual examinations under the IWE program are particularly important for detecting through-wall corrosion and degradation of metallic liners and shells.

In summary, the regulatory criteria require: (1) maintenance of the carbon steel base metal to prevent corrosion and leakage, (2) periodic leakage rate testing and inspections as specified in Appendix J and RG 1.163, and (3) corrective actions if degradation or unacceptable leakage is detected. These measures collectively ensure the integrity of the carbon steel beneath degraded cladding.

APPENDIX J TO PART 50—PRIMARY REACTOR CONTAINMENT LEAKAGE TESTING FOR WATER-COOLED POWER REACTORS

I. Introduction
A. The primary reactor containment for a water-cooled power reactor is subject to potential leakage of radioactive material, especially under accident conditions. The containment, including penetrations and isolation valves, must be designed, constructed, and maintained to ensure that leakage is within allowable limits. 

B. The purpose of the tests required by this appendix is to assure that leakage through the primary reactor containment and systems and components penetrating containment, or otherwise connected to the containment atmosphere, does not exceed allowable leakage rates specified in the technical specifications or associated bases. 

II. Types of Tests
A. Type A Test: Integrated Leakage Rate Test. This test measures the overall leakage rate of the primary reactor containment.

B. Type B and C Tests: Local Leakage Rate Tests. These tests measure the leakage rate of containment penetrations and isolation valves.

III. Test Requirements
A. The test program must ensure that the containment structure, including carbon steel base metal beneath stainless steel cladding, is maintained in a condition that precludes corrosion and leakage. data.query: What are the regulatory acceptance criteria for materials used in containment liners to ensure resistance to corrosion and leakage?
data.answer:
The regulatory acceptance criteria for materials used in containment liners to ensure resistance to corrosion and leakage are established primarily through the requirements of Appendix J to 10 CFR Part 50, relevant General Design Criteria (GDCs), and associated regulatory guidance. According to DSRS 6.2.6 (Section II), materials must conform to the requirements of Appendix J, which mandates that the containment, including liners, must maintain integrity and leak-tightness as designed. Specifically, the minimum acceptable design containment leakage rate should not exceed 0.1 percent per day, and periodic testing (CILRTs and local leakage rate tests) must demonstrate that leakage rates remain within allowable limits specified in the plant’s technical specifications (DSRS 6.2.6; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Sections I-IV).

Appendix J further requires that containment liner materials be selected, fabricated, and maintained to prevent corrosion and degradation that could compromise leak-tight integrity (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J, Section I.B and IV.A). The materials must be resistant to corrosion and degradation throughout the service life of the plant, and the effectiveness of these materials is verified through periodic integrated and local leakage rate tests (Appendix J, Sections II and III).

Regulatory Guide 1.163 (Section C) reinforces these requirements by specifying that licensees must implement an IWE/IWL Containment Inservice Inspection Program in accordance with the ASME BPV Code, Section XI, as required by 10 CFR 50.55a. This program must address both accessible and inaccessible areas of the containment structure, including liners, and utilize appropriate inspection techniques to detect potential degradation, especially in areas susceptible to corrosion.

In summary, acceptance criteria require that containment liner materials be demonstrably resistant to corrosion and leakage, verified through periodic testing and inspection programs, and that measured leakage rates do not exceed technical specification limits throughout the plant’s service life (DSRS 6.2.6; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J; RG 1.163).

APPENDIX J TO PART 50—PRIMARY REACTOR CONTAINMENT LEAKAGE TESTING FOR WATER-COOLED POWER REACTORS

I. Introduction
A. The primary reactor containment for water-cooled power reactors is subject to certain leakage testing requirements to assure that (1) leakage through the containment or systems and components penetrating the containment shall not exceed allowable leakage rate values as specified in the technical specifications or associated bases, and (2) periodic surveillance of containment penetrations and isolation valves is performed so that proper maintenance and repairs are made during the service life of the containment and systems and components penetrating the containment.

B. The requirements set forth in this appendix apply to all water-cooled power reactors, except as provided in paragraph III.A of this appendix. The requirements are intended to ensure that the containment, including containment liners and penetrations, maintains its integrity and leak-tightness as designed. The containment materials, including liners, must be selected and maintained to prevent corrosion and degradation that could lead to leakage.

II. Types of Tests
A. Type A Test: Integrated leakage rate tests to measure the overall leakage rate of the primary reactor containment.
B. Type B and C Tests: Local leakage rate tests to measure leakage across each containment penetration, including containment liners and isolation valves.

III. Test Methods and Procedures
A. The test methods and procedures used must be capable of detecting and measuring leakage rates as specified in the technical specifications. The containment liner materials must be resistant to corrosion and degradation to ensure that the measured leakage rates remain within allowable limits throughout the service life of the plant.

IV. Acceptance Criteria
A. The measured leakage rates must not exceed the allowable leakage rate values specified in the technical specifications or associated bases. The materials used for containment liners must be selected, fabricated, and maintained to ensure that corrosion or other degradation does not compromise the leak-tight integrity of the containment.

data.query: How do regulatory requirements for containment leakage testing address the potential for localized corrosion, such as pitting, in stainless steel liners exposed to borated water, and what are the implications for underlying carbon steel structures?
data.answer:
Regulatory requirements for containment leakage testing address the potential for localized corrosion, such as pitting in stainless steel liners exposed to borated water, through a combination of leakage rate testing and visual inspections. According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix J (Section III.B and V.A), the containment leakage testing program must include test methods capable of detecting and measuring leakage resulting from structural defects, including those due to corrosion or other degradation mechanisms in the containment liner or penetrations. If measured leakage rates exceed allowable limits, the cause—including the possibility of localized corrosion such as pitting—must be determined, and corrective actions implemented to restore containment integrity.

DSRS 6.2.6 further emphasizes compliance with General Design Criterion 53, which requires provisions for periodic inspection, surveillance, and testing of containment penetrations and components most likely to be sources of leakage. The review process ensures that applicants have identified potential leakage paths and established adequate test provisions to confirm specified leakage rates, including bypass leakage (DSRS 6.2.6, Section III).

Regulatory Guide 1.163 clarifies that the containment leakage testing program (ILRTs and LLRTs) works in conjunction with the ASME BPV Code, Section XI, Subsection IWE inservice inspection program. Visual inspections of accessible containment surfaces are required before each Type A test and at periodic intervals, specifically to detect structural deterioration such as through-wall corrosion or pitting that could compromise leak-tight integrity. Operating experience indicates that such localized corrosion is more reliably detected by these visual examinations than by integrated leakage rate tests alone (RG 1.163, Section B).

The implications for underlying carbon steel structures are that if pitting or localized corrosion in the stainless steel liner is detected, it may indicate a breach that could expose the carbon steel substrate to borated water, increasing the risk of further corrosion and structural degradation. Therefore, the regulatory framework ensures early detection and corrective action to maintain the integrity of both the liner and the underlying structures.

data.query: How do general design criteria for testing safety systems relate to the NRC's expectations for first-of-a-kind tests of emergency core cooling system features in standardized reactor designs?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for testing safety systems, as outlined in 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A, establish the NRC's expectations that emergency core cooling systems (ECCS) must be designed to allow for periodic inspection and testing to ensure their integrity and capability (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 35). Specifically, GDC 35 requires that the ECCS be testable to demonstrate its effectiveness under accident conditions, and GDC 36 and 37 further require that the system permit appropriate periodic inspection, pressure, and functional testing throughout the plant's life (DSRS 6.3, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA).

For standardized reactor designs, especially those incorporating first-of-a-kind (FOAK) features, the NRC expects that the design bases and test programs explicitly address how these new or unique ECCS features will be tested. Regulatory Guide 1.68 emphasizes that FOAK systems or components must have their in-plant functional testing requirements identified early in the design process, so that these requirements are incorporated into the final test design and the initial test program (ITP). Applicants for design certification (DC) or combined licenses (COL) must identify FOAK tests for safety-related systems, and the NRC will verify that these tests are included in the ITP (RG 1.68, B. DISCUSSION).

In summary, the NRC's expectations, grounded in the GDCs and supporting guidance, are that standardized reactor designs must ensure ECCS features—including FOAK features—are designed to permit comprehensive testing and inspection, and that specific FOAK test requirements are identified and incorporated into the plant's test program to demonstrate safety system performance (DSRS 6.3; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A; RG 1.68).

data.query: What regulatory considerations guide the determination of whether a first-of-a-kind test should be performed on only the initial module of a standardized nuclear power plant design?
data.answer:
The determination of whether a first-of-a-kind (FOAK) test should be performed only on the initial module of a standardized nuclear power plant design is guided by several regulatory considerations. According to Appendix N to 10 CFR Part 50, Sections II and III, the NRC may authorize or require FOAK tests on the initial unit(s) to confirm the adequacy of the standardized design. The extent and nature of these tests are determined on a case-by-case basis, considering the presence of unique, unusual, or enhanced safety features and the degree of standardization achieved in the design. The Commission also decides the number of units on which FOAK tests must be performed, again based on these factors (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix N, Sections II and III).

DSRS 14.2 further clarifies that for FOAK or unique plant features, the applicant must provide plans for preoperational and initial startup testing, including design and test acceptance criteria. These requirements apply to both Design Certification (DC) and Combined License (COL) applicants, ensuring that FOAK features meet their design basis through the Initial Test Program (ITP) (DSRS 14.2, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA). Additionally, 10 CFR 50.43(e) requires sufficient data and testing to demonstrate the performance of safety features, especially for designs that differ significantly from previously licensed reactors.

Regulatory Guide 1.68 emphasizes early identification of FOAK SSCs and the need for in-plant functional testing to verify their performance. It notes that prototype or FOAK tests may be required on the initial plant(s) and that the NRC will verify inclusion of such tests in the ITP (RG 1.68, Section B).

In summary, the NRC determines the need for and scope of FOAK testing on the initial module(s) based on the uniqueness of design features, the degree of standardization, and the need to confirm safety performance. The decision is made on a case-by-case basis, with requirements articulated in 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix N, DSRS 14.2, and RG 1.68.

Appendix N to Part 50—Standardization of Nuclear Power Plant Designs: Permits To Construct and Licenses To Operate Nuclear Power Reactors of Identical Design at Multiple Sites

Section I—Introduction

This appendix sets out procedures and criteria for the review and approval of applications for permits to construct and licenses to operate nuclear power reactors of identical design to be located at multiple sites. The objective is to achieve standardization of nuclear power plant designs and to facilitate the licensing of such plants. 

Section II—Scope

The procedures and criteria in this appendix apply to applications for permits to construct and licenses to operate nuclear power reactors of identical design to be located at multiple sites. The Commission may authorize or require, as appropriate, the conduct of first-of-a-kind tests on the initial unit(s) to confirm the adequacy of the standardized design. The extent and nature of such tests will be determined on a case-by-case basis, considering the extent to which the reactor incorporates unique, unusual, or enhanced safety features, and the degree of standardization achieved in the design.

Section III—Procedures and Criteria

(a) The Commission may issue permits to construct and licenses to operate nuclear power reactors of identical design at multiple sites, provided that the applications demonstrate that the design is standardized and that the design meets applicable safety requirements. 

(b) The Commission may require, as a condition of the license, that first-of-a-kind tests be performed on the initial unit(s) to confirm the adequacy of the standardized design. The need for such tests and the number of units on which they must be performed will be determined by the Commission, taking into account the extent to which the reactor incorporates unique, unusual, or enhanced safety features, and the degree of standardization achieved in the design.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for ensuring control room habitability during design basis accidents?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for ensuring control room habitability during design basis accidents are primarily established in General Design Criteria (GDC) 4, 5, and 19 of Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, as well as specific provisions in 10 CFR 50.34(f)(2)(xxviii) and related guidance documents.

GDC 19 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) requires that a control room be provided from which actions can be taken to operate the nuclear power unit safely under normal and accident conditions, including loss-of-coolant accidents (LOCAs). The control room must provide adequate radiation protection to permit access and occupancy under accident conditions without personnel receiving radiation exposures in excess of 5 rem whole body, or its equivalent to any part of the body, for the duration of the accident. For applicants and licensees applying after January 10, 1997, or those using an alternative source term under 10 CFR 50.67, the limit is specified as 0.05 Sv (5 rem) total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) (SRP 6.4, Section II; RG 1.183, Section A).

GDC 4 requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety, including the control room and its ventilation system, be designed to accommodate environmental conditions associated with postulated accidents and be protected against dynamic effects such as missiles and pipe ruptures (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4).

Additionally, the NRC requires evaluation of control room habitability against hazardous chemical releases. RG 1.78 provides acceptable methods for assessing control room habitability during postulated hazardous chemical releases, using Immediately Dangerous to Life or Health (IDLH) values as the metric for operator safety. Detailed evaluations must consider accident type, release characteristics, atmospheric dispersion, and control room air exchange rates (RG 1.78, Section C).

In summary, NRC regulations require that the control room be designed and evaluated to ensure operator protection from both radiological and chemical hazards during design basis accidents, with specific dose and toxicity limits, and that the design accommodates environmental and dynamic effects associated with such accidents.

evidence_chain.evidence_text: This regulatory guide (RG) describes approaches and technical bases that are acceptable to the staff of the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) to meet regulatory requirements for evaluating the habitability of a nuclear power plant (NPP) control room (CR) during a postulated hazardous chemical release. ... The driver of this RG is Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) Part 50, “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities,” Appendix A, “General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants,” General Design Criterion (GDC) 19, “Control Room,” (Ref. 1). GDC 19 requires operating reactor licensees to provide a CR from which actions can be taken to maintain the nuclear power unit in a safe condition under accident conditions, including loss-of-coolant accidents. ... This RG contains technical bases and guidelines that are acceptable to the NRC staff for use in assessing the habitability of a CR during and after a postulated external release of hazardous chemicals (e.g., vapor and gaseous) from a stationary source on site and multiple mobile sources off site, based on the immediately dangerous to life or health (IDLH) values (Ref. 2). ... When performing a detailed evaluation of CR habitability during a hazardous chemical release using this guidance, the metric applicants and licensees should use for each chemical is the IDLH that can be tolerated without physical incapacitation of a CR operator. In deriving the toxicity level in the CR, the detailed calculations should consider several factors, such as accident type; release characterization (e.g., release rate, duration); atmospheric dispersion characteristics, including prevailing meteorological conditions at the site; and the air exchange rate of the CR. The checklist for the determinations of the toxicity level (i.e., concentration) in the CR, based on the toxic chemical and CR air quality parameter values, is as follows: (1) name of the most hazardous chemical, (2) type of source (stationary or mobile) during the accidental release; (3) maximum quantity or concentration measured (if available); (4) IDLH values (i.e., ppm or mg/m3); (5) average continuous release rate of hazardous chemical; (6) vapor pressure (torr) of hazardous chemical (at local ambient plant temperature); (7) fraction of chemical flashed and rate of boiloff when spilling occurs; (8) total plume travel distance between the CR and the chemicals; and (9) local meteorological data.

data.query: How do regulatory expectations for control room habitability systems relate to the classification of systems as safety-related or non-safety-related?
data.answer:
Regulatory expectations for control room habitability systems are closely tied to the classification of systems as safety-related or non-safety-related, primarily through the application of General Design Criteria (GDC) 4 and 19 from Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50. According to SRP 6.4 Section II and the technical rationale, control room habitability systems must ensure that the control room remains functional and provides adequate protection for operators during normal and accident conditions, including loss-of-coolant accidents (LOCAs). GDC 4 requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety—including those supporting control room habitability—be designed to withstand environmental and dynamic effects associated with postulated accidents (SRP 6.4; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4).

GDC 19 specifically mandates that the control room must allow safe operation and provide adequate radiation protection under accident conditions. Regulatory Guides such as RG 1.78 and RG 1.183 clarify that meeting GDC 19 involves ensuring habitability through protection from hazardous chemicals and radiological releases, and that safety-related systems may be credited in dose analyses because their classification ensures reliability in performing their safety function (RG 1.183, Section B; RG 1.78, Section A).

Thus, regulatory expectations require that habitability systems or their credited components be classified as safety-related when their function is essential to maintaining control room habitability under accident conditions. This classification ensures the systems’ reliability and robustness, as required by GDC 4 and GDC 19. Non-safety-related systems may be present, but only safety-related systems can be credited for regulatory compliance in analyses where reliability is critical to operator protection and plant safety (SRP 6.4; RG 1.183).

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
Requirements
Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations:
1. General Design Criterion 4 (GDC 4), "Environmental and Dynamic Effects Design Bases,” as it relates to SSCs important to safety being designed to accommodate the effects of and to be compatible with the environmental conditions associated with postulated accidents.
2. General Design Criterion 5 (GDC 5), "Sharing of Structures, Systems and Components," as it relates to ensuring that sharing among nuclear power units of SSCs important to safety will not significantly impair the ability to perform safety functions, including, in the event of an accident in one unit, an orderly shutdown and cooldown of the remaining unit(s).
3. General Design Criterion 19 (GDC 19), "Control Room," as it relates to maintaining the nuclear power unit in a safe condition under accident conditions and providing adequate radiation protection.
...
Technical Rationale
The technical rationale for application of these acceptance criteria to the areas of review addressed by this SRP section is discussed in the following paragraphs:  
1. Compliance with GDC 4 requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed to accommodate the effects of, and be compatible with, environmental conditions associated with normal operation, maintenance, testing, and postulated accidents, including loss-of-coolant accidents (LOCAs).  These structures, systems, and components shall be appropriately protected against dynamic effects (e.g., the effects of missiles, pipe whipping, and discharging fluids) that may result from equipment failures and from events and conditions outside the nuclear power unit.
The function of the control room habitability system is to provide a suitable and controlled environment for the control room and equipment located therein during normal operation, anticipated operational occurrences, and during and after postulated accidents, including LOCAs.  GDC 4 applies to this SRP section because the reviewer verifies that the control room will remain functional throughout the course of operating and accident events and that operators will be able to carry out their responsibilities without being subject to undue stress.
Meeting the requirements of GDC 4 provides assurance that the control room habitability system will function as designed, thereby providing protection to plant operators against the effects of accidental releases of toxic and radiological gases.
...
3. Compliance with GDC 19 requires provision of a control room from which actions can be taken (a) to operate the nuclear power unit safely under normal conditions and (b) to maintain the plant in a safe state under accident conditions, including LOCAs.
GDC 19 applies to this SRP section because the reviewer verifies that adequate radiation protection and protection from hazardous chemical releases will be provided to permit access to and occupancy of the control room under accident conditions. 
Regulatory Guides 1.52 and 1.78 present methods acceptable to the staff for meeting control room occupancy protection requirements.
Regulatory Guides 1.195, 1.196 and 1.197 provide acceptable guidance for meeting control room habitability requirements.  For future reactors or for plants implementing an alternate source term (AST) pursuant to 10 CFR 50.67, the guidance on dose analysis of Regulatory Guide 1.183 is applicable in place of Regulatory Guide 1.195. 
Meeting the requirements of GDC 19 provides assurance that adequate protection will be maintained to permit access to and occupancy of the control room under accident conditions.

data.query: For a nuclear power plant design that does not credit operator actions for accident mitigation, what combined regulatory provisions govern the use and crediting of engineered safety features for control room habitability, including requirements for system classification, operability, emergency power, and failure assumptions?
data.answer:
For a nuclear power plant design that does not credit operator actions for accident mitigation, the combined regulatory provisions governing the use and crediting of engineered safety features for control room habitability are primarily established by General Design Criteria (GDC) 4 and 19 in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, as well as related NRC guidance documents.

GDC 4 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety—including those ensuring control room habitability—be designed to accommodate the effects of postulated accidents and environmental conditions, and to be protected against dynamic effects from equipment failures and external events. Importantly, GDC 4 specifies that operator action for accident mitigation cannot be credited unless it is demonstrated to be feasible within the available time and environmental conditions (10CFR [2]).

GDC 19 requires that the control room be designed to allow safe operation and maintenance of the plant under both normal and accident conditions, including loss-of-coolant accidents, and to provide adequate radiation protection to permit access and occupancy without exceeding specified dose limits (SRP 6.4 [1]; RG 1.183 [4]). For current plants, this limit is 5 rem whole body (SRP 6.4 [1]), or 0.05 Sv (5 rem) TEDE for newer applications or those using an alternative source term.

SRP 6.4 further details acceptance criteria for engineered safety features, including: (1) system classification as safety-related, (2) operability requirements such that a single failure of an active component does not result in loss of function, (3) provision of emergency power, and (4) adherence to standards such as Regulatory Guide 1.52 and ASME AG-1 for emergency filtration systems. The design must also consider failure assumptions, such as single active failures, and must not rely on operator actions for accident mitigation unless justified (SRP 6.4 [1]).

Regulatory Guide 1.78 provides additional guidance for evaluating control room habitability against hazardous chemical releases, emphasizing engineered features (e.g., filtered ventilation, isolation dampers) and not relying on operator actions (RG 1.78 [3]). RG 1.183 reinforces that defense-in-depth is maintained by relying on safety-related, redundant, and independent engineered systems, not compensatory operator actions (RG 1.183 [4]).

In summary, the regulatory framework requires that engineered safety features for control room habitability be classified as safety-related, designed for single failure tolerance, provided with emergency power, and evaluated under conservative failure assumptions, without crediting operator actions unless specifically justified.

evidence_chain.section: Appendix A to Part 50—General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants, GDC 4
evidence_chain.evidence_text: General Design Criterion 4—Environmental and dynamic effects design bases. Structures, systems, and components important to safety shall be designed to accommodate the effects of and to be compatible with the environmental conditions associated with normal operation, maintenance, testing, and postulated accidents, including loss-of-coolant accidents. These structures, systems, and components shall be appropriately protected against dynamic effects, including the effects of missiles, pipe whipping, and discharging fluids, that may result from equipment failures and from events and conditions outside the nuclear power unit. The design shall reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe environmental conditions and the most severe dynamic effects postulated to occur at the location of the structures, systems, and components, including combinations of environmental conditions and dynamic effects. The design shall not credit the use of operator action for accident mitigation unless it can be demonstrated that the operator action can be accomplished in the time available and under the environmental conditions expected. The design shall also provide for the capability to test and inspect safety-related structures, systems, and components to ensure their continued functional capability. The design bases for these structures, systems, and components shall be established and documented.

C.  STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE
This section includes the staff regulatory guidance for evaluating the habitability of a NPP CR during a postulated hazardous chemical release. Any hazardous chemical stored on site within a half (½) kilometer (km) [1,640 feet (ft)] of the CR in a quantity greater than 45 kilograms (kg) [(100 pounds (lb)] should be considered for CR habitability evaluation. Hazardous chemicals should not be stored within 0.1 km (330 ft) of a CR or its fresh air inlets, including ventilation system intakes and locations of possible infiltration such as penetrations. Licensees are encouraged to conduct periodic surveys of stationary and mobile sources of hazardous chemicals near their plant sites to keep the site-specific inventories up to date.  However, this RG also provides essential assumptions and criteria for screening out release events that need not be considered in the evaluation of CR habitability. The following criteria identify the release events that need not be considered further for CR habitability evaluation.

...

3. Control Room Habitability Evaluation

When performing a detailed evaluation of CR habitability during a hazardous chemical release using this guidance, the metric applicants and licensees should use for each chemical is the IDLH that can be tolerated without physical incapacitation of a CR operator. In deriving the toxicity level in the CR, the detailed calculations should consider several factors, such as accident type; release characterization (e.g., release rate, duration); atmospheric dispersion characteristics, including prevailing meteorological conditions at the site; and the air exchange rate of the CR.  The checklist for the determinations of the toxicity level (i.e., concentration) in the CR, based on the toxic chemical and CR air quality parameter values, is as follows: (1) name of the most hazardous chemical, (2) type of source (stationary or mobile) during the accidental release; (3) maximum quantity or concentration measured (if available); (4) IDLH values (i.e., ppm or mg/m3); (5) average continuous release rate of hazardous chemical; (6) vapor pressure (torr) of hazardous chemical (at local ambient plant temperature); (7) fraction of chemical flashed and rate of boiloff when spilling occurs; (8) total plume travel distance between the CR and the chemicals; and (9) local meteorological data.

For determining the air quality in the CR for habitability evaluation, the NRC recommends the following 7  considerations: (1) the design height of air intake windows; (2) the volume size of CR; (3) the air-exchange rate of CR; (4) the flow rate as cubic feet per minute of the CR; (5) the unfiltered makeup or inleakage air for the CR; (6) the filtered makeup and recirculated air under normal and emergency operations; and (7) the use of a filtered nuclear air-cleaning system or personal breathing-air supplying device during an emergency.

1.1.2 Defense in Depth

Licensees should evaluate their proposed uses of an AST, and the associated proposed facility modifications and changes to procedures, to determine whether the proposed changes are consistent with the principle that adequate defense in depth is maintained to compensate for uncertainties in accident progression and analysis data. Consistency with the defense-in-depth philosophy is maintained if system redundancy, independence, and diversity are preserved commensurate with the expected accident frequency, consequences of challenges to the system, and uncertainties. For facilities to which the GDC (see Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50) apply, compliance with these criteria is required. Modifications proposed for the facility generally should not create a need for compensatory programmatic activities (e.g., reliance on manual operator actions, use of potassium iodide as a prophylactic drug) or self-contained breathing apparatus or post-accident entries into vital areas to accomplish safety functions. The NRC staff expects that the use of the AST will not result in a net decrease in the level of defense in depth provided by the facility’s design and operation. The NRC staff will review the proposed changes to ensure that the defense-in-depth philosophy is maintained.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for providing a habitable control room for nuclear power plant operators during design basis accidents?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for providing a habitable control room for nuclear power plant operators during design basis accidents are primarily established in General Design Criterion 19 (GDC 19) of Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, as well as related criteria and regulations. GDC 19 requires that a control room be provided from which actions can be taken to operate the nuclear power unit safely under normal conditions and to maintain it in a safe condition under accident conditions, including loss-of-coolant accidents (SRP 6.4; RG 1.183, Section A). The control room must provide adequate radiation protection to permit access and occupancy under accident conditions without personnel receiving radiation exposures in excess of 5 rem whole body, or its equivalent to any part of the body, for the duration of the accident (SRP 6.4, Section II; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 19). For applicants and licensees after January 10, 1997, or those using an alternative source term under 10 CFR 50.67, the dose limit is specified as 0.05 Sv (5 rem) total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) (SRP 6.4, Section II).

Additionally, GDC 4 requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety, including the control room and its ventilation system, be designed to accommodate environmental conditions and dynamic effects associated with postulated accidents (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4; SRP 6.4). GDC 5 addresses the sharing of SSCs among units to ensure safety functions are not impaired (SRP 6.4).

For protection against hazardous chemicals, NRC guidance (RG 1.78, Section C) specifies that control room habitability evaluations must ensure that chemical concentrations do not exceed immediately dangerous to life or health (IDLH) values, considering factors such as accident type, release characteristics, air exchange rates, and air filtration. The design should ensure that operators are not physically incapacitated and can perform necessary safety functions during and after a hazardous chemical release.

In summary, NRC requirements mandate that the control room must remain habitable during design basis accidents, with radiation and chemical exposures not exceeding specified limits, and that the design must account for environmental, dynamic, and chemical hazards to ensure operator safety and the ability to maintain safe plant conditions (SRP 6.4; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4, 5, 19; RG 1.78; RG 1.183).

The driver of this RG is Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) Part 50, “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities,” Appendix A, “General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants,” General Design Criterion (GDC) 19, “Control Room,” (Ref. 1). This RG contains technical bases and guidelines that are acceptable to the NRC staff for use in assessing the habitability of a CR during and after a postulated external release of hazardous chemicals (e.g., vapor and gaseous) from a stationary source on site and multiple mobile sources off site, based on the immediately dangerous to life or health (IDLH) values (Ref. 2). ... When performing a detailed evaluation of CR habitability during a hazardous chemical release using this guidance, the metric applicants and licensees should use for each chemical is the IDLH that can be tolerated without physical incapacitation of a CR operator. data.query: How do NRC regulations define the relationship between safety-related classification of control room habitability systems and the credited use of engineered safety features for mitigating airborne radioactive material during accident scenarios?
data.answer:
NRC regulations establish a direct relationship between the safety-related classification of control room habitability systems and the credited use of engineered safety features (ESFs) for mitigating airborne radioactive material during accident scenarios. According to SRP 6.4 (Section II), control room habitability systems must meet the requirements of General Design Criterion (GDC) 4 and GDC 19 from Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50. GDC 4 requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety—including those ensuring control room habitability—be designed to withstand environmental conditions associated with postulated accidents (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4). GDC 19 specifically requires that adequate radiation protection be provided to permit access and occupancy of the control room under accident conditions, with dose limits not exceeding 5 rem whole body or its equivalent for the duration of the accident (SRP 6.4, II.6.A-B).

Regulatory Guide 1.183 (Section B, C) clarifies that safety-related systems may be credited in radiological consequence analyses for mitigating airborne radioactive material, provided their safety-related classification ensures reliability in performing their safety function. The NRC staff evaluates the credited use of ESFs—such as emergency standby atmosphere filtration systems—based on their safety-related classification and reliability, as these attributes are essential for maintaining defense in depth and ensuring compliance with the GDCs (RG 1.183, C.1.1.2). This means only systems classified as safety-related, and thus subject to rigorous design, qualification, and maintenance requirements, can be credited for mitigating airborne radioactive material in the control room during accident scenarios.

In summary, NRC regulations require that only safety-related, reliable habitability systems and ESFs can be credited for mitigating airborne radioactive material in the control room, as this classification ensures compliance with GDC 4 and 19 and supports the defense-in-depth philosophy (SRP 6.4; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A; RG 1.183).

1.1.2 Defense in Depth

Licensees should evaluate their proposed uses of an AST, and the associated proposed facility modifications and changes to procedures, to determine whether the proposed changes are consistent with the principle that adequate defense in depth is maintained to compensate for uncertainties in accident progression and analysis data. Consistency with the defense-in-depth philosophy is maintained if system redundancy, independence, and diversity are preserved commensurate with the expected accident frequency, consequences of challenges to the system, and uncertainties. For facilities to which the GDC (see Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50) apply, compliance with these criteria is required. Modifications proposed for the facility generally should not create a need for compensatory programmatic activities (e.g., reliance on manual operator actions, use of potassium iodide as a prophylactic drug) or self-contained breathing apparatus or post-accident entries into vital areas to accomplish safety functions. The NRC staff will review the adequacy of defense in depth for each proposed use of an AST on a case-by-case basis. The staff will consider the credited use of engineered safety features (ESFs) for mitigating airborne radioactive material in the control room and offsite in the context of the safety-related classification of these systems and their reliability in performing their safety function.

data.query: For a nuclear power plant design that does not credit operator actions for accident mitigation, what combined regulatory guidance and review standards determine whether control room habitability systems must be classified as safety-related, and how does this affect the assumptions allowed in radiological consequence analyses for the control room?
data.answer:
The determination of whether control room habitability systems must be classified as safety-related in a nuclear power plant design that does not credit operator actions for accident mitigation is governed by a combination of regulatory requirements and guidance. The primary regulatory basis is General Design Criterion 19 (GDC 19) from 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, which requires that adequate radiation protection be provided to permit access and occupancy of the control room under accident conditions, ensuring that personnel do not receive radiation exposures in excess of 5 rem whole body (or its equivalent) for the duration of the accident (SRP 6.4, Section II; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 19).

SRP 6.4, Section II, further clarifies that compliance with GDC 19 requires provision of a control room from which the plant can be operated safely under both normal and accident conditions, and that adequate radiation protection must be maintained. Regulatory Guides such as RG 1.78 and RG 1.183 provide acceptable methods for evaluating and demonstrating control room habitability and dose consequences.

According to RG 1.183, Section 4.2, control room habitability systems (e.g., filtration, pressurization, isolation) may only be credited in radiological consequence analyses if they are classified as safety-related and are designed to perform their intended function under accident conditions. If these systems are not safety-related, the analysis must assume they are unavailable for accident mitigation, and the resulting control room doses must be evaluated without their mitigating effects. This approach is consistent with the guidance in SRP 6.4 and the applicable GDCs.

Therefore, in designs that do not credit operator actions for accident mitigation, control room habitability systems must be classified as safety-related if their function is to be credited in the radiological consequence analysis. If not classified as safety-related, their mitigating effects cannot be assumed, and the analysis must demonstrate compliance with GDC 19 dose limits without them.

evidence_chain.section: Section 4.2 Control Room Dose Consequences
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
4.2 Control Room Dose Consequences

The control room dose consequence analysis should be performed to demonstrate compliance with GDC 19 or equivalent requirements. The analysis should assume that the control room is occupied by personnel necessary to operate the plant safely under accident conditions. The analysis should use the AST and the assumptions described in this guide, including those in the applicable appendices. The analysis should not credit operator actions for accident mitigation unless such actions are performed from within the control room and are consistent with the assumptions of the analysis. If operator actions outside the control room are credited, the applicant or licensee should provide justification that such actions can be performed without exceeding applicable dose criteria. 

The control room habitability systems (e.g., filtration, pressurization, and isolation systems) may be credited in the analysis if they are classified as safety-related and are designed to perform their intended function under accident conditions. If the control room habitability systems are not safety-related, the analysis should assume that these systems are not available for accident mitigation, and the resulting control room doses should be evaluated accordingly. The classification of control room habitability systems as safety-related should be consistent with the guidance in SRP Section 6.4 and the applicable GDCs.
