data.query: When radiation is detected in the main condenser offgas stream, what combined regulatory requirements and review standards govern the need for isolation of the steam source and the design of isolation provisions, including any required valves or support systems?
data.answer:
When radiation is detected in the main condenser (MC) offgas stream, the regulatory requirements and review standards governing the need for isolation of the steam source and the design of isolation provisions are primarily based on General Design Criterion 60 (GDC 60) of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, and are further detailed in Standard Review Plan (SRP) Sections 10.4.1 and 11.3, as well as Regulatory Guides (RG) 1.143 and 4.21.

GDC 60 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) requires that the nuclear power unit design include means to suitably control the release of radioactive materials in gaseous and liquid effluents during normal operation and anticipated operational occurrences. This includes the use of suitable isolation and containment provisions, such as valves, to prevent excessive releases of radioactivity to the environment.

SRP 10.4.1 (Sections II and III) specifies that the MC system, in conjunction with the main steam system, must have provisions to detect loss of condenser vacuum and effect isolation of the steam source. For direct cycle plants, it is acceptable if the detection system in the MC can actuate the main steam isolation valves to limit the quantity of steam lost to the MC. The design must ensure that radioactive releases are kept as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA), in accordance with 10 CFR 50, Appendix I.

SRP 11.3 (Items 10 and 11) further requires that automatic control features and the placement of isolation valves and radiation detectors on process piping and effluent discharge lines ensure timely closure of such valves upon detection of elevated radioactivity. The review also considers the interdependence of radiation monitoring instrumentation with other system parameters and the logic for alarming and isolating process flows to comply with dose and effluent limits under 10 CFR Part 20 and Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50.

RG 1.143 provides accepted methods for the design and classification of radwaste system structures, systems, and components (SSCs), including valves, specifying applicable codes and standards (e.g., ANSI/ASME B31.3 for piping and valves) and material requirements to ensure reliability and compatibility with the radioactive environment. RG 4.21 emphasizes the minimization of contamination, early detection, and prompt response to unintended releases, supporting the need for robust isolation provisions.

In summary, the need for and design of isolation provisions, including required valves and support systems, are governed by GDC 60, SRP 10.4.1 and 11.3, and RGs 1.143 and 4.21, which collectively require reliable detection and isolation mechanisms to prevent excessive radioactive releases, ensure timely response to elevated radiation, and maintain ALARA principles.

evidence_chain.section: A. INTRODUCTION
evidence_chain.evidence_text: This guide describes a method acceptable to the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) for use in the implementation of Title 10, Section 20.1406, “Minimization of Contamination,” of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR 20.1406) (Ref. 1). License, approval, and certification applicants should strive to minimize contamination and radioactive waste generation over the total life cycle of a facility, from initial facility layout and design through procedures for operation and concluding with final decontamination and dismantling at the time of decommissioning. ... The purpose of this regulatory guide is to present guidance that will assist applicants covered by 10 CFR 20.1406 in effectively implementing this licensing requirement. The guidance consists of specific design considerations drawn from nuclear industry experience and lessons learned from decommissioning. These have been combined to support the development of a contaminant management philosophy. The principles embodied in this philosophy are threefold: (1) prevention of unintended releases; (2) early detection, if there is unintended release of radioactive contamination; and (3) prompt assessment to support a timely and appropriate response. Applying these principles requires the use of sound design, proven engineering practices, conservative radiation protection principles, and attention to operational practices. All of this should be considered in the context of the life cycle of the facility from the early planning stages through the final plans for decommissioning and waste disposal. This guide describes some of the mechanisms that can be employed for facility life-cycle planning to meet the requirements of 10 CFR 20.1406.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for controlling and monitoring radioactive liquid releases from main condensers in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for controlling and monitoring radioactive liquid releases from main condensers in nuclear power plants are primarily established by General Design Criterion 60 (GDC 60) of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, and further detailed in NRC guidance such as SRP 10.4.1 and SRP 11.3. 

According to GDC 60 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 60), the nuclear power unit design must include means to suitably control the release of radioactive materials in both gaseous and liquid effluents during normal operation and anticipated operational occurrences. The design must also provide for monitoring these releases at appropriate locations to collect data on the quantities and concentrations of radioactive materials released to the environment, and to monitor the performance of systems that control these releases (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 60).

SRP 10.4.1 clarifies that the main condenser (MC) system design is acceptable if it includes provisions to prevent excessive releases of radioactivity to the environment, even in the event of system failures. The MC design must ensure that radioactive materials deposited in the condenser during normal operation are controlled and that uncontrolled releases are prevented. Compliance with GDC 60 also requires that releases are kept as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA), in accordance with 10 CFR 50, Appendix I (SRP 10.4.1, Section II).

Additionally, SRP 11.3 references requirements from 10 CFR Part 20 (including 10 CFR 20.1301, 20.1302, and 20.1406) and 10 CFR 50.34a, which set dose limits for the public, require minimization of contamination, and establish design objectives for effluent control systems. The design and operation of systems handling radioactive liquid releases must ensure that public dose limits are not exceeded, contamination is minimized, and releases are ALARA (SRP 11.3, Section II).

In summary, the regulatory requirements mandate that main condenser systems must be designed and operated to control and monitor radioactive liquid releases, prevent excessive or uncontrolled releases, provide adequate monitoring, and ensure compliance with dose limits and ALARA principles, as specified in GDC 60, 10 CFR Part 20, and 10 CFR 50, Appendix I.

data.query: How do the general design criteria for radioactive material control apply to the design features of main condenser hotwells in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The general design criteria for radioactive material control, specifically General Design Criterion 60 (GDC 60) from 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, require that nuclear power plant designs include means to suitably control the release of radioactive materials in gaseous and liquid effluents during normal operation and anticipated operational occurrences. This criterion is directly applicable to the design features of main condenser (MC) hotwells, as these components can accumulate radioactive materials—particularly in boiling water reactors (BWRs) during normal operation, and in pressurized water reactors (PWRs) in the event of a primary-to-secondary steam generator tube leak (SRP 10.4.1, Section II; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 60).

To meet GDC 60, the MC hotwell design must include provisions to prevent excessive or uncontrolled releases of radioactivity to the environment, even in the event of system failures. This includes structural integrity under seismic events, as well as features to prevent, detect, and control leaks and spills (SRP 10.4.1, Section II; RG 1.143, Section 1.2). Specifically, components such as tanks and hotwells outside containment should have liquid level monitoring, alarms, routing of overflows and drains to the liquid radwaste system, and containment features (e.g., curbs, dikes) to prevent unmonitored releases (RG 1.143, Section 1.2.1–1.2.5).

Additionally, the design should minimize facility contamination by limiting leakage and providing for early detection and containment of leaks (RG 4.21, Section 1.2–1.3). Monitoring and surveillance are essential to ensure prompt detection and response to leaks, supporting the ALARA (as low as reasonably achievable) principle for radioactive releases (SRP 10.4.1, Section II; RG 4.21, Section 1.3).

In summary, the general design criteria require that MC hotwells incorporate design features for monitoring, containment, leak prevention, and routing of radioactive liquids to controlled systems, thereby ensuring that radioactive releases are suitably controlled and minimized in accordance with regulatory requirements.

evidence_chain.section: C. REGULATORY POSITION, 1. Minimizing Facility Contamination
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
1.1 General Statement   

In general, an applicant should minimize radioactive contamination of the facility by using structure, system, and component (SSC) designs and operational procedures that limit leakage and/or control the spread of contamination.  The design and operational procedures should provide for the early detection of leaks thus allowing prompt assessment to support a timely and appropriate response.  Applicants should note that 10 CFR 20.1406 requires that contamination be minimized “…to the extent practicable...”  This implies that other competing concerns such as the implication to safety systems and the overall cost should be considered.  Thus the minimization of facility contamination must be considered in the context of overall facility safety.   

1.2 Minimization of Leaks and Spills and Provision of Containment

Through design, worker practices, preventive maintenance, and effective operating procedures, applicants covered by 10 CFR 20.1406 should strive to minimize leaks and spills, provide containment in areas where such events might occur, and provide for detection that supports timely assessment and appropriate response.  This approach should be applied in a risk-informed and performance-based manner considering the nature of the hazard.  Radiologically significant leaks and spills need to be addressed, and containment should be considered where practical and cost effective.  Areas where licensed materials are used and stored should be designed to facilitate maintenance and operations (including cleanup).  Radiological work should be restricted to a localized section of the facility in order to minimize the potential area requiring decontamination.

1.3 Prompt Detection of Leakage  

The facility should be designed such that any SSC that has the potential for leakage is provided with adequate leak detection capability to the extent practical.  In addition to design considerations to control and, if possible, prevent radioactive system leakage, it is important during operations to be able to promptly detect leakage as close as possible to the leakage source to allow timely intervention and to prevent the potential for widespread contamination.  Thus, monitoring and routine surveillance programs are an important part of minimizing potential contamination.  This approach should include the placement of instruments to detect leakage at readily accessible locations and the use of operational practices that will enable early detection of contamination.  Because leakage detection is only the first step in minimizing contamination, the applicant also should be prepared to provide a timely assessment and response based on the location and characteristics of the leak or spill.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for the design and operation of main condensers in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for the design and operation of main condensers (MC) in nuclear power plants are primarily established to ensure control of radioactive material releases and to maintain public and environmental safety. According to SRP 10.4.1 Section II, the design must meet the requirements of General Design Criterion 60 (GDC 60) from 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, which mandates that the nuclear power unit design includes means to suitably control the release of radioactive materials in gaseous and liquid effluents, ensuring exposures are kept as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA). The design must also provide for suitable sampling, monitoring, and alarm systems for effluents (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 60).

Specifically, the MC design is acceptable if it includes provisions to prevent excessive releases of radioactivity to the environment resulting from failures of structures, systems, or components. For new BWR plants, seismic analyses must demonstrate that condenser anchorages and piping inlet nozzles maintain structural integrity during and after a safe shutdown earthquake (SSE) (SRP 10.4.1 II.1.A). If there is potential for explosive mixtures, the MC must be designed to withstand explosions, and dual instrumentation must be provided to detect, annunciate, and control such hazards (SRP 10.4.1 II.1.B, referencing SRP 11.3 II.6).

Additionally, the design and operation must ensure compliance with dose limits and effluent concentration limits specified in 10 CFR Part 20 and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I, and must minimize contamination and radioactive waste generation as required by 10 CFR 20.1406 (SRP 11.3 II). The applicant must also propose inspections, tests, analyses, and acceptance criteria (ITAAC) to provide reasonable assurance that the plant will operate in accordance with NRC regulations (10 CFR 52.47(b)(1), 10 CFR 52.80(a)).

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria require that main condensers are designed and operated to prevent excessive radioactive releases, withstand credible hazards, and ensure effluent controls and monitoring are in place, all in accordance with the referenced regulatory requirements.

Requirements

The relevant requirements of the Commission’s regulations for the gaseous waste management system (GWMS) are as follows:

1. 10 CFR Part 20, Subpart D, establishes standards for protection against radiation from radioactive materials released in gaseous effluents to unrestricted areas, including dose limits for individual members of the public.
2. 10 CFR 20.1301 and 10 CFR 20.1302, which specify dose limits for individual members of the public.
3. 10 CFR Part 20, Appendix B, Table 2, Column 1, and Note 4, which specify concentration limits for radioactive materials in gaseous effluents released to unrestricted areas.
4. 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I, Sections II.A, II.B, II.C, and II.D, which specify numerical guides for design objectives and limiting conditions for operation to meet the ALARA criterion for radioactive material in gaseous effluents released to unrestricted areas.
5. 10 CFR 50.34a, which requires applicants to include in their applications a description of the design features and operating procedures to keep releases of radioactive materials in effluents to unrestricted areas ALARA.
6. 10 CFR 20.1406, which requires applicants to describe how facility design and procedures for operation will minimize, to the extent practicable, contamination of the facility and the environment, facilitate eventual decommissioning, and minimize, to the extent practicable, the generation of radioactive waste.

4. The design and operation of the GWMS are such that releases of radioactive materials in gaseous effluents to unrestricted areas are ALARA, as required by 10 CFR 50.34a and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I.

data.query: How do the regulatory requirements for main condenser design relate to the overall safety analysis report content requirements for a nuclear power plant application?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for main condenser (MC) design are directly linked to the overall safety analysis report (SAR) content requirements for a nuclear power plant application. According to SRP 10.4.1, the MC system must be designed to control the release of radioactive material to the environment, with acceptance criteria based on compliance with General Design Criterion 60 (GDC 60) from Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50. GDC 60 specifically requires that the plant design includes means to suitably control releases of radioactive materials in effluents and to handle radioactive solid wastes during normal operation and anticipated operational occurrences (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 60).

The SAR must describe how the MC system meets these requirements, including the design features that prevent excessive releases of radioactivity in the event of system failures (SRP 10.4.1, Section II). The SAR is also reviewed to ensure that any degraded operation of the MC does not adversely affect the reactor primary or secondary systems.

Furthermore, for applications under 10 CFR Part 52 (design certification or combined license), the SAR must include proposed inspections, tests, analyses, and acceptance criteria (ITAAC) necessary to provide reasonable assurance that the plant will be constructed and operated in accordance with regulatory requirements (SRP 10.4.1, referencing 10 CFR 52.47(b)(1) and 10 CFR 52.80(a)). These ITAAC are essential components of the SAR and are also referenced in SRP 14.3.10, which addresses emergency planning and preparedness, further emphasizing the need for comprehensive documentation of system design and operational controls in the SAR.

Additionally, SRP 11.3 and RG 1.143 highlight the importance of quality assurance provisions and the need for the SAR to provide sufficient information to confirm that failures of essential systems, such as the MC, will not compromise public health and safety. The SAR must demonstrate compliance with quality assurance criteria and design bases for protection against natural phenomena, as outlined in Appendix A and B to 10 CFR Part 50 (RG 1.143).

In summary, the regulatory requirements for MC design are integral to the SAR content, ensuring that the plant's design, operational controls, and quality assurance measures collectively provide reasonable assurance of safety and regulatory compliance.

evidence_chain.section: A. INTRODUCTION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
In 10 CFR Part 50, "Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities," § 50.34, "Contents of Applications; Technical Information," requires that each application for a construction permit include a preliminary safety analysis report. Part of the information required is related to quality assurance and the preliminary design of the facility, including, among other things, the principal design criteria for the facility. Appendix B, "Quality Assurance Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants and Fuel Reprocessing Plants," to 10 CFR Part 50 establishes overall quality assurance requirements for structures, systems, and components important to safety. Appendix A, ''General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants," to 10 CFR Part 50 establishes minimum requirements for the principal design criteria for light-water-cooled nuclear power plants.

Criterion 1, "Quality Standards and Records,'' of Appendix A requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with the importance to safety of the safety function to be performed and that a quality assurance program be established and implemented in order to provide adequate assurance that these structures, systems, and components will satisfactorily perform their safety function.

Criterion 2, "Design Bases for Protection Against Natural Phenomena," of Appendix A requires, among other things, that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena such as earthquakes, tornados, or flooding without loss of capability to perform their safety functions. The design bases for these structures, systems, and components are to reflect the importance of the safety functions to be performed.

Criterion 60, "Control of Releases of Radioactive Materials to the Environment,'' of Appendix A requires that the nuclear power unit design include means to suitably control the release of radioactive materials in gaseous and liquid effluents and to handle radioactive solid waste produced during normal reactor operation, including anticipated operational occurrences. The release of radioactive materials from external man-induced events and design basis accidents must also be controlled.

This regulatory guide is being revised to provide design guidance acceptable to the NRC staff in regard to natural phenomena hazards, internal and external man-induced hazards, and quality group classification and quality assurance provisions for radioactive waste management systems, structures, and components.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for monitoring and controlling leakage of circulating water into the main condenser in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for monitoring and controlling leakage of circulating water into the main condenser in nuclear power plants are primarily established to prevent excessive releases of radioactive materials to the environment. According to SRP 10.4.1, the main condenser (MC) system must incorporate design features that detect, control, and facilitate correction of cooling water leakage into the condensate. The review of the MC system focuses on these features to ensure that any potential leakage does not result in unacceptable releases of radioactivity.

The acceptance criteria for the MC system are based on compliance with General Design Criterion 60 (GDC 60) from 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A. GDC 60 requires that the nuclear power unit design includes means to suitably control the release of radioactive materials in both gaseous and liquid effluents during normal operation and anticipated operational occurrences. Specifically, the design must provide for suitable control points and sampling connections in systems where radioactive materials may be released, and means must be provided for monitoring such releases in accordance with applicable requirements (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 60).

In summary, the MC system must be designed to: (1) prevent corrosion or erosion of condenser tubes, (2) detect and control leakage of cooling water into the condensate, (3) facilitate correction of such leakage, and (4) provide monitoring and sampling capabilities to ensure compliance with regulatory limits on radioactive releases. These measures collectively ensure that radioactive releases from the main condenser are kept as low as reasonably achievable, in accordance with 10 CFR 50, Appendix I (SRP 10.4.1, II. Acceptance Criteria; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 60).

data.query: How do general design criteria for environmental and radiological protection apply to the detection and correction of circulating water system leakage into the main condenser?
data.answer:
The general design criteria for environmental and radiological protection, particularly General Design Criterion 60 (GDC 60) from 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, require that nuclear power plant designs include means to suitably control the release of radioactive materials in gaseous and liquid effluents during normal operation and anticipated operational occurrences. Specifically, for the main condenser and circulating water system, these criteria are implemented by incorporating design features that detect, control, and facilitate correction of cooling water leakage into the main condenser (SRP 10.4.1, Section II).

The main condenser system must be designed to prevent corrosion or erosion of condenser tubes, detect leakage of cooling water into the condensate, and preclude accidental releases of radioactive materials to the environment in excess of regulatory limits. Compliance with GDC 60 is demonstrated when the design includes provisions to monitor and control such releases, ensuring that offsite doses do not exceed the limits specified in Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 60).

Supporting guidance, such as RG 1.143 (Section 1.2), further specifies that systems and components outside containment that may contain radioactive liquids should be designed to prevent uncontrolled releases, include monitoring provisions (e.g., liquid level alarms), and prevent leakage from entering unmonitored or nonradioactive systems. SRP 11.3 (Items 8 and 11) emphasizes the importance of design features and monitoring instrumentation to avoid uncontrolled and unmonitored releases, and to prevent contamination of nonradioactive systems, referencing industry guidance and regulatory bulletins.

In summary, the general design criteria require that the main condenser and associated systems incorporate features to detect and correct circulating water system leakage, thereby preventing unmonitored or excessive radiological releases to the environment, in accordance with GDC 60 and related NRC guidance.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for monitoring and detecting leakage from the circulating water system into the main condenser in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for monitoring and detecting leakage from the circulating water system into the main condenser in nuclear power plants are established to ensure control and minimization of radioactive releases to the environment. According to SRP 10.4.1, the main condenser system must incorporate design features that prevent, detect, control, and facilitate correction of cooling water leakage into the condensate. Specifically, the system must include means to detect radioactive leakage into or out of the system and preclude accidental releases of radioactive materials exceeding established limits. Instrumentation must be in place to monitor condensate quality and detect main condenser tube leakage, as referenced in SRP Section 9.3.2, and measures must be implemented to monitor the inventory of radioactive materials in the main condenser, as detailed in SRP Section 11.5. 

These requirements are grounded in General Design Criterion (GDC) 60 from 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, which mandates that nuclear power unit designs include suitable means to control and monitor the release of radioactive materials in both gaseous and liquid effluents during normal operation and anticipated operational occurrences. The design must ensure that such releases and resulting radiation exposures are kept as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA). Compliance with GDC 60 is demonstrated by providing adequate monitoring and control provisions in the main condenser system to detect and address leakage, thereby minimizing the risk of environmental contamination.

References: SRP 10.4.1, Sections I-III; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 60.

data.query: How do general design criteria for environmental protection and control of radioactive material releases apply to the detection and correction of circulating water system inleakage into the main condenser?
data.answer:
The general design criteria for environmental protection and control of radioactive material releases, specifically General Design Criterion (GDC) 60 as outlined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, require that nuclear power unit designs include provisions to limit the release of radioactive materials in effluents to as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA) during normal operation and anticipated operational occurrences. This includes providing means for monitoring, control, and surveillance of such releases (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 60).

According to SRP 10.4.1, these criteria directly apply to the main condenser (MC) system, which can be a pathway for radioactive material release if circulating water system inleakage occurs. The SRP specifies that the MC design must incorporate features to detect, control, and facilitate correction of cooling water leakage into the condensate. Such inleakage could introduce impurities or dilute radioactive materials, potentially leading to uncontrolled releases. Therefore, the design must include measures to prevent corrosion or erosion of condenser tubes, detect inleakage promptly, and enable corrective actions to minimize the risk of radioactive material release to the environment. Compliance with GDC 60 is demonstrated when these provisions are in place, ensuring that both gaseous and liquid radioactive effluents from the MC are controlled and kept ALARA, in accordance with regulatory requirements (SRP 10.4.1, Section II; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 60).

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for protecting safety-related structures, systems, and components from flooding caused by circulating water system pipe ruptures?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for protecting safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) from flooding caused by circulating water system (CWS) pipe ruptures are primarily established in General Design Criterion 4 (GDC 4) of Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50 and further detailed in SRP 10.4.5 Section II. GDC 4 requires that SSCs important to safety be designed to accommodate the effects of, and be compatible with, environmental conditions associated with both normal operation and postulated accidents, including the dynamic effects of discharging fluids resulting from equipment failures such as pipe ruptures. Specifically, SSCs must be appropriately protected against flooding and other dynamic effects that may result from such failures (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4).

SRP 10.4.5 Section II elaborates that, to meet GDC 4, the CWS design must include provisions to accommodate the effects of water discharge from a failure of CWS components or piping. This includes providing means to prevent, detect, and control flooding in safety-related areas to ensure that the safety function of SSCs is not compromised by leakage from the CWS. Additionally, any malfunction or failure of CWS components or piping, including expansion joints, should not have unacceptable adverse effects on the functional performance of safety-related SSCs. Applicants must either comply with these acceptance criteria or justify alternative approaches that provide equivalent protection (SRP 10.4.5, Section II).

In summary, the regulatory requirements mandate design features and procedural measures that prevent or mitigate flooding from CWS pipe ruptures to ensure the continued functionality of safety-related SSCs, as specified in GDC 4 and detailed in SRP 10.4.5.

data.query: How do general design criteria for environmental and flood protection interact with the requirements for the layout and grading of areas surrounding safety-related buildings in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The general design criteria for environmental and flood protection, specifically General Design Criterion 4 (GDC 4) as outlined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, interact directly with the requirements for the layout and grading of areas surrounding safety-related buildings in nuclear power plants by mandating that structures, systems, and components important to safety are designed to withstand and be compatible with environmental conditions, including those resulting from normal operation, maintenance, testing, and postulated accidents (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4). This includes protection against dynamic effects such as flooding, pipe whipping, and discharging fluids that may arise from equipment failures or external events.

According to SRP 10.4.5, Section II, the acceptance criteria for meeting GDC 4 require that the design of systems like the circulating water system (CWS) must include provisions to prevent, detect, and control flooding of safety-related areas. This ensures that the safety function of systems or components is not compromised by water leakage or discharge. The layout and grading of areas around safety-related buildings must therefore be configured to direct potential floodwaters away from these structures, or otherwise mitigate the risk of flooding, so that the intended safety functions are preserved. The technical rationale emphasizes that even non-safety-related systems, such as the CWS, must be designed to minimize adverse environmental impacts on safety-related systems and components (SRP 10.4.5, Section II).

In summary, the interaction is that the general design criteria establish the regulatory basis for environmental and flood protection, which in turn informs the specific requirements for site layout and grading to ensure that safety-related buildings and their functions are not adversely affected by flooding or other environmental hazards.

data.query: In the context of nuclear power plant design, what combined regulatory standards and guidance address the evaluation of site grading and drainage to ensure that flooding from a circulating water system pipe rupture does not compromise the safety functions of nearby structures, systems, and components?
data.answer:
The evaluation of site grading and drainage to ensure that flooding from a circulating water system (CWS) pipe rupture does not compromise the safety functions of nearby structures, systems, and components is addressed through a combination of regulatory standards and guidance. Specifically, General Design Criterion (GDC) 4 in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50 requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed to accommodate environmental and dynamic effects, including those resulting from discharging fluids due to equipment failures such as pipe ruptures (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4). This criterion mandates appropriate protection against such effects to ensure safety functions are not compromised.

Standard Review Plan (SRP) Section 10.4.5 further elaborates on these requirements by specifying that the CWS design must include provisions to prevent or detect and control flooding of safety-related areas. This ensures that leakage from the CWS does not preclude the intended safety function of any system or component. SRP 10.4.5 also references the need to evaluate the effects of CWS pipe failures in conjunction with other SRP sections, such as SRP 3.4.1, which addresses internal flooding and protective measures for safety-related equipment, and SRP 3.6.1, which covers the review of high- and moderate-energy pipe breaks, including those in the CWS.

In summary, the combined regulatory framework of GDC 4 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) and the guidance in SRP 10.4.5, along with related SRP sections, provide the basis for evaluating site grading and drainage to ensure that flooding from a CWS pipe rupture does not adversely affect the safety functions of nearby structures, systems, and components.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for the design and performance of expansion joints in the circulating water system of a nuclear power plant?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for the design and performance of expansion joints in the circulating water system (CWS) of a nuclear power plant are grounded in General Design Criterion 4 (GDC 4) from Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50 and the guidance provided in SRP 10.4.5, Section II. Specifically, expansion joints, as components of the CWS, must be designed to accommodate the effects of and be compatible with environmental conditions associated with normal operation, maintenance, testing, and postulated accidents, including loss-of-coolant accidents (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4). The design must ensure protection against dynamic effects such as those resulting from equipment failures, including pipe whipping and discharging fluids (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4).

According to SRP 10.4.5, Section II, the acceptance criteria require that the CWS design, including expansion joints, provides means to prevent, detect, and control flooding of safety-related areas so that the intended safety function of systems or components is not compromised due to leakage from the CWS. Furthermore, any malfunction or failure of a CWS component or piping, including expansion joints, must not have unacceptable adverse effects on the functional performance capabilities of safety-related systems or components. Applicants must either comply with these criteria or justify alternative approaches that provide acceptable methods of compliance with NRC regulations (SRP 10.4.5, Section II).

data.query: How do the general design criteria for protection against dynamic effects relate to the requirements for analyzing hydraulic transients, such as water hammer, in the circulating water system of a nuclear facility?
data.answer:
The general design criteria for protection against dynamic effects, specifically General Design Criterion 4 (GDC 4) as outlined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, require that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety be designed to accommodate and be compatible with environmental and dynamic effects, including those resulting from equipment failures and discharging fluids (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4). In the context of the circulating water system (CWS) of a nuclear facility, this means the design must address the potential for dynamic effects such as hydraulic transients, including water hammer, which can result from sudden changes in flow or pressure due to component or piping failures.

SRP 10.4.5 further clarifies that to meet GDC 4, the CWS design must include provisions to accommodate the effects of discharging water from failures, and specifically, the design must minimize hydraulic transients and their effects on the functional capability and integrity of system components (SRP 10.4.5, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA and III. REVIEW PROCEDURES). This includes providing means to prevent or control flooding of safety-related areas and ensuring that failures in the CWS do not adversely affect the performance of safety-related systems or components.

Therefore, the requirements for analyzing hydraulic transients, such as water hammer, are directly related to GDC 4's mandate to protect SSCs from dynamic effects. The analysis and mitigation of such transients are necessary to demonstrate that the CWS design will not compromise safety functions due to dynamic loads or fluid discharges resulting from failures. This relationship is established in both the regulatory basis (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4) and the NRC's Standard Review Plan (SRP 10.4.5).

Appendix S requires that for SSE ground motions, SSCs will remain functional and within applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits.  The required safety functions of SSCs must be assured during and after the vibratory ground motion through design, testing, or qualification methods.  The evaluation must take into account SSI effects and the expected duration of the vibratory motion.  If the OBE is set at one-third or less of the SSE, an explicit analysis or design is not required.  If the OBE is set at a value greater than one-third of the SSE, an analysis and design must be performed to demonstrate that the applicable stress, strain, and deformation limits are satisfied.  Appendix S also requires that the horizontal component of the SSE ground motion in the free-field at the foundation level of the structures must be an appropriate response spectrum with a PGA of at least 0.1g.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for leak detection in the circulating water system of a nuclear power plant?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for leak detection in the circulating water system (CWS) of a nuclear power plant are primarily established to ensure that safety-related areas are protected from flooding due to potential leaks or failures in the CWS. According to SRP 10.4.5, Section II (Acceptance Criteria), compliance with General Design Criterion (GDC) 4 is achieved when the CWS design includes provisions to accommodate the effects of discharging water resulting from component or piping failures. Specifically, the system must provide means to prevent, detect, and control flooding in safety-related areas so that the safety function of any system or component is not compromised by leakage from the CWS. The review procedures (Section III) further require verification of the CWS's capability to detect leaks and to secure the system quickly and effectively in the event of a leak.

Additionally, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4, requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed to withstand environmental and dynamic effects, including those from discharging fluids due to equipment failures. This includes ensuring that such components are protected against flooding and other dynamic effects that could result from leaks or ruptures. However, the regulation allows for the exclusion of certain dynamic effects from the design basis if analyses demonstrate that the probability of such failures is extremely low.

In summary, the regulatory requirements mandate that the CWS must have provisions for leak detection and control to prevent flooding of safety-related areas, and the system must be capable of quickly securing itself in the event of a leak, as outlined in SRP 10.4.5 and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4.

data.query: How do general design criteria for protection against environmental and dynamic effects apply to the design of leak detection systems in auxiliary water systems?
data.answer: The general design criteria for protection against environmental and dynamic effects, specifically General Design Criterion 4 (GDC 4), apply to the design of leak detection systems in auxiliary water systems by requiring that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety are designed to accommodate and be compatible with environmental conditions and dynamic effects resulting from both normal operation and postulated accidents (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4). According to SRP 10.4.5, GDC 4 mandates that the design must include provisions to address the effects of discharging water due to failures in components or piping, such as those in the circulating water system (CWS), which is analogous to auxiliary water systems. Specifically, the design must provide means to prevent, detect, and control flooding in safety-related areas to ensure that the safety function of systems or components is not compromised by leakage. The reviewer is tasked with verifying the capability of the system to detect leaks and to secure the system quickly and effectively. While the CWS itself may not be safety-related, GDC 4 establishes design limits to minimize the potential for adverse environmental conditions, such as flooding, that could affect safety-related SSCs. Therefore, leak detection systems in auxiliary water systems must be designed to promptly identify and control leaks to prevent environmental and dynamic effects (e.g., flooding, pipe whipping, discharging fluids) from impairing the function of safety-related equipment, in accordance with the requirements outlined in SRP 10.4.5 and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4.

data.query: When evaluating the circulating water system for a nuclear power plant, what combined regulatory requirements from general design criteria, review standards, and regulatory guides must be considered to ensure adequate leak detection and protection against environmental hazards?
data.answer:
When evaluating the circulating water system (CWS) for a nuclear power plant, several combined regulatory requirements must be considered to ensure adequate leak detection and protection against environmental hazards. According to SRP 10.4.5 Section II (Acceptance Criteria), the primary regulatory basis is General Design Criterion 4 (GDC 4) from Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50. GDC 4 requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed to accommodate environmental and dynamic effects, including those from normal operation, maintenance, testing, and postulated accidents. Specifically, these components must be protected against dynamic effects such as discharging fluids resulting from equipment failures (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 4).

SRP 10.4.5 further clarifies that the CWS design must include provisions to accommodate the effects of water discharge from component or piping failures. This includes providing means to prevent, detect, and control flooding of safety-related areas, ensuring that leakage from the CWS does not preclude the intended safety function of any system or component. Additionally, any malfunction or failure in the CWS, including expansion joints, must not have unacceptable adverse effects on the performance of safety-related systems or components.

Furthermore, compliance with 10 CFR 52.47(b)(1) and 10 CFR 52.80(a) is required, mandating that applications for design certification and combined licenses include proposed inspections, tests, analyses, and acceptance criteria (ITAAC) to provide reasonable assurance that the plant will be constructed and operated in accordance with NRC regulations and the Atomic Energy Act.

In summary, the combined requirements from GDC 4, the Standard Review Plan (SRP 10.4.5), and relevant sections of 10 CFR Parts 50 and 52 ensure that the CWS is designed with adequate leak detection and environmental hazard protection, with specific emphasis on preventing and controlling flooding and ensuring the continued functionality of safety-related systems.

data.query: What is the NRC's acceptance criterion for the development of a site-specific chemistry control program for the condensate cleanup system at nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC's acceptance criterion for the development of a site-specific chemistry control program for the condensate cleanup system at nuclear power plants is grounded in ensuring compliance with General Design Criterion (GDC) 14 of Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50. GDC 14 requires that the reactor coolant pressure boundary be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to have an extremely low probability of abnormal leakage, rapidly propagating failure, and gross rupture. To meet these regulatory requirements, the Standard Review Plan (SRP) Section 10.4.6 specifies that applicants must develop chemistry control programs that adhere to the water chemistry guidelines referenced in the SRP.

For boiling-water reactor (BWR) plants, SRP Section 5.4.8 provides the criteria for acceptable water purity, which refers to the latest version of the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) 'BWR Water Chemistry Guidelines' and the technical specifications for BWR reactor coolant systems. For pressurized-water reactor (PWR) plants, SRP Section 5.4.2.1 provides the criteria for acceptable secondary water chemistry, referencing the latest EPRI 'PWR Secondary Water Chemistry Guidelines.'

Applicants are required to identify any differences between their proposed chemistry control program and the SRP acceptance criteria, and to justify how any alternatives provide acceptable compliance with NRC regulations. Thus, the NRC's acceptance criterion is that the site-specific chemistry control program for the condensate cleanup system must be consistent with the referenced EPRI guidelines and technical specifications, thereby supporting the integrity of the reactor coolant pressure boundary as required by GDC 14.

References: SRP 10.4.6 Section II; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 14.

evidence_chain.section: Appendix A to Part 50—General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants, Criterion 14
evidence_chain.evidence_text: General Design Criterion 14—Reactor coolant pressure boundary. The reactor coolant pressure boundary shall be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested so as to have an extremely low probability of abnormal leakage, of rapidly propagating failure, and of gross rupture. Means shall be provided for detecting and, to the extent practical, identifying the location of the source of reactor coolant leakage. The design of the reactor coolant pressure boundary shall be such that the boundary will behave in a nonbrittle manner and the probability of rapidly propagating fracture is minimized. Appropriate margin shall be provided to allow for uncertainties in determining—(a) the effects of irradiation on material properties, (b) residual, steady state, and transient stresses, and (c) size of flaws. The design shall reflect consideration of the most severe postulated service conditions, including the effects of anticipated operational occurrences and system hydrostatic tests.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for controlling radioactive material concentrations in the reactor coolant system to ensure public dose limits are not exceeded?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for controlling radioactive material concentrations in the reactor coolant system to ensure public dose limits are not exceeded are grounded in several key regulations and guidance documents. According to DSRS 11.1 (Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA), the requirements are based on compliance with 10 CFR Part 20, which sets limits for radioactive material in effluents to unrestricted areas, and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I, which provides numerical guides for design objectives to ensure releases are as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA). Specifically, 10 CFR 50.34a requires applicants to describe design objectives and equipment for controlling releases of radioactive material in both gaseous and liquid effluents during normal operations and anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs). The design and operational procedures must ensure that effluent concentrations and resulting public doses do not exceed the limits specified in Part 20 and meet the ALARA principle as outlined in Appendix I to Part 50.

Additionally, General Design Criteria (GDC) 60 and 61 require that the reactor design includes means to suitably control and safely store radioactive materials, ensuring radiological safety under both normal and accident conditions. The coolant source terms used for design basis calculations must be determined using models and parameters consistent with Regulatory Guide 1.112, NUREG-0017, and ANSI/ANS 18.1-1999, adjusted for the specific reactor design. The effectiveness of the radwaste systems (liquid and gaseous waste management) is evaluated to confirm that they can adequately treat coolant and ensure effluent releases meet the numerical design objectives and concentration limits, including the unity criterion of Appendix B, Table 2 to 10 CFR Part 20.

In summary, the NRC requires that radioactive material concentrations in the reactor coolant system be controlled through design, operational procedures, and waste management systems to ensure that public dose limits are not exceeded, in accordance with 10 CFR Parts 20 and 50, and associated guidance.

evidence_chain.section: § 50.34a Design objectives for equipment to control releases of radioactive material in effluents—nuclear power reactors
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
§ 50.34a Design objectives for equipment to control releases of radioactive material in effluents—nuclear power reactors.

(a) Each applicant for a construction permit or operating license for a nuclear power reactor to be constructed and operated on a site for which a construction permit was issued after January 1, 1975, shall include in its application a description of the design objectives for equipment to be installed to control releases of radioactive material in gaseous and liquid effluents produced during normal reactor operations, including anticipated operational occurrences. The design objectives for equipment to control releases of radioactive material in effluents shall be such that, in conjunction with the limitations on operation required by § 50.36a, the quantities of radioactive materials, including iodine, in effluents released to unrestricted areas will be kept as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA) and within the dose objectives specified in Appendix I to this part.

(b) Each applicant shall include in its application the means to be employed for keeping levels of radioactive material in effluents to unrestricted areas as low as is reasonably achievable, including the use of operating procedures and equipment design features. The application shall include a description of the process and effluent control systems, including the means for collecting, monitoring, processing, storing, and disposing of radioactive wastes and for controlling the release of radioactive material in effluents to unrestricted areas.

data.query: How do NRC regulations for occupational and public radiation dose limits interact with the requirements for evaluating reactor coolant system activity concentrations in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
NRC regulations for occupational and public radiation dose limits, as established in 10 CFR Part 20, directly interact with requirements for evaluating reactor coolant system activity concentrations in nuclear power plants by serving as the regulatory basis for assessing and controlling radioactive releases and exposures. According to DSRS 11.1 (Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA and I. AREAS OF REVIEW), the design basis coolant source term is used to estimate inventories of radioactivity in system components, which in turn informs the adequacy of shielding, placement of radiation monitoring equipment, and design of ventilation systems to maintain doses to workers and the public ALARA (as low as reasonably achievable), consistent with 10 CFR Part 20, Subparts G and H.

The calculated primary and secondary coolant concentrations are used to evaluate the performance of liquid and gaseous waste management systems, ensuring that radioactive effluents meet the numerical design objectives of Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50 and the effluent concentration limits of 10 CFR Part 20, Appendix B. The acceptance criteria require that operational source terms used in dose calculations for potential radioactivity in liquid and gaseous effluents to unrestricted areas must demonstrate compliance with the dose limits of Part 20 and the ALARA principle.

10 CFR 50.34(a)(3) further requires that applications for nuclear power plants include estimates of radionuclide releases, descriptions of effluent control and monitoring equipment, and analyses demonstrating that releases and resultant doses to individuals are within Part 20 limits and ALARA. Thus, the evaluation of reactor coolant system activity concentrations is intrinsically linked to ensuring that occupational and public dose limits are not exceeded, and that plant design and operation maintain exposures as low as reasonably achievable, as mandated by NRC regulations.

data.query: When determining a conservative yet realistic failed fuel fraction for source term calculations in a pressurized water reactor, what combined NRC regulatory provisions and review standards govern the selection of methodology, key parameters, and assumptions to ensure compliance with dose limits for both workers and the public?
data.answer:
The determination of a conservative yet realistic failed fuel fraction for source term calculations in a pressurized water reactor (PWR) is governed by a combination of NRC regulatory provisions and review standards to ensure compliance with dose limits for both workers and the public. According to DSRS 11.1 (Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA), the design basis coolant source term, which includes assumptions about failed fuel fractions (typically 0.25 to 1 percent for PWRs), is used to derive radioactivity inventories, assess shielding adequacy, define radiation zones, and confirm the placement of monitoring equipment and ventilation systems. The methodology, key parameters, and assumptions must be consistent with the requirements of 10 CFR Part 20 (operational source term and effluent limits), 10 CFR 50.34 (analysis of radiological consequences and demonstration of safety), 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix I (design objectives for effluents and ALARA), and General Design Criterion 60 (control of radioactive releases).

DSRS 11.1 further specifies that acceptable source term values are those determined using models and parameters consistent with Regulatory Guide 1.112, NUREG-0017 (PWR-GALE86 code), and ANSI/ANS 18.1-1999, adjusted as necessary for specific reactor designs. These documents provide detailed methodologies for calculating releases of radioactive materials and establishing operational source terms. The analysis must demonstrate that the facility can be operated without undue risk to public health and safety, as required by 10 CFR 50.34(a), by evaluating the radiological consequences of normal operation, anticipated operational occurrences, and postulated accidents, including the identification of potential sources and quantities of radioactive material, release pathways, and resultant doses.

In summary, the selection of failed fuel fraction and associated source term methodology must align with the regulatory framework outlined in DSRS 11.1, 10 CFR Parts 20 and 50, Appendix I, and GDC 60, and utilize NRC-endorsed calculation models to ensure compliance with dose limits and ALARA principles.

evidence_chain.section: II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
The design basis coolant source term is used to derive inventories of radioactivity in system components, assess the adequacy of shielding in maintaining doses to workers and public as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA), define ambient radiation exposure levels and zones, and confirm the proper placement of radiation monitoring equipment in plant areas and operating conditions, and the design of ventilation systems provided for maintaining doses to workers ALARA, consistent with Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) Part 20, Subparts G and H.  The design basis source term is based on a combination of assumptions of failed fuel fractions (e.g., 0.25 to 1 percent) for PWRs, or the reactor coolant system isotopic concentrations, including fission products and significant corrosion and activation products, equivalent to operation for a full fuel cycle at the technical specification limits for halogens (I-131 dose equivalent) and noble gases (Xe-133 dose equivalent), and steam generator technical specification limits on primary to secondary leakage and, as warranted, presence of neutron activation products in secondary coolant.

Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations:

1. 10 CFR Part 20, as it relates to determining the operational source term that is used in calculations associated with potential radioactivity in liquid and gaseous effluents to unrestricted areas.

2. 10 CFR 50.34(a) and (b), 10 CFR 52.47(a)(5), and 10 CFR 52.79(a)(3), and 10 CFR 52.79(a)(1)(i) and (ii), as they relate to the kinds and quantities of radioactive materials expected to be produced and released during normal operations and AOOs to be within the limits of Part 20 and Part 50, Appendix I design objectives.

3. 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I, as it relates to determining the operational source term that is used in calculations associated with potential radioactivity in liquid and gaseous effluents considered in the context of numerical guides for design objectives and limiting conditions for operation to meet the criterion “as low as is reasonably achievable” for radioactive material contained in light-water reactor effluents.

4. General Design Criterion 60 (GDC) as it relates to determining the operational source term that is used in calculations associated with potential radioactivity in liquid and gaseous effluents released into unrestricted areas, such that a nuclear power unit design shall include means to control suitably the release of radioactive materials in gaseous and liquid effluents produced during normal reactor operation and AOOs.

In general, coolant source terms used as the design basis for expected releases have been found acceptable if these values are determined using models and parameters that are consistent with Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.112, “Calculation of Releases of Radioactive Materials in Gaseous and Liquid Effluents from Light-Water-Cooled Nuclear Power Reactors,” NUREG-0017 (PWR-GALE86 code), and the guidance provided in (ANSI/ANS) 18.1-1999 once adjusted to reflect the design features of SMRs.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for limiting public radiation exposure from normal operations of a nuclear power plant?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for limiting public radiation exposure from normal operations of a nuclear power plant are primarily established in 10 CFR Part 20, 10 CFR 50.34(a) and (b), 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix I, and General Design Criteria (GDC) 60 and 61. According to DSRS 11.1 Section II, these requirements mandate that the operational source term (the amount and type of radioactive material released) must be determined and used in calculations for potential radioactivity in liquid and gaseous effluents to unrestricted areas. 

Specifically, 10 CFR Part 20 sets the general standards for protection against radiation, including dose limits for individual members of the public. 10 CFR 50.34a requires applicants to describe design features that ensure radioactive effluent releases are kept as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA) and to provide means for monitoring such releases. Appendix I to Part 50 provides numerical guides for design objectives and limiting conditions for operation, ensuring that effluent releases from light-water-cooled nuclear power reactors meet the ALARA criterion. 

GDC 60 requires that nuclear power unit designs include means to suitably control the release of radioactive materials in effluents during normal operation and anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs). GDC 61 addresses the design of facilities and shielding for the safe storage and handling of radioactive materials to ensure radiological safety under normal and postulated accident conditions. 

In summary, the NRC requires that radioactive releases to the environment during normal operations be minimized and controlled through design, operational limits, and monitoring, ensuring public exposure remains within regulatory limits and as low as reasonably achievable, as detailed in 10 CFR Part 20, 10 CFR 50.34a, Appendix I to Part 50, and GDC 60 and 61 (DSRS 11.1 Section II; 10 CFR 50.34a and Appendix I).

The calculated concentrations of radioactive materials in the primary and secondary coolant systems serve as critical inputs for evaluating the performance of the liquid and gaseous waste management systems (LWMS and GWMS). Specifically, the regulation mandates reasonable assurance that the operation of the facility will not result in public doses above the limits in 10 CFR Part 20. Thus, the evaluation of coolant radioactivity is foundational to demonstrating compliance with these public dose limits and regulatory requirements.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
§ 50.34a Design objectives for equipment to control releases of radioactive material in effluents—nuclear power reactors.

(a) Each applicant for a construction permit or operating license for a nuclear power reactor to be constructed and operated on a site for which the application was filed after January 2, 1971, shall include in its application a description of the design objectives for equipment to be installed to control releases of radioactive material in gaseous and liquid effluents produced during normal reactor operations, including anticipated operational occurrences. The applicant shall also provide reasonable assurance that the collective dose to persons in the population within 80 kilometers (50 miles) of the reactor from radioactive materials released in liquid effluents during any calendar year will not exceed 0.003 man-sievert (300 man-rem), and that the collective dose from radioactive materials released in gaseous effluents during any calendar year will not exceed 0.005 man-sievert (500 man-rem). The applicant shall also provide reasonable assurance that the operation of the facility will not result in doses to individual members of the public in unrestricted areas in excess of the limits specified in 10 CFR part 20.

data.query: When determining a conservative and realistic failed fuel fraction for source term calculations, what combined regulatory expectations apply regarding the selection of representative plant data, statistical treatment of fuel failure rates, and documentation of supporting data quality?
data.answer:
When determining a conservative and realistic failed fuel fraction for source term calculations, NRC regulatory expectations require a combination of technical rigor and thorough documentation. According to DSRS 11.1, the design basis coolant source term must be based on assumptions of failed fuel fractions (e.g., 0.25 to 1 percent for PWRs) or equivalent isotopic concentrations, reflecting operation at technical specification limits. The selection of these fractions should use models and parameters consistent with Regulatory Guide 1.112, NUREG-0017 (PWR-GALE86 code), and ANSI/ANS 18.1-1999, with adjustments documented if design features differ (DSRS 11.1, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA). Any deviations from standard parameters or calculation methods due to differences in plant design or operation must be justified with sufficient supporting information to enable independent NRC staff evaluation.

Statistically, the treatment of fuel failure rates must be based on representative plant data, and any adjustments to standard code parameters must be clearly documented, including the rationale and supporting data. The application must also include a description of the quality of the data used, detailing sources, collection methods, and procedures to ensure data accuracy and reliability (10 CFR 50.34(g)). This ensures that the safety analysis is based on high-quality, traceable data, and that the NRC can independently verify the basis for the selected failed fuel fraction. Overall, the regulatory expectation is for a transparent, well-documented approach that uses representative data, appropriate statistical methods, and robust data quality assurance.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for limiting radioactive material releases in liquid and gaseous effluents from nuclear power plants?
data.answer: The regulatory requirements for limiting radioactive material releases in liquid and gaseous effluents from nuclear power plants are established primarily in 10 CFR Part 20, 10 CFR Part 50 (including Appendix I), and related guidance documents. According to DSRS 11.1 (Section II. Acceptance Criteria), these requirements ensure that the operational source term used in calculations for potential radioactivity in effluents to unrestricted areas meets the limits set forth in these regulations. Specifically, 10 CFR 50.34a requires that equipment be designed to control releases such that radioactive material in both liquid and gaseous effluents is kept as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA). For liquid effluents, the annual average concentrations released to unrestricted areas must not exceed the values in Table 2 of Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 20, and for gaseous effluents, the limits are those in Table 1, Column 1 of Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 20. Additionally, the collective dose commitment from liquid effluents must not exceed 3 man-rem per year to the total body or any organ (except the thyroid, which is limited to 10 man-rem per year), and for gaseous effluents, the limits are 5 man-rem per year to the total body or any organ (except the thyroid, which is limited to 15 man-rem per year) (10 CFR 50.34a(b)). The design and operation of systems for managing these effluents must also comply with General Design Criteria 60 and 61, and use calculation models consistent with Regulatory Guide 1.112 and NUREG-0017. The overall objective is to ensure that effluent releases are within regulatory limits and ALARA, protecting public health and safety.

data.query: How do NRC regulations for radioactive effluent control interact with source term assumptions for primary coolant activity in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
NRC regulations for radioactive effluent control are closely linked to the source term assumptions for primary coolant activity in nuclear power plants. According to DSRS 11.1, source terms—specifically radionuclide concentrations in primary and secondary coolant—are derived from operational reactor experience and are used to estimate radioactivity levels in process and effluent streams. These concentrations are not the sole basis for plant and radioactive waste management system (RWMS) design, but they are essential inputs for evaluating the performance of liquid and gaseous waste management systems (LWMS and GWMS) under DSRS Sections 11.2 and 11.3. The effectiveness of these systems is assessed to ensure that radioactive effluents meet the numerical design objectives of Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50 and the concentration limits of Appendix B, Table 2 to 10 CFR Part 20 (DSRS 11.1).

10 CFR § 50.34a further requires that applicants describe the design objectives for effluent control equipment, ensuring that releases of radioactive material in effluents during normal operation and anticipated operational occurrences are kept as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA) and do not exceed regulatory limits. The design and evaluation of effluent control systems must be based on reasonable source term assumptions, including primary coolant activity, to provide assurance of compliance with these requirements (10 CFR § 50.34a).

In summary, NRC regulations require that source term assumptions for primary coolant activity inform the design and evaluation of effluent control systems. These systems must be capable of treating radioactive materials in effluents to meet regulatory limits and ALARA objectives, thereby ensuring public and environmental protection.

(a) Each applicant for a construction permit or operating license for a nuclear power reactor to be constructed and operated on a site for which a construction permit was issued after January 1, 1975, shall include in its application a description of the design objectives for equipment to be installed to control releases of radioactive material in gaseous and liquid effluents produced during normal reactor operations, including anticipated operational occurrences. The design objectives for such equipment must be to keep levels of radioactive material in effluents to unrestricted areas as low as is reasonably achievable. The applicant shall also provide a description of the process and effluent control systems, including means for measuring the concentration of radioactive material in effluents and for collecting samples of such effluents when the reactor is operating under steady-state conditions. The description must include the means for monitoring and controlling the release of radioactive materials in effluents to ensure compliance with the requirements of part 20 of this chapter.

(b) The applicant shall provide reasonable assurance that the radioactive material in effluents released to unrestricted areas during normal operation, including anticipated operational occurrences, will not exceed the numerical guides given in appendix I to this part. The applicant shall also provide reasonable assurance that the design of the facility includes means to limit the release of radioactive materials in effluents during normal operation, including anticipated operational occurrences, to levels that are as low as is reasonably achievable.

data.query: When recycled reactor coolant is returned to the primary system, what regulatory standards and review criteria must be considered to ensure that tritium buildup and subsequent liquid and gaseous effluent releases remain within acceptable limits for public and occupational dose?
data.answer:
When recycled reactor coolant is returned to the primary system, several regulatory standards and review criteria must be considered to ensure that tritium buildup and subsequent liquid and gaseous effluent releases remain within acceptable limits for public and occupational dose. The primary regulatory framework includes:

1. 10 CFR Part 20: This regulation governs the operational source term for calculations associated with potential radioactivity in liquid and gaseous effluents to unrestricted areas, ensuring doses to the public are as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA) (DSRS 11.1, II; DSRS 11.2, II.1). Specifically, 10 CFR 20.1101(b) requires procedures and engineering controls to maintain public doses ALARA, and 10 CFR 20.1301/1302 and Appendix B, Table 2, set effluent concentration limits and dose criteria (DSRS 11.2, II.2).

2. 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I: This appendix provides numerical design objectives for radioactive material releases in liquid and gaseous effluents, requiring that releases during normal operation and anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs) be kept ALARA (DSRS 11.1, II.3; 10 CFR 50.34a(b); DSRS 11.2, II.12). The design must ensure that the numerical guides for design objectives are not exceeded (10 CFR 50.34a(b)).

3. General Design Criterion (GDC) 60: The reactor design must include means to suitably control the release of radioactive materials in effluents during normal operation and AOOs (DSRS 11.1, II.4; DSRS 11.2, II.10).

4. Review Methodology: The NRC expects that coolant source terms and effluent release calculations use models and parameters consistent with Regulatory Guide 1.112, NUREG-0017 (PWR-GALE86), and ANSI/ANS 18.1-1999, adjusted for specific reactor designs (DSRS 11.1, II).

5. System Design and Interfaces: The design and operation of the Liquid Waste Management System (LWMS) and Gaseous Waste Management System (GWMS) must be reviewed to ensure they can adequately treat recycled coolant and control effluent releases (DSRS 11.1, II; DSRS 11.2, I, II). The boundaries, interfaces, and methods for diverting or terminating releases must be clearly defined and controlled (DSRS 11.2, I.21).

In summary, compliance with 10 CFR Part 20, 10 CFR Part 50 (including Appendix I and GDC 60), and the use of NRC-endorsed calculation methodologies are required to ensure tritium and other radioactive releases from recycled coolant remain within regulatory limits and ALARA.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for limiting radioactive effluent releases from nuclear power plants to protect public health and safety?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for limiting radioactive effluent releases from nuclear power plants are established to protect public health and safety by ensuring that radioactive materials released to the environment are controlled and minimized. According to DSRS 11.1 (Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA), these requirements are grounded in several key regulations:

1. 10 CFR Part 20: This regulation sets limits on the concentration of radioactive materials in liquid and gaseous effluents released to unrestricted areas, ensuring that operational source terms used in calculations reflect potential releases.

2. 10 CFR 50.34(a) and (b), 10 CFR 52.47(a)(5), 10 CFR 52.79(a)(3), and 10 CFR 52.79(a)(1)(i) and (ii): These sections require that the kinds and quantities of radioactive materials expected to be produced and released during normal operations and anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs) remain within the limits of Part 20 and the design objectives of Part 50, Appendix I.

3. 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I: This appendix provides numerical guides for design objectives and limiting conditions for operation, requiring that radioactive material in effluents be kept 'as low as is reasonably achievable' (ALARA). Applicants must demonstrate compliance with these design objectives.

4. General Design Criteria (GDC) 60 and 61: These criteria require that plant designs include means to suitably control the release of radioactive materials in effluents and ensure safe storage and handling of radioactive materials.

Specifically, 10 CFR 50.34a requires that equipment be designed to ensure that the collective dose to the population within 80 kilometers (50 miles) from liquid effluents does not exceed 0.003 man-sieverts (300 man-rem) per year to the total body or any organ (except the thyroid), and from gaseous effluents does not exceed 0.005 man-sieverts (500 man-rem) to the total body or 0.015 man-sieverts (1500 man-rem) to the thyroid. Additionally, annual average concentrations of radioactive material in effluents must not exceed the limits in Table 2 of Appendix B to Part 20. Licensees must also use procedures and equipment to minimize releases to the environment to the extent practicable (10 CFR 50.34a(a)).

In summary, NRC regulations require nuclear power plants to design and operate effluent control systems that limit radioactive releases to levels protective of public health and safety, comply with specific dose and concentration limits, and apply ALARA principles.
