data.query: How do regulatory requirements for radioactive waste management interact with dose limits for members of the public in the context of liquid and gaseous effluent releases from nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
Regulatory requirements for radioactive waste management at nuclear power plants are closely linked to dose limits for members of the public, particularly regarding the release of liquid and gaseous effluents. According to DSRS 11.1 (Section II. Acceptance Criteria), the effectiveness of liquid and gaseous waste management systems (LWMS and GWMS) is evaluated to ensure that effluent releases meet both the numerical design objectives of Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50 and the effluent concentration limits specified in 10 CFR Part 20, Appendix B, Table 2, Note 4. These requirements are designed to ensure that radioactive releases to unrestricted areas do not exceed regulatory dose limits for the public.

Specifically, Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50 (Sections II.A and II.B) sets numerical dose objectives for effluent releases: for liquid effluents, the annual dose to any member of the public in unrestricted areas must not exceed 3 millirems to the total body or 10 millirems to any organ (excluding tritium and dissolved gases). For gaseous effluents, the annual dose must not exceed 5 millirems to the total body, 15 millirems to the skin, or 15 millirems to any organ. These limits are intended to ensure that releases are kept as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA), as required by 10 CFR 50.34a and 50.36a.

In summary, the regulatory requirements for radioactive waste management systems are structured to ensure that the design and operation of nuclear power plants control liquid and gaseous effluent releases such that the resulting public doses do not exceed the specified limits in Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50, while also meeting the ALARA principle and the effluent concentration limits of 10 CFR Part 20.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appendix I to Part 50—Numerical Guides for Design Objectives and Limiting Conditions for Operation To Meet the Criterion “As Low as is Reasonably Achievable” for Radioactive Material in Light-Water-Cooled Nuclear Power Reactor Effluents

I. Introduction
Section 50.34a provides that each applicant for a license to operate a light-water-cooled nuclear power reactor will include in its application a description of the design features of the facility provided to meet the requirements of § 50.34a(a) and an analysis of the manner in which the facility has been designed and will be operated to ensure that the release of radioactive materials in effluents to unrestricted areas will be kept as low as is reasonably achievable. Section 50.36a requires technical specifications to keep releases of radioactive materials to unrestricted areas during normal operation, including anticipated operational occurrences, as low as is reasonably achievable. This appendix provides numerical guides to meet these requirements for design objectives and limiting conditions for operation.

II. Design Objectives for Light-Water-Cooled Nuclear Power Reactors
A. The calculated annual total quantity of radioactive material, except tritium and dissolved gases, released from each light-water-cooled nuclear power reactor to unrestricted areas in liquid effluents will not result in an estimated annual dose or dose commitment to any member of the public in the unrestricted area in excess of 3 millirems to the total body or 10 millirems to any organ.
B. The calculated annual total quantity of radioactive material released from each light-water-cooled nuclear power reactor to unrestricted areas in gaseous effluents will not result in an estimated annual dose or dose commitment to any member of the public in the unrestricted area in excess of 5 millirems to the total body or 15 millirems to the skin, or 15 millirems to any organ.

data.query: For a nuclear power plant that recycles liquid radioactive waste back into the reactor coolant system, what combined regulatory provisions from radioactive waste management requirements, effluent release controls, and regulatory guidance must be considered to ensure that buildup and release of radionuclides such as tritium remain within acceptable limits for both liquid and gaseous pathways?
data.answer:
For a nuclear power plant that recycles liquid radioactive waste back into the reactor coolant system, several combined regulatory provisions must be considered to ensure that the buildup and release of radionuclides, such as tritium, remain within acceptable limits for both liquid and gaseous pathways. According to DSRS 11.1 (Section II. Acceptance Criteria), the effectiveness of the liquid waste management system (LWMS) and gaseous waste management system (GWMS) must be evaluated to ensure that radioactive effluents meet the numerical design objectives of Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50 and the concentration limits and unity criterion of Appendix B, Table 2 to 10 CFR Part 20. 

The acceptance criteria require compliance with:
- 10 CFR Part 20, which governs operational source terms and effluent concentration limits to unrestricted areas.
- 10 CFR 50.34(a) and (b), and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I, which set design objectives for effluent releases and require that releases be kept as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA).
- General Design Criteria (GDC) 60 and 61, which mandate suitable controls for the release and safe storage/handling of radioactive materials.

Specifically, 10 CFR 50.34a requires that the facility's design and operation ensure radioactive material in effluents to unrestricted areas are ALARA and within Appendix I numerical guides. For liquid effluents (excluding tritium and dissolved gases), the annual dose to any member of the public must not exceed 3 millirem to the total body or 10 millirem to any organ. For gaseous effluents, the limits are 5 millirem to the total body and 15 millirem to the skin or any organ (10 CFR 50.34a(b)).

Regulatory guidance documents such as RG 1.112 (for calculating releases), RG 1.110 (cost-benefit analysis), and RG 1.140 (ventilation system design and maintenance) must also be followed. The use of models and parameters consistent with RG 1.112, NUREG-0017 (GALE86 code), and ANSI/ANS 18.1-1999 is recommended for determining coolant source terms and expected releases.

In summary, compliance with the above regulatory requirements and guidance ensures that the buildup and release of radionuclides, including tritium, from recycled liquid radioactive waste remain within acceptable limits for both liquid and gaseous pathways.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for controlling radioactive effluent releases to ensure public dose limits are not exceeded?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for controlling radioactive effluent releases to ensure public dose limits are not exceeded are grounded in several key NRC regulations. According to DSRS 11.1 (Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA), the primary requirements are based on 10 CFR Part 20, which sets standards for protection against radiation, including dose limits for members of the public. Specifically, effluent releases must be controlled such that doses to the public do not exceed the limits specified in 10 CFR 20.1301.

Additionally, 10 CFR 50.34(a) and (b), as well as 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I, require applicants to demonstrate that the kinds and quantities of radioactive materials expected to be released during normal operations and anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs) are within these limits and meet the design objectives for keeping releases as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA). Applicants must provide sufficient information to show that their systems can adequately treat effluents to meet both the numerical design objectives of Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50 and the concentration limits and unity criterion of Appendix B, Table 2 to 10 CFR Part 20.

Furthermore, General Design Criteria 60 and 61 require that nuclear power unit designs include means to suitably control the release of radioactive materials in both gaseous and liquid effluents and ensure safe storage and handling of radioactive materials.

Per 10 CFR 50.34a, applicants must describe facility design features and operational procedures intended to keep effluent releases ALARA and within public dose limits. License applications must also include technical specifications for limiting conditions for operation, surveillance, and reporting requirements to ensure ongoing compliance with Part 20 dose limits.

In summary, the regulatory framework requires robust design, operational controls, and technical specifications to ensure that radioactive effluent releases are minimized and public dose limits are not exceeded, as detailed in DSRS 11.1, 10 CFR Part 20, 10 CFR 50.34a, and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory guides for radioactive waste management interface with requirements for monitoring and limiting tritium releases in liquid and gaseous effluents?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory guides for radioactive waste management interface directly with requirements for monitoring and limiting tritium releases in both liquid and gaseous effluents through a structured framework of guidance and regulatory criteria. According to DSRS 11.1, the NRC endorses the use of Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.112 for calculating releases of radioactive materials, including tritium, in liquid and gaseous effluents from nuclear power plants. This guide, along with supporting codes such as NUREG-0017 (PWR-GALE86), provides the methodologies and models for estimating expected releases, ensuring consistency with regulatory expectations. The calculated source terms are then used to evaluate the performance of the liquid waste management system (LWMS) and gaseous waste management system (GWMS), as described in DSRS Sections 11.2 and 11.3, to verify that these systems can adequately treat effluents to meet regulatory limits.

The regulatory basis for these evaluations is found in Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50, which sets numerical design objectives for radioactive material in effluents, including specific dose limits for tritium in gaseous releases (5 millirems to the total body or 15 millirems to the skin annually) and for other radionuclides in liquid releases (excluding tritium, which is not subject to the same liquid effluent dose limits). These objectives supplement the effluent concentration limits in Appendix B, Table 2 to 10 CFR Part 20, and reinforce the ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) principle. Thus, NRC regulatory guides provide the technical basis and calculation methods, while the regulations establish the dose and concentration limits that must be met for tritium and other radionuclides in both liquid and gaseous effluents.

evidence_chain.section: Appendix I to Part 50
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appendix I to Part 50—Numerical Guides for Design Objectives and Limiting Conditions for Operation To Meet the Criterion “As Low as is Reasonably Achievable” for Radioactive Material in Light-Water-Cooled Nuclear Power Reactor Effluents

I. Introduction
Section 50.34a provides numerical guides for the design objectives and limiting conditions for operation of nuclear power reactors to meet the criterion of keeping radioactive material in effluents to unrestricted areas as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA). These guides are intended to supplement the requirements of § 20.1301 of this chapter that radioactive material in effluents released to unrestricted areas not exceed the limits specified in Table 2 of Appendix B to Part 20 of this chapter. The guides are also intended to supplement the requirements that the exposure of individuals to radiation resulting from the operation of a nuclear power reactor be kept as low as is reasonably achievable.

II. Design Objectives for Light-Water-Cooled Nuclear Power Reactors
A. The design objectives for light-water-cooled nuclear power reactors are:
1. The calculated annual total quantity of radioactive material, except tritium and dissolved or entrained noble gases, released from each light-water-cooled nuclear power reactor to unrestricted areas in liquid effluents shall not result in an estimated annual dose or dose commitment to any individual in an unrestricted area, from all pathways of exposure, in excess of 3 millirems to the total body or 10 millirems to any organ.
2. The calculated annual total quantity of radioactive material, including tritium and all radioactive noble gases, released from each light-water-cooled nuclear power reactor to unrestricted areas in gaseous effluents shall not result in an estimated annual dose or dose commitment to any individual in an unrestricted area, from all pathways of exposure, in excess of 5 millirems to the total body or 15 millirems to the skin.

data.query: When evaluating tritium buildup in the reactor coolant system due to recycling of processed coolant, what combined regulatory standards and guidance must be applied to ensure that calculated source terms and effluent release rates are conservative and meet NRC acceptance criteria?
data.answer:
When evaluating tritium buildup in the reactor coolant system due to recycling of processed coolant, the NRC requires that combined regulatory standards and guidance be applied to ensure calculated source terms and effluent release rates are conservative and meet acceptance criteria. According to DSRS 11.1 (Section II), the primary regulatory requirements include:

- 10 CFR Part 20, which governs the determination of operational source terms for calculations of potential radioactivity in liquid and gaseous effluents to unrestricted areas.
- 10 CFR 50.34(a) and (b), 10 CFR 52.47(a)(5), and 10 CFR 52.79(a)(3), which require that the kinds and quantities of radioactive materials expected to be produced and released during normal operations and anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs) remain within the limits of Part 20 and the design objectives of Part 50, Appendix I.
- 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I, which sets numerical guides for design objectives and limiting conditions for operation, ensuring releases are as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA).
- General Design Criteria (GDC) 60 and 61, which require the design to include means to suitably control and safely store radioactive materials in effluents and other systems.

For source term and effluent release calculations, coolant source terms are considered acceptable if determined using models and parameters consistent with Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.112, NUREG-0017 (PWR-GALE86 code), and ANSI/ANS 18.1-1999, adjusted for specific reactor design features. Additional relevant guidance includes RG 1.110 (cost-benefit analysis), RG 1.140 (ventilation system design), and DC/COL-ISG-5 (GALE86 Code application).

10 CFR 50.34a further requires that the application describe design objectives and means to control releases, ensuring calculated annual average releases do not exceed Appendix I numerical guides, and that equipment is designed for periodic testing and inspection to maintain compliance.

In summary, compliance with these combined regulations and guidance ensures that tritium source term and effluent release calculations are conservative and meet NRC acceptance criteria (DSRS 11.1 Section II; 10 CFR 50.34a).

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for the design and operation of liquid radioactive waste management systems in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for the design and operation of liquid radioactive waste management systems (LWMS) in nuclear power plants are established to ensure that radioactive releases to the environment are minimized and controlled, protecting public health and safety. According to SRP 11.2, the NRC reviews LWMS to verify compliance with regulatory limits on liquid effluent discharges and associated public doses, ensuring releases and doses are as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA). The review encompasses system design, objectives, criteria, treatment methods, system interfaces, bypass routes, expected releases, and provisions for preventing and mitigating uncontrolled or unmonitored releases (SRP 11.2).

Per 10 CFR 50.34a, the design objectives require that, at the boundary of the unrestricted area, the annual dose to any member of the public from liquid effluents must not exceed 3 millirems to the total body or 10 millirems to any organ (except the thyroid, which may receive up to 15 millirems). The design must also ensure effluent levels are ALARA (10 CFR 50.34a).

RG 1.143 provides detailed design and construction criteria for LWMS, including the use of appropriate materials (excluding iron and plastic pipe), adherence to ASME codes, containment provisions for maximum liquid inventory, and requirements for leakage control, inspection, testing, and quality assurance (RG 1.143, C.1.1, C.4). Systems must facilitate access, operation, and maintenance to maintain occupational exposures ALARA, and pressure-retaining components should use welded construction where practicable.

RG 4.21 emphasizes minimizing facility contamination through design and operational procedures that limit leakage, provide containment, and enable early leak detection and response. The design should facilitate maintenance and restrict radiological work to localized areas to minimize decontamination needs. Leak detection capabilities and monitoring programs are required to ensure prompt identification and response to leaks (RG 4.21, C.1.1–1.3).

In summary, NRC acceptance criteria require LWMS to be designed and operated to meet dose limits, minimize releases and contamination, ensure robust containment and leak detection, and comply with applicable codes and quality assurance provisions.

evidence_chain.section: C. REGULATORY POSITION (1. Minimizing Facility Contamination, 1.1–1.3)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
C.  REGULATORY POSITION   

1.  Minimizing Facility Contamination  

1.1 General Statement   

In general, an applicant should minimize radioactive contamination of the facility by using structure, system, and component (SSC) designs and operational procedures that limit leakage and/or control the spread of contamination.  The design and operational procedures should provide for the early detection of leaks thus allowing prompt assessment to support a timely and appropriate response.  Applicants should note that 10 CFR 20.1406 requires that contamination be minimized “…to the extent practicable...”  This implies that other competing concerns such as the implication to safety systems and the overall cost should be considered.  Thus the minimization of facility contamination must be considered in the context of overall facility safety.   

1.2 Minimization of Leaks and Spills and Provision of Containment

Through design, worker practices, preventive maintenance, and effective operating procedures, applicants covered by 10 CFR 20.1406 should strive to minimize leaks and spills, provide containment in areas where such events might occur, and provide for detection that supports timely assessment and appropriate response.  This approach should be applied in a risk-informed and performance-based manner considering the nature of the hazard.  Radiologically significant leaks and spills need to be addressed, and containment should be considered where practical and cost effective.  Areas where licensed materials are used and stored should be designed to facilitate maintenance and operations (including cleanup).  Radiological work should be restricted to a localized section of the facility in order to minimize the potential area requiring decontamination.

1.3 Prompt Detection of Leakage  

The facility should be designed such that any SSC that has the potential for leakage is provided with adequate leak detection capability to the extent practical.  In addition to design considerations to control and, if possible, prevent radioactive system leakage, it is important during operations to be able to promptly detect leakage as close as possible to the leakage source to allow timely intervention and to prevent the potential for widespread contamination.  Thus, monitoring and routine surveillance programs are an important part of minimizing potential contamination.  This approach should include the placement of instruments to detect leakage at readily accessible locations and the use of operational practices that will enable early detection of contamination.  Because leakage detection is only the first step in minimizing contamination, the applicant also should be prepared to provide a timely assessment and response based on the location and characteristics of the leak or spill.

data.query: How do the requirements for quality assurance in radioactive waste management systems relate to the criteria for seismic and flood protection in nuclear facilities?
data.answer:
The requirements for quality assurance (QA) in radioactive waste management systems are closely related to the criteria for seismic and flood protection in nuclear facilities, as both are grounded in the overarching regulatory framework established by 10 CFR Part 50, particularly Appendix A (General Design Criteria) and Appendix B (Quality Assurance Criteria).

According to SRP 11.2 and Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.143, QA provisions for radioactive waste management structures, systems, and components (SSCs) are established to ensure that these SSCs are designed, constructed, and maintained to perform their safety functions under both normal and adverse conditions, including natural phenomena such as earthquakes and floods (SRP 11.2, RG 1.143 Section A, C.7). Specifically, Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 50 requires a QA program commensurate with the safety importance of the SSCs, ensuring that design, procurement, fabrication, and construction activities meet the necessary quality standards (RG 1.143, Section C.7).

Appendix A, Criterion 1, mandates that SSCs important to safety be subject to quality standards and QA programs to assure their performance (RG 1.143, Section A). Criterion 2 further requires that these SSCs be designed to withstand natural phenomena, including seismic and flood events, without loss of safety function. The design bases for these protections must reflect the safety significance of the SSCs (SRP 3.3.1, 3.4.2, 3.7.1; RG 1.143, Section A).

Thus, the QA requirements ensure that the design, construction, and operation of radioactive waste management systems are robust enough to meet the seismic and flood protection criteria. This is achieved by applying appropriate quality group classifications, codes, and standards (SRP 11.2), and by documenting and maintaining records of QA measures (RG 1.143, Section C.7). The QA program thereby provides assurance that SSCs will perform as required during natural phenomena, directly supporting compliance with seismic and flood protection criteria.

In 10 CFR Part 50, "Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities," § 50.34, "Contents of Applications; Technical Information," requires that each application for a construction permit include a preliminary safety analysis report. Part of the information required is related to quality assurance and the preliminary design of the facility, including, among other things, the principal design criteria for the facility. Appendix B, "Quality Assurance Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants and Fuel Reprocessing Plants," to 10 CFR Part 50 establishes overall quality assurance requirements for structures, systems, and components important to safety. Appendix A, ''General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants," to 10 CFR Part 50 establishes minimum requirements for the principal design criteria for light-water-cooled nuclear power plants.

Criterion 1, "Quality Standards and Records,'' of Appendix A requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with the importance to safety of the safety function to be performed and that a quality assurance program be established and implemented in order to provide adequate assurance that these structures, systems, and components will satisfactorily perform their safety function.  

Criterion 2, "Design Bases for Protection Against Natural Phenomena," of Appendix A requires, among other things, that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena such as earthquakes, tornados, or flooding without loss of capability to perform their safety functions. The design bases for these structures, systems, and components are to reflect the importance of the safety functions to be performed. ...

This regulatory guide is being revised to provide design guidance acceptable to the NRC staff in regard to natural phenomena hazards, internal and external man-induced hazards, and quality group classification and quality assurance provisions for radioactive waste management systems, structures, and components.
...
7. QUALITY ASSURANCE FOR RADWASTE MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS
Since the impact of these systems on safety is limited, the extent of control required by Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 50 is similarly limited. To ensure that systems will perform their intended functions, a quality assurance program sufficient to ensure that all design, construction, and testing provisions are met should be established and documented. A quality assurance program acceptable to the NRC staff is presented in ANSI/ANS-55.6-1993, "Liquid Radioactive Waste Processing System for Pressurized Water Reactor Plants."

Section 4.3, "Quality Assurance," of ANSI/ANS 55.6-1993 provides quality assurance guidance that is acceptable to the NRC staff for the system designer and procurer and for the system constructor. The design, procurement, fabrication, and construction activities should conform to the quality control provisions of the codes and standards specified in Table 1 of this guide. In addition, or when not covered by the referenced codes and standards, sufficient records should be maintained to furnish evidence that quality assurance measures are being implemented. The records should include results of reviews and inspections and should be identifiable and retrievable.

II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
Requirements
Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations:

GDC 2 requires that SSCs important to safety shall be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena such as earthquakes, tornados, hurricanes, floods, tsunami, and seiches without loss of capability to perform their safety functions as it relates to natural phenomena.  The design bases for these SSCs shall reflect appropriate combinations of the effects of normal and accident conditions with the effects of the natural phenomena.  
2. 10 CFR 52.47(b)(1), which requires that a DC application contain the proposed inspections, tests, analyses, and acceptance criteria (ITAAC) that are necessary and sufficient to provide reasonable assurance that, if the inspections, tests, and analyses are performed and the acceptance criteria met, a plant that incorporates the design certification is built and will operate in accordance with the design certification, the provisions of the Atomic Energy Act, and the NRC's regulations; 
3. 10 CFR 52.80(a), which requires that a COL application contain the proposed inspections, tests, and analyses, including those applicable to emergency planning, that the licensee shall perform, and the acceptance criteria that are necessary and sufficient to provide reasonable assurance that, if the inspections, tests, and analyses are performed and the acceptance criteria met, the facility has been constructed and will operate in conformity with the combined license, the provisions of the Atomic Energy Act, and the NRC's regulations.

SRP Acceptance Criteria
Specific SRP acceptance criteria acceptable to meet the relevant requirements of the NRC’s regulations identified above are as follows for the review described in this SRP section.  The SRP is not a substitute for the NRC’s regulations, and compliance with it is not required. However, an applicant is required to identify differences between the design features, analytical techniques, and procedural measures proposed for its facility and the SRP acceptance criteria and evaluate how the proposed alternatives to the SRP acceptance criteria provide acceptable methods of compliance with the NRC regulations
The design of a structure that must withstand the effects of the highest flood and groundwater levels is acceptable if the relevant requirements of GDC 2, "Design Bases for Protection Against Natural Phenomena," are complied with. The criteria necessary to meet the relevant requirements of GDC 2 are as follows:
1. The highest flood and groundwater levels and the associated static and dynamic effects, if any, used in the design shall be the most severe ones that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated.
2. In most situations, the highest flood level is below the proposed plant grade and only its hydrostatic effects need be considered. Unless the hydrostatic head associated with the highest flood and groundwater levels is relieved by utilizing a drainage or a pumping system around the foundations of a structures, hydrostatic pressure has to be considered as a structural load on basement walls and the foundation slab of a structure. In consideration of any uplifting or floating of a structure, the total buoyancy force may be based on the highest flood level or the highest groundwater level excluding wave action. However, wave action should be included in the calculation for lateral and overturning movements of a structure.
3. Where the flood level is above the proposed plant grade, the dynamic loads of wave action should be considered.  Procedures for determining such dynamic loads are acceptable if they are in accordance with or equivalent to those delineated in the U.S. Army Coastal Engineering Research Center, “Shore Protection Manual” (Vol. I, June 2002, reprinted from 1973 edition and  Vol. II, June 2002, reprinted from 1973 edition) or in EM 1110-2-1100, Coastal Engineering Manual, Part II, Chapter 1, “Water Wave Mechanics,” U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, April 30, 2002 as applicable.
Any other methods proposed should be provided with adequate justification and are reviewed on a case by case basis.

data.query: For a nuclear power plant's liquid waste management system, what combined regulatory provisions from general design criteria, regulatory guides on waste management, and review standards on environmental protection must be considered to ensure compliance with NRC requirements for system design, operation, and accident mitigation?
data.answer:
To ensure compliance with NRC requirements for the design, operation, and accident mitigation of a nuclear power plant's liquid waste management system (LWMS), a combination of regulatory provisions from general design criteria, regulatory guides, and review standards must be considered:

1. General Design Criteria (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A): The LWMS must meet the minimum requirements for principal design criteria, including:
- Criterion 1: Quality standards and records, requiring quality assurance programs for structures, systems, and components important to safety (RG 1.143, Section A; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B).
- Criterion 2: Protection against natural phenomena, ensuring systems can withstand events like earthquakes or flooding (RG 1.143, Section A).
- Criterion 60: Control of releases of radioactive materials, mandating suitable means to control liquid effluent releases during normal operation, anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs), and design basis accidents (RG 1.143, Section A).

2. Regulatory Guides:
- RG 1.143 provides acceptable methods for design, construction, installation, and testing of radioactive waste management systems, including quality group classification, accident mitigation (e.g., tank overflow controls, dikes, retention basins), and protection against both natural and man-induced hazards (RG 1.143, Section A; SRP 11.2).
- RG 4.21 addresses minimization of contamination and radioactive waste generation throughout the facility life cycle, emphasizing prevention of unintended releases, early detection, and prompt response, as required by 10 CFR 20.1406 (RG 4.21, Section A; SRP 11.2).

3. Review Standards (SRP 11.2):
- The NRC reviews LWMS design objectives, criteria, treatment methods, system interfaces, and accident mitigation features to ensure compliance with effluent and dose limits (SRP 11.2, Section I).
- The review includes evaluation of provisions for preventing and mitigating uncontrolled or unmonitored releases, such as tank overflow controls and containment features, referencing RG 1.143 and RG 4.21 (SRP 11.2, Section I).

4. Regulatory Requirements (10 CFR 50.34a, 50.36a):
- Applications must describe design objectives for effluent control equipment to ensure doses are ALARA and within regulatory limits (10 CFR 50.34a).
- Technical specifications must include limiting conditions and surveillance to prevent effluent releases exceeding 10 CFR 20.1301 limits (10 CFR 50.36a).

In summary, compliance requires integrating general design criteria, NRC-accepted design and operational guidance, and review standards to ensure robust control, monitoring, and mitigation of radioactive liquid releases throughout the plant’s life cycle.

§ 50.34 Contents of applications; technical information.
(a) Preliminary safety analysis report. Each application for a construction permit shall include a preliminary safety analysis report. The preliminary safety analysis report shall describe the facility, present design bases and limits on its operation, and present a safety analysis of the structures, systems, and components of the facility as a whole. The analysis must assess the facility’s capability to prevent or mitigate the consequences of postulated accidents that could result in potential offsite exposures. ...

§ 50.34a Design objectives for equipment to control releases of radioactive material in effluents—nuclear power reactors.
(a) Each applicant for a license to operate a nuclear power reactor shall include in its application a description of the design objectives for equipment to be installed to control releases of radioactive material in gaseous and liquid effluents produced during normal reactor operations, including anticipated operational occurrences. The design objectives must provide reasonable assurance that the collective dose to persons in the population surrounding the plant can be kept as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA) and that the annual dose to any individual in an unrestricted area from external exposure to such effluents will not exceed the limits specified in § 20.1301 of this chapter.

§ 50.36a Technical specifications on effluents from nuclear power reactors.
(a) Each license authorizing operation of a nuclear power reactor will include technical specifications, including requirements for limiting conditions for operation and surveillance to assure that the operation of the facility will not result in releases of radioactive materials in effluents that would exceed the limits specified in § 20.1301 of this chapter.

This regulatory guide has been revised to provide guidance to licensees and applicants on methods acceptable to the staff for complying with the NRC's regulations in the design, construction, installation, and testing the structures, systems, and components of radioactive waste management facilities in light-water-reactor nuclear power plants. 

In 10 CFR Part 50, "Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities," § 50.34, "Contents of Applications; Technical Information," requires that each application for a construction permit include a preliminary safety analysis report. Part of the information required is related to quality assurance and the preliminary design of the facility, including, among other things, the principal design criteria for the facility. Appendix B, "Quality Assurance Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants and Fuel Reprocessing Plants," to 10 CFR Part 50 establishes overall quality assurance requirements for structures, systems, and components important to safety. Appendix A, ''General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants," to 10 CFR Part 50 establishes minimum requirements for the principal design criteria for light-water-cooled nuclear power plants.

Criterion 1, "Quality Standards and Records,'' of Appendix A requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with the importance to safety of the safety function to be performed and that a quality assurance program be established and implemented in order to provide adequate assurance that these structures, systems, and components will satisfactorily perform their safety function.

The release of radioactive materials from external man-induced events and design basis accidents must also be controlled.

This regulatory guide is being revised to provide design guidance acceptable to the NRC staff in regard to natural phenomena hazards, internal and external man-induced hazards, and quality group classification and quality assurance provisions for radioactive waste management systems, structures, and components. evidence_chain.section: A. INTRODUCTION
evidence_chain.evidence_text: This guide describes a method acceptable to the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) for use in the implementation of Title 10, Section 20.1406, “Minimization of Contamination,” of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR 20.1406) (Ref. 1). License, approval, and certification applicants should strive to minimize contamination and radioactive waste generation over the total life cycle of a facility, from initial facility layout and design through procedures for operation and concluding with final decontamination and dismantling at the time of decommissioning. ... The purpose of this regulatory guide is to present guidance that will assist applicants covered by 10 CFR 20.1406 in effectively implementing this licensing requirement. The guidance consists of specific design considerations drawn from nuclear industry experience and lessons learned from decommissioning. These have been combined to support the development of a contaminant management philosophy. The principles embodied in this philosophy are threefold: (1) prevention of unintended releases; (2) early detection, if there is unintended release of radioactive contamination; and (3) prompt assessment to support a timely and appropriate response. Applying these principles requires the use of sound design, proven engineering practices, conservative radiation protection principles, and attention to operational practices. All of this should be considered in the context of the life cycle of the facility from the early planning stages through the final plans for decommissioning and waste disposal. This guide describes some of the mechanisms that can be employed for facility life-cycle planning to meet the requirements of 10 CFR 20.1406.

data.query: What is the NRC's acceptance criterion for the assumed failed fuel fraction when evaluating radiation source terms for shielding design in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC's acceptance criterion for the assumed failed fuel fraction when evaluating radiation source terms for shielding design in nuclear power plants depends on the scenario being analyzed. For normal operation and shielding/ventilation design, DSRS 12.2 (Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA) specifies that the source term is acceptable if it is based on an assumed 0.25-percent fuel cladding defect rate for pressurized-water reactors (PWRs), or on reactor coolant system isotopic concentrations equivalent to operation for a full fuel cycle at the technical specification limits for halogens (I-131 dose equivalent) and noble gases (Xe-133 dose equivalent). This criterion is used to establish the routine source term for shielding calculations under normal operating conditions.

For accident scenarios, such as the maximum hypothetical loss-of-coolant accident (LOCA), Regulatory Guide 1.183 (Appendix A, Section A.1.1) states that it is acceptable to assume that 100 percent of the fuel rods in the reactor core fail and contribute to the accident source term. This conservative assumption ensures that the calculated source term bounds the consequences of any credible accident involving significant core damage and provides a basis for evaluating the adequacy of shielding and radiological protection systems under accident conditions.

In summary, the NRC acceptance criterion is 0.25-percent failed fuel for normal operation shielding design (DSRS 12.2), and 100 percent failed fuel for accident source term evaluations (RG 1.183 Appendix A).

evidence_chain.section: Appendix A: Assumptions for Evaluating the Radiological Consequences of Light-Water Reactor Maximum Hypothetical Loss-of-Coolant Accidents
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appendix A: Assumptions for Evaluating the Radiological Consequences of Light-Water Reactor Maximum Hypothetical Loss-of-Coolant Accidents

A.1.1 Fraction of Failed Fuel

For the maximum hypothetical accident (MHA) LOCA, the NRC staff finds it acceptable to assume that 100 percent of the fuel rods in the reactor core fail and contribute to the accident source term. This assumption is consistent with the deterministic approach for evaluating the adequacy of engineered safety features and containment systems. The assumed complete core involvement ensures that the calculated source term bounds the consequences of any credible accident involving significant core damage. This approach is intended to provide a conservative basis for the design and evaluation of shielding and other radiological protection systems.

A.1.2 Fission Product Inventory

The fission product inventory should be calculated based on the total core inventory at the time of the accident, assuming equilibrium conditions at the licensed core power level and the maximum fuel burnup permitted by the technical specifications.

data.query: How do regulatory requirements for radiation protection of workers relate to the assumptions made for failed fuel fraction in the design of shielding and ventilation systems?
data.answer:
Regulatory requirements for radiation protection of workers are directly linked to the assumptions made for failed fuel fraction in the design of shielding and ventilation systems. According to DSRS 12.2, the NRC reviews the applicant’s safety analysis to ensure that radiation protection design features comply with regulations such as 10 CFR 20.1101(b), which mandates that occupational radiation exposure (ORE) be maintained as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA). The design of shielding and ventilation systems must be based on source term descriptions that include all relevant information, such as the methods, models, and assumptions used—specifically, the assumed fraction of failed fuel. For pressurized-water reactors (PWRs), the NRC accepts a basis of 0.25-percent fuel cladding defects or equivalent isotopic concentrations for the design of shielding and ventilation systems. These assumptions are critical inputs to shielding codes and facility design features, ensuring that occupational and public exposures remain within regulatory limits.

Furthermore, Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50 reinforces that design objectives for effluent control systems must ensure releases are ALARA and do not exceed specified numerical guides. The failed fuel fraction assumption directly affects the calculated source term, which in turn determines the required shielding and ventilation to protect workers and the public. Thus, regulatory requirements for worker protection are operationalized through conservative assumptions about failed fuel fraction, ensuring that the design of shielding and ventilation systems is robust enough to maintain exposures within regulatory limits and ALARA principles (DSRS 12.2; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I).

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) staff will review the applicant’s final safety analysis report (FSAR) for a design certification (DC) or combined license (COL). The staff reviews radiation sources in normal operations, anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs), and accident conditions used as the bases for determining the radiation protection design features provided to ensure compliance with the Commission’s requirements. The requirements include: (1) Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) 20.1101(b), to maintain occupational radiation exposure (ORE) as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA), (2) 10 CFR Part 20, Subpart H, “Respiratory Protection and Controls To Restrict Internal Exposure in Restricted Areas,” and (3) 10 CFR 20.1301(e) and 40 CFR Part 190, to control the exposure of members of the public from direct radiation sources. ...

Descriptions should be provided for all radiation sources that require (1) shielding (e.g., provided for ORE 20.1101(b), 20.1201, 20.1202, or public 20.1301(e) radiation exposure control), (2) special ventilation systems, ... The source descriptions should include all pertinent information required for (1) input to shielding codes used in the design process, (2) establishment of related facility design features, (3) development of plans and procedures, (4) assessment of radiation (public or occupational, as appropriate) exposure, and (5) determination of radiation dose to electrical equipment important to safety as described in 10 CFR 50.49. Unless described within other sections of the FSAR, source descriptions should include the methods, models, and assumptions used as the bases for all values provided in FSAR Section 12.2. ...

Shielding and ventilation design fission product source terms will be acceptable if developed using these bases:

1. 0.25-percent fuel cladding defects for pressurized-water reactors (PWRs) or the reactor coolant system isotopic concentrations, including fission products and significant corrosion and activation products, equivalent to operation for a full fuel cycle at the technical specification limits for halogens (I-131 dose equivalent) and noble gases (Xe-133 dose equivalent).

evidence_chain.section: Appendix I to Part 50
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appendix I to Part 50—Numerical Guides for Design Objectives and Limiting Conditions for Operation To Meet the Criterion “As Low as is Reasonably Achievable” for Radioactive Material in Light-Water-Cooled Nuclear Power Reactor Effluents

I. Introduction
Section 50.34a provides that each applicant for a license to operate a light-water-cooled nuclear power reactor will include in its application a description of the design features of the installation to be provided for the control of releases of radioactive material in effluents to the environment. The design objectives for equipment to control releases of radioactive material in effluents are to be such that, in the absence of unusual operating conditions, the quantities of radioactive materials released in liquid and gaseous effluents during normal operation, including anticipated operational occurrences, will be kept as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA) and, in any event, will not exceed the numerical guides set forth in this appendix. These numerical guides are not to be regarded as limits, but as design objectives which are to be used in the design of nuclear power reactors for the purpose of ensuring that releases of radioactive materials in effluents are kept as low as is reasonably achievable.

data.query: For a new nuclear power plant design, what regulatory standards and review criteria must be met to demonstrate that the assumed failed fuel fraction is sufficiently conservative to ensure adequate radiation protection for workers and the public, as well as appropriate design of shielding, ventilation, radwaste handling, and equipment qualification?
data.answer:
To demonstrate that the assumed failed fuel fraction is sufficiently conservative for a new nuclear power plant design, several regulatory standards and review criteria must be met, as outlined in the provided evidence:

1. Source Term Development: The shielding and ventilation design fission product source terms must be based on conservative assumptions, such as a 0.25-percent fuel cladding defect rate for PWRs or isotopic concentrations equivalent to operation at technical specification limits for key radionuclides (DSRS 12.2, II). The source term should also account for activated corrosion products and neutron activation, using reactor operating experience and core physics calculations.

2. Safety Analysis Requirements: The Preliminary Safety Analysis Report (PSAR) must include a detailed analysis of the structures, systems, and components (SSCs), emphasizing how the design criteria are met and assessing the risk to public health and safety from radioactive releases, including the assumed failed fuel fraction. The analysis must demonstrate that the design is sufficiently conservative to ensure adequate radiation protection for workers and the public, and that shielding, ventilation, radwaste handling, and equipment qualification are appropriately addressed (10 CFR 50.34(a)(4)).

3. Accident Source Term and Dose Criteria: The fission product inventory for accident analyses should be based on the maximum core inventory for the highest burnup and enrichment sought, using conservative irradiation histories (RG 1.183, 3.1). Release fractions should be based on NRC-approved values or justified plant-specific analyses, ensuring conservatism for uncertainties in accident progression and fuel performance (RG 1.183, 3.2). The calculated doses to workers and the public must not exceed the reference values in 10 CFR 50.67, 10 CFR 50.34, and GDC 19 (RG 1.183, 4.4).

4. Radwaste System Design: Radwaste management systems must be classified according to the potential radiological release, with more stringent requirements (RW-IIa) if unmitigated releases could exceed 500 mrem/year at the site boundary or 5 rem/year to personnel (RG 1.143, Regulatory Position 5). This ensures that radwaste systems are designed to maintain exposures as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA).

5. Quality Standards: SSCs important to safety, including those involved in shielding, ventilation, and radwaste handling, must be designed, fabricated, and tested to quality standards commensurate with their safety function (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 1; RG 1.26, C.3). Systems containing radioactive material whose failure could result in offsite doses exceeding 0.1 rem must meet Quality Group C standards (RG 1.26, C.3.d).

In summary, the assumed failed fuel fraction must be justified as conservative through detailed safety analysis, adherence to NRC-accepted source term methodologies, compliance with dose limits, and application of appropriate quality and safety classifications for all relevant systems.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Shielding and ventilation design fission product source terms will be acceptable if developed using these bases:

1. 0.25-percent fuel cladding defects for pressurized-water reactors (PWRs) or the reactor coolant system isotopic concentrations, including fission products and significant corrosion and activation products, equivalent to operation for a full fuel cycle at the technical specification limits for halogens (I-131 dose equivalent) and noble gases (Xe-133 dose equivalent).  

2. Post-accident shielding (for vital area access, including work in the area) source terms from RG 1.183, modified for NuScale-specific design attributes, which were developed using relevant industry operating experience.   

3. Direct exposure to members of the public due to radiation from neutron activation products is less than the limits of 10 CFR 20.1301(e).

§ 50.34 Contents of applications; technical information.

(a) Preliminary safety analysis report. Each application for a construction permit shall include a preliminary safety analysis report. (3) A description and analysis of the structures, systems, and components of the facility, with emphasis upon performance requirements, the bases, and the manner in which the design criteria are met.

The fission product inventory used in the accident source term should be based on the maximum core inventory of each radionuclide of interest, calculated for the maximum fuel burnup and enrichment for which approval is sought. evidence_chain.evidence_text:
The design and construction of radioactive waste management and steam generator blowdown systems should provide assurance that radiation exposures to operating personnel and to the general public are as low as is reasonably achievable. One aspect of this consideration is ensuring that these systems are designed to quality standards that enhance system reliability, operability, and availability. ...

5. CLASSIFICATION OF RADWASTE SYSTEMS FOR DESIGN PURPOSES
There are three safety classes, or classifications, for radwaste management facilities:  RW-IIa (High Hazard), RW-IIb (Hazardous), and RW-IIc (Non-Safety).  RW-IIa is the most stringent class and RW-IIc is the least stringent.  These classifications were developed primarily for natural phenomena and man-induced hazard design.  The radiological release criteria (500 millirem at the unprotected area boundary and 5 rem to facility personnel within the protected boundary) was selected to be consistent with the criteria of 10 CFR Part 20, “Standards for Protection Against Radiation.” This safety classification is applied to SSCs as follows.

5.1 For a given structure housing radwaste processing systems or components, if the total design basis unmitigated radiological release (considering the maximum inventory) at the boundary of the unprotected area is greater than 500 millirem per year or the maximum unmitigated exposure to site personnel within the protected area is greater than 5 rem per year, the external structures are classified as RW-IIa.

5.2 For a given structure housing radwaste processing systems or components, if the total design basis unmitigated radiological release (considering the maximum inventory) at the boundary of the unprotected area is less than 500 millirem per year and the maximum unmitigated exposure to site personnel within the protected area is less than 5 rem per year, the external structure is classified as RW-IIb.

5.3 Any systems or components in a RW-IIa facility (see Regulatory Position 5.1) that store, process, or handle radioactive waste in excess of the A1 quantities given in Appendix A, “Determination of A1 and A2,” to 10 CFR Part 71, “Packaging and Transportation of Radioactive Material,” are classified as RW-IIa. These systems or components that process radioactive waste in excess of the A2 quantities but less than the A1 quantities given in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 71 are classified as RW-IIb. All other components are classified as RW-IIc. This classification may be modified for specific radwaste components.

5.4 Any systems or components in a RW-IIb structure (see Regulatory Position 5.2) that are used to store or process specified radioactive waste in excess of the A1 quantities given in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 71 are classified as RW-IIb. All other systems or components are classified as RW-IIc.

The unprotected area boundary mentioned in Regulatory Position 5.1 is shown in Figure 1. A flowchart of the Safety Classification Process is shown in Figure 2. The classifications discussed in Regulatory Positions 5.1 through 5.4 are not intended to apply to radwaste storage facilities if they do not contain any systems or components that exceed the quantities specified in Regulatory Positions 5.1 through 5.4.

data.query: What is the NRC's acceptance criterion for the assumed fraction of failed fuel rods when evaluating radiation source terms in nuclear power plant design?
data.answer:
The NRC's acceptance criterion for the assumed fraction of failed fuel rods when evaluating radiation source terms in nuclear power plant design depends on the scenario being analyzed. For normal operation and shielding/ventilation design, DSRS 12.2 specifies that the source term is acceptable if it is based on an assumed 0.25-percent fuel cladding defect rate for pressurized-water reactors (PWRs), or on reactor coolant system isotopic concentrations equivalent to operation for a full fuel cycle at technical specification limits for key radionuclides (DSRS 12.2, Section II). 

For design basis accident scenarios, such as the maximum hypothetical loss-of-coolant accident (LOCA), Regulatory Guide 1.183 (Appendix A) requires the conservative assumption that 100 percent of the fuel rods in the core fail and are available for release of fission products. This deterministic approach is intended to test the adequacy of containment and safety systems under the most severe credible accident conditions, rather than to represent a realistic or best-estimate scenario (RG 1.183, Appendix A.1).

Additionally, 10 CFR 50.34 requires that the safety assessment in license applications include an evaluation of the potential radiological consequences of postulated accidents, using assumptions (including the fraction of failed fuel rods) that are consistent with the facility's design and operation and provide an adequate margin of safety (10 CFR 50.34(a)(1)).

In summary, the NRC acceptance criterion is 0.25-percent failed fuel rods for normal operation source term evaluations, and 100 percent failed fuel rods for design basis accident source term evaluations.

data.query: How do regulatory requirements for radiation protection of workers and the public relate to the assumptions made about fuel cladding defects in the calculation of radioactive source terms?
data.answer:
Regulatory requirements for radiation protection of workers and the public are directly linked to the assumptions made about fuel cladding defects in the calculation of radioactive source terms. According to DSRS 12.2, shielding and ventilation design source terms are considered acceptable if they are based on conservative assumptions, such as a 0.25-percent fuel cladding defect rate for pressurized-water reactors (PWRs), or equivalent reactor coolant system isotopic concentrations for a full fuel cycle at technical specification limits for key radionuclides (e.g., I-131 and Xe-133). These assumptions are used to ensure that all radiation sources requiring shielding, special ventilation, storage, access control, procedures, or monitoring are adequately described and accounted for in facility design and operational planning (DSRS 12.2, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA).

The regulatory framework, as outlined in RG 1.183, requires that dose consequence analyses for design basis accidents (DBAs) use intentionally conservative assumptions to address uncertainties in accident progression and fission product behavior. For example, the maximum hypothetical accident (MHA), such as a loss-of-coolant accident (LOCA) with substantial core melt, is modeled with a deterministic source term representing significant fuel failure, regardless of the presence of safety systems designed to prevent such failures. This approach ensures that the design and operation of safety-related systems, including containment and shielding, are robust enough to protect both workers and the public under worst-case credible scenarios (RG 1.183, A. INTRODUCTION; B. DISCUSSION).

In summary, the regulatory requirements for radiation protection are met by using conservative fuel cladding defect assumptions in source term calculations, which form the basis for designing facility features and operational controls to limit radiation exposures to workers and the public, as required by 10 CFR Parts 20 and 50.

data.query: For a new light water reactor design, what combined regulatory standards and guidance documents must be considered to ensure that the assumed failed fuel fraction used in shielding and ventilation system design is both conservative and consistent with operational experience and NRC licensing precedent?
data.answer:
To ensure that the assumed failed fuel fraction used in shielding and ventilation system design for a new light water reactor is both conservative and consistent with operational experience and NRC licensing precedent, several combined regulatory standards and guidance documents must be considered:

1. DSRS 12.2 (Section II. Acceptance Criteria) specifies that shielding and ventilation design source terms are acceptable if based on a 0.25-percent fuel cladding defect assumption for PWRs, or on reactor coolant system isotopic concentrations equivalent to operation at technical specification limits for key radionuclides. The source terms must be grounded in applicable reactor operating experience and justified if allowances are made for corrosion product buildup. The methods for determining source terms should be consistent with ANSI/ANS 18.1 and RG 1.112, modified as appropriate for the specific reactor design, and must reflect relevant industry operating experience (DSRS 12.2).

2. Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.183 (Sections 3.1 and 3.2) requires that the fission product inventory and release fractions used in accident source term calculations be based on conservative assumptions, operational experience, and NRC licensing precedent. The inventory should be calculated using the maximum steady-state power and fuel burnup, and the release fractions should be justified, documented, and account for uncertainties, using the best available experimental data (RG 1.183).

3. 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I, and related sections (Appendix A, GDC 1 and 60) require that radioactive material releases be kept as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA), and that design features and technical specifications reflect this principle. The design must include means to control releases and ensure quality standards for safety-related structures, systems, and components (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I; RG 1.143; RG 1.26).

4. RG 1.143 and RG 1.26 provide further guidance on quality assurance, classification, and design criteria for radioactive waste management and other systems handling radioactive material, emphasizing the use of industry practices and operational history in design decisions (RG 1.143, RG 1.26).

In summary, the failed fuel fraction and associated source terms must be based on conservative, experience-based assumptions as outlined in DSRS 12.2, RG 1.183, and ANSI/ANS 18.1, and must comply with the ALARA requirements and quality standards of 10 CFR Part 50 and associated regulatory guides.

Appendix I to Part 50—Numerical Guides for Design Objectives and Limiting Conditions for Operation To Meet the Criterion “As Low as is Reasonably Achievable” for Radioactive Material in Light-Water-Cooled Nuclear Power Reactor Effluents

I. Introduction
Section 50.34a provides that each applicant for a license to operate a light-water-cooled nuclear power reactor will include in its application a description of the design features of the facility, and the proposed technical specifications, as they relate to keeping levels of radioactive material in effluents to unrestricted areas as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA). evidence_chain.evidence_text:
3.1 Fission Product Inventory

The fission product inventory used in the accident source term should be based on the maximum core inventory of each radionuclide at the time of the postulated accident. The inventory should be calculated using the maximum steady-state power level permitted by the technical specifications and the maximum fuel burnup for the fuel in the core at the time of the accident. The inventory should be determined using a method that is consistent with operational experience and NRC licensing precedent. The method should be conservative and should account for uncertainties in the calculation of the inventory. The inventory should be calculated for each radionuclide of interest, including those that contribute significantly to the dose consequences of the accident.

3.2 Release Fractions

The release fractions for each radionuclide group should be based on the best available experimental data and should be consistent with operational experience and NRC licensing precedent. The release fractions should be conservative and should account for uncertainties in the data. The release fractions should be applied to the calculated fission product inventory to determine the amount of each radionuclide released from the fuel during the accident. The release fractions used in the analysis should be documented and justified in the safety analysis report.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for determining decontamination factors for liquid radioactive waste treatment systems using filtration media such as granulated activated charcoal?
data.answer: According to DSRS 12.2 Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA, the NRC acceptance criteria for determining decontamination factors for liquid radioactive waste treatment systems using filtration media such as granulated activated charcoal are based on providing detailed descriptions of all radiation sources relevant to shielding, ventilation, storage, access control, procedures, and monitoring equipment. The source descriptions must include all pertinent information required for input to shielding codes, facility design features, plans and procedures, exposure assessments, and determination of radiation dose to safety-related electrical equipment as described in 10 CFR 50.49. Specifically, the quantities of radioactive material in systems connected to the reactor coolant system are considered acceptable if the values are based on the methods presented in ANSI/ANS Standard 18.1 and Regulatory Guide 1.112, with modifications for design-specific attributes and informed by relevant industry operating experience. These methods and assumptions must be clearly described in the FSAR (Final Safety Analysis Report) Section 12.2, and the types and quantities of radioactive material, including those resulting from neutron activation, should be tabulated in FSAR Subsection 11.1 or 12.2. Therefore, acceptance is contingent upon the use of recognized methods and standards, transparent documentation of assumptions and models, and comprehensive tabulation of radioactive material quantities as the basis for decontamination factor determinations.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for identifying and characterizing all sources of radiation exposure to workers and the public from contained sources in a nuclear facility?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for identifying and characterizing all sources of radiation exposure to workers and the public from contained sources in a nuclear facility are grounded in compliance with specific regulatory requirements and detailed technical guidance. According to DSRS 12.2 Section II, applicants must meet the requirements of 10 CFR Part 20 (including 10 CFR 20.1101, 20.1201, 20.1202, 20.1203, 20.1204, 20.1206, 20.1207, and 20.1301) and 40 CFR Part 190, which set occupational and public dose limits and require comprehensive radiation protection programs. All radiation sources requiring shielding, special ventilation, storage, access control, procedures, or monitoring must be described in detail, including isotope, quantity, form, use, and location, with plan scale drawings and quantitative source parameters. Methods, models, and assumptions used for source term calculations must be specified.

RG 1.183 Section 4.4 further requires that analyses identify and characterize all sources of radiation exposure (direct and airborne) to workers and the public, using NRC-accepted methodologies and considering plant-specific and accident-specific parameters. Dose criteria for design basis accidents are set at 25 rem TEDE at the exclusion area boundary and low population zone, and 5 rem TEDE for control room personnel, per 10 CFR 50.67 and GDC 19.

RG 1.143 (Sections 4 and 5) and RG 1.26 provide additional criteria for radioactive waste management systems, requiring that exposures be as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA) and that system design and classification reflect potential unmitigated exposures (e.g., 500 mrem/year at the unprotected area boundary and 5 rem/year to personnel within the protected area). RG 1.29 and RG 1.26 specify that systems containing radioactive material must be classified and designed based on potential offsite doses, with seismic and quality assurance requirements applied if postulated failures could result in doses exceeding 0.5 rem (RG 1.29) or 0.1 rem (RG 1.26).

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria require comprehensive identification, characterization, and documentation of all contained radiation sources, with detailed quantitative and locational information, adherence to dose limits for workers and the public, and system design and classification based on potential radiological consequences, as specified in DSRS 12.2, RG 1.183, RG 1.143, RG 1.26, and RG 1.29.

II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

Requirements

Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following NRC regulations:

1. 10 CFR 20.1101, “Radiation Protection Programs”; 10 CFR 20.1201, “Occupational Dose Limits for Adults”; 10 CFR 20.1202, “Compliance with Requirements for Summation of External and Internal Doses”; and 10 CFR 20.1206, “Planned Special Exposures”; as they relate to limiting occupational radiation doses.   

2. 10 CFR 20.1203, “Determination of External Dose from Airborne Radioactive Material,” and 10 CFR 20.1204, “Determination of Internal Exposure,” as they relate to limiting average concentrations of airborne radioactive materials to protect individuals and control the intake (inhalation or absorption) of such materials.   

3. 10 CFR 20.1207, “Occupational Dose Limits for Minors,” as it relates to limiting exposure to minors to one-tenth of limits for adults.   

4. 10 CFR 20.1301, “Radiation Dose Limits for Individual Members of the Public,” and 40 CFR Part 190, “Environmental Radiation Protection Standards for Nuclear Power Operations,” as they relate to the determination of radiation levels and radioactive materials concentrations within the components of the plant that could affect direct radiation exposure to members of the public.  

... [list continues] ...

Compliance with the following specific acceptance criteria is necessary to meet the relevant requirements of the regulations identified above.

Descriptions should be provided for all radiation sources that require (1) shielding (e.g., provided for ORE 20.1101(b), 20.1201, 20.1202, or public 20.1301(e) radiation exposure control), (2) special ventilation systems, (3) special storage locations and conditions, (4) traffic or access control, (5) special plans or procedures, or (6) monitoring equipment. The source descriptions should include all pertinent information required for (1) input to shielding codes used in the design process, (2) establishment of related facility design features, (3) development of plans and procedures, (4) assessment of radiation (public or occupational, as appropriate) exposure, and (5) determination of radiation dose to electrical equipment important to safety as described in 10 CFR 50.49. Unless described within other sections of the FSAR, source descriptions should include the methods, models, and assumptions used as the bases for all values provided in FSAR Section 12.2. A listing of isotope, quantity, form, and use of all required radiation sources containing byproduct, source, and special nuclear material exceeding 3.7x10^9 Bq (100 millicuries) that may warrant shielding design consideration should be provided.

For contained sources, the description should include plan scale drawings of each floor of the plant that show all sources identified so they easily can be related to tables containing the pertinent and necessary quantitative source parameters. Their position should be located accurately, indicating the approximate size and shape. The information about neutron and gamma source terms from the core, reactor pressure vessel, irradiated components inside the reactor vessel, irradiated components inside containment, irradiated portions of the containment vessel, irradiated components and materials present outside of the containment vessel, and adjacent operating reactors should be described in sufficient detail to allow determination of the radiation fields that could occur in areas that may require occupancy, may contain certain electrical equipment important to safety as described in 10 CFR 50.49, or could be a source of radioactive material available to systems outside of the containment vessel. Use to the extent practicable relevant experience from operating reactors. Airborne sources created by leakage, opening formerly closed containers, storage of leaking fuel elements, direct neutron activation of shielding materials and other plant materials, and other mechanisms should be identified by location and magnitude so that they can be used for designing appropriate ventilation systems and in specifying appropriate monitoring systems. Airborne radioactivity concentrations in frequently occupied areas should be a small fraction of the concentrations related to 10 CFR 20.1203, 10 CFR 20.1204, and Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 20. The assumptions made in arriving at quantitative values for these various sources should be specified, either in this section or by reference to FSAR Chapter 11, and other relevant interfacing sections of the FSAR.

evidence_chain.section: Section 4.4 Acceptance Criteria
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
4.4 Acceptance Criteria

The NRC staff finds the following dose criteria acceptable for evaluating the radiological consequences of design basis accidents using an AST:

• For offsite dose consequences, the total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) at the exclusion area boundary (EAB) and the low population zone (LPZ) outer boundary should not exceed the dose reference values specified in 10 CFR 50.67(a)(1)(i) and (ii), which are 25 rem (0.25 Sv) TEDE at the EAB and 25 rem (0.25 Sv) TEDE at the LPZ outer boundary, respectively, for the duration of the accident.

• For control room dose consequences, the TEDE to an individual occupying the control room should not exceed the dose reference value specified in GDC 19, which is 5 rem (0.05 Sv) TEDE for the duration of the accident.

The analyses should identify and characterize all sources of radiation exposure to workers and the public from contained sources, including direct radiation and airborne releases, and should use the assumptions and methodologies described in this guide and its appendices. The analyses should also consider the impacts of plant-specific features, site characteristics, and accident-specific parameters as described in Section 5 of this guide.

The design and construction of radioactive waste management and steam generator blowdown systems should provide assurance that radiation exposures to operating personnel and to the general public are as low as is reasonably achievable. One aspect of this consideration is ensuring that these systems are designed to quality standards that enhance system reliability, operability, and availability. ...

4.1 Radioactive waste management SSCs should be designed to control leakage and facilitate access, operation, inspection, testing, and maintenance in order to maintain radiation exposures to operating and maintenance personnel as low as is reasonably achievable. 5. CLASSIFICATION OF RADWASTE SYSTEMS FOR DESIGN PURPOSES
There are three safety classes, or classifications, for radwaste management facilities: RW-IIa (High Hazard), RW-IIb (Hazardous), and RW-IIc (Non-Safety). ... The radiological release criteria (500 millirem at the unprotected area boundary and 5 rem to facility personnel within the protected boundary) was selected to be consistent with the criteria of 10 CFR Part 20, 'Standards for Protection Against Radiation.' This safety classification is applied to SSCs as follows.
5.1 For a given structure housing radwaste processing systems or components, if the total design basis unmitigated radiological release (considering the maximum inventory) at the boundary of the unprotected area is greater than 500 millirem per year or the maximum unmitigated exposure to site personnel within the protected area is greater than 5 rem per year, the external structures are classified as RW-IIa.

data.query: How do NRC requirements for radiation source term characterization relate to the methods and assumptions that must be documented for radiation protection in nuclear facility design?
data.answer:
NRC requirements for radiation source term characterization are closely linked to the methods and assumptions that must be documented for radiation protection in nuclear facility design. According to DSRS 12.2, all radiation sources requiring shielding, special ventilation, storage, access control, procedures, or monitoring must be described in detail. These descriptions must include all pertinent information necessary for input to shielding codes, facility design features, development of plans and procedures, exposure assessments, and equipment qualification (DSRS 12.2, Section II). Importantly, the methods, models, and assumptions used to derive quantitative source term values must be explicitly specified, either within the section or by reference to other FSAR chapters, ensuring transparency and traceability in the design basis.

Regulatory Guide 1.183 further establishes acceptable methods for accident source term (AST) characterization, emphasizing that licensees must maintain clear, logical, and consistent design bases and demonstrate that safety margins are preserved, including margins for analysis uncertainties (RG 1.183, Section C.1.1.1). Any changes to source term assumptions or methodologies that could affect safety margins require NRC approval, and all such uses must be technically justified and documented.

SRP 15.0.3 reinforces that the NRC reviews both the accident source terms and the methods and assumptions used in radiological consequence analyses. The application must provide sufficient design information, including the methodologies and assumptions for source term characterization, to demonstrate compliance with regulatory dose acceptance criteria (SRP 15.0.3, Sections I, II, III). The staff relies on the regulatory positions in RG 1.183 for evaluating these methodologies and assumptions.

In summary, NRC requirements mandate that all methods and assumptions used in radiation source term characterization be thoroughly documented and justified in the facility’s licensing basis, as these form the foundation for radiation protection features in nuclear facility design.
