evidence_chain.section: C. STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE, 1. Implementation of Accident Source Term, 1.1 Generic Considerations, 1.1.1 Safety Margins
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
C. STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE

This section and the appendices to this RG contain regulatory positions that establish a method acceptable to the NRC staff for complying with regulations for DBA dose consequence analysis using an AST.
This RG applies to MHA LOCA models for applicants and licensees using zirconium-alloy cladded uranium dioxide (UO2) fuel rod designs with reactor core burnups up to a maximum rod-average of 68 gigawatt-days per metric ton uranium (GWd/MTU) (and fuel enrichments up to 8 weight-percent uranium-235), including chromium-coated cladding (thicknesses less than 50 microns (μm)) and chromia-doped (up to 0.16 weight-percent) fuel. It is not applicable for other fuel-clad combinations, including fuel with iron-chromium-aluminum (FeCrAl) alloy cladding.
This RG applies to non-LOCA models for applicants and licensees with reactor core burnups up to a maximum rod-average burnup of 68 GWd/MTU (and fuel enrichments up to 8 weight-percent uranium-235) for currently approved (as of the issuance of this RG) zirconium-alloy cladded UO2 fuel rod designs at power levels below the burnup-dependent power envelopes depicted in figure 1 of this guide.

1. Implementation of Accident Source Term

1.1 Generic Considerations

As used in this guide, the AST is an accident source term derived principally from SAND2011-0128; it differs from the TID-14844 and NUREG-1465 source terms used in the original and revised design and licensing of operating reactor facilities. ASTs may also be used by applicants for new LWRs, including advanced evolutionary and passive LWRs, under 10 CFR Part 50 and 10 CFR Part 52, and for existing operating reactor licensees under 10 CFR 50.34 and 10 CFR 50.67. This guide identifies an AST that is acceptable to the NRC staff and describes significant characteristics of other source terms that may be found acceptable. While the staff recognizes several potential uses of an AST, it is not possible to foresee all possible uses. Licensees may pursue technically justifiable uses of the ASTs in the most flexible manner in license amendments so long as these uses are compatible with maintaining a clear, logical, and consistent design basis and continue to comply with NRC regulations. These license amendment requests should demonstrate that the facility, as modified, will continue to provide sufficient safety margins, with adequate defense in depth to address unanticipated events and to compensate for uncertainties in accident progression and analysis assumptions and parameter inputs.

1.1.1 Safety Margins

Licensees should evaluate their proposed uses of this guide, and the associated proposed facility modifications and changes to procedures, to determine whether the proposed changes are consistent with the principle that sufficient safety margins are maintained, including a margin to account for analysis uncertainties. The safety margins are products of specific values and limits in the technical specifications (which cannot be changed without NRC approval) and other values, such as assumed accident or transient initial conditions or assumed safety system response times. For example, changes, or the net effect of multiple changes, that result in a reduction in safety margins may require prior NRC approval. If the initial AST implementation, consistent with the guidance in RG 1.183, Revision 1, is approved by the staff and becomes part of the facility design basis, licensees may use 10 CFR 50.59, “Changes, tests and experiments,” and its supporting guidance to assess facility modifications and changes to procedures that are described in the updated FSAR.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
The staff reviews the radiological consequences of potential design basis accidents (DBAs) in six parts: (1) review of selected bounding design basis accidents, (2) review of accident source terms, (3) review of the major structures, systems, and components of the facility that are intended to mitigate the radiological consequences of a DBA, (4) review of the characteristics of fission product releases from the proposed site (for CP, OL and COL reviews) or reference site (for the DC review) to the environment, (5) review of the meteorological characteristics of the proposed site for the CP, OL or COL review (reference site for DC review), and (6) review of the total calculated radiological consequence dose at the exclusion area boundary (EAB), low population zone (LPZ) and control room from the bounding DBAs. ... The application must contain sufficient nuclear plant design information for the staff to review in making a determination regarding the acceptability of the proposed site using the radiological consequence evaluation factors identified in 10 CFR 50.34(a)(1) and General Design Criterion (GDC) 19.

... The plant design features intended to mitigate the radiological consequences of accidents, site atmospheric dispersion characteristics and the distances to the exclusion area boundary (EAB) and to the low population zone (LPZ) outer boundary are acceptable if the total calculated radiological consequences for the postulated fission product release fall within the following exposure acceptance criteria specified in 10 CFR 50.34(a)(1)(ii)(D):
A. An individual located at any point on the boundary of the exclusion area for any 2-hour period following the onset of the postulated fission product release, would not receive a radiation dose in excess of 25 rem total effective dose equivalent (TEDE), and
B. An individual located at any point on the outer boundary of the LPZ, who is exposed to the radioactive cloud resulting from the postulated fission product release (during the entire period of its passage), would not receive a radiation dose in excess of 25 rem TEDE.

... For the methodology and assumptions for calculating the radiological consequences of postulated accidents, the staff will use, where applicable, the regulatory positions stated in Regulatory Guide 1.183, “Alternative Radiological Source Terms for Evaluating Design Basis Accidents at Nuclear Power Reactors”.

data.query: For a liquid radioactive waste system in a nuclear power plant, what combined regulatory provisions require that all radiation sources, including those from waste processing components such as granular activated carbon vessels, are identified, characterized, and their source term assumptions justified using accepted models and methodologies?
data.answer:
The combined regulatory provisions requiring identification, characterization, and justification of all radiation sources—including those from waste processing components such as granular activated carbon vessels—in a liquid radioactive waste system are established through several NRC documents and regulations. 

First, DSRS 12.2 (Sections I and II) mandates that the applicant’s FSAR must describe all radiation sources in the plant, including those in radioactive waste management systems. This includes specifying isotopic composition, location, source strength, geometry, and the basis for these values. The FSAR must also detail the methods, models, and assumptions used for source term values, referencing FSAR Chapter 11 and other relevant sections as needed. All sources requiring shielding, special ventilation, storage, access control, or monitoring must be described, and the information must be sufficient for shielding design, exposure assessment, and safety evaluations (DSRS 12.2, I. AREAS OF REVIEW and II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA).

Second, 10 CFR Part 50 (§ 50.34, § 50.36a, and Appendix I) requires that applications include a description and analysis of facility systems, including those for controlling and limiting radioactive effluents and exposures. Technical specifications must ensure effluent releases are as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA) and within regulatory dose objectives (10 CFR 50.34, 50.36a, Appendix I).

Third, Regulatory Guide 1.183 (Sections 1.3 and 1.5) provides accepted methodologies, requiring comprehensive identification and characterization of all radioactivity sources that could contribute to radiological consequences, including waste processing components like activated carbon beds. The source term assumptions must be justified using NRC-accepted models and methodologies, and applicants must provide detailed descriptions and justifications for all source terms and their transport.

In summary, DSRS 12.2, 10 CFR Part 50, and RG 1.183 collectively require that all radiation sources—including those from liquid waste processing components—are identified, characterized, and justified using accepted models and methodologies, with supporting information provided in the FSAR and technical submittals.

evidence_chain.section: C. STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE, 1.3 Scope of Required Analyses and 1.5 Submittal Requirements and Information
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
1.3 Scope of Required Analyses

The implementation of an AST must include a comprehensive review of all affected design basis accident analyses. The scope of the required analyses includes, but is not limited to, the following:

• All radiological consequence analyses that use a source term, including those for the control room, exclusion area boundary, and low population zone, must be updated to reflect the AST and associated assumptions.
• The analyses must identify and characterize all sources of radioactivity that could contribute to the radiological consequences of the analyzed accidents. This includes sources from the reactor core, spent fuel, and other plant systems and components that may contain or process radioactive material, such as waste processing systems (e.g., liquid and gaseous waste management systems, including components such as filters, ion exchangers, and activated carbon beds).
• The source term assumptions must be justified using models and methodologies that are generally accepted by the NRC staff. The applicant or licensee should provide sufficient information to demonstrate that the models and methodologies used are appropriate for the specific application and are consistent with the current state of knowledge regarding fission product behavior and transport.
• The analyses should consider the potential for holdup, retention, and decontamination of radioactive material within plant systems and components, and the assumptions regarding these processes should be clearly identified and justified.

1.5 Submittal Requirements and Information

Applicants and licensees should provide the following information in their submittals:
• A description of the source term(s) used in the analyses, including the basis for the selection of the source term and any plant- or fuel-specific modifications.
• Identification and characterization of all sources of radioactivity considered in the analyses, including those from waste processing components such as granular activated carbon vessels.
• Justification for the models and methodologies used to estimate the source terms and their transport, including references to NRC-accepted guidance or technical literature.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for identifying and accounting for post-accident radiation sources in nuclear power plant containment?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for identifying and accounting for post-accident radiation sources in nuclear power plant containment are established through a combination of regulations, guidance documents, and review standards. According to DSRS 12.2, applicants must provide a detailed description of radiation sources during accident conditions in the Final Safety Analysis Report (FSAR). This includes specifying the isotopic composition, location, source strength, geometry, and the basis for these values. The description must cover all sources requiring shielding, special ventilation, storage, access control, special procedures, or monitoring equipment, and must include information necessary for shielding design, facility features, procedure development, exposure assessment, and equipment qualification (DSRS 12.2, Sections I and II).

Regulatory Guide 1.183 further specifies that the accident source term (AST) must be characterized by the magnitude, composition, physical and chemical form, and timing of radioactive material released from the fuel to containment. The AST should include all significant dose contributors, release fractions for each radionuclide group, timing of release phases, radionuclide composition, and chemical forms, with supporting models and assumptions. Analyses must account for transport, retention, and removal of radionuclides within containment and plant systems, as well as the impact of engineered safety features (RG 1.183, Section C.3).

SRP 15.0.3 and 10 CFR 50.34(a)(1) require that the identification and accounting of post-accident sources support the evaluation of offsite and control room radiological consequences, ensuring calculated doses do not exceed regulatory limits (25 rem TEDE at the exclusion area boundary and low population zone, and 5 rem TEDE for control room personnel). These requirements ensure that the design and operational features of the plant adequately mitigate the radiological consequences of postulated accidents (SRP 15.0.3, II. Acceptance Criteria).

In summary, NRC regulations require comprehensive identification, quantification, and documentation of post-accident radiation sources in containment, with detailed supporting analyses to demonstrate compliance with dose limits and to inform the design of radiation protection features.

Appendix I to Part 50—Numerical Guides for Design Objectives and Limiting Conditions for Operation To Meet the Criterion “As Low as is Reasonably Achievable” for Radioactive Material in Light-Water-Cooled Nuclear Power Reactor Effluents

I. Introduction
Section 50.34a provides that each applicant for a license to operate a light-water-cooled nuclear power reactor will include in its application a description of the design features of the facility and the operating procedures developed to keep releases of radioactive material to unrestricted areas during normal operation, including anticipated operational occurrences, as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA). The guides set forth in this appendix are intended to provide numerical values for use in the design objectives and limiting conditions for operation for radioactive material in effluents from light-water-cooled nuclear power reactors to meet the ALARA criterion. These guides are not intended to be used as limits for accidental releases or as a basis for design objectives for containment or other engineered safety features for postulated accidents. The guides are intended to be used in conjunction with the requirements of § 50.34a and the technical specifications required by § 50.36a.

evidence_chain.section: Section C.3 (Accident Source Term)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
3. Accident Source Term

The accident source term is defined by the magnitude, composition, physical and chemical form, and timing of the radioactive material released from the fuel and transported to the containment. The AST described in this guide is based on SAND2011-0128 and is characterized by the following attributes:

• Fission product inventory: The inventory of radionuclides available for release is based on the core inventory at the time of the accident, calculated using reactor operating history, fuel burnup, and decay time assumptions. The inventory should include all significant contributors to dose, including noble gases, iodine, cesium, tellurium, and other relevant radionuclides.

• Release fractions: The fractions of the core inventory released to the containment are specified for each radionuclide group and are based on empirical data and mechanistic models. These fractions account for the physical and chemical behavior of fission products during the accident progression.

• Timing of release phases: The release of radionuclides is divided into distinct phases (e.g., gap release, early in-vessel release, late in-vessel release, ex-vessel release), each with specified timing and magnitude. The timing assumptions are based on mechanistic understanding of accident progression and are intended to bound the range of credible accident scenarios.

• Radionuclide composition: The composition of the released material is specified for each release phase, including the relative abundances of different radionuclides and their chemical forms (e.g., elemental iodine, cesium iodide).

• Chemical form: The chemical forms of released radionuclides are specified based on experimental data and mechanistic models. For example, iodine may be released as a mixture of elemental iodine, iodide, and organic iodides, with specified fractions for each form.

Applicants and licensees should use the source term attributes specified in this guide, or justify alternative assumptions, in their analyses of post-accident radionuclide concentrations in containment and plant systems. The analyses should account for the transport, retention, and removal of radionuclides within the containment and other plant systems, as well as any engineered safety features that may affect the source term or its consequences.

data.query: How do NRC regulations require the use of isotopic inventories and release fractions to estimate post-accident radiation levels within containment areas?
data.answer: NRC regulations require the use of isotopic inventories and release fractions as fundamental components in estimating post-accident radiation levels within containment areas. According to 10 CFR 50.34(a)(3), applications must describe the means for controlling and limiting the release of radioactive effluents, specifically including the use of source terms—such as isotopic inventories and release fractions—to estimate post-accident radiation levels within containment. The technical basis for these estimates is further detailed in Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.183, Section 3, which defines the accident source term as the product of the fission product inventory in the core and the fraction of that inventory released to the containment during an accident. The fission product inventory should be calculated using NRC-approved methods (e.g., ORIGEN code), accounting for the operating history and burnup to determine the maximum core inventory of each radionuclide. Release fractions, which represent the portion of the inventory released under specific accident scenarios, are applied to the calculated inventory to determine the source term for dose consequence analyses. RG 1.183 provides default release fractions for various accident types, with plant-specific justification required for deviations. The Design-Specific Review Standard (DSRS) 12.2 further requires applicants to provide detailed tabulations of calculated concentrations of radioactive material by nuclide for accident conditions, including the models and parameters used. These values are used in shield design calculations, equipment qualification, and ventilation system design to ensure compliance with radiation protection requirements. Thus, NRC regulations mandate a systematic approach: calculate the isotopic inventory, apply scenario-specific release fractions, and use the resulting source term to estimate post-accident radiation levels for safety analysis and facility design (10 CFR 50.34; RG 1.183 Section 3; DSRS 12.2).

§ 50.34 Contents of applications; technical information.
(a) Preliminary safety analysis report. Each application for a construction permit shall include a preliminary safety analysis report. The preliminary safety analysis report shall describe the facility, present the design bases and the limits on its operation, and present a safety analysis of the structures, systems, and components of the facility as a whole. (4) An analysis and evaluation of the design and performance of structures, systems, and components with respect to the prevention of accidents and the mitigation of the consequences of accidents, including the identification of postulated accidents and the use of source terms to estimate the radiological consequences of such accidents.

evidence_chain.section: Section 3, Accident Source Term (pp. 18-19)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
3. Accident Source Term

The accident source term is defined by the composition, magnitude, chemical and physical form, and timing of the release of radioactive material from the fuel to the containment. The source term is determined by the fission product inventory in the core and the fraction of that inventory released to the containment during the accident. The following sections describe the methodology for determining the fission product inventory and release fractions for use in accident analyses.

3.1 Fission Product Inventory

The fission product inventory should be calculated for the core at the time of the accident using a method that accounts for the operating history, including power level and burnup. The inventory should be based on the maximum core inventory of each radionuclide of interest, considering the most limiting combination of power history and decay time. Acceptable methods for calculating the fission product inventory include the use of computer codes such as ORIGEN or other NRC-approved methods.

3.2 Release Fractions

The fraction of the fission product inventory released from the fuel to the containment (release fraction) should be based on the accident scenario being analyzed. For the maximum hypothetical accident (MHA) LOCA, the release fractions provided in Table 3 of this guide, which are derived from SAND2011-0128, should be used unless a plant-specific or fuel-specific justification is provided for alternative values. For other accident scenarios, such as fuel handling accidents or non-LOCA events, the release fractions should be determined using the guidance in Appendices B through I of this guide, as applicable. The release fractions should be applied to the calculated fission product inventory to determine the source term for dose consequence analyses.

5. CLASSIFICATION OF RADWASTE SYSTEMS FOR DESIGN PURPOSES
There are three safety classes, or classifications, for radwaste management facilities:  RW-IIa (High Hazard), RW-IIb (Hazardous), and RW-IIc (Non-Safety).
... The radiological release criteria (500 millirem at the unprotected area boundary and 5 rem to facility personnel within the protected boundary) was selected to be consistent with the criteria of 10 CFR Part 20, "Standards for Protection Against Radiation." This safety classification is applied to SSCs as follows.
5.1 For a given structure housing radwaste processing systems or components, if the total design basis unmitigated radiological release (considering the maximum inventory) at the boundary of the unprotected area is greater than 500 millirem per year or the maximum unmitigated exposure to site personnel within the protected area is greater than 5 rem per year, the external structures are classified as RW-IIa.
5.2 For a given structure housing radwaste processing systems or components, if the total design basis unmitigated radiological release (considering the maximum inventory) at the boundary of the unprotected area is less than 500 millirem per year and the maximum unmitigated exposure to site personnel within the protected area is less than 5 rem per year, the external structure is classified as RW-IIb.
5.3 Any systems or components in a RW-IIa facility (see Regulatory Position 5.1) that store, process, or handle radioactive waste in excess of the A1 quantities given in Appendix A, "Determination of A1 and A2," to 10 CFR Part 71, "Packaging and Transportation of Radioactive Material," are classified as RW-IIa. These systems or components that process radioactive waste in excess of the A2 quantities but less than the A1 quantities given in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 71 are classified as RW-IIb. All other components are classified as RW-IIc. This classification may be modified for specific radwaste components.
5.4 Any systems or components in a RW-IIb structure (see Regulatory Position 5.2) that are used to store or process specified radioactive waste in excess of the A1 quantities given in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 71 are classified as RW-IIb. All other systems or components are classified as RW-IIc.
The unprotected area boundary mentioned in Regulatory Position 5.1 is shown in Figure 1. A flowchart of the Safety Classification Process is shown in Figure 2. The classifications discussed in Regulatory Positions 5.1 through 5.4 are not intended to apply to radwaste storage facilities if they do not contain any systems or components that exceed the quantities specified in Regulatory Positions 5.1 through 5.4.

data.query: When determining post-accident radiation levels in various plant areas, what combined NRC regulatory provisions and review standards govern the identification of isotopic inventories, application of release fractions, and consideration of containment aerosol removal mechanisms?
data.answer:
The determination of post-accident radiation levels in various plant areas is governed by a combination of NRC regulations, regulatory guides, and review standards that address the identification of isotopic inventories, application of release fractions, and consideration of containment aerosol removal mechanisms.

According to 10 CFR 50.34(a)(3) and (a)(6), applications must identify the kinds and quantities of radioactive materials expected to be produced, handled, or released, and must justify the assumptions, models, and methods used in the safety analysis, including those for source term, release fractions, and removal mechanisms such as containment aerosol removal (10 CFR Part 50 § 50.34).

DSRS 12.2 further specifies that the NRC reviews the applicant’s FSAR for detailed descriptions of isotopic composition, source strength, and the basis for these values, as well as the models and parameters used in calculations. The DSRS references RG 1.183 for accident source term assumptions, RG 1.7 for radionuclide concentrations, RG 1.112 for source term calculations, and ANSI/ANS 18.1 for estimation methods (DSRS 12.2, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA).

RG 1.183 (Sections 3.1–3.3, 4) provides the accepted methodology for calculating the fission product inventory (using NRC-approved codes like ORIGEN), applying release fractions (from sources such as SAND2011-0128), and considering the timing of release phases. It also requires that dose calculations account for removal mechanisms (e.g., sprays, deposition, filtration) consistent with guidance in NUREG-1465 and SAND2011-0128, and that credit for such mechanisms is only given if their performance can be reasonably assured.

Additionally, RG 1.143 and RG 1.26 provide guidance on quality assurance and classification of systems important to safety, referencing the requirements of 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A (notably GDC 1 and GDC 60) for the control and quality of radioactive material handling and release systems.

In summary, the combined regulatory framework requires applicants to use NRC-accepted methods for identifying isotopic inventories, applying release fractions, and crediting containment aerosol removal mechanisms, as detailed in 10 CFR 50.34, DSRS 12.2, RG 1.183, and supporting regulatory guides.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
3. Accident Source Term

The accident source term is defined by the quantity, timing, chemical and physical form, and location of the radioactive material released from the fuel and transported to the containment. The source term is determined by the following attributes:

3.1 Fission Product Inventory
The fission product inventory is the quantity of radioactive material available for release from the fuel. The inventory should be calculated using a method acceptable to the NRC staff, such as the ORIGEN code or other NRC-approved methods, based on the maximum fuel burnup and enrichment for the core. The inventory should be determined for the core at the end of the fuel cycle, assuming equilibrium core conditions, unless a different approach is justified.

3.2 Release Fractions
The release fractions are the fractions of the fission product inventory released from the fuel to the containment atmosphere during the accident. The release fractions for the various chemical groups (noble gases, halogens, alkali metals, tellurium, lanthanides, and actinides) should be based on the values provided in SAND2011-0128 or other NRC-approved sources. The release fractions should be applied to the calculated fission product inventory to determine the quantity of each radionuclide group released to the containment.

3.3 Timing of Release Phases
The timing of the release phases should be consistent with the accident progression and the physical phenomena governing the release and transport of fission products. The timing should be based on the values provided in SAND2011-0128 or other NRC-approved sources. The timing of the release phases affects the calculation of doses to plant personnel and the public.

4. Dose Calculation Methodology

The dose calculation methodology should account for the removal of radioactive material from the containment atmosphere by natural and engineered processes, such as containment sprays, natural deposition, and filtration. The methodology should be consistent with the guidance provided in NUREG-1465, SAND2011-0128, and other NRC-approved sources. The removal mechanisms should be credited only if their performance can be demonstrated with reasonable assurance.

This regulatory guide has been revised to provide guidance to licensees and applicants on methods acceptable to the staff for complying with the NRC's regulations in the design, construction, installation, and testing the structures, systems, and components of radioactive waste management facilities in light-water-reactor nuclear power plants. 

In 10 CFR Part 50, "Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities," § 50.34, "Contents of Applications; Technical Information," requires that each application for a construction permit include a preliminary safety analysis report.  Part of the information required is related to quality assurance and the preliminary design of the facility, including, among other things, the principal design criteria for the facility.  Appendix B, "Quality Assurance Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants and Fuel Reprocessing Plants," to 10 CFR Part 50 establishes overall quality assurance requirements for structures, systems, and components important to safety.  Appendix A, ''General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants," to 10 CFR Part 50 establishes minimum requirements for the principal design criteria for light-water-cooled nuclear power plants.

Criterion 60, "Control of Releases of Radioactive Materials to the Environment,'' of Appendix A requires that the nuclear power unit design include means to suitably control the release of radioactive materials in gaseous and liquid effluents and to handle radioactive solid waste produced during normal reactor operation, including anticipated operational occurrences.  The release of radioactive materials from external man-induced events and design basis accidents must also be controlled.

ANSI/ANS Standards 55.1-1992, "Solid Radioactive Waste Processing System for Light Water Cooled Reactor Plants," 55.4-1993, "Gaseous Radioactive Waste Processing Systems for Light Water Plants," and 55.6-1993, "Liquid Radioactive Waste Processing Systems for Light Water Reactor Plants," have been reviewed for applicability to this guide.  These ANSI/ANS Standards provide a wider range of guidance than that provided in Sections 11.2, "Liquid Waste Management System"; 11.3, "Gaseous Waste Management System"; and 11.4, "Solid Waste Management System," of Chapter 11, "Radioactive Waste Management," of NUREG-0800, "Standard Review Plan for the Review of Safety Analysis Reports for Nuclear Power Plants."  As appropriate, guidance from the ANSI/ANS standards has been incorporated by reference.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for identifying and evaluating post-accident radiation sources in nuclear power plant containment areas?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for identifying and evaluating post-accident radiation sources in nuclear power plant containment areas are established through a combination of regulations, guidance documents, and review standards. According to 10 CFR 50.34(a), applicants must provide a safety analysis that identifies and evaluates sources of radiation under accident conditions, including post-accident scenarios, and describe the means for controlling and monitoring these sources to ensure occupational and public exposures are ALARA (10CFR [2]).

DSRS 12.2 specifies that the FSAR must include detailed descriptions of all radiation sources during accident conditions, including isotopic composition, location, source strength, geometry, and the basis for these values. The descriptions must support shielding design, ventilation, storage, access control, monitoring, and exposure assessment, and must include plan drawings showing source locations and quantitative parameters (DSRS [1], Section I and II). The methods, models, and assumptions used to derive these values must be documented.

Regulatory Guide 1.183 provides an accepted methodology for accident source term evaluation. It requires calculation of the fission product inventory at the time of the postulated accident, using maximum core inventory parameters. Release fractions for each radionuclide, based on empirical data and accident progression analyses, must be applied to determine the quantity released into containment. The timing and phases of release (e.g., gap, early in-vessel, late in-vessel) must be documented and justified (RG 1.183 [3], Sections 3.1–3.3).

In summary, NRC requirements mandate a comprehensive identification and evaluation of post-accident radiation sources in containment, including detailed source characterization, location mapping, release quantification, and timing analysis, all documented in the FSAR using NRC-accepted methods and consistent with regulatory criteria for radiation protection and facility design.

evidence_chain.section: Section C.3 (Accident Source Term), including 3.1, 3.2, 3.3
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
3. Accident Source Term

The accident source term is defined as the magnitude and characteristics of the radioactive material released from the fuel, transported through the reactor coolant system, and released into the containment as a result of a postulated accident. The source term includes the quantity, chemical and physical form, and timing of the release of radioactive material. The NRC staff finds the following approach acceptable for identifying and evaluating post-accident radiation sources in containment areas:

3.1 Fission Product Inventory
The fission product inventory should be calculated for the core at the time of the postulated accident, using the maximum core inventory for the fuel type, enrichment, and burnup. The inventory should be based on the maximum steady-state power level and the maximum fuel burnup, consistent with the facility’s technical specifications and operating history. The inventory should include all significant radionuclides that contribute to the dose consequences of the accident.

3.2 Release Fractions
The fraction of the fission product inventory released from the fuel, transported through the reactor coolant system, and released into the containment should be based on the release fractions specified in this guide (see Table 3 and Appendices). These fractions are based on empirical data and analyses of severe accident progression and fission product behavior. The release fractions should be applied to the calculated fission product inventory to determine the quantity of each radionuclide released into the containment.

3.3 Timing of Release Phases
The timing of the release of radioactive material into the containment should be based on the phases of the accident progression (e.g., gap release, early in-vessel release, late in-vessel release, ex-vessel release). The timing and duration of each phase should be consistent with the accident scenario and the characteristics of the reactor design. The timing assumptions should be documented and justified in the analysis.

evidence_chain.section: Regulatory Position 5. CLASSIFICATION OF RADWASTE SYSTEMS FOR DESIGN PURPOSES
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
5. CLASSIFICATION OF RADWASTE SYSTEMS FOR DESIGN PURPOSES
There are three safety classes, or classifications, for radwaste management facilities:  RW-IIa (High Hazard), RW-IIb (Hazardous), and RW-IIc (Non-Safety).  These classifications were developed primarily for natural phenomena and man-induced hazard design.  The radiological release criteria (500 millirem at the unprotected area boundary and 5 rem to facility personnel within the protected boundary) was selected to be consistent with the criteria of 10 CFR Part 20, “Standards for Protection Against Radiation.” This safety classification is applied to SSCs as follows.
5.1 For a given structure housing radwaste processing systems or components, if the total design basis unmitigated radiological release (considering the maximum inventory) at the boundary of the unprotected area is greater than 500 millirem per year or the maximum unmitigated exposure to site personnel within the protected area is greater than 5 rem per year, the external structures are classified as RW-IIa.
5.2 For a given structure housing radwaste processing systems or components, if the total design basis unmitigated radiological release (considering the maximum inventory) at the boundary of the unprotected area is less than 500 millirem per year and the maximum unmitigated exposure to site personnel within the protected area is less than 5 rem per year, the external structure is classified as RW-IIb.
5.3 Any systems or components in a RW-IIa facility (see Regulatory Position 5.1) that store, process, or handle radioactive waste in excess of the A1 quantities given in Appendix A, “Determination of A1 and A2,” to 10 CFR Part 71, “Packaging and Transportation of Radioactive Material,” are classified as RW-IIa.  These systems or components that process radioactive waste in excess of the A2 quantities but less than the A1 quantities given in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 71 are classified as RW-IIb.  All other components are classified as RW-IIc.  This classification may be modified for specific radwaste components.
5.4 Any systems or components in a RW-IIb structure (see Regulatory Position 5.2) that are used to store or process specified radioactive waste in excess of the A1 quantities given in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 71 are classified as RW-IIb.  All other systems or components are classified as RW-IIc.
The unprotected area boundary mentioned in Regulatory Position 5.1 is shown in Figure 1.  A flowchart of the Safety Classification Process is shown in Figure 2.  The classifications discussed in Regulatory Positions 5.1 through 5.4 are not intended to apply to radwaste storage facilities if they do not contain any systems or components that exceed the quantities specified in Regulatory Positions 5.1 through 5.4.

data.query: How do NRC regulations ensure that post-accident isotopic inventories are used to assess radiation levels in various areas of a nuclear facility, and how do these requirements relate to the control of occupational radiation exposure?
data.answer:
NRC regulations ensure that post-accident isotopic inventories are used to assess radiation levels in various areas of a nuclear facility through a combination of regulatory requirements and guidance on safety analysis and facility design. According to 10 CFR 50.34(a) and (b), applicants for construction permits and operating licenses must include in their safety analysis reports an identification of the isotopic inventory of radioactive materials expected to be present following postulated accidents. This inventory must be used to assess radiation levels in various facility areas, specifically for the purpose of controlling occupational radiation exposure and demonstrating compliance with Part 20 requirements, including keeping exposures as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA).

The Design-Specific Review Standard (DSRS) 12.2 further details that the NRC reviews the applicant’s safety analysis for radiation sources during normal, anticipated, and accident conditions. The analysis must include tabulated concentrations of radioactive materials by nuclide for areas occupied by personnel, and describe the models and parameters used for these calculations. This information is essential for input to shielding design, facility features, development of procedures, and assessment of occupational and public radiation exposure, as well as for determining doses to safety-related equipment (DSRS 12.2, Sections I and II).

Regulatory Guide 1.183 (Sections 3.3, 3.4, and 4.3) provides an accepted method for determining the timing and composition of post-accident releases, specifying that the isotopic inventory should reflect the core at the time of the accident and include all significant contributors to dose. The guide instructs applicants to use these inventories and associated assumptions to evaluate radiological consequences for facility areas beyond the control room, including those requiring access for accident mitigation and recovery. The results of these analyses are used to ensure occupational exposures remain within regulatory limits and are ALARA.

In summary, NRC regulations require detailed post-accident isotopic inventories to be used in radiation assessments for all relevant facility areas, directly supporting the control of occupational radiation exposure through design, procedural, and operational measures (10 CFR 50.34; DSRS 12.2; RG 1.183).

evidence_chain.section: Sections 3.3, 3.4, and 4.3
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
3.3 Timing of Release Phases

The timing of the release phases for the AST is based on the physical phenomena associated with the progression of a severe core damage accident. The release phases are as follows:

• Gap release: The gap release phase is assumed to occur instantaneously at the onset of the accident. The gap release consists of the fission products that are present in the fuel-cladding gap and are released promptly upon cladding failure.

• Early in-vessel release: The early in-vessel release phase is assumed to begin immediately after the gap release and to continue for 30 minutes. This phase is characterized by the release of fission products from the fuel as the core is heated and fuel damage progresses.

• Late in-vessel release: The late in-vessel release phase is assumed to begin at the end of the early in-vessel release phase and to continue for 1 hour. This phase is characterized by the release of fission products as the core continues to degrade and melt.

• Ex-vessel release: The ex-vessel release phase is assumed to begin at the end of the late in-vessel release phase and to continue for 1 hour. This phase is characterized by the release of fission products as molten core material interacts with structures outside the reactor vessel.

3.4 Radionuclide Composition

The radionuclide composition of the AST is based on the isotopic inventory of the core at the time of the accident. The isotopic inventory should be determined using a core burnup representative of the end of the fuel cycle, unless a different burnup is justified. The inventory should include all significant fission products and activation products that contribute to the dose consequences of the accident.

4.3 Other Dose Consequences

Applicants and licensees should evaluate the radiological consequences of DBAs for areas of the facility other than the control room and offsite locations, as appropriate. These evaluations should consider the potential for occupational radiation exposure during and following an accident, including access to vital areas required for accident mitigation and recovery. The analyses should use the AST and associated assumptions described in this guide to determine the post-accident radiation levels in these areas. The results should be used to ensure that occupational radiation exposures are maintained within regulatory limits and are as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA).

data.query: When evaluating post-accident radiation levels in different plant areas, what combined regulatory requirements and review standards must be applied to the assumptions and calculations for isotopic concentrations, release fractions, and aerosol removal rates in containment, and how do these ensure adequate protection for workers and the public?
data.answer:
When evaluating post-accident radiation levels in different plant areas, the combined regulatory requirements and review standards mandate a comprehensive and conservative approach to the assumptions and calculations for isotopic concentrations, release fractions, and aerosol removal rates in containment. According to DSRS 12.2 (Section II), the analysis must meet the requirements of 10 CFR Part 20 (including §§ 20.1101, 20.1201, 20.1203, and 20.1301), 10 CFR 50.34(f)(2)(vii), GDC 19, and GDC 61, which collectively limit occupational and public radiation doses and require the identification and control of radioactive materials and their concentrations. 

10 CFR 50.34(a) further requires that the safety analysis report include detailed descriptions of the methods and assumptions used to determine potential releases, isotopic concentrations, release fractions, and removal mechanisms (such as aerosol removal rates) in containment, as well as the resulting radiation doses to workers and the public. 

Regulatory Guide 1.183 (Sections 2, 5, and Appendix A) provides an NRC-accepted method for these analyses, specifying that the isotopic composition should be based on representative fission product inventories, release fractions should reflect mechanistic understanding, and removal mechanisms (e.g., aerosol deposition, plateout, containment sprays) must be considered. The analysis must use conservative, accident-specific assumptions, be well-documented, and justify the data and methods used. 

These combined requirements and standards ensure that the evaluation is grounded in current scientific understanding and is sufficiently conservative to provide reasonable assurance of adequate protection for workers and the public by limiting exposures and controlling radioactive material concentrations under post-accident conditions.

evidence_chain.section: II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following NRC regulations: 

1. 10 CFR 20.1101, “Radiation Protection Programs”; 10 CFR 20.1201, “Occupational Dose Limits for Adults”; 10 CFR 20.1202, “Compliance with Requirements for Summation of External and Internal Doses”; and 10 CFR 20.1206, “Planned Special Exposures”; as they relate to limiting occupational radiation doses.   

2. 10 CFR 20.1203, “Determination of External Dose from Airborne Radioactive Material,” and 10 CFR 20.1204, “Determination of Internal Exposure,” as they relate to limiting average concentrations of airborne radioactive materials to protect individuals and control the intake (inhalation or absorption) of such materials.   

4. 10 CFR 20.1301, “Radiation Dose Limits for Individual Members of the Public,” and 40 CFR Part 190, “Environmental Radiation Protection Standards for Nuclear Power Operations,” as they relate to the determination of radiation levels and radioactive materials concentrations within the components of the plant that could affect direct radiation exposure to members of the public.  

6. General Design Criterion (GDC) 61, “Fuel storage and Handling and Radioactivity Control,” found in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, as it relates to systems that may contain radioactive materials.   

7. 10 CFR 50.34(f)(2)(vii) and GDC 19, “Control Room,” as they relate to the acceptable radiation conditions in the plant under accident conditions, and the source term release assumptions used to calculate those conditions.

The following regulatory guides (RGs), standards, and NRC technical report designations (NUREGs) provide information, recommendations, and guidance and, in general, describe a basis acceptable to the NRC staff for implementing the requirements... 

1. RG 1.183, as it relates to the assumptions used in evaluating the concentrations of radionuclides in containment and plant systems following a loss-of-coolant accident.   

2. RG 1.7, as it relates to radionuclides in systems used for determining gaseous concentrations in containment following an accident. 

3. RG 1.112, as it relates to complying with NRC regulations under 10 CFR 20.1301, concerning the calculation of realistic radiation levels and radioactive materials source terms for the evaluation of waste treatment systems.   

5. American National Standards Institute/American Nuclear Society (ANSI/ANS) Standard 18.1, as it relates to methods and data used to estimate typical long-term concentrations of principal radionuclides in fluid streams of light-water-cooled nuclear power plants. These methods and data must be modified by the applicant to reflect NuScale-specific design attributes, which were developed using relevant industry operating experience.  

Shielding and ventilation design fission product source terms will be acceptable if developed using these bases: 

1. 0.25-percent fuel cladding defects for pressurized-water reactors (PWRs) or the reactor coolant system isotopic concentrations, including fission products and significant corrosion and activation products, equivalent to operation for a full fuel cycle at the technical specification limits for halogens (I-131 dose equivalent) and noble gases (Xe-133 dose equivalent).  

2. Post-accident shielding (for vital area access, including work in the area) source terms from RG 1.183, modified for NuScale-specific design attributes, which were developed using relevant industry operating experience.   

Base coolant and corrosion activation products source terms on applicable reactor operating experience.  Address the buildup of activated corrosion products in various components and systems. Explain any allowances made in design source terms for the buildup of activated corrosion products. Base neutron and prompt gamma source terms on reactor core physics calculations and applicable reactor operating experience.

evidence_chain.section: C. STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE (Sections 2, 3, 5; Appendix A)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
C. STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE

This section and the appendices to this RG contain regulatory positions that establish a method acceptable to the NRC staff for complying with regulations for DBA dose consequence analysis using an AST.
...
2. Attributes of an Acceptable Accident Source Term

An acceptable accident source term for use in design basis radiological consequence analyses should include the following attributes:
• The isotopic composition of the source term should be based on a representative fission product inventory for the fuel type, enrichment, and burnup, as described in section 3.1 of this guide.
• The release fractions for each radionuclide group should be based on the mechanistic understanding of fission product release and transport, as described in section 3.2 of this guide.
• The timing of the release phases should be consistent with the accident progression and containment response, as described in section 3.3 of this guide.
• The chemical form of the released radionuclides should be considered, as described in section 3.5 of this guide.
• The removal of radionuclides from the containment atmosphere by natural processes (e.g., aerosol deposition, plateout, and containment sprays) should be considered, as described in section 5.2 and Appendix A of this guide.

5. Analysis Assumptions and Methodology

5.1 General Considerations

The analysis should use conservative assumptions regarding the initial conditions, system performance, and accident progression. The methodology should be consistent with the guidance provided in this RG and should be documented in sufficient detail to allow for independent NRC staff review. The analysis should address the following:
• The isotopic inventory used in the source term calculation.
• The release fractions and timing for each radionuclide group.
• The chemical and physical form of the released radionuclides.
• The removal mechanisms for radionuclides within containment and other plant systems.
• The transport of radionuclides to various plant areas and to the environment.
• The calculation of doses to workers and the public, including the use of appropriate dose conversion factors and occupancy factors.

5.2 Accident-Specific Assumptions

The analysis should use accident-specific assumptions for the evaluation of radionuclide concentrations, release fractions, and removal rates, as provided in the appendices to this guide (e.g., Appendix A for LOCA). These assumptions should be based on the best available data and should be justified in the analysis documentation.

These combined requirements and review standards ensure that the assumptions and calculations for isotopic concentrations, release fractions, and aerosol removal rates are based on current scientific understanding and are sufficiently conservative to provide reasonable assurance of adequate protection for workers and the public.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for identifying and quantifying post-accident radiation sources in nuclear power plant containment?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for identifying and quantifying post-accident radiation sources in nuclear power plant containment are detailed in several key documents. According to DSRS 12.2, applicants must provide a comprehensive description of radiation sources during accident conditions in the Final Safety Analysis Report (FSAR). This includes the isotopic composition, location, source strength, geometry, and the basis for these values. The description must cover all radiation sources relevant for shielding, dose assessment, and radiation protection design, and must include methods, models, and assumptions used for quantification (DSRS 12.2, II. Acceptance Criteria).

10 CFR 50.34(a)(1) requires that the safety analysis report identify and quantify the sources of radiation that may be released following postulated accidents, including the pathways by which these sources might reach the environment and result in exposures to individuals and population groups (10 CFR 50.34(a)(1)).

Regulatory Guide 1.183 provides the accepted methodology for defining the accident source term (AST). The AST must specify the magnitude, composition, physical and chemical form, and timing of radioactive material released from the core into containment. This includes calculating the fission product inventory based on core power, burnup, and irradiation history, specifying release fractions for each radionuclide group, and detailing the timing and phases of release. The chemical and physical forms, especially of iodine, must be specified to support dose consequence analyses (RG 1.183, Section 3).

SRP 15.0.3 further clarifies that the application must provide isotopic quantities and rates of fission product release as a function of time, as well as the chemical forms of released radionuclides, to support the evaluation of radiological consequences at the exclusion area boundary, low population zone, and control room (SRP 15.0.3, I. AREAS OF REVIEW).

In summary, NRC requirements mandate a detailed, quantitative, and methodologically justified identification of post-accident radiation sources, including isotopic inventories, release fractions, timing, chemical forms, and supporting assumptions, as documented in the FSAR and in accordance with 10 CFR 50.34, RG 1.183, and related guidance.

evidence_chain.section: Section 3: Accident Source Term (pages 18-24)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
3. Accident Source Term

The accident source term is defined by the magnitude, composition, physical and chemical form, and timing of the radioactive material released from the fuel and subsequently from the reactor core into the containment. The AST described in this guide is based on SAND2011-0128 and is characterized by the following attributes:

• Fission product inventory: The inventory of radionuclides available for release is calculated based on the maximum core inventory at the time of the accident, considering the core power level, fuel burnup, and irradiation history. The inventory should include all significant contributors to dose, including noble gases, iodine, cesium, tellurium, and other relevant radionuclides.

• Release fractions: The fractions of the core inventory released to the containment are specified for each radionuclide group and are based on experimental data and analyses of severe accidents. These fractions are provided in Table 3 of this guide and are intended to be conservative for design basis accident analyses.

• Timing of release phases: The release of radionuclides is divided into distinct phases (gap release, early in-vessel, late in-vessel, ex-vessel), each with specified durations and release rates. The timing and magnitude of releases for each phase are provided in Table 4 of this guide.

• Radionuclide composition: The composition of the released material is specified for each phase, with particular attention to the chemical and physical forms of iodine (e.g., elemental, particulate, organic) and other dose-significant radionuclides.

• Chemical form: The chemical forms of released radionuclides, especially iodine, are specified to support dose consequence analyses. The default assumption is that 95 percent of the released iodine is in the elemental form and 5 percent is in the particulate form, unless plant-specific data support alternative fractions.

Applicants and licensees should use these attributes in their analyses to identify and quantify post-accident radiation sources in containment and plant systems following a loss-of-coolant accident. The methodology for calculating the fission product inventory and applying the release fractions and timing is described in detail in Sections 3.1 through 3.5 of this guide.

data.query: How do NRC review standards require the use of isotopic inventories and release fractions to support post-accident radiation source term calculations?
data.answer:
NRC review standards require that isotopic inventories and release fractions be rigorously used to support post-accident radiation source term calculations. According to DSRS 12.2 (Section II. Acceptance Criteria), applicants must provide detailed descriptions of all radiation sources, including isotope, quantity, form, and use, particularly for sources that may impact shielding design or require special controls. The methods, models, and assumptions used to derive these values must be specified, and the information should be sufficient to support shielding, ventilation, and monitoring system design, as well as dose assessments for both occupational and public exposures.

Regulatory Guide 1.183 (Section 3) further details the acceptable approach for accident source term (AST) calculations. The fission product inventory must be calculated for the core or affected fuel, accounting for burnup, enrichment, and irradiation history, and should include all significant radionuclides contributing to dose consequences. Conservative assumptions regarding irradiation history and decay time are acceptable, and inventories should be calculated using validated codes such as ORIGEN. Release fractions for each radionuclide group must be consistent with NRC-approved values (e.g., SAND2011-0128) and should be applied to the calculated inventory to determine the quantity of each radionuclide released during an accident. These fractions must reflect the physical and chemical behavior of radionuclides under the specific accident scenario.

10 CFR 50.34 requires that the safety analysis report include an analysis of the facility’s capability to control and limit radioactive releases, and to estimate potential radiation doses to workers and the public in the event of an accident. This analysis must be based on the calculated isotopic inventories and the application of appropriate release fractions, as described above.

In summary, NRC standards require applicants to use validated methods to determine isotopic inventories and apply NRC-approved release fractions to support post-accident source term calculations, ensuring that all assumptions and methodologies are clearly documented and justified in the safety analysis.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
3. Accident Source Term

The accident source term is defined by the magnitude, composition, chemical form, and timing of the radioactive material released from the fuel and transported to the environment. The NRC staff finds the following attributes acceptable for use in DBA radiological consequence analyses using an AST:

3.1 Fission Product Inventory

The fission product inventory should be calculated for the core or affected fuel using a method that accounts for the fuel burnup, enrichment, and irradiation history. The inventory should include all significant radionuclides that contribute to the dose consequences of the analyzed accident. The inventory should be based on the maximum fuel rod average burnup and enrichment for the fuel in the core at the time of the accident. The use of conservative assumptions regarding the irradiation history and decay time is acceptable. The inventory should be calculated using a recognized and validated computer code (e.g., ORIGEN or equivalent).

3.2 Release Fractions

The release fractions for each radionuclide group (noble gases, halogens, alkali metals, alkaline earths, lanthanides, actinides, and others) should be consistent with the values provided in SAND2011-0128 or other NRC-approved sources. The release fractions should be applied to the calculated fission product inventory to determine the quantity of each radionuclide released from the fuel. The release fractions should reflect the physical and chemical behavior of the radionuclides during the accident scenario being analyzed. For non-LOCA events, the release fractions should be determined using the methodology described in Appendix I of this guide or other NRC-approved methods.

data.query: When determining post-accident radiation levels in areas adjacent to containment, what combined regulatory guidance and review standards govern the selection and application of isotopic inventories, release fractions, and aerosol removal rates?
data.answer:
The determination of post-accident radiation levels in areas adjacent to containment is governed by a combination of regulatory requirements, guidance documents, and review standards that specify the selection and application of isotopic inventories, release fractions, and aerosol removal rates.

According to DSRS 12.2 (Section II), the NRC staff reviews the calculated concentrations of radioactive material by nuclide for accident conditions, including the models and parameters used. The acceptance criteria are based on compliance with NRC regulations such as 10 CFR 50.34(f)(2)(vii), GDC 19, and GDC 61 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A), which require control of radioactive material and provision of suitable shielding and containment to limit radiation exposure and offsite doses (see [2]).

The primary regulatory guidance for accident source term assumptions is Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.183, as referenced in DSRS 12.2 and SRP 15.0.3. RG 1.183 (Sections 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, and 5.1) specifies that the isotopic inventory should be based on the maximum core inventory for each radionuclide, calculated for the burnup and power level that maximize the inventory, and should account for irradiation and decay history. Release fractions for each radionuclide group should use values from SAND2011-0128 (summarized in RG 1.183 Table 3), unless justified otherwise. Aerosol removal rates and other engineered safety feature removal mechanisms should be based on experimental data or conservative assumptions, and must be consistent with the design and performance of the systems.

Additional guidance is provided by ANSI/ANS Standard 18.1 (for source term estimation methods), RG 1.112 (for waste system source terms), and NUREG-0737 (for post-accident source identification), as cited in DSRS 12.2. The Standard Review Plan (SRP) 15.0.3 confirms that RG 1.183 is the accepted basis for methodology and assumptions in radiological consequence analyses, including the use of bounding isotopic inventories and release fractions.

In summary, the selection and application of isotopic inventories, release fractions, and aerosol removal rates for post-accident radiation level determination are governed by 10 CFR Part 50 (GDC 19 and 61), RG 1.183, ANSI/ANS 18.1, RG 1.112, and supporting NRC review standards as detailed in DSRS 12.2 and SRP 15.0.3.

3. Accident Source Term

The accident source term is defined by the magnitude, composition, chemical form, and timing of the release of radioactive material to the containment. The NRC staff finds the following attributes acceptable for use in design basis accident analyses:

3.1 Fission Product Inventory

The fission product inventory should be based on the maximum core inventory of each radionuclide of interest, calculated for the burnup and power level that maximize the inventory for each isotope, consistent with the fuel management strategy and operating history. The inventory should be determined using a method that accounts for the irradiation and decay history of the fuel, including the effects of shutdowns and power changes. The inventory should include all significant contributors to dose, including noble gases, iodine, cesium, tellurium, and other relevant radionuclides.

3.2 Release Fractions

The release fractions for each radionuclide group should be based on the values provided in SAND2011-0128, as summarized in Table 3 of this guide, unless a plant-specific or event-specific analysis justifies alternative values. The release fractions are intended to be conservative and reflect the fraction of the core inventory released to the containment under the assumed accident conditions. For non-LOCA events, release fractions should be determined using the methodology described in Appendix I of this guide, which is based on ANSI/ANS-5.4-2011 (Ref. 7), or a plant-specific analysis that is technically justified.

3.3 Timing of Release Phases

The timing of the release phases should be consistent with the accident progression and the physical and chemical behavior of the radionuclides. The NRC staff finds the timing assumptions in SAND2011-0128 acceptable for use in design basis analyses. The timing should be documented and justified in the analysis.

5. Analysis Assumptions and Methodology

5.1 General Considerations

The analysis should use conservative assumptions regarding system performance, operator actions, and environmental conditions. The methodology should be consistent with the guidance in this RG and should be documented in sufficient detail to allow independent review. The analysis should account for the removal of aerosols and other radionuclides by engineered safety features, such as containment sprays and filters, using removal rates that are consistent with the design and performance of the systems. The removal rates should be based on experimental data or conservative assumptions, as described in this guide.

SRP Acceptance Criteria
Specific SRP acceptance criteria acceptable to meet the relevant requirements of the NRC's regulations identified above are as follows for the review described in this SRP section. ...
Appropriate sections of the following Regulatory Guides are used by the staff for the identified acceptance criteria.

Regulatory Guide 1.23, “Onsite Meteorological Programs,” presents criteria for an acceptable onsite meteorological monitoring program and the resulting meteorological database that may be used in this SRP section as input to the atmospheric dispersion estimates.

Regulatory Guide 1.78, “Evaluating the Habitability of a Nuclear Power Plant Control Room During a Postulated Hazardous Chemical Release,” presents criteria for characterizing atmospheric dispersion conditions for evaluating the consequences of airborne hazardous material releases to the control room. 

Regulatory Guide 1.145, "Atmospheric Dispersion Models for Potential Accident Consequence Assessments at Nuclear Power Plants," presents criteria for characterizing atmospheric dispersion conditions for evaluating the consequences of radiological releases to the EAB and LPZ. 

Regulatory Guide 1.194, “Atmospheric Relative Concentrations for Control room Radiological Habitability Assessments at Nuclear Power Plants,” presents criteria for characterizing atmospheric dispersion conditions for evaluating the consequences of radiological releases to the control room.  

Older plants licenced under 10 CFR Part 50 may have also used the following regulatory guides instead of Regulatory Guide 1.145 for characterizing atmospheric dispersion conditions for evaluating the consequences of radiological releases to the EAB and LPZ:
Regulatory Guide 1.3, “Assumptions Used for Evaluating the Potential Radiological Consequences of a Loss of Coolant Accident for Boiling Water Reactors”.
Regulatory Guide 1.4, “Assumptions Used for Evaluating the Potential Radiological Consequences of a Loss of Coolant Accident for Pressurized Water Reactors”.
Regulatory Guide 1.5, “Assumptions Used for Evaluating the Potential Radiological Consequences of a Steam Line Break Accident for Boiling Water Reactors”.
Regulatory Guide 1.24, “Assumptions Used for Evaluating the Potential Radiological Consequences of a Pressurized Water Reactor Radioactive Gas Storage Tank Failure”.
Regulatory Guide 1.25, “Assumptions Used for Evaluating the Potential Radiological Consequences of a Fuel Handling Accident in the Fuel Handling and Storage Facility for Boiling and Pressurized Water Reactors”.
Regulatory Guide 1.77, “Assumptions Used for Evaluating a Control Rod Ejection Accident for Pressurized Water Reactors”.
Regulatory Guide 1.98, “Assumptions Used for Evaluating the Potential Radiological Consequences of a Radioactive Offgas System Failure in a Boiling Water Reactor”.

New reactor applicant atmospheric dispersion estimates should reasonably reflect current staff positions and state-of-the-art atmospheric dispersion knowledge.  Specifically for CP, OL, COL, or ESP reviews, the following information should be provided:
1. A description of the atmospheric dispersion models used to calculate χ/Q values for accidental releases of radioactive and hazardous materials to the atmosphere.  The models should be documented in detail and substantiated within the limits of the model so that the staff can evaluate their appropriateness of use with regards to release characteristics, plant configuration, plume density, meteorological conditions, and site topography.
2. Meteorological data used for the evaluation (as input to the dispersion models) which represent annual cycles of hourly values of wind direction, wind speed, and atmospheric stability for each mode of accidental release. Any dispersion estimates should be calculated from the most representative meteorological data available for the site. Guidance on appropriate onsite meteorological data is provided in Regulatory Guide 1.23.  This information is also reviewed in SRP Section 2.3.3.
3. A discussion of atmospheric diffusion parameters, such as lateral and vertical plume spread (σy and σz) as a function of distance, topography, and atmospheric conditions, should be related to measured meteorological data.  The methodology for establishing these relationships should be appropriate for estimating the consequences of accidents within the range of distances which are of interest with respect to site characteristics and established regulatory criteria.
4. The methods for generating these distributions should be adequately described.  Guidance for calculating EAB and LPZ atmospheric dispersion factors is provided in Regulatory Guide 1.145.
5. Atmospheric dispersion factors used for the assessment of consequences related to atmospheric radioactive releases to the control room for design basis, other accidents, and for onsite and offsite releases of hazardous airborne materials should be provided. data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for controlling airborne radioactive material concentrations in areas accessible to workers within a nuclear power plant?
data.answer: The NRC regulatory requirements for controlling airborne radioactive material concentrations in areas accessible to workers within a nuclear power plant are grounded in several key regulations and guidance documents. According to DSRS 12.2, the NRC reviews the applicant’s final safety analysis report to ensure compliance with requirements such as 10 CFR 20.1101(b), which mandates maintaining occupational radiation exposure (ORE) as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA). Additionally, 10 CFR Part 20, Subpart H, addresses respiratory protection and controls to restrict internal exposure in restricted areas. The NRC requires that airborne radioactivity concentrations in frequently occupied areas be a small fraction of the limits specified in 10 CFR 20.1203, 10 CFR 20.1204, and Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 20. These sections relate to limiting average concentrations of airborne radioactive materials to protect individuals and control intake via inhalation or absorption. The design and operation of ventilation systems and personnel protective measures must be based on calculated concentrations of radioactive material expected during normal operation, anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs), and accident conditions. Furthermore, 10 CFR 50.34a requires that equipment to control releases of radioactive material in gaseous effluents be designed to keep average annual releases during normal operation and AOOs as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA), and to ensure compliance with 10 CFR Part 20, particularly §§ 20.1301 and 20.1302. In summary, NRC regulations require nuclear power plants to design and operate systems that limit airborne radioactive material concentrations in worker-accessible areas to levels that are ALARA and well below regulatory limits, with specific attention to internal dose limits and respiratory protection.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
§ 50.34a Design objectives for equipment to control releases of radioactive material in effluents—nuclear power reactors.

(a) Each applicant for a construction permit or operating license for a nuclear power reactor to be constructed and operated on a site for which a construction permit was issued after January 1, 1975, shall include in its application a description of the design objectives for equipment to be installed to control the release of radioactive material in gaseous and liquid effluents produced during normal reactor operations, including anticipated operational occurrences. The design objectives for equipment to control the release of radioactive material in gaseous effluents shall be to keep average annual releases during normal operation, including anticipated operational occurrences, to levels that are as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA). The design objectives for equipment to control the release of radioactive material in liquid effluents shall be to keep average annual releases during normal operation, including anticipated operational occurrences, to levels that are as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA). data.query: How do NRC regulations for radiation protection programs relate to the design features required for ventilation systems in nuclear power plant reactor buildings?
data.answer:
NRC regulations for radiation protection programs are closely linked to the design features required for ventilation systems in nuclear power plant reactor buildings. According to DSRS 12.2, the NRC reviews the applicant’s safety analysis to ensure that radiation protection design features, including ventilation systems, comply with regulatory requirements such as 10 CFR 20.1101(b), which mandates that occupational radiation exposure (ORE) be kept as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA). The design of ventilation systems must account for airborne radioactive material sources, with detailed descriptions and calculations of expected concentrations during normal operations, anticipated operational occurrences, and accident conditions. These concentrations must be a small fraction of the limits specified in 10 CFR 20.1203, 10 CFR 20.1204, and Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 20, to protect both workers and the public.

Furthermore, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I, requires that the design features of reactor installations include equipment to control releases of radioactive materials in effluents, with the objective of keeping public doses from such releases as low as reasonably achievable and within specified numerical guides. These guides serve as design objectives and are to be used alongside the ALARA principle outlined in 10 CFR 20.1101(b).

In summary, NRC regulations require that ventilation system design in reactor buildings be based on a thorough assessment of airborne radioactive sources, with features and controls that ensure compliance with ALARA and dose limits for both occupational and public exposure, as detailed in DSRS 12.2 and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I.
