data.query: When evaluating airborne tritium and other radionuclide concentrations in a reactor building, what regulatory guidance and acceptance criteria must be considered regarding assumed environmental conditions, ventilation flow rates, and design features to ensure compliance with occupational dose limits?
data.answer:
When evaluating airborne tritium and other radionuclide concentrations in a reactor building, several regulatory guidance documents and acceptance criteria must be considered to ensure compliance with occupational dose limits:

1. Environmental Conditions and Ventilation Flow Rates: According to DSRS 12.2 (Section II), the NRC staff reviews the description of airborne radioactive material sources, including calculated concentrations by nuclide for various plant areas under normal, AOO, and accident conditions. The assumptions for environmental conditions (e.g., temperature, pressure, humidity) and ventilation flow rates must be specified and justified, either directly or by reference to the FSAR. RG 1.183 (Section 5) further requires that analyses use conservative, clearly identified, and justified assumptions for environmental conditions and ventilation flow rates, consistent with facility design and operation. The most limiting set of assumptions should be considered for each scenario.

2. Design Features: The design features of the facility, such as containment, filtration, shielding, and ventilation, must be described and justified in the analysis (DSRS 12.2; RG 1.183, Section 5.2). For tritium, DSRS 12.2 specifies that concentrations should be based on a primary coolant concentration of 1.3x10^5 Bq/gm (3.5 μCi/gm), or an alternate value with supporting methods and assumptions.

3. Acceptance Criteria: Airborne radioactivity concentrations in frequently occupied areas should be a small fraction of the limits in 10 CFR 20.1203, 10 CFR 20.1204, and Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 20 (DSRS 12.2). For effluent releases, Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50 sets annual dose objectives for unrestricted areas (e.g., 5 mrem total body, 15 mrem skin, 10 mrem to any organ from tritium and long-lived particulates).

4. Atmospheric Dispersion and Meteorological Assumptions: RG 1.183 (Section 5.3), SRP 2.3.4, and RG 1.145 require the use of conservative, site-specific meteorological data (windspeed, direction, stability) for dispersion modeling. The models and input parameters must be justified and reflect current staff positions and state-of-the-art knowledge. Regulatory Guide 1.23 provides criteria for meteorological data collection.

In summary, compliance is demonstrated by using conservative, justified assumptions for environmental conditions, ventilation, and facility design; by ensuring airborne concentrations are a small fraction of regulatory limits; and by applying accepted models and site-specific meteorological data for dispersion and dose assessments.

I. Introduction
Section 50.34a provides that each applicant for a license to operate a light-water-cooled nuclear power reactor will include in its application a description of the design features of the facility and the procedures for operation of the facility to be used to keep releases of radioactive material to unrestricted areas during normal operation, including anticipated operational occurrences, as low as is reasonably achievable. A. The design objectives for radioactive material in gaseous effluents are:
1. The calculated annual (calendar year) dose to any individual in an unrestricted area from radioactive materials released in gaseous effluents from each light-water-cooled nuclear power reactor shall not exceed:
(a) 5 millirems to the total body; and
(b) 15 millirems to the skin.
2. The calculated annual (calendar year) dose to any individual in an unrestricted area from tritium and all radioactive materials in particulate form with half-lives greater than 8 days in gaseous effluents from each light-water-cooled nuclear power reactor shall not exceed 10 millirems to any organ.
B. The licensee shall establish operating procedures and equipment design features to ensure that the releases of radioactive materials in effluents to unrestricted areas are kept as low as is reasonably achievable.

evidence_chain.section: Section 5: Analysis Assumptions and Methodology (pages 30-32)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
5. Analysis Assumptions and Methodology

5.1 General Considerations

The assumptions used in the radiological consequence analyses should be consistent with the design and operation of the facility and should be justified. The analyses should use conservative assumptions regarding the initial conditions, system performance, and operator actions. The assumptions should be clearly identified and justified in the analysis. The analyses should consider the most limiting set of assumptions for each accident scenario. The analyses should also consider the effects of uncertainties in the input parameters and models used in the analysis.

5.2 Accident-Specific Assumptions

The assumptions used in the radiological consequence analyses should be based on the specific accident scenario being analyzed. The analyses should consider the following factors:
• The type and magnitude of the source term
• The timing and duration of the release
• The location and geometry of the release point
• The environmental conditions (e.g., temperature, pressure, humidity)
• The ventilation flow rates and pathways
• The design features of the facility (e.g., containment, filtration, shielding)
• The occupancy and location of personnel
• The duration of exposure
• The use of protective measures (e.g., respiratory protection, evacuation)

The analyses should use conservative assumptions for each of these factors, consistent with the design and operation of the facility. The assumptions should be clearly identified and justified in the analysis.

5.3 Atmospheric Dispersion Modeling and Meteorology Assumptions

The analyses should use conservative assumptions for atmospheric dispersion and meteorological conditions. The analyses should consider the most limiting meteorological conditions for each accident scenario. The analyses should use appropriate models and input parameters for atmospheric dispersion, consistent with the guidance in NUREG-0800, SRP Section 2.3.4, and Regulatory Guide 1.145, "Atmospheric Dispersion Models for Potential Accident Consequence Assessments at Nuclear Power Plants."

evidence_chain.section: C. REGULATORY POSITION, 1.1 Meteorological Data Input
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
C. REGULATORY POSITION
This section identifies acceptable methods for (1) calculating atmospheric relative concentration (xJQ) values, (2) determining X/Q values on a directional basis, (3) determining XJQ values on an overall site basis, and (4) choosing X/Q values to be used in evaluations of the types of events described in Regulatory Guides 1.3 and 1.4.
Selection of conservative, less detailed site parameters for the evaluation may be sufficient to establish compliance with regulatory guidelines.
1. CALCULATION OF ATMOSPHERIC RELATIVE CON-
CENTRATION (X/Q) VALUES
Equations and parameters presented in this section should be used unless unusual siting, meteorological, or terrain conditions dictate the use of other models or considerations. Site-specific atmospheric diffusion tests covering a full range of conditions may be used as a basis for modifying the equations and parameters.
1.1 Meteorological Data Input
The meteorological data needed for X/Q calculations include windspeed, wind direction, and a measure of atmospheric stability. These data should represent hourly averages as defined in Regulatory Guide 1.23.
Wind direction should be classed into 16 compass directions (22.5-degree sectors centered on true north, north-northeast, etc.).
Atmospheric stability should be determined by vertical AT between the release height and the 10-meter level. Acceptable stability classes are given in Regulatory Guide 1.23. If other well-documented parameters are used to determine plume dispersion (with appropriate justification), the models described in this guide may require modification. A well-documented parameter is one that is substantiated by diffusion data collected in terrain conditions similar to those at the nuclear power plant site being considered.
Calms should be defined as hourly average windspeeds below the vane or anemometer starting speed, whichever is higher (to reflect limitations in instrumentation). If the instrumentation program conforms to the regulatory position in Regulatory Guide 1.23, calms should be assigned a windspeed equal to the vane or anemometer starting speed, whichever is higher. Otherwise, consideration of a conservative evaluation of calms, taking into account the limitations of the windspeed measurement system, will be necessary. Wind directions during calm conditions should be assigned in proportion to the directional distribution of noncalm winds with speeds less than 1.5 meters per second.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for controlling airborne radioactive material concentrations in areas accessible to workers in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for controlling airborne radioactive material concentrations in areas accessible to workers in nuclear power plants are grounded in several NRC regulations and guidance documents. The primary requirements are to ensure occupational radiation exposure is maintained as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA) and within specified dose limits.

According to DSRS 12.2, the NRC reviews the applicant’s safety analysis to ensure compliance with 10 CFR 20.1101(b) (ALARA), 10 CFR Part 20 Subpart H (controls to restrict internal exposure), and 10 CFR 20.1201 (occupational dose limits for adults). Specifically, airborne radioactivity concentrations in frequently occupied areas should be a small fraction of the limits specified in 10 CFR 20.1203 and 10 CFR 20.1204, as well as Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 20. These sections require limiting average concentrations of airborne radioactive materials to protect individuals and control intake via inhalation or absorption.

Design objectives for equipment controlling releases of radioactive material in gaseous effluents are specified in 10 CFR 50.34a, which requires that annual average concentrations at the boundary of unrestricted areas not exceed values in Table 2 of Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 20.

RG 1.183 provides guidance for control room habitability, requiring that doses to control room occupants under accident conditions not exceed a total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) of 5 rem for the duration of the accident, per 10 CFR 50.67 and GDC 19. The analysis must account for all credible airborne pathways and consider engineered safety features such as filtration and isolation.

RG 1.143 and RG 1.26 further require that systems handling radioactive materials be designed to quality standards that ensure reliability and facilitate ALARA practices. Structures are classified based on potential radiological releases, with more stringent requirements for higher potential exposures (e.g., >5 rem/year to personnel).

In summary, the regulatory framework requires nuclear power plants to design, operate, and maintain systems to control airborne radioactive material concentrations in worker-accessible areas, ensuring exposures are ALARA and within regulatory dose limits, with specific design and operational controls for both normal and accident conditions (DSRS 12.2; 10 CFR 20.1101, 20.1201, 20.1203, 20.1204; 10 CFR 50.34a; RG 1.183; RG 1.143; RG 1.26).

§ 50.34a Design objectives for equipment to control releases of radioactive material in effluents—nuclear power reactors.

(a) In order to keep levels of radioactive material in effluents to unrestricted areas as low as is reasonably achievable, each applicant for a construction permit or operating license for a nuclear power reactor to be located on a site for which a construction permit was issued after January 1, 1975, shall include in its application a description of the design objectives for equipment to be installed to control releases of radioactive material in gaseous and liquid effluents produced during normal reactor operations, including anticipated operational occurrences. The design objectives for equipment to control releases of radioactive material in gaseous effluents must be such that, at the boundary of the unrestricted area, the radioactive material in gaseous effluents will not result in an annual average concentration exceeding the values specified in Table 2 of Appendix B to part 20 of this chapter. The design objectives for equipment to control releases of radioactive material in liquid effluents must be such that, at the boundary of the unrestricted area, the radioactive material in liquid effluents will not result in an annual average concentration exceeding the values specified in Table 2 of Appendix B to part 20 of this chapter.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
C. STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE

This section and the appendices to this RG contain regulatory positions that establish a method acceptable to the NRC staff for complying with regulations for DBA dose consequence analysis using an AST.
...
4. Dose Calculation Methodology
...
4.2 Control Room Dose Consequences

The control room dose consequence analysis should be performed using the AST and the assumptions and methods described in this guide. The analysis should demonstrate that the calculated doses to control room occupants do not exceed the dose acceptance criteria specified in 10 CFR 50.67 and GDC 19. The analysis should consider the following:

• The control room should be assumed to be occupied continuously for the duration of the accident, unless justified otherwise.
• The analysis should account for the ingress of airborne radioactive material into the control room from all credible pathways, including direct leakage, ventilation system intake, and other penetrations.
• The control room habitability systems, including filtration and isolation features, may be credited if their performance is demonstrated to be reliable and consistent with the facility’s design basis.
• The analysis should use the AST release fractions, timing, and chemical forms as described in this guide.
• The analysis should consider the effects of engineered safety features, such as filtration and isolation, on the concentrations of airborne radioactive material in the control room.
• The calculated doses should be compared to the acceptance criteria in 10 CFR 50.67 and GDC 19.

4.4 Acceptance Criteria

The calculated doses to control room occupants and at the exclusion area boundary and low population zone should not exceed the dose reference values specified in 10 CFR 50.67 and GDC 19. Specifically, for control room habitability, GDC 19 requires that adequate radiation protection be provided to permit access and occupancy of the control room under accident conditions without exceeding a total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) of 5 rem (0.05 Sv) or its equivalent to any individual for the duration of the accident.

data.query: How do NRC regulations for occupational dose limits relate to the requirements for ventilation system design in areas where airborne radioactive materials may be present?
data.answer:
NRC regulations for occupational dose limits are directly related to the requirements for ventilation system design in areas where airborne radioactive materials may be present. According to DSRS 12.2, the NRC reviews the design features of ventilation systems to ensure compliance with occupational dose limits specified in 10 CFR 20.1201 (Occupational Dose Limits for Adults) and related sections. The design must account for airborne radioactive material concentrations during normal operations, anticipated operational occurrences, and accident conditions, ensuring that occupational exposures are kept as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA) per 10 CFR 20.1101(b). The NRC also requires that the design includes measures to control internal exposures, as outlined in 10 CFR Part 20, Subpart H, and that dose assessments consider both external and internal exposures from airborne materials (10 CFR 20.1203 and 20.1204).

Additionally, Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50 provides numerical design objectives for controlling releases of radioactive materials in effluents, emphasizing ALARA principles. Ventilation systems must be designed to control the venting and release of airborne radioactive materials, including provisions for holding or filtering such materials to meet these objectives.

Regulatory Guide 1.183 further specifies that control room ventilation systems must be designed to ensure that operator doses do not exceed the limits in GDC 19 and 10 CFR 50.67(b)(2), accounting for potential airborne radioactive material ingress during accident conditions. RG 1.143 reinforces that radioactive waste management systems, including ventilation, should be designed to minimize occupational exposures and control leakage, referencing the dose limits in 10 CFR Part 20.

In summary, NRC occupational dose limits establish the regulatory basis for the design and operation of ventilation systems in areas with potential airborne radioactive materials, requiring that such systems be engineered to limit both internal and external exposures to workers and to maintain doses ALARA, in accordance with the cited regulations and guidance documents.

I. Introduction

A. The calculated annual total quantity of radioactive material, except tritium and noble gases, released from each light-water-cooled nuclear power reactor to the atmosphere will not result in an estimated annual dose or dose commitment to any individual in an unrestricted area, from all pathways of exposure, in excess of 5 mrem to the total body or any organ, except the thyroid, which shall not exceed 15 mrem.

4.2 Control Room Dose Consequences

The control room dose analysis should demonstrate that the dose to control room operators does not exceed the dose criteria specified in GDC 19, as implemented by 10 CFR 50.34(f)(2)(xxviii) and 10 CFR 50.67(b)(2). The analysis should consider the potential for airborne radioactive material to enter the control room envelope and should include the following assumptions, unless otherwise justified:

• The control room envelope is assumed to be occupied by at least one operator for the duration of the accident.
• The control room ventilation system is assumed to be operating in its normal mode at the time of the accident and is switched to the emergency mode in accordance with the plant’s emergency operating procedures.
• The control room envelope is assumed to be isolated from unfiltered inleakage as soon as practicable, but not later than the time specified in the plant’s emergency operating procedures.
• The analysis should account for the unfiltered inleakage of airborne radioactive material into the control room envelope, including contributions from both direct leakage and transfer through ventilation system components.
• The analysis should use the assumed concentrations of radionuclides in the containment and plant systems, as described in Appendices A through H of this guide, to evaluate the potential for airborne radioactive material to be transported to the control room envelope.

The design of the control room ventilation system should ensure that the dose to operators does not exceed the limits specified in GDC 19 and 10 CFR 50.67(b)(2), taking into account the potential for airborne radioactive material to enter the control room envelope during accident conditions.

data.query: When evaluating airborne tritium concentrations in a reactor building, what regulatory guidance and review standards must be considered for establishing the assumptions regarding ventilation rates, atmospheric conditions, and design features to ensure compliance with occupational exposure limits?
data.answer:
When evaluating airborne tritium concentrations in a reactor building, regulatory guidance and review standards require that assumptions regarding ventilation rates, atmospheric conditions, and design features be clearly specified, justified, and consistent with NRC requirements. According to DSRS 12.2 (Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA), the NRC staff reviews the description of airborne radioactive material sources, including the models and parameters used for calculations, as documented in the FSAR. The assumptions for ventilation rates and atmospheric conditions must be specified and referenced, ensuring that airborne concentrations in occupied areas remain a small fraction of the limits in 10 CFR 20.1203, 10 CFR 20.1204, and Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 20. The guidance also references RG 1.183 for acceptable assumptions in evaluating radionuclide concentrations and ANSI/ANS 18.1 for methods and data to estimate typical long-term concentrations, which must be adapted to the specific plant design.

Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50 further requires that the design of ventilation and effluent control systems be based on expected types and quantities of radioactive materials, their physical and chemical forms, and anticipated operating conditions, including process upsets and maintenance. The design must ensure effluent concentrations are as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA) and comply with the limits in Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 20.

RG 1.183 (Section 5) emphasizes that all analysis assumptions, including those for ventilation and atmospheric dispersion, must be conservative, justified, and clearly identified. The NRC reviews these assumptions to ensure they are appropriate for the facility and scenario. Atmospheric dispersion models and meteorological assumptions must be consistent with NRC guidance and account for site-specific characteristics and uncertainties.

In summary, compliance is ensured by: (1) specifying and justifying all assumptions in the FSAR, (2) using NRC-accepted methods and standards (e.g., RG 1.183, ANSI/ANS 18.1), (3) designing systems to meet ALARA and regulatory limits, and (4) employing conservative, justified assumptions for ventilation, atmospheric conditions, and design features as reviewed by the NRC.

Appendix I to Part 50—Numerical Guides for Design Objectives and Limiting Conditions for Operation To Meet the Criterion “As Low as is Reasonably Achievable” for Radioactive Material in Light-Water-Cooled Nuclear Power Reactor Effluents

I. Introduction
Section 50.34a provides numerical guides for design objectives and limiting conditions for operation to meet the criterion “as low as is reasonably achievable” for radioactive material in light-water-cooled nuclear power reactor effluents. The guides are intended to provide a basis for evaluating the adequacy of the design and operation of systems for controlling radioactive material in gaseous and liquid effluents produced during normal operation, including anticipated operational occurrences. The guides are not intended to be used as limits for individual occupational exposures or for releases during accident conditions.

II. Design Objectives
A. The design of nuclear power reactors shall include means to control the release of radioactive materials in effluents during normal operation, including anticipated operational occurrences, to levels as low as is reasonably achievable. The design objectives for light-water-cooled nuclear power reactors are:
1. The calculated annual average concentration of radioactive material in gaseous effluents released to unrestricted areas shall not exceed the values specified in Table 2 of Appendix B to part 20 of this chapter.
2. The design of the ventilation and offgas systems, and the selection of process and effluent control equipment, shall be based on the expected types and quantities of radioactive materials produced, the physical and chemical forms of the effluents, and the anticipated operating conditions, including the effects of process upsets and maintenance operations.
3. The design shall provide for appropriate sampling and monitoring systems to measure the concentrations and total quantities of radioactive materials released in effluents.

B. The design objectives shall be used in conjunction with the requirements of part 20 of this chapter, including the occupational dose limits and the limits on concentrations of radioactive material in air in restricted and unrestricted areas.

evidence_chain.section: Section 5: Analysis Assumptions and Methodology (5.1, 5.2, 5.3)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
5. Analysis Assumptions and Methodology

5.1 General Considerations

The assumptions used in the radiological consequence analyses should be consistent with the design and operation of the facility and should be justified. The analyses should use conservative assumptions to account for uncertainties in accident progression, fission product transport, and atmospheric dispersion. The assumptions should be clearly identified and justified in the submittal. The NRC staff will review the assumptions to ensure that they are appropriate for the specific facility and accident scenario being analyzed.

5.2 Accident-Specific Assumptions

The assumptions used in the analysis should reflect the specific accident scenario being evaluated. For example, the assumptions regarding the timing and magnitude of releases, the operation of engineered safety features, and the behavior of radionuclides in the plant systems should be based on the best available information and should be justified. The analysis should consider the potential for retention and removal of radionuclides by plant systems and components, as well as the potential for re-entrainment and release to the environment.

5.3 Atmospheric Dispersion Modeling and Meteorology Assumptions

The analysis should use appropriate atmospheric dispersion models and meteorological assumptions to estimate the transport and dispersion of radionuclides in the environment. The models and assumptions should be consistent with NRC guidance and should be justified based on the characteristics of the site and the accident scenario. The analysis should consider the potential for variations in meteorological conditions and should use conservative assumptions to account for uncertainties. The NRC staff will review the models and assumptions to ensure that they are appropriate for the specific facility and accident scenario being analyzed.

data.query: How do NRC regulations define the limits for airborne radioactive material concentrations in controlled areas of a nuclear facility, and what are the general requirements for maintaining these concentrations within permissible levels?

NRC regulations define the limits for airborne radioactive material concentrations in controlled areas of a nuclear facility primarily by referencing the requirements in 10 CFR Part 20, specifically 10 CFR 20.1203, 10 CFR 20.1204, and Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 20. According to DSRS 12.2, the concentrations of airborne radioactive material in frequently occupied areas should be a small fraction of the limits specified in these regulations. The facility must provide a detailed description and tabulation of expected airborne concentrations by nuclide during normal operation, anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs), and accident conditions. These values are used for the design of ventilation systems, personnel protective measures, and dose assessment. The NRC requires that all sources of airborne radioactivity, including those from leakage, storage, and activation, be identified and quantified to ensure appropriate design and monitoring.

Additionally, 10 CFR 50.34a requires that the design objectives for equipment controlling releases of radioactive material in gaseous effluents ensure that, at the site boundary, the annual average concentration does not exceed the values in Table 2 of Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 20. Furthermore, releases must be kept as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA). The general requirements for maintaining concentrations within permissible levels include implementing special ventilation systems, monitoring equipment, and radiation protection programs as outlined in 10 CFR 20.1101 and related sections. These measures collectively ensure that occupational exposures are minimized and regulatory limits are not exceeded.

§ 50.34a Design objectives for equipment to control releases of radioactive material in effluents—nuclear power reactors.

(a) Each applicant for a construction permit or operating license for a nuclear power reactor to be constructed on or after January 1, 1975, shall include in its application a description of the design objectives for equipment to be installed to control releases of radioactive material in gaseous and liquid effluents produced during normal reactor operations, including anticipated operational occurrences. data.query: How should assumptions regarding evaporation rates from pools be incorporated into the methodology for calculating airborne activity concentrations to ensure compliance with regulatory limits for occupational exposure?
data.answer:
Assumptions regarding evaporation rates from pools must be explicitly incorporated into the methodology for calculating airborne activity concentrations to ensure compliance with regulatory limits for occupational exposure. According to DSRS 12.2, the description of airborne radioactive material sources, including those arising from evaporation, should be detailed in the facility's safety analysis report (FSAR). This includes a tabulation of calculated concentrations by nuclide for various plant areas during normal operation, anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs), and accident conditions. The models and parameters used for these calculations, including evaporation rates, must be specified and justified, either directly or by reference to relevant FSAR sections (DSRS 12.2, Areas of Review and Acceptance Criteria).

Furthermore, Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50 requires that the design of systems for controlling radioactive material in effluents must consider anticipated releases, specifically including those resulting from evaporation from pools (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I, Section III.A). The methodology should use the best available information on the expected quantities and types of radioactive material released during normal operation. The calculated airborne concentrations in occupied areas should be a small fraction of the regulatory limits specified in 10 CFR 20.1203, 10 CFR 20.1204, and Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 20 (DSRS 12.2, Acceptance Criteria).

In summary, evaporation rates from pools must be identified as a source term, quantified with justified assumptions, and incorporated into airborne activity concentration calculations. These calculations must be documented and referenced in the FSAR to demonstrate that occupational exposures remain well below regulatory limits.

data.answer:
NRC regulatory requirements for airborne radioactive material concentrations are closely linked to the assumptions made about evaporation rates from pools in nuclear power plant facilities. According to DSRS 12.2, the NRC staff reviews the description of airborne radioactive material sources, including those arising from evaporation, to ensure that ventilation systems and personnel protective measures are adequately designed. The calculated concentrations of airborne radioactive material must be tabulated for various plant areas and operational conditions, and the models and parameters used—including those for evaporation—must be specified (DSRS 12.2, Areas of Review and Acceptance Criteria).

Regulatory requirements mandate that airborne radioactivity concentrations in frequently occupied areas remain a small fraction of the limits specified in 10 CFR 20.1203, 10 CFR 20.1204, and Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 20 (DSRS 12.2). RG 1.183, Appendix A, Section A.1.2.2.2, provides specific guidance for evaluating airborne radioactivity from pool evaporation, particularly following a loss-of-coolant accident (LOCA). It states that analyses should conservatively assume the entire pool surface is available for evaporation unless otherwise justified, and that evaporation rates should be based on maximum credible pool temperature, surface area, and ventilation conditions. These conservative assumptions ensure that calculated airborne concentrations are not underestimated and are consistent with accident-specific regulatory guidance.

In summary, NRC regulatory requirements for airborne radioactive material concentrations require that evaporation rates from pools be conservatively estimated and explicitly documented, as these rates directly affect the calculated airborne concentrations used for compliance with regulatory limits and for the design of plant safety systems (DSRS 12.2; 10 CFR 50.34a; RG 1.183, Appendix A, Section A.1.2.2.2).

According to DSRS 12.2, the NRC reviews the description of airborne radioactive material sources in the plant as part of the design of ventilation systems, personnel protective measures, and dose assessment. The NRC expects that the assumptions and values for these parameters be clearly specified in the FSAR (Final Safety Analysis Report), either in Chapter 12 or by reference to Chapter 11. data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for controlling radioactive material deposition, such as crud, on reactor core surfaces in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for controlling radioactive material deposition, such as crud, on reactor core surfaces in nuclear power plants are grounded in several NRC documents and regulations. According to DSRS 12.2 (Section II. Acceptance Criteria), applicants must base source terms for coolant and corrosion activation products—including the buildup of activated corrosion products (crud)—on applicable reactor operating experience and reactor core physics calculations. The buildup of such products in various components and systems must be addressed, and any allowances made in design source terms for this buildup must be explained. These source terms are used in shield design, equipment qualification, and ventilation system design calculations, and must be documented in the Final Safety Analysis Report (FSAR).

10 CFR Part 50, specifically § 50.34 and § 50.34a, requires that the FSAR include a description and analysis of structures, systems, and components, emphasizing how the design minimizes contamination and facilitates decommissioning. § 50.34a further requires applicants to describe design objectives and principal features intended to minimize, to the extent practicable, contamination of the facility and the environment, including the control of radioactive material deposition and the minimization of radioactive waste generation.

Regulatory Guide 1.183 (Appendix A) provides accepted methods for evaluating the radiological consequences of accidents, including assumptions for plateout (deposition), holdup, and decontamination factors. For radioiodines, a decontamination factor (DF) of 3 may be applied to account for removal by plateout and holdup in the reactor coolant system, provided this is justified for the specific plant design. For other radionuclides, removal by plateout or decontamination should not be credited unless supported by plant-specific data or analysis. The potential for resuspension or re-entrainment of deposited material (crud) during accident conditions must also be considered, and any credit for removal mechanisms must be justified.

In summary, regulatory requirements mandate that the buildup and control of radioactive material deposition (crud) be addressed in design and safety analyses, with appropriate documentation, justification, and minimization measures as specified in DSRS 12.2, 10 CFR 50.34/50.34a, and RG 1.183.

The source term used for determining shielding and ventilation design of PWR components provided for purification of secondary coolant should consider isotopic concentrations associated with operation at the Technical Specifications allowed limits for primary-to-secondary leakage and/or the secondary coolant specific activity concentrations, in addition to any direct neutron activation products.

The tables of source parameters, which can be placed in FSAR Chapter 12 or referenced to FSAR Chapter 11, will be acceptable if the accompanying text, either in this section or other referenced sections, makes clear how the values are used in a shield design calculation, equipment qualification, or ventilation system design during normal operation. A.1.3.2. Plateout, Holdup, and Decontamination Factors

The evaluation of the radiological consequences of a LOCA should consider the removal of radioactive material by plateout, holdup, and decontamination in the reactor coolant system (RCS) and associated systems. The following assumptions are acceptable to the NRC staff:

• For noble gases, no removal by plateout, holdup, or decontamination should be assumed.
• For radioiodines, a removal factor (decontamination factor, DF) of 3 may be applied to account for plateout, holdup, and decontamination in the RCS and associated systems prior to release to containment. This DF is consistent with the values used in NUREG-1465 and SAND2011-0128.
• For other radionuclides, removal by plateout, holdup, or decontamination should not be credited unless justified by plant-specific data or analysis.

The evaluation should also consider the potential for resuspension or re-entrainment of deposited material (crud) during accident conditions. If credit is taken for removal mechanisms, the analysis should provide justification that the assumed DFs are appropriate for the plant design and accident scenario being evaluated.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory guides for radiation protection programs relate to requirements for minimizing radioactive material buildup on reactor core surfaces?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory guides for radiation protection programs are closely related to requirements for minimizing radioactive material buildup on reactor core surfaces through their emphasis on design features and operational practices that reduce contamination and facilitate radiation protection. According to DSRS 12.2, acceptance criteria for radiation protection programs are based on compliance with 10 CFR 20.1101 (Radiation Protection Programs) and 10 CFR 20.1406 (Minimization of Contamination), which require applicants to describe how facility design minimizes contamination and the generation of radioactive waste, and facilitates decommissioning. The DSRS further specifies that applicants must address the buildup of activated corrosion products in reactor components and systems, and explain how design source terms account for such buildup, thereby directly linking radiation protection program guidance to the minimization of radioactive material accumulation on core surfaces (DSRS 12.2, Section II).

Regulatory Guide 1.143 provides additional guidance, recommending that radioactive waste management systems be designed to control leakage and facilitate maintenance, inspection, and operation, all with the goal of keeping radiation exposures as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA). This includes ensuring that systems are constructed to quality standards that enhance reliability and operability, which indirectly supports minimizing radioactive material buildup by reducing the potential for contamination and facilitating effective waste management (RG 1.143, Sections B and C.4.1).

Furthermore, 10 CFR 50.34 and 50.34a require applicants to describe design features that prevent or minimize the release of radioactive materials, including those that could result from the buildup of radioactive material on reactor core surfaces, and to demonstrate that effluent releases are ALARA (10 CFR 50.34(a)(3), 50.34a(a)). Thus, NRC regulatory guides and requirements collectively ensure that radiation protection programs incorporate design and operational measures to minimize radioactive material buildup on reactor core surfaces.

data.query: For a new light-water reactor design, what combined regulatory requirements and guidance govern the estimation of radiation source terms and dose rates in plant areas, considering the potential for increased crud deposition and activation on core surfaces during outages?
data.answer:
The estimation of radiation source terms and dose rates in plant areas for a new light-water reactor design is governed by a combination of regulatory requirements and guidance documents, with specific attention to the effects of increased crud deposition and activation on core surfaces during outages.

The primary regulatory requirements are found in Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR), including:
- 10 CFR 20.1101(b), which mandates maintaining occupational radiation exposure (ORE) as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA),
- 10 CFR Part 20, Subpart H, for internal exposure controls,
- 10 CFR 20.1301(e) and 40 CFR Part 190, for public exposure limits,
- 10 CFR 50.34, which requires the identification and evaluation of radioactive material sources (including those from normal operations and postulated accidents) and the assessment of their radiological consequences (10 CFR Part 50 §50.34(a)(2), (5)),
- General Design Criteria (GDC) 19 and 61 in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, which address control room habitability and radioactive material control, respectively (DSRS 12.2; SRP 15.0.3).

Guidance for implementing these requirements includes:
- Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.183, which provides acceptable methods for accident source term (AST) development and dose consequence analysis, including defense-in-depth considerations and accounting for uncertainties (RG 1.183 Section 1.1, 1.1.2; SRP 15.0.3),
- RG 1.112 and ANSI/ANS 18.1, which address methods for estimating long-term concentrations of principal radionuclides and require modification to reflect plant-specific design and operating experience, including the buildup of activated corrosion products (DSRS 12.2),
- NUREG-0737 and RG 1.7 for post-accident source identification and gaseous radionuclide concentrations,
- DSRS 12.2, which specifically requires that source terms for coolant and corrosion activation products be based on applicable reactor operating experience, and that the buildup of activated corrosion products (crud) in components and systems be addressed, including allowances in design source terms for such buildup.

In summary, applicants must base source term and dose rate estimates on regulatory requirements in 10 CFR Parts 20 and 50, GDC 19 and 61, and use guidance from RG 1.183, RG 1.112, ANSI/ANS 18.1, and related documents. The estimation process must explicitly consider the potential for increased crud deposition and activation during outages, using operating experience and plant-specific data to justify assumptions and design allowances (DSRS 12.2; 10 CFR 50.34; RG 1.183).

C. STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE

This section and the appendices to this RG contain regulatory positions that establish a method acceptable to the NRC staff for complying with regulations for DBA dose consequence analysis using an AST. 
This RG applies to MHA LOCA models for applicants and licensees using zirconium-alloy cladded uranium dioxide (UO2) fuel rod designs with reactor core burnups up to a maximum rod-average of 68 gigawatt-days per metric ton uranium (GWd/MTU) (and fuel enrichments up to 8 weight-percent uranium-235), including chromium-coated cladding (thicknesses less than 50 microns (μm)) and chromia-doped (up to 0.16 weight-percent) fuel. It is not applicable for other fuel-clad combinations, including fuel with iron-chromium-aluminum (FeCrAl) alloy cladding. 
This RG applies to non-LOCA models for applicants and licensees with reactor core burnups up to a maximum rod-average burnup of 68 GWd/MTU (and fuel enrichments up to 8 weight-percent uranium-235) for currently approved (as of the issuance of this RG) zirconium-alloy cladded UO2 fuel rod designs at power levels below the burnup-dependent power envelopes depicted in figure 1 of this guide.

1. Implementation of Accident Source Term

1.1 Generic Considerations

As used in this guide, the AST is an accident source term derived principally from SAND2011-0128; it differs from the TID-14844 and NUREG-1465 source terms used in the original and revised design and licensing of operating reactor facilities. ASTs may also be used by applicants for new LWRs, including advanced evolutionary and passive LWRs, under 10 CFR Part 50 and 10 CFR Part 52, and for existing operating reactor licensees under 10 CFR 50.34 and 10 CFR 50.67. This guide identifies an AST that is acceptable to the NRC staff and describes significant characteristics of other source terms that may be found acceptable. ...

Licensees should evaluate their proposed uses of this guide, and the associated proposed facility modifications and changes to procedures, to determine whether the proposed changes are consistent with the principle that sufficient safety margins are maintained, including a margin to account for analysis uncertainties. ...

1.1.2 Defense in Depth

Licensees should evaluate their proposed uses of an AST, and the associated proposed facility modifications and changes to procedures, to determine whether the proposed changes are consistent with the principle that adequate defense in depth is maintained to compensate for uncertainties in accident progression and analysis data. Consistency with the defense-in-depth philosophy is maintained if system redundancy, independence, and diversity are preserved commensurate with the expected accident frequency, consequences of challenges to the system, and uncertainties. For facilities to which the GDC (see Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50) apply, compliance with these criteria is required.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for accounting for the production and control of tritium as a radioactive material in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for accounting for the production and control of tritium as a radioactive material in nuclear power plants are grounded in several regulations and guidance documents. Tritium, as a radioactive material, must be managed to ensure occupational and public safety, and its production, storage, and release are subject to specific controls.

According to DSRS 12.2 (Section II), tritium concentrations in plant systems must be based on specified or justified values, and compliance must be demonstrated with key NRC regulations, including:
- 10 CFR 20.1101 (Radiation Protection Programs), 20.1201–20.1206 (Occupational Dose Limits and Exposure Determination), and 20.1301 (Public Dose Limits), which require limiting occupational and public radiation doses and controlling airborne concentrations and intakes of radioactive materials, including tritium.
- 10 CFR 20.1801 requires secure storage and control of licensed materials, including tritium, to prevent unauthorized removal.
- General Design Criterion (GDC) 61 (Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50) mandates that systems containing radioactive materials, such as tritium, are designed to control and limit releases.

10 CFR 50.34a and 50.36a require that plant designs include equipment and technical specifications to control radioactive effluent releases, including tritium, to unrestricted areas, keeping them as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA) and within the numerical guides of Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50. Operating procedures for effluent control and recordkeeping are also required.

RG 1.143 provides design guidance for radioactive waste management systems, including those handling tritiated liquids. Systems must be designed to prevent uncontrolled releases, monitor liquid levels, and route all radioactive liquid waste (including tritiated water) to appropriate treatment systems. RG 1.26 further specifies quality standards for systems containing radioactive materials, ensuring reliability and safety.

In summary, NRC requirements mandate that nuclear power plants account for tritium production and control through robust design, operational controls, monitoring, and recordkeeping, ensuring occupational and public exposures are minimized and within regulatory limits (DSRS 12.2; 10 CFR 20, 50; RG 1.143; RG 1.26).

§ 50.34a Design objectives for equipment to control releases of radioactive material in effluents—nuclear power reactors.
(a) Each applicant for a construction permit or operating license for a nuclear power reactor to be constructed and operated on a site for which a construction permit was issued after January 1, 1975, shall include in its application a description of the design objectives for equipment to be installed to control releases of radioactive material in gaseous and liquid effluents produced during normal reactor operations, including anticipated operational occurrences. The AST is composed of the following radionuclide groups: noble gases, iodine, cesium, tellurium, strontium, ruthenium, and other fission products. The chemical form of tritium, if included, should be justified by the applicant or licensee based on the expected accident conditions and the form in which tritium would be released.

data.query: How do NRC regulations for radiation protection programs interact with requirements for monitoring and controlling the buildup of radioactive isotopes such as deuterium and tritium in reactor systems?
data.answer:
NRC regulations for radiation protection programs are closely integrated with requirements for monitoring and controlling the buildup of radioactive isotopes such as deuterium and tritium in reactor systems. According to DSRS 12.2, the NRC reviews the applicant’s safety analysis to ensure compliance with 10 CFR Part 20, including maintaining occupational radiation exposure (ORE) as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA), controlling internal exposures, and minimizing contamination (10 CFR 20.1406). The FSAR must include calculated concentrations of radioactive materials, by nuclide, including tritium, during normal and off-normal conditions, and justify the methods and assumptions used.

Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50 requires that reactor designs include features to control releases of radioactive materials in effluents, with numerical guides for annual doses to the public, supporting ALARA objectives. These guides inform technical specifications and operational controls for effluent releases, including those containing tritium.

Regulatory Guide 1.183 (Section 3.4) specifies that accident source term analyses must account for activation products such as tritium and deuterium, considering their buildup in reactor coolant and potential release during accidents. The NRC reviews the justification for radionuclide inventories and the methods used.

Regulatory Guide 1.143 emphasizes that radioactive waste management systems, including those handling tritiated water, must be designed to control leakage and facilitate safe operation and maintenance, maintaining exposures ALARA and meeting the dose criteria of 10 CFR Part 20. Systems are classified by hazard potential, with design requirements commensurate with the risk of radiological release.

Finally, Regulatory Guide 1.26 provides quality classification guidance for components containing radioactive material, ensuring that systems capable of containing or releasing significant quantities of radioactive isotopes are designed, fabricated, and maintained to appropriate quality standards per GDC 1 of 10 CFR Part 50.

In summary, NRC regulations require a comprehensive radiation protection program that includes monitoring, controlling, and analyzing the buildup and potential release of radioactive isotopes like deuterium and tritium, with design, operational, and quality assurance requirements grounded in 10 CFR Parts 20 and 50, and detailed in NRC regulatory guides.

The radionuclide composition of the accident source term should be based on the inventory of fission products and activation products in the reactor core at the time of the postulated accident. data.query: For a nuclear facility with ongoing tritium production, what regulatory review standards and guidance documents outline the acceptable methods, modeling approaches, and assumptions for evaluating the impact of deuterium buildup on tritium production rates over the operational life of the plant, and how should these be justified if alternative approaches are used?
data.answer:
The regulatory review standards and guidance documents relevant to evaluating the impact of deuterium buildup on tritium production rates in a nuclear facility are primarily outlined in the Design-Specific Review Standard (DSRS) Section 12.2, 10 CFR Part 50 § 50.34, and several NRC Regulatory Guides (RGs).

DSRS 12.2 specifies that source descriptions must include the methods, models, and assumptions used as the basis for all values provided in the FSAR, including those related to tritium production. The assumptions and quantitative values should be clearly specified, either directly or by reference to other FSAR sections. For tritium, acceptable methods are those based on ANSI/ANS Standard 18.1 and RG 1.112, modified as appropriate for plant-specific attributes, and developed using relevant industry operating experience. If alternative values or methods are used, the application must provide the supporting methods, models, and assumptions (DSRS 12.2, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA).

10 CFR Part 50 § 50.34 requires that the safety analysis report identify the analytical methods and assumptions used in deriving design bases and evaluating accident consequences. If an applicant proposes methods or assumptions different from those previously approved or generally accepted, justification for their use must be provided (§ 50.34(a)).

Regulatory Guides such as RG 1.183, RG 1.143, and RG 1.26 describe acceptable methods for compliance and clarify that alternative approaches may be used if adequately justified. RG 1.183 and RG 1.26 emphasize that while RGs are not regulations, alternative methods are acceptable if supported by a sufficient basis for issuance or continuance of a permit or license. RG 1.143 further notes that alternative means may be proposed for meeting applicable regulations, provided they are justified and ensure that exposures are as low as reasonably achievable.

In summary, acceptable methods and modeling approaches for evaluating deuterium buildup impacts on tritium production should be based on established standards (e.g., ANSI/ANS 18.1, RG 1.112) and clearly documented in the FSAR. If alternative approaches are used, the applicant must provide detailed justification, including the technical basis and consistency with regulatory requirements, as required by DSRS 12.2 and 10 CFR § 50.34, and as described in the referenced RGs.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
§ 50.34 Contents of applications; technical information.

(a) Preliminary safety analysis report. Each application for a construction permit shall include a preliminary safety analysis report. The preliminary safety analysis report shall describe the facility, present the design bases and the limits on its operation, and present a safety analysis of the structures, systems, and components of the facility as a whole. The analysis must assess the facility’s capability to withstand the effects of accidents and to prevent or mitigate their consequences. The report must include the principal design criteria for the facility, with identification of those criteria that are based on generally accepted engineering practices, and must include information on the design bases and the means for ensuring that the design bases will be met. The report must also include a description and analysis of the structures, systems, and components of the facility with respect to their safety functions, reliability, and capability to perform their intended functions under postulated accident conditions. The report must identify the analytical methods used and the assumptions made in deriving the design bases for the facility and in evaluating the consequences of postulated accidents. If the applicant proposes to use methods or assumptions different from those previously approved or generally accepted, the applicant must provide justification for their use.

data.answer: According to DSRS 12.2, the NRC regulatory requirement for accounting for tritium as a radioactive material source in reactor coolant systems specifies that, for nuclear power plants designed for the recycling of tritiated water, tritium concentrations in contained sources and airborne concentrations in specified regions should be based on a primary coolant concentration of 1.3x10^5 Bq/gm (3.5 μCi/gm), unless an alternate value is justified with supporting methods, models, and assumptions in the application. data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for identifying and characterizing all sources of radiation exposure to workers and the public from contained sources in a nuclear facility?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for identifying and characterizing all sources of radiation exposure to workers and the public from contained sources in a nuclear facility are primarily outlined in DSRS 12.2, Section II, and are grounded in compliance with several key NRC regulations, including 10 CFR Part 20 and 10 CFR Part 50. Specifically, the criteria require:

1. Comprehensive identification and description of all radiation sources that may contribute to occupational or public exposure, including those requiring shielding, special ventilation, storage, access control, special procedures, or monitoring equipment (DSRS 12.2, II).
2. Source descriptions must include all pertinent information necessary for shielding design, facility design features, development of plans and procedures, exposure assessment, and determination of radiation dose to safety-related equipment (DSRS 12.2, II).
3. For contained sources, plan scale drawings must show the location, size, and shape of each source, correlated with tables of quantitative source parameters (DSRS 12.2, II).
4. The description must cover neutron and gamma source terms from the reactor core, irradiated components, containment vessel, and adjacent reactors, as well as airborne sources from leakage or activation, with sufficient detail to determine potential radiation fields in occupied or safety-significant areas (DSRS 12.2, II).
5. Quantitative values for source terms must be based on specified methods, models, and assumptions, with references to supporting FSAR sections (DSRS 12.2, II).
6. Airborne radioactivity concentrations in frequently occupied areas must be a small fraction of regulatory limits (10 CFR 20.1203, 20.1204, and Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 20) (DSRS 12.2, II).

Supporting regulatory guidance (RG 1.143, Sections 4 and 5) further requires that radioactive waste management systems be designed to control leakage and maintain exposures as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA), with safety classifications based on potential unmitigated exposures (e.g., 500 mrem/year at the site boundary or 5 rem/year to personnel). RG 1.183 provides acceptable methods for source term characterization in accident analyses, and RG 1.26 and RG 1.29 specify quality and seismic design requirements for systems containing radioactive material, with dose-based thresholds for classification and design.

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria demand a thorough, quantitative, and location-specific characterization of all radiation sources, supported by appropriate design, procedural, and monitoring controls, to ensure compliance with regulatory dose limits for both workers and the public.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

Requirements

Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following NRC regulations:

1. 10 CFR 20.1101, “Radiation Protection Programs”; 10 CFR 20.1201, “Occupational Dose Limits for Adults”; 10 CFR 20.1202, “Compliance with Requirements for Summation of External and Internal Doses”; and 10 CFR 20.1206, “Planned Special Exposures”; as they relate to limiting occupational radiation doses.   

2. 10 CFR 20.1203, “Determination of External Dose from Airborne Radioactive Material,” and 10 CFR 20.1204, “Determination of Internal Exposure,” as they relate to limiting average concentrations of airborne radioactive materials to protect individuals and control the intake (inhalation or absorption) of such materials.   

3. 10 CFR 20.1207, “Occupational Dose Limits for Minors,” as it relates to limiting exposure to minors to one-tenth of limits for adults.   

4. 10 CFR 20.1301, “Radiation Dose Limits for Individual Members of the Public,” and 40 CFR Part 190, “Environmental Radiation Protection Standards for Nuclear Power Operations,” as they relate to the determination of radiation levels and radioactive materials concentrations within the components of the plant that could affect direct radiation exposure to members of the public.  

... [list continues] ...

Compliance with the following specific acceptance criteria is necessary to meet the relevant requirements of the regulations identified above.

Descriptions should be provided for all radiation sources that require (1) shielding (e.g., provided for ORE 20.1101(b), 20.1201, 20.1202, or public 20.1301(e) radiation exposure control), (2) special ventilation systems, (3) special storage locations and conditions, (4) traffic or access control, (5) special plans or procedures, or (6) monitoring equipment. The source descriptions should include all pertinent information required for (1) input to shielding codes used in the design process, (2) establishment of related facility design features, (3) development of plans and procedures, (4) assessment of radiation (public or occupational, as appropriate) exposure, and (5) determination of radiation dose to electrical equipment important to safety as described in 10 CFR 50.49. Unless described within other sections of the FSAR, source descriptions should include the methods, models, and assumptions used as the bases for all values provided in FSAR Section 12.2. A listing of isotope, quantity, form, and use of all required radiation sources containing byproduct, source, and special nuclear material exceeding 3.7x10^9 Bq (100 millicuries) that may warrant shielding design consideration should be provided.

For contained sources, the description should include plan scale drawings of each floor of the plant that show all sources identified so they easily can be related to tables containing the pertinent and necessary quantitative source parameters. Their position should be located accurately, indicating the approximate size and shape. The information about neutron and gamma source terms from the core, reactor pressure vessel, irradiated components inside the reactor vessel, irradiated components inside containment, irradiated portions of the containment vessel, irradiated components and materials present outside of the containment vessel, and adjacent operating reactors should be described in sufficient detail to allow determination of the radiation fields that could occur in areas that may require occupancy, may contain certain electrical equipment important to safety as described in 10 CFR 50.49, or could be a source of radioactive material available to systems outside of the containment vessel. Use to the extent practicable relevant experience from operating reactors. Airborne sources created by leakage, opening formerly closed containers, storage of leaking fuel elements, direct neutron activation of shielding materials and other plant materials, and other mechanisms should be identified by location and magnitude so that they can be used for designing appropriate ventilation systems and in specifying appropriate monitoring systems. Airborne radioactivity concentrations in frequently occupied areas should be a small fraction of the concentrations related to 10 CFR 20.1203, 10 CFR 20.1204, and Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 20. The assumptions made in arriving at quantitative values for these various sources should be specified, either in this section or by reference to FSAR Chapter 11, and other relevant interfacing sections of the FSAR.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
C. STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE

This section and the appendices to this RG contain regulatory positions that establish a method acceptable to the NRC staff for complying with regulations for DBA dose consequence analysis using an AST.
...
3. Accident Source Term

The accident source term is characterized by the composition and magnitude of the radioactive material, the chemical and physical properties of the material, and the timing of the release to the containment. The NRC staff considered the applicability of the revised source terms to operating reactors and determined that the current analytical approach, based on the source term in Technical Information Document (TID)-14844, “Calculation of Distance Factors for Power and Test Reactor Sites,” issued March 1962 (Ref. 10), would continue to be adequate to protect public health and safety. Operating reactors licensed under that approach would not be required to reanalyze accidents using the revised source terms. However, the NRC staff determined that some operating reactor licensees might request to use an AST in analyses to support cost-beneficial licensing actions.

The NRC staff therefore initiated several actions to provide a regulatory basis for operating reactor licensees to use an AST3 in design basis analyses. These initiatives resulted in the development and issuance of the final rule for 10 CFR 50.67 (64 FR 72001; December 23, 1999) and the subsequent issuance of RG 1.183, Revision 0, in July 2000, as implementing guidance for the rule.

Several RGs and SRP chapters describe the NRC’s traditional methods for calculating the radiological consequences of DBAs. The staff developed that guidance to be consistent with the TID-14844 source term and the wholebody and thyroid dose guidelines stated in 10 CFR 100.11, “Determination of exclusion area, low population zone, and population center distance” (Ref. 11). Many of those analysis assumptions and methods in that guidance are inconsistent with the AST and with the total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) criteria in 10 CFR 50.34, 10 CFR Part 52, and 10 CFR 50.67. This guide provides assumptions and methods that are acceptable to the NRC staff for performing design basis radiological analyses using an AST.

data.query: How do NRC requirements for radiation zone classification relate to the need for comprehensive identification of radioactive material inventories in waste storage areas?
data.answer:
NRC requirements for radiation zone classification are closely linked to the comprehensive identification of radioactive material inventories in waste storage areas. According to DSRS 12.2 (Section II. Acceptance Criteria), detailed descriptions of all radiation sources—including isotope, quantity, form, and use—are required for sources that may necessitate shielding, special storage, access control, or monitoring. This information is essential for input to shielding design, facility layout, exposure assessment, and the development of safety procedures. Accurate inventories, including plan drawings showing source locations and quantitative parameters, enable the determination of potential radiation fields and the need for protective measures in waste storage areas.

Regulatory Guide 1.143 (Section 5) further establishes that the safety classification of radwaste systems and components is based on the maximum inventory of radioactive material present. The classification (RW-IIa, RW-IIb, RW-IIc) depends on whether the unmitigated radiological release or exposure exceeds specific thresholds (e.g., 500 millirem/year at the unprotected area boundary or 5 rem/year to personnel). The inventory data are thus critical for determining the appropriate safety class, which in turn dictates the design and operational requirements for the storage area.

In summary, comprehensive identification and documentation of radioactive material inventories are fundamental to both the classification of radiation zones and the safety classification of waste storage systems, ensuring that appropriate controls and protective measures are implemented as required by NRC regulations (DSRS 12.2; RG 1.143, Section 5).

evidence_chain.section: Regulatory Position 5. CLASSIFICATION OF RADWASTE SYSTEMS FOR DESIGN PURPOSES
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
5. CLASSIFICATION OF RADWASTE SYSTEMS FOR DESIGN PURPOSES
There are three safety classes, or classifications, for radwaste management facilities:  RW-IIa (High Hazard), RW-IIb (Hazardous), and RW-IIc (Non-Safety).
RW-IIa is the most stringent class and RW-IIc is the least stringent.  These classifications were developed primarily for natural phenomena and man-induced hazard design.  The radiological release criteria (500 millirem at the unprotected area boundary and 5 rem to facility personnel within the protected boundary) was selected to be consistent with the criteria of 10 CFR Part 20, “Standards for Protection Against Radiation.” This safety classification is applied to SSCs as follows.
5.1 For a given structure housing radwaste processing systems or components, if the total design basis unmitigated radiological release (considering the maximum inventory) at the boundary of the unprotected area is greater than 500 millirem per year or the maximum unmitigated exposure to site personnel within the protected area is greater than 5 rem per year, the external structures are classified as RW-IIa.
5.2 For a given structure housing radwaste processing systems or components, if the total design basis unmitigated radiological release (considering the maximum inventory) at the boundary of the unprotected area is less than 500 millirem per year and the maximum unmitigated exposure to site personnel within the protected area is less than 5 rem per year, the external structure is classified as RW-IIb.
5.3 Any systems or components in a RW-IIa facility (see Regulatory Position 5.1) that store, process, or handle radioactive waste in excess of the A1 quantities given in Appendix A, “Determination of A1 and A2,” to 10 CFR Part 71, “Packaging and Transportation of Radioactive Material,” are classified as RW-IIa.  These systems or components that process radioactive waste in excess of the A2 quantities but less than the A1 quantities given in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 71 are classified as RW-IIb.  All other components are classified as RW-IIc.  This classification may be modified for specific radwaste components.
5.4 Any systems or components in a RW-IIb structure (see Regulatory Position 5.2) that are used to store or process specified radioactive waste in excess of the A1 quantities given in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 71 are classified as RW-IIb.  All other systems or components are classified as RW-IIc.
The unprotected area boundary mentioned in Regulatory Position 5.1 is shown in Figure 1.  A flowchart of the Safety Classification Process is shown in Figure 2.  The classifications discussed in Regulatory Positions 5.1 through 5.4 are not intended to apply to radwaste storage facilities if they do not contain any systems or components that exceed the quantities specified in Regulatory Positions 5.1 through 5.4.

data.query: When establishing radiation zone designations in a radioactive waste building, what combined regulatory provisions require that all major sources, including specific waste storage areas, are identified, their radionuclide inventories characterized, and their potential dose rates evaluated for worker protection?
data.answer:
The combined regulatory provisions requiring identification, characterization, and evaluation of all major sources—including specific waste storage areas—when establishing radiation zone designations in a radioactive waste building are found in DSRS 12.2 (Section II. Acceptance Criteria) and Regulatory Guide 1.143 (Regulatory Positions 4 and 5).

DSRS 12.2 mandates that descriptions be provided for all radiation sources requiring shielding, special storage, access control, or monitoring. These descriptions must include isotope, quantity, form, and use for all sources exceeding 3.7x10^9 Bq (100 millicuries), and must be detailed enough to support shielding design, facility features, exposure assessment, and dose determination. The guidance further requires plan scale drawings showing the location, size, and shape of each source, and quantitative source parameters. Both contained and airborne sources must be identified by location and magnitude to inform ventilation and monitoring system design. This ensures that all major sources, including waste storage areas, are identified, their radionuclide inventories characterized, and their potential dose rates evaluated for worker protection (DSRS 12.2, Section II).

Regulatory Guide 1.143 reinforces these requirements by specifying that radioactive waste management systems must be designed to maintain exposures as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA) and that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) must be classified based on the maximum inventory and potential unmitigated exposures. The classification system (RW-IIa, RW-IIb, RW-IIc) is based on the potential radiological release and dose to personnel, directly linking inventory characterization and dose evaluation to facility design and zone designation (RG 1.143, Regulatory Positions 4 and 5).

Together, these provisions require comprehensive identification, inventory characterization, and dose rate evaluation for all major sources in radioactive waste buildings to ensure adequate worker protection.

data.query: What are the NRC requirements for establishing qualification criteria for management and supervisory positions within the technical support organization of a nuclear power plant?
data.answer:
The NRC requires that applicants for nuclear power plants establish clear qualification criteria for management and supervisory positions within the technical support organization. According to SRP 13.1.1, applicants must provide detailed descriptions of educational and experience requirements for each management and supervisory position, including those providing technical support for plant operations. These requirements must be specified for each identified position or class of positions (SRP 13.1.1, Section III). Furthermore, applicants must commit that the experience and qualifications of management and technical support staff meet or exceed those endorsed by Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.8 (SRP 13.1.1, Section III.f).

RG 1.8 endorses ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, which sets forth the minimum experiential, professional, and educational requirements for such positions. The NRC staff accepts these criteria, with specific exceptions and clarifications, such as limiting temporary appointments of unqualified middle managers to one year and requiring that such appointees be supported by a qualified staff member (RG 1.8, Section C.1.1). This ensures that only qualified personnel are assigned to positions with specific requirements, maintaining the integrity of technical support functions.

Additionally, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, Criterion II, mandates that the quality assurance program must include measures to ensure that personnel performing and supervising activities affecting quality have the requisite experience, knowledge, and qualifications. Supervisors must possess qualifications commensurate with the scope, complexity, and importance of the activities they oversee, and appropriate indoctrination and training must be provided to maintain proficiency (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, Criterion II).

In summary, NRC requirements mandate that qualification criteria for management and supervisory positions in the technical support organization be clearly defined, meet or exceed the standards in RG 1.8 (and ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014), and ensure that personnel have the necessary education, experience, and training to safely and effectively perform their duties.

evidence_chain.section: C. STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, “Selection, Qualification, and Training of Personnel for Nuclear Power Plants,” provides criteria for the selection, qualification, and training of personnel for nuclear power plants for complying with the qualifications and training requirements of 10 CFR Parts 50 and 52. The NRC staff endorses ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, with the following exceptions and clarifications.

1. QUALIFICATION

The qualification criteria described in Section 4 of ANSI/ANS- 3.1-2014 are acceptable to the NRC staff with the following exceptions and clarifications. The minimum qualification requirements for positions as described in ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, including the exceptions and clarifications in this RG, represent the minimum experiential, professional, and educational requirements necessary to ensure that assigned personnel can independently evaluate risks and safely execute the responsibilities associated with the positions. To conform to this guidance, an individual assigned to a specific position must meet the requirements for that position.

1.1 Section 4.3, Middle Manager Level

Temporary appointments of unqualified middle managers shall be limited to one year in duration. During the temporary appointment, an unqualified middle manager shall be provided a single, directly-reporting staff member who meets the middle manager qualification position requirements to assist in decision-making.  The intention of this exception is to emphasize the importance of assigning qualified personnel to positions with specific requirements as described in ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, while allowing licensees adequate flexibility to manage human resources.  This flexibility is not intended to allow purposeful long-term assignment of unqualified personnel to middle manager positions or to allow multiple consecutive assignments of unqualified middle managers to a position.
