data.query: How do NRC regulations for radiation protection and decommissioning influence the qualification requirements for technical support and management personnel in nuclear facility organizations?
data.answer:
NRC regulations for radiation protection and decommissioning directly influence the qualification requirements for technical support and management personnel in nuclear facility organizations by mandating specific educational, experiential, and professional standards. According to SRP 13.1.1, applicants must describe and ensure that the qualifications of technical support and management personnel, particularly those involved in health physics (radiation protection), meet or exceed the standards endorsed by Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.8. This includes compliance with 10 CFR 50.34, which requires a detailed description of the organizational structure, qualifications, and responsibilities of facility personnel, as well as the managerial and administrative controls for safe operation and decommissioning (10 CFR Part 50 § 50.34(b)(7), (8), (9)).

RG 1.8 further specifies that the NRC endorses ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, which sets forth minimum qualification criteria for nuclear power plant personnel. For radiation protection management (RPM), the guidance requires not only the educational and experience requirements outlined in ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014 Section 4.3.3, but also additional onsite experience for new RPMs and relevant supervisory experience in in-field radiation protection activities. Temporary RPMs must also have first-line supervisory experience in radiation protection, and cannot serve in the role for more than one year without meeting full requirements.

Collectively, these requirements ensure that personnel responsible for radiation protection and decommissioning are technically qualified to manage radiological risks and implement NRC-mandated programs, thereby supporting the safe operation and eventual decommissioning of nuclear facilities (SRP 13.1.1; RG 1.8; 10 CFR 50.34).

data.query: For a nuclear facility's management and technical support organization, what combined regulatory guidance and review standards outline the process for defining qualification requirements for positions that provide technical support to the operating organization, and how should these requirements address both operational safety and long-term site decommissioning considerations?
data.answer:
The process for defining qualification requirements for positions providing technical support to the operating organization at a nuclear facility is outlined through a combination of regulatory guidance and review standards, primarily found in SRP 13.1.1, Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.8, and 10 CFR Part 50. 

SRP 13.1.1 (Section III) specifies that applicants must describe the educational and experience requirements for each identified technical support position, including management and supervisory roles. The applicant must ensure that the qualifications and experience of management and technical support staff meet or exceed those endorsed by RG 1.8, which is explicitly referenced as the standard for qualification and training of personnel (SRP 13.1.1, III; RG 1.8, Section C).

RG 1.8 endorses ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014 (with exceptions and clarifications), which provides detailed criteria for selection, qualification, and training of nuclear power plant personnel. Section 4 of ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, as accepted by RG 1.8, sets minimum experiential, professional, and educational requirements to ensure personnel can independently evaluate risks and safely execute their responsibilities (RG 1.8, Section C).

10 CFR 50.34(a)(6) and (9), and 50.34(b)(6), require applicants to describe the managerial and administrative controls, including the qualifications and responsibilities of management and technical personnel, as well as the organizational structure and technical qualifications necessary for safe operation and long-term activities. These requirements encompass both operational safety and long-term considerations such as decommissioning, as the technical qualifications and organizational controls must be sufficient for all phases of facility operation (10 CFR 50.34).

In summary, the combined guidance of SRP 13.1.1, RG 1.8 (endorsing ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014), and 10 CFR Part 50 establishes that qualification requirements for technical support positions must be clearly defined, documented, and meet or exceed NRC-endorsed standards, addressing both operational safety and the capability to support long-term site activities, including decommissioning.

data.query: What are the NRC requirements for establishing qualification criteria for management and supervisory positions within the technical support organization at a nuclear power plant?
data.answer:
The NRC requires that nuclear power plant applicants establish and document qualification criteria for management and supervisory positions within the technical support organization, as outlined in several regulatory documents. According to SRP 13.1.1, applicants must provide detailed descriptions of the educational and experience requirements for management and supervisory positions, including those within technical support units. Specifically, the applicant must describe the general educational and experience requirements for identified positions, and provide specific requirements for management and supervisory roles (SRP 13.1.1, Section III.c.iv, vi, and b). Furthermore, the applicant must commit that the qualifications and experience of management and technical support staff meet or exceed those endorsed by Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.8.

RG 1.8 endorses ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, which sets forth the criteria for selection, qualification, and training of nuclear power plant personnel. The NRC staff accepts the qualification criteria in Section 4 of ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, with certain exceptions and clarifications. For example, temporary appointments of unqualified middle managers are limited to one year, and such appointees must be supported by a qualified staff member. Additionally, operations middle managers and senior managers responsible for operations must hold a senior operator’s license, and shift managers must hold an active senior operator’s license while supervising plant operations (RG 1.8, Section C.1.1).

Finally, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, Criterion II, requires the establishment of a quality assurance program that includes indoctrination and training of personnel performing activities affecting quality, ensuring suitable proficiency is achieved and maintained. This requirement applies to all personnel, including management and supervisory staff, whose activities affect safety-related functions.

In summary, NRC requirements mandate that qualification criteria for management and supervisory positions in the technical support organization be clearly defined, documented, and consistent with the standards in RG 1.8 (ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014), and that these criteria are integrated into the plant’s quality assurance program as required by 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B.

1. QUALIFICATION

The qualification criteria described in Section 4 of ANSI/ANS- 3.1-2014 are acceptable to the NRC staff with the following exceptions and clarifications. The minimum qualification requirements for positions as described in ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, including the exceptions and clarifications in this RG, represent the minimum experiential, professional, and educational requirements necessary to ensure that assigned personnel can independently evaluate risks and safely execute the responsibilities associated with the positions. 1.1 Section 4.3, Middle Manager Level

Temporary appointments of unqualified middle managers shall be limited to one year in duration. During the temporary appointment, an unqualified middle manager shall be provided a single, directly-reporting staff member who meets the middle manager qualification position requirements to assist in decision-making.  The intention of this exception is to emphasize the importance of assigning qualified personnel to positions with specific requirements as described in ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, while allowing licensees adequate flexibility to manage human resources.  This flexibility is not intended to allow purposeful long-term assignment of unqualified personnel to middle manager positions or to allow multiple consecutive assignments of unqualified middle managers to a position.

At all times, an operations middle manager (Section 4.3.6) or a senior manager assigned responsibility for operations (Section 4.2) shall hold a senior operator’s license. A shift manager (Section 4.3.7) shall hold an active senior operator’s license while directly supervising plant operations.

data.query: How do NRC regulations regarding organizational structure interact with requirements for personnel qualifications in technical support organizations at nuclear facilities?
data.answer:
NRC regulations establish a clear interaction between organizational structure requirements and personnel qualification requirements for technical support organizations at nuclear facilities. According to SRP 13.1.1, the NRC reviews both the organizational structure—including organization charts, lines of authority, and personnel responsibilities—and the qualification and experience requirements for management and staff positions within technical support organizations. Applicants must provide detailed descriptions of the educational and experience requirements for each identified position, particularly for management and supervisory roles, and must ensure that these qualifications meet or exceed those endorsed by Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.8 (SRP 13.1.1, Section III).

10 CFR 50.34(b)(6) and (9) further require that license applications include descriptions of the organizational structure, assigned responsibilities, and the qualifications of both the applicant and operating personnel. This includes information on education, training, and experience to demonstrate that personnel are qualified to operate and maintain the facility safely (10 CFR 50.34).

RG 1.8 provides the NRC-endorsed method for meeting these requirements, referencing ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014 for the selection, qualification, and training of personnel. The guide clarifies that the minimum qualification requirements outlined in ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, as accepted by the NRC, represent the necessary experiential, professional, and educational standards for technical support positions. Thus, the organizational structure must be designed to ensure that all technical support roles are filled by individuals who meet these minimum qualifications (RG 1.8, Section C).

In summary, NRC regulations require that the organizational structure of technical support organizations at nuclear facilities is closely aligned with, and supports, the assignment of qualified personnel to all positions, ensuring safe and effective facility operation.

data.query: For a new nuclear power plant, what combined regulatory requirements and guidance documents must be considered when developing qualification standards for management and supervisory personnel who provide technical support to the operating organization, and how do these requirements ensure adequate technical resources are available?
data.answer:
When developing qualification standards for management and supervisory personnel who provide technical support to the operating organization of a new nuclear power plant, applicants must consider a combination of regulatory requirements and guidance documents. The primary regulatory requirements are found in 10 CFR Part 50, including Appendix B (Criteria II and III), which mandates a documented quality assurance program and design control measures, ensuring that responsible individuals have sufficient authority, organizational freedom, and qualifications (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, Criteria II and III; [2]). 

Applicants must also address the requirements of 10 CFR 50.34(b)(6)(i), which requires information on organizational structure and personnel qualifications, and 10 CFR 52.79(a)(26), which requires similar information for combined license applications ([3], RG 1.8, Introduction and Discussion). 

Guidance for meeting these requirements is provided by Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.8, which endorses ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014 (with exceptions and clarifications), specifying minimum experiential, professional, and educational requirements for technical support and management positions ([3], RG 1.8, Section C). SRP 13.1.1 further requires that applicants commit to meeting or exceeding the qualifications endorsed by RG 1.8 ([1], SRP 13.1.1, III.1.f). 

Additional relevant guidance includes SRP 13.2.1, which reinforces the commitment to RG 1.8 and ANSI/ANS-3.1, and SRP 13.5.1, which references qualification requirements for individuals involved in test procedure development and review, as described in Section 4.4.6 of ANS 3.1 ([4], SRP 13.2.1; [5], SRP 13.5.1).

These combined requirements and guidance ensure that technical support management and supervisory personnel are qualified to provide adequate technical resources by mandating documented qualification standards, periodic evaluation, and adherence to industry-accepted standards, thereby supporting safe and effective plant operation.

Criterion II—Quality Assurance Program
The applicant shall establish at the earliest practicable time, consistent with the schedule for accomplishing the activities, a quality assurance program which complies with the requirements of this appendix. Measures shall be established to assure that applicable regulatory requirements and the design basis, as defined in 10 CFR Part 50, are correctly translated into specifications, drawings, procedures, and instructions. This regulatory guide (RG) describes methods acceptable to the staff of the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) for complying with those portions of the Commission’s regulations associated with the selection, qualifications, and training for nuclear power plant personnel.

data.query: What are the NRC requirements for the training and qualification of non-licensed plant staff at nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC requires that non-licensed plant staff at nuclear power plants undergo a comprehensive training and qualification program to ensure safe and effective facility operation. According to SRP 13.2.2 Section III, the training program must include initial training, periodic retraining (at least every two years), and qualification for all non-licensed staff. The program must cover technical training specific to each position, as well as training in physical security, emergency protection, radiological emergency, administrative procedures, radiation protection, fire protection, quality assurance, and fitness for duty. 

Applicants must commit to following Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.8, which endorses ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014 (and previously ANSI/ANS-3.1-1993), specifying minimum qualification, education, experience, and training requirements for each position. The training must be based on a systems approach to training (SAT) as defined in 10 CFR 55.4, and must be established, implemented, and maintained at least 18 months prior to fuel load (SRP 13.2.2 Section III). 

10 CFR 50.120(b) further requires that the training program be derived from SAT, include all non-licensed positions performing safety-related functions, and be periodically evaluated and revised for effectiveness. Records of training and qualification must be maintained for at least three years after employment ends or until license termination (10 CFR 50.120(c)). 

In summary, NRC requirements mandate a structured, SAT-based training and qualification program for non-licensed plant staff, with periodic retraining, comprehensive subject coverage, and adherence to regulatory guidance and standards (SRP 13.2.2 Section III; RG 1.8 Section C; 10 CFR 50.120).

evidence_chain.section: § 50.120 Training and qualification of nuclear power plant personnel
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
§ 50.120 Training and qualification of nuclear power plant personnel.

(a) Applicability. The requirements of this section apply to each holder of an operating license issued under this part and each holder of a combined license issued under part 52 of this chapter after the Commission has made the finding under § 52.103(g) of this chapter.

(b) Requirements. Each licensee shall establish, implement, and maintain a training program for the training and qualification of nuclear power plant personnel. The training program must provide for the training and qualification of personnel to perform their assigned functions. The training program must be derived from a systems approach to training as defined in 10 CFR 55.4. The training program must include those non-licensed plant staff positions that perform safety-related functions as identified by the facility licensee. The training program must be periodically evaluated and revised as necessary to ensure its continued effectiveness.

(c) Records. The licensee shall maintain records of the training and qualification of nuclear power plant personnel who have been trained and qualified under the training program required by this section. These records must be retained for at least three years after the individual has left the employment of the licensee or until the Commission terminates the facility license, whichever is earlier.

data.query: How do NRC regulations for licensed operator training programs relate to the requirements for non-licensed plant staff training at nuclear facilities?
data.answer:
NRC regulations require both licensed operator and non-licensed plant staff training programs at nuclear facilities to be developed, implemented, and maintained using a systems approach to training (SAT), as defined in 10 CFR 55.4 (see SRP 13.2.2; 10 CFR 50.120(b)). While the licensed operator training program is specifically addressed in SRP 13.2.1 and must meet the requirements of 10 CFR 55.4 and 10 CFR 55.59, the non-licensed plant staff training program must also be SAT-based and cover additional areas such as physical security, emergency protection, radiological emergency, administrative procedures, radiation protection, fire protection, quality assurance, and fitness for duty (SRP 13.2.2).

Both programs are required by 10 CFR 50.120, which mandates that licensees establish, implement, and maintain training programs for all nuclear power plant personnel, including both licensed operators and non-licensed staff. Regulatory Guide 1.8, which is endorsed in both SRP 13.2.1 and 13.2.2, further clarifies that ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014 provides acceptable criteria for the selection, qualification, and training of all plant personnel, with minimum qualifications and training requirements specified for each position (RG 1.8, Section C).

In summary, NRC regulations establish a unified framework for training both licensed operators and non-licensed plant staff, requiring both groups to be trained under a SAT program that meets the standards set forth in 10 CFR 50.120, 10 CFR 55.4, and RG 1.8/ANSI/ANS-3.1. The main distinction is that licensed operator training must also meet the specific requirements of 10 CFR Part 55, while non-licensed staff training must address a broader range of plant support functions.

data.query: When developing training programs for both licensed operators and non-licensed plant staff at a nuclear power plant, what combined regulatory requirements and guidance must be met regarding program content, scheduling, and personnel categories to ensure compliance with NRC standards?
data.answer:
To ensure compliance with NRC standards when developing training programs for both licensed operators and non-licensed plant staff at a nuclear power plant, several combined regulatory requirements and guidance documents must be met regarding program content, scheduling, and personnel categories.

1. Personnel Categories: Training programs must address both licensed operators (including reactor operators and senior reactor operators) and non-licensed plant staff (such as non-licensed operators, shift supervisors, shift technical advisors, maintenance personnel, radiological protection technicians, chemistry technicians, and engineering support personnel) (SRP 13.2.2, Section I; 10 CFR 50.120(b)).

2. Program Content: The training must cover technical knowledge specific to each position and include areas such as physical security, emergency protection, radiological emergency, administrative procedures, radiation protection, fire protection, quality assurance, and fitness for duty for non-licensed staff (SRP 13.2.2, Section I). Licensed operator training must include classroom, on-the-job, and simulator training, and address all subjects required by 10 CFR Part 55 (SRP 13.2.1, Section I.e).

3. Regulatory Commitments: Programs must commit to the guidance of RG 1.8 (endorsing ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014 for selection, qualification, and training), RG 1.149 (for simulation facilities), and, for COL applicants, NEI 06-13A (SRP 13.2.1 and 13.2.2, Section I). The training must be based on a systems approach to training (SAT) as defined in 10 CFR 55.4 (SRP 13.2.1, III.d; SRP 13.2.2, I.d.vii; 10 CFR 50.120(b)).

4. Scheduling: Both licensed operator and non-licensed staff training programs must be established, implemented, and maintained at least 18 months prior to fuel load, with detailed schedules relative to the expected fuel load date and preoperational test period (SRP 13.2.1, I; SRP 13.2.2, I.d.v). Retraining/requalification must be periodic: for non-licensed staff, at least every two years (SRP 13.2.2, I.e); for licensed operators, requalification must be continuous and not exceed two years (SRP 13.2.1, I.f; 10 CFR 55.59).

5. Documentation and Effectiveness: Licensees must maintain records of training, qualification, and program effectiveness (10 CFR 50.120(b)).

6. Administrative Procedures: Administrative controls, including shift relief, turnover, working hours, and crane operations, must conform to referenced standards and regulatory guides (SRP 13.5.1, II).

In summary, compliance requires a SAT-based training program for all relevant personnel categories, adherence to referenced regulatory guides and standards, detailed content and scheduling, periodic retraining, and robust administrative controls, as specified in SRP 13.2.1, SRP 13.2.2, RG 1.8, 10 CFR 50.120, and related regulations.

The NRC staff endorses ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, with the following exceptions and clarifications.

1. QUALIFICATION

The qualification criteria described in Section 4 of ANSI/ANS- 3.1-2014 are acceptable to the NRC staff with the following exceptions and clarifications. The minimum qualification requirements for positions as described in ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, including the exceptions and clarifications in this RG, represent the minimum experiential, professional, and educational requirements necessary to ensure that assigned personnel can independently evaluate risks and safely execute the responsibilities associated with the positions. To conform to this guidance, an individual assigned to a specific position must meet the requirements for that position.

evidence_chain.section: § 50.120 Training and qualification of nuclear power plant personnel
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
§ 50.120 Training and qualification of nuclear power plant personnel.

(a) Applicability. The requirements of this section apply to each holder of an operating license issued under this part and each holder of a combined license issued under part 52 of this chapter after the Commission has made the finding under § 52.103(g) of this chapter.

(b) Requirements. Each licensee shall establish, implement, and maintain a training program. The training program must provide for the training and qualification of personnel to operate and maintain the facility safely and meet the requirements of 10 CFR 55.4 and 10 CFR 55.31 for licensed operators, and the requirements of 10 CFR 19.12 for instruction of workers. The training program must include the following categories of personnel:

(1) Non-licensed plant staff (including maintenance, technical, and supervisory personnel);
(2) Licensed operators; and
(3) Senior licensed operators.

The training program must be derived from a systems approach to training as defined in 10 CFR 55.4. The program must provide for periodic retraining and requalification of personnel. The licensee shall maintain records of the training and qualification of personnel and the program's effectiveness.

data.query: What are the NRC requirements for emergency planning regarding the provision of adequate facilities and equipment to support emergency response functions at a nuclear power plant site?
data.answer:
The NRC requires that nuclear power plant licensees provide adequate facilities and equipment to support emergency response functions as part of their emergency planning. According to 10 CFR 50.47(b)(8), the onsite emergency response plan must identify and describe the emergency facilities and equipment, and demonstrate that arrangements have been made for timely access to these resources. The plan must specifically address the adequacy of facilities such as the technical support center, operational support center, and emergency operations facility. Additionally, it must cover the communications systems, radiological monitoring equipment, and other necessary resources to support emergency response. The plan is also required to describe the processes for maintenance, testing, and upgrading of these facilities and equipment to ensure their continued availability and capability.

Supporting guidance, as referenced in SRP 13.3, includes NUREG-0654/FEMA-REP-1, Rev. 1, and NUREG-0696, which provide detailed criteria for the development and evaluation of emergency response facilities and systems. The NRC reviews emergency plans to confirm that any necessary updates to existing facilities and equipment are identified and implemented, ensuring compliance with the standards in 10 CFR 50.47(b) and Appendix E to 10 CFR Part 50. This comprehensive approach ensures that emergency response functions are adequately supported by appropriate and reliable facilities and equipment at nuclear power plant sites.

data.query: How do NRC requirements for emergency response facilities ensure that the technical support center provides radiological protection for personnel equivalent to that of the main control room during accident conditions?
data.answer:
NRC requirements ensure that the Technical Support Center (TSC) provides radiological protection for personnel equivalent to that of the main control room during accident conditions through a combination of regulatory mandates and detailed guidance. According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix E, Section IV.B, the TSC must be 'located and designed to provide for radiological protection of occupants during accident conditions, including the capability to maintain dose to personnel below the limits established for emergency workers, and, to the extent practicable, to provide a level of protection equivalent to that provided for the main control room.' This requirement is further supported by the standards in 10 CFR 50.47(b)(8), which mandate adequate emergency facilities and equipment to support emergency response.

The NRC’s Standard Review Plan (SRP 13.3) specifies that compliance with these requirements is determined using guidance from NUREG-0696, which details the functional criteria for emergency response facilities, including the TSC. NUREG-0696 addresses the need for a habitable TSC with adequate space, data retrieval, and communications, and emphasizes radiological protection comparable to the main control room. Supplement 1 to NUREG-0737 and Regulatory Guide 1.97 further clarify the instrumentation and monitoring requirements to ensure that both the main control room and the TSC can assess plant and environmental conditions during and after an accident.

In summary, NRC regulations and guidance collectively require that the TSC be designed and equipped to protect its occupants from radiological hazards during emergencies, aiming for a level of protection equivalent to the main control room, as practicable, thereby ensuring the safety of emergency response personnel (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix E, Section IV; SRP 13.3; NUREG-0696).

data.query: What structural features are required for a technical support center to meet NRC standards for habitability and emergency operations?
data.answer:
To meet NRC standards for habitability and emergency operations, a technical support center (TSC) must incorporate several specific structural features. According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix E, Section IV.A.1, the TSC must be located onsite but outside the control room and any area that could become uninhabitable due to a radiological accident. This ensures the TSC remains operational during emergencies. The TSC must provide adequate communications, radiological monitoring, and habitability features to support effective emergency response. It must be capable of accommodating key technical support personnel and protecting them from radiological and other hazards likely to result from an accident. Additionally, the TSC must be equipped with the necessary instrumentation, displays, and controls to allow technical support personnel to assess plant conditions and recommend corrective actions.

SRP 13.3 further clarifies that the TSC should have adequate space, data retrieval capabilities, and dedicated communications equipment. The acceptance criteria reference NUREG-0696, which provides detailed guidance on the facilities and systems required to support emergency response, and NUREG-0654/FEMA-REP-1, Rev. 1, which establishes an acceptable basis for emergency plans and procedures. These documents, endorsed by Regulatory Guide 1.101, Rev. 2, are considered acceptable methods for complying with NRC standards in 10 CFR 50.47.

In summary, the TSC must be structurally designed to remain habitable and functional during emergencies, with sufficient space, protection, communications, monitoring, and assessment capabilities as outlined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix E, and supported by SRP 13.3 and referenced guidance documents.

evidence_chain.section: Appendix E to Part 50—Emergency Planning and Preparedness for Production and Utilization Facilities, Section IV.A.1
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appendix E to Part 50—Emergency Planning and Preparedness for Production and Utilization Facilities

Section IV. Emergency Response Organization

A. Each licensee shall establish an emergency response organization with the capability to respond to emergency situations. The organization shall include, but not be limited to, the following facilities and equipment:

1. A technical support center (TSC) located onsite, but outside the control room and outside any area that may become uninhabitable as a result of a radiological accident. The TSC shall be provided with adequate communications, radiological monitoring, and habitability features to permit effective emergency response. The TSC shall have the capability to accommodate key technical support personnel and provide for their protection from radiological and other hazards likely to result from an accident. The TSC shall be provided with the necessary instrumentation, displays, and controls to allow technical support personnel to assess plant conditions and recommend corrective actions.

2. An operations support center (OSC) and an emergency operations facility (EOF) with similar requirements for communications, habitability, and radiological protection, as appropriate to their functions.

data.query: What are the NRC requirements for the technical support center to have backup power to maintain emergency response functions during a loss of offsite power?
data.answer:
The NRC requires that the technical support center (TSC) at nuclear power plants be equipped with backup power to ensure that emergency response functions can be maintained during a loss of offsite power. Specifically, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix E, Section IV.2(b) mandates that licensees provide emergency power for emergency response facilities and equipment, including the TSC, to ensure continuity of emergency response functions during a loss of offsite power (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix E, Section IV.2(b)). This requirement is further supported by 10 CFR 50.47(b)(8), which states that adequate emergency facilities and equipment must be provided and maintained.

The Standard Review Plan (SRP 13.3) and associated guidance documents, such as NUREG-0696 and NUREG-0654/FEMA-REP-1, are used to determine compliance with these regulations. These documents specify that the TSC must be habitable and have adequate space, data retrieval capabilities, and dedicated communications equipment, all of which must remain operational during emergencies, including loss of offsite power (SRP 13.3, Section II).

Regulatory Guide 1.32 and IEEE Std. 308-2020 provide acceptable methods for designing and testing electric power systems, including requirements for onsite and offsite power systems to support emergency functions (RG 1.32, Section C). In the event of a station blackout, RG 1.155 (Regulatory Position 3.2 and 3.3) recommends that battery capacity be sufficient to support required loads for the duration of the blackout, and, if necessary, additional batteries or independent charging systems (such as dedicated diesel generators) should be provided to ensure continued operation of emergency response facilities like the TSC.

In summary, NRC regulations and guidance require that the TSC have reliable backup power—typically through batteries and/or independent generators—to maintain emergency response capabilities during a loss of offsite power, in accordance with 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix E, and supporting regulatory guidance.

data.query: How do NRC regulations for emergency planning require the technical support center to provide access to key plant parameters and ensure data availability during accident conditions?
data.answer:
NRC regulations require that the Technical Support Center (TSC) be equipped to provide access to key plant parameters and ensure data availability during accident conditions through several specific provisions. According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix E, Section IV.A, each licensee must establish a TSC that enables the acquisition, display, and evaluation of information necessary for technical staff to assess plant conditions, perform accident assessment, and determine mitigation strategies. The TSC must have direct communications with the control room, plant systems, and other emergency response facilities, and must have access to plant parameter data and radiological information. Furthermore, the TSC is required to remain habitable and functional during accident conditions, including scenarios involving loss of offsite power (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix E, Section IV.A).

Supporting guidance in SRP 13.3 elaborates that the TSC must have adequate space, data retrieval capabilities, and dedicated communications equipment. The review of information systems important to safety, including instrumentation to assess plant conditions during and after an accident, is addressed under SRP Section 7.5. This includes the Safety Parameter Display System (SPDS), which provides critical plant data to emergency response personnel. Additionally, Section VI of Appendix E to 10 CFR Part 50 requires an Emergency Response Data System (ERDS), which ensures near real-time electronic data transmission from the licensee’s onsite computer system to the NRC Operations Center during emergencies. NUREG-1394 provides the minimum standards for ERDS implementation. Collectively, these requirements ensure that the TSC has reliable access to essential plant parameters and maintains data availability to support effective emergency response during accident conditions.

data.query: For a new nuclear power plant design, what combined regulatory requirements and guidance specify the necessary features of the technical support center related to data acquisition, display, backup power, and the ability to support emergency response functions, including the display of meteorological and radiological information during accident scenarios?
data.answer:
The combined regulatory requirements and guidance for the Technical Support Center (TSC) in a new nuclear power plant design specify several key features related to data acquisition, display, backup power, and emergency response support, including the display of meteorological and radiological information during accident scenarios.

According to Appendix E to 10 CFR Part 50, Section IV.A, each licensee must establish and maintain an onsite TSC equipped to acquire and display data from the reactor and associated systems, including radiological and meteorological information, and must have backup power sources to maintain these functions during emergencies. The TSC must also support emergency response functions such as communications, data assessment, and coordination with offsite authorities (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix E, Section IV.A; [2]).

SRP 13.3 further clarifies that the TSC must be habitable, have adequate space, data retrieval capabilities, dedicated communications equipment, and the ability to display meteorological and radiological data. The TSC must comply with the standards in 10 CFR 50.47(b), Appendix E to 10 CFR Part 50, and guidance in NUREG-0654/FEMA-REP-1, NUREG-0696, and Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.101. NUREG-0696 and Supplement 1 to NUREG-0737 specify the need for reliable meteorological variable indication in the TSC and other emergency facilities ([1]).

RG 1.23 and RG 1.97 provide acceptable methods for implementing these requirements. RG 1.23 states that meteorological data (wind speed, direction, atmospheric stability) must be available in the TSC and provided to the NRC’s Emergency Response Data System (ERDS) in near real-time, supporting ongoing assessment of atmospheric transport and diffusion following an accidental release ([3]). RG 1.97, endorsing IEEE Std. 497-2016, requires instrumentation for monitoring plant and environmental variables (including radiological releases) over ranges appropriate for accident conditions, with sufficient margin and reliability to support emergency response and accident management ([4]).

In summary, the TSC must have: (1) systems for acquiring and displaying reactor, radiological, and meteorological data; (2) backup power to maintain these functions during emergencies; (3) communications and data assessment capabilities; and (4) compliance with ERDS data transmission requirements. These features are mandated by 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix E, and further detailed in SRP 13.3, NUREG-0654/FEMA-REP-1, NUREG-0696, RG 1.23, and RG 1.97.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory expectations regarding the use of conservatively biased initial conditions versus nominal initial conditions when analyzing limiting radiological consequences for steam system piping failure events in pressurized water reactors?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory expectations regarding the use of conservatively biased initial conditions versus nominal initial conditions in the analysis of limiting radiological consequences for steam system piping failure events in pressurized water reactors are clearly articulated in DSRS 15.1.5. Specifically, the NRC expects that initial plant conditions and postulated system failures should be selected to maximize the consequences of the accident, not merely reflect nominal or average values. Sensitivity studies are required to determine the most conservative combination of power level and plant operating mode, and these studies should be documented and justified in the technical submittal (DSRS 15.1.5, Section II). For example, the initial core flow assumed in the analysis should be chosen based on which value (minimum or maximum) leads to the most limiting consequences, with justification provided for the selected value.

Additionally, DSRS 4.4 emphasizes that uncertainties in process parameters and calculational methods must be addressed, typically by ensuring at least a 95-percent probability at the 95-percent confidence level that safety limits are not exceeded. This further supports the use of conservative assumptions rather than nominal values when analyzing accident scenarios (DSRS 4.4, Section II).

Regulatory Guide 1.68 and SRP 14.2 reinforce the requirement that the assumptions used in safety analyses must be verified for correctness or conservatism, and any exceptions or alternatives must be adequately justified and reviewed on a case-by-case basis (RG 1.68, Sections A and B; SRP 14.2, Section II).

In summary, NRC regulatory guidance requires the use of conservatively biased initial conditions—those that maximize the limiting radiological consequences—rather than nominal initial conditions, with the basis for these choices clearly justified and documented.

data.query: How do general design criteria for protection against anticipated operational occurrences relate to the regulatory expectations for conservative assumptions in the analysis of steam system piping failures inside and outside containment?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for protection against anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs) establish regulatory expectations for the use of conservative assumptions in the analysis of steam system piping failures both inside and outside containment. Specifically, DSRS 15.1.5 outlines that analyses must use initial plant conditions and postulated system failures that maximize the consequences of the accident, requiring sensitivity studies to determine the most conservative combination of parameters (DSRS 15.1.5, Section II). For example, the assumption of a loss of offsite power (LOOP) must be considered in addition to any limiting single active failure, as required by GDC 17, to ensure that the safety functions of onsite and offsite power systems are maintained and that fuel design limits and reactor coolant pressure boundary conditions are not exceeded during AOOs.

GDC 13 further requires instrumentation and controls to monitor and maintain variables within prescribed ranges during normal operation, AOOs, and accident conditions (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 13). This supports the need for conservative assumptions in analyses to ensure that instrumentation and control systems can adequately respond to worst-case scenarios.

Additionally, DSRS 4.4 emphasizes that uncertainties in process parameters, core design, and calculational methods must be treated with at least a 95-percent probability at the 95-percent confidence level, ensuring that the analysis of thermal margins and fuel design limits is conservative and robust (DSRS 4.4, Section II). This approach ensures that the most limiting conditions are considered, consistent with the intent of the GDCs to protect public health and safety during AOOs, including steam system piping failures.

In summary, the GDCs require that analyses of steam system piping failures inside and outside containment use conservative assumptions regarding initial conditions, system failures, and uncertainties, as detailed in DSRS 15.1.5 and DSRS 4.4, to ensure compliance with regulatory requirements for safety system performance during AOOs.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
There are certain assumptions regarding important parameters used to describe the initial plant conditions and postulated system failures which should be used. These are listed below:

1. The reactor power level, other plant operating mode parameters assumed at the initiation of the transient should correspond to the operating condition that maximizes the consequences of the accident. Sensitivity studies will be required to determine the most conservative combination of power level and plant operating mode. These sensitivity studies may be presented in a generic report and referenced in the technical submittal.

2. Assumptions as to the loss of offsite power (LOOP) and the time of loss should be made to study their effects on the consequences of the accident. A LOOP could occur simultaneously with the pipe break or during the accident, or offsite power might not be lost. Analyses should be made to determine the most conservative assumption appropriate to the particular plant design. The reviewer should note that the assumption that offsite power is not lost may maximize heat removal from the core and reactor system and thereby maximize containment pressure and reactivity feedback within the core. The analyses should take account of the effect that LOOP has on the main feedwater pump trips, on the initiation of the decay heat removal system and the effects on the sequence of events for these accidents. For new applications, LOOP should be considered in addition to any limiting single active failure. (This position is based upon interpretation of GDC 17, as documented in the final safety analysis report (FSAR) for the ABB-CE System 80+ DC.)

... 

The technical rationale for application of these acceptance criteria to the areas of review addressed by this DSRS section is discussed in the following paragraphs:   

1. Compliance with GDC 13 requires the provision of instrumentation to monitor variables and systems over their anticipated ranges and of appropriate controls that can maintain listed variables and systems within prescribed operating ranges.
...
2. Compliance with GDC 17 requires in part that onsite and offsite electrical power systems be provided to permit functioning of structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety. The safety function for each power system (assuming the other system is not functioning) shall be to provide sufficient capacity and capability to ensure that (1) the specified acceptable fuel design limits and the design conditions of the reactor coolant pressure boundary are not exceeded as a result of anticipated operational occurrences, and (2) the core is cooled and containment integrity and other vital functions are maintained.

GDC 17 is applicable to this section because it requires that the LOOP be considered not as a single failure event, but assumed in the analyses for each event without changing the event category. data.query: What regulatory guidance addresses the selection of initial conditions and key assumptions, such as heat transfer and tube plugging, to ensure conservative outcomes in the minimum critical heat flux ratio analysis for steam line break events?
data.answer:
The regulatory guidance addressing the selection of initial conditions and key assumptions—such as heat transfer and tube plugging—to ensure conservative outcomes in the minimum critical heat flux ratio (MCHFR) analysis for steam line break events is primarily found in DSRS 15.1.5, with supporting criteria from DSRS 4.4, 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A, SRP 14.2, and RG 1.68.

DSRS 15.1.5 (Section II) specifies that initial plant conditions and postulated system failures must be chosen to maximize the consequences of the accident, thereby ensuring conservative analysis. This includes selecting the reactor power level and plant operating mode that yield the most limiting results, performing sensitivity studies to justify these choices, and considering the effects of loss of offsite power, control rod positions, core burnup, and initial core flow. For example, the guidance notes that maximum initial core flow may be more conservative for steam line break analysis due to its impact on RCS cooldown and recriticality potential, and the assumed value must be justified.

DSRS 4.4 (Section II) further requires that uncertainties in process parameters (e.g., reactor power, coolant flow, temperature, and pressure) and calculational methods be treated with at least a 95-percent probability at the 95-percent confidence level. This includes accounting for uncertainties in instrumentation and the origins of each uncertainty parameter, ensuring that the assessment of thermal margin (including CHF) is robust and conservative.

10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 13, establishes the foundational requirement for instrumentation and control to monitor and maintain key plant variables within prescribed limits during both normal and accident conditions, supporting the selection of conservative initial conditions and assumptions.

SRP 14.2 and RG 1.68 emphasize the need for initial test programs and validation of analytical models and assumptions used in accident analyses, including those related to heat transfer and tube plugging. These documents require that the correctness or conservatism of assumptions be verified through testing and that the performance of safety-related SSCs be demonstrated under conditions representative of those assumed in the safety analysis.

In summary, DSRS 15.1.5 provides direct guidance on selecting conservative initial conditions and key assumptions for MCHFR analysis in steam line break events, supported by requirements for uncertainty treatment (DSRS 4.4), instrumentation (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A), and validation through testing (SRP 14.2, RG 1.68).

evidence_chain.section: II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
There are certain assumptions regarding important parameters used to describe the initial plant conditions and postulated system failures which should be used. These are listed below:

1. The reactor power level, other plant operating mode parameters assumed at the initiation of the transient should correspond to the operating condition that maximizes the consequences of the accident. Sensitivity studies will be required to determine the most conservative combination of power level and plant operating mode. These sensitivity studies may be presented in a generic report and referenced in the technical submittal.

2. Assumptions as to the loss of offsite power (LOOP) and the time of loss should be made to study their effects on the consequences of the accident. ... Analyses should be made to determine the most conservative assumption appropriate to the particular plant design. ...

5. The maximum-worth control rod should be assumed to be held in the fully withdrawn position. An appropriate rod reactivity worth versus rod position curve should be used. Local power peaking at the location of the stuck out control rod should be considered. Local power peaking will affect the DNBR analysis in the initial period as the safety rods are entering the core and during any subsequent return to power resulting from reactivity addition to the core from the cooldown.

6. The core burnup (time in core life) should be selected to yield the most limiting combination of moderator temperature reactivity feedback, void reactivity feedback, Doppler reactivity feedback, axial power profile, and radial power distribution.

7. The initial core flow assumed for the analysis of the steam line rupture accident should be chosen conservatively. If the minimum core flow allowed by the technical specifications is assumed, the minimum DNBR margin results; however, for the analysis of steam line break accidents, this may not be the most conservative assumption. For example, maximum initial core flow results in increased RCS cooldown and depressurization, decreased shutdown margin, and an increased possibility that the core will become critical and return to power. Because it is not clear what initial core flow is most conservative, the assumed value should be justified.

evidence_chain.section: B. DISCUSSION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
The applicant for an OL under 10 CFR Part 50, or a COL under 10 CFR Part 52, is responsible for ensuring that a suitable initial (preoperational and startup) test program will be conducted for the facility.  The primary objectives of a suitable program are:  

1. Provide additional assurance that the facility has been adequately designed. 

2. Validate, to the extent practical, the analytical models. 

3. Verify the correctness or conservatism of assumptions used to predict plant responses to anticipated transients and postulated accidents. 

4. Provide assurance that construction and installation of equipment in the facility have been accomplished in accordance with design. 

5. Familiarize the plant’s operating and technical staff with the operation of the facility.  

6. Verify by trial use, to the extent practical, that the facility operating procedures and emergency procedures are adequate.   

The ITP may include system and component tests, monitoring of SSC performance, and inspection and surveillance test activities for plant SSCs.  An ITP satisfying these objectives should provide the necessary assurance that the facility can be operated in accordance with design requirements and in a manner that will not endanger the health and safety of the public.

As previously noted, the ITP consists of preoperational and initial startup tests.  “Preoperational testing,” as used in this regulatory guide, consists of those tests conducted following completion of construction inspections and tests, but before fuel loading, to demonstrate, to the extent practical, the capability of SSCs to meet the performance requirements to satisfy the design criteria.  

Initial startup testing, as used in this regulatory guide, consists of equipment performance tests completed during and after fuel loading.  These performance tests are normally completed during fuel loading, pre-critical, initial criticality, low power and power ascension phases to confirm the design bases and demonstrate, to the extent practical, that the plant will operate in accordance with design and that it is capable of responding to anticipated transients and postulated accidents as specified in the FSAR.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for the analysis of loss of non-emergency AC power to station auxiliaries in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for the analysis of loss of non-emergency AC power to station auxiliaries in nuclear power plants are primarily outlined in DSRS 15.2.6, Section II. The criteria are based on compliance with several General Design Criteria (GDCs) from 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, specifically GDC 10 (Reactor Design), GDC 13 (Instrumentation and Control), GDC 15 (Reactor Coolant System Design), and GDC 26 (Reactivity Control System Redundancy and Capability). The specific acceptance criteria are as follows:

1. The pressure in the reactor coolant and main steam systems must be maintained below 110 percent of their design values.
2. Fuel cladding integrity must be ensured by keeping the minimum departure from nucleate boiling ratio (DNBR) above the 95/95 DNBR limit, as described in DSRS Section 4.4, which requires at least a 95-percent probability at the 95-percent confidence level that the hottest fuel rod does not experience a boiling crisis during normal operation or anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs).
3. An incident of moderate frequency, such as loss of non-emergency AC power, should not escalate to a more serious plant condition without other independent faults.
4. The analysis must consider the most limiting single failure, as defined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, and satisfy the positions of Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.53, which endorses IEEE Std 379-2000 for the application of the single-failure criterion to safety systems.
5. Analytical models used in the transient analysis must be NRC-approved and employ suitably conservative parameter values, including:
   - Initial power level at licensed core thermal power plus a 2% allowance for measurement uncertainty (unless justified otherwise).
   - Conservative scram characteristics, assuming maximum time delay and the most reactive rod stuck out.
   - Core burn-up conditions that yield the most limiting combination of reactivity feedbacks and power distributions.
   - Mitigating system actuation at setpoints that account for instrument inaccuracy, in accordance with RG 1.105.

Additionally, the applicant must provide abstracts of planned tests to verify the performance of systems, structures, and components (SSCs) used for safe shutdown and cooldown, including test objectives, methods, and acceptance criteria (SRP 14.2). These criteria collectively ensure that the plant remains within safety limits and that fuel and pressure boundary integrity are maintained during the loss of non-emergency AC power events.

II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

Requirements

Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations:

1. General Design Criterion (GDC) 10, “Reactor Design,” as to reactor coolant system (RCS) design with appropriate margin so specified acceptable fuel design limits are not exceeded during normal operation including anticipated operational occurrences.

2. GDC 13, “Instrumentation and Control,” as to the availability of instrumentation to monitor variables and systems over their anticipated ranges to assure adequate safety, and of appropriate controls to maintain these variables and systems within prescribed operating ranges.

3. GDC 15, “Reactor Coolant System Design,” as to design of the RCS and its auxiliaries with appropriate margin so the pressure boundary is not breached during normal operation including anticipated operational occurrences.

4. GDC 26, “Reactivity Control System Redundancy and Capability,” as to reliable control of reactivity changes so specified acceptable fuel design limits are not exceeded in anticipated operational occurrences. This control is accomplished by appropriate margin for malfunctions like stuck rods.

DSRS Acceptance Criteria

Specific DSRS acceptance criteria acceptable to meet the relevant requirements of the NRC’s regulations identified above are set forth below. ...

Specific criteria necessary to meet the relevant requirements of GDCs 10, 13, 15, and 26 for events of moderate frequency ... are as follow:

1. Pressure in the reactor coolant and main steam systems should be maintained below 110 percent of the design values.

2. Fuel cladding integrity should be maintained by keeping the minimum departure from nucleate boiling ratio (DNBR) above the 95/95 DNBR limit based on acceptable correlations (see DSRS Section 4.4).

3. An incident of moderate frequency should not generate a more serious plant condition without other faults occurring independently.

4. For the requirements of GDCs 10 and 15, the positions of Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.105, “Setpoints for Safety-Related Systems,” affect the plant response to the type of transient addressed in this DSRS section.

5. The most limiting plant system single failure, as defined in the “Definitions and Explanations” of Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) Part 50, Appendix A, must be assumed in the analysis and must satisfy the positions of RG 1.53, “Application of the Single-Failure Criterion to Nuclear Power Plant Protection Systems.”

The applicant’s analysis of the loss-of-ac-power transient should be based on an acceptable and NRC-approved model. ... The parameter values in the analytical model should be suitably conservative. The following values are acceptable:

A. The initial power level is taken as the licensed core thermal power plus an allowance of 2 percent to account for power measurement uncertainties unless the applicant can justify a lower power level.

B. Conservative scram characteristics are assumed (i.e., for the maximum time delay with the most reactive rod held out of the core).

C. The core burn-up is selected to yield the most limiting combination of moderator temperature reactivity feedback, void reactivity feedback, Doppler reactivity feedback, power profile, and radial power distribution.

D. Mitigating systems should be assumed to be actuated in the analyses at setpoints with allowance for instrument inaccuracy in accordance with RG 1.105. Compliance with RG 1.105 is determined.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating the loss of non-emergency AC power to station auxiliaries in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating the loss of non-emergency AC power to station auxiliaries in nuclear power plants are grounded in compliance with several General Design Criteria (GDCs) and regulatory guidance. According to DSRS 15.2.6 (Section II), the relevant GDCs are:

- GDC 10 (Reactor Design): The reactor coolant system (RCS) must be designed with sufficient margin to ensure that specified acceptable fuel design limits are not exceeded during normal operation and anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs) (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 10).
- GDC 13 (Instrumentation and Control): Instrumentation must be available to monitor variables and systems over their anticipated ranges to assure adequate safety, and appropriate controls must be available to maintain these variables and systems within prescribed operating ranges.
- GDC 15 (Reactor Coolant System Design): The RCS and its auxiliaries must be designed with appropriate margin so the pressure boundary is not breached during normal operation and AOOs.
- GDC 26 (Reactivity Control System Redundancy and Capability): Reliable control of reactivity changes must be ensured so that specified acceptable fuel design limits are not exceeded in AOOs.

Specific DSRS acceptance criteria for events of moderate frequency, such as loss of non-emergency AC power, include:
1. Reactor coolant and main steam system pressures must remain below 110% of design values.
2. Fuel cladding integrity must be maintained by keeping the minimum departure from nucleate boiling ratio (DNBR) above the 95/95 DNBR limit, as detailed in DSRS Section 4.4.
3. The event should not escalate to a more serious plant condition without additional independent faults.
4. Setpoints for safety-related systems must conform to RG 1.105.
5. The analysis must assume the most limiting single failure, as defined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, and satisfy the single-failure criterion per RG 1.53 and IEEE Std 379-2000.

Additionally, SRP 14.2 requires that applicants provide test abstracts demonstrating the performance of systems, structures, and components (SSCs) used for safe shutdown and cooldown under such conditions, including acceptance criteria to verify functional adequacy.

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria focus on maintaining fuel and pressure boundary integrity, ensuring reliable instrumentation and control, applying the single-failure criterion, and verifying system performance through testing, as specified in DSRS 15.2.6, 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A, RG 1.53, and SRP 14.2.

II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

Requirements

Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations:

1. General Design Criterion (GDC), 10 Reactor Design.   
2. GDC 12, Suppression of Reactor Power Oscillations .  
3. Section 52.47(b)(1) Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR 52.47(b)(1)), which requires that a DC application contain the proposed ITAAC that are necessary and sufficient to provide reasonable assurance that, if the inspections, tests, and analyses are performed and the acceptance criteria met, a facility that incorporates the design certification has been constructed and will be operated in conformity with the design certification, the provisions of the Atomic Energy Act (AEA), and the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s (NRC) rules and regulations.   
4. 10 CFR 52.80(a), which requires that a COL application contain the proposed inspections, tests, and analyses, including those applicable to emergency planning, that the licensee shall perform, and the acceptance criteria that are necessary and sufficient to provide reasonable assurance that, if the inspections, tests, and analyses are performed and the acceptance criteria met, the facility has been constructed and will operate in conformity with the combined license, the provisions of the AEA, and the NRC's rules and regulations.   

DSRS Acceptance Criteria

Specific DSRS acceptance criteria acceptable to meet the relevant requirements of the NRC’s regulations identified above are set forth below.  The DSRS is not a substitute for the NRC’s regulations, and compliance with it is not required.  As an alternative, and as described in more detail below, an applicant may identify the differences between a DSRS section and the design features (DC and COL applications only), analytical techniques, and procedural measures proposed in an application and discuss how the proposed alternative provides an acceptable method of complying with the NRC regulations that underlie the DSRS acceptance criteria.

Specific criteria necessary to meet the requirements of GDC 10 and GDC 12 are as follows:

1. SRP Section 4.2 specifies the acceptance criteria for the evaluation of fuel design limits.  One criterion provides assurance that there be at least a 95-percent probability at the 95-percent confidence level that the hot fuel rod in the core does not experience a boiling crisis during normal operation or AOOs.   

Uncertainties in the values of process parameters (e.g., reactor power, coolant flow rate, core bypass flow, inlet temperature and pressure, nuclear and engineering hot channel factors), core design parameters, and calculational methods used in the assessment of thermal margin should be treated with at least a 95-percent probability at the 95-percent confidence level.  The assessment of thermal margin should also consider the uncertainties in instrumentation.  The origin of each uncertainty parameter, such as fabrication uncertainty, computational uncertainty, or measurement uncertainty e.g., reactor power, coolant temperature, flow, should be identified.  Each uncertainty parameter should be identified as statistical or deterministic and should clearly describe the methodologies used to combine uncertainties.   

The following is an example of acceptable approaches to meeting this criterion:   

A. For CHF correlations, there should be a 95-percent probability at the 95-percent confidence level that the hot rod in the core does not experience a boiling crisis during normal operation or AOOs.   

Correlations of CHF are continually being revised as a result of additional experimental data, changes in fuel assembly design, and improved calculational techniques involving coolant mixing and the effect of axial power distributions.

data.query: How do general design criteria for safety system independence relate to the regulatory requirements for analyzing the loss of non-emergency AC power events in nuclear facilities?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for safety system independence are directly related to the regulatory requirements for analyzing loss of non-emergency AC power events in nuclear facilities. According to DSRS 15.2.6, the analysis of such events must demonstrate compliance with several GDCs, including GDC 10, 13, 15, and 26, as outlined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A. These criteria require that the reactor core and associated systems are designed with sufficient margin to prevent exceeding fuel design limits (GDC 10), ensure adequate instrumentation and control (GDC 13), maintain the integrity of the reactor coolant system (GDC 15), and provide reliable reactivity control (GDC 26).

A key aspect of these requirements is the application of the single-failure criterion, as specified in RG 1.53 and referenced in DSRS 15.2.6. This criterion mandates that safety systems must be capable of performing their required functions even in the presence of any single failure, including during a loss of non-emergency AC power. The analysis must assume the most limiting single failure, ensuring that the safety systems remain independent and effective under such conditions. RG 1.53 further clarifies that this includes failures in electrical power, instrumentation, and control systems, and that conformance with IEEE standards (such as IEEE Std 379-2000) is an acceptable method for demonstrating compliance.

In summary, the general design criteria for safety system independence ensure that, during a loss of non-emergency AC power event, the plant's safety systems are sufficiently independent and robust to handle the event and any single failure, thereby maintaining core and fuel integrity, system monitoring, and control as required by NRC regulations (DSRS 15.2.6; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 10, 13, 15, 26; RG 1.53).

evidence_chain.section: II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA and Technical Rationale
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

Requirements

Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations:

1. General Design Criterion (GDC) 10, “Reactor Design,” as to reactor coolant system (RCS) design with appropriate margin so specified acceptable fuel design limits are not exceeded during normal operation including anticipated operational occurrences.

2. GDC 13, “Instrumentation and Control,” as to the availability of instrumentation to monitor variables and systems over their anticipated ranges to assure adequate safety, and of appropriate controls to maintain these variables and systems within prescribed operating ranges.

3. GDC 15, “Reactor Coolant System Design,” as to design of the RCS and its auxiliaries with appropriate margin so the pressure boundary is not breached during normal operation including anticipated operational occurrences.

4. GDC 26, “Reactivity Control System Redundancy and Capability,” as to reliable control of reactivity changes so specified acceptable fuel design limits are not exceeded in anticipated operational occurrences. This control is accomplished by appropriate margin for malfunctions like stuck rods.

...

5. The most limiting plant system single failure, as defined in the “Definitions and Explanations” of Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) Part 50, Appendix A, must be assumed in the analysis and must satisfy the positions of RG 1.53, “Application of the Single-Failure Criterion to Nuclear Power Plant Protection Systems.”

The applicant’s analysis of the loss-of-ac-power transient should be based on an acceptable and NRC-approved model. ...

Technical Rationale

The technical rationale for application of these acceptance criteria to the areas of review addressed by this DSRS section is discussed in the following paragraphs:

1. GDC 10 requires that the reactor core and its coolant, control, and protection systems be designed with appropriate margin so specified acceptable fuel design limits are not exceeded during any condition of normal operation, including the effects of anticipated operational occurrences.

GDC 10 applies to this section because the reviewer evaluates the consequences of the loss of nonemergency ac power to the station auxiliaries. This anticipated operational occurrence creates a potential for specified acceptable fuel design limits to be exceeded. Within seconds after the loss of power, the turbine and the reactor both trip, and the pressure and temperature of the reactor coolant increase. RG 1.53 provides guidance for application of the single-failure criterion to the design and analysis of nuclear power plant protection systems. RG 1.105 describes a method acceptable to the staff for keeping instrument setpoints within the technical specification limits.

GDC 10 requirements provide assurance that specified acceptable fuel design limits are not exceeded and that fuel cladding integrity is maintained in loss of nonemergency ac power to the station auxiliaries.

2. GDC 13 requires the provision of instrumentation that is capable of monitoring variables and systems over their anticipated ranges to assure adequate safety, and of controls that can maintain these variables and systems within prescribed operating ranges.

GDC 13 applies to this section because the reviewer evaluates the sequence of events, including automatic actuations of protection systems, and manual actions, and determines whether the sequence of events is justified, based upon the expected values of the relevant monitored parameters and instrument indications.

3. GDC 15 requires that the RCS and its auxiliary, control, and protection systems be designed with sufficient margin so design conditions of the reactor coolant pressure boundary are not exceeded during any condition of normal operation, including anticipated operational occurrences. GDC 15 applies to this section because the reviewer evaluates the consequences of the loss of nonemergency ac power to the station auxiliaries. This transient is an anticipated operational occurrence, and the reactor coolant pressure must be analyzed to confirm whether the pressure acceptance criterion is satisfied.

GDC 15 requirements provide assurance that the design conditions of the reactor coolant pressure boundary are not exceeded in the loss of nonemergency ac power to the station auxiliaries.

4. GDC 26 requires that one of the reactivity control systems consist of control rods capable of reliably controlling reactivity changes with appropriate margin for malfunctions like stuck rods so that specified acceptable fuel design limits are not exceeded under conditions of normal operation, including anticipated operational occurrences.

GDC 26 applies because the transient analyzed in this section involves the movement of control rods in response to the loss of nonemergency ac power and because rod misalignment, including stuck rods, can produce thermal-hydraulic conditions more severe than otherwise. GDC 26 requires a thermal margin sufficient to accommodate these conditions. Under DSRS Section 15.2.6 these margins are examined where applicable for whether the thermal criteria remain satisfied.

data.query: When evaluating the loss of non-emergency AC power to station auxiliaries, what combined regulatory guidance and review standards inform the identification and justification of the most limiting single failure for reactor coolant system pressure and minimum critical heat flux ratio analyses?
data.answer:
The identification and justification of the most limiting single failure for reactor coolant system (RCS) pressure and minimum critical heat flux ratio (MCHFR) analyses during a loss of non-emergency AC power to station auxiliaries are informed by a combination of regulatory guidance and review standards. According to DSRS 15.2.6 (Section II), the analysis must assume the most limiting plant system single failure as defined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, and must satisfy the positions of Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.53. RG 1.53 references IEEE Std 279-1971 and IEEE Std 603-1991, which require that safety systems perform all required functions for a design basis event in the presence of any single detectable failure, including those that could occur prior to or during the event. Conformance with IEEE Std 379-2000 is also deemed acceptable for applying the single-failure criterion to safety systems, including electrical power and control systems.

For RCS pressure and MCHFR analyses, DSRS 15.2.6 specifies that pressure in the reactor coolant and main steam systems must remain below 110% of design values, and fuel cladding integrity must be maintained by keeping the minimum DNBR above the 95/95 DNBR limit, as further detailed in DSRS 4.4. DSRS 4.4 requires that uncertainties in process parameters and instrumentation be considered, ensuring at least a 95% probability at the 95% confidence level that the hot fuel rod does not experience a boiling crisis during normal operation or anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs). These criteria are grounded in General Design Criterion (GDC) 10 of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, which mandates appropriate margins to assure fuel design limits are not exceeded.

In summary, the combined regulatory guidance from DSRS 15.2.6, DSRS 4.4, RG 1.53, and the requirements of GDC 10 inform both the identification of the most limiting single failure and the justification for its selection in RCS pressure and MCHFR analyses during loss of non-emergency AC power.

evidence_chain.section: Review Interfaces (Section I, Areas of Review)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Review Interfaces
Other SRP sections interface with this section as follows:
1. For COL and OL applicants, the QA staff reviews the information provided by the applicant to ensure that the overall ITP is acceptable.  The relevant technical reviewers ensure, for their particular areas of review, that specific test objectives, test methods, and acceptance criteria are acceptable and consistent with the design requirements for the facility in accordance with the technical reviewers’ guidance.  The QA staff also evaluates the nuclear steam supply system (NSSS) vendor involvement in the development of the plant ITP, including NSSS vendor review of test procedures.
2. For DC reviews, in addition to reviewing the ITP to ensure that the overall program is acceptable, the QA staff performs coordination activities, as requested by other reviewers, for testing issues related to Tier 1.  However, the relevant technical reviewers are responsible for the review of the individual systems in Tier 1 in accordance with the technical reviewer guidance.  For example, the relevant technical reviewers responsible for reviewing the design of a specific system and/or design feature will assess certain tests, such as (1) those for the reactor systems, containment systems, electrical power systems, emergency core cooling systems, security systems, and related features or (2) those identified for design-specific or unique (for example, first-of-a-kind) plant features.  For those areas of review identified above, additional acceptance criteria and/or review methods beyond those described in this section are specified in other RGs (for example, RG 1.20).  These acceptance criteria and/or review methods are also of use in the overall evaluation of issues related to the ITP, such as (1) the adequacy of testing proposed for specific SSCs and/or design features and (2) the design parameters, characteristics, and performance criteria that should be satisfactorily demonstrated by testing.
