data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for analyzing the loss of non-emergency AC power to the station auxiliaries in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for analyzing the loss of non-emergency AC power to the station auxiliaries in nuclear power plants are grounded in the requirements of General Design Criteria (GDC) 10, 13, 15, and 26 as specified in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, and further detailed in DSRS 15.2.6 Section II. The key acceptance criteria include:

1. The reactor coolant and main steam system pressures must remain below 110 percent of their design values during the event (DSRS 15.2.6, II.1).
2. Fuel cladding integrity must be maintained by ensuring the minimum departure from nucleate boiling ratio (DNBR) stays above the 95/95 DNBR limit, using acceptable correlations (DSRS 15.2.6, II.2; see also DSRS Section 4.4).
3. The analyzed event, classified as an incident of moderate frequency, should not escalate to a more serious plant condition unless other faults occur independently (DSRS 15.2.6, II.3).
4. The analysis must consider the most limiting single failure, as defined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, and satisfy the positions of Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.53, which endorses the application of the single-failure criterion per IEEE Std 379-2000 (DSRS 15.2.6, II.5; RG 1.53, C).
5. Instrumentation and controls must be available to monitor and maintain variables within prescribed ranges, as required by GDC 13 (DSRS 15.2.6, II; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 13).

These criteria ensure that the reactor core and associated systems are designed with sufficient margin to prevent exceeding specified fuel design limits and to maintain system integrity during the loss of non-emergency AC power to station auxiliaries.

data.query: How do the requirements for single failure criteria interact with the analysis of loss of non-emergency AC power events in nuclear power plant safety evaluations?
data.answer:
The requirements for the single failure criterion are integral to the analysis of loss of non-emergency AC power events in nuclear power plant safety evaluations. According to DSRS 15.2.6, the analysis must assume the most limiting single failure, as defined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, and must satisfy the positions of Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.53. The single failure criterion, as defined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, requires that for any single failure of active or passive components, the system(s) must still be able to accomplish their safety function. This means that during the analysis of a loss of non-emergency AC power event, the safety-related systems required to respond must be shown to perform their functions even in the presence of a single failure, including any consequential failures resulting from the initial occurrence.

RG 1.53 further clarifies that the protection system must be capable of proper protective action at the system level despite any single failure, and that the safety system must perform all required safety functions for a design basis event in the presence of any single detectable failure, all failures caused by that single failure, and all failures and spurious actions caused by the event itself. The single failure could occur before or during the event. Conformance with IEEE Std 379-2000 is considered an acceptable method for demonstrating compliance with these requirements for electrical power, instrumentation, and control systems.

In summary, the single failure criterion ensures that safety evaluations for loss of non-emergency AC power events demonstrate the continued capability of safety-related systems to perform their functions, even if a single failure occurs, as required by 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, and as described in DSRS 15.2.6 and RG 1.53.

evidence_chain.section: Appendix A to Part 50 – General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants (Definitions and Explanations)
evidence_chain.evidence_text: "Single failure means an occurrence which results in the loss of capability of a component to perform its intended safety functions. Multiple failures resulting from a single occurrence are considered to be a single failure. An occurrence which results in a loss of function of a component(s) and any consequential loss of function(s) of other component(s) that are required to accomplish the same safety function is considered a single failure. The single failure criterion is that, for any single failure of active or passive components, the system(s) must be able to accomplish its safety function. The analysis of the loss of non-emergency ac power events must consider the single failure criterion as defined above, ensuring that safety-related systems required to respond to such events are capable of performing their functions in the presence of a single failure. data.query: In the context of a loss of non-emergency AC power event, what combined regulatory provisions from general design criteria, review standards, and regulatory guides govern the identification and analysis of the most limiting single failure affecting feedwater isolation valves and its impact on steam generator pressure?
data.answer:
The identification and analysis of the most limiting single failure affecting feedwater isolation valves during a loss of non-emergency AC power event are governed by a combination of general design criteria, review standards, and regulatory guides. According to DSRS 15.2.6 (Section II), the analysis must assume the most limiting plant system single failure as defined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, and must satisfy the positions of Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.53. Specifically, General Design Criterion (GDC) 10 requires that the reactor core and associated systems be designed with appropriate margin to ensure that specified acceptable fuel design limits are not exceeded during normal operation and anticipated operational occurrences (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 10). GDC 15 further requires that the reactor coolant system and its auxiliaries be designed to prevent breach of the pressure boundary under these conditions.

RG 1.53 provides the accepted method for applying the single-failure criterion, referencing IEEE Std 279-1971 and IEEE Std 603-1991, which require that safety systems perform all required functions in the presence of any single detectable failure, including those affecting feedwater isolation valves. The analysis must consider that such a failure could occur before or during the event and must ensure that protective actions (such as isolation of feedwater) are still achieved to prevent exceeding steam generator pressure limits. Conformance with IEEE Std 379-2000 is considered acceptable for demonstrating compliance with the single-failure criterion for safety-related systems, including electrical power, instrumentation, and control systems relevant to feedwater isolation.

In summary, the regulatory provisions from GDCs 10 and 15, DSRS 15.2.6, and RG 1.53 collectively require that the most limiting single failure be identified and analyzed for its impact on steam generator pressure, ensuring that safety limits are not exceeded even in the presence of such a failure.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating reactor coolant system and steam generator pressure responses during a loss of non-emergency AC power to the station auxiliaries?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating reactor coolant system (RCS) and steam generator pressure responses during a loss of non-emergency AC power to the station auxiliaries are primarily established to ensure compliance with General Design Criteria (GDC) 10, 13, 15, and 26, as outlined in DSRS 15.2.6 Section II. Specifically:

1. The pressure in the reactor coolant and main steam systems must be maintained below 110 percent of their design values during the event (DSRS 15.2.6, II. Acceptance Criteria, item 1).
2. Fuel cladding integrity must be preserved by ensuring the minimum departure from nucleate boiling ratio (DNBR) remains above the 95/95 DNBR limit, based on acceptable correlations (DSRS 15.2.6, II. Acceptance Criteria, item 2; DSRS 4.4, II. Acceptance Criteria). This means there should be at least a 95-percent probability at the 95-percent confidence level that the hottest fuel rod does not experience a boiling crisis during such anticipated operational occurrences (DSRS 4.4, II. Acceptance Criteria).
3. The event should not escalate to a more serious plant condition without the occurrence of additional, independent faults (DSRS 15.2.6, II. Acceptance Criteria, item 3).
4. The analysis must assume the most limiting single failure, as defined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, and satisfy the positions of Regulatory Guide 1.53 regarding the single-failure criterion (DSRS 15.2.6, II. Acceptance Criteria, item 5; RG 1.53, C. Regulatory Position).
5. Instrumentation and controls must be available to monitor and maintain system variables within prescribed ranges (DSRS 15.2.6, II. Acceptance Criteria, item 2; GDC 13).

These criteria ensure that the RCS and steam generator pressure responses do not compromise fuel or pressure boundary integrity and that the plant remains within safe operational limits during a loss of non-emergency AC power to station auxiliaries.

data.query: What are the regulatory acceptance criteria for the analysis of a loss of normal feedwater flow event in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The regulatory acceptance criteria for the analysis of a loss of normal feedwater flow event in nuclear power plants are established to ensure compliance with several General Design Criteria (GDC) from 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, specifically GDC 10, 13, 15, 17, and 26 (DSRS 15.2.7, Section II). The main objectives are to confirm that fuel damage and system pressure limits are not exceeded, sufficient decay heat removal (DHR) capacity exists for long-term plant stabilization, and that plant protection system setpoints account for measurement uncertainties per Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.105. The analysis must also consider single failures, operator errors, and the performance of nonsafety-related systems, consistent with RG 1.206.

Specific acceptance criteria include:
- Reactor coolant and main steam system pressures must remain below 110% of design values during the event (DSRS 15.2.7, II.2.A).
- Fuel cladding integrity must be maintained by ensuring the minimum departure from nucleate boiling ratio (DNBR) remains above the 95/95 DNBR limit, or other specific acceptable fuel design limits (DSRS 15.2.7, II.2.B; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 10).
- The event should not escalate to a more serious condition without additional independent faults (DSRS 15.2.7, II.2.C).
- Instrumentation and control setpoints must be selected with adequate allowance for uncertainties (DSRS 15.2.7, II.1.C; RG 1.105).
- The most limiting single failure must be identified and assumed in the analysis, in accordance with RG 1.53 and GDC 17 (DSRS 15.2.7, II.2.E; RG 1.53).
- The analysis must evaluate the performance of nonsafety-related systems and the impact of single failures in both active and passive systems, referencing guidance in SECY-77-439, SECY-94-084, and RG 1.206 (DSRS 15.2.7, II.2.F).

These criteria ensure that the plant design and safety analysis adequately address the loss of normal feedwater event, maintaining core integrity and preventing escalation to more severe conditions.

data.query: How do general design criteria for reactor protection systems relate to the requirements for analyzing loss of normal feedwater flow events?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for reactor protection systems are directly related to the requirements for analyzing loss of normal feedwater flow events, as outlined in DSRS 15.2.7 and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A. Specifically, GDC 10, 13, 15, 17, and 26 establish the foundational safety requirements that must be met during such events:

- GDC 10 (Reactor Design) requires that the reactor core and associated systems be designed with sufficient margin to ensure that specified acceptable fuel design limits (SAFDLs) are not exceeded during normal operation and anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs), which include loss of normal feedwater events (DSRS 15.2.7; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 10).

- GDC 13 (Instrumentation and Control) mandates the provision of instrumentation capable of monitoring key variables and systems over their anticipated ranges, ensuring that protection systems can detect and respond to loss of feedwater events appropriately (DSRS 15.2.7).

- GDC 15 (Reactor Coolant System Design) requires that the reactor coolant system and associated protection systems be designed with sufficient margin to prevent exceeding the design conditions of the reactor coolant pressure boundary during AOOs, such as loss of feedwater (DSRS 15.2.7).

- GDC 17 (Electric Power Systems) ensures that both onsite and offsite power systems are available to support safety functions during AOOs, including loss of feedwater, so that SAFDLs and pressure boundary limits are not exceeded (DSRS 15.2.7).

- GDC 26 (Reactivity Control System Redundancy and Capability) requires two independent reactivity control systems to reliably control reactivity changes, ensuring fuel design limits are not exceeded during events like loss of feedwater (DSRS 15.2.7).

Additionally, the analysis of loss of normal feedwater events must consider single failures, operator errors, and the performance of nonsafety-related systems, consistent with regulatory guidance (DSRS 15.2.7; RG 1.53). Instrument setpoints used in transient analyses must include adequate allowance for measurement uncertainties (DSRS 15.2.7; RG 1.105 referenced therein).

In summary, the GDC provide the regulatory basis for the design and analysis of reactor protection systems to ensure that, during a loss of normal feedwater event, the plant remains within safety limits for fuel integrity and pressure boundaries, with appropriate instrumentation, redundancy, and power supply as required by NRC regulations.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations:

1. General Design Criteria (GDC) 10, Reactor Design
2. GDC 13, Instrumentation and Control
3. GDC 15, Reactor Coolant System Design

5. GDC 26, Reactivity Control System Redundancy and Capability

...

The basic objective in the review of the loss of normal feedwater transient is to confirm that the following criteria are met:

A. The plant responds to the loss of feedwater transient in such a way that the criteria regarding fuel damage and system pressure are met.

B. There is sufficient capacity for long-term DHR for the plant to reach a stabilized condition.

C. The plant protection systems’ setpoints assumed in the transient analyses are selected with adequate allowance for measurement uncertainties as delineated in Regulatory Guide 1.105.

D. The event evaluation takes into consideration single failures, operator errors, and performance of nonsafety-related systems that are consistent with regulatory guidelines set forth in RG 1.206.

...

The technical rationale for application of these acceptance criteria to the areas of review addressed by this DSRS section is discussed in the following paragraphs:

1. Compliance with GDC 10 requires that the reactor core and associated coolant, control, and protection systems be designed with appropriate margin to ensure that SAFDLs are not exceeded during any condition of normal operation, including the effects of anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs).

GDC 10 is applicable to DSRS Section 15.2.7 because this section evaluates the loss of normal feedwater flow transient. A part of the evaluation relates to the reactor coolant system being designed with appropriate margin to ensure that SAFDLs are not exceeded during normal operations including AOOs. Regulatory Guide 1.105 provides guidance for ensuring that instrument setpoints are initially within and remain within the TS limits.

Meeting the requirements of GDC 10 provides assurance that SAFDLs are not exceeded for the initiating events evaluated in this DSRS section involving a decrease in heat removal by the secondary system.

2. GDC 13 requires the provision of instrumentation that is capable of monitoring variables and systems over their anticipated ranges to assure adequate safety, and of controls that can maintain these variables and systems within prescribed operating ranges.

GDC 13 applies to this section because the reviewer evaluates the sequences of events, including automatic actuations of protection systems, and manual actions and determines whether the sequence of events is justified, based upon the expected values of the relevant monitored parameters and instrument indications.

3. Compliance with GDC 15 requires that the reactor coolant system and associated auxiliary, control, and protection systems shall be designed with sufficient margin to ensure that the design conditions of the reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) are not exceeded during any condition of normal operation, including AOOs.

GDC 15 is applicable to DSRS Section 15.2.7 because this section evaluates the consequences of the events of a loss of normal feedwater flow transient that result in a decrease in heat removal by the secondary system with the potential for causing the reactor coolant system pressure to change in response to the increase in reactor coolant temperature.

Meeting the requirements of GDC 15 provides assurance that the design conditions of the RCPB are not exceeded for the initiating events evaluated in this DSRS section involving a decrease in heat removal by the secondary system.

4. Compliance with GDC 17 requires (in part) that an onsite and an offsite electric power system shall be provided to permit functioning of SSCs important to safety. The safety function for each system (assuming the other system is not functioning) shall be to provide sufficient capacity and capability to ensure that SAFDLs and design conditions of the RCPB are not exceeded as a result of AOOs. GDC 17 is applicable to DSRS Section 15.2.7 because the loss of normal feedwater flow transient is an AOO.

Meeting the requirements of GDC 17 provides assurance that SAFDLs and design conditions of the RCPB are not exceeded as a result of a loss of normal feedwater.

5. Compliance with GDC 26 requires that two independent reactivity control systems be provided that are capable of reliably controlling reactivity changes to ensure that acceptable fuel design limits are not exceeded.

GDC 26 is applicable to DSRS Section 15.2.7 because this section evaluates the consequences of the events of a loss of normal feedwater flow that result in a decrease in heat removal by the secondary system with the potential for causing changes in reactivity within the core that could cause the thermal design criteria for the fuel cladding to be exceeded. DSRS Section 15.2.7 ensures that the thermal margin be sufficient to accommodate these conditions and ensures that the appropriate margins for malfunctions of reactivity controls, such as stuck rods, are accounted for.

Meeting the requirements of GDC 26 provides assurance that SAFDLs are not exceeded by ensuring that there is appropriate margin for malfunctions of the reactivity control system.

The NRC issued RG 1.232, “Guidance for Developing Principal Design Criteria for Non-Light-Water Reactors” (Ref. 12), to provide guidance on how the GDC in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, may be adapted for non-LWR designs.

• NUREG-0800, “Standard Review Plan for the Review of Safety Analysis Reports for Nuclear Power Plants (LWR Edition)” (Ref. 20), is the standard review plan (SRP) for the NRC staff. It contains guidance related to safety reviews of applications and describes methods or approaches that the staff previously has found acceptable for meeting NRC requirements.

Purpose of Regulatory Guides

The NRC issues RGs to describe to the public methods that the staff considers acceptable for use in implementing specific parts of the agency’s regulations, to explain techniques that the staff uses in evaluating specific problems or postulated events, and to provide guidance to applicants. Regulatory guides are not substitutes for regulations and compliance with them is not required. Methods and solutions that differ from those set forth in RGs will be deemed acceptable if they provide a basis for the findings required for the issuance or continuance of a permit or license by the Commission.

data.query: How do the general design criteria for reactor coolant pressure boundary integrity relate to the regulatory expectations for evaluating uncertainties in heat transfer during feedwater system pipe break events?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) integrity, particularly GDC 31 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 31), require that the RCPB be designed with sufficient margin to ensure nonbrittle behavior and minimize the probability of rapidly propagating fracture under all operating, maintenance, testing, and postulated accident conditions, including feedwater system pipe break events. This design must explicitly account for uncertainties in material properties, flaw sizes, irradiation effects, residual and transient stresses, and the analytical methods used (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 31).

In the context of evaluating feedwater system pipe break events, DSRS 15.2.8 specifies that the review must confirm the RCPB remains safe for break sizes up to a double-ended rupture of the largest feedwater line. The acceptance criteria for such events are grounded in GDC 31, which mandates consideration of uncertainties in heat transfer and stress conditions that could arise from either excessive cooldown or heatup of the reactor coolant system (RCS) due to the event. The severity of these anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs) and their impact on RCPB stress are assessed in the safety analysis report (SAR) and reviewed per DSRS 15.2.8.

Analytical models used to evaluate these events must be sufficiently detailed to simulate the primary and secondary systems, including the pressurizer, and must justify their conservatism through sensitivity studies and comparison to test data. Assumptions regarding heat transfer, such as condensation in the pressurizer, are specifically reviewed for their impact on pressure and temperature transients (DSRS 15.2.8, Section III).

Furthermore, the fracture toughness requirements of Appendix G to 10 CFR Part 50, as referenced in SRP 5.2.3 and DSRS 5.3.1, ensure that RCPB materials are tested and qualified to withstand the stresses and uncertainties associated with such transients. Surveillance programs per Appendix H further monitor material property changes over time, accounting for uncertainties in service conditions (DSRS 5.3.1).

In summary, the general design criteria require that uncertainties in heat transfer and resulting RCPB stresses during feedwater system pipe break events be explicitly evaluated and bounded in the safety analysis, with conservative analytical methods and robust material qualification and surveillance programs to ensure boundary integrity.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for minimizing the probability of rapidly propagating fracture in the reactor coolant pressure boundary during feedwater system pipe break transients?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for minimizing the probability of rapidly propagating fracture in the reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) during feedwater system pipe break transients are established primarily by General Design Criterion (GDC) 31, as referenced in both DSRS 15.2.8 and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A. GDC 31 mandates that the RCPB must be designed with sufficient margin to ensure nonbrittle behavior and to minimize the probability of rapidly propagating fracture under all conditions, including operation, maintenance, testing, and postulated accident scenarios such as feedwater system pipe breaks. 

Specifically, the design must account for:
- Service temperatures and other environmental conditions experienced by the boundary material during all operational and accident conditions (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 31).
- Material properties, including the effects of irradiation, and uncertainties in determining these properties (DSRS 15.2.8; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 31).
- Residual, steady state, and transient stresses, as well as flaw sizes (DSRS 15.2.8; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 31).
- Provisions for detecting flaws and periodic inspection to ensure the required margin is maintained throughout the service life (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 31).

DSRS 15.2.8 clarifies that these requirements apply specifically to feedwater system pipe breaks, which can cause rapid changes in reactor coolant system (RCS) temperature and pressure, potentially imposing undue stress on the RCPB. The severity of such anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs) must be assessed in the Safety Analysis Report (SAR) and reviewed to ensure compliance with these criteria.

In summary, the regulatory requirements focus on ensuring the RCPB is robust against brittle fracture by considering all relevant material, operational, and accident-related factors, with ongoing inspection and testing to maintain safety margins.

data.query: How do general design criteria for reactor coolant pressure boundary integrity relate to the evaluation of uncertainties in heat transfer assumptions during feedwater system pipe break events?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) integrity, specifically GDC 31 as outlined in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, require that the RCPB be designed with sufficient margin to ensure nonbrittle behavior and minimize the probability of rapidly propagating fracture under all conditions, including postulated accidents such as feedwater system pipe breaks. GDC 31 explicitly mandates that the design must account for uncertainties in material properties, flaw sizes, irradiation effects, material degradation, uncertainties in design analyses, and inspection capabilities (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 31).

DSRS 15.2.8 clarifies the application of GDC 31 to feedwater system pipe break events, noting that such breaks can cause transient reactor coolant temperature and pressure conditions that may adversely affect the RCPB. The evaluation of these events must consider the severity of anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs) and the associated uncertainties in heat transfer assumptions, as these directly impact the thermal and mechanical stresses experienced by the RCPB during such transients (DSRS 15.2.8, Section II).

Furthermore, DSRS 4.4 provides detailed guidance on the treatment of uncertainties in process parameters and calculational methods when assessing thermal margins, requiring that uncertainties be addressed with at least a 95-percent probability at the 95-percent confidence level. This includes uncertainties in reactor power, coolant flow, temperature, and other parameters relevant to heat transfer during AOOs, such as feedwater system pipe breaks. The methodologies for combining and characterizing these uncertainties must be clearly described (DSRS 4.4, Section II).

In summary, the general design criteria for RCPB integrity require that uncertainties in heat transfer assumptions—such as those arising during feedwater system pipe break events—be systematically evaluated and incorporated into the design and safety analysis to ensure the RCPB maintains its integrity under all credible conditions.

SRP Section 14.2 does not specify the acceptance criteria for the evaluation of fuel design limits or the evaluation of uncertainties in heat transfer assumptions during feedwater system pipe break events. Instead, SRP 14.2 focuses on the requirements and acceptance criteria for the Initial Plant Test Program (ITP), including preoperational and startup testing, administrative controls, test procedures, and the demonstration that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) meet performance requirements and design criteria. The section references other SRP sections and regulatory guides (e.g., RG 1.68) for specific technical acceptance criteria and test objectives, and notes that technical reviewers are responsible for ensuring that test objectives, methods, and acceptance criteria are consistent with the design requirements for the facility in accordance with their guidance. For example: 

'The relevant technical reviewers ensure, for their particular areas of review, that specific test objectives, test methods, and acceptance criteria are acceptable and consistent with the design requirements for the facility in accordance with the technical reviewers’ guidance.' (Review Interfaces)

'For those areas of review identified above, additional acceptance criteria and/or review methods beyond those described in this section are specified in other RGs (for example, RG 1.20). These acceptance criteria and/or review methods are also of use in the overall evaluation of issues related to the ITP, such as (1) the adequacy of testing proposed for specific SSCs and/or design features and (2) the design parameters, characteristics, and performance criteria that should be satisfactorily demonstrated by testing.' (Review Interfaces)

Therefore, SRP 14.2 does not provide the specific fuel design limits or methodologies for evaluating uncertainties in heat transfer assumptions; these are addressed in other SRP sections such as SRP 4.2.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for minimizing the probability of rapidly propagating fracture in feedwater system piping during postulated pipe break transients?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for minimizing the probability of rapidly propagating fracture in feedwater system piping during postulated pipe break transients are primarily established by General Design Criterion (GDC) 31 of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A. GDC 31 mandates that the reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) must be designed with sufficient margin to ensure nonbrittle behavior and to minimize the probability of rapidly propagating fracture under operating, maintenance, testing, and postulated accident conditions. This includes consideration of service temperatures, material properties (including effects of irradiation), residual and transient stresses, and flaw sizes (DSRS 15.2.8, Section II; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 31).

The design must also account for system depressurization provisions and inservice inspection and testing to assure continued boundary integrity (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 31). The NRC’s Standard Review Plan (SRP) further clarifies that compliance with GDC 14 and GDC 15 is required, ensuring that the RCPB is designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to have an extremely low probability of abnormal leakage, rapidly propagating failure, and gross rupture, and that design conditions are not exceeded during any operational or postulated transient, including pipe breaks (SRP 3.9.1, II; SRP 3.9.3, II).

Applicants must provide a comprehensive list of transients, including postulated pipe breaks, for fatigue analysis of all Code Class 1 components. The selected transients must conservatively estimate the magnitude and frequency of temperature and pressure conditions, and the resulting loads and load combinations must be used as the basis for RCPB design (SRP 3.9.1, II). Additionally, analyses and testing must confirm that piping systems and supports can withstand flow-induced dynamic loadings and that adverse flow conditions, such as those leading to strong pressure pulsations or vibrations, are addressed (SRP 3.9.2, I).

In summary, the requirements are grounded in GDC 31, supported by GDC 14 and 15, and implemented through detailed design, analysis, and testing criteria as outlined in the DSRS and SRP sections referenced above.

The purpose of the analyses is to assess the vibration behavior of the components, including the definition of the input-forcing functions, and estimation of the consequent vibration and alternating stress levels. The analyses should verify the structural integrity of reactor internals for flow-induced vibration (FIV), acoustic resonance (AR), acoustic-induced vibration (AIV), and mechanical-induced vibration (MIV). Flow excitation mechanisms such as vortex-induced vibration, flow-excited acoustic resonance, fluid-elastic instability, and turbulence buffeting as well as other flow excitations of flow separation, reattachment, and impinging flow instabilities should be considered. These mechanisms are often nonlinear and their adverse effects cannot be predicted by linear extrapolation of existing plant data. In some cases, the instabilities in these flow fields can couple with acoustic or structural resonances, causing high dynamic loads throughout the steam system and RPV. These self-excited loads can be orders of magnitude higher than those which do not couple to acoustic or structural resonances. A complete assessment of the likelihood of any potential self-excitation mechanisms that lead to adverse flow effects at steady state and anticipated transient conditions that correspond to preoperational, startup test, and normal operating conditions is needed.

data.query: How do regulatory standards for uncertainty analysis in safety-related heat transfer calculations relate to the requirements for demonstrating adequate protection against pipe rupture in feedwater systems?
data.answer:
Regulatory standards for uncertainty analysis in safety-related heat transfer calculations are closely tied to the requirements for demonstrating adequate protection against pipe rupture in feedwater systems. According to DSRS 15.2.8, the NRC reviews the analytical thermal-hydraulic methods used by applicants to ensure that mathematical modeling and computer codes are either previously accepted or adequately justified. This review includes an evaluation of parameter values, initial conditions, nuclear design parameters, and the conservatism of the methods compared to test data. Sensitivity studies are specifically required to identify the most conservative combination of power level and plant operating mode, and these studies must account for uncertainties in material properties, effects of irradiation, stresses, and flaw sizes (DSRS 15.2.8, Sections II and III).

These requirements directly support compliance with General Design Criterion (GDC) 31 from 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, which mandates that the reactor coolant pressure boundary—including feedwater system piping—be designed with sufficient margin to prevent brittle fracture and minimize the probability of rapidly propagating fractures. GDC 31 explicitly requires consideration of uncertainties in material properties, flaw sizes, irradiation effects, loading rates, temperature changes, and other relevant factors. Thus, the uncertainty analysis in heat transfer calculations is essential for demonstrating that the design adequately protects against pipe rupture by ensuring that all relevant uncertainties are conservatively addressed, as required by both DSRS 15.2.8 and GDC 31.

While 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2, establishes the broader requirement for considering the most severe natural phenomena in the design bases, SRP 2.3.1 provides the specific procedural requirement to identify the relevant state climatic division(s) as part of the climate evaluation process.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for including 0% occurrence values in the evaluation of meteorological data for nuclear facility siting?
data.answer:
Based on the provided evidence, the NRC does not specify explicit regulatory requirements for including 0% occurrence values (i.e., events that have not been observed in the historical record) in the evaluation of meteorological data for nuclear facility siting. According to SRP 2.3.1, meteorological averages and extremes should be estimated using long-term historical data, and the selection of critical meteorological data must be justified and substantiated using standard practices and data sources such as NOAA and regulatory guides. The procedures should ensure that the data used are representative and reasonable for the site in question. 

10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2, requires that the design bases for safety-related structures, systems, and components reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in the data. This implies that the evaluation should be based on actual historical occurrences and does not mandate the inclusion of events with 0% historical occurrence.

RG 1.76 further supports this approach by describing the use of extensive historical tornado databases to define design-basis wind speeds and strike probabilities. The guide emphasizes the use of observed data and statistical analysis of historical occurrences to determine exceedance frequencies for design-basis events. If less-conservative values are proposed, a comprehensive justification is required, but there is no mention of including 0% occurrence values in the analysis.

In summary, NRC regulatory requirements focus on the use of historical data and observed extremes, with appropriate justification and margin for uncertainties, rather than mandating the inclusion of 0% occurrence values in meteorological evaluations for nuclear facility siting.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for determining the ambient air temperature used in atmospheric dispersion analyses for nuclear facility siting?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for determining the ambient air temperature used in atmospheric dispersion analyses for nuclear facility siting are grounded in both regulatory criteria and accepted guidance. According to SRP 2.3.1, Section II (Acceptance Criteria), ambient temperature and humidity statistics must be established as site characteristics or parameters, depending on the application type (ESP, CP, OL, COL, or DC). Specifically, the statistics should include values such as the 2% and 1% annual exceedance and 100-year maximum dry bulb temperature and coincident wet bulb temperature, as well as the 98% and 99% annual exceedance and 100-year minimum dry bulb temperature. These statistics are used for the design of plant heat sink systems and HVAC systems.

The data for these statistics should be derived from nearby representative climatic stations or from appropriate standards, with suitable corrections for local conditions (SRP 2.3.1, II.7). Reference 23 in the SRP provides a method for estimating 100-year return period extreme temperature values based on annual extremes.

The regulatory basis for these requirements is found in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, which requires consideration of the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site, with sufficient margin for data limitations (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2). Additionally, 10 CFR Part 100 (§100.10(c)(2), §100.20(c)(2), and §100.21(d)) requires that regional meteorological characteristics, including ambient temperature, be considered in site acceptability and safety analyses.

Regulatory guides such as RG 1.206 and RG 1.76 clarify that while these guides provide acceptable methods for compliance, alternative approaches may be used if they meet the regulatory requirements. In summary, the NRC requires that ambient air temperature statistics for dispersion analyses be based on representative, corrected historical data, and that these values reflect the most severe conditions with appropriate safety margins, as specified in the cited regulations and guidance documents.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for determining the design-basis tornado wind speed for nuclear power plant safety-related structures?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for determining the design-basis tornado wind speed for nuclear power plant safety-related structures are grounded in several key documents and criteria. According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, safety-related structures, systems, and components must be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including tornadoes, based on the most severe events historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2). The Standard Review Plan (SRP) 2.3.1 further specifies that tornado parameters should be based on Regulatory Guide 1.76 (RG 1.76), unless an applicant provides a justified, site-specific technical evaluation for alternative parameters. Any deviations from RG 1.76 must be clearly identified and justified by the applicant (SRP 2.3.1, Section II).

Regulatory Guide 1.76 provides the NRC-accepted method for selecting design-basis tornado parameters. It defines three tornado intensity regions within the United States, each with specific maximum wind speeds and other parameters (RG 1.76, Section C). For example, Region I requires a maximum wind speed of 103 m/s (230 mph), Region II 89 m/s (200 mph), and Region III 72 m/s (160 mph), with a standard radius of maximum rotational speed of 45.7 meters (150 feet) for all regions. These values are considered generally acceptable by the NRC. If less-conservative values are proposed, a comprehensive technical justification is required.

In summary, the NRC requires that design-basis tornado wind speeds for nuclear power plant safety-related structures be determined using the regional parameters in RG 1.76, unless a justified, site-specific analysis supports alternative values, in accordance with the requirements of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2, and as described in SRP 2.3.1.

data.query: What is the NRC regulatory requirement for determining the 50-year return period 3-second gust wind speed at a nuclear power plant site?
data.answer: The NRC regulatory requirement for determining the 50-year return period 3-second gust wind speed at a nuclear power plant site is grounded in the need to ensure that structures, systems, and components important to safety are designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site, with appropriate margins for uncertainties in the data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; SRP 2.3.1). Specifically, SRP 2.3.1 states that the basic (straight-line) 100-year return period 3-second gust wind speed should be used, based on appropriate standards and with corrections for local conditions. While the SRP references the 100-year return period as the standard for design, it does not explicitly specify a 50-year return period for the 3-second gust wind speed. Instead, the regulatory focus is on using the most severe historical data, typically represented by the 100-year return period, and ensuring compliance with 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2, and 10 CFR Part 100 requirements for meteorological characterization. Regulatory Guide 1.76 provides further guidance for tornado wind speeds, but its design-basis tornado wind speeds are based on exceedance frequencies (e.g., 10^-7 per year) rather than a specific 50-year return period for straight-line winds. data.query: How do NRC regulatory standards define the required exceedance probability for normal ambient site temperature characteristics when evaluating site suitability for a nuclear power plant?
data.answer: NRC regulatory standards define the required exceedance probability for normal ambient site temperature characteristics primarily through the use of annual exceedance probabilities and return period statistics. According to SRP 2.3.1, Section II (Acceptance Criteria), ambient temperature and humidity statistics used in site suitability evaluations must include values such as the 2% and 1% annual exceedance and 100-year maximum dry bulb temperature and coincident wet bulb temperature, as well as the 2% and 1% annual exceedance and 100-year maximum wet bulb temperature (non-coincident). For minimum temperatures, the 98% and 99% annual exceedance and 100-year minimum dry bulb temperature are required. These statistics are used to establish heat loads for the design of normal plant heat sink systems and other safety-related systems. The data should be derived from representative climatic stations or appropriate standards, with corrections for local conditions as needed. While 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2, requires that design bases reflect the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site with sufficient margin, it does not specify exceedance probabilities for ambient temperature. The specific exceedance probabilities for tornado wind speeds (e.g., 10^-7 per year) in RG 1.76 do not apply to normal ambient temperature characteristics. Therefore, for ambient temperature, the NRC requires the use of 2% and 1% annual exceedance probabilities and 100-year return period values as defined in SRP 2.3.1.

data.query: In the context of demonstrating that site characteristics fall within approved design parameters, how do NRC requirements address the use of specific statistical exceedance levels for temperature data?
data.answer:
NRC requirements for demonstrating that site characteristics fall within approved design parameters specifically address the use of statistical exceedance levels for temperature data. According to SRP 2.3.1, Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA, ambient temperature and humidity statistics must be evaluated using specific statistical thresholds, including 2% and 1% annual exceedance levels and 100-year maximum and minimum values for dry bulb and wet bulb temperatures. These statistics are used to establish heat loads for the design of normal plant heat sink systems, post-accident containment heat removal systems, and plant HVAC systems. The data should be derived from nearby representative climatic stations or appropriate standards, with corrections for local conditions as necessary. The SRP also references methods for estimating 100-year return period extreme temperature values based on annual extremes (SRP 2.3.1, II.6.e and II.7).

While 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2, requires that design bases reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site, it does not specify particular statistical exceedance levels for temperature. Instead, it emphasizes the need for sufficient margin and consideration of the accuracy and quantity of historical data. The use of specific exceedance levels (e.g., 2%, 1%, 100-year values) for temperature is thus grounded in NRC staff guidance (SRP 2.3.1) rather than explicit regulatory text.

In summary, NRC requirements, as detailed in SRP 2.3.1, mandate the use of defined statistical exceedance levels for temperature data to ensure that site characteristics are appropriately bounded by approved design parameters.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for determining the design basis wind speed at a nuclear power plant site?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for determining the design basis wind speed at a nuclear power plant site are grounded in several key regulations and guidance documents. According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety must be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including wind events such as tornadoes and hurricanes. The design bases must reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; SRP 2.3.1, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA).

Additionally, 10 CFR Part 100 (§100.10(c)(2), §100.20(c)(2), and §100.21(d)) requires that the regional meteorological characteristics, including maximum probable wind speed, be identified and characterized to ensure the site poses no undue risk (SRP 2.3.1, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA).

The Standard Review Plan (SRP) 2.3.1 further specifies that the basic (straight-line) 100-year return period 3-second gust wind speed should be determined based on appropriate standards and corrected for local conditions. For tornadoes, Regulatory Guide 1.76 provides an accepted method, establishing that the design-basis tornado wind speeds should correspond to an exceedance frequency of 10^-7 per year. The guide defines three regions in the contiguous United States with maximum wind speeds of 103 m/s (230 mph), 89 m/s (200 mph), and 72 m/s (160 mph), depending on the site's geographic location. If less-conservative values are proposed, a comprehensive justification is required (RG 1.76, Sections B and C).

In summary, the NRC requires that the design basis wind speed be determined by considering the most severe historical wind phenomena for the site, using appropriate standards and regulatory guidance, and ensuring sufficient safety margins to account for uncertainties.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory guides address the evaluation and reporting of calm wind frequency in onsite meteorological monitoring for nuclear power plant siting?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory guides address the evaluation and reporting of calm wind frequency in onsite meteorological monitoring for nuclear power plant siting through a combination of specific measurement, analysis, and reporting requirements. According to SRP 2.3.2, applicants must provide local summaries of meteorological data based on onsite measurements in accordance with Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.23, and present these data as specified in RG 1.206 and other referenced documents. The SRP explicitly requires the inclusion of wind roses and annual joint frequency distributions of wind speed and direction by atmospheric stability, using the criteria in RG 1.23, ensuring that calm wind periods are captured and reported.

RG 1.23 defines 'calm' as any wind speed below the starting threshold of the wind speed or direction sensor, and requires wind speed and direction measurements at specified heights. It also specifies the minimum duration of onsite meteorological data collection (e.g., at least 12 to 24 consecutive months, with 3 or more years preferred) to ensure representativeness and completeness of the data, including calm wind occurrences.

RG 1.206 further details that applicants must describe their onsite meteorological monitoring program, including instrumentation, data collection, and analysis methods. Specifically, it requires the calculation and reporting of the frequency of calm winds (defined as wind speeds less than or equal to 1 m/s), and mandates that this information be included in the wind speed distribution analysis. The guide also requires justification for the threshold used to define calm winds and a summary of results, including tables and figures presenting calm wind frequency.

Collectively, these regulatory guides ensure that calm wind frequency is systematically evaluated and transparently reported, supporting the assessment of atmospheric dispersion conditions critical for nuclear power plant safety analyses (SRP 2.3.2; RG 1.23, Section C; RG 1.206, Section 2.3.2.1).

Further, it specifies:

In the 'Review Procedures' section, it reinforces: 

'The wind and atmospheric stability data should be based on onsite data, because airflow and vertical temperature structure, which can vary substantially from one location to another, are necessary for assessment of atmospheric diffusion conditions at the site.'

These requirements ensure that calm wind frequency (i.e., periods of low or zero wind speed) is captured in the joint frequency distributions and wind roses, as prescribed by Regulatory Guide 1.23, which provides detailed guidance on the measurement and reporting of wind speed, including calm conditions.

data.query: What are the NRC expectations for identifying and discussing potential causes of unusually high calm wind observations in the context of meteorological data quality assurance?
data.answer:
The NRC expects applicants and licensees to implement a robust data quality assurance program for meteorological data, with specific attention to identifying and discussing potential causes of unusually high calm wind observations. According to Regulatory Guide 1.23, Section C.4.1, the data review and validation process should include routine examination of wind speed and direction data to detect periods with unusually high frequencies of calm winds or other anomalies. If such periods are observed, the applicant or licensee is expected to investigate and discuss potential causes, which may include instrument threshold limitations, siting issues, or local obstructions. The applicant must also provide justification for the representativeness of the data, ensuring that any anomalies do not compromise the reliability of the meteorological assessments.

Regulatory Guide 1.206, Section 2.3.2, further requires that the Safety Analysis Report include a summary and evaluation of onsite meteorological measurements, explicitly identifying and discussing any unusual or anomalous data, such as high calm wind observations. The discussion should evaluate the potential causes of these anomalies and assess the representativeness and reliability of the data for safety analyses. Procedures for ensuring data quality, including calibration, maintenance, and validation activities, must also be described.

Standard Review Plan 2.3.2, Section III, reinforces the need to consider local site characteristics that could cause deviations in meteorological data, and to reference all relevant supporting data sources. Collectively, these documents establish that the NRC expects a thorough, documented investigation and discussion of unusually high calm wind observations, including their potential causes and implications for data quality and safety analysis.

4. Data Quality Assurance

4.1 Data Review and Validation

The applicant or licensee should establish and implement a data review and validation program to ensure the quality and representativeness of the meteorological data collected. The program should include procedures for the routine review of data to identify and correct errors, malfunctions, or unusual patterns. This review should include, but not be limited to, the following:

• Examination of wind speed and direction data for periods of unusually high frequencies of calm winds or other anomalies. If unusually high calm frequencies are observed, the applicant or licensee should investigate and discuss potential causes, such as instrument threshold limitations, siting issues, or local obstructions, and provide justification for the representativeness of the data.

• Comparison of data from redundant or nearby sensors, if available, to identify inconsistencies or instrument malfunctions.

• Review of data for consistency with expected meteorological patterns for the site and region, including seasonal and diurnal variations.

• Documentation of all data review activities, identified issues, corrective actions taken, and justification for the use of data in assessments.

The applicant or licensee should provide a summary of the data review and validation process, including a discussion of any identified data quality issues and their resolution, in the application or annual reports, as appropriate.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for the inspection frequency of guyed wires and tower anchors used in safety-related structures at nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for the inspection frequency of guyed wires and tower anchors used in safety-related structures, such as meteorological towers at nuclear power plants, are primarily addressed through a combination of quality assurance and maintenance provisions. According to Regulatory Guide 1.23, Section C.4, the meteorological monitoring system—including supporting structures like towers, guyed wires, and anchors—must be maintained under a documented quality assurance program. This program must include periodic inspection, maintenance, and calibration. Specifically, a visual inspection of the tower, guyed wires, and anchors is required at least annually to ensure structural integrity and proper tensioning. The frequency may need to be increased based on manufacturer recommendations, environmental conditions, or operational experience, especially in areas prone to severe weather. Any deficiencies found during inspections must be corrected promptly to maintain system reliability.

These requirements are consistent with the broader regulatory basis found in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A (General Design Criteria 1, 2, and 4), which mandates that safety-related structures be designed, constructed, and maintained to quality standards that ensure their safety function, including resistance to natural phenomena and environmental effects. Standard Review Plan (SRP) 2.3.3 further emphasizes the importance of evaluating inspection and maintenance procedures and their frequency to ensure continued acceptable performance of safety-related instrumentation and structures.

In summary, NRC regulations require at least annual visual inspections of guyed wires and tower anchors, with the possibility of more frequent inspections as warranted by site-specific factors, all within a documented quality assurance framework (RG 1.23, Section C.4; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A; SRP 2.3.3).

The meteorological monitoring system should be maintained in accordance with a documented quality assurance program. The program should include provisions for periodic inspection, maintenance, and calibration of all meteorological sensors, data acquisition systems, and supporting structures (e.g., towers, guyed wires, and anchors). The frequency of inspection and maintenance should be sufficient to ensure reliable operation of the system and should be based on manufacturer recommendations, environmental conditions, and operational experience. At a minimum, a visual inspection of the tower, guyed wires, and anchors should be performed at least annually to ensure structural integrity and proper tensioning. More frequent inspections may be warranted in areas subject to severe weather conditions or where operational experience indicates a need.

Calibration of meteorological sensors should be performed at intervals recommended by the manufacturer or as indicated by operational experience. Calibration records should be maintained and available for inspection. Any deficiencies identified during inspections or calibrations should be corrected promptly to ensure the continued reliability of the meteorological monitoring system.

Appendix A to Part 50—General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants

Criterion 1—Quality standards and records. Structures, systems, and components important to safety shall be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with the importance of the safety functions to be performed. Where generally recognized codes and standards are used, they shall be identified and evaluated to determine their applicability, adequacy, and sufficiency and shall be supplemented or modified as necessary to assure a quality product in keeping with the required safety function. A quality assurance program shall be established and implemented in order to provide adequate assurance that these structures, systems, and components will satisfactorily perform their safety functions. Appropriate records of the design, fabrication, erection, and testing of structures, systems, and components important to safety shall be maintained.

Criterion 2—Design bases for protection against natural phenomena. Structures, systems, and components important to safety shall be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena such as earthquakes, tornadoes, hurricanes, floods, tsunami, and seiches without loss of capability to perform their safety functions. The design bases for these structures, systems, and components shall reflect: (1) Appropriate consideration of the most severe of the natural phenomena that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated, (2) appropriate combinations of the effects of normal and accident conditions with the effects of the natural phenomena, and (3) the importance of the safety functions to be performed.

Criterion 4—Environmental and dynamic effects design bases. Structures, systems, and components important to safety shall be designed to accommodate the effects of and to be compatible with the environmental conditions associated with normal operation, maintenance, testing, and postulated accidents, including loss-of-coolant accidents. In addition, these structures, systems, and components shall be appropriately protected against dynamic effects, including the effects of missiles, pipe whipping, and discharging fluids, that may result from equipment failures and from events and conditions outside the nuclear power unit.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for the digital sampling rate of onsite meteorological data collected during preoperational and operational monitoring at nuclear power plant sites?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for the digital sampling rate of onsite meteorological data at nuclear power plant sites are primarily outlined in Regulatory Guide 1.23 (RG 1.23) and referenced in Standard Review Plan Section 2.3.3 (SRP 2.3.3). According to RG 1.23, the meteorological monitoring system must provide continuous measurements of required parameters, with data recorded at intervals not exceeding 15 minutes. Specifically, for emergency response purposes, the system must be capable of providing near-real-time data, with a digital sampling rate of at least once every 15 minutes. However, a higher sampling rate, such as once per minute, is preferable—particularly for wind speed, wind direction, and vertical temperature difference—to better support emergency response and dose assessment activities (RG 1.23, Section C.4.1). 

SRP 2.3.3 further clarifies that the adequacy of the frequency and mode (instantaneous or average) of sampling is evaluated as part of the NRC staff review, and references RG 1.23 for specific criteria. The review ensures that the data acquisition system meets the required accuracy and frequency for both preoperational and operational monitoring programs (SRP 2.3.3, Sections II and III). 

In summary, the minimum NRC requirement is a digital sampling rate of at least once every 15 minutes, with a preference for higher rates (e.g., once per minute) for key parameters, as detailed in RG 1.23 and supported by SRP 2.3.3.

data.query: What are the NRC requirements for the description of meteorological monitoring programs at nuclear power plant sites?
data.answer:
The NRC requires that applicants for nuclear power plant licenses provide a detailed description of their meteorological monitoring programs as part of their application. According to SRP 2.3.3, the description must include both pre-operational and operational monitoring programs, depending on the application type (CP, ESP, COL, OL). The monitoring program description should cover meteorological measurements at the site and any offsite satellite facilities, and must include: (a) a site map showing tower location and relevant features, (b) distances to nearby obstructions, (c) measurements made, (d) elevations of measurements, (e) instrument exposure, (f) instrument descriptions, (g) instrument performance specifications, (h) calibration and maintenance procedures and frequencies, (i) data output and recording systems, and (j) data processing, archiving, and analysis procedures (SRP 2.3.3, II.1).

Meteorological data must be presented as joint frequency distributions of wind speed and direction by atmospheric stability class, and as hour-by-hour listings of hourly-averaged parameters, in the format described in Regulatory Guide 1.23 (SRP 2.3.3, II.2). Any deviations from RG 1.23 must be identified and justified (SRP 2.3.3, II.3).

RG 1.23 provides further guidance, stating that the onsite meteorological measurements program should support assessments of atmospheric dispersion, radiological consequences of accidents, routine effluent releases, control room habitability, emergency response, and environmental impacts. The minimum data requirements are: a representative consecutive 12-month period for a construction permit, a 24-month period (including the most recent year) for an operating license, and a consecutive 24-month period (not older than 10 years) for an ESP or COL not referencing an ESP. Three or more years of data are preferable if available (RG 1.23, B. DISCUSSION).

In summary, the NRC requires a comprehensive, well-documented meteorological monitoring program, with data and program details conforming to the guidance in RG 1.23, to ensure adequate assessment of site safety and environmental impacts.

This revised regulatory guide provides licensees and applicants with improved guidance concerning criteria for an onsite meteorological measurements program that the staff of the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) considers acceptable for the collection of basic meteorological data needed to support plant licensing and operation. ...

An onsite meteorological measurements program at a nuclear power plant site should be capable of providing the meteorological information needed to make the following assessments:

• a conservative assessment by both the applicant and the regulatory staff of the habitability of the control room during postulated design-basis radiological accidents and hazardous chemical releases to demonstrate that the control room can remain occupied under accident conditions in accordance with GDC 19
• a near-real-time ongoing assessment by the licensee of atmospheric transport and diffusion immediately following an accidental release of airborne radioactive materials to provide input to the evaluation of the consequences of radioactive releases to the atmosphere and to aid in the implementation of emergency response decisions in accordance with the requirements in Appendix E to 10 CFR Part 50
• an assessment by the licensee of natural phenomena being experienced or projected beyond usual levels (e.g., high winds) for the purposes of emergency classification in accordance with 10 CFR 50.47(b)(4) and Section IV.B of Appendix E to 10 CFR Part 50
• a realistic assessment by both the applicant and the regulatory staff of the potential dispersion of radioactive materials from, and the radiological consequences of, a spectrum of accidents to aid in evaluating the environmental risk posed by a nuclear power plant in accordance with Subpart A to 10 CFR Part 51
• a realistic assessment by both the applicant and the regulatory staff of nonradiological environmental effects, such as fogging, icing, and salt drift from cooling towers or ponds, to aid in evaluating the environmental impact of a nuclear power plant in accordance with Subpart A to 10 CFR Part 51

data.query: How do NRC regulatory guides distinguish between preoperational and operational meteorological monitoring program requirements for nuclear power plant sites?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory guides distinguish between preoperational and operational meteorological monitoring program requirements primarily in terms of timing, data collection duration, and specific measurement needs. According to SRP 2.3.3 (Section II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA), the preoperational monitoring program must be described for construction permit (CP) and early site permit (ESP) applications, as well as for combined license (COL) applications that do not reference an ESP. In contrast, the operational monitoring program is required for operating license (OL) and COL applications, and for ESP applications that include complete emergency response plans. Both programs require detailed descriptions of meteorological measurements, including site maps, instrument specifications, calibration procedures, and data processing methods.

Regulatory Guide 1.23 further specifies the minimum onsite meteorological data required: for a CP, a representative consecutive 12-month period; for an OL, a consecutive 24-month period including the most recent year; and for an ESP or COL without an ESP, a consecutive 24-month period not older than 10 years. Preoperational programs at sites with cooling towers or similar heat sinks must include ambient temperature and atmospheric moisture measurements to assess environmental impacts such as vapor plumes and fogging. These specific measurements are generally not required during the operational phase unless mandated by the plant’s Environmental Protection Program under 10 CFR 50.36b or 10 CFR 51.50.

Additionally, RG 4.21 emphasizes that site characterization and environmental monitoring should begin before construction to establish baseline conditions and inform future operational monitoring. This ensures that both preoperational and operational programs are tailored to the site’s unique environmental and design features.

In summary, NRC regulatory guides require more extensive and specific data collection during the preoperational phase to establish baseline conditions and assess potential impacts, while operational monitoring focuses on ongoing compliance and may have reduced measurement requirements unless otherwise specified.

For systems that directly interface with the environment, the first indication of a leak may be detection in an environmental monitoring system. To control and mitigate such events, it is prudent to have a comprehensive understanding of the interface with environmental systems and the features that will control the movement of contamination in the environment. A conceptual site model based on site characterization and facility design and construction can be a significant tool in (1) understanding the site, (2) planning and implementing a contaminant monitoring program, and (3) planning and implementing mitigative actions. data.query: When preparing a safety analysis report for a new nuclear power plant, what are the combined regulatory expectations for separately describing preoperational and operational meteorological monitoring programs, and how should these descriptions address data collection, instrumentation, and program objectives according to NRC review standards and regulatory guides?
data.answer:
When preparing a safety analysis report (SAR) for a new nuclear power plant, NRC regulatory expectations require that preoperational and operational meteorological monitoring programs be described separately, with each program tailored to the stage of licensing and plant operation (SRP 2.3.3, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA). For construction permit (CP), early site permit (ESP), and combined license (COL) applications not referencing an ESP, the preoperational program must be described. For operating license (OL) and COL applications, as well as ESPs with integrated emergency response plans, the operational program must be described.

The SAR must include detailed descriptions addressing:
- Data collection: The program should specify the meteorological parameters to be measured (wind speed and direction, vertical temperature difference, ambient temperature, precipitation, and, where applicable, atmospheric moisture), the duration and representativeness of the data set (e.g., at least 12 months for CP, 24 months for OL or COL, with 3+ years preferred), and the procedures for data processing, archiving, and analysis (SRP 2.3.3; RG 1.23, C. REGULATORY POSITION).
- Instrumentation: The SAR should provide a site map showing tower locations, measurement elevations (typically 10 m and 60 m above ground), instrument descriptions and specifications, exposure, calibration and maintenance procedures, and data output/recording systems (SRP 2.3.3; RG 1.23, Section 2; RG 1.145, 1.1; RG 1.194, 3.1).
- Program objectives: The monitoring program must support site characterization, environmental impact assessments, consequence analyses for routine and accident releases, and emergency preparedness (10 CFR 50.34(a)(3); RG 1.23, C. REGULATORY POSITION).

The SAR should demonstrate that the meteorological data are representative of site conditions, free from local effects, and collected using quality assurance provisions (RG 1.194, 3.1). The monitoring program must also address how data are reviewed for quality and completeness, and how instrumentation limitations (e.g., calm wind conditions) are handled (RG 1.145, 1.1).

In summary, the SAR must provide a comprehensive, stage-appropriate description of both preoperational and operational meteorological monitoring programs, addressing data collection, instrumentation, and program objectives in accordance with SRP 2.3.3, RG 1.23, RG 1.145, RG 1.194, and 10 CFR 50.34.

evidence_chain.section: C. REGULATORY POSITION, 1.1 Meteorological Data Input
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
1.1 Meteorological Data Input
The meteorological data needed for X/Q calculations include windspeed, wind direction, and a measure of atmospheric stability. These data should represent hourly averages as defined in Regulatory Guide 1.23.
Wind direction should be classed into 16 compass directions (22.5-degree sectors centered on true north, north-northeast, etc.).
Atmospheric stability should be determined by vertical AT between the release height and the 10-meter level. Acceptable stability classes are given in Regulatory Guide 1.23. If other well-documented parameters are used to determine plume dispersion (with appropriate justification), the models described in this guide may require modification. A well-documented parameter is one that is substantiated by diffusion data collected in terrain conditions similar to those at the nuclear power plant site being considered.
Calms should be defined as hourly average windspeeds below the vane or anemometer starting speed, whichever is higher (to reflect limitations in instrumentation). If the instrumentation program conforms to the regulatory position in Regulatory Guide 1.23, calms should be assigned a windspeed equal to the vane or anemometer starting speed, whichever is higher. Otherwise, consideration of a conservative evaluation of calms, taking into account the limitations of the windspeed measurement system, will be necessary. Wind directions during calm conditions should be assigned in proportion to the directional distribution of noncalm winds with speeds less than 1.5 meters per second.3

evidence_chain.section: 3.1 Meteorological Data Input
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
3.1 Meteorological Data Input
The meteorological data needed for χ/Q calculations include wind speed, wind direction, and a measure of atmospheric stability. These data should be obtained from an onsite meteorological measurement program based on the guidance of Safety Guide 23, “Onsite Meteorological Programs” (Ref. 12), that includes quality assurance provisions consistent with Appendix B to 10 CFR Part 50. The meteorological data set used in these assessments should represent hourly averages as defined in Safety Guide 23. Data should be representative of the overall site conditions and be free from local effects such as building and cooling tower wakes, brush and vegetation, or terrain. Collected data should be reviewed to identify instrumentation problems and missing or anomalous observations (see Ref. 13). The size of the data set used in the χ/Q assessments should be sufficiently large such that it is representative of long-term meteorological trends at the site. The NRC staff considers 5 years of hourly observations to be representative of long-term trends at most sites. With sufficient justification of its representativeness, however, the minimum meteorological data set is one complete year (including all four seasons) of hourly observations.

Wind direction should be expressed as the direction from which the wind is blowing (i.e., the upwind direction from the center of the site) referenced from true north.

Atmospheric stability should be determined by the vertical temperature difference (ΔT) measured over the difference in height appropriate for the projected release height (including plume rise as applicable). A table of ∆T values in units of degrees Centigrade per 100 meters (°C/100m) versus stability class is given in Safety Guide 23 (Ref. 12). If other well-documented methodologies are used to estimate atmospheric stability (with appropriate justification), the models described in this guide may require modification. A well-documented methodology is one that is substantiated by diffusion data for conditions similar to those at the nuclear power plant site involved.

Appendix A provides information on the structure and content of the meteorological data set and input parameters used by the ARCON96 code.
