data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for the use of atmospheric dispersion models to estimate x/Q and D/Q values for offsite radiological assessments?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for the use of atmospheric dispersion models to estimate χ/Q and D/Q values for offsite radiological assessments are detailed in SRP 2.3.5, which references several regulatory guides and requirements. The criteria are based on compliance with 10 CFR 20 (public dose limits), 10 CFR 50.34a and Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50 (effluent release objectives), and 10 CFR 100.21(c)(2) (site atmospheric dispersion characteristics) (SRP 2.3.5, II).

Applicants must provide a detailed description of the dispersion and deposition models used, including documentation of their accuracy, validity, source configuration, input parameters, topography, and site appropriateness (SRP 2.3.5, II). The models should be substantiated and sufficiently documented to allow NRC review. Regulatory Guide 1.23 specifies requirements for onsite meteorological data collection, including windspeed, wind direction, and atmospheric stability, with vertical temperature difference (ΔT) as the preferred method for stability classification (RG 1.23, Section C.2.2). Meteorological data should be hourly averages and representative of the site (RG 1.145, 1.1).

Regulatory Guide 1.111 provides guidance for calculating χ/Q and D/Q values, which must be estimated for maximum annual average conditions at or beyond the site boundary and at specific receptor locations, using appropriate meteorological data for each release point. Values should also be estimated for 16 radial sectors out to 50 miles (SRP 2.3.5, II; RG 1.111). The models and assumptions, including treatment of plume meander, building wake effects, and other site-specific phenomena, must be described and justified (RG 1.206, 2.3.5.2).

For control room assessments, the ARCON96 code (as described in RG 1.194) is acceptable for χ/Q calculations, with the 95th percentile χ/Q determined for each source-receptor combination and for specified averaging periods (0-2, 2-8, 8-24, 24-96, 96-720 hours) (RG 1.194, C.2). Conservative, bounding parameters should be used, and the period of most adverse release should coincide with the most unfavorable dispersion conditions.

In summary, the NRC requires that atmospheric dispersion models be well-documented, use site-representative meteorological data (preferably ΔT for stability), and follow the methodologies and sector/distance requirements in RG 1.111, RG 1.145, and RG 1.194, as referenced in SRP 2.3.5 and RG 1.206.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
An onsite meteorological measurements program at a nuclear power plant site should be capable of providing the meteorological information needed to make the following assessments:
• a conservative assessment by both the applicant and the regulatory staff of the potential dispersion of radioactive material from, and the radiological consequences of, design-basis accidents to aid in evaluating the acceptability of a site and the adequacy of engineered safety features for a nuclear power plant in accordance with 10 CFR Part 100 criteria
• an assessment by both the applicant and the regulatory staff of the maximum potential annual radiation dose to the public resulting from the routine release of radioactive materials in gaseous effluents to assist in demonstrating that operations will be or are being conducted within the limits of 10 CFR Part 20 and Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50, and to ensure that effluent control equipment design objectives and proposed operating procedures meet the Commission’s requirements for keeping levels of radioactive material in effluents to unrestricted areas as low as practicable
...
Vertical temperature difference is the preferred method for determining Pasquill stability classes at nuclear power plants for licensing purposes because it is an effective indicator for the worst-case stability conditions (e.g., Pasquill stability classes E, F, and G). Also, certain Gaussian plume models endorsed by the NRC (such as the models referenced in Regulatory Guides 1.145 and 1.194, Refs. 9 and 11) are based on empirically derived plume meander factors from field tracer studies that used ΔT to classify atmospheric stability. Alternative methods may be used to classify atmospheric stability for licensing purposes if appropriate justification is provided. However, the use of alternative methods to classify atmospheric stability may require modifications of the models described in Regulatory Guides 1.145 and 1.194.

Alternative methods may be appropriate for classifying atmospheric stability for emergency response purposes if these methods can be shown to be compatible with the plant’s emergency response dose assessment methodology.

The applicant should describe the methods used to estimate atmospheric dispersion factors (χ/Q and D/Q) for offsite and control room radiological assessments. The description should include the following:

• The meteorological data used as input to the models, including the period of record, data quality, and representativeness of the data for the site.
• The locations for which dispersion factors are estimated (e.g., exclusion area boundary, low population zone, nearest residence, control room intake).
• The averaging times and release durations considered in the analyses.
• The treatment of plume meander, building wake effects, and other site-specific phenomena that may affect dispersion.
• The results of the dispersion analyses, including tabulated χ/Q and D/Q values for the locations of interest.

The NRC staff acceptance criteria for atmospheric dispersion estimates are described in NUREG-0800, Section 2.3.5, which references Regulatory Guide 1.23 for onsite meteorological measurements and Regulatory Guide 1.145 for atmospheric dispersion models. The applicant should demonstrate that the methods used are consistent with these guidance documents or provide justification for alternative approaches.

evidence_chain.section: C. REGULATORY POSITION (including subsections 1.1, 1.2, 1.3)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
C. REGULATORY POSITION
This section identifies acceptable methods for (1) calculating atmospheric relative concentration (xJQ) values, (2) determining X/Q values on a directional basis, (3) determining XJQ values on an overall site basis, and (4) choosing X/Q values to be used in evaluations of the types of events described in Regulatory Guides 1.3 and 1.4.
Selection of conservative, less detailed site parameters for the evaluation may be sufficient to establish compliance with regulatory guidelines.
1. CALCULATION OF ATMOSPHERIC RELATIVE CON-CENTRATION (X/Q) VALUES
Equations and parameters presented in this section should be used unless unusual siting, meteorological, or terrain conditions dictate the use of other models or considerations. Site-specific atmospheric diffusion tests covering a full range of conditions may be used as a basis for modifying the equations and parameters.
1.1 Meteorological Data Input
The meteorological data needed for X/Q calculations include windspeed, wind direction, and a measure of atmospheric stability. These data should represent hourly averages as defined in Regulatory Guide 1.23.
Wind direction should be classed into 16 compass directions (22.5-degree sectors centered on true north, north-northeast, etc.).
Atmospheric stability should be determined by vertical AT between the release height and the 10-meter level. Acceptable stability classes are given in Regulatory Guide 1.23. If other well-documented parameters are used to determine plume dispersion (with appropriate justification), the models described in this guide may require modification. A well-documented parameter is one that is substantiated by diffusion data collected in terrain conditions similar to those at the nuclear power plant site being considered.
Calms should be defined as hourly average windspeeds below the vane or anemometer starting speed, whichever is higher (to reflect limitations in instrumentation). If the instrumentation program conforms to the regulatory position in Regulatory Guide 1.23, calms should be assigned a windspeed equal to the vane or anemometer starting speed, whichever is higher. Otherwise, consideration of a conservative evaluation of calms, taking into account the limitations of the windspeed measurement system, will be necessary. Wind directions during calm conditions should be assigned in proportion to the directional distribution of noncalm winds with speeds less than 1.5 meters per second.3
1.2 Determination of Distances for X/Q Calculations
For each wind direction sector, XJQ values for each significant release point should be calculated at an appropriate exclusion area boundary distance and outer low population zone (LPZ) boundary distance. The following procedure should be used to determine these distances. The procedure takes into consideration the possibility of curved airflow trajectories, plume segmentation (particularly in low wind, stable conditions), and the potential for windspeed and wind direction frequency shifts from year to year.
For each of the 16 sectors, the distance for exclusion area boundary or outer LPZ boundary X/Q calculation should be the minimum distance from the stack or, in the case of releases through vents or building penetrations, the nearest point on the building to the exclusion area boundary or outer LPZ boundary within a 45-degree sector centered on the compass direction of interest.
For stack releases, the maximum ground-level concentration in a sector may occur beyond the exclusion area boundary distance or outer LPZ boundary distance. Therefore, for stack releases, X/Q calculations should be made in each sector at each minimum boundary distance and at various distances beyond the exclusion area boundary distance to determine the maximum relative concentration for consideration in subsequent calculations.
1.3 Calculation of X/Q Values at Exclusion Area Boundary Distances
Relative concentrations that can be assumed to apply at the exclusion area boundary for 2 hours immediately following an accident should be determined.4 Calculations based on meteorological data representing a 1-hour average should be assumed to apply for the entire 2-hour period. This assumption is reasonably conservative considering the small variation of xIQ values with averaging time (Ref. 8). If releases associated with a postulated event are estimated to occur in a period of less than 20 minutes, the applicability of these models should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis.
Procedures for calculating "2-hour" X/Q values depend on the mode of release. The procedures are described below.

evidence_chain.section: C. REGULATORY POSITION, 2. GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
C.  REGULATORY POSITION

2. GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS
The May 9, 1997, version of the ARCON96 code as described in Revision 1 of NUREG/CR-6331 (Ref. 1) is an acceptable methodology for assessing control room χ/Q values for use in design basis accident (DBA) radiological analyses, subject to the positions in this guide, unless unusual siting, building arrangement, release characterization, source-receptor configuration, meteorological regimes, or terrain conditions indicate otherwise. These latter situations need to be addressed on a case-by-case basis.

Although the ARCON96 code, when used as described in this guide, can provide an improved basis for determining site-specific χ/Q values, holders of operating licenses may continue to use χ/Q values determined with methodologies previously approved by the NRC staff and documented in the facility’s final safety analysis report (FSAR) to the extent that these values are appropriate for the application in which they are being used. Licensees may also continue to use the licensing basis methodology for determining χ/Q values for newly identified source-receptor combinations or re-generating the approved χ/Q values using more recently collected meteorological data sets. The ARCON96 code and the other models addressed in this guide may be used voluntarily, subject to the guidance herein, as a replacement for the existing licensing basis methodology for determining χ/Q values for design basis control room radiological habitability. Since the existing licensing basis methodology remains valid, a licensee may use the ARCON96 code and the other models addressed in this guide on a selective basis, that is, it is not necessary that existing χ/Q values be updated. The NRC staff does expect that the methodologies will be applied consistently in any particular accident assessment.

For each of the source-to-receptor combinations, the 95th percentile χ/Q should be determined. Values for parameters used as input to the χ/Q assessment should be selected consistent with achieving this confidence level. Selection of conservative, bounding source-to-receptor combinations and less detailed site parameters for the χ/Q evaluation may be sufficient to establish compliance with regulatory guidelines.

Control room χ/Q values are generally determined for each of the following averaging periods: 0-8 hours (or 0-2 hours and 2-8 hours), 8-24 hours, 24-96 hours, 96-720 hours. The period of the most adverse release of radioactive materials to the environment should be assumed to occur coincident with the period of most unfavorable atmospheric dispersion. If the 0-2 hour χ/Q is calculated, this value should be used coincident with the limiting portion of the release to the environment. The 2-8 hour χ/Q value is used for the remaining 6 hours of the first 8-hour time period. Part of this 6-hour interval may occur before or after the limiting 2-hour period. The 8-24, 24-96, and 96-720 hour χ/Q values should similarly be used for the remainder of the release duration. For facilities using the traditional TID-14844 (Ref. 11) source term, the 2-hour period will generally coincide with the start of the event. For facilities with design basis analyses that include an alternative source term, the 2-hour period is often the onset of the in-vessel release phase. In any case, the start of this period should be determined as a part of the analyses for each facility.

data.query: What are the regulatory expectations for identifying and evaluating the interface between a nuclear power plant and the surrounding hydrosphere to ensure adequate protection against hydrologic hazards?
data.answer:
The regulatory expectations for identifying and evaluating the interface between a nuclear power plant and the surrounding hydrosphere are clearly defined in NRC guidance and regulations. According to SRP 2.4.1 (Sections I and II), applicants must provide a comprehensive description of the plant’s interface with the hydrosphere, including site location, major hydrological features, surface and groundwater characteristics, and water supply. This description must include quantitative data on hydrologic features (e.g., record high and low flows, hydrologic anomalies) and detailed site maps showing topography, drainage patterns, flood-prone areas, and the locations of all external plant structures and components.

The evaluation must meet the requirements of 10 CFR Part 100 (site evaluation), 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2 (design bases for protection against natural phenomena), and relevant sections of 10 CFR Part 52 for new applications. Specifically, GDC 2 requires that safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data (SRP 2.4.1, RG 1.59, SRP 3.4.2).

RG 1.59 (Section C) further clarifies that the design basis flood (DBF) must consider the worst site-related flood, including probable maximum flood (PMF), seismically induced floods, hurricanes, seiches, surges, and heavy precipitation. The analysis must also account for dam failures, coincident wind-generated wave activity, and reasonable combinations of less-severe floods with seismic events if their combined probability is significant. The methods used for estimating these hazards must be conservative and justified, as outlined in RG 1.59 and SRP 3.4.2.

In summary, the NRC expects a thorough, conservative, and well-documented evaluation of the hydrosphere interface, ensuring that all relevant hydrologic hazards are identified, characterized, and incorporated into the plant’s design bases to protect safety-related SSCs and ensure public health and safety.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
A. INTRODUCTION
General Design Criterion 2, "Design Bases for Protection Against Natural Phenomena," of Appendix A, "General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants," to 10 CFR Part 50, "Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities," requires, in part, that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena such as floods, tsunami, and seiches without loss of capability to perform their safety functions. Criterion 2 also requires that design bases for these structures, systems, and components reflect (1) appropriate consideration of the most severe of the natural phenomena that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding region, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy and quantity of the historical data and the period of time in which the data have been accumulated, (2) appropriate combinations of the effects of normal and accident conditions with the effects of the natural phenomena, and (3) the importance of the safety functions to be performed.  
...
C. REGULATORY POSITION
1. The conditions resulting from the worst site-related flood probable at a nuclear power plant (e.g., PMF, seismically induced flood, hurricane, seiche, surge, heavy local precipitation) with attendant wind-generated wave activity constitute the design basis flood conditions that safety-related structures, systems, and components identified in Regulatory Guide 1.29 (see footnote 3) must be designed to withstand and retain capability for cold shutdown and maintenance thereof.  

a. The PMF on streams, as defined in Appendix A and based on the analytical techniques summarized in Appendices A and B of this guide, provides an acceptable level of conservatism for estimating flood levels caused by severe hydrometeorological conditions.  

b. Along lakeshores, coastlines, and estuaries, estimates of flood levels resulting from severe surges, seiches, and wave action caused by hydrometeorological activity should be based on criteria comparable in conservatism to those used for Probable Maximum Floods. Criteria and analytical techniques providing this level of conservatism for the analysis of these events are summarized in Appendix A of this guide. Appendix C of this guide presents an acceptable method for estimating the still-water level of the Probable Maximum Surge from hurricanes at open-coast sites on the Atlantic Ocean and Gulf of Mexico.  

c. Flood conditions that could be caused by dam failures from earthquakes should also be considered in establishing the design basis flood. Analytical techniques for evaluating the hydrologic effects of seismically induced dam failures discussed herein are presented in Appendix A of this guide. Techniques for evaluating the effects of tsunami will be presented in a future appendix.  

d. Where upstream dams or other features that provide flood protection are present, in addition to the analyses of the most severe floods that may be induced by either hydrometeorological or seismic mechanisms, reasonable combinations of less-severe flood conditions and seismic events should also be considered to the extent needed for a consistent level of conservatism. The effect of such combinations on the flood conditions at the plant site should be evaluated in cases where the probability of such combinations occurring at the same time and having significant consequences is at least comparable to the probability associated with the most severe hydrometeorological or seismically induced flood.  

e. The effects of coincident wind-generated wave activity to the water levels associated with the worst site-related flood possible (as determined from paragraphs a, b, c, or d above) should be added to generally define the upper limit of flood potential. Acceptable procedures are contained in Appendix A of this guide.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
Requirements
Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations:  
1. GDC 2 requires that SSCs important to safety shall be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena such as earthquakes, tornados, hurricanes, floods, tsunami, and seiches without loss of capability to perform their safety functions as it relates to natural phenomena.  The design bases for these SSCs shall reflect appropriate combinations of the effects of normal and accident conditions with the effects of the natural phenomena.  
...
The design of a structure that must withstand the effects of the highest flood and groundwater levels is acceptable if the relevant requirements of GDC 2, "Design Bases for Protection Against Natural Phenomena," are complied with. The criteria necessary to meet the relevant requirements of GDC 2 are as follows:
1. The highest flood and groundwater levels and the associated static and dynamic effects, if any, used in the design shall be the most severe ones that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated.
2. In most situations, the highest flood level is below the proposed plant grade and only its hydrostatic effects need be considered. Unless the hydrostatic head associated with the highest flood and groundwater levels is relieved by utilizing a drainage or a pumping system around the foundations of a structures, hydrostatic pressure has to be considered as a structural load on basement walls and the foundation slab of a structure. In consideration of any uplifting or floating of a structure, the total buoyancy force may be based on the highest flood level or the highest groundwater level excluding wave action. However, wave action should be included in the calculation for lateral and overturning movements of a structure.
3. Where the flood level is above the proposed plant grade, the dynamic loads of wave action should be considered. Procedures for determining such dynamic loads are acceptable if they are in accordance with or equivalent to those delineated in the U.S. Army Coastal Engineering Research Center, “Shore Protection Manual” (Vol. I, June 2002, reprinted from 1973 edition and  Vol. II, June 2002, reprinted from 1973 edition) or in EM 1110-2-1100, Coastal Engineering Manual, Part II, Chapter 1, “Water Wave Mechanics,” U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, April 30, 2002 as applicable.
Any other methods proposed should be provided with adequate justification and are reviewed on a case by case basis.

data.query: How do regulatory requirements for site safety analysis ensure that the most conservative plausible conceptual models are selected when evaluating hydrologic causal mechanisms at a nuclear power plant site?
data.answer:
Regulatory requirements for site safety analysis at nuclear power plant sites ensure the selection of the most conservative plausible conceptual models for evaluating hydrologic causal mechanisms through a combination of explicit review procedures, technical rationales, and acceptance criteria grounded in federal regulations and NRC guidance. 

According to SRP 2.4.1 (Section III. REVIEW PROCEDURES and II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA / Technical Rationale), the NRC staff reviews a variety of alternate conceptual models based on the site's geological and hydrological characteristics. The most adverse of these models, particularly in terms of contaminant movement, must be used to derive a conservative bounding estimate of travel time. This approach requires consideration of all relevant pathways and physiographic conditions to ensure the most severe impact on people and the environment is evaluated. The technical rationale is rooted in General Design Criterion (GDC) 2 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A), which mandates that safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data.

Regulatory Guide 1.59 (Sections B and C) further reinforces this conservatism by requiring that the design basis flood conditions represent the worst site-related flood probable, such as the Probable Maximum Flood (PMF), and that analytical techniques used provide an acceptable level of conservatism. Reasonable combinations of less-severe flood conditions must also be considered if their probability and consequences are comparable to the most severe events. SRP 3.4.2 and RG 1.29 cross-reference these requirements, emphasizing that the highest flood and groundwater levels, and associated effects, must be used in design, again with sufficient margin for data limitations.

In summary, the regulatory framework compels applicants to consider and select the most conservative plausible conceptual models by requiring evaluation of the most severe hydrologic phenomena, use of bounding estimates, and explicit consideration of uncertainties and combinations of events, as detailed in SRP 2.4.1, 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A (GDC 2), RG 1.59, and SRP 3.4.2.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory requirements ensure that site elevation data are clearly defined and consistently presented in licensing documents for nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory requirements ensure that site elevation data are clearly defined and consistently presented in licensing documents for nuclear power plants through a combination of regulatory mandates, guidance, and review criteria. According to 10 CFR 50.34(a)(3), applications must include a description and safety assessment of the site, explicitly requiring the inclusion of site and plant elevations with respect to probable maximum flood levels, groundwater levels, and other relevant data. This ensures that elevation data are a fundamental part of the licensing documentation (10 CFR Part 50 § 50.34).

The Standard Review Plan (SRP) 2.4.1 further details the acceptance criteria and review procedures, requiring that applications provide comprehensive descriptions and elevations of safety-related structures, facilities, and access points. These must be sufficiently complete to allow evaluation of flood design bases. The SRP specifies that topographic maps of good quality and sufficient scale, as well as detailed tabulations of elevation-storage relationships, must be included. Additionally, spatially referenced data such as elevation contours and detailed topographic and bathymetric maps are required to support the safety conclusions (SRP 2.4.1, Sections II and III).

Regulatory Guide 1.59 provides further guidance on the use of elevation data in the context of flood hazard analysis, referencing ANSI standards and providing methods for estimating probable maximum flood (PMF) levels. Appendix B of RG 1.59 includes tabulated PMF peak discharge data and maps with isolines of equal PMF peak discharge, which are used to determine appropriate flood elevations for site evaluation. The guide also describes the process for transposing and adjusting PMF data to the specific site, ensuring consistency in how elevation data are applied and presented (RG 1.59, C. REGULATORY POSITION; Appendix B).

Together, these requirements and guidance documents ensure that site elevation data are clearly defined, consistently presented, and rigorously reviewed as part of the licensing process for nuclear power plants.

data.query: In what ways do general design criteria for site protection relate to the regulatory expectations for the use of standardized units and contour intervals in site topography figures?
data.answer:
The general design criteria for site protection, particularly General Design Criterion (GDC) 2 as specified in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A (see [2]), require that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area. This includes consideration of the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which historical data have been accumulated. To meet these regulatory expectations, site characterization—including topography—must be sufficiently detailed and accurate to support robust safety analyses.

SRP 2.4.1 (Section II) further clarifies that site topographic maps must be of good quality and sufficient scale to allow independent analysis of pre- and post-construction drainage patterns, and that flood maps should be of appropriate scale and quality (see [1]). The use of standardized units and appropriate contour intervals in site topography figures is essential to ensure that the data are clear, interpretable, and consistent with hydrologic and geologic data from authoritative sources such as the USGS, NOAA, NRCS, and USACE. This standardization supports the NRC’s ability to independently verify applicant analyses and ensures that the design bases for protection against natural phenomena are based on reliable and comparable data.

Additionally, SRP 2.4.1 (Section III) notes that spatially referenced data, including topographic and bathymetric data with elevation contours, are reviewed by NRC staff, and that these data may be presented in GIS format with clear descriptions of the software and methods used. This reinforces the expectation for standardized, high-quality data presentation.

In summary, the general design criteria for site protection are directly related to regulatory expectations for the use of standardized units and contour intervals in site topography figures, as these practices ensure the accuracy, clarity, and reliability of the data used to evaluate site safety against natural phenomena, in accordance with GDC 2 and supporting NRC guidance (see [1], [2], [5]).

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for determining the design basis flood for nuclear power plant sites located near streams and rivers?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for determining the design basis flood (DBF) for nuclear power plant sites located near streams and rivers are established to ensure that safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) are protected against the most severe flooding events that could reasonably be expected at the site. According to SRP 2.4.3 Section II, the requirements are grounded in several NRC regulations, including 10 CFR Part 100 (site evaluation), 10 CFR 100.23(d) (siting factors for seismically induced floods), 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2 (protection against natural phenomena), and relevant sections of 10 CFR Part 52 for ESP and COL applications.

Applicants must identify and evaluate hydrological features of the site, considering the most severe natural phenomena historically reported, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in data (SRP 2.4.3 II; 10 CFR 50.34(a)(3)(i)-(iii)). Specifically, for streams and rivers, the design basis must be based on conservative assumptions regarding hydrometeorologic characteristics, including: (a) watershed area, (b) probable maximum precipitation (PMP) and its hyetograph, (c) maximum probable maximum flood (PMF) water surface elevation with coincident wind-waves, and (d) hydraulic characteristics describing dynamic effects of the PMF on SSCs important to safety (SRP 2.4.3 II.1).

Regulatory Guide 1.59 provides further guidance, stating that the PMF, as defined in ANSI N170-1976 and supplemented by NRC staff guidance, is the acceptable basis for estimating flood levels from severe hydrometeorological conditions. The guide also allows for alternative, NRC-accepted methods for estimating PMF, provided they are sufficiently conservative (RG 1.59, C.1, Appendix A, Appendix B). Safety-related SSCs identified per RG 1.29 must be designed to withstand these flood conditions (RG 1.29, RG 1.59).

In summary, the DBF for nuclear power plants near streams and rivers must be conservatively determined using the PMF, considering site-specific hydrological and meteorological data, and must ensure the protection of safety-related SSCs as required by NRC regulations and guidance.

data.query: How do general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena relate to the selection of conceptual models used in flood hazard assessments for nuclear facility siting?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for protection against natural phenomena, specifically GDC 2 as outlined in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, directly inform the selection and application of conceptual models used in flood hazard assessments for nuclear facility siting. GDC 2 requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin to account for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2; RG 1.59, Section A).

In practice, this means that the conceptual models chosen for flood hazard assessments—such as those estimating the Probable Maximum Flood (PMF), seismically induced floods, or storm surges—must be conservative and reflect the worst-case scenarios that could reasonably occur at the site. The Standard Review Plan (SRP 2.4.3) specifies that these models should be based on conservative assumptions regarding hydrometeorologic characteristics, watershed area, and other relevant factors, ensuring that the design bases for SSCs are robust against uncertainties in historical data and physical limitations of natural phenomena. The use of deterministic approaches is recommended to ensure that the severity of design basis events is not underestimated (SRP 2.4.3, Section II).

Regulatory Guide 1.59 further clarifies that the design basis flood conditions should be established using methodologies that provide an acceptable level of conservatism, such as those found in ANSI N170-1976, and that these methods are endorsed by the NRC for estimating PMF and related phenomena (RG 1.59, Section C). Thus, the general design criteria mandate that the conceptual models used in flood hazard assessments must be sufficiently conservative to ensure the safety of nuclear facilities under the most severe credible natural events.

evidence_chain.section: A. INTRODUCTION; C. REGULATORY POSITION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
A. INTRODUCTION
General Design Criterion 2, "Design Bases for Protection Against Natural Phenomena," of Appendix A, "General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants," to 10 CFR Part 50, "Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities," requires, in part, that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena such as floods, tsunami, and seiches without loss of capability to perform their safety functions. Criterion 2 also requires that design bases for these structures, systems, and components reflect (1) appropriate consideration of the most severe of the natural phenomena that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding region, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy and quantity of the historical data and the period of time in which the data have been accumulated, (2) appropriate combinations of the effects of normal and accident conditions with the effects of the natural phenomena, and (3) the importance of the safety functions to be performed.  
...
This guide discusses the design basis floods that nuclear power plants should be designed to withstand without loss of capability for cold shutdown and maintenance thereof. ... The material previously contained in Appendix A, "Probable Maximum and Seismically Induced Floods on Streams," has been replaced by American National Standards Institute (ANSI) Standard N170-1976, "Standards for Determining Design Basis Flooding at Power Reactor Sites," which has been endorsed as acceptable by the NRC staff with the exception noted in Appendix A. In addition to information on stream flooding, ANSI N170-1976 contains methodology for estimating probable maximum surges and seiches at estuaries and coastal areas on oceans and large lakes. Appendix B gives timesaving alternative methods of estimating the probable maximum flood along streams, and Appendix C gives a simplified method of estimating probable maximum surges on the Atlantic and Gulf coasts.
...
C. REGULATORY POSITION
1. The conditions resulting from the worst site-related flood probable at a nuclear power plant (e.g., PMF, seismically induced flood, hurricane, seiche, surge, heavy local precipitation) with attendant wind-generated wave activity constitute the design basis flood conditions that safety-related structures, systems, and components identified in Regulatory Guide 1.29 ... must be designed to withstand and retain capability for cold shutdown and maintenance thereof.

a. The PMF on streams, as defined in Appendix A and based on the analytical techniques summarized in Appendices A and B of this guide, provides an acceptable level of conservatism for estimating flood levels caused by severe hydrometeorological conditions.

b. Along lakeshores, coastlines, and estuaries, estimates of flood levels resulting from severe surges, seiches, and wave action caused by hydrometeorological activity should be based on criteria comparable in conservatism to those used for Probable Maximum Floods. Criteria and analytical techniques providing this level of conservatism for the analysis of these events are summarized in Appendix A of this guide. Appendix C of this guide presents an acceptable method for estimating the still-water level of the Probable Maximum Surge from hurricanes at open-coast sites on the Atlantic Ocean and Gulf of Mexico.

data.query: What are the NRC requirements for considering combined natural phenomena events when establishing the design basis flood for nuclear power plant sites?
data.answer:
The NRC requires that the design basis flood (DBF) for nuclear power plant sites be established by considering both the most severe individual natural phenomena and appropriate combinations of such phenomena that could reasonably occur at the site. According to 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion 2, the design bases for safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) must reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties, and must also account for appropriate combinations of the effects of normal and accident conditions with the effects of natural phenomena (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2).

SRP 2.4.3 further clarifies that compliance with GDC 2 requires consideration of the most severe natural phenomena and their combinations, including the effects of site-related proximity, seismic, and non-seismic information as they relate to flooding (SRP 2.4.3, II and III).

Regulatory Guide 1.59 provides detailed guidance on combined natural phenomena events, stating that the DBF should be based on the most severe flood conditions reasonably predicted to occur, including those resulting from severe hydrometeorological conditions, seismic activity, or both. For sites on streams, the Probable Maximum Flood (PMF) is typically used, while for lakes, seashores, or estuaries, the DBF may be determined by the most severe combination of hydrometeorological parameters (e.g., Probable Maximum Hurricane, Seiche, Surge) or reasonable combinations of less severe events. RG 1.59 emphasizes that seismically induced floods and their reasonable combinations with hydrometeorological floods should be considered, especially if the combined effects are more severe or more probable than the most severe single event. Analyses should not be limited to the most severe single event but should also include reasonable combinations of less-severe events if their joint probability and consequences are comparable to the most severe event (RG 1.59, B. DISCUSSION).

In summary, NRC requirements mandate that the DBF be established by evaluating both the most severe individual natural phenomena and reasonable combinations of such events, ensuring a conservative and comprehensive approach to flood hazard assessment for nuclear power plant safety.

evidence_chain.section: B. DISCUSSION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
B. DISCUSSION
Nuclear power plants should be designed to prevent the loss of capability for cold shutdown and maintenance thereof resulting from the most severe flood conditions that can reasonably be predicted to occur at a site as a result of severe hydrometeorological conditions, seismic activity, or both. ...
The conditions resulting from the worst site-related flood probable at the nuclear power plant (e.g., PMF, seismically induced flood, seiche, surge, severe local precipitation) with attendant wind-generated wave activity constitute the design basis flood conditions that safety-related structures, systems, and components identified in Regulatory Guide 1.29 should be designed to withstand and retain capability for cold shutdown and maintenance thereof.  
For sites along streams, the PMF generally provides the design basis flood. For sites along lakes or seashores, a flood condition of comparable severity could be produced by the most severe combination of hydrometeorological parameters reasonably possible, such as may be produced by a Probable Maximum Hurricane or by a Probable Maximum Seiche. On estuaries, a Probable Maximum River Flood, a Probable Maximum Surge, a Probable Maximum Seiche, or a reasonable combination of less severe phenomenologically caused flooding events should be considered in arriving at design basis flood conditions comparable in frequency of occurrence with a PMF on streams.  
In addition to floods produced by severe hydrometeorological conditions, the most severe seismically induced floods reasonably possible should be considered for each site. ... Consideration of seismically induced floods should include the same range of seismic events as is postulated for the design of the nuclear plant. ... In the case of seismically induced floods along rivers, lakes, and estuaries that may be produced by events less severe than a Safe Shutdown Earthquake, consideration should be given to the coincident occurrence of floods due to severe hydrometeorological conditions, but only where the effects on the plant are worse than and the probability of such combined events may be greater than an individual occurrence of the most severe event of either type. Appendix A contains acceptable combinations of such events. ...
Analyses of only the most severe flood conditions may not indicate potential threats to safety-related systems that might result from combinations of flood conditions thought to be less severe. Therefore, reasonable combinations of less-severe flood conditions should also be considered to the extent needed for a consistent level of conservatism. Such combinations should be evaluated in cases where the probability of their existing at the same time and having significant consequences is at least comparable to that associated with the most severe hydrometeorological or seismically induced flood.

data.query: How do NRC regulations address the consideration of long-term sea level rise in determining the design basis flood elevation for nuclear facilities?
data.answer:
NRC regulations do not explicitly require the consideration of long-term sea level rise when determining the design basis flood elevation for nuclear facilities. According to SRP 2.4.3, the Standard Review Plan (SRP) focuses on the use of the probable maximum flood (PMF) and probable maximum precipitation (PMP) as the basis for flood hazard evaluation, emphasizing conservative assumptions and the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area. The relevant regulatory requirements, such as 10 CFR Part 100 and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, require consideration of the most severe natural phenomena with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data, but do not specifically mandate the inclusion of future or long-term sea level rise (SRP 2.4.3, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA).

Regulatory Guide 1.59 further clarifies that the design basis flood for coastal and lakeshore sites should be based on the most severe combination of hydrometeorological parameters reasonably possible, such as a Probable Maximum Hurricane or Probable Maximum Surge, using conservative analytical techniques (RG 1.59, B. Discussion; C. Regulatory Position). While these methods are intended to be highly conservative, they are based on current and historical data and do not explicitly require projections of future sea level rise.

However, SRP 2.4.3 does note that 'long-term environmental changes and changes to the region resulting from human or natural causes may have introduced changes to the site characteristics that could be relevant to the design basis.' This suggests that if long-term sea level rise is recognized as a relevant change, it could be considered in the review process, but it is not an explicit regulatory requirement.

In summary, NRC regulations and guidance require conservative estimation of flood hazards based on the most severe historically reported natural phenomena, but do not explicitly require consideration of long-term sea level rise in determining the design basis flood elevation.

data.query: How do regulatory requirements for protection against natural phenomena relate to the methods used for estimating runoff from extreme precipitation events at nuclear facility sites?
data.answer:
Regulatory requirements for protection against natural phenomena at nuclear facility sites are directly linked to the methods used for estimating runoff from extreme precipitation events, such as probable maximum precipitation (PMP) and probable maximum flood (PMF). According to SRP 2.4.3 (Section II), the NRC mandates that site evaluations and facility designs must consider the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data (referencing 10 CFR Part 100, 10 CFR 50 Appendix A GDC 2, and related sections). Specifically, estimates of runoff from extreme precipitation are required to establish design bases for flooding in streams, rivers, and site drainage. These estimates must be based on conservative hydrometeorologic assumptions, including watershed area, PMP depth and hyetograph, and PMF water surface elevations, to ensure safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSC) are protected.

10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2 further requires that SSCs important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of floods and other natural phenomena, reflecting the most severe events with appropriate safety margins. Regulatory Guide 1.59 provides detailed guidance on developing hydrometeorological design bases, endorsing the use of conservative analytical techniques and alternative methods (such as those in ANSI N170-1976 and RG 1.59 Appendix B) for estimating PMF. These methods, including timesaving alternatives and enveloping isolines, are accepted by the NRC for their conservatism and are used to determine the design basis flood conditions that SSCs must withstand.

In summary, regulatory requirements ensure that the methods for estimating runoff from extreme precipitation are conservative, well-documented, and justified, forming the technical basis for flood protection measures at nuclear facility sites (SRP 2.4.3 II; 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A GDC 2; RG 1.59 A, C, Appendix B).

evidence_chain.section: II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
Requirements
Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations:
1. 10 CFR Part 100, as it relates to identifying and evaluating hydrological features of the site. The requirements to consider physical site characteristics in site evaluations are specified in 10 CFR 100.10(c) for applications before January 10, 1997, and in 10 CFR 100.20(c) for applications on or after January 10, 1997.
2. 10 CFR 100.23(d) sets forth the criteria to determine the siting factors for plant design bases with respect to seismically induced floods and water waves at the site.
3. 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, for CP and OL applications, as it relates to consideration of the most severe of the natural phenomena that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated.
4. 10 CFR 52.17(a)(1)(vi), for ESP applications, and 10 CFR 52.79(a)(1)(iii), for COL applications, as they relate to identifying hydrologic site characteristics with appropriate consideration of the most severe of the natural phenomena that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area and with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated.

SRP Acceptance Criteria
Specific SRP acceptance criteria acceptable to meet the relevant requirements of the NRC’s regulations identified above are as follows for the review described in this SRP section. ...
Appropriate sections of the following Regulatory Guides are used by the staff for the identified acceptance criteria:
Regulatory Guide 1.27 describes the applicable ultimate heat sink capabilities.
Regulatory Guide 1.29 identifies seismic design bases for SSC important to safety.
Regulatory Guide 1.59, as supplemented by current best practices, provides guidance for developing the hydrometeorological design bases.
Regulatory Guide 1.102 describes acceptable flood protection to prevent the safety-related facilities from being adversely affected.

1. Design Bases for Flooding in Streams and Rivers. To meet the requirements of GDC 2, 10 CFR 52.17, and 10 CFR Part 100, estimates of the following characteristics are needed, and should be based on conservative assumptions of hydrometeorologic characteristics in the drainage area: (a) the area of the watershed used to estimate flooding in streams and rivers, (b) the total depth of PMP and the PMP hyetograph, (c) the maximum PMF water surface elevation in streams and rivers with coincident wind-waves, and (d) hydraulic characteristics that describe dynamic effects of PMF on SSC important to safety. If a potential hazard to SSC important to safety exists, the applicant should document and justify the design bases of affected facilities.

2. Design Bases for Site Drainage. To meet the requirements of GDC 2, 10 CFR 52.17 and 10 CFR Part 100, estimates of the following characteristics are needed: the runoff from the immediate site area and the drainage from areas adjacent to the site, including the roofs of safety related structures. Flood response characteristics should be identified to estimate flooding adjacent to and on the plant site. The effects of erosion and sedimentation during the flooding should be identified and their effects on SSC important to safety should be determined. If a potential hazard to SSC important to safety exists, the applicant should document and justify the design bases of affected facilities.

evidence_chain.section: Appendix A to Part 50—General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants (Criteria 2, 3, 4)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appendix A to Part 50—General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants

Criterion 2—Design bases for protection against natural phenomena. Structures, systems, and components important to safety shall be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena such as earthquakes, tornadoes, hurricanes, floods, tsunami, and seiches without loss of capability to perform their safety functions. The design bases for these structures, systems, and components shall reflect: (1) Appropriate consideration of the most severe of the natural phenomena that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated, (2) appropriate combinations of the effects of normal and accident conditions with the effects of the natural phenomena, and (3) the importance of the safety functions to be performed.

Criterion 3—Fire protection. Structures, systems, and components important to safety shall be designed and located to minimize, consistent with other safety requirements, the probability and effect of fires and explosions. Noncombustible and heat-resistant materials shall be used wherever practical throughout the plant, particularly in locations such as the control room, the cable spreading rooms, and the reactor containment. Fire detection and fighting systems of appropriate capacity and capability shall be provided and designed to minimize the adverse effects of fires on structures, systems, and components important to safety. Firefighting systems shall be designed to ensure that their rupture or inadvertent operation does not significantly impair the safety capability of these structures, systems, and components.

Criterion 4—Environmental and dynamic effects design bases. Structures, systems, and components important to safety shall be designed to accommodate the effects of and to be compatible with the environmental conditions associated with normal operation, maintenance, testing, and postulated accidents, including loss-of-coolant accidents. In addition, these structures, systems, and components shall be appropriately protected against dynamic effects, including the effects of missiles, pipe whipping, and discharging fluids, that may result from equipment failures and from events and conditions outside the nuclear power unit.

data.query: What regulatory considerations govern the use of hydrologic modeling approaches, such as the unit hydrograph method, for evaluating site flooding potential under probable maximum precipitation conditions?
data.answer:
The regulatory considerations governing the use of hydrologic modeling approaches, such as the unit hydrograph method, for evaluating site flooding potential under probable maximum precipitation (PMP) conditions are detailed in several NRC documents. According to SRP 2.4.3 (Section III), runoff models like the unit hydrograph method or other standard runoff discharge estimates are used to estimate discharge on the site drainage system under local PMP. The appropriateness of the selected runoff model must be evaluated, considering the hydrologic characteristics of the watershed; for diverse watersheds, distributed models are encouraged over lumped models. The NRC staff reviews the applicant’s model choice, compares coefficients and parameters to documented locations, and may perform independent analyses to verify results, ensuring conformity with acceptance criteria (SRP 2.4.3, III; SRP 2.4.2, III).

Regulatory Guide 1.59 (Section C; Appendix B) further specifies that the probable maximum flood (PMF), derived from PMP, constitutes the design basis for flood protection of safety-related structures. Analytical techniques for PMF estimation, including those in standard hydrology texts and NRC-accepted methods, are recommended. Appendix B of RG 1.59 provides alternative methods for estimating PMF peak discharge, including the use of tabulated PMF values and isoline maps, with guidance on their applicability and limitations. Applicants may use these methods, and results are generally accepted by NRC staff if appropriately justified.

Additionally, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2, requires that safety-related structures be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena, including floods, with appropriate consideration of historical data and sufficient safety margins. This regulatory basis underpins the requirement for conservative and site-appropriate hydrologic modeling.

In summary, the NRC requires that hydrologic modeling for site flooding under PMP conditions use accepted, justified methods; that model parameters be validated against documented data; and that the results provide a conservative basis for flood protection of safety-related structures, in accordance with SRP 2.4.3, SRP 2.4.2, RG 1.59, and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for determining base flow in the context of flood hazard analyses for nuclear power plant siting?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for determining base flow in the context of flood hazard analyses for nuclear power plant siting are grounded in a comprehensive evaluation of the drainage area, hydrologic and hydraulic characteristics, and the use of conservative, accepted methodologies. According to SRP 2.4.3 (Section III), the drainage area contributing runoff to the plant site must be delineated using topographic or digital elevation data, and the probable maximum precipitation (PMP) for this area is determined using NOAA/NWS hydrometeorological reports. The rainfall-runoff response, which includes base flow as part of the total streamflow, is characterized by rainfall losses and overland flow mechanisms. The NRC staff reviews the applicant’s flood estimates using currently available methods and may require additional data or independent analysis if discrepancies are found.

Regulatory Guide 1.59 (Sections A, B, and C) endorses the use of ANSI N170-1976 for determining design basis flooding, which includes methodologies for estimating the probable maximum flood (PMF) on streams. The PMF, which incorporates base flow as part of the total flow, is generally used as the design basis flood. Analytical techniques for PMF estimation, as described in Appendices A and B of RG 1.59, are considered acceptable and provide a conservative approach to flood estimation.

10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2, requires that structures, systems, and components important to safety be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena, including floods, with appropriate consideration of historical data and sufficient safety margins. SRP 2.4.2 and 2.4.4 further require documentation and review of all potential flood sources, including base flow, and the use of historical streamflow records and accepted hydrologic models (e.g., USACE models) for flood routing and peak flow determination.

In summary, the regulatory requirements mandate the use of conservative, accepted methodologies for delineating drainage areas, estimating PMP and PMF (which include base flow), and verifying these estimates through review of historical data and accepted hydrologic models, as detailed in SRP 2.4.3, RG 1.59, and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A.

evidence_chain.section: III. REVIEW PROCEDURES
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
The drainage area that contributes runoff to the location on the stream network adjacent to the plant site should be evaluated by delineating ridge lines on a topographic map. More recently, automated drainage network and contributing area delineation procedures have also become available that use digital elevation and digitized stream network data from the United States Geological Survey. The staff reviews the applicant’s flood estimates using currently available methods. If a significant discrepancy exists in drainage areas between the two estimates, the staff will need the applicant to provide more data to support its estimate, or to accept the staff’s estimate and re-analyze flooding of the streams and rivers.

Probable maximum precipitation on the drainage area estimated above determines in the probable maximum flood adjacent to the plant site. The PMP is estimated for the drainage area using currently applicable National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Weather Service (NWS) hydrometeorological reports (HMR). The rainfall-runoff response characterized by rainfall losses and overland flow mechanisms in the drainage area results in flooding that propagates downstream via the stream network. The staff may consult the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) and other appropriate State and Federal agencies to determine the appropriate rainfall-runoff response functions and other watershed parameters. In its review of the PMF on streams and rivers, the staff may verify the applicant’s estimate, perform its own independent analysis, or accept an estimate from a Federal or State agency that has the authority and responsibility to carry out these estimates. In its independent analysis, the staff should use currently accepted runoff generation and flood routing methods, such as those made available by the USACE, and hydraulic characteristics such as velocities and momentum fluxes that may assist in estimation of dynamic effects of the PMF on SSC. The staff’s estimates are compared with the applicant’s estimates to determine conformity to the acceptance criteria in Subsection II of this SRP section.

data.query: How do the general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena relate to the regulatory requirements for estimating base flow when determining probable maximum flood discharge at a nuclear power plant site?
data.answer:
The general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena, specifically General Design Criterion (GDC) 2 from Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, require that nuclear power plant structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including floods, without loss of safety function. GDC 2 mandates that the design bases for these SSCs reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; RG 1.29; RG 1.59).

In relation to estimating base flow when determining probable maximum flood (PMF) discharge at a nuclear power plant site, these criteria are operationalized through regulatory requirements and guidance. SRP 2.4.3 specifies that, to meet GDC 2 and related regulations (10 CFR Part 100, 10 CFR 52.17), estimates of PMF characteristics—including base flow—must be based on conservative assumptions regarding hydrometeorologic conditions in the drainage area. This ensures that the design basis flood accounts for the most severe plausible conditions, consistent with the intent of GDC 2 (SRP 2.4.3, II. Acceptance Criteria).

Regulatory Guide 1.59 further elaborates that design basis floods, including PMF, should be determined using methods that provide sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data. Appendix B of RG 1.59 provides alternative methods for estimating PMF peak discharge, including the use of tabulated PMF determinations and regional maps, which incorporate conservative assumptions about base flow and other hydrologic parameters (RG 1.59, Appendix B, B.3, B.3.1).

In summary, the general design criteria require that the estimation of base flow for PMF discharge determination be conservative and reflect the most severe historical conditions, thereby ensuring that nuclear plant SSCs remain protected against extreme natural flooding events.

data.query: What is the NRC acceptance criterion for conservatism in the selection of rainfall-runoff response functions used in probable maximum flood (PMF) analyses for nuclear power plant siting?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criterion for conservatism in the selection of rainfall-runoff response functions used in probable maximum flood (PMF) analyses for nuclear power plant siting is that the analyses must be based on conservative assumptions regarding hydrometeorologic characteristics in the drainage area. According to SRP 2.4.3, Section II, estimates of watershed area, probable maximum precipitation (PMP) depth and hyetograph, maximum PMF water surface elevation, and hydraulic characteristics must all be conservatively determined to meet the requirements of GDC 2, 10 CFR 52.17, and 10 CFR Part 100. The SRP emphasizes the use of a deterministic approach, rather than a probabilistic one, to avoid underestimating the severity of rare natural phenomena due to limited historical data. This approach ensures that the practical physical limitations of natural phenomena are accounted for, providing a conservative basis for design.

Regulatory Guide 1.59 further clarifies that the PMF, as defined and estimated using accepted analytical techniques (including those of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and NRC-accepted methods), provides an acceptable level of conservatism for flood level estimation. The guide notes that the procedures used are highly conservative due to enveloping methods and that reasonable combinations of less-severe flood conditions should also be considered if their combined probability and consequences are comparable to the most severe event. Limitations of generalized methods must be carefully evaluated for site-specific applicability.

In summary, the NRC requires that rainfall-runoff response functions for PMF analyses be selected and applied using conservative, deterministic assumptions and methods, as detailed in SRP 2.4.3 (Section II) and RG 1.59 (Section C, Appendix B), to ensure the safety of nuclear power plant design bases.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for evaluating the effects of upstream dam failures on nuclear power plant safety-related structures, systems, and components?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for evaluating the effects of upstream dam failures on nuclear power plant safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) are established to ensure that such hazards are adequately considered in plant design and safety analysis. According to SRP 2.4.4 (Section II), the hydrological design basis must account for potential hazards from the failure of upstream, onsite, and downstream water control structures. The evaluation must meet the requirements of 10 CFR Part 100 (specifically 10 CFR 100.10(c), 10 CFR 100.20(c), and 10 CFR 100.23(d)), and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, which require consideration of the most severe natural phenomena, including floods from dam failures, with appropriate conservatism and margin for uncertainties in historical data.

The SRP specifies that analyses must include:
1. Conservative estimates of flood waves from severe breaching of upstream dams, considering full reservoir levels and coincident flow rates, to determine the maximum flood elevation that could affect safety-related SSCs.
2. Evaluation of domino-type or cascading dam failures, including those induced by seismic or hydrological events, to identify the worst-case flood scenario at the plant site.
3. Assessment of dynamic effects (e.g., velocities, momentum fluxes) of flood waves on SSCs important to safety, with documentation and inclusion in design bases if hazards are identified.

10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2 and 4, further require that SSCs important to safety be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including floods, and be protected against dynamic effects from external events such as dam failures.

Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.59 (Sections B and C) provides acceptable methods for evaluating seismically induced floods from dam failures, including consideration of the Safe Shutdown Earthquake and the potential for cascading dam failures. RG 1.29 and RG 1.143 provide additional guidance on the classification and design of SSCs, including radwaste systems, to ensure they meet seismic and flood protection requirements.

In summary, the regulatory framework requires a conservative, comprehensive evaluation of upstream dam failure scenarios, including cascading failures and dynamic flood effects, to ensure that all safety-related SSCs are adequately protected and can perform their safety functions during such events (SRP 2.4.4, 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix A, RG 1.59, RG 1.29, RG 1.143).

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
In this section of the safety analysis report (SAR), the hydrological design basis is developed to ensure that any potential hazard to the safety-related facilities due to the failure of onsite, upstream, and downstream water control structures are considered in plant design. ... 

II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
Requirements
Acceptance criteria are based on meeting the relevant requirements of the following Commission regulations:
1. 10 CFR Part 100, as it relates to identifying and evaluating hydrological features of the site. The requirements to consider physical site characteristics in site evaluations are specified in 10 CFR 100.10(c) for applications before January 10, 1997, and in 10 CFR 100.20(c) for applications on or after January 10, 1997.
2. 10 CFR 100.23(d) sets forth the criteria to determine the siting factors for plant design bases with respect to seismically induced floods and water waves at the site.
3. 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2, for CP and OL applications, as it relates to consideration of the most severe of the natural phenomena that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated.
...
SRP Acceptance Criteria
Specific SRP acceptance criteria acceptable to meet the relevant requirements of the NRC’s regulations identified above are as follows for the review described in this SRP section. ...
1. Flood Waves from Severe Breaching of an Upstream Dam: To meet the requirements of GDC 2, 10 CFR 52.17, 10 CFR Part 100, and 10 CFR 100.23(d), estimates of the following characteristics are needed, and should be based on conservative assumptions of hydrometeorological, geological, and seismic characteristics in the drainage area: (a) modes of assumed dam breaches or failures, (b) consideration of flood control reservoirs at full pool level, and (c) conservatism of coincident flow rates and water surface elevations. Flood waves produced by postulated dam failure scenarios should be routed to the proposed plant site to conservatively estimate the most severe flood water surface elevation that may affect SSC important to safety.
2. Domino-Type or Cascading Dam Failures: To meet the requirements of GDC 2, 10 CFR 52.17, 10 CFR Part 100, and 10 CFR 100.23(d), an appropriate configuration of the cascade of dam failures and its potential to produce the largest flood adjacent to the plant site is needed. Several possible cascading dam failures should be investigated, including those induced by seismic and hydrological failures. The failure modes should be conservatively chosen and the resulting flood waves should be conservatively routed to the proposed plant site to estimate the most severe flood water surface elevation that may affect SSC important to safety.
3. Dynamic Effects on Structures: To meet the requirements of GDC 2, 10 CFR 52.17, and 10 CFR Part 100, an estimate of dynamic effects of flood waves, such as velocities and momentum fluxes, on SSC important to safety is needed. If a potential hazard to SSC important to safety exists from dynamic effects of flood waves, it should be documented and included in the design bases of affected facilities.

evidence_chain.section: Appendix A to Part 50—General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants (Criteria 2 and 4)
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appendix A to Part 50—General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants

Criterion 2—Design bases for protection against natural phenomena. Structures, systems, and components important to safety shall be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena such as earthquakes, tornadoes, hurricanes, floods, tsunami, and seiches without loss of capability to perform their safety functions. The design bases for these structures, systems, and components shall reflect: (1) Appropriate consideration of the most severe of the natural phenomena that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated, (2) appropriate combinations of the effects of normal and accident conditions with the effects of the natural phenomena, and (3) the importance of the safety functions to be performed.

Criterion 4—Environmental and dynamic effects design bases. Structures, systems, and components important to safety shall be designed to accommodate the effects of and to be compatible with the environmental conditions associated with normal operation, maintenance, testing, and postulated accidents, including loss of coolant accidents. These structures, systems, and components shall be appropriately protected against dynamic effects, including the effects of missiles, pipe whipping, and discharging fluids, that may result from equipment failures and from events and conditions outside the nuclear power unit. However, dynamic effects associated with postulated pipe ruptures within the containment may be excluded from the design basis when analyses reviewed and approved by the Commission demonstrate that the probability of fluid system piping rupture is extremely low under conditions consistent with the design basis for the piping.

evidence_chain.section: B. DISCUSSION and C. REGULATORY POSITION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
In addition to floods produced by severe hydrometeorological conditions, the most severe seismically induced floods reasonably possible should be considered for each site. Along streams and estuaries, seismically induced floods may be produced by dam failures or landslides. ... Consideration of seismically induced floods should include the same range of seismic events as is postulated for the design of the nuclear plant. For instance, the analysis of floods caused by dam failures, landslides, or tsunami requires consideration of seismic events of the severity of the Safe Shutdown Earthquake occurring at the location that would produce the worst such flood at the nuclear power plant site. In the case of seismically induced floods along rivers, lakes, and estuaries that may be produced by events less severe than a Safe Shutdown Earthquake, consideration should be given to the coincident occurrence of floods due to severe hydrometeorological conditions, but only where the effects on the plant are worse than and the probability of such combined events may be greater than an individual occurrence of the most severe event of either type. Appendix A contains acceptable combinations of such events. For the specific case of seismically induced floods due to dam failures, an evaluation should be made of flood waves that may be caused by domino-type dam failures triggered by a seismically induced failure of a critically located dam and of flood waves that may be caused by multiple dam failures in a region where dams may be located close enough together that a single seismic event can cause multiple failures.

... Flood conditions that could be caused by dam failures from earthquakes should also be considered in establishing the design basis flood. Analytical techniques for evaluating the hydrologic effects of seismically induced dam failures discussed herein are presented in Appendix A of this guide.

data.query: How do general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena relate to the evaluation of flood waves resulting from cascading dam failures at nuclear power plant sites?
data.answer:
The general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena, specifically General Design Criterion (GDC) 2 from Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, require that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety at nuclear power plants be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including floods, without loss of safety function. This requirement is directly related to the evaluation of flood waves resulting from cascading (domino-type) dam failures at nuclear power plant sites.

According to SRP 2.4.4, to meet GDC 2 and related regulations (10 CFR Part 100, 10 CFR 100.23(d)), the evaluation must consider the most severe flood scenarios, including those caused by cascading dam failures. The analysis should use conservative assumptions regarding dam breach modes, reservoir levels, and coincident flow rates. Several possible cascading dam failure scenarios, including those induced by seismic or hydrological events, must be investigated to estimate the most severe flood water surface elevation that could affect SSCs important to safety (SRP 2.4.4, Section II).

Regulatory Guide 1.59 further clarifies that the design basis flood for a nuclear power plant must include the worst site-related flood, which encompasses floods from severe hydrometeorological conditions and seismically induced dam failures. Specifically, it requires evaluation of flood waves from domino-type dam failures triggered by seismic events, considering the severity of the Safe Shutdown Earthquake (RG 1.59, Sections B and C). The analysis must ensure that safety-related SSCs can withstand these flood conditions and maintain their safety functions.

In summary, the general design criteria mandate that the evaluation of flood waves from cascading dam failures is an integral part of establishing the design basis flood for nuclear power plant safety. This ensures that SSCs important to safety are adequately protected against the most severe, credible natural phenomena, including complex dam failure scenarios (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; SRP 2.4.4; RG 1.59).

Criterion 2 also requires that design bases for these structures, systems, and components reflect (1) appropriate consideration of the most severe of the natural phenomena that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding region, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy and quantity of the historical data and the period of time in which the data have been accumulated, (2) appropriate combinations of the effects of normal and accident conditions with the effects of the natural phenomena, and (3) the importance of the safety functions to be performed. ...
