2.5.4.5 - Excavation and Backfill. In meeting the requirements of 10 CFR Part 50, the presentation of the data concerning excavation, backfill, and earthwork analyses is acceptable if:
A. The sources and quantities of backfill and borrow are identified and are shown to have been adequately investigated by borings, pits, and laboratory property and strength testing (dynamic and static); long term solubility properties and dissolution behavior during the life of the facility have been determined; and these data are included, interpreted, and summarized.
B. The engineering properties of the backfill and the criteria for placement and control are specified, including compaction, moisture content, lift thickness, and other parameters necessary to ensure that the backfill will perform as required for the support of safety-related structures.
C. The quality control program for backfill placement is described, including the frequency and type of field testing (e.g., density, moisture content, compaction tests), acceptance criteria, and corrective actions for nonconforming material or placement.
D. The applicant provides evidence that the backfill will not adversely affect the stability or settlement of safety-related structures, including analyses or test fills as appropriate.
E. The applicant provides a discussion of the monitoring program to verify that the backfill and foundation conditions remain acceptable during construction and operation.

The staff reviews the applicant’s excavation and backfill plans, specifications, and quality control procedures to ensure that the engineering properties of the backfill are appropriate for the intended use and that adequate quality control measures are in place to ensure that the backfill is placed and compacted in accordance with the specified criteria. The staff also reviews the applicant’s analyses and monitoring programs to ensure that the backfill will not adversely affect the stability or settlement of safety-related structures.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appendix B to Part 50—Quality Assurance Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants and Fuel Reprocessing Plants

I. Introduction

A. General. Quality assurance comprises all those planned and systematic actions necessary to provide adequate confidence that a structure, system, or component will perform satisfactorily in service. The quality assurance program provides control over activities affecting the quality of structures, systems, and components, to an extent consistent with their importance to safety. The activities affecting quality include designing, purchasing, fabricating, handling, shipping, storing, cleaning, erecting, installing, inspecting, testing, operating, maintaining, repairing, refueling, and modifying.

II. Quality Assurance Program

A. Establishment and Execution. The applicant shall establish at the earliest practicable time, consistent with the schedule for accomplishing the activities, a quality assurance program which complies with the requirements of this appendix. The applicant shall execute the activities affecting quality in accordance with the requirements of the quality assurance program.

III. Design Control

Measures shall be established to assure that applicable regulatory requirements and the design basis, as defined in Appendix A, for those structures, systems, and components to which this appendix applies are correctly translated into specifications, drawings, procedures, and instructions. These measures shall provide for verifying or checking the adequacy of design, such as by the performance of design reviews, by the use of alternate or simplified calculational methods, or by the performance of a suitable testing program. The design control measures shall include provisions to assure that appropriate quality standards are specified and included in design documents and that deviations from such standards are controlled. Design changes, including field changes, shall be subject to design control measures commensurate with those applied to the original design.

4.3. Reconstituted or Remolded Samples  
All tests of strength and dynamic responses of in situ soils, whether cohesive or cohesionless, should use high-quality, undisturbed samples.  In some instances, however, reconstituted or remolded samples may be used when representative undisturbed samples cannot be obtained.  Remolded samples are also used as representative of compacted fill or backfill material for new construction.   
Reconstituted specimens representative of in situ material should be molded to the in situ density and moisture content as determined from actual field measurements.    

4.5. Laboratory Testing Program 

a. The study of soil and rock mechanics covers the investigation, description, classification, testing, and analysis of soil and rock to determine their interaction with structures built in, upon, or with them.   The physical properties of soils and rocks should be determined by carrying out tests on samples of soil in a laboratory.  These tests fall into two main categories:  classification tests and engineering properties tests.  Classification tests indicate the general type of soil and the engineering category to which it belongs.  Specific tests to determine engineering properties require careful consideration of field conditions, various design loading conditions, material properties, and possible problems at the site.  The focus of laboratory investigations should depend on the design requirements and nature of problems encountered or suspected at the site.   

5.2. Soil Testing  
a. Laboratory personnel should perform classification tests and engineering properties tests according to an accepted and published method.   Appendix A shows laboratory procedures for some of the most common tests, along with other related references.   These include the following:  
(1) water content 
(2) permeability 
(3) unit weights 
(4) consolidation 
(5) void ratio 
(6) direct shear 
(7) porosity 
(8) triaxial compression 
(9) saturation 
(10) unconfined compression 
(11) Atterberg limits 
(12) relative density 
(13) specific gravity 
(14) grain size analysis 
(15) erodibility 
(16) compaction 

b. The number of tests required in a laboratory investigation program will depend on the type of material, the quality of samples, the purpose and relative importance of the test, and the scatter of test data.  In general, investigators should first identify and classify all soils and rocks sampled at the site using appropriate index and classification tests.  The Unified Soil Classification System (ASTM D2487) should be used to describe soils and prepare soil profiles, while ASTM D5878, “Standard Guide for Using Rock Mass Classification Systems for Engineering Purposes” (Ref. 26) should be used to classify rock mass for specific engineering purposes.  Further tests required to establish physical and engineering properties should be sufficient to define the range of values for material properties.  The number of tests should be sufficient to cover the range of values expected under field conditions.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating the potential impact of subsurface fractures on the stability of foundations for nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating the potential impact of subsurface fractures on the stability of foundations for nuclear power plants are grounded in several regulatory requirements and guidance documents. According to SRP 2.5.4, Section II (including 2.5.4.1 Geologic Features), the evaluation must ensure compliance with 10 CFR 50.55a(a)(1), which requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) be designed, constructed, and inspected to quality standards commensurate with their safety function. General Design Criterion 2 (GDC 2) in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, further requires that SSCs important to safety be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data.

Specifically, the acceptance criteria require a thorough geotechnical evaluation of the site, including detailed site investigations to provide unambiguous representation of the geology (SRP 2.5.4.1). All areas or zones of actual or potential surface or subsurface alteration, such as fractures, solution cavities, or structural weaknesses, must be identified and adequately evaluated for their impact on stability. The investigations must be sufficient in scope and technique to provide best estimate material properties and their variability (SRP 2.5.4, II).

Cross-referencing SRP 2.5.3, the NRC requires that the geologic and seismic characteristics of the site and its environs be investigated in sufficient detail to permit adequate evaluation of potential surface and subsurface deformation, including fractures. If such features are present, the applicant must demonstrate that their effects are within the design basis of the facility (SRP 2.5.3, II.6).

Regulatory Guides such as RG 1.138 emphasize that laboratory tests on soil and rock must be thorough, with representative and critical samples tested to establish the range of material properties, including those affected by fractures. RG 1.198 further notes that zones of weakness, such as those created by fractures, must be quantitatively analyzed for their potential to cause differential settlement or instability, especially under seismic loading.

In summary, the NRC acceptance criteria require comprehensive identification, characterization, and evaluation of subsurface fractures and related geologic features to ensure that foundation stability is maintained under all relevant loading conditions, and that the design basis of the facility accounts for their potential impacts.

evidence_chain.section: SCREENING TECHNIQUES FOR EVALUATION OF LIQUEFACTION POTENTIAL (pp. 1.198-6 to 1.198-7)
evidence_chain.evidence_text: Potentially liquefiable soils may not pose a liquefaction risk to the facility if they are insufficiently thick and of limited lateral extent. If, however, they are very loose and continue laterally over a sufficient area, they can represent hazardous planes of weakness and sliding and may thus pose other hazards with respect to translational site instability, lateral spreading, or related ground displacement. During an earthquake, a loss of bearing capacity may occur beneath shallow foundations of structures supported on relatively stable strata above the liquefiable soils. The reduction in the lateral capacity and the addition in the lateral loads to the deep foundations may also occur if the soils surrounding deep foundations liquefy (Martin and Lew, 1999). When suitably sound lateral containment is provided to eliminate potential sliding on liquefied layers, potentially liquefiable zones of finite thickness occurring at any depth may be deemed to pose no significant sliding risk but may, however, be susceptible to differential settlement and ground oscillation. Where considerations of such differential settlement or relative displacement between structures or components of the facility have safety significance, quantitative analyses of the settlement and the deformations, including effects of earthquakes, will be required even though the soils involved may be judged seismically stable to liquefaction effects.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating liquefaction potential of soils at nuclear power plant sites, including consideration of surface backfill materials?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating the liquefaction potential of soils at nuclear power plant sites are established to ensure that all soils, including surface backfill materials, are thoroughly assessed for earthquake-induced instability. According to SRP 2.5.4.8, the evaluation must address the potential for liquefaction and strength degradation using both deterministic and probabilistic procedures, based on soil properties obtained from state-of-the-practice laboratory and field tests. All subsurface soils, including surface backfill, must be included in the evaluation, and the consequences of liquefaction, such as foundation settlement, must be considered. The applicant must demonstrate that all zones potentially subject to liquefaction or strain-softening have been adequately sampled and tested, with relative density, consolidation behavior, and static and dynamic strength properly defined. 

10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, further requires that the evaluation of liquefaction potential consider the properties of soils and rocks, including any surface backfill materials, and the effects of groundwater. If liquefaction or permanent ground displacement is possible, appropriate engineering measures must be implemented to ensure plant safety. The properties of all backfill and in situ soils affecting seismic response must be determined by appropriate field and laboratory tests, and the design must account for liquefaction or ground failure in these materials.

RG 1.198 provides accepted methods for site characterization, recommending the use of CPT and SPT for initial investigations, with sufficient coverage to identify potentially liquefiable soils and their saturation status. If potentially liquefiable soils are present, their resistance to liquefaction must be evaluated, and decisions made regarding removal, remediation, or further analysis. The factor of safety against liquefaction should be determined using empirical procedures.

RG 1.138 specifies that laboratory tests on backfill or compacted fill should use reconstituted samples molded to in situ density and moisture content. Laboratory investigations must determine key parameters such as relative density, static and dynamic strength, and wave velocities, with analyses addressing liquefaction potential, settlement, and dynamic stability.

In summary, the NRC requires a comprehensive, site-specific evaluation of liquefaction potential for all soils, including surface backfill, using state-of-the-practice testing and analysis methods, with results informing design and safety measures. (SRP 2.5.4.8; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S; RG 1.198, Sections 1-3; RG 1.138, Sections C.4.3, C.4.5)

evidence_chain.section: 2.5.4.8 - Liquefaction Potential
evidence_chain.evidence_text: 2.5.4.8 - Liquefaction Potential. In meeting the requirements of 10 CFR 100.23 and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, the evaluation of liquefaction potential is acceptable if the applicant provides a thorough evaluation of the potential for earthquake-induced instability of soil resulting from liquefaction and strength degradation. The evaluation should be based on soil properties obtained by proper and state-of-the-practice laboratory and field tests and involve application of both deterministic and probabilistic procedures. The evaluation should include all subsurface soils, including surface backfill materials, and should address the consequences of liquefaction, such as settlement of foundations. The applicant should demonstrate that all zones which could become unstable due to liquefaction or strain-softening phenomena have been adequately sampled and tested. The relative density of the soils at the site should be determined, and the consolidation behavior as well as static and dynamic strength should be adequately defined. The evaluation should be consistent with the guidance provided in RG 1.198, which describes acceptable methods for assessing seismic soil liquefaction at nuclear power plant sites.

evidence_chain.section: Appendix S to Part 50—Earthquake Engineering Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appendix S to Part 50—Earthquake Engineering Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants

I. Introduction

This appendix establishes the minimum requirements for earthquake engineering criteria for nuclear power plants. These requirements are intended to provide reasonable assurance that nuclear power plant structures, systems, and components important to safety will withstand the effects of earthquakes and other dynamic events without loss of capability to perform their safety functions.

II. Requirements

1. Seismic Design Bases. The design bases for nuclear power plants must include consideration of the most severe earthquakes that have been historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for the limited accuracy, quantity, and period of time in which the historical data have been accumulated. The potential for surface deformation, including liquefaction and slope instability, must be evaluated for the site and the surrounding area. The evaluation must include consideration of the properties of soils and rocks, including any surface backfill materials, and the effects of ground water. If the potential for liquefaction or other permanent ground displacement exists, appropriate engineering measures must be taken to ensure the safety of the plant.

2. Site Grading and Backfill. The properties of all backfill and in situ soils that could affect the response of the plant to seismic events must be determined by appropriate field and laboratory tests. The design must account for the potential for liquefaction or other ground failure in these materials.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
C.   REGULATORY POSITION
1. SITE CHARACTERIZATION
1.1 General
The initial phase of the site characterization program should include borings with their locations and depths chosen so that the site geology and foundation conditions are sufficiently defined in lateral extent and depth to provide the data for the designs for all structures and excavations.  This phase should include borings with SPT tests or CPT tests for determining penetration resistance and soil characteristics for measuring classification and water content determinations.
CPT should be the tool of choice for initial site characterization studies in support of liquefaction potential assessment.  The CPT results should be used to select localities and depths for subsequent SPT borings or boreholes and other sampling efforts.  Coverage of the site with CPT and SPT borings should be adequate to (1) establish general soil conditions, distribution of soil types, homogeneity, and ground-water elevation; (2) identify soils that might liquefy; and (3) assist in specifying the locations of additional borings and geophysical surveys aimed at detailed seismic response evaluation. 
For the in situ investigation of the strength of soils containing gravels or cobbles and their potential for liquefaction, the tool of choice is the Becker Hammer Tool or shear wave velocity measurement.
...
2. SCREENING TECHNIQUES FOR EVALUATING LIQUEFACTION POTENTIAL
Based on the initial site characterization, an early evaluation of the potential for seismically induced ground failure should be made.  The liquefaction hazard evaluation should address three basic questions:  (1) Are potentially liquefiable soils present? (2) If so, are they saturated or could they become saturated at some future date? and (3) If so, are they of sufficient thickness or lateral extent to pose a risk to the survival or function of the project?  These evaluations should make assessments as to whether the site is clearly safe or if soils clearly will liquefy.  If the results of the screening evaluation are unclear, more detailed evaluations should be conducted.
3. PROCEDURES FOR EVALUATING LIQUEFACTION POTENTIAL
3.1 General
If evaluations of the site investigations indicate the presence of potentially liquefiable soils, the resistance of these soils to liquefaction must be evaluated.  It should also be determined whether the potentially liquefiable soils should be removed, whether remedial action should be undertaken, whether further field and laboratory investigations are needed, or whether detailed stability and deformation analysis could demonstrate that an acceptable margin of safety is maintained for the design structures even if liquefaction is assumed to occur.
3.2 Factor of Safety Against Liquefaction
The factor of safety, FS, is used in empirical procedures for the evaluation of liquefaction potential.  Interpretations of the FS should be used with caution...

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for protecting nuclear power plant structures against the effects of extreme wind events?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for protecting nuclear power plant structures against the effects of extreme wind events, such as tornadoes and hurricanes, are primarily established in 10 CFR 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2. GDC 2 requires that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety must be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including extreme wind events, without loss of capability to perform their safety functions. The design bases must reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2; [2]).

The Standard Review Plan (SRP) 3.3.1 further specifies that the wind used in the design should be the most severe historically reported, with sufficient margin, and that design wind speed, recurrence interval, speed variation with height, and gust factors should be determined per SRP Sections 2.3.1 and 2.3.2 ([1]). The procedures for converting wind speed to equivalent pressure should follow ASCE/SEI 7-05 standards ([1]).

SRP 2.3.1 and 2.3.2 require that tornado parameters be based on Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.76, or justified site-specific data, and that the basic 100-year return period 3-second gust wind speed be used, with corrections for local conditions ([3], [4]). Local meteorological data, including wind roses and frequency distributions, should be documented as per Regulatory Guide 1.23 ([4]).

RG 1.76 provides NRC-accepted methods for selecting design-basis tornado parameters and tornado-generated missile spectra, specifying that nuclear power plants should be designed to withstand the design-basis tornado for their region, as defined in RG 1.76 Table 1, and the associated missile spectrum in Table 2 ([5]).

In summary, NRC regulations require nuclear power plant safety-related structures to be designed against the most severe credible wind events, using conservative, well-documented meteorological data and NRC-accepted methodologies, ensuring continued safety function during and after such events.

data.query: How do general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena relate to the determination of design wind speeds for nuclear power plant safety-related structures?
data.answer:
The general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena, specifically General Design Criterion (GDC) 2 in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, require that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety at nuclear power plants be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including wind events such as tornadoes and hurricanes, without loss of their safety functions (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; [2]). The determination of design wind speeds for safety-related structures is directly tied to this requirement. 

According to SRP 3.3.1, the wind used in the design must be the most severe wind historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin to account for uncertainties in the historical data (SRP 3.3.1, II; [1]). This approach ensures that the design bases for SSCs reflect appropriate combinations of normal, accident, and natural phenomena conditions, as required by GDC 2 ([1], [2]). 

SRP 2.3.1 and 2.3.2 further specify that the basic (straight-line) 100-year return period 3-second gust wind speed should be used, based on appropriate standards and corrected for local conditions (SRP 2.3.1, II; [3]). The technical rationale is that compliance with GDC 2, along with related regulations (10 CFR 100.10(c)(2), 100.20(c)(2), 100.21(d)), ensures that the most severe meteorological conditions at the site are identified and considered in the design ([3], [4]). 

Additionally, Regulatory Guide 1.23 supports the need for onsite meteorological measurements to document wind conditions and provide data for both safety analysis and emergency preparedness (RG 1.23, A, B; [5]). 

In summary, the general design criteria mandate that design wind speeds for safety-related structures be based on the most severe historically reported winds for the site, with appropriate margins, to ensure SSCs can perform their safety functions during extreme wind events, as detailed in GDC 2 and supporting NRC guidance ([1], [2], [3], [4], [5]).

data.query: How do general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena relate to the determination of design basis wind speeds for nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The general design criteria (GDC) for protection against natural phenomena, specifically GDC 2 as set forth in Appendix A to 10 CFR Part 50, require that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety at nuclear power plants be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including wind events such as tornadoes and hurricanes, without loss of safety function (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; SRP 3.3.1, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA). The determination of design basis wind speeds is directly tied to this requirement. GDC 2 mandates that the design bases for SSCs reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 2; SRP 2.3.1, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA).

Standard Review Plan (SRP) Sections 2.3.1 and 2.3.2 provide the specific acceptance criteria for determining design basis wind speeds. These criteria require that the wind used in the design be the most severe historically reported, with suitable margin, and that parameters such as recurrence interval, speed variation with height, and gust factors be established based on appropriate standards and local conditions (SRP 3.3.1, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA; SRP 2.3.1, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA; SRP 2.3.2, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA). For example, SRP 2.3.1 specifies that the basic 100-year return period 3-second gust wind speed should be used, adjusted for local conditions.

The technical rationale for these requirements is to ensure that the most severe meteorological conditions at the site are identified and incorporated into the plant's design basis, thereby providing assurance that SSCs will maintain their safety functions under extreme wind events (SRP 2.3.1, Technical Rationale; SRP 2.3.2, Technical Rationale). Regulatory Guide 1.23 further supports this by recommending onsite meteorological measurements to accurately characterize site wind conditions for both design and operational needs (RG 1.23, A. INTRODUCTION, B. DISCUSSION).

In summary, the general design criteria for protection against natural phenomena establish the regulatory basis for determining design basis wind speeds, requiring that nuclear power plants be designed to withstand the most severe credible wind events, as characterized by historical data and site-specific meteorological assessments.

data.query: What is the regulatory basis for ensuring that selected wind speeds used in nuclear facility design meet the requirements for protection against natural hazards?
data.answer:
The regulatory basis for ensuring that selected wind speeds used in nuclear facility design meet requirements for protection against natural hazards is primarily established in 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criterion (GDC) 2. GDC 2 mandates that structures, systems, and components (SSCs) important to safety must be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, including severe wind events such as tornadoes and hurricanes, without loss of safety function. The design bases must reflect appropriate consideration of the most severe natural phenomena historically reported for the site and surrounding area, with sufficient margin for uncertainties in historical data (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2; SRP 3.3.1, Section II; SRP 2.3.1, Section II; SRP 2.3.2, Section II).

The Standard Review Plan (SRP) further specifies that the wind speed used in design should be the most severe historically reported, with sufficient margin for data limitations. The design wind speed, recurrence interval, speed variation with height, and gust factors must be determined using approved values and methodologies, as detailed in SRP Sections 2.3.1 and 2.3.2 (SRP 3.3.1, Section II). SRP 2.3.1 recommends using the basic 100-year return period 3-second gust wind speed, adjusted for local conditions, as a standard for design.

Additionally, 10 CFR 100.10(c)(2), 100.20(c)(2), and 100.21(d) require that meteorological characteristics, including maximum probable wind speed, be identified and characterized to ensure site acceptability and that no undue risk is posed by site-specific physical characteristics (SRP 2.3.1, Section II; SRP 2.3.2, Section II).

Regulatory Guide 1.23 provides accepted methods for measuring wind speed and direction, specifying instrument placement and siting to ensure data are representative of site conditions (RG 1.23, Sections C.2 and C.3).

In summary, the regulatory basis is grounded in GDC 2 and related NRC regulations, with detailed acceptance criteria and methodologies provided in the SRP and RG 1.23 to ensure that wind speeds used in nuclear facility design adequately protect against natural hazards.

Wind speed and direction should be measured on one open-lattice tower or mast measured at heights of approximately 10 meters (33 feet) and 60 meters (197 feet) above ground level. Factors to be considered in selecting the appropriate measurement locations and installation of the instruments include the prevailing wind direction, topography, and location of manmade and vegetation obstructions.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating the uniformity of soil and rock layer structures in seismic soil-structure interaction analyses for nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for evaluating the uniformity of soil and rock layer structures in seismic soil-structure interaction (SSI) analyses for nuclear power plants are grounded in several key regulatory and guidance documents. According to SRP 3.7.1 (Section II), the supporting media for Seismic Category I structures must be thoroughly described, including soil layering characteristics and their variability, to assess the applicability of SSI analysis methods. The competent material is generally defined as in-situ material with a minimum shear wave velocity of 1,000 fps, and any remaining soft soil or backfill must be considered in the analysis.

SRP 2.5.2 (Subsection 2.5.2.5) requires a detailed description of subsurface materials, including the thickness, lateral extent, and physical properties of each soil and rock layer. The uniformity of these layers must be evaluated through appropriate field and laboratory investigations (e.g., borings, sampling, in situ and laboratory testing). The dynamic properties, such as shear wave velocity profiles, must be determined using methods acceptable to the NRC (e.g., those in RG 1.208 and RG 1.138), and the appropriateness of these methods for site conditions must be demonstrated.

SRP 2.5.4.2 further specifies that state-of-the-art methods should be used to determine static and dynamic engineering properties of all foundation soils and rocks to sufficient depth. The applicant must provide quantitative criteria for sampling and testing, address spatial variability (horizontal and vertical), and use multiple methods to determine critical parameters like shear wave velocity. The number of measurements must be sufficient to represent field conditions, and all zones susceptible to instability (e.g., liquefaction) must be adequately sampled and tested.

SRP 3.7.2 emphasizes that SSI analyses must account for the random nature and uncertainties of soil and rock configurations, including the lack of lateral uniformity, and that the procedures for incorporating strain-dependent properties, layering, and property variation must be reviewed. The modeling assumptions and validation must also be documented.

In summary, the NRC requires a comprehensive, data-driven evaluation of soil and rock uniformity using multiple, validated methods, with explicit consideration of spatial variability and uncertainties, to ensure the adequacy of SSI analyses for nuclear power plant safety (SRP 3.7.1, SRP 2.5.2, SRP 2.5.4, SRP 3.7.2; 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 2).

In meeting the requirements of 10 CFR Parts 50 and 100, the description of properties of underlying materials is considered acceptable if state-of-the-art methods are used to determine the static and dynamic engineering properties of all foundation soils and rocks in the site area to sufficient depth that impact behavior during construction and over the life of the facility, including during postulated seismic events. ... The relative density of the soils at the site should be determined. evidence_chain.section: I. AREAS OF REVIEW, 4. Soil-Structure Interaction
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
4. Soil-Structure Interaction.  The design ground motion response spectra at the foundation level (foundation input response spectra (FIRS)) are defined in the free-field, i.e., without the presence of structures, as described in SRP Section 3.7.1, and Interim Staff Guidance (ISG) DC/COL-ISG-01 and DC/COL-ISG-017.  Performance-based free-field surface response spectra (PBSRS) are also defined at the free ground surface to ensure the performance adequacy of the soil columns used in the deterministic SSI analysis.  The FIRS and PBSRS should be developed in a consistent manner.  They are probabilistically determined performance-based spectra generated using the soil columns corresponding to the building.  The properties of the soil columns usually consist of 60 or more randomized sets of properties similar to those used in the probabilistic seismic hazard analysis (PSHA) process.  For sites with soil layers near the surface that will be completely excavated to expose competent material, and replaced with extended compacted backfill layers, the FIRS and PBSRS are determined considering the effect of the backfill layers in the site profiles that will exist after completion of excavation and backfilling.  FIRS at the foundation should also be developed as free-field outcrop motions, not as in-column motions.  Competent material is generally considered to be in-situ material having a minimum shear wave velocity of 1,000 feet/second (fps).

As applicable, the modeling methods (including technical bases) used in the seismic system analysis to account for SSI are reviewed.  The factors to be considered in accepting a particular modeling method include: (1) the extent of embedment, (2) the layering of the soil/rock strata, and (3) the boundary of the soil-structure model.  All SSI analyses should recognize the uncertainties prevalent throughout the phenomenon, and include consideration of the following:

A. The random nature of the soil and rock configuration and material characteristics.

B. Uncertainty in soil constitutive modeling (soil stiffness, damping, etc.).

C. Nonlinear soil behavior.

D. Coupling between the structures and soil.

E. Lack of lateral uniformity in the site soil profile that is usually assumed to be uniformly layered in all horizontal directions in SSI analyses.

F. Effects of the flexibility of soil/rock.

G. Effects of the flexibility of basemat, sidewalls and interior structures.

H. The effect of pore water on structural responses, including the effects of variability of ground-water level with time.

I. Effects of potential separation or loss of contact between the structure (embedded portion of the structure and foundation mat) and the soil during the earthquake.

J. If incoherence effects to reduce high frequency motions are included in the SSI response, consideration of the potential variation of the Coherency Function described in DC/COL-ISG-01 with depth should be included in the evaluation.

The procedures by which strain-dependent soil properties (damping, shear modulus, pore pressure development), layering, and variation of soil properties are incorporated in the analysis are reviewed.  Assumptions for modeling the soil-structure system and computer program validation documents are also reviewed.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory expectations for coordinating nuclear power plant maintenance activities that may impact the reliability of the transmission system?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory expectations for coordinating nuclear power plant maintenance activities that may impact the reliability of the transmission system are primarily governed by 10 CFR 50.65(a)(4), as referenced in SRP 8.2, Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.160, and the regulation itself. Before performing maintenance activities—including those in the switchyard or other areas that could affect the transmission system—licensees are required to assess and manage any increase in risk that may result from the proposed activities. This assessment must consider both the likelihood and consequences of events that would require critical structures, systems, and components (SSCs) to perform their intended safety functions (10 CFR 50.65(a)(4); RG 1.160, Section B).

The NRC expects that plant management is aware of and can control maintenance activities in the switchyard, as these can directly affect plant operations and the reliability of offsite power (RG 1.160, Switchyard Maintenance Activities). The risk assessment should be commensurate with the safety significance of the SSCs involved and may use either qualitative or quantitative methods. If the assessment identifies an increased risk, appropriate compensatory actions must be taken to manage that risk (10 CFR 50.65(a)(4)).

Additionally, the NRC endorses guidance in RG 1.160 and RG 1.182, which reference industry guidelines (such as NUMARC 93-01) for monitoring the effectiveness of maintenance, including grid-risk-sensitive activities that could increase the likelihood of a plant trip or loss of offsite power (SRP 8.2, II.A and II.B). These expectations apply during all conditions of plant operation, including shutdown (RG 1.160, Section B).

In summary, the NRC requires a structured risk assessment and management process for maintenance activities that could impact transmission system reliability, with a focus on maintaining the capability of safety-related SSCs and taking compensatory actions as needed.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory expectations for inspection, testing, and monitoring programs to detect degradation of inaccessible or underground power cables that support equipment within the scope of the Maintenance Rule?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory expectations for inspection, testing, and monitoring programs to detect degradation of inaccessible or underground power cables that support equipment within the scope of the Maintenance Rule are grounded in several key requirements and guidance documents. General Design Criterion (GDC) 18 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A) requires that electric power systems important to safety be designed to permit appropriate periodic inspection and testing of important areas and features, including wiring and insulation, to assess system continuity and component condition. This includes the capability to periodically test operability and functional performance (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, GDC 18).

The Standard Review Plan (SRP) 8.2 further clarifies that compliance with GDC 18 is demonstrated through inspection and testing of offsite power systems, and that the Maintenance Rule (10 CFR 50.65) applies to the assessment and management of risk from maintenance activities. Specifically, Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.160 is referenced as an acceptable method for monitoring the effectiveness of maintenance activities, including those affecting onsite emergency AC power sources (SRP 8.2, II.8.A).

RG 1.160, which endorses portions of NUMARC 93-01, provides that licensees should use existing activities, such as technical specification surveillance testing, to satisfy monitoring requirements for structures, systems, and components (SSCs) within the Maintenance Rule scope. Licensees are expected to monitor the performance or condition of SSCs against established goals to provide reasonable assurance of their capability to fulfill intended functions. If performance or condition does not meet these goals, corrective action must be taken. Monitoring is not required if effective preventive maintenance ensures continued functionality (RG 1.160, B. DISCUSSION).

In summary, NRC expects licensees to establish and implement inspection, testing, and monitoring programs that provide reasonable assurance of the continued functionality of inaccessible or underground power cables within the Maintenance Rule scope. These programs should include periodic inspection and testing, performance monitoring against established goals, and corrective actions as necessary, with flexibility in how these requirements are met, provided the underlying safety objectives are achieved.

data.query: How do regulatory requirements for the Maintenance Rule influence the development and frequency of inspection and testing programs for underground or inaccessible power cables in nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
Regulatory requirements for the Maintenance Rule, as specified in 10 CFR 50.65 and interpreted in SRP 8.2 and RG 1.160, directly influence the development and frequency of inspection and testing programs for underground or inaccessible power cables in nuclear power plants. The Maintenance Rule mandates that licensees monitor the performance or condition of structures, systems, or components (SSCs) against licensee-established goals to ensure these SSCs can fulfill their intended functions (10 CFR 50.65(a)(1); RG 1.160). This monitoring must be sufficient to provide reasonable assurance of reliability and safety, and goals should be informed by safety significance and industry-wide operating experience (RG 1.160).

For underground or inaccessible power cables, this means that licensees must establish appropriate monitoring and preventive maintenance activities, which may include inspections and testing, to ensure cable integrity and functionality. If performance or condition does not meet established goals, corrective actions are required (RG 1.160). The frequency and scope of these activities must be evaluated at least every refueling cycle, not to exceed 24 months, and adjusted as necessary to balance failure prevention with minimizing unavailability due to maintenance (RG 1.160).

Before performing maintenance activities, including inspections and testing, licensees are required to assess and manage any increase in risk, considering the aggregate impact on plant safety and defense-in-depth (10 CFR 50.65(a)(4); SRP 8.2). The results of this risk assessment must inform the planning and scheduling of maintenance activities to minimize risk to public health and safety (10 CFR 50.65(a)(4)).

In summary, the Maintenance Rule requires a structured, risk-informed approach to the development and frequency of inspection and testing programs for underground or inaccessible power cables, with periodic evaluation and adjustment based on performance, risk, and industry experience (10 CFR 50.65; RG 1.160; SRP 8.2).

The relevant part of the maintenance rule current states:

The requirements of this section are applicable during all conditions of plant operation, including normal shutdown operations.

(a) (1) Each holder of an operating license for a nuclear power plant under this part and each holder of a combined license under part 52 of this chapter after the Commission makes the finding under § 52.103(g) of this chapter, shall monitor the performance or condition of structures, systems, or components, against licensee-established goals, in a manner sufficient to provide reasonable assurance that these structures, systems, and components, as defined in paragraph (b) of this section, are capable of fulfilling their intended functions. (2)  Monitoring as specified in paragraph (a)(1) of this section is not required where it has been demonstrated that the performance or condition of a structure, system, or component is being effectively controlled through the performance of appropriate preventive maintenance, such that the structure, system, or component remains capable of performing its intended function.

(3)  Performance and condition monitoring activities and associated goals and preventive maintenance activities shall be evaluated at least every refueling cycle provided the interval between evaluations does not exceed 24 months. The evaluations shall take into account, where practical, industry-wide operating experience. The scope of the assessment may be limited to structures, systems, and components that a risk-informed evaluation process has shown to be significant to public health and safety.

(b) The scope of the monitoring program specified in paragraph (a)(1) of this section shall include safety related and nonsafety related structures, systems, and components, as follows: ...

Use of Existing Licensee Programs

The NRC staff encourages licensees to use, to the maximum extent practicable, activities currently being conducted, such as technical specification surveillance testing, to satisfy monitoring requirements. Such activities could be integrated with, and provide the basis for, the requisite level of monitoring. data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for chemicals used as oxygen scavengers in nuclear plant condensate and feedwater systems?
data.answer: The NRC acceptance criteria for chemicals used as oxygen scavengers in nuclear plant condensate and feedwater systems are established to ensure the integrity of the reactor coolant pressure boundary, as required by General Design Criterion 14 (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, Criterion 14). Specifically, the NRC relies on water chemistry guidelines to control the use of such chemicals. For boiling-water reactor (BWR) plants, SRP Section 10.4.6 directs reviewers to SRP Section 5.4.8, which references the latest Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) 'BWR Water Chemistry Guidelines' and the plant's technical specifications for acceptable water purity. For pressurized-water reactor (PWR) plants, SRP Section 10.4.6 refers to SRP Section 5.4.2.1, which in turn references the latest EPRI 'PWR Secondary Water Chemistry Guidelines.' These guidelines specify the types and concentrations of chemicals, including oxygen scavengers, that are acceptable for use to prevent corrosion and maintain the integrity of system materials. The NRC acceptance criteria, therefore, require that any oxygen scavenger chemicals used must conform to the recommendations and limits set forth in the applicable EPRI water chemistry guidelines and the plant's technical specifications, ensuring compliance with the regulatory requirements for reactor coolant pressure boundary integrity.

evidence_chain.section: Appendix A to Part 50—General Design Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants, Criterion 14
evidence_chain.evidence_text: General Design Criterion 14—Reactor coolant pressure boundary. The reactor coolant pressure boundary shall be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested so as to have an extremely low probability of abnormal leakage, of rapidly propagating failure, and of gross rupture. Means shall be provided for detecting and, to the extent practical, identifying the location of the source of reactor coolant leakage. The design of the reactor coolant pressure boundary shall be such that the boundary will behave in a nonbrittle manner and the probability of rapidly propagating fracture is minimized. Appropriate margin shall be provided to allow for uncertainties in determining the effects of irradiation on material properties, uncertainties in determining the stresses and sizes of flaws, and uncertainties in methods of analysis. The design shall reflect consideration of the most severe conditions of normal operation, including anticipated operational occurrences, and postulated accidents.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory requirements for radioactive liquid effluent releases relate to the dose limits for members of the public and the dose objectives for nuclear power plant operations?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory requirements for radioactive liquid effluent releases are directly linked to both dose limits for members of the public and dose objectives for nuclear power plant operations. According to 10 CFR Part 50, § 50.34a, nuclear power reactor applicants must design and operate equipment to control releases of radioactive material in liquid effluents such that the annual dose to any member of the public does not exceed 0.003 rem (3 mSv) to the total body or any organ, except the thyroid, which has a higher limit of 0.01 rem (10 mSv). These requirements ensure that releases to unrestricted areas remain within strict regulatory limits.

Additionally, the NRC emphasizes the ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) principle, requiring that radioactive material in effluents be minimized beyond just meeting dose limits (SRP 11.2, I. AREAS OF REVIEW). The NRC staff reviews plant systems to ensure compliance with both the regulatory dose limits (10 CFR Part 20 and Part 50) and the ALARA objective, confirming that public health and safety are adequately protected even in the event of subsystem failures.

Regulatory guidance (RG 1.143, Section C.5) further reinforces these requirements by specifying design and classification criteria for radioactive waste management systems. These criteria are consistent with the dose limits of 10 CFR Part 20 and ensure that system reliability and operability support both compliance with dose limits and the ALARA objective.

In summary, NRC requirements for liquid effluent releases mandate compliance with specific public dose limits and require plant systems to be designed and operated to keep exposures as low as reasonably achievable, integrating both regulatory limits and operational dose objectives.

data.query: What information should be provided in a regulatory review to demonstrate compliance with both the dose objectives for liquid effluent releases and the annual dose limits for individual members of the public?
data.answer:
To demonstrate compliance with both the dose objectives for liquid effluent releases and the annual dose limits for individual members of the public, a regulatory review should include the following information:

1. Description of Plant Systems and Equipment: The review must provide detailed descriptions of the liquid waste management system (LWMS), including design, design objectives, design criteria, methods of treatment, system interfaces, bypass routes, expected releases, and calculation methods for deriving effluent source terms and releases (SRP 11.2, Section I; 10 CFR 50.34a(a), (b)).

2. Effluent Control and Monitoring: The application should describe the process and effluent control systems, as well as effluent monitoring and sampling systems, to ensure compliance with technical specifications and regulatory limits (10 CFR 50.34a(b)).

3. ALARA and Regulatory Limits: The review must demonstrate that the means employed keep radioactive material levels in effluents to unrestricted areas as low as is reasonably achievable (ALARA) and meet the requirements of 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I, and 10 CFR Part 20 (SRP 11.2, Section I; 10 CFR 50.34a(a), (b)).

4. Source Terms and Exposure Pathways: The review should include expected flow rates, radionuclide concentrations, decontamination factors, holdup/decay times, and a bounding assessment of radioactive liquid effluents for all defined release points. It should also consider potential exposure pathways such as ingestion of aquatic food, drinking water, irrigation, and recreational water use (SRP 11.2, Section I).

5. Quality Assurance and SSC Classification: The review should address quality assurance provisions for radioactive waste management structures, systems, and components (SSCs), using the guidelines of RG 1.143, and classify SSCs according to their potential radiological impact (RG 1.143, Regulatory Position 1, 5).

6. Minimization of Contamination: The application should describe how facility design and operational procedures minimize contamination and radioactive waste generation, facilitate decommissioning, and prevent unintended releases, in accordance with 10 CFR 20.1406 and RG 4.21 (RG 4.21, Section A).

By providing this information, the applicant demonstrates the capability to comply with dose objectives for liquid effluent releases and annual dose limits for individual members of the public, as required by NRC regulations.

evidence_chain.section: A. INTRODUCTION
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
This guide describes a method acceptable to the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) for use in the implementation of Title 10, Section 20.1406, “Minimization of Contamination,” of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR 20.1406) (Ref. 1). License, approval, and certification applicants should strive to minimize contamination and radioactive waste generation over the total life cycle of a facility, from initial facility layout and design through procedures for operation and concluding with final decontamination and dismantling at the time of decommissioning.

10 CFR 20.1406 applies to applicants for licenses (other than early site permits and renewals), design certifications, approvals of standard designs, and manufacturing licenses. The regulation requires the submittal of design information and operational procedures for (1) minimizing radioactive waste generation and contamination of the facility and the environment, and (2) facilitating decommissioning. As specifically stated in 10 CFR 20.1406:

(a) Applicants for licenses, other than early site permits and manufacturing licenses under part 52 of this chapter and renewals, whose applications are submitted after August 20, 1997, shall describe in the application how facility design and procedures for operation will minimize, to the extent practicable, contamination of the facility and the environment, facilitate eventual decommissioning, and minimize, to the extent practicable, the generation of radioactive waste.

...

The purpose of this regulatory guide is to present guidance that will assist applicants covered by 10 CFR 20.1406 in effectively implementing this licensing requirement. The guidance consists of specific design considerations drawn from nuclear industry experience and lessons learned from decommissioning. These have been combined to support the development of a contaminant management philosophy. The principles embodied in this philosophy are threefold: (1) prevention of unintended releases; (2) early detection, if there is unintended release of radioactive contamination; and (3) prompt assessment to support a timely and appropriate response. Applying these principles requires the use of sound design, proven engineering practices, conservative radiation protection principles, and attention to operational practices. All of this should be considered in the context of the life cycle of the facility from the early planning stages through the final plans for decommissioning and waste disposal. This guide describes some of the mechanisms that can be employed for facility life-cycle planning to meet the requirements of 10 CFR 20.1406.

data.query: What is the NRC regulatory requirement for limiting radiation doses to members of the public from nuclear facility operations?
data.answer: The NRC regulatory requirement for limiting radiation doses to members of the public from nuclear facility operations is primarily established in Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) Part 20, which sets standards for protection against radiation. Specifically, compliance with 10 CFR 20.1301 and 10 CFR 20.1302 is required to control doses to members of the public from radioactive effluent releases (SRP 11.2, I. AREAS OF REVIEW). In addition, Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50 provides numerical guides for design objectives and limiting conditions for operation to ensure that radioactive material in effluents released to unrestricted areas is kept 'as low as is reasonably achievable' (ALARA). According to Appendix I, the annual dose or dose commitment to any member of the public from liquid effluent releases to unrestricted areas must not exceed 3 millirems to the total body or 10 millirems to any organ (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix I, II.A). These values serve as design objectives and limiting conditions for operation, forming the basis for technical specifications required by NRC regulations. The NRC reviews facility designs and operations to ensure these requirements are met and that public health and safety are adequately protected.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appendix I to Part 50—Numerical Guides for Design Objectives and Limiting Conditions for Operation To Meet the Criterion “As Low as is Reasonably Achievable” for Radioactive Material in Light-Water-Cooled Nuclear Power Reactor Effluents

I. Introduction
Section 50.34a provides that each applicant for a license to operate a light-water-cooled nuclear power reactor will include in its application a description of the design features of the facility provided to meet the objective of keeping levels of radioactive material in effluents to unrestricted areas as low as is reasonably achievable. Section 50.36a provides that each license authorizing operation of a light-water-cooled nuclear power reactor will include technical specifications on limiting conditions for operation for radioactive material in effluents released to unrestricted areas. This appendix provides numerical guides to meet the criterion “as low as is reasonably achievable” for radioactive material in effluents released to unrestricted areas. These guides are not to be construed as limits, but as design objectives and limiting conditions for operation. The guides are intended to provide a basis for the technical specifications required by § 50.36a and for the design objectives required by § 50.34a.

II. Guides for Effluents
A. The annual dose or dose commitment to any member of the public due to releases of radioactive materials in liquid effluents to unrestricted areas shall not exceed 3 millirems to the total body or 10 millirems to any organ.

data.query: How do NRC regulations address the evaluation of potential recirculation pathways in liquid radioactive effluent releases to ensure compliance with dose limits for members of the public?
data.answer:
NRC regulations require a comprehensive evaluation of potential recirculation pathways in liquid radioactive effluent releases to ensure compliance with public dose limits. According to 10 CFR 50.34a(b), applicants must provide reasonable assurance that facility design includes means to control, monitor, and reduce radioactive material in effluents, and specifically must describe the means for evaluating potential recirculation pathways and their impact on public dose. The Standard Review Plan (SRP) 11.2 further details that the NRC staff reviews the liquid waste management system (LWMS) design, including system interfaces, bypass routes, and calculation methods for effluent releases. The review considers site-specific exposure pathways such as ingestion of aquatic food, drinking water, irrigation, and recreational water use, as well as the impacts of accidental releases to groundwater or surface water, referencing SRP Sections 2.4.1, 2.4.12, and 2.4.13.

SRP 2.4.1 emphasizes the need to evaluate alternate conceptual models of site hydrology, using the most adverse model to conservatively estimate contaminant travel times and impacts, considering both surface and groundwater pathways. Regulatory Guide 1.143 outlines design features for systems and components containing radioactive liquids, such as monitoring, containment, and routing of potential leaks to the liquid radwaste system, to prevent uncontrolled releases and unmonitored pathways. Regulatory Guide 4.21 advises applicants to identify potential contaminant pathways through surface and subsurface media early in the licensing process and to implement onsite monitoring programs for early detection and response to leaks and spills, thereby preventing offsite migration via unmonitored pathways.

Collectively, these requirements and guidance documents ensure that potential recirculation pathways are systematically evaluated and controlled, supporting compliance with dose limits for members of the public as specified in 10 CFR 20.1301 and Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
§ 50.34a Design objectives for equipment to control releases of radioactive material in effluents—nuclear power reactors.

(a) Each applicant for a construction permit or operating license for a nuclear power reactor to be constructed or operated on or after January 1, 1979, shall include in its application a description of the design objectives for equipment to be installed to control the release of radioactive material in effluents to unrestricted areas. The design objectives shall be such that, in addition to complying with the requirements set forth in § 20.1301 of this chapter, the calculated annual average releases of radioactive material in gaseous and liquid effluents (including consideration of anticipated operational occurrences) from each reactor to unrestricted areas will not result in an estimated annual dose or dose commitment to any member of the public in the unrestricted area, from all pathways, in excess of the values specified in Appendix I to this part.

(b) To meet the design objectives, the applicant shall provide reasonable assurance that the design of the facility includes means to control, monitor, and, to the extent practicable, reduce radioactive material in effluents. The applicant shall also provide a description of the process and effluent monitoring and control systems, including the capability to assess the impact of radioactive effluent releases, and the means for evaluating potential recirculation pathways and their impact on dose to members of the public.

1.2 SSCs Outside Containment that Contain Radioactive Liquids
All SSCs located outside the reactor containment that contain radioactive materials in liquid form should be classified as described in Regulatory Position 5 and designed in accordance with Regulatory Position 6. In addition, any such component should be designed to prevent uncontrolled releases of radioactive materials caused by spillage in buildings or from outdoor components. The following design features should be included for such components and should meet the criteria contained in Sections 5.2, 5.3, and 5.4 of ANSI/ANS 55.1-1992.
1.2.1. All tanks inside and outside the plant, including the condensate storage tanks, should have provisions to monitor liquid levels. Designated high-liquid-level conditions should actuate alarms both locally and in the control room.
1.2.2. All radwaste tanks, overflows, drains, and sample lines should be routed to the liquid radwaste treatment system. Retention by an intermediate sump or drain tank that is designed for handling radioactive materials and that has provisions for routing to the liquid radwaste system is acceptable. 
1.2.3. Indoor radwaste tanks should have curbs or elevated thresholds with floor drains routed to the liquid radwaste treatment system. Retention by an intermediate sump or drain tank that is designed for handling radioactive materials and that has provisions for routing to the liquid radwaste system is acceptable.
1.2.4. The design should include provisions to prevent leakage from entering unmonitored and nonradioactive systems and ductwork in the area.
1.2.5. Outdoor tanks should have a dike or retention pond capable of preventing runoff in the event of a tank overflow and should have provisions for sampling collected liquids and routing them to the liquid radwaste treatment system.

data.query: What regulatory guidance is provided for assessing the impact of site-specific discharge structures or canals on the potential for recirculation of liquid radioactive effluents?
data.answer:
Regulatory guidance for assessing the impact of site-specific discharge structures or canals on the potential for recirculation of liquid radioactive effluents is primarily provided in Standard Review Plan (SRP) Sections 11.2 and 10.4, as well as Regulatory Guide (RG) 4.21. 

SRP 11.2 (items 16 and 20) specifies that for plant designs with impoundment facilities and cooling ponds/canals used for discharging liquid radioactive effluents, the review should include descriptions of design features that minimize contamination of plant discharge blowdown systems and the environment, in accordance with 10 CFR 20.1406 and RG 4.21. The review also considers the liquid effluent discharge path to the circulating water system and plant blowdown to unrestricted areas, referencing SRP Section 10.4 for guidance on site-specific balance of plant design features (SRP 11.2, items 16 and 20).

RG 4.21, Section C.2, provides further guidance by recommending the development of a conceptual site model based on site characterization and facility design to understand and control the movement of contamination in the environment. This includes identifying potential release mechanisms, scenarios, and pathways, as well as implementing early detection systems for leakage and contaminant migration. RG 4.21 also advises that applicants should consider the final site configuration to prevent offsite migration of radionuclides and develop an onsite monitoring program as part of the radiological environmental monitoring program (RG 4.21, C.2.1–2.3).

Additionally, SRP 10.4.1 emphasizes the importance of design features that control the release of radioactive material to the environment, including means to detect radioactive leakage and prevent accidental releases. The design must meet the requirements of General Design Criterion 60 (GDC 60), ensuring that failures do not result in excessive releases (SRP 10.4.1, I, II).

In summary, the regulatory guidance requires a comprehensive assessment of site-specific discharge structures or canals, focusing on design features, site characterization, monitoring, and early detection to minimize and control the potential for recirculation and environmental contamination of liquid radioactive effluents.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
2. Minimizing Contamination of the Environment

2.1 Development of a Conceptual Site Model Development

In general, system design features and operational procedures that prevent and/or control releases within the facility also contribute to minimizing contamination of the environment. For systems that directly interface with the environment, the first indication of a leak may be detection in an environmental monitoring system. To control and mitigate such events, it is prudent to have a comprehensive understanding of the interface with environmental systems and the features that will control the movement of contamination in the environment. A conceptual site model based on site characterization and facility design and construction can be a significant tool in (1) understanding the site, (2) planning and implementing a contaminant monitoring program, and (3) planning and implementing mitigative actions. Therefore, the site should be characterized before construction to assess the impact that the facility will have on the site hydrogeology following construction. In addition to the conceptual site model, attention should be given to identifying the potential release mechanisms, release scenarios, and possible location of contaminant releases.

2.2 Provision for Early Detection of Leakage and Contaminant Migration

Systems or structures that are buried or in contact with soil are particularly susceptible to undetected leakage. Undetected leakage commonly occurs in areas where it is not possible to conduct regular inspections; therefore, these leaks are often not identified in a timely manner. To minimize contamination of the environment, systems should be designed to facilitate early detection of leakage and contaminant migration.

2.3 Final Site Configuration

Applicants covered by 10 CFR 20.1406 should consider the site configuration following construction to aid in preventing the offsite migration of radionuclides via an unmonitored pathway. 10 CFR 20.1406 applicants should identify, as early as practical in the licensing process, the potential pathways of radioactive contaminants through the surface and subsurface. Applicants covered by 10 CFR 20.1406(a) should develop an onsite monitoring program, as an integral part of the radiological environmental monitoring program. The program should provide early detection and quantification of leaks and spills and maintain a current baseline of radiological and hydrogeological parameters. Plans for responding to the detection of leaks and spills should reflect the final facility design and site configuration.

data.query: How do NRC regulatory requirements for radioactive liquid effluent releases establish dose objectives for members of the public, and how do these objectives relate to annual dose limits for individuals outside the site boundary?
data.answer:
NRC regulatory requirements for radioactive liquid effluent releases establish dose objectives for members of the public through a combination of design objectives and annual dose limits. According to 10 CFR 50.34a(a), applicants for nuclear power reactor licenses must describe design objectives and the means to control releases of radioactive material in liquid effluents, ensuring that these releases are as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA). Specifically, the collective dose commitment to members of the public from liquid effluents must not exceed 3 man-rem per year to the total body or any organ (except the thyroid) of any individual outside the site boundary. Additionally, the dose to any individual member of the public must not exceed the limits specified in 10 CFR 20.1301.

Section 10 CFR 50.34a(b) further requires that equipment design and operational procedures ensure the annual dose or dose commitment to any member of the public outside the site boundary from radioactive materials in liquid effluents does not exceed the dose limits in 10 CFR 20.1301. The Standard Review Plan (SRP) 11.3 reinforces this by stating that NRC staff evaluate compliance with these regulatory limits and associated doses, ensuring that releases and doses are ALARA and that public health and safety are adequately protected. The review includes independent source terms and dose calculations to assess compliance with both the design objectives of Appendix I to 10 CFR Part 50 and the annual dose limits of 10 CFR 20.1301.

In summary, the NRC establishes dose objectives for liquid effluent releases to ensure both collective and individual doses to the public are minimized and do not exceed regulatory limits, with the annual dose limits for individuals outside the site boundary serving as an upper bound for compliance (10 CFR 50.34a, 10 CFR 20.1301; SRP 11.3).

data.query: What regulatory guidance describes the expectations for providing detailed breakdowns of individual and population doses by exposure pathway and organ in the context of radioactive effluent releases from nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The regulatory guidance describing the expectations for providing detailed breakdowns of individual and population doses by exposure pathway and organ in the context of radioactive effluent releases from nuclear power plants is primarily found in 10 CFR Part 50, specifically § 50.34(a)(3). This section requires that the preliminary safety analysis report (PSAR) included in a construction permit application must assess the risk to public health and safety from facility operation. The PSAR must include an analysis of the kind and quantity of radioactive materials expected to be produced, the means for controlling and limiting radioactive effluents, and an assessment of potential radiation doses to individuals and population groups in the vicinity of the facility. Importantly, this assessment must consider exposure pathways and doses to individual organs or tissues, as appropriate (10 CFR § 50.34(a)(3)).

Further, Standard Review Plan (SRP) Section 11.3 provides detailed guidance for NRC staff reviewing these analyses. It references the use of Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.112, NUREG-0016 (for BWRs), NUREG-0017 (for PWRs), and ANSI/ANS 18.1-1999 for the calculation of releases and dose assessments. These documents provide methodologies for calculating and presenting effluent releases and resulting doses, including breakdowns by exposure pathway (such as ingestion, inhalation, and external exposure) and by organ, to ensure compliance with NRC requirements and ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) objectives (SRP 11.3, Review Interfaces).

In summary, the expectations for detailed breakdowns of doses by exposure pathway and organ are established in 10 CFR § 50.34(a)(3), with implementation guidance provided in SRP Section 11.3 and referenced calculation guides.

data.query: What are the NRC acceptance criteria for onsite storage of radioactive waste at nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The NRC acceptance criteria for onsite storage of radioactive waste at nuclear power plants are outlined in several regulatory documents, primarily SRP 11.4, Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.143, and RG 4.21. According to SRP 11.4, the NRC reviews provisions for onsite waste storage, including design volumes, radionuclide concentrations, radioactivity inventories, storage area layout, equipment use, storage capacity, fire protection, ventilation, shielding, and expected storage durations (SRP 11.4, I.14). The design and safety classifications of storage systems, structures, and components (SSCs) must follow the guidance in RG 1.143, which includes considerations for natural phenomena and man-induced hazards (SRP 11.4, I.16).

RG 1.143 specifies that SSCs for solid radwaste storage should be designed and tested according to applicable codes and standards (Section C.3.1), with materials compatible with the waste environment (C.3.2). Foundations and walls of storage structures must be designed to contain the maximum expected liquid inventory and withstand natural and man-induced hazards, as detailed in Tables 1-4 of RG 1.143 (C.3.3, C.6.2.1). Safety classifications (RW-IIa, RW-IIb, RW-IIc) are assigned based on hazard potential (C.5).

RG 4.21 further requires that, when offsite disposal is unavailable, licensees must develop additional onsite storage capacity and integrate these operations into existing waste management programs. Licensees should also plan for decontamination and decommissioning of storage facilities and periodically reassess stored waste to ensure future disposal remains feasible (RG 4.21, C.4).

In summary, NRC acceptance criteria require robust design, safety classification, hazard protection, integration with waste management programs, and ongoing reassessment and planning for decommissioning, as specified in SRP 11.4, RG 1.143, and RG 4.21.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for the storage of low-level radioactive waste at nuclear facilities?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for the storage of low-level radioactive waste (LLRW) at nuclear facilities are grounded in a combination of regulations, guidance documents, and standard review plans. Facilities must design, operate, and maintain storage systems to ensure safety, minimize releases, and comply with waste classification and dose limits.

According to SRP 11.4, the NRC reviews the design and operation of systems for managing, treating, processing, and storing LLRW, including both short- and long-term onsite storage provisions if offsite disposal is unavailable. The review includes design objectives, criteria, treatment methods, expected waste volumes, radioactivity inventories, storage capacity, fire protection, ventilation, shielding, and storage durations (SRP 11.4, pp. 11.4-2 to 11.4-5).

10 CFR Part 50 (§ 50.34 and § 50.36a) requires that applications include a safety analysis of structures, systems, and components, with technical specifications for effluent controls to ensure releases are as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA) and within dose limits set by 10 CFR 20.1301 (10 CFR Part 50).

Regulatory Guide 1.143 provides accepted design and material standards for solid radwaste systems, including requirements for pressure-retaining components, compatibility with waste environments, and structural design to contain maximum expected liquid inventories. Buildings housing radwaste systems must be designed to withstand natural phenomena and man-induced hazards, with foundations and walls up to spill height meeting specified criteria (RG 1.143, Regulatory Positions 3 and 6).

RG 4.21 advises that when offsite disposal is unavailable, licensees must develop additional onsite storage capacity, integrate storage operations into waste management programs, address decontamination and decommissioning, and periodically reassess stored waste in light of evolving disposal requirements (RG 4.21, Section C.4).

SRP 11.2 further emphasizes the need for quality assurance, safety classifications, and provisions to prevent and control releases from tank overflows, referencing RG 1.143 and RG 4.21 for design and operational guidance (SRP 11.2, pp. 11.2-2 to 11.2-4).

In summary, NRC requirements for LLRW storage at nuclear facilities include robust design and operational controls, compliance with effluent and dose limits, adherence to material and structural standards, integration with waste management programs, and ongoing reassessment to ensure continued safety and regulatory compliance.
