data.query: What are the NRC requirements for describing the development of plant maintenance programs in a nuclear power plant licensing application?
data.answer: The NRC requires that a nuclear power plant licensing application include a detailed description of the development of plant maintenance programs. According to SRP 13.1.1 (Section I, 13.1.1-3 to 13.1.1-4), the application must describe the development and implementation of plant maintenance programs as part of the applicant’s preoperational responsibilities. This includes specifying how responsibilities are assigned within the management organization, the organizational units involved, staffing levels, qualifications, and the interface with contractors and technical support. Additionally, 10 CFR 50.34 (sections (6) and (9)) mandates that the application provide a description of managerial and administrative controls to assure safe operation, including maintenance of equipment. The application must also describe the maintenance program for structures, systems, and components, addressing objectives, scope, and implementation, and demonstrate compliance with § 50.65 regarding monitoring the effectiveness of maintenance. The program must ensure that all relevant components can fulfill their intended safety functions. Furthermore, RG 1.8 (Section C) endorses ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014 for personnel qualification and training, emphasizing that individuals responsible for maintenance programs must meet minimum qualification requirements, including education, experience, and training, to ensure safe and effective program execution. The guidance also clarifies the requirements for management and supervisory positions involved in maintenance program development and oversight. In summary, the NRC expects a comprehensive, structured, and well-documented approach to the development of plant maintenance programs, with clear organizational responsibilities, qualified personnel, and compliance with regulatory requirements.

evidence_chain.section: C. STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
C.  STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE

ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, “Selection, Qualification, and Training of Personnel for Nuclear Power Plants,” provides criteria for the selection, qualification, and training of personnel for nuclear power plants for complying with the qualifications and training requirements of 10 CFR Parts 50 and 52. The NRC staff endorses ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, with the following exceptions and clarifications.

1. QUALIFICATION

 The qualification criteria described in Section 4 of ANSI/ANS- 3.1-2014 are acceptable to the NRC staff with the following exceptions and clarifications. The minimum qualification requirements for positions as described in ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, including the exceptions and clarifications in this RG, represent the minimum experiential, professional, and educational requirements necessary to ensure that assigned personnel can independently evaluate risks and safely execute the responsibilities associated with the positions. To conform to this guidance, an individual assigned to a specific position must meet the requirements for that position.

1.1 Section 4.3, Middle Manager Level

Temporary appointments of unqualified middle managers shall be limited to one year in duration. During the temporary appointment, an unqualified middle manager shall be provided a single, directly-reporting staff member who meets the middle manager qualification position requirements to assist in decision-making.  The intention of this exception is to emphasize the importance of assigning qualified personnel to positions with specific requirements as described in ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, while allowing licensees adequate flexibility to manage human resources.  This flexibility is not intended to allow purposeful long-term assignment of unqualified personnel to middle manager positions or to allow multiple consecutive assignments of unqualified middle managers to a position.  

At all times, an operations middle manager (Section 4.3.6) or a senior manager assigned responsibility for operations (Section 4.2) shall hold a senior operator’s license. A shift manager (Section 4.3.7) shall hold an active senior operator’s license while directly supervising plant operations.

1.2 Section 4.3.1, Training

Section 4.3.1 states, “The training middle manager is the individual responsible for management of the initial and continuing training programs, and shall meet the following requirements.” This section is clarified as follows: “The training middle manager is the onsite member of the power plant staff responsible for management of the initial and continuing training programs, and shall meet the following requirements.”

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for describing the relationship between the nuclear organization and the broader corporate organization in a nuclear power plant application?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for describing the relationship between the nuclear organization and the broader corporate organization in a nuclear power plant application are detailed in several regulatory documents. According to SRP 13.1.1 (Section III. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA), the applicant must provide organizational charts of the corporate-level management and technical support organizations, and explicitly describe the relationship of the nuclear-oriented part of the organization to the rest of the corporate organization. This includes identifying and describing the organizational groups and individual positions responsible for all aspects of the project, and how the organization integrates management of activities supporting construction, operation, and maintenance. The applicant must also identify the corporate officer responsible for nuclear activities, ensuring this individual has no ancillary responsibilities that could detract from nuclear safety matters.

RG 1.206 (Section C.1.1) further requires the application to describe the applicant’s organizational structure as it relates to the proposed facility, including the relationship between the applicant and its parent, affiliates, and contractors. The application should detail the corporate and management structure, lines of authority and responsibility for facility operation, and the relationship to any parent or holding company or other entities that may exercise control over the applicant or facility.

Additionally, RG 1.8 (Section A) and 10 CFR 50.34(b)(6)(i) require information on organizational structure, allocations of responsibilities and authorities, and personnel qualification requirements. These requirements ensure the NRC can assess the applicant’s technical and organizational capability to operate the facility safely, as also referenced in 10 CFR 50.80 regarding license transfers.

In summary, the application must clearly delineate the nuclear organization’s structure, its integration and relationship with the broader corporate organization, and the lines of authority and responsibility, supported by organizational charts and descriptive information, as specified in SRP 13.1.1, RG 1.206, RG 1.8, and relevant CFR sections.

evidence_chain.section: § 50.80 Transfer of licenses
evidence_chain.evidence_text: § 50.80 Transfer of licenses. (a) No license for a production or utilization facility, or any right thereunder, shall be transferred, assigned, or in any manner disposed of, either voluntarily or involuntarily, directly or indirectly, through transfer of control of any license to any person, unless the Commission shall, after securing full information, find that the transfer is in accordance with the provisions of the Act, and shall give its consent in writing. The Commission may require any person who is to acquire ownership or control of the facility or of the license to submit as part of the application, such information as it deems necessary to enable it to find that the proposed transferee is qualified to be the holder of the license and that the transfer is otherwise consistent with applicable provisions of law, and to enable the Commission to determine whether the applicant is financially qualified and has the necessary technical and organizational capability to operate the facility in a manner that will protect the public health and safety and promote the common defense and security. (b) An application for transfer of license must include as much of the information described in §§ 50.33 and 50.34 as is relevant to the transfer, as well as a written statement describing the proposed transaction, and the identity, technical and financial qualifications of the proposed transferee, and the proposed transferee’s plans for the facility.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for describing the assignment and implementation of design, construction, and preoperation responsibilities within an applicant’s organizational structure for a nuclear power plant?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for describing the assignment and implementation of design, construction, and preoperation responsibilities within an applicant’s organizational structure for a nuclear power plant are detailed in several key documents. According to SRP 13.1.1, applicants must provide a comprehensive description of their management, engineering, and technical support organizations, including organizational charts, lines of authority, and personnel responsibilities for the project. This includes specifying the number of persons assigned, qualification and experience requirements for management and staff, and how responsibilities are assigned and implemented within organizational units (SRP 13.1.1-2 to 13.1.1-4).

Applicants must delineate responsibilities for principal site-related engineering studies, plant and ancillary system design, review and approval of design features, procurement, construction management, document control, and preoperational activities such as test program management, staff training, and maintenance program development. The description must clarify which organizational units are responsible for each function, the qualifications required, and how management interfaces with contractors and technical organizations (SRP 13.1.1).

10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, Section I, requires that the applicant establish and execute a quality assurance program, clearly delineating in writing the authority and duties of all persons and organizations performing activities affecting safety-related functions. While work may be delegated to contractors or consultants, the applicant retains ultimate responsibility. Quality assurance functions must be performed by individuals or organizations independent from those performing the work, with sufficient authority and organizational freedom to identify and resolve quality issues (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, Section I).

Additionally, 10 CFR 50.34(b)(6)(i) and 10 CFR 52.79(a)(26) require that applications include information on organizational structure, allocations of responsibilities and authorities, and personnel qualification requirements. Regulatory Guide 1.8 and ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, as endorsed by the NRC, provide acceptable criteria for personnel selection, qualification, and training (RG 1.8, Section C).

In summary, the NRC requires applicants to provide detailed, documented descriptions of how design, construction, and preoperation responsibilities are assigned and implemented, including organizational structure, authority, qualifications, and quality assurance measures, as specified in SRP 13.1.1, 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix B, and related guidance.

evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appendix B to Part 50—Quality Assurance Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants and Fuel Reprocessing Plants

I. ORGANIZATION
A. The applicant shall be responsible for the establishment and execution of the quality assurance program. The applicant may delegate to others, such as contractors, agents, or consultants, the work of establishing and executing the quality assurance program, or any part thereof, but shall retain responsibility therefor. The authority and duties of persons and organizations performing activities affecting the safety-related functions of structures, systems, and components shall be clearly established and delineated in writing. These activities include performing the functions associated with attaining quality objectives, such as designing, purchasing, fabricating, handling, shipping, storing, cleaning, erecting, installing, inspecting, testing, operating, maintaining, repairing, refueling, and modifying. Such persons and organizations shall have sufficient authority and organizational freedom to identify quality problems; to initiate, recommend, or provide solutions; and to verify implementation of solutions. The applicant shall require contractors or subcontractors to provide such assurance. The persons and organizations performing quality assurance functions must have direct access to the levels of management necessary to perform their functions.

B. The quality assurance functions shall be performed by persons or organizations other than those who performed the work, but who may be from the same organization. These persons or organizations shall have sufficient authority and organizational freedom to identify quality problems; to initiate, recommend, or provide solutions; and to verify implementation of solutions.

data.query: What are the NRC requirements for identifying the organizational units responsible for the design, construction, and preoperational phases of a nuclear power plant project?
data.answer:
The NRC requires applicants for nuclear power plant licenses to clearly identify and describe the organizational units responsible for the design, construction, and preoperational phases of a project. According to SRP 13.1.1 (Sections I and III), the application must include organizational charts and descriptions of management, engineering, and technical support organizations, specifying lines of authority, personnel responsibilities, and the number and qualifications of staff assigned to each unit. The applicant must detail how responsibilities are assigned and implemented within these units, including the responsible working or performance-level organizational unit, and provide general educational and experience requirements for key positions.

SRP 13.1.1 further requires that the applicant demonstrate, through organizational charts and functional descriptions, that all groups and positions responsible for project implementation—including design, construction, preoperational testing, and technical support—are identified. The applicant must also describe how integrated management of activities is achieved, how qualified personnel are obtained, and how responsibilities for contractor oversight and safety are fulfilled, including the roles of architect-engineers (AEs) and nuclear steam supply system (NSSS) vendors.

10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, Criterion I, mandates that the applicant establish and delineate in writing the authority and duties of all persons and organizations performing activities affecting safety-related functions. The applicant must identify individuals with overall authority and responsibility for the quality assurance program, ensuring they have sufficient organizational freedom and authority, including independence from cost and schedule pressures when safety is at stake.

Regulatory Guide 1.8 and 10 CFR 50.34(b)(6)(i) reinforce the requirement to provide information on organizational structure, responsibilities, authorities, and personnel qualification requirements. SRP 13.5.1 and SRP 13.2.1 further specify that the responsibilities of organizational units for test program development, review, and approval must be defined, and that the qualifications of personnel involved in these activities must meet established standards (e.g., ANSI/ANS-3.1).

In summary, NRC requirements mandate comprehensive identification and description of all organizational units and positions responsible for the design, construction, and preoperational phases, including their authority, responsibilities, qualifications, and oversight mechanisms, as detailed in SRP 13.1.1, 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix B, and related guidance.

evidence_chain.section: Appendix B to Part 50—Quality Assurance Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants and Fuel Reprocessing Plants, Criterion I—Organization
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
ORGANIZATION
A. The applicant shall be responsible for the establishment and execution of the quality assurance program. The applicant may delegate to others, such as contractors, agents, or consultants, the work of establishing and executing the quality assurance program, or any part thereof, but shall retain responsibility therefor. The applicant shall clearly establish and delineate in writing the authority and duties of persons and organizations performing activities affecting the safety-related functions of structures, systems, and components. These activities include performing the functions associated with attaining quality objectives, such as designing, purchasing, fabricating, handling, shipping, storing, cleaning, erecting, installing, inspecting, testing, operating, maintaining, repairing, refueling, and modifying. Such persons and organizations performing quality assurance functions must have sufficient authority and organizational freedom to identify quality problems; to initiate, recommend, or provide solutions; and to verify implementation of solutions.

B. The applicant (or designee) shall identify the individual(s) within the applicant's organization who have the overall authority and responsibility for the establishment and execution of the quality assurance program. These individual(s) shall have sufficient organizational freedom and authority to accomplish this responsibility, including sufficient independence from cost and schedule when opposed to safety considerations. The individual(s) assigned responsibility for quality assurance functions must have direct access to the levels of management necessary to effect corrective measures.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for describing the estimated number of personnel assigned to the design, construction, and preoperational phases of a nuclear power plant project?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for describing the estimated number of personnel assigned to the design, construction, and preoperational phases of a nuclear power plant project are specified in several key documents. According to 10 CFR 50.34(a)(6), an application must include a description of the applicant's organization, including the responsibilities and authorities of each position, and the minimum number of personnel proposed for the operation and maintenance of the facility. Importantly, the applicant must also provide a description of the estimated number of personnel, by category, to be assigned to the design, construction, and preoperational phases of the facility.

SRP 13.1.1 further clarifies that the application should include an organizational description with charts, lines of authority, personnel responsibilities, and the number of persons assigned to the project. Specifically, it requires the estimated number of persons to be assigned to each organizational unit responsible for the project during the design, construction, and preoperational phases. The applicant should also describe the educational and experience requirements for each identified position or class of positions.

Regulatory Guide 1.206, Section C.1.1, provides additional guidance, stating that the application should specify the estimated number of personnel assigned to each phase, identify the principal organizations responsible, and describe the management and technical support organizations, including personnel numbers, qualifications, and responsibilities. The application should also outline plans for recruiting, training, and qualifying personnel for both construction and operation.

In summary, NRC regulations and guidance require applicants to provide detailed estimates of personnel numbers by phase and organizational unit, along with descriptions of responsibilities, qualifications, and plans for recruitment and training (10 CFR 50.34(a)(6); SRP 13.1.1; RG 1.206 C.1.1).

data.query: What are the NRC requirements for the general educational background and experience of personnel responsible for the design, construction, and preoperation phases of a nuclear power plant?
data.answer:
The NRC requires that personnel responsible for the design, construction, and preoperation phases of a nuclear power plant possess appropriate educational backgrounds and experience commensurate with their responsibilities. According to SRP 13.1.1, applicants must provide descriptions of the general educational and experience requirements for identified positions or classes of positions, including management and supervisory roles. This includes specifying requirements for technical support positions in areas such as nuclear, mechanical, structural, electrical, thermal-hydraulic, metallurgical, materials, and instrumentation and controls engineering. 

Furthermore, SRP 13.1.1 states that the experience and qualifications of management and technical support staff must meet or exceed those endorsed by Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.8. RG 1.8 endorses ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, which provides detailed criteria for the selection, qualification, and training of nuclear power plant personnel. The NRC accepts the minimum qualification requirements described in Section 4 of ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, with certain exceptions and clarifications, as the baseline for educational and experiential qualifications. These requirements ensure that personnel can independently evaluate risks and safely execute their responsibilities.

Additionally, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, Criterion II, mandates that the quality assurance program for nuclear power plants be established and executed by qualified personnel. It requires provisions for indoctrination and training to ensure suitable proficiency for all activities affecting quality, including design, construction, and preoperation. The program must be documented and periodically reviewed to maintain compliance.

In summary, NRC requirements stipulate that personnel involved in design, construction, and preoperation must have qualifications and experience as described in ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014 (as endorsed by RG 1.8), and that quality assurance activities must be performed by qualified and properly trained personnel, as required by 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B.

evidence_chain.section: Appendix B to Part 50—Quality Assurance Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants and Fuel Reprocessing Plants, Criterion II—Quality Assurance Program
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Criterion II—Quality Assurance Program

The applicant shall establish at the earliest practicable time, consistent with the schedule for accomplishing the activities, a quality assurance program which complies with the requirements of this appendix. The applicant shall identify the structures, systems, and components to be covered by the quality assurance program, the major organizations participating in the program, and the designated functions and responsibilities of these organizations. The applicant shall also identify the levels of authority and lines of communication for activities affecting quality. These activities include designing, purchasing, fabricating, handling, shipping, storing, cleaning, erecting, installing, inspecting, testing, operating, maintaining, repairing, refueling, and modifying. The quality assurance program shall provide control over activities affecting quality to an extent consistent with their importance to safety. The program shall be established and executed by qualified personnel. Provisions shall be established for indoctrination and training of personnel performing activities affecting quality as necessary to assure that suitable proficiency is achieved and maintained. The program shall be documented by written policies, procedures, or instructions and shall be carried out in accordance with these policies, procedures, or instructions. The program and its implementation shall be reviewed periodically as specified by the applicant.

data.query: What are the NRC requirements for describing the interfaces between a license applicant's management and the nuclear steam supply system supplier and architect-engineer during design, construction, and preoperational phases?
data.answer: The NRC requires license applicants to provide detailed descriptions of the interfaces between their management and the nuclear steam supply system (NSSS) supplier and architect-engineer (AE) during the design, construction, and preoperational phases. According to SRP 13.1.1, the application must include organizational descriptions with charts, lines of authority, and personnel responsibilities, as well as the number of persons assigned and qualification/experience requirements for management and staff. Specifically, the applicant must describe how responsibilities are assigned and implemented within organizational units, identify the responsible working units, estimate staffing levels, and specify educational and experience requirements for key positions. Importantly, the applicant must explain how its management interfaces with the NSSS and AE organizations to jointly address emerging risk insights as probabilistic risk assessments mature, and how they resolve combined license (COL) items that cannot be addressed prior to license issuance, as referenced in DC/COL-ISG-015. The applicant is also required to describe the review process for contractor work by its own staff. While 10 CFR 50.80 addresses license transfers and the need to demonstrate technical and financial qualifications, the specific requirements for describing management interfaces during design, construction, and preoperational phases are detailed in SRP 13.1.1, Section I (pages 13.1.1-2 to 13.1.1-4).

evidence_chain.section: § 50.80 Transfer of licenses
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
§ 50.80 Transfer of licenses.
(a) No license for a production or utilization facility, or any right thereunder, shall be transferred, assigned, or in any manner disposed of, either voluntarily or involuntarily, directly or indirectly, through transfer of control of any license to any person, unless the Commission shall give its consent in writing. An application for transfer of license must include as much of the information described in §§ 50.33 and 50.34 as is relevant to the transfer, as well as a written statement describing the proposed transaction, and the identity, technical and financial qualifications of the proposed transferee, and the proposed transferee’s plans for the facility (including any changes the proposed transferee intends to make in the facility or the facility’s operation). The Commission may require additional information such as the applicant’s technical and financial qualifications, as it deems appropriate for the transfer review. The Commission will approve an application for the transfer of a license if the Commission determines: (1) That the proposed transferee is qualified to be the holder of the license; and (2) That the transfer is otherwise consistent with applicable provisions of law, regulations, and orders issued by the Commission.

data.query: What are the NRC requirements for the qualifications and responsibilities of personnel involved in the design, construction, and preoperational testing phases of a nuclear power plant?
data.answer:
The NRC requirements for the qualifications and responsibilities of personnel involved in the design, construction, and preoperational testing phases of a nuclear power plant are established through a combination of regulatory guidance, standards, and quality assurance criteria. According to SRP 13.1.1, applicants must provide detailed descriptions of organizational structure, lines of authority, personnel responsibilities, and qualification/experience requirements for management and staff positions involved in these phases. This includes specifying how responsibilities are assigned, the organizational units responsible, the number of personnel, and the general educational and experience requirements for each position, especially for management and supervisory roles. The applicant must also ensure that contractor work is reviewed by qualified applicant staff (SRP 13.1.1, Section I, III).

The NRC endorses ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014 (as clarified in RG 1.8) as the standard for selection, qualification, and training of nuclear power plant personnel. This standard sets minimum experiential, professional, and educational requirements for each position to ensure personnel can independently evaluate risks and safely execute their responsibilities. For middle manager positions, temporary appointments of unqualified individuals are limited to one year and must be supported by a qualified staff member. Operations middle managers and shift managers must hold a senior operator’s license (RG 1.8, Section C).

Additionally, 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, Criteria I and II, require the applicant to establish and execute a quality assurance program covering all activities affecting safety-related functions, including design, construction, and testing. The authority and duties of all personnel must be clearly defined in writing, and those performing quality assurance functions must be organizationally independent from those performing the work to ensure objectivity. The quality assurance program must be established as early as practicable and must identify all major organizations, their responsibilities, and the controls over activities affecting quality (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, Criteria I and II).

In summary, NRC requirements mandate clear organizational structure, defined responsibilities, and minimum qualification standards for all personnel involved in design, construction, and preoperational testing, with oversight and quality assurance controls in place as specified in SRP 13.1.1, RG 1.8, and 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B.

evidence_chain.section: C. STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
C.  STAFF REGULATORY GUIDANCE

ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, “Selection, Qualification, and Training of Personnel for Nuclear Power Plants,” provides criteria for the selection, qualification, and training of personnel for nuclear power plants for complying with the qualifications and training requirements of 10 CFR Parts 50 and 52. The NRC staff endorses ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, with the following exceptions and clarifications.

1. QUALIFICATION

 The qualification criteria described in Section 4 of ANSI/ANS- 3.1-2014 are acceptable to the NRC staff with the following exceptions and clarifications. The minimum qualification requirements for positions as described in ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, including the exceptions and clarifications in this RG, represent the minimum experiential, professional, and educational requirements necessary to ensure that assigned personnel can independently evaluate risks and safely execute the responsibilities associated with the positions. To conform to this guidance, an individual assigned to a specific position must meet the requirements for that position.

1.1 Section 4.3, Middle Manager Level

Temporary appointments of unqualified middle managers shall be limited to one year in duration. During the temporary appointment, an unqualified middle manager shall be provided a single, directly-reporting staff member who meets the middle manager qualification position requirements to assist in decision-making.  The intention of this exception is to emphasize the importance of assigning qualified personnel to positions with specific requirements as described in ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014, while allowing licensees adequate flexibility to manage human resources.  This flexibility is not intended to allow purposeful long-term assignment of unqualified personnel to middle manager positions or to allow multiple consecutive assignments of unqualified middle managers to a position.  

At all times, an operations middle manager (Section 4.3.6) or a senior manager assigned responsibility for operations (Section 4.2) shall hold a senior operator’s license. A shift manager (Section 4.3.7) shall hold an active senior operator’s license while directly supervising plant operations.

evidence_chain.section: Appendix B to Part 50—Quality Assurance Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants and Fuel Reprocessing Plants, Criterion I—Organization and Criterion II—Quality Assurance Program
evidence_chain.evidence_text:
Appendix B to Part 50—Quality Assurance Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants and Fuel Reprocessing Plants

I. Introduction

A. Applicability

The quality assurance program applies to all activities affecting the safety-related functions of structures, systems, and components. These activities include designing, purchasing, fabricating, handling, shipping, storing, cleaning, erecting, installing, inspecting, testing, operating, maintaining, repairing, refueling, and modifying.

II. Quality Assurance Criteria

Criterion I—Organization

The applicant shall be responsible for the establishment and execution of the quality assurance program. The applicant may delegate to others, such as contractors, agents, or consultants, the work of establishing and executing the quality assurance program, or any part thereof, but shall retain responsibility therefor. The authority and duties of persons and organizations performing activities affecting the safety-related functions of structures, systems, and components shall be clearly established and delineated in writing. These activities include performing the functions associated with attaining quality objectives, such as designing, purchasing, fabricating, and so forth, as enumerated in paragraph A of the Introduction. Such persons and organizations shall have sufficient authority and organizational freedom to identify quality problems; to initiate, recommend, or provide solutions; and to verify implementation of solutions. These persons and organizations performing quality assurance functions must be different from those performing the work, to the extent necessary to permit objective accomplishment of quality assurance functions.

Criterion II—Quality Assurance Program

The applicant shall establish at the earliest practicable time, consistent with the schedule for accomplishing the activities, a quality assurance program which complies with the requirements of this appendix. The applicant shall identify the structures, systems, and components to be covered by the quality assurance program, as well as the major organizations participating in the program, together with their responsibilities and authorities. The program shall provide control over activities affecting the quality of the identified structures, systems, and components, to an extent consistent with their importance to safety. These activities include designing, purchasing, fabricating, handling, shipping, storing, cleaning, erecting, installing, inspecting, testing, operating, maintaining, repairing, refueling, and modifying.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for identifying management and supervisory positions responsible for design, construction, and preoperational activities at a nuclear power plant?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for identifying management and supervisory positions responsible for design, construction, and preoperational activities at a nuclear power plant are detailed in several key documents. According to SRP 13.1.1, Section III, the applicant must clearly identify and describe, through organizational charts and position descriptions, all organizational groups and individual positions responsible for implementing all aspects of the project, including design, construction, and the initial test program. The applicant must also define how the organization manages these activities, ensures sufficient experience and qualifications among personnel, and maintains clear lines of authority and communication (SRP 13.1.1, III.a.i-viii, c, e, g). The corporate officer responsible for nuclear activities must be identified, with a commitment that this individual will focus solely on nuclear safety matters (SRP 13.1.1, III.b).

10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, Criterion I, further requires that the applicant establish a quality assurance program, clearly delineate the authority and duties of persons and organizations performing activities affecting quality, and assign qualified personnel to these functions. The individuals or organizations responsible for quality-affecting activities must be identified in writing and have sufficient authority and organizational freedom to address quality issues (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, Criterion I.A-B).

Additionally, Regulatory Guide 1.8 endorses ANSI/ANS-3.1-2014 for the selection, qualification, and training of personnel, specifying that minimum qualification requirements must be met for each position. Middle and senior managers responsible for operations must meet specific qualification standards, including holding a senior operator’s license where applicable (RG 1.8, Section C.1, C.1.1).

In summary, NRC regulations require applicants to clearly identify, describe, and qualify management and supervisory positions responsible for design, construction, and preoperational activities, ensuring clear authority, communication, and adherence to quality assurance and personnel qualification standards.

data.query: What are the NRC regulatory requirements for including early plans for providing technical support for the operation of a nuclear facility in a license application?
data.answer:
The NRC regulatory requirements for including early plans for providing technical support for the operation of a nuclear facility in a license application are clearly outlined in several regulatory documents. According to SRP 13.1.1, Section I and III, applicants must provide descriptions of early plans for technical support as part of their organizational and operational planning. Specifically, the application should identify and describe the organizational groups and individual positions responsible for implementing all aspects of the project, including those responsible for providing technical support for facility operation (SRP 13.1.1, Section III.a.i).

The acceptance criteria for these plans are based on compliance with several regulations, notably 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, which requires a description of the quality assurance program, including the organizational structure, functional responsibilities, levels of authority, and lines of communication for activities affecting quality (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B, Criterion I). The applicant must also address indoctrination and training of personnel to ensure proficiency in activities affecting quality.

Additionally, 10 CFR 50.34(b)(6)(i) and 10 CFR 52.79(a)(26) require that the license application include detailed information about the applicant’s organizational structure, allocation of responsibilities and authorities, and personnel qualification requirements for operation (RG 1.8, Section A). These requirements ensure that the NRC can evaluate whether the applicant has established adequate early plans and organizational arrangements to provide technical support for safe and effective facility operation.

In summary, the NRC requires that license applications include early plans for technical support, with clear organizational descriptions, responsibilities, and personnel qualifications, as detailed in SRP 13.1.1, 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix B, 10 CFR 50.34, and 10 CFR 52.79.

data.query: What are the NRC requirements for defining emergency classification levels in a nuclear power plant emergency plan?
data.answer:
The NRC requires that nuclear power plant emergency plans define emergency classification levels according to a standard scheme, as specified in 10 CFR 50.47(b)(4) and Appendix E to 10 CFR Part 50. The emergency classification scheme must include four levels: Notification of Unusual Event, Alert, Site Area Emergency, and General Emergency. The bases for these classifications must include facility system and effluent parameters, and the emergency action levels (EALs) must be based on plant system instrumentation, radiation monitors, or other suitable and reliable means (10 CFR 50.47(b)(4)). The emergency plan must describe both the classification scheme and the methods for determining the EALs.

SRP 13.3 further clarifies that the emergency plan should follow the emergency classification level scheme described in Appendix 1 and Supplement 3 to NUREG-0654, and generally use the methodology outlined in NEI 99-01, as endorsed by Regulatory Guide 1.101. However, for new or advanced reactor designs, the unique characteristics of the plant and site must be addressed in the development of EALs. The format of the EAL scheme should follow the convention established in Regulatory Information Summary 2003-18. Additionally, initial emergency actions and EALs must be discussed and agreed upon with State and local governmental authorities, with confirmation of such agreement included in the emergency plan if the EALs differ from those of existing reactors at the site (SRP 13.3, Section II).

In summary, NRC requirements mandate a four-level emergency classification scheme, with EALs based on reliable plant parameters, and require coordination with State and local authorities, as detailed in 10 CFR 50.47(b)(4), Appendix E, and SRP 13.3.

data.query: How do NRC regulations require the use of endorsed guidance documents when developing emergency action level schemes for nuclear power plants, and what is the relationship between these guidance documents and the emergency plan?
data.answer:
NRC regulations require that emergency action level (EAL) schemes for nuclear power plants be developed in accordance with a standard framework, as specified in 10 CFR 50.47(b)(4) and Appendix E to 10 CFR Part 50. The regulations mandate that EALs be based on plant system and effluent parameters and be consistent with the emergency classification scheme outlined in Appendix E. The NRC must approve the EALs, and their bases must be described in the emergency plan (10 CFR 50.47(b)(4)).

Endorsed guidance documents, such as NUREG-0654 (Appendix 1 and Supplement 3), NEI 99-01 (Revision 4), and Regulatory Guide 1.101, provide methodologies and conventions for developing EAL schemes. The Standard Review Plan (SRP 13.3, Section II) states that the emergency plan should include an EAL scheme as described in these guidance documents. While the NRC anticipates that applicants will use the methodology in NEI 99-01 (Revision 4), it acknowledges that unique reactor or site characteristics may require modifications. In such cases, the emergency plan must address these differences and provide confirmation of agreement with State and local authorities if the EALs differ from those used for existing reactors at the site.

The relationship between the guidance documents and the emergency plan is that the guidance provides the recommended structure and methodology for EAL development, while the emergency plan documents the specific EAL scheme adopted by the licensee, including its bases and any necessary adaptations. The emergency plan must demonstrate consistency with NRC-endorsed guidance unless justified otherwise and must include evidence of coordination with State and local authorities when deviations occur.

References: SRP 13.3 Section II; 10 CFR 50.47(b)(4).

data.query: For a new nuclear power plant, what combined regulatory requirements and NRC-endorsed guidance govern the development and approval of an emergency action level scheme, including the process for addressing site-specific information and the inclusion of digital instrumentation and control systems?
data.answer:
The development and approval of an emergency action level (EAL) scheme for a new nuclear power plant are governed by a combination of regulatory requirements and NRC-endorsed guidance. The primary regulatory basis is 10 CFR 50.47(b)(4), which mandates that licensees implement a standard emergency classification and action level scheme. This scheme must be based on plant system and effluent parameters and be consistent with the EAL scheme described in NUREG–0654/FEMA–REP–1, Revision 1, or other NRC-endorsed guidance. The regulation further requires that EALs address site-specific information, including the consideration of digital instrumentation and control systems, as appropriate. EALs must be submitted to the NRC for approval and updated as necessary to reflect changes in plant design, procedures, or equipment, including digital systems, to maintain consistency with NRC-endorsed guidance (10 CFR 50.47(b)(4)).

The Standard Review Plan (SRP) 13.3 further clarifies that the emergency plan should include an EAL scheme as described in Appendix 1 and Supplement 3 to NUREG-0654, and that the NRC anticipates use of a scheme similar to that in NEI 99-01, Revision 4, as endorsed by Regulatory Guide 1.101. However, for advanced reactor designs, site- and design-specific characteristics must be addressed in the EAL development. The format should follow conventions established in Regulatory Information Summary 2003-18. Additionally, if the EALs differ from those for existing reactors at the site, the applicant must provide confirmation of agreement with State and local authorities in the emergency plan (SRP 13.3, Section II).

In summary, the EAL scheme must be developed using NRC-endorsed guidance, tailored to site-specific and design-specific features (including digital I&C systems), and formally approved by the NRC, with coordination with State and local authorities as required.

data.query: What are the NRC requirements for establishing agreements with offsite agencies that have emergency response roles within the Emergency Planning Zones?
data.answer:
The NRC requires licensees to establish formal arrangements and written agreements with offsite agencies that have emergency response roles within the Emergency Planning Zones (EPZs). According to Appendix E to 10 CFR Part 50, Sections IV.A, IV.D, and IV.E, emergency plans must describe arrangements for notification and coordination with offsite authorities and organizations responsible for emergency response, including the means for requesting offsite assistance (Section IV.A.2). Specifically, arrangements must be made for requesting and effectively using assistance from fire and law enforcement agencies, ambulance services, hospitals, and other relevant offsite organizations (Section IV.D).

Furthermore, written agreements are required with local and State law enforcement agencies, fire departments, hospitals, ambulance services, and any other organizations with which arrangements for assistance have been made. These agreements must clearly set forth the authorities, responsibilities, and resources of the supporting organizations (Section IV.E).

The NRC reviews these arrangements and agreements as part of its licensing process, ensuring compliance with 10 CFR 50.47(b) and the guidance in NUREG-0654/FEMA-REP-1, Rev. 1, as referenced in SRP 13.3. This ensures that all emergency response roles within the EPZs are clearly defined, coordinated, and supported by formal agreements, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of emergency preparedness and response.

data.query: How do NRC regulations require coordination between a nuclear facility and local law enforcement agencies to ensure effective emergency response, and what criteria must be included in such agreements?
data.answer:
NRC regulations require nuclear facilities to establish and document formal coordination with local law enforcement agencies (LLEAs) and other offsite response organizations to ensure effective emergency response. According to 10 CFR 50.33(g), license applications must describe arrangements for: (1) informing each offsite response organization, including local police, about the facility’s nature and characteristics; (2) providing training for personnel who may respond to emergencies, including joint exercises; (3) involving these organizations in the development of emergency plans; and (4) ensuring prompt notification of these organizations in the event of an emergency. The application must include any formal agreements made with LLEAs and other relevant organizations.

Further, SRP 13.3 specifies that emergency response plans must meet the standards of 10 CFR 50.47(b) and Appendix E to 10 CFR Part 50. Section IV.B of Appendix E requires that initial emergency actions be discussed and agreed upon by State and local governmental authorities, with confirmation of such agreements (e.g., signed letters) included in the emergency plan. Compliance is evaluated using guidance such as NUREG-0654/FEMA-REP-1, which provides an acceptable basis for developing and improving radiological emergency plans and procedures.

In summary, NRC regulations mandate documented, formal arrangements with LLEAs that address notification, training, participation in planning, and agreement on emergency actions, as detailed in 10 CFR 50.33(g), SRP 13.3, and Appendix E to 10 CFR Part 50.

data.query: How do NRC regulations define the minimum staffing requirements for onsite emergency response organizations at nuclear power plants, and how should these requirements be reflected in organizational diagrams and staffing tables?
data.answer:
NRC regulations define the minimum staffing requirements for onsite emergency response organizations at nuclear power plants primarily through 10 CFR 50.47(b) and the guidance endorsed in SRP 13.3. According to 10 CFR 50.47(b)(2), emergency plans must demonstrate that the emergency response organization (ERO) has sufficient staff to respond to radiological emergencies and to augment its initial response on a continuous basis. The regulations require that the emergency plans specify the minimum number of staff and the positions that must be filled on a shift basis. Additionally, the plans must describe the functions of the ERO, the assignments for performing emergency response functions, and the means for notification, recall, and assembly of offsite response organizations (10 CFR 50.47(b)(2)).

SRP 13.3 further clarifies that compliance with these requirements is determined using guidance from Regulatory Guide 1.101, which endorses NUREG-0654/FEMA-REP-1, Rev. 1. This document establishes an acceptable basis for developing radiological emergency plans and procedures, including staffing. The applicant must identify any differences from the SRP acceptance criteria and justify how their proposed alternatives provide acceptable compliance with NRC regulations. For combined license (COL) applications, the NRC staff reviews the Emergency Planning program description and implementation milestones, including review of the FSAR Table 13.x to ensure that minimum staffing and organizational requirements are addressed.

Organizational diagrams and staffing tables must clearly reflect the minimum number of staff and the specific positions required on each shift, as well as the structure and assignments of the ERO, in accordance with the regulatory requirements and guidance documents referenced above.

data.query: What are the regulatory expectations for ensuring clear interfaces and coordination between onsite emergency functional areas and offsite support agencies during a nuclear plant emergency?
data.answer:
The regulatory expectations for ensuring clear interfaces and coordination between onsite emergency functional areas and offsite support agencies during a nuclear plant emergency are established primarily in 10 CFR 50.47(b) and further detailed in NRC guidance documents. According to 10 CFR 50.47(b)(2), onsite emergency response plans must be coordinated with offsite emergency response plans. This coordination includes providing for prompt notification of offsite response organizations and establishing means to request and effectively integrate offsite assistance. The emergency plans must explicitly describe the interfaces and coordination mechanisms between onsite and offsite response organizations, covering notification, communication, and coordination of emergency response activities. Additionally, 10 CFR 50.47(b)(6) requires that emergency response plans are coordinated with appropriate local, State, and Federal agencies, including arrangements for requesting and integrating offsite assistance and resources.

The NRC, in consultation with FEMA, evaluates the adequacy of these plans, as outlined in SRP 13.3. The NRC relies on guidance such as Regulatory Guide 1.101 and NUREG-0654/FEMA-REP-1, Rev. 1, which provide acceptable methods for demonstrating compliance with these requirements. These documents emphasize the need for clear, documented procedures and arrangements that ensure effective communication and coordination between onsite and offsite entities during an emergency. The NRC reviews emergency plans to ensure these interfaces are well-defined and that there is reasonable assurance that adequate protective measures can and will be taken in the event of a radiological emergency (SRP 13.3; 10 CFR 50.47(b)).

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for the frequency of communication system testing between nuclear power plant emergency response facilities and the NRC Headquarters Operations Center?

However, based on the provided evidence, the specific frequency for testing communication systems between emergency response facilities and the NRC Headquarters Operations Center is not explicitly stated in the cited regulations or guidance. The requirements direct licensees to follow the standards and guidance documents referenced, which contain the detailed procedures and frequencies for such testing.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for public education and information programs in nuclear power plant emergency planning?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for public education and information programs in nuclear power plant emergency planning are established primarily in 10 CFR 50.33(k), 10 CFR 50.47(b), and Appendix E to 10 CFR Part 50, as well as supporting guidance documents such as NUREG-0654/FEMA-REP-1, Rev. 1. According to 10 CFR 50.33(k), applicants for a nuclear power reactor license must demonstrate that they have developed and will maintain an emergency plan that includes provisions for informing and educating the public living within the plume exposure pathway Emergency Planning Zone (EPZ). This includes describing the means for notification and the actions to be taken by the public in the event of an emergency. Additionally, the applicant must make arrangements to provide information to the public during an emergency, including notification, instructions, and periodic updates, as specified in the emergency plan (10 CFR 50.33(k)(2)-(3)).

SRP 13.3 further clarifies that compliance with these requirements is determined by meeting the standards of 10 CFR 50.47(b) and the applicable requirements of Appendix E to 10 CFR Part 50, using the guidance in NUREG-0654/FEMA-REP-1, Rev. 1. Specifically, Appendix 3 of NUREG-0654/FEMA-REP-1 provides guidance on prompt alerting and notification of the population, and Supplement 3 offers criteria for protective action recommendations for the public during severe accidents. These documents collectively establish the acceptable basis for developing radiological emergency plans and procedures, including public education and information programs, to ensure the public is adequately informed and prepared for potential emergencies.

References: SRP 13.3, Section II; 10 CFR 50.33(k); NUREG-0654/FEMA-REP-1, Rev. 1.

data.query: How do NRC regulations require coordination of public education efforts when emergency planning zones of two nuclear facilities overlap?
data.answer: NRC regulations require that when emergency planning zones (EPZs) of two nuclear facilities overlap, the emergency plans—including public education efforts—must be coordinated to ensure effective emergency response and public safety. According to 10 CFR § 50.47(d) and (j), applicants must provide assurance that emergency plans are coordinated in cases where EPZs overlap, specifically to maintain necessary emergency response capabilities and to ensure the public receives accurate and timely information. Section 50.47(b)(10) further requires that there be means for prompt public education and information regarding appropriate actions within the EPZs in the event of an accident. The Standard Review Plan (SRP) 13.3 reinforces this by stating that the NRC reviews whether applicants have addressed exercise requirements for co-located licensees and the conduct of emergency preparedness activities, including coordination of the Alert and Notification System (ANS) and public information efforts. The NRC also consults with FEMA to evaluate the preparedness of state and local governments responsible for protective actions within overlapping EPZs. Thus, NRC regulations mandate coordinated public education and information dissemination efforts among licensees and relevant authorities to ensure the public within overlapping EPZs is adequately informed and protected.

data.query: What are the regulatory expectations for the timely activation and staffing of emergency response facilities, such as the Technical Support Center and Emergency Operations Facility, during a nuclear power plant emergency?
data.answer:
The regulatory expectations for the timely activation and staffing of emergency response facilities, such as the Technical Support Center (TSC) and Emergency Operations Facility (EOF), during a nuclear power plant emergency are established primarily in 10 CFR 50.47(b) and Appendix E to 10 CFR Part 50. According to 10 CFR 50.47(b)(8), licensees must provide and maintain adequate emergency facilities and equipment to support emergency response. Section 50.47(b)(2) further requires that onsite emergency response plans describe the means for notification, activation, and staffing of emergency response facilities, including the TSC and EOF, in a timely manner, ensuring these facilities are activated and staffed in accordance with Appendix E requirements.

The Standard Review Plan (SRP) 13.3 specifies that compliance is determined using guidance from Regulatory Guide 1.101, which endorses NUREG-0654/FEMA-REP-1 and NUREG-0696. NUREG-0696 provides detailed guidance on the facilities and systems to be provided by licensees to support emergency response, including requirements for habitable TSCs with adequate space, data retrieval, and communications capabilities. Supplement 1 to NUREG-0737 further clarifies requirements for upgrading emergency response facilities and meeting the criteria of 10 CFR 50.47(b)(6), (8), (9), and Section IV.E of Appendix E.

In summary, licensees must ensure that emergency response facilities are promptly activated and staffed as described in their emergency plans, with adequate instrumentation, communications, and support systems, as outlined in the referenced regulations and guidance documents (10 CFR 50.47(b), Appendix E, SRP 13.3, NUREG-0654/FEMA-REP-1, NUREG-0696, and Supplement 1 to NUREG-0737).

data.query: How do NRC regulations address the capability of an Emergency Operations Facility to support simultaneous emergency responses for multiple nuclear units, and what criteria must be met to ensure adequate response?
data.answer:
NRC regulations require that the Emergency Operations Facility (EOF) at a multi-unit nuclear site be capable of supporting simultaneous emergency responses for all units. According to Appendix E to 10 CFR Part 50, Section IV.F.2.c, co-located licensees (those sharing an EOF or emergency planning zone) must participate in a joint exercise every 8 years that simulates an event affecting multiple units. This exercise must demonstrate the EOF’s ability to coordinate emergency response activities, allocate resources, and support simultaneous responses for multiple units, thereby testing the adequacy of emergency plans and the capability of emergency response personnel and facilities (10 CFR Part 50, Appendix E, Section IV.F.2.c).

Regulatory Guide 1.206, Section C.1.5, further clarifies that applicants must describe and justify the EOF’s capability to perform its intended functions for all units, including during simultaneous emergencies. The EOF must have sufficient space, communications, equipment, and staffing to support the emergency response organization for each unit. The emergency plan should include an analysis or justification that the EOF can support the maximum credible number of simultaneous emergencies expected at the site, and address coordination among units and with offsite authorities, as well as command and control provisions during multi-unit events (RG 1.206, C.1.5).

The Standard Review Plan (SRP 13.3) instructs reviewers to evaluate whether the emergency planning program, including the EOF, is adequately extended to new reactors at an existing site. This includes confirming that any necessary updates to emergency facilities and equipment are identified and implemented, and that exercise requirements for co-located licensees are met (SRP 13.3, I. Areas of Review).

In summary, NRC regulations require that the EOF be demonstrably capable of supporting simultaneous emergency responses for multiple units, with criteria including adequate facilities, staffing, communications, and coordination, as verified through periodic joint exercises and documented analyses.

data.query: How do regulatory review standards require that offsite dose assessment models account for both site-specific source characteristics and local meteorological conditions when estimating radiological consequences during an emergency?
data.answer:
Regulatory review standards require that offsite dose assessment models explicitly account for both site-specific source characteristics and local meteorological conditions when estimating radiological consequences during an emergency. According to 10 CFR 50.47(b)(8) and (c)(1), emergency plans must include means for assessing and monitoring actual or potential offsite radiological consequences, which necessitates the use of models that reflect the unique characteristics of the site and its environment (10CFR §50.47).

Supporting this, SRP 13.3 references Appendix 2 to NUREG-0654/FEMA-REP-1 and Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.23, which provide acceptance criteria for meteorological measurements. RG 1.23 (Section C.3) specifies that onsite meteorological measurement programs must provide data representative of the atmospheric conditions into which radioactive material will be released and transported. This includes careful siting of meteorological instruments to ensure measurements accurately reflect the site's meteorology, considering factors such as prevailing wind direction, topography, and obstructions.

RG 1.145 (Section C.1.1) further details that atmospheric dispersion models must use site-specific meteorological data—specifically wind speed, wind direction (in 16 compass sectors), and atmospheric stability (as defined in RG 1.23)—to calculate atmospheric relative concentration (X/Q) values. The guide allows for the use of site-specific diffusion tests and requires that any alternative parameters or models be substantiated by data from terrain conditions similar to the site.

Additionally, RG 1.97 (Section C.4) requires that accident monitoring instrumentation have sufficient range and accuracy to cover predicted accident conditions, including those involving fuel damage, ensuring that source term characteristics are adequately captured.

In summary, regulatory standards mandate that offsite dose assessment models incorporate both the unique source term characteristics of the facility and detailed, representative local meteorological data to ensure accurate estimation of radiological consequences during emergencies (SRP 13.3; 10CFR §50.47; RG 1.23; RG 1.145; RG 1.97).

The procedures also allow evaluations of atmospheric dispersion for directionally variable distances such as a noncircular exclusion area boundary.

C. REGULATORY POSITION
This section identifies acceptable methods for (1) calculating atmospheric relative concentration (x/Q) values, (2) determining X/Q values on a directional basis, (3) determining X/Q values on an overall site basis, and (4) choosing X/Q values to be used in evaluations of the types of events described in Regulatory Guides 1.3 and 1.4.

Selection of conservative, less detailed site parameters for the evaluation may be sufficient to establish compliance with regulatory guidelines.

1. CALCULATION OF ATMOSPHERIC RELATIVE CONCENTRATION (X/Q) VALUES
Equations and parameters presented in this section should be used unless unusual siting, meteorological, or terrain conditions dictate the use of other models or considerations. Site-specific atmospheric diffusion tests covering a full range of conditions may be used as a basis for modifying the equations and parameters.

1.1 Meteorological Data Input
The meteorological data needed for X/Q calculations include windspeed, wind direction, and a measure of atmospheric stability. These data should represent hourly averages as defined in Regulatory Guide 1.23.

Wind direction should be classed into 16 compass directions (22.5-degree sectors centered on true north, north-northeast, etc.).

Atmospheric stability should be determined by vertical ΔT between the release height and the 10-meter level. Acceptable stability classes are given in Regulatory Guide 1.23. If other well-documented parameters are used to determine plume dispersion (with appropriate justification), the models described in this guide may require modification. A well-documented parameter is one that is substantiated by diffusion data collected in terrain conditions similar to those at the nuclear power plant site being considered.

data.query: What are the regulatory expectations for incorporating local terrain features and building effects into atmospheric dispersion modeling for emergency preparedness at nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The regulatory expectations for incorporating local terrain features and building effects into atmospheric dispersion modeling for emergency preparedness at nuclear power plants are grounded in both the Standard Review Plan (SRP) and federal regulations. According to SRP 13.3, the review of emergency preparedness plans must consider natural and manmade features and physical characteristics unique to the site, including those that could significantly impact emergency planning (SRP 13.3, Review Interfaces, item 1). Specifically, the acceptance criteria reference 10 CFR 50.33(g), 10 CFR 50.47(c)(2), and Appendix E to 10 CFR Part 50, which require that the size and adequacy of the Emergency Planning Zone (EPZ) be determined in relation to local emergency response needs and capabilities, as influenced by factors such as demography, topography, land characteristics, and access routes (SRP 13.3, II. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA, item 10).

Further, 10 CFR 50.33(g) explicitly requires that license applications describe the site’s topography and other features of the site and surrounding area, including meteorology, as they may affect the safety of the facility. This includes providing information on how these features could influence atmospheric dispersion, which is critical for emergency preparedness (10 CFR 50.33(g)).

In summary, regulatory expectations require applicants to identify and incorporate local terrain features and building effects into atmospheric dispersion modeling to ensure that emergency preparedness plans and EPZs are appropriately tailored to the unique characteristics of the site. This ensures that emergency response measures are based on realistic assessments of how radioactive materials could disperse in the event of an accident, considering the influence of site-specific features.

data.query: What are the regulatory requirements for emergency preparedness related to security-based events at nuclear power plants?
data.answer:
The regulatory requirements for emergency preparedness related to security-based events at nuclear power plants are established through a combination of NRC regulations and guidance documents. According to SRP 13.3, the review of emergency preparedness is conducted against several key regulations, including 10 CFR 50.33, 10 CFR 50.34, 10 CFR 50.47, 10 CFR 50.54, 10 CFR 50.72, Appendix E to 10 CFR Part 50, 10 CFR Part 52, 10 CFR 73.71, and 10 CFR Part 100. These regulations collectively require licensees to develop, implement, and maintain emergency plans that address a range of emergencies, including those resulting from security-based events (SRP 13.3, Section I and II).

Specifically, 10 CFR 50.33(g) requires applicants to describe their plans for emergency preparedness, including the means for coping with emergencies that may result from security-based events (10 CFR 50.33(g)). Appendix E to 10 CFR Part 50 further details the requirements for emergency planning. Additionally, NRC Orders, such as the Interim Compensatory Measures (ICMs) B.5.c, B.5.d, and B.5.e issued on February 25, 2002, impose additional requirements on operating commercial nuclear power plants to address security-based emergency plans and preparedness (SRP 13.3, Section II.G).

Notification and reporting requirements for security-based events are specified in 10 CFR 50.72 and 10 CFR 73.71, which mandate timely notification of the NRC for emergency class declarations, reporting of safeguards events, and maintaining open communication lines (SRP 13.3, Section II.F).

Finally, SRP 13.6 provides further guidance on the review of security-based events and physical security, tailored to the specific type of licensing action (SRP 13.6, Section I).

In summary, emergency preparedness for security-based events at nuclear power plants is governed by a comprehensive set of regulations and NRC orders, requiring robust planning, notification, and reporting mechanisms as part of the overall emergency preparedness program.

data.query: How do NRC regulations address the need for arrangements with offsite medical facilities to provide treatment for radiological and non-radiological injuries resulting from a nuclear emergency?
data.answer: NRC regulations explicitly require applicants for licenses to construct and operate nuclear facilities to address arrangements with offsite medical facilities for the treatment of both radiological and non-radiological injuries resulting from a nuclear emergency. According to 10 CFR 50.33(g), each application must describe the arrangements made with local hospitals or other offsite medical facilities to provide medical services for onsite individuals who may be injured during normal operation or as a result of an accident, including those who may be contaminated with radioactive material. This requirement ensures that both radiological and non-radiological injuries are considered in emergency planning. Furthermore, the Standard Review Plan (SRP) 13.3 specifies that emergency response plans, both onsite and offsite, must meet the standards established in 10 CFR 50.47(b) and the applicable requirements of Appendix E to 10 CFR Part 50. In summary, NRC regulations mandate that applicants establish and document arrangements with offsite medical facilities to ensure adequate medical response capabilities for all types of injuries that may occur during a nuclear emergency, as detailed in 10 CFR 50.33(g) and reinforced by the SRP 13.3 guidance.

data.query: What is the regulatory basis for including specialized radiological emergency medical centers, such as national radiological emergency assistance centers, in the list of offsite medical support resources for nuclear power plant emergency plans?
data.answer:
The regulatory basis for including specialized radiological emergency medical centers, such as national radiological emergency assistance centers, in the list of offsite medical support resources for nuclear power plant emergency plans is grounded in several NRC regulations and guidance documents. Specifically, 10 CFR 50.47(b)(12) requires that 'arrangements are made for medical services for contaminated injured individuals.' This standard mandates that emergency plans must ensure the availability of appropriate medical support for individuals who may be contaminated or injured during a radiological emergency. 

Further, the Standard Review Plan (SRP) 13.3, Section II, Acceptance Criteria, clarifies that compliance with 10 CFR 50.47(b) and Appendix E to 10 CFR Part 50 is determined using guidance from Regulatory Guide 1.101, which endorses NUREG-0654/FEMA-REP-1, Rev. 1. This guidance establishes acceptable methods for developing radiological emergency plans, including the identification and arrangement of offsite medical support resources. The SRP also references the need for coordination with offsite organizations capable of augmenting the planned response (10 CFR 50.47(b)(3)), which would include specialized radiological emergency medical centers. 

Therefore, the inclusion of specialized radiological emergency medical centers in emergency plans is based on the regulatory requirement to provide for medical services for contaminated injured individuals (10 CFR 50.47(b)(12)), and the broader requirement to identify and arrange for assistance from organizations capable of augmenting the emergency response (10 CFR 50.47(b)(3)), as interpreted and implemented through NRC-endorsed guidance (SRP 13.3, RG 1.101, and NUREG-0654/FEMA-REP-1).

evidence_chain.section: § 50.47 Emergency plans (specifically § 50.47(b))
evidence_chain.evidence_text: (b) Emergency plans for nuclear power reactors. Each applicant for a license to operate a nuclear power reactor shall submit radiological emergency response plans for the plant in accordance with the criteria in appendix E and the planning standards of this section. The NRC will base its finding on the adequacy of these plans on whether the applicant's plans provide reasonable assurance that adequate protective measures can and will be taken in the event of a radiological emergency. The following planning standards must be met: (1) Primary responsibilities for emergency response by the nuclear facility licensee and by State and local organizations within the emergency planning zones have been assigned, the emergency responsibilities of the various supporting organizations have been specifically established, and each principal response organization has staff to respond and to augment its initial response on a continuous basis. (2) Onsite and offsite emergency response plans for nuclear power reactors must be coordinated to the extent that such coordination is necessary to ensure an integrated response. (3) Arrangements for requesting and effectively using assistance resources have been made, arrangements to accommodate State and local staff at the licensee's Emergency Operations Facility have been made, and other organizations capable of augmenting the planned response have been identified. (4) A standard emergency classification and action level scheme, the bases of which include facility system and effluent parameters, is in use by the nuclear facility licensee, and State and local response plans call for reliance on information provided by facility licensees for determinations of minimum initial offsite response measures. (5) Procedures have been established for notification, by the licensee, of State and local response organizations and for notification of emergency personnel by all organizations; the content of initial and followup messages to response organizations and the public has been established; and means to provide early notification and clear instruction to the populace within the plume exposure pathway Emergency Planning Zone have been established. (6) Provisions exist for prompt communications among principal response organizations to emergency personnel and to the public. (7) Information is made available to the public on a periodic basis on how they will be notified and what their initial actions should be in an emergency (e.g., listening to a local broadcast station and remaining indoors), and information is made available on a periodic basis on the principal protective actions (e.g., evacuation, sheltering, and use of potassium iodide (KI), as appropriate). (8) Adequate emergency facilities and equipment to support the emergency response are provided and maintained. (9) Adequate methods, systems, and equipment for assessing and monitoring actual or potential offsite consequences of a radiological emergency condition are in use. (10) A range of protective actions has been developed for the plume exposure pathway Emergency Planning Zone for emergency workers and the public. Evacuation time estimates have been developed. (11) Means for controlling radiological exposures, including exposure control methods for emergency workers, are provided. (12) Arrangements are made for medical services for contaminated injured individuals. (13) Radiological emergency response training is provided to those who may be called on to assist in an emergency. (14) Exercises are conducted to test the adequacy of emergency plans and to develop and maintain key skills.
